name: Deathbound
detailed_description: JOIN OUR DISCORD About the Game Gain the skills, memories and identities of fallen warriors throughout the world. Combine their unique personalities and combat styles and switch between them seamlessly. The essences you absorb form your party. Deathbound features a robust party system that allows players to craft a playstyle through talent trees. Seamlessly switch between fallen warriors to harness their skills and abilities. Each party member’s affiliation in life will affect their synergy in death. Unleash the combined powers of fallen warriors with devastating Morphstrikes. Utilize different attack styles to pull-off powerful combinations and finishing blows to defeat all who oppose you. Ziêminal is a world that mixes a technological past and a medieval present, home to diverse cultures. The city of Akratya is rich in lore and dangers. Explore a city falling into ruin under the shadow of a grand crusade. From the body-filled streets to arenas and places of worship. With its imposing brutalist architecture and melding of technology, it’s a city bound for oblivion. Face challenging enemies crafted to push you to your limits. Their very nature is based on the five stages of grief, with each new encounter commanding the attention of any soul who dare face them.

short_description: Deathbound is a unique Soulslike. Build a party of four characters and instantly morph between them in and out of combat. Combine their abilities to pull off devastating attacks and slay those who stand before you.

_childDocuments_.review: Being frozen in place when using any item is not a fun mechanic and makes the combat frustrating and not fun. Another dislike I have is that you are constantly watching 4 health bars and 4 stamina bars since if even one of the four bound characters equipped die it is game over. I would like it better if they died individually until they are all dead then game over or 1 shared Health bar. Why have individual health bars if only 1 dies it's game over?Did not receive the ultimate edition Skins or dlc. I don't know how you could not have "Skins" ready for your ultimate edition of your game for launch.. By the time you release them I will have moved to something better to play. DLC thats fine but skins really? My opinion of this game has not changed. I will probably never play it again. Waste of money unless you are starved for souls like games but don't care how janky it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the many great ideas, it all comes down to the fact that Deathbound's battles are often almost unenjoyable. This is mostly due to the low-level animations, the hitbox sliding back and forth, the sometimes blatantly cheating opponents who turn on us before every hit, as well as the camera that shows the events too closely. This segment (especially after a very polished From Software game) just seems painfully primitive and carved with an axe, in which knowledge is secondary in many cases, instead it often depends on luck whether you succeed in defeating the given enemy or not. It's a shame, because the significant changes made to the gameplay could have made it an inevitable classic in the increasingly crowded genre of soulslike games, but instead, one can only welcome a smart but not really clever attempt, in which despite the opportunity, the development team could not take full advantage of it.

_childDocuments_.review: I for one love what they've done with the combat in Deathbound. I wish the game was longer.I truly believe a lot of the souls ''community'' is scared of change. As soon as small bits of the formula are changed they're afraid to learn new aspects and combat systems and just frustrated and review bomb. It stops devs from trying new things and stops the genre from progressing. Pro:-Voice acting is great, I really enjoyed the conversation and arguments between spirits.-Combat system. The morph system is great. (explained more below)-World looks decent because of the lighting used in a lot of places.  (also a con)-Plenty of shortcuts although many quite predictable. -Loot EVERYWHERE. There's space behind a corner where they could have placed loot? THERE WILL BE LOOT.-Story from different views - as you have many spirits they all see the story unfold with their own political/religious viewpoint.-Heat system is a nice take on having ranged/magic users without limiting ammo/magic-Great barrel/wooden box physics...Neutral: - Equipment/upgrades. Very bland. Only found one set of rings to be useful.- Leveling up - Interesting. It works. That's about it. At least it looks nice.Con-8 crashes in 13 hours -Shadows is connected to lighting? Turning down shadows also makes a lot of the lighting situations turn off.-Performance goes from 60 to 30 depending on particle effects. Some effects severely make the game suffer and some are used only once in the game. (for example the weird fireworks glitter when you arrive in the lift to the boss)-Can't set your own controls. Why not? This is 2024 :(  HOWEVER. It made me use control scheme B and the game works much better to have your spirits connected to the X/Y/B/A buttons.COMBAT Dev tries something new and a lot of people seem to misunderstand it or simply don't want to learn it.There basically are no healing potions and stamina is tied to health. But you have 4 different health and stamina bars. Your other spirits gain health when the active one deals damage. So you basically heal by being aggressive.You morph during dashes to use the stamina from other spirits so you don't run out while evading.You morph during attacks to do extra damage BUT more importantly morph striking gives you I-frames and it is immensely satisfying to dodge attacks this way. The only slight downside is that once you master it it does make the game too easy. Especially the last half of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: There is something baffling about developers with interesting ideas and the inability to encase those ideas into a clockwork of functioning, enjoyable systems.  is the latest example I've seen of a team with good intentions, messing up the execution so badly.I am not going to bother you with things like the presentation. It's a budget title and that is depicted clearly, so there is no reason to throw shade here. What did strike me as odd is the lack of artistic merit though - we've seen many games ( comes to mind) where the tech didn't really complement the looks of the game, but the Art itself created an enjoyable whole. Here, we are looking at a pastel-themed approach, without any interesting assets to complement the designs. Adding salt to injury, it's strange to see someone aim at creating a narrative-driven, emotion-provoking game without a shred of memorable music. Granted, there barely is any, but even when it's there, there's nothing that will stick to mind. Droning sounds in place of ambience and your standard "now it's stress time" Boss themes do little to alleviate the issue. As stated above, the creators tried to provide us with a Soulslike that bends the rules of the genre, forging a more story-driven, characters-centric adventure. The plural in "characters" is not a typo, since you will be leading a small team of bound "Essences" through the gameworld, for the better part of 15 hours. There is a good notion here, but the implementation is bland and problematic: The characters are unappealing and simplistic in appearence, their animations stiff, the writing extremely basic and the voice acting swings wildly between servicable and offensively incompetent. There is a character early on trying to mimic a slavic accent that is of particularly bad taste, creating an abnoxious caricature. The peak of my misery here came in the form of an area, a revisited level from early on in the game. Here, you are stalked by a Nemesis-type villain while attacked by everything else in the environment. This frustrating situtation reaches its climax by introducing a gank Boss fight, in a three phase arena with a huge pit in the middle. All XP you are carrying can be lost in any of the three parts, forcing you to make progress through all previous ones in order to reacquire. Die in any of these three parts and you will have to do it all over again, fighting through two dozen enemies whilst trying not to perish again, least you lose all you were carrying. For a game that comes out almost ten years after  - the previously worst offender when it comes to such flawed designs - it is impossible to make any excuses. I was just sitting there, staring in awe, wondering why the game's more niche ideas had to be implemented in such a flawed manner. EDIT: Since the release of this Review, the Devs have answered and improved the Boss Battle mentioned. I hope they will keep calibrating and adding to the game, in order to push it closer to its initial potential. As it stands right now, it still needs work, at least in my humble opinion. - FiOth

_childDocuments_.review: played the demo for this game when it first released and wasn't planning on buying it but here i am after giving it some time for people to drop some feedback and to see what the final product would be like. is it good? meh. is it bad? meh. im on the fence about it but im leaving a positive because it is clear the devs at least put a lot of effort into making the game unique in the soulslike genre with the party system, classes, story and world. the gameplay is clunky but can be fun at times, the level design is pretty linear, and the story isn't really memorable but it suffices for a game like this. it does feel like more effort was put into the first half of the game and then it kinda drops off/becomes very repetitive, as well as looks repetitive towards the end. almost like a strong start, but poor execution to finish it. for the price it is, i will recommend the game but just know you are not getting a Sekiro, Dark Souls or Elden Ring out of this game. commending the devs for the work they put in and im sure they will continue to keep it going as much as they can, just as they did with the demo feedback they received. it's OKAY!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game packed full of great ideas but sadly the execution of these ideas leaves me with an unfulfilling and ultimately not fun experience. I don't think the ideas are fundamentally broken, they could be tweaked with some balance passes and slight adjustments. The main issue I have with this game is the fact that it heavily encourages you to be constantly switching between characters but at the same time it is often not possible to switch to certain characters because they have taken too damage making them essentially useless and then you are hamstrung by being stuck on fewer characters so can't participate properly in combat and it takes SO LONG to heal the party. It just isn't fun I'm sorry. This is a great idea that needs a rework. I don't know what needs to happen to fix this but taking damage is currently far too punishing since stamina is tied to health it makes the character useless and if one character dies they all die. We need to have a mechanic to bring them back into the fight quicker because this just feels bad.Other than that, the voice acting and story are not something that interests me so I really want that core gameplay experience to be improved. I really wanted to like this, but the more I play it the more frustrated I am getting and at this point thinking about giving up.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played many a soulslike, and enjoyed almost all of them. Tried this one for stream since I got it for free, and I genuinely cannot figure out who this game is for.It has some good and interesting mechanics, but they're held back by what the game does wrong.I like the multiple character premise, but instead of giving each one some unique mechanic, they simply divide up the standard soulslike moveset between them. One has a ranged weapon and can backstab, one casts spells, one is regular swordbro, one is spear-user, etc.I like that the magic system relies on rechargeable heat instead of MP or cast limits, but the magic feels slow, low impact, and the heat regen is abysmal.I like that the level upgrades affect all characters, but they're all barely-noticeable increases, the highest I ever saw was 5%. I like that the "poppable souls" also give health and have a secondary use, but it makes them primary heals when the normal heal *takes away health from the other three on your team*. It doesn't refill, it SHARES.I like the follow-up attack system, but there's no gap-closers for melee characters, meaning you only ever get use out of it going from melee to melee or ranged to ranged.Add onto that the fact that it's riddled with bugs, bad animations, unskippable exposition forced down your throat with every new character, slow and clunky combat, nothing more than the illusion of exploration in levels, and a convoluted story that explains precisely nothing to you from the beginning and expects you to be okay with that, and I really can't recommend this game to anyone at all.TL;DR: Game has good ideas, but nothing is executed well. Shame, really, as it has promise. I got it for free, and still kind of want a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough, i wanted to finish it before posting a review. So to make it short i really like this game despite of its flaws. It´s not perfect, not FromSoft level but hey if everybody could as good as FromSoft then they wouldn´t be that special.I really like how they treated the party based thing and i wasn´t a fan of the idea at all! I played the demo and didn´t like it tbh. Mostly because it was a mess and too much info at once but i also thought that the actual 1.0 would take more time to explain everything and you would discover all the essences one after the other along the main quest. And that´s what happened, i liked the feeling of progression (that wasn´t in the demo for obvious reasons).Like any Soulslike you´re weak in the beginning and that´s what i like, to start weak and grow stronger as the build comes together and it totally worked here. At the end of the game, the enemies that were bulliyng me at the start of the game (even in the middle) got destroyed when i finally got my build together and i was comfortable with the/my playstyle.The settings and atmosphere reminds me of Immortal Unchained or Hellpoint for some reasons. There is some bugs, some jank and a LOT of frustrating moment (i struggled with a boss called Dragon of the Deep for an hour, killed him just to see that they nerfed it the day after....should have been waiting)I read and seen a lot of negative things about this game but i tried anyway and loved it (game reviewers can be lame when it comes to challenging games, like they want to be able to claim they finished a hard game without the game being actually hard...i don´t know).I was in need of a Soulslike after the Elden Ring DLC and i even replayed Bloodborne but i was looking for a NEW Soulslike, Deathbound was perfect at that moment. I´m totally gonna play NG+ and check the other endings (assuming there is several) and try some new essences combinations.Thanks a lot to the devs and team for this great game!

_childDocuments_.review: I finished Deathbound and I loved it :DI'm not good at writing reviews, but here’s my take after a 20-hour playthrough:You get to choose 4 characters, and the game really pushes you to adapt to its unique system and use all of them, especially for stamina management and healing. Once you get the hang of it, it’s seriously a blast. The conflicts and synergies between characters can either make the game easier or harder, depending on how you set it up, which is my favorite part. The bosses are great, the combat is engaging, and the enemy variety is decent for a short linear game.Some of the levels were a pain to get through, but I wasn't exactly aware of the conflict-synergy stat back then, so it could've been my fault for not using the right setup. Either way, overcoming a tough level was super satisfying.I haven’t unlocked the “Untouchable” achievement yet, so it seems like I haven’t mastered the mechanics 100%, but I’m starting NG+ to work on that and complete all the achievements. It looks like you can get everything done in 2 playthroughs since there are (at least) 2 endings and ways to complete the game.Game design and aesthetics are amazing! I didn’t dive into the story, so I can’t comment on its quality. It seems interesting, but I’m all about the gameplay, especially in Soulslikes. Not an expert on voice acting and music either; they don’t really factor into my experience.Compared to other games, I'd say it's a MUCH-improved version of Mortal Shell. Is it clunky? Yes. But so is DS1 and it's still a great game. Plus, the devs are clearly invested, so I’m sure there will be patches and improvements down the line.If you’re into games that let you tweak the difficulty and love a fresh take on the Souls formula, this one’s definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathbound gets a 6/10 on gameplay and a 9/10 on setting. Should you purchase and invest the time in playing the game? That's really going to depend on what you're willing to be flexible with. My partner played the demo and couldn't get past the clunky combat. I've been playing for a few hours and can't wait to see more. I'm a sucker for the world setting. Its the definition of anachronistic. You've got a medieval styled crusader running around in the dystopia of some post-apocalypse. There's LED lights, and a broadsword in the same moment and I'm in love with it. Also MASSIVE shout out to the art design/level designer. I don't care if this is all built on easily available assets or not, you did well in the placement of objects and setting the mood/vibe. The unique feature of this game is being able to swap between different characters "essences" mid-combat with relative ease. I enjoyed collecting new essences and learning their unique skill sets. The world setting and this feature are enough to keep me pushing through the rougher parts of the game.Small shout out to the voice actors who seemed like they had fun with their roles. I liked the banter between the characters as I ran around. It made the world feel more alive. This is where the game falls apart and it can be immersion breaking a lot of times. Deathbound has got a lot of heart, and you can tell the devs really love Soulslike games. This game feels like a D&D campaign with a new DM who's big on story and worldbuilding, but shaky on the rules and combat.  It's not a bad time, and there's plenty to enjoy. You can walk away at the end of a session having had a LOT of fun, but it never quite reaches its full potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly fun.Indie souls-like, I was not expecting much, but surprisingly engaging, clearly done with love and care, even though there are still some rough edges.Good:* Good combat, slow and methodical, movement is a bit clunky though.* Engaging levelling/skill tree.* The "switch" mechanic is fun to use. I also liked how they introduce each new "form"/character with a memory of their past life. Nothing mind blowing, but it shows the "care" given by the developers.* Solid performance -- but the graphics are also ok, not bad but not triple-A either.Needs improvement:* Movement is a bit clunky.* Equipment upgrading is lackluster -- no weapon/armor customization, you only upgrade your rings and trinket (at least so far).Overall I'm impressed given this is one of the first games from this Studio (from what I've heard). Looking forward to what they come up with next.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathbound is an overall interesting and refreshing take on the "Souslike" formula.  Building a party of 4 characters (called Essences) and managing their individual life and stamina bars as you weave combos and dodge attacks while keeping up aggression.The story is engaging enough to carry the roughly 8 to 12 hour experience for a single playthrough. It's told a bit more straightforward than most games in the genre - which I appreciate - even if it doesn't tread particularly new ground.  The final moments of the story feel a little rushed and not as coherent but it was still simple enough to keep it paced together.On the topic of the characters, not all of them are created equal in my opinion.  Some are clearly better than others, seemingly better tested and balanced.  Of the 7 characters, the two mages felt particularly bad to use with the way the combat system worked, along with the heat system.  I won't go into a lot of detail here, trying to keep it succint but both systems seemed heavily at odds with each other and clunky.Each character's weapon and armor are permently set to them, which is fine, leaving gear as a single artefact and 2 rings.  I found almost every piece of gear to be so incredibly niche or oddly specific with some odd drawbacks that very little of it interested me enough to even really use it.  A few late-game pieces finally got me to use my upgrade materials, but even then it felt like it had minimal impact.  The game isn't particularly difficult - which is not a bad thing, not every Soulslike needs to be - so the above mentioned item situation isn't a real problem.  However, the very backend of the game does seem to artificially inflate the difficulty.  Enemy placement gets a lot more tedious and the "secret" boss felt particularly rushed in design.  It is a shame, as the final hour of the game added a bit of a stain on an otherwise great game.All in all, I enjoyed my time with Deathbound and think it is worth the time of every fan of Soulslikes.  Go in with the proper expectations - this is NOT Dark Souls, it is NOT Bloodborne, it is NOT Elden ring.. nor is it trying to be.  Deathbound is very much its own game, and if you approach it on its own terms, it will offer you a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for: Players looking for a mixture of fast paced, action packed, souls-like game with linear storylineNot Recommended for: Players hoping to try out their souls-like experience or looking for a similar souls-like experienceDeathbound is a mixture of souls-like with a fusion of character switching action packed combat, allowing for brisk experience with a linear gameplay. It combines elements from souls-like games having to manage your stamina with attacks being executed before queuing another action and switching in order to fully utilize combat and survival. This makes it more invigorating albeit daunting at times due to how unbalanced the structure of the levels are designed, enemies count on areas, model clipping and character staggering on both ends. It's and somewhat fast paced, but the intro for the game makes it incredibly misleading as just a BASE souls-like game. Characters are called essences which you can switch to but entirely they are the Character Classes of the game, you have at least 7 of them (I missed one) but they are missable and will often come later. They range from your Typical Knight Class, Assassin/Rogue, Tank, Mage, Amazon (Spear) and Brawler that does Capoeira (pretty cool and awesome if you ask me). Unfortunately you cannot customize these characters Aesthetics or gear in any way shape or form. You also have a restricted character leveling system which means you cannot focus on specific stats such as stamina or vigor (crucial stats for any souls-like game) they are sort of skill trees that interconnect with one another and have their own "nodes" for essences that give their abilities a boost. However, these don't really give you a lot as an individual essence in the field, but once you've gotten the rhythm of adjusting to the combat, then you'll see its effects.Syncing is a mechanic that allows your character to gain with active and off field in order initiate a power attack while switching. Filling up this bar is essential in order to deal massive damage against tank types or multiple enemies in the field. It can be obtained by simply attacking the enemies, performing staggers and perfect dashing (rolling in terms of this game).Dashing is replaced instead of rolling which is bad and inconvenient as some essence have their own unique form of it (brawler does a back flip instead) and it makes it more difficult to apply in situations and understanding the hitboxes of enemies more complicated, however, switching characters midway (specially when attacking) allows for brief invincibility which is encouraged. You can restore your HP in so many ways with multiple downsides to it, being able to heal by attacking enemies, you mostly heal off field character/s instead of the active one forcing you to constantly switch strategies on the fly. Using an Essence Enhancer (Flasks) also heals your Active character but drains off field characters instead. There's also Essence Crystals that yields a risk reward mechanic which gives you x amount of Crystals for XP/Upgrades in exchange for x amount of HP. This meant that you'll have the XP in your set up as you fight enemies, which can also drop if you die.Later on as you gather many essence (your character class as a bundle) you're able to fully understand and optimize your strategy, being able to evolve from slowly awaiting attacks to bum rushing and switching like a dual pistol. The level design is atmospheric but lacks depth and is completely dark most of the time. Empty even, as it fails to give world building a chance. Attacks do have weight on them and feels just right, but enemies feel like sponges or rock even being able to withstand almost all attacks with minimal exception from others that can be staggered from normal attacks. Your character/s however are almost always vulnerable, even with poise, it feels like you're denied the combo you wish to perform.Inventory and UI system is dull and unintuitive, with you only being able to use or access your ACTUAL items by putting them in your belt. As well as only being able to equip TWO rings and ONE artefact besides having a lot. The terminology also confuses me and descriptions for some skills and uses are incredibly vague with having a lore description instead of actually telling you what it does.Overall I'd give this game a 6/10 and my verdict is that this is a fun experience with mixing souls-like game with a variety of mechanics, It does fail to execute it to a polished and proper degree as the level design in most places are not only dark, narrow and constricted but also is filled with enemies that can overwhelm you early on. The most awful part for the game was the unnecessary Chase sequence with you rotating around the area, facing hordes of enemies and some of them sniping you, looking for key items to unlock a door just leads back to the same place and the "nemesis" having to chase you even in safe areas. I'd like to thank GamingCypher for gifting this game for me! it's been a treat playing through! please check out their website!

_childDocuments_.review: I just love it!Atmospheric, spectacular, sufficiently difficult, sometimes annoying yet captivating!The mixing of the modern and the old world is a bit strange, since I didn't read the story, but I immediately poured almost 3 hours into the game.Anyone who reads the story will surely get the picture.I also like that the tutorial is not the typical press wasd, but actually shows what and how in given situations.I like the introduction of the characters, for each the game tells the story of the given character and what it specializes in and how to use it.It follows that there are several characters in the game, each of them has its own characteristics. For example, one is an assassin, the other is a wizard, the third is a warrior, etc.We can switch between them and, if we switch while fighting, we can also use an ultimate skill. I haven't seen a multi-character solution in a game like Souls Like, but this is quite amazing!XP farming is also simple, yet effective.There are also separate items that provide more exp, more damage, etc.It's worth looking around the map and looting, as you can get useful items.I didn't encounter any bugs during the game, so this is a huge plus point, although the game crashed once, but only once in 3 hours.So I recommend it to everyone!
_childDocuments_.name: Deathbound

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I would not call this a souls-like. There are core elements of a souls-like, but overall this game is it's own thing entirely. As a vet of souls games, I'm always looking for something similar that has a fresh, new difficulty curve that also feels rewarding and this checks both of those boxes. There are certain game play elements that I feel like need to be refined or changed but overall, this game has been an enjoyable experience. If I had to chose one thing to gripe about, it would be that the game overall feels slightly imbalanced and I would've liked to see more enemy variety and area variety. But neither of these were significant enough to turn me off from playing through it. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: In summary, after playing through the game (about 13 hours) and the first few areas in NG+, I think I've come to the conclusion that it's a solid "Meh". It'll scratch the souls itch but isn't too difficult outside of a few fights. Recommended only if you really need something.- First, the overall gameplay is fine but janky. There's nothing particularly wrong with it IMO but swapping characters does take a bit of getting used to when first starting out. I mostly stuck to the same 2 or 3 characters in my party and used the 4th for utility rather than actual combat. By the end, you'll have the options of sword & shield, spear, hammer, capoeira, dagger & crossbow, and 2 flavors of mage. - Then there's healing, arguable the most important ability you have as a player in a souls-like. The estus equivalent item heals your currently active character at the cost of damaging your other bound characters. This caused me to almost never use it. I ended up relying on the healing gained by your non-active characters when you damage an enemy simply because it didn't feel like there was a downside. It's also possible to heal through other consumables but those are either a health-redistribution item or your XP poppables.- The story itself was pretty bland IMO but the world lore was interesting enough. Most of it comes in the form of piecing together the stories of each character leading up to their deaths through memories scattered throughout the levels. A lot of side characters overlap and seeing them double-cross each other through political intrigue was cool. My only issue with them are that the characters in the memories have a sort of warble filter added to their voices which I find distracting.- There's also a handful of cutscenes but outside of the first one and the intros to bosses they feel shoehorned in. The opening cutscenes are very stylized but that style is never used again. The first boss has cutscenes for each of its 3 phases but they are super short and feel pointless except the last one where it takes off its blindfold. Simple things like that just make the whole experience feel strange.- Lastly, there's really no music in the game. What is there is bland, forgettable, "time to stress during the bossfight" music.Overall, if you really need a souls-like to play, you could do a lot worse. I just don't think this one should be your first choice.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, this game might seem to have a slow-paced combat system, which could be a turnoff for some players. However, this initial sluggishness is part of a larger design choice. Once you start unlocking more characters, known as Essences, the gameplay evolves into a fast-paced and dynamic experience. It’s important to be mindful of how the game conditions you to play more cautiously in the beginning, but rest assured that the pace will pick up significantly as you progress.One aspect that might take some getting used to is the Stamina Hunger mechanic. It requires patience and a thoughtful approach, but it’s well worth mastering. Make sure to use the tools the game provides to their fullest potential, as it’s incredibly rewarding to successfully manage your stamina and execute Morphs mid-battle to defeat enemies.Unlocking new Essences is where the game truly shines. Each new character brings a sense of empowerment, as the morph system becomes increasingly complex and satisfying. This progression is where the game hooks you, making you feel like your efforts are genuinely paying off.However, the Sync Bar mechanics could be more intuitive. I recommend always keeping one in reserve for Dash Morphs, especially when you encounter enemies at inopportune moments.The story itself is relatively simple, but that simplicity works in the game’s favor. It allows you to focus on the gameplay and immerse yourself in the world without getting bogged down by overly complex narratives. You’ll find yourself gradually becoming attached to the Essences and their unique personalities. Agaros is my favorite so far.Additionally, I really appreciated the Synergy and Conflict mechanic between Bound Essences. It’s a shame this feature feels a bit slept on at launch. I think this is one area where the developers could focus on enhancing the experience without disrupting the overall balance of the game.In conclusion, while the game requires a bit of patience and adjustment early on, it rewards those who stick with it by delivering an increasingly engaging and powerful experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A Promising Indie Game with a Unique Sci-Fi Fantasy TwistIn the ever-growing world of indie gaming, Deathbound, the debut game from a new Brazilian development team is surely an awesome new entry. While some reviewers have hastily compared it to the Dark Souls series, this comparison, though understandable due to its Soulslike nature, is somewhat unfair. Unlike the large-scale productions of FromSoftware, Deathbound was crafted by a small team, and despite the lack of years of development or a massive budget, it manages to carve out its own niche, offering a rich and engaging experience.A Narrative with DepthOne of the standout features of Deathbound is its narrative depth, a quality often lacking in the Soulslike genre. As a fan of story-driven games, I’ve always felt the absence of a strong narrative in most Souls games (with the perhaps the exception of Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice). Deathbound, however, fills this gap admirably, offering a well-crafted story that blends sci-fi and fantasy elements into a grimdark, medieval, post-apocalyptic world. The game’s mythology, while relatively straightforward, is imbued with a fairy tale-like quality, featuring immortals, mortals, and deities of life and death. The developers seem to have had fun crafting this world, evident in the imaginative portrayal of a society clinging to the remnants of a lost, advanced civilization. The way modern items are interpreted through the eyes of a less technologically advanced populace is both intriguing and entertaining.The narrative unfolds through interactions with various playable characters, each bringing their own perspective and backstory to the table. While the story is more detailed than the average Soulslike, it still requires players to engage with it actively, piecing together the lore through dialogue, environmental storytelling, and item descriptions. This method may not appeal to everyone, but for those who enjoy digging deeper into a game's world, Deathbound offers plenty to uncover.Character DynamicsThe interactions between the characters are a highlight, both in terms of narrative and gameplay. My personal favorites were Mamdile, Haodai, and Yulia, each bringing a unique flavor to the game. Anna, however, fell a bit flat for me due to a questionable choice in her voice acting. Her overly cheery and quirky demeanor didn’t quite align with her role as an assassin, creating a dissonance that was hard to overlook. Agharos, on the other hand, provided some comic relief, albeit as a somewhat caricatured character. Despite this, he has some memorable moments that players can unlock as they progress through the game. Olivia shares the same issue, while more serious in tone, and also has her share of significant scenes.The game features mandatory "Reveries" — sequences that delve into the characters' pasts. Unfortunately, I found these segments to be the least engaging aspect of the narrative. They were often convoluted and lacked coherence. Exceptions to this were Haodai’s and Mamdile’s Reveries — which unfortunately come rather late in the game, as the capoeira master is one of the more interesting characters both gameplay and story wise. Where Deathbound’s storytelling truly shines is in its "Echoes of the Past" and "Essences" interactions. These moments are more directly connected to the game's main story and feature the enigmatic Soulon, the character you spend much of the game pursuing. The Essences are particularly well-crafted, each with its own motivations and shades of moral ambiguity, adding a layer of depth to the narrative that I thoroughly enjoyed.Mastering Combat and MechanicsWhen it comes to gameplay, Deathbound holds its own, particularly through its innovative morphing mechanic. This feature, which allows players to shift between different forms and abilities, is the key to mastering the game. It took me some time to get the hang of it, but once I did, the game became increasingly enjoyable. The enemies are varied, with each type requiring a different approach, making the choice of which Essence to use crucial to survival. Consumables also play a significant role in combat, offering players numerous ways to make their journey through the game’s challenging world a bit easier. However, the combat is not without its flaws. The most noticeable issue is the occasional problem of hit detection in tight spaces, where attacks sometimes pass right through enemies. This can be frustrating, especially in a game that demands precision. Hopefully, this is something the developers will address in future updates.The difficulty of Deathbound is in line with what fans of the genre expect — tough but fair. Mastering the morphing mechanic opens the door to some truly epic battles, and the satisfaction of overcoming these challenges is immense.ConclusionIn conclusion, Deathbound is an impressive indie title that stands strong even when compared to larger, more established Triple I games. It's a solid entry into the Soulslike arena, with a unique narrative, interesting characters, and innovative mechanics that set it apart from its peers. The game’s smaller scope does little to detract from the overall experience, and it’s clear that the development team put a lot of heart and soul into this project. I’m excited to see where this studio goes next, and I would love to see a Deathbound II that delves even deeper into the fascinating world of Zenminal. If they continue on this path, refining their craft and expanding their vision, I hope that they’ll make a significant mark on the gaming industry.

_childDocuments_.review: Deathbound is a fun, but flawed, take on the Soulslike formula. A few weird design choices, like the lack of fast travel and an unhelpful healing flask, keep this from being a true gem. This is a recommendation with caveats: if you're done Eldening those Rings and want a more linear, focused experience, Deathbound is worth a stab.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying I only really played this for four hours so it's more or less a first impressions kind of review. I also received this title for free and went in with little to no information prior. I say what I say with deep interest in titles like this and the uniqueness its mechanics bring to genre. So thank you for the opportunity. Now here's my Ted Talk lol. The  is that the visuals, concept, and core mechanics of the game are really interesting. I really enjoy them and think the game and its gimmick are really promising. And yet with that, it feels rather unpolished in the execution of the swapping mechanic as it leaves you exposed more times than it should of even when executed properly. Given that the game wants you to do this as much as possible, that leaves a lot of times you will notice this flaw. I'd still recommend the game for its style and for the uniqueness of its swapping system... Just approach the game knowing that it could use some more refining for sure if you do pick up the title. I love the setting and design of the game meshing the medieval elements with the future tech elements, it's an aesthetic I've enjoyed in other titles and love to see in a souls-like format. The diversity in each of the characters feels really nice and being able to approach different combat styles in the same run is an incredible aspect. I think the game with its core gimmick of character swapping and the mechanics that come from it is really enthralling of a concept and when it works, it is pretty cool... however, that mechanic is also flawed in its execution. The animation for the swap I feel is way too slow, especially in a genre that requires reflexive action, responsive controls, and consistent defensive mechanics. The animation for switching between characters, even when done at a 'perfect' timing, feels too lengthy and leaves way for you to be easily punished by attacks. Whether that is because the enemy isn't easily stagger-able or there's a third party who isn't directly affected by your attacks, given they may be a ranged unit or something. The amount of times I'd get a chunk of my health eaten away because I decided to use the game's core mechanic offensively or defensively, was more times than not. At first it was just like "Haha quirky mechanic." But after enemies got more 'advanced', it became a more noticeable flaw. Not to mention, if you do happen to get hit during the beginning of that swap, it cancels it all together. Thus leaving you in a position where you are heavily punished. Sure you could boil it down to "well just getting better at timing it", but even when a perfect swap is performed, the dangers still exist, especially against bosses. I even had a moment where everything slowed down from the perfect swap, excluding a crossbow bolt that got fired before the slow down ended. That moved at full speed while I was caught in the slow down still. So it staggered me, allowed for the time slow to end, and for me to get immediately punished by the melee enemies near me since it cancelled my follow up.There also is the other issue, the combat feels a bit floaty. Often my impacts don't feel too weighty, I get staggered from the smallest thing but enemies just keep on attacking. I can get stun locked over and over until I am just dead. While I could swing at them repetitively and they just shrug it off and counter me. Even chaining together 3 well timed swap attacks, can amount to me being hit directly after as if I didn't just do the thing the game wants me to do, not once, not twice, but thrice. Leaving that to be a more risky decision than a rewarding one.I think as far as changes for either the future of this game or maybe a sequel in the same world, it could benefit from a greatly smaller windows from swaps, more weight behind your attacks, potentially a brief i-frame window during swapping and associated attacks/riposte from that mechanic, and also minor protections against persistent stun locks. Whether that latter change is a point at which your character is knocked down/back with a momentary immunity as they recover, or simply allowing for you to break punishing combos with rolls/swaps. I think being able to swap while being hit is also something that could help the game, as a way to recover (or save a near death character stuck in animation) and pick back up your momentum after having taking a hit. The game has a lot of promise and I was really excited to check it out, but I'm not fully sure if I personally can sift through it to see everything through in the end. Just because it feels like a majority of my deaths would not be from challenging boss mechanics or enemy routing but instead simply fighting with the almost RNG chance that I'm going to get punished for using the game's core gimmick. When it works, it feels so rewarding, and when it doesn't... It is the game's loudest problem. When designing a souls-like, you really need every cog in the offensive and defensive systems to move consistently, having that (for better lack of a word) 'jank' to it, will cause players to be frustrated at the lack of responsiveness. No one wants to die because the game's mechanics betray you. That all being said, where this may be the end of the road for myself, I do think that it's worth checking out. Especially if you manage to get Deathbound during a sale or as a gift. It just comes down to trying to approach the game a lot more cautiously than you would another souls-like. As playing hyper aggressive and taking on crowds will likely allow for that aforementioned jank to become painfully more apparently. Chip away tactics and making use of ranged units will be your friend. I hope that with time some changes will be made and I can finish my journey into this world of life and death.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best Souls Like I have ever played (my previous best was Salt and Sanctuary). The main reason being originiality and game design. It is a short and sweet demonstration of its unique combat that does not overstay its welcome and on average has decent boss fights.Now for a more in depth look at why this game is actually good and the negative reviews or people saying the game is mid are very wrong IMO.1. Game Design. The central mechanic and what makes this game special is the Essence/Character System. Unlike a Souls Game where you can freely choose your equipment you have 7 different preset geared out characters that of which you can choose 4 at a time. Depending on where on the d pad you assign them, you receive unique boni or high risk, high reward trade offs. The entire game is designed around this system and every single aspect of the gameplay exists to make it work. At first it starts off just like a regular souls game with one sword and board character and an estus like heal. The more essences you get, the more the gameplay shifts around being all 4 characters at once, shifting between them mid combo or dodge and taking advantage of certain synergies between them. As the enemies get stronger you can't simply stay as your main character. How do they force you to cycle frequently? Unlike a souls game your estus does not get stronger and in fact damages your other essences, so your main healing is an innate life steal each essence has that only works for the currently dormant essences. So basically you fight as one and take damage, then switch to another one to heal it back up again. That is how it deviates from the traditional souls formula. Another factor is the heat mechanic for the 2 mage characters that you want to reduce back down by switching to another essence or else you will take damage. The last incentive is synergy which is basically a combo meter that allow for powerful, character specific attacks once filled or other switch related mechanics. Once you figure out when to dodge more or morph strike you can really become incredibly strong and almost unkillable. But this is the core of this game and if you don't find the mechanic enticing you will not have fun. Staying on your favourite character is a huge detriment and the game is not balanced around that. 2. Gameplay. In general this game has weighty slow paced combat. I would say it is a bit faster than DS1 or 2 but quite a bit slower than DS3. Once you commit to an action, you cannot cancel out of any animation, meaning that it is more focused on decision making than reaction speed. The enemies are all about the same speed as you and I would say it is balanced quite well. There is quite a lot of juice and I would say that the SFX are really great and make the game have great game feel. For me the game was easier than other souls likes, but still demanded my full attention to not die. A single essence can die in a few hits and if you are not focused on when to switch. Getting trapped in a corner means certain death, just like any Souls Game. I would say that the combat is more active in comparison as in the later stages you don't have the downtime of needing to heal, since you are constantly just attacking and morphing. The characters all have their advantages, but I would say that some are stronger than others, but even with the worst one's you can easily beat the game. The beginning is very, very forgiving with the later stages becoming more difficult. Enemy variety is ok, ish, but especially in the last two areas it is stretched thin and you will not see anything new. There could have defintely been one or two more enemy types to keep it fresher. But thankfully the bosses get a lot better, when the enemy variety shows its cracks. Level design is on the very upper echalon of all souls likes. It might be the best I have seen in any of the non Fromsoftware games. Tons of logical layouts with previews of future areas and hints at what will await you next. A lot of looping level design, wich most souls fans will appreciate.3. Art. I would say the art direction ranges from great to sub par. Some areas look gorgeous and have a clear vision (church of life, essence labs). Others are empty and fairly generic (Lower Acrathyia). Enemy designs are often creative (mostly bosses and corrupted abominations), but some are generic (death cult) and uninspring. The Characters in general are unique from each other, but some are again much less visually fleshed out than others. For example Anna just looks like a generic rogue, but Olivia has a much more original design with a lot more going on. There barely is any music, but what is there mostly serves a secondary role. Like exciting boss music and some environmental stuff. Nothing I would listen to in my free time, but it is passable. The writing in general is decent and I was engaged with the story. The lore is fairly intruiging and all characters are often more than just blank states of stereo types with some motivation and behavioural quirks etc. It isn't ground breaking, but also not just generic just to be there. There were people passionate trying to create world for their game. The voice acting performance does not support this very often. Most of them are passable at best and really don't bring the characters to life like you would hope they would. More of a result of having a smaller indie studio that cannot allocate tons of resources there. But I still think that having voice acting at all in an indie project like this is commendable, especially considering that there is quite a lot of dialogue.4. Technical Stuff.In this category it comes off ok, but not good. I had 2 crashes in my 17 hours and one of them was at a very crucial moment. There is quite a lot of jank with dialogue not being played at correct times, enemies glitching inside the level or you getting stuck on the environment. Performance for me has been excellent, but massive stutters in transitions from area to area. I get what is happening, but other games manage to hide these loading zones a lot better.  But nothing completely gamebreaking and the most important part, the gameplay, is quite polished. Acceptable for quite an ambitious project for such a small studio, but of course there could be improvement. For me this is on average an 8.5/10 games with great focus and vision seperating it from the pack of other souls likes. It does not try to beat Fromsoftware, it tries to learn from them and change up the script in a meaningful way. I can see myself craving this game instead of other Fromsoft titles, which is very rare for souls likes. There is no reason for me to play Lords of the Fallen when I can play Elden Ring. But there are reasons to play Deatbound instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Ambitious Idea but in practice the game falls flat.Aesthetic is dope, I vibe with the dark graphic novel style but unfortunately thats the only thing I find appealing about the game.COMBAT:  clunky/repetitive - light attack/heavy attack for melee classesSTAMINA/HEALTH Hybrid - Damage to health equally damages your stamina.(Killed the game for me)STORY LINE: Almost incoherent and doesn't have weight to it. _childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, everything about this game's controls was clunky from the beginning. Here is a list from the first 45 minutes I played (on controller) :- The left joystick, which controls movement, also controls the camera for some reason. This means that even if I adjusted the camera with the right joystick, every time I went left or right when not locked on to enemies, the camera would turn suddenly. Never found an option to turn it off and it made exploration unbearable for me.- When trying to interact with objects, I often had difficulties finding the right position to do so. The positionning is so tight that I often had to try two or three times to open doors.- The timing for perfect blocks or parries seemed off.- The game crashed once.- Dodging seemed to be only I-frames with no boost in speed, at least on the first character, which made the dodge... not dodge?- Every room looked exactly the same and there was no mini-map, making navigation very difficult.This completely killed my will to play in under an hour. I felt like I was fighting the controls more than the enemies. This is not good for a souls-like. Unfortunate, as the premise and gimmick sounded very fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Great Game"Deathbound" has a reason to exist above the sea of mediocre games. The setting and core mechanics are unique enough to make this indie soulslike stand out, even with limited resources. It's worth playing and offers great hope for the Brazilian game dev scene.The Good, the Bad, and the NemesisThe setting of "Deathbound" is very interesting and quite unique. The post-apocalyptic world with medieval characters and plot would be enough to make it worthwhile, but the elegant nods to Brazilian culture and the use of classic soulslike item descriptions make it great in my opinion.The world is great, but the main cast brings it to life. I wasn't expecting much in terms of character backstories or the depth of connections formed during the game when I first looked at the title, but it’s now obvious to me that the team put a lot of care into it. The choice of the main cast is a good start, with conflicting views and intertwining plots, and it’s followed by a solid introduction that focuses on the characters' themes. Beyond that, the gameplay uses this cast really well, with more descriptions defining relationships between characters and their lives in general.The lore and story are a step down but still good. It's not easy to create a complex world, and the team did a good job. I would have liked more environmental storytelling, like in the "not-football" stadium, and a more fleshed-out ending to the main story.The game starts to show its flaws in the game design—a linear path with shortcuts to checkpoints, very reminiscent of Dark Souls 1, and pretty standard. The main problem is the variety and density of enemies, most noticeable closer to the end, and even worse when our pursuer is present. I understand the limitations of an indie game, and the elite enemies are, for the most part, good, but a few more enemy variations and better placement in some areas would make the game smoother to play and more fun overall.The worst part, in my opinion, is the bosses. "Deathbound" is not a big game, but by the end, I was having trouble thinking of good bosses that weren't just elite enemies. And this genre relies on its bosses most of the time. There are some good fights, like the last one, but most of them are on the easy side, with simple mechanics—boring or just unfun. Two cases deserve special mention: Eithalos with its enemy spawn + AOE. I get that he's a summoner, but it didn’t work out. And the Nemesis enemy, who is hyped up throughout the game, makes some stages miserable, and in the end, is just like an elite soldier.On a final note, the graphics are not great but are fine and didn’t break the immersion for me. The game runs okay and is smooth enough to make the fights enjoyable.In conclusion, "Deathbound" is a great accomplishment for the devs and a worthwhile experience. It is not perfect, but most of its flaws are a consequence of being an indie project, and they can be fixed in future titles. Most importantly, the soul, or essence as they say, is there, and as a Brazilian, I'm proud to see this game and will be waiting for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the negative reviews put you off, this is a true soulslike and has decent combat and other souls elements.Those who are used to spamming dodge/roll or attack button will have a hard time because the game priorize strategy and timming for everything ... and that is great, because when you fight big foes and get the timming correct, specially when transmorphing, it is so satisfying.... of couse you can dash, parry, and even do some cool movements with specific characters, all good stuff.Some bosses are really tough and require learning their attacks and switching back and forth between the essences, then you can combo them to do maximum damage.Of couse the game is not up to the FromSoftware standands in terms of animation, graphics etc, but for a indie game from small and unknown studio this is really a acomplishment and think it is worth my money.Vai Brasil!!!!!1

_childDocuments_.review: The Soulsbladebornekiroringcorerdtree-like genre comes in three flavors now.- --- - the Soulsoulsoulsouls-like, with a focus on stamina management, RPG mechanics, and exploration- - - the Bladekiro-like, offering a more linear experience with an emphasis on memory-based Quick Time Event combat- -- - the Ringcorerdtree-like, with a focus on customization, delayed attacks, and screen-obscuring particle effects falls squarely into the first category.You play as Therone, as "Souls veteran" who is always . He will make anyone else die who does not "play the right way," considering them heretics who "cheat not only the church, but themselves."Therone unwillingly teams up with a cast of characters with wildly varying accents.Also, the game provides concrete answers about "Nito, the first to die," who is the subject of countless YouTube lore videos. As it turns out, Nito was an African American football player. So simple, yet everyone overlooked it.For the first 4-5 hours, I really liked the game. It started off almost too easy, but ramped up to a normal Soulslike difficulty experience.However, after 5 hours, the game can get very difficult, frustratingly so. I started enjoying it a lot less until I spent a little time grinding levels.The game offers tons of experience, though. You can literally kill 4-8 enemies and gain a level, then kill those same enemies again to level up.Progression is very marginal, like most Soulslikes, but this is a genre of marginal advantages for marginal victories. A 3% health gain feels like an insulting waste of time until you beat a boss with 2% of your health remaining.The "estus flask" type of healing in the game is nearly useless, as it drains the health of your non-active party members to heal the active one. I think I healed less than 5 times all game and regretted it each time.Instead, the game wants you to rely on morphing to another character who has more health. It is always pushing you to do morphs - dodges, strikes, ultimate strikes.When doing damage to enemies, non-active party members regain some health (life steal).As designed, it also puts a lot of pressure on the player to be aggressive but safe when all of your party members are low on health. It punishes you for putting yourself in a bad spot, but rewards you for playing well.And stamina is correlated to how much health you have left.I can see this being very divisive, as it renders some Soulslike habits useless or punishing. And until you get a handle on when and how to morph safely, it can feel very unnatural.Some bosses are fine, good even. I don't think Soulslikes are exclusively about bosses, but are just as much about the dungeon crawling experience.Thankfully,  has both good dungeon crawling and mostly good bosses.I beat a couple bosses on the first try, but most took several tries.One particular boss took about a dozen tries, and the final boss took maybe half a dozen.I got to the infamous  boss at level 47 and could not beat him. Once I leveled up to 55, it was still very challenging, but was able to beat it in another 3-4 tries.Overall, it feels mostly balanced appropriately. The ease of gaining experience to level up helps with this.Besides a couple of extremely frustrating parts, I enjoyed most of this game. I think the frustrations will be smoothed over with patches in the future. At that point, this might be a very smooth and enjoyable experience, although offering a pretty standard Soulslike difficulty.Overall, this is a good Soulslike worth trying. Similar to , it punishes some Soulslike habits. It should be celebrated for trying to break out of the mold a bit, even if the morph mechanics could use some polishing.

Deathbound is a one-of-a-kind party-based soulslike set in a callous world where Faith and Science clash.

The forbidden city of Akratya is an unforgiving land that cannot be conquered alone. Bind with fallen warriors found throughout your crusade and dynamically transform between the characters seamlessly mid-combat with the unique 4-hero party system.

Face challenging enemies crafted to push you to your limits. Their very nature is based on the five stages of grief, with each new encounter commanding the attention of any soul who dare face them.

name: Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin
detailed_description: ●Notice of Change in System Requirements As a result of NVIDIA announcing the end of support for certain GPUs from October 4, 2021, the minimum and recommended system requirements for this game have changed. Please make sure to check the updated requirements before purchase. About the Game *This content is also available as part of one or more bundles. Please check your previous purchases to avoid duplication. Hatch, raise, and live alongside monsters as a Monster Rider in this fun-filled RPG set in the Monster Hunter universe. ◆ Story What you've been entrusted with could bring hope or terror… It is the night of a festival in Mahana, the central village of Hakolo Island. Rathalos all around the world are vanishing. You are the grandchild of Red, whose Monstie was Guardian Ratha, the revered protector of Hakolo Island. Upon setting out to gain experience as a Rider, you encounter Ena, a Wyverian girl who once knew Red. In order to protect the egg that Guardian Ratha has entrusted her with, you decide to leave the island together. There are strange things happening everywhere. As you try to figure out what is causing these environmental abnormalities, the egg finally hatches. A flightless Rathalos with small wings bursts out of the egg. ◆ Go Egg Collecting and Hatch Some Monstie Travel Companions Form bonds with monsters as you embark on a Rider's journey! The monsters you befriend during this enthralling adventure become your loyal Monsties. There is a diverse range of monsters that inhabit every nook and cranny of this world. Throughout your daring escapades, you can become pals with fearsome and unique monsters such as Brachydios, Seregios, Nargacuga, Tigrex, Zinogre, Kushala Daora, and Teostra! Find more monsters along the way and add them to your party! Eggs can be found in Monster Dens that randomly appear in the field. There are even some rare dens that pop up infrequently where you can get your hands on elusive monster eggs and ones that contain hard-to-find genes. Once you have made it safely out of the Monster Den, bring the egg to the Stables and hatch it to get a new Monstie for your journey! These are special skills that you can perform while riding a Monstie. Depending on the Monstie, you can gain an ability such as dashing, flying, or swimming. There are also other actions that allow you to search for items more effectively when out in the field. ◆ Monstie Growth Line up genes to level up your Monsties! After hatching Monsties, you can strengthen them through battles and the Rite of Channeling. The Rite of Channeling is a ritual that allows you to transfer a gene from one Monstie to another. By doing this, you can awaken a new ability in the Monstie receiving the gene, thereby creating your own original Monstie. During the ritual, you can choose which slot you will place the gene in. This gives you the opportunity to enhance your Monsties by awakening new skills and abilities in interesting combinations. ◆ Turn-Based Battles Master the three attack types to gain the upper hand during turn-based battles! The improved turn-based combat system allows you to experience the excitement of the main Monster Hunter titles while engaging in epic, strategic fights with monsters you encounter during your adventure. There are three attack types: Power, Speed, and Technical. By predicting your opponent's attack type and winning a Head-to-Head, you can inflict massive damage as well as greatly fill your Kinship Gauge. Duke it out using the weapons and armor that the Monster Hunter series is known for! Six weapon types from the familiar Monster Hunter series lineup are available in this game too. Master each of their unique characteristics and forge equipment to fit your individual playing style. Layered armor is also available, so you can hunt in style while wearing your favorite equipment. ◆ Multiplayer In Multiplayer, you can connect with players from around the world! Team up in Co-Op Expedition Quests or face off against each other in Versus Battles. If one of you engages a monster while out in the field, the other player can enter the fray and lend a helping hand. Join forces with other Riders from all over the globe to search for rare eggs and take down fearsome monsters together. ◆ Downloadable Content From hairstyles for your Rider to outfits for Ena and Navirou, there is a wide assortment of exciting downloadable content available. You can purchase downloadable content individually or in packs. You can even get all of the available downloadable content at once for a bargain with the All-In Extra Content Pack! Give the characters a fresh look and take your adventure to new heights!

short_description: A new adventure awaits you in this second installment of the turn-based RPG series set in the world of Monster Hunter! Become a Rider and form bonds with friendly monsters known as Monsties to fight alongside them as you take part in an epic story.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a captivating RPG that beautifully expands the Monster Hunter universe, offering a delightful blend of storytelling, exploration, and turn-based combat. The game features a rich and immersive story that follows your character's journey as a Monster Rider, filled with memorable characters and emotional moments. The narrative effectively draws players into the world and keeps them invested in the outcome. The visuals are vibrant and colorful, bringing the world and its inhabitants to life. The character designs and animations are charming, making every interaction feel delightful. The turn-based combat encourages players to think strategically about their moves, utilizing the strengths of their monsters while countering opponents. The addition of the "Kinship" mechanic allows for powerful combo attacks, adding depth to battles. Players can hatch, raise, and bond with various monsters, creating a strong emotional connection. This feature adds a unique and personal touch to the gameplay, as players develop their own team of companions. Overall, Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a fantastic RPG that successfully combines a heartfelt narrative with engaging gameplay mechanics. It’s a perfect entry point for newcomers and a delightful experience for fans of the Monster Hunter franchise!
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is everything you could want in a Pokemonesque Monster Hunter Game. The gameplay is intuitive, fun and complex in a rewarding way. The collection of Monsties within this game is phenomenal each being unique and exciting to use, rewarding strategy in both story content and multiplayer. The story is top class, funny, charming and emotional at times. The varied cast of characters all hit their marks being memorable and different enough from one another while many of them provide a similar role as a light to build up the MC's motivations and actions. Without spoilers the ending to the story is phenomenal and the early post game content is rewarding for time put in and gives a refreshing air to the overworld that you trek through in the main game. Looking forward to updates in the future. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Like if Pokemon made a baby with Monster Hunter.Simple Rock/Paper/Scissors type combat dealing with "Power", "Technique" and "Speed" based moves with incredibly over the top anime stylized attacks from your Monsties and allies.  It gets hilarious how ridiculous some of the attacks can be.  Definitely worth a good amount of time and still looking forward to sinking some more hours into it.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good RPG that shares Similarities with collection JRPGs like Pokemon and DigimonYou don't even need high specs to run the game, I was able to run this on a regular laptop without any issues.I managed to get to the end of the game's story while collecting most of the monsters, so the game's length is about 40-60 hours, not including the post game which could be another 60 hours.The game's core mechanics are solid while being fun enough to continue through long hours, and you're able to kill weaker monsters instantly if you're over leveled enough.All in all, buy it if you feel playing a great collection JRPG!

_childDocuments_.review: Wings of Ruin is a strange one, to me... I've put in 40ish hours as of this review, and I'll probably put more into it at some point either for the post-game or a second play through, but this is one of those games where I wish Steam had a middling option rather than a thumbs up or down. For every good choice or interesting route the game takes with its gameplay or mechanics, there's always a counterpoint that drags it down in return... and the fact that I literally had to mod a character out of the game just so that I could make an attempt at enjoying the story is laughable (I'm looking at you, Navirou).All in all the gameplay is good, and even interesting when you dig into the gene system for your critters, if a bit shallow, but the the game was clearly designed for a younger audience so expect an annoyingly hand-holdy tooltip system and npc dialogue that will continue to explain things at you long after you've reached the endgame as if you've only just started. Think of it along the lines of Pokemon Sword/Shield - at its core, a decent game... but I can't give it a thumbs up for anyone who doesn't have an extremely high tolerance for nonsense.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I begin? This was a game I greatly regret sleeping on for so long.I'm a diehard JRPG fan, and among them played many monster collectors like Shin Magami Tensei, Digimon, Symphonia 2, the pokemon franchise, and DQ monsters. I can proudly add this title to my shelf. It stands out to me how much thought was put into the game's combat mechanics, The game's cornerstone, head to heads seems like a simple Rock paper scissors mechanic that ends up expanding into other interwoven game mechanics inspired by the mothership franchise. Rage mode and monster actions change behaviours, part breaking affects their move pools. Status effects can be used offensivsly and defensively to help your party.  All the monhun mechanics are translated over into this head to head system intuitively. Riding is this game's super meter, and building it requires you to actively participate and learn how to make the most of the system.Compared to the juggernaut Franchise pokemon where battles are more of a chore of mashing A through menus to snowplough through the game, you actually activate your neurons and think on what your next move is after reading the field.This is hugely rewarding as your motivated to fight, not just to grind up numbers, but because fights are both really fun and you improve on your own as a player.  This also plays into its monster recruiting, You paintball monsters and raid dens to get a shot at stealing their eggs. The monster pool is best described as quality over quantity. With many monsters from the core franchise up to worlds able to be hatched and raised at your mounts.The monsters all have unique moves and are loaded with personality, each species feeling like their own character with great animations.The monsters field skills as you ride them to get around actively encourage you to build a diverse team for many reasons besides being a bigger bag of stats with an element on it. Getting a swimming or climing monster in your group feels like a big deal with the involved process of getting an egg. Story is a fairly kid-friendly boy becoming a man in their forebearer's footsteps stuff you see a lot of in JRPGs and such, with a healthy seasoning of monster hunter lore and personality. Its engaging, and the game isnt beating you over the head too hard with the usual suspects. (Navirou the Felyne can be a polarizing character however, acting as the comic-releif voice surrigate for the mute protagonist.)Graphically its style focus over technical focus as it was originally a switch title. But never feels like one. And tbe open world areas are typical of a monster hunter franchise, beautiful ecology-scapes. World's endemic life making the area even more lively. Audio is also typical monster hunter affair, great music tracks and meaty sound design. And even the switch version featured fully voiced cutscenes, something neither switch pokemon games could even attempt, but standard for many JROGs in the late playstation 2 era. Lastly the game's combat system also enables co-op through its buddy system. In the story an NPC and their monstie join in battle with you, and the full head to head system cross interacts and compounds. Later on you can invite a friend to join you in fights online to take on the game's bigger targets.This game was the boogeyman under Pokemon Company's bed, and legends arceus tried its best and failed at appropriating ideas from MH Stories.As the old addage goes; imitation is the greatest form of flattery.If you want a fresh take on a monster collector, or want to experience what Pokemon Legends Arceus wished it could be, or a Mon-Hun fan who loves everything Monster Hunter. You will not be dissapointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a turn-based RPG set in the Monster Hunter world. To say it draws inspiration from the Pokemon franchise is an understatement - most of its mechanics are taken at least somewhat from Pokemon games.I mean that in no ill intent - if you like Pokemon games, this game will probably be up your alley.This game also uses many classic mechanics and features from the standard Monster Hunter games, which add a nice spice to the game.This is a very chill game all about collecting all the different monsters you can. It's story-driven, sure, but even though the plot is more complex than in standard Monster Hunter games, I won't say it's significantly better. The story in this game isn't mind-shattering, but rather there to get the game moving.The turn-based combat, while fairly simple and not too challenging, is still fun. Just like in Monster Hunter fashion, you need to figure out what the monsters you're fighting are weak to, and preparation for a fight is greatly rewarded. However, this game isn't too hard. You really don't need to grind or stay on your toes, you'll usually win encounters.The graphics are stylized and charming, and the music is nice. In my personal opinion, the anime-esque nature of this game is not a welcome addition, but this is simply a matter of taste.In short, MHS2 is a fun game that has plenty of content for those who want to collect 'em all. It's not really challenging, it's not really interesting in terms of story, but it's harmless fun. If you like Pokemon, you'll probably like this game, but if you're looking for a great story like in other RPGs or challenging gameplay like in regular Monster Hunter, you may be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Aloha,This is my reivew for Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin, a JRPG that puts you in the role of a monster rider instead of a hunter unlike the other games in the series. You follow the story of the wings of ruin, where a terrible prophecy fortells doom to the world. The game delivers the standard JRPG tropes [friendship is power] and the usual play cycle [fight, get xp, level up, repeat] and you travel from one area to the next solving mysteries regarding the legendary wings of ruin.The Good: probably the best JRPG I've played in recent memory, colourful well crafted cell shaded graphics and fun environments, cool monster designs, a memorable cast of characters, wonderful orchestral music, the story while having some predictable plot points [see if you can spot Lysanderoth in the first hour of the game], it is a fun romp with great game play mechanics. Also, it should be a design document for making a good RPG, it has lots of quality of life improvements which will make the next JRPG I play seem antiquated [quick finish battles, teleport to checkpoints, fastmode, skip cut scenes, and more]. The Bad: the sidekick character is pretty annoying, but the game is designed for children, so I can see how they would have enjoyed him; that being said, despite being made for children, it doesn't feel like a kids game, except for the light tone, and I authentically enjoyed the game, despite it being far outside what I usually play [rogue-likes, dark souls, h-games].The Ugly: the Lysanderoth character reveal was only lacking a "I would have gotten away with it if it wasn't for you meddling kids!" line because I guessed it after he first appeared with his mask.The Last Word: this is one of the funnest and most comfy JRPG's I've played since Cyberdimension Neptunia; and after two years of pandemic, my life becoming an unrecognisable mess, this whimsical romp filled my heart with joy and gave much needed relief during one of the darkest winters of my life, and I hope you consider purchasing it, and hope you will enjoy it too.
