_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is not a terribly bad game but it isn't the most appealing one either especially once you get past the initial excitement of capturing monsters. Then again, I'm a 33 year old man and it's probably my fault for attempting to play a game that's targeted at a younger audience.The pros:1) The anime-style graphics are pretty good lookingThe cons:1) The story is pretty dull and if you're one of those who's obsessed with capturing all monsties, it's going to slow down the game play even more. Having a silent protagonist really just drags everything down to a crawl.2) The game is super repetitive - the dungeons are all fairly standard. But what's worse is every time you reach a new chapter, it's all about doing the same stuff again.3) The battle mechanics is too simple (not in terms of difficulty, but the concept of it). The fact that the creators of the game had a quick battle system meant they knew the battles were going to tire gamers out. And while I appreciate the quick battle system, maybe they should have tried creating a more compelling experience in the first place?4) The open world is big but empty. Ends up being very hollow.5) The sound system of the game is quite unbalanced. A lot of the time you;re going to be wondering if there's any BGM at all. (Yes you can tune it yourself in the settings section but the default settings should have worked a lot better to begin with)6) The dialogues are probably the worst aspect of the game. Again, this is from a perspective of a 33 year old man, so I'm probably not the intended audience. But boy does the writing sucks. It's written for a 10 year old with loads of kiddo-type dialogues and humour that annoys the ♥♥♥♥ out of me. It's one thing to try to create an anime-styled game, it's another to create a childish game for kids watching PAW Patrol.Overall, it's a 4/10 but if you're like me who bought the game at full price, it's closer to a 3/10.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a monster collecting game that actually had effort put into it then this game is for you.Monster Hunter Stories 2 takes aspects from the main games and turns it into a turn-based RPG and mostly succeeds in this. My main issue in the gameplay is more in the endgame department where I sometimes just get 1-shotted by normal attacks by the hardest monsters, even at level 90. While it is possible to prevent this, it is a bit too punishing for getting hit once.The story of the game is fine, nothing too noteworthy but not bad. The pacing around the 2nd and 3rd town isn't great though, the 3rd town honestly bored me a bit 'cus it really didn't add anything to the story for so long. I also wish you could choose your battle theme as hearing the same big monster theme in co-op quests gets a bit tiring. This is probably the only time I'm gonna give Pokémon a point as those games always have awesome music.I'm not a graphics guy but I really like this game's art style. Seeing the monsters in a more stylized art style is pretty charming to me and I would love a mainline game in this art style. Also high quality animations, this game has them. _childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a fantastic spin-off title to the much longer running Monster Hunter series of games and is a sequel to Monster Hunter Stories for the nintendo 3DS, telling the story of your main character and a small collection of characters as you try to discover the secrets behind strange events happening in the world and put a stop to it.The games story is rather run of the mill, small isolated town main character leaves home on a larger than life adventure alongside a macguffin beast companion with the end goal to defeat a world ending threat, despite this however in all three of my play through's (once on the nintendo switch twice here on steam) I found myself becoming attached to these characters and compelled to save this world i've been shown, however this may not stand true for everyone which is okay.The main draw of the game however is all the mechanics, the best way to experience the game is to play it for yourself as the nuances of combat crafting collecting and dungeon raiding that form the gameplay loop is engaging and exciting especially if you are fond of turn based rpg's and yet remains faithful in most aspects the the main series of games making it great for fans of those games as well making it in my personal opinion this and the original stories great ways for new fans of the MH series to dip their feet into the series and get a feel for it's rules and mechanics.Now don't let the 2 in the title scare you off, while this is a sequel and several characters from the 3DS title do return in this game at no point will you be alienated by the game for not playing the original. Most characters are given a short run down to the player by Navirou and are treated in a way that contains them to this games story alone allowing specific returning characters to interact with the plot without needing that prior knowledge, at that point having played the first game just allows you to be put in awe at how these characters have grown since the first game and go "OH MY GOD I REMEMBER THEM!"If you're still not sold on the game a free demo of the game is available for free on the steam market and takes you all the way to the first boss fight of the game, allowing you to experience all the basics and get a strong feel for the game and if you decide to purchase the game in full your demo progress will be transferred over so you won't loose anything, so take a swing at it! Happy hunting hunter's and rider's, I hope to see you in game.

_childDocuments_.review: MHST2 takes the great foundation laid down by the 3DS title Monster Hunter Stories and builds upon it. The graphics have been massively updated and while the cell-shading, colorful palettes stuck around, the character, armor, and monster designs are a little less cutesy and closer to the main series in proportion, although still with significantly less detail. This is a massive boon to the game as the design work of Monster Hunter has always been one of its (or, in my opinion, *the*) best assets to bring it above the competition.        The turn-based combat in this game uses the attack patterns in the Monster Hunter franchise as its inspiration to prevent it from becoming too predictable and dull. While the predecessor had an element of strict memorization and even randomness to spice up combat and make it challenging, this game tries to broadcast each set of moves an enemy will make clearly which looses a lot of the difficulty and can make combat a bit boring for skilled players. I don't mind this as I enjoy turn-based monster taming games primarily as a lower-effort engagement brightened by strong creature designs and longer-term goals, which MHST2 is perfect for, but if your main complaint about monster taming games is that few are as high engagement and challenging as Shin Megami Tensei you're looking in the wrong place.       Fans of franchises like Digimon, Pokemon, or Yokai-Watch will find that the beautiful and varied monsters and their interesting and unique animations, the wide and varied selection of armors and weaponry, and easier gameplay feeds their needs very well. In fact, if your main gripe about those games is that you can't explore the colorful and interesting worlds flying on the back of a Birdramon or leaping up cliffs on a Gogoat, this is exactly the game for that itch. Pokemon Let's Go Pikachu and Eevee took a lot of inspiration from the first game in this series to implement their own follow/ride mechanics and this still stands as the strongest representation of that.  If you love games that let you feel like you can really get attatched to your mounts or pets, this is for you.TL;DR breakdownGameplay - CasualCompletionist suitability - A lot of RNG grind for eggs, will be time consumingGraphics - Beautiful and consistent but not particularly resource intensiveStory - Nothing special, but cute enoughMusic - FantasticReplayablility - High

_childDocuments_.review: MIXED REVIEWI wouldn't bother with this game unless you're a diehard Monster Hunter fanboy, you like the concept of Pokemon and would like to use Stories as a gateway into the MonHun series, or if you're buying this for a young child. I'll try to outline why.-Positive points-* It's Monster Hunter* It's a cute and comfortable game* It has multiplayer: both co-op and PvP* The story is nice and ties in with the first game, and the Monster Hunter Stories anime. Chronologically the events happen after the anime, and I suggest you watch that first if it's the selling point for you.-Negative points-Difficulty is almost nonexistent through most of the playthrough. This is because Monsters can almost 100% of the time be predicted which type of attack they're going to do. It wasn't like this in Stories 1, there they had random chance of using at least one of 2 attack styles in a Rock/Paper/Scissor design. Here they instead operate in modes, e.g. Glavenus will always use Power attacks in normal mode. When he fire charges his throat, he will always use Speed attacks. When he heats his tailblade, he will always use Tech attacks. This means that you can sync attack every enemy monster attack which denies any incoming damage. Very few monster attacks will not be Head to Head type attacks, and usually it's the 3rd or 4th attack after the Monster enrages or goes into a special mode, which is identifiable by the fact the monster will (most of the time) not have a target indicator going to either you or your monstie. When this happens, you can do a kinship attack to also bypass that, and force the monster to skip a turn right back to the start of the normal > enrage > alternative mode flowchart. This behavior holds up all the way throughout the story and in the post-story gameplay. There's VERY few monsters who can not be beaten with this strategy, few enough to be counted on one hand. One could argue difficulty shouldn't be expected in this game because it's clearly marketed towards children, but Stories 1 had difficulty aplenty. There's also a big difference between the difficulty being totally absent, and low difficulty. Stories 2 also has a "skip fight" button in random encounters (so not e.g. story or boss encounters) where you outlevel your opponent by a certain amount. In theory this sounds nice for things that would die in one hit, but that's not how this was implemented. It took me one hour of doing side quests in the last area for the "skip fight" button to start appearing, letting me instakill encounters that would otherwise require 5-10 minutes to clear normally, with the added benefit of getting an automatic S rank which spits out insane amount of loot for you. This one personally ruins a lot of the game's appeal for me, since for me Monster Hunter is a lot about tracking your "career" (e.g. amount of monsters slayed and materials gathered), but both of these statistics become meaningless when you have an autowin button on most of the fights. Post game High Rank encounters seem to be an exception, but that assumes you spend multiple tens of hours going through the story first, and in my book any game that doesn't start to get enjoyable until you're at the end is not worth playing.Finally, raising Monsties is also not particularly rewarding. At all times, your entire party will gain XP from an encounter, so there's no room for enjoying the feeling of putting in effort into raising and leveling a certain Monster. Just drop it in your party and hit the instakill button, and boom your new Monstie will be maxed out within half an hour without ever sending it to battle.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend? The answer is "yes, but..."It's a great game from what I've played of it, but the thing that kills it for me is the rock-paper-scissors combat and how cookie cutter it is. Every monster species is a pre-determined rock, paper, or scissor. Every attack they use, barring some special attacks, will be that type. When there's a phase change (such as enraging), they'll switch to a different type and use that for the entirety of that phase, at which point they'll switch back. There's no variability outside of that, making combat extremely predictable once you find out their type.This means that every fight effectively boils down to "what type attack are they using on turn one", switching your monster to counter it, and just spamming "head to heads" until phase change, at which point you repeat those three steps. Nothing in the game has felt threatening. It's possible I'm just well out of the target age demographic and am too min-maxy with it.If combat was less predictable, I feel that I'd enjoy the game more. All it would need is more randomness in attack types during phases rather than locking it to one type, plus a neutral.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up as I have an interest in Monster Hunter, and am a fan of creature collectors, and having put 140 hours into this game I can easily say it's one of my favourite games. The story is ok, with some cool/emotional moments, and the characters are decent, despite getting a lot of flak I actually quite like Navirou. The start is a little slow and the initial pool of available monsters is small, but it eventually speeds up quite a lot.The game plays similarly to other creature collectors, you travel the world conscripting the local wildlife into your merry band and command them to destroy your enemies, but rather than defeating them in battle and then capturing them, you instead channel your inner loot goblin and steal the eggs right out of the nest, have the newborn imprint on you, and then have dragon junior fight alongside you, and you can ride them as mounts. There are over a hundred different monsters to collect, and many of them have useful abilities when exploring the world, like breaking boulders, leaping across chasms, turning invisible to sneak past unwanted fights etc.Once you and your monsters reach a high enough level, most fights in that area become significantly faster as you get the option to instantly win, which makes leveling up new monsters much faster. The game eventually gives you access to special missions you can send inactive monsters on so they still gain experience and level up when not in your party, so you can do less grinding with them.All monsters have 9 geneslots, which is where their abilities, both passive and active, can be found, and partway through the game you gain the ability to take genes from monsters and put them in other ones, enabling you to customise and tailor your party exactly the way you want, so you can specialise certain monsters for particular fights etc, and its quite fun trying to come up with your own builds and test them out.Combat in this game is a mix of both Monster Hunter and the typical creature collector turn based gameplay. Both you and your monsters fight, with your monsters having a selection of moves pokemon style, whereas you craft and wield multiple weapon types, from the sword and shield, bows, axes etc, and your moveset changes depending on what you have equipped during that battle. You can have 3 weapons equipped at a time, and can switch between them during a fight, you also have access to various traps, sonic and flash bombs, barrel bombs, paintballs etc.Monsters have both elemental and weapon type weaknesses, and moves both yours and monsters, have one of 3 types: Power, Speed, and Technical, which mostly comes into play during head to head fights during a battle. Power beats Technical, Technical beats Speed, Speed beats Power, so taking advantage of this, in addition to elemental and weapon weaknesses, is important for winning fights. Winning head to heads, using certain moves etc, fill up a special kinship gauge. Once this is full, you get the option to ride your monster, restoring health and enabling you to use a special kinship move which plays a special cutscene and does a lot of damage.Once you beat the main story there is a considerable amount of post story content, such as new quests, new monster variations, and a new zone called the Elders Lair, which is where you will find some of the toughest fights in the game.I cannot say anything about the multiplayer, coop or PvP, as I don't have much interest in those, but if you are a fan of Monster Hunter or creature collectors/turn based combat games in general, or looking to get into them, I highly recommend this game, it's a ton of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom did a good job on this game, I play Monster Hunter games, and occasionally RPGs like this, and in my opinion Stories 2 is a better turn-based RPG game than Monster Hunter Rise is a Monster Hunter game.Some people draw similarities between this and Pokemon, I can't comment because I don't play Pokemon, but I think it's more like Dragon Quest meets Monster Hunter.  I say that because you actually fight with your main character in this, and in some of the Dragon Quest games you could recruit and use monsters in combat as regular party members (5 for example).  Pokemon is also a kid's game that you can faceroll I'm told, but this game has a semblance of a challenge to it, so there's a lot of strategy involved in the combat in this.  You got rock/paper/scissors with 3 types of attacks, you got double attacks that cancel a monster's attack if you use rock/paper/scissors correctly, you got monsters with multiple states where they change their attack types, you got element and status vulnerabilities, a robust selection of items you can use in combat to counter specific monster attacks, like flash bombs on fliers, and sonic bombs on stuff that burrows into the ground, healing items, buffing items, items to inflict status effects (including traps).  The monster genes (passive buffs and attacks) can be fully customized once you reach a certain point in the game, so there's builds for monsters and player characters.  So it's a pretty robust selection of options you got here, and you'll need to use them wisely.  Don't buy this for the multiplayer, I can tell you straight up it's garbo.  Buy this as a single player RPG game, and forget that multiplayer exists.  If you liked Dragon Quest XI, you'll probably like this.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you're a monster hunter and JRPG fan this is one of the best games everStory: 6.5/10Nothing spectacular here, the story is serviceable enough but there's nothing that really made it stand out too much, with it being a kid's game and all. It goes more or less the way you would expect a game like this to go. It actually sort of feels like a rehash of the first game, and if you did not play the first one you might be a little bit confused on who some of the later characters introduced are. Not too big of a worry though as it has minimal impact on the actual story of the game itselfGraphics: 9/10It's no Monster Hunter World, but the graphics fit the game quite nicely and every monster looks more or less the same as their counterpart in the mainline games (with a bit of differences here and there - I don't remember Azure Rathalos being this bright blue)Animations are superbly done - each monster follows the exact same animations as they would in the mainline game for idle / attacking animations and moreKinship skills are also a big plus and a joy to look at just for the sheer spectacle of being anything between a super cheesy ham attack to launching what is essentially a nuke at your opponent and possibly leaving a crater where they standMusic: 9/10The BGMs are all amazingly done, you can hear the actual monster's theme mixed into the boss battle theme during their boss intro cutscenes, each area has day / night music that plays when you first enter them and it is, in general, very fitting and a joy to listen toGameplay: 9.5/10Rock, paper, scissors with a few twists here and there, each monster you fight have fixed patterns they follow and it's up to you the player to figure it out and play around them. This is emphasized to the extreme when it comes to the hard mode bosses which more or less instantly or heavily punish you if you don't know how to counter their patterns properly to cancel their attacks every round. Surprisingly addicting even in the post game.Certain monster mechanics from the mainline series remain in the game as well, such as monsters falling over when you break their legs or other specific parts, or even them toppling themselves over if certain parts are broken upon performing certain attacks.My only gripe is that the post game more or less dictates that you MUST play online / co-op rooms in order to find the end game monsties, as the other option of trying to spawn a super rare high rank monster den is extremely tedious and can take hours to pay offFinal Score: 34/40Story may not be anything special and drags the game down a little, but everything else makes up for it and creates what is in essence a very enjoyable game, particularly for monster hunter fans.

Fortunately Capcom decided to give the series another chance on much better hardware, and because of this I not only got to enjoy Monster Hunter Stories, I actually kind of regret not giving it a fair chance sooner.✪ The Rite of Channeling allows you to keep your favorite Monsties with you for as long as you'd like without ever worrying about them becoming obsolete.✪ The tale it tells makes it a if my time going above and beyond was well-spent.✪ It's carried by an excellent take on turn-based combat.✪ It does an excellent job translating just about everything that makes them special into a fantastic JRPG.✪ For those into the competitive side of things, you can host your own lobbies with overrides that ensure you and your opponent are balanced, which doubles as a nice way to counter anyone who didn't acquire their monsties, skills or levels legitimately.✪ Those interested in co-op have three different quest types to enjoy with a buddy, random, or AI.✪ There's a whole lot to do after the credits, properly called "Post-Game Content", and a  highlighting new activities to do in co-op and Monsties to collect for those itching for more content. ✘ Much like Monster Hunter World and Monster Hunter Rise, you'd better make darn sure you're satisfied with the way your character looks, because changing it is gonna cost you actual money again. ✘ Though you can change just about every keybind and the general feeling of mouse and keyboard was great, there are a few things that didn't make sense or could have been done better. • It's a shame this game has no kind of photo mode, because even in its most repetitious biomes, it is full of so many vibrant visuals and delightful characters that I'd love to run around taking pictures without the game's permanently fixated menu getting in the way. • You can sort your Monsties by Level, Rarity and when you Acquired them, but there's no way to organize your Monsties beyond these means.• Waiting for Monster Hunter Rise to release on PC became a much bigger struggle than I thought it would.Monster Hunter Stories 2 is among the most delightful games I've ever played. With so many ways to play, so much to do and even more on the way at no extra cost, not only do we have a new standard for turn-based RPGs, but what was already a fantastic franchise—which doubles as my favorite franchise—has become even better. It's a really good time to be a Monster Hunter fan.[𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗼]■ Post-Story Free Roam: Yes■ Chapter Select: No■ New Game+: No (at time of writing) ■ DLC: Yes; strictly cosmetic.■ Optional Content: Immense; side quests aplenty, with post-game content and even a post-game to the post-game. There's a whole lot to do beyond the main story.■ Update Frequency: Steady; Capcom is doing a decent job handling patches and fan feedback, with the Roadmap providing several incentives to return.■ Accessibility Options: None, from what I could gather in the Options via the Main Menu and in-game.■ Plan to 100%: Yes, but slowly because of how grindy Genes are.■ Replay Worthy : The story? Yes. The 100%? No chance.For more information and a much longer review, !

_childDocuments_.review: Due to MHW being my favorite game I really wanted to like this one. The lack of difficulty and the repetitious combat were kind of a let down but good enough for some simple entertainment. What killed this game for me was the highly annoying mascot Navirou who is the surrogate voice for the silent protagonist please god why do you speak in contemporary slang and why are you so annoying and please god why wont you ever shut the %$#@ up!? Ahem, sorry.So the combat... It starts strong. Its flashy, the battle theme hypes you up, it moves pretty quick, but then you realize that's it. What you see is what you get. The combat is a rock-paper-scissors system. The issue is every monster has a certain type and will almost always use that type of attack. Unless its mad, then it will always use a different specific attack type. Its incredibly predictable and successfully countering your attacker mean you don't take any damage. Sure you and your monsties get different abilities but they're all tied to an attack type. Just use the abilities that counters what you're fighting and you cannot lose.Then there's Navirou the tie in mascot character from the first game. It seems like everyone who likes him in MHS2 carried that affection from the first game. Apparently he's a legendary bad butt. Just like every other mascot character who's a self proclaimed hero, he's absolutely worthless. He never shuts up and his hint prompts seem to actively hinder game play (also they never ever ever stop, please make them stop). Also, Navirou completely shatters the immersion due to using more modern contemporary slang and dialogue. It's like he got isekai'ed straight from New York in the late 90's and he NEEDS you to know about his donut addiction. You will never stop hearing this dialogue which is used to constantly ram words down your throat or ruin dramatic moments with comedic quips because "this is a children's game (for some reason) and a child cant handle any emotion besides fart humor" etc. Really this is what did it for me. I cant play a game where the mascot, without any consent ever, speaks for you and makes you look like a total idiot. Why did they take away one of the BEST things about the monster hunter franchise, the palicos, and give you this annoying abomination instead? Getting a palico companion that looks and acts like one from the main titles would've easily elevated this game from a 5/10 to a 7/10 game, well as long as the only noises it makes are the cute mews and hisses that we typically get.Tl;dr: This game is literally for children. This is what you buy your toddler to play because they wanted to play Monster Hunter with you but aren't good enough at games yet. This game didn't pick a whimsical childish style to leverage nostalgia or contrast with some darker themes. It looks like a kids game because it is a kid's game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never been a fan of the mainline Monster Hunter series of games, mostly because there really wasn't any "story" at all beyond hunting monsters. The Monster Hunter Stories spin-off games fixes that, and also turns the game into a much-more playable turn-based roleplaying game style. _childDocuments_.review: MHS2 is a pretty good game. The monsters and their attacks look and feel good visually. It's fun to create interesting builds for individual monsters, or to just min-max and create absolute powerhouses. During that first run through each area, I enjoyed pulling up all the different patterned eggs and predicting based on the surrounding mobs what it'd be.The story is a little kiddy and pretty simple overall, but I guess it serves to take the edge off. It assumes you played the first game, which I didn't, but that fact kind of made the world feel somewhat more lived in. The postgame, however, offers more challenges and is really where the build-crafting shines. I suppose that's true to Monster Hunter as a franchise.I completed the Book of Genes, which kind of led to some burnout and is alone what added ~50 hrs to my play time. You don't have to do it unless you're cursed with seeking achievements, which I am blighted by. Most of the best genes (XL tier) are the easiest to obtain.Multiplayer scene is dead but if you have a buddy playing alongside you then the multiplayer content actually isn't half bad.End of the day, I got to ride and command a Nergigante. So, it's not perfect, but it's a recommendation in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s Monster Hunter but with a twist that turned into a turn based, creature collector game. It has a lot of typical Monster Hunter stuff so you’ll feel right at home if you’ve played a Monster Hunter game.However, I found that the game starts off strong but gets boring as time goes on. Despite having ‘stories’ in its name, the story is pretty bland and dull. The protag is silent which doesn’t help. The combat is okay at the start but gets repetitive quickly. Because of these issues I was not able to complete it and found myself playing purely to try and get my money's worth, I had to drop it.It has positives too, like any Monster Hunter game, there are a ton of equipment sets and a ton of grinding to do if you’re into that. The game also runs well and there are no real problems with the PC port which is always nice to see. Although keep in mind, it's a port of a Switch game, and has not been enhanced for PC, so don’t expect amazing graphics but it running well is enough for me.It’s hard for me to recommend due to not being able to complete it. I would much rather play Monster Hunter World than this, but at the same time I don’t think it’s a bad game, it’s just not really for me. This could easily have been a thumbs down review too.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this because I heard it's a better Pokemon game and while I wouldn't say it's better than the original Pokemon experience it's definitely a great game on its own that hits some of the same notes.As I am not a big Monster Hunter player it took me a while to get into this game because lots of things are not explained well enough but by now I can say it was well worth it. The game gets better and better over time and just keeps evolving as you go on - there's a lot to learn and see here!Calling the combat rock-paper-scissoresque also doesn't do it justice because it's actually surprisingly deep. While the combat mechanics itself might be simple, success mainly depends on knowledge and timing, thus the game kind of forces you to observe and get to know each Monster you encounter and collect so that you can then perform better against it and/or with it. It's a great way to keep you involved and actually care about the world.The story and characters feel like a sunday morning kids cartoon but not in a bad way. Suprisingly enough, as goofy as it can be, it's somewhat charming instead of cringy.---Honestly I wasn't sure about this game up until about 15h into it but by now I'm very glad I gave it a chance to grow on me because it absolutely did!

_childDocuments_.review: Its a pretty cool game, made even better by the number and variety of monsters that you can befriend. As someone whose played Monster Hunter titles since I was like 8, its pretty awesome to pull together a team of monsters that I've grown to like from other MH entries. As soon as I was able to, I grabbed a Great Jaggi and have been using it ever since; I'm almost certain that every Monster is a viable option in this game, including some of the usually useless herbivores like Aptonoth and Apceros. It also helps that even if your base monsters genetic information sucks, you can pull together abilities and passives from other monsters to make them stronger. The grind for levels is made easier as well by a handy feature that lets you instantly complete a battle if you level is higher than a wild monster's by a specific margin, letting you plow through entire areas of monsters for some steady exp. The story of the game itself seems pretty standard if anything, I can already see the twist coming from like 10 miles away, but honestly that's fine, I really just came here to ride and battle with my favorite monsters.Overall I'd give this game a solid 9/10, its been engaging and entertaining. I honestly hope they release a third MHStories just so that we'd have even MORE monsters to work with.

Also the kinship skills are well done even tho it kinda reminds me a bit of stuff like dragonball from time to time but seeing a Kulu Ya Ku fumble an explosive egg into the monster you are fighting is already a favorite of mine. Storywise the game is a monster hunter game as always there is something happening that makes monsters mad, we have to investigate and find the cause and hunt that. At least it is the story so far and since we hatch eggs, we have to take care of a rathalos egg.I haven't encountered any bugs, game is running smooth as it should so for everybody who wants to enjoy monster hunter in a way more relaxed way, go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is coming from the perspective of someone who has played all the mainline Monster Hunter games and also the first Monster Hunter Stories game both on the Nintendo 3DS and the mobile port. MH Stories 2 evokes a whole wide range of emotions that ultimately is an enjoyable experience. Well atleast after getting through the very slow start.Negatives first, this game has starts okay but then really drags in the snow region. Both storywise and gameplaywise, the snow region is the worst time I ever had playing through the game. I was considering dropping the game, but I somehow didn't. The snow region does not reflect the whole quality of the game as a whole and for newcomers, just hold on til the next region where the story and gameplay ramps up in quality.  Still on the negatives section, there is no value in exploring the world. The world you venture in ultimately is split into three types of places, which is the towns, the big wide regional map, and the sub-areas that connects the big maps. The big wide regional maps are the highlights and are very beautiful with its artstyle and elevation in heights. But ultimately its all just very generic that kinda doesn't look like a Monster Hunter world other than the monsters roaming in it. Sub-areas connecting the big region maps have repetitive designs that gets old very, very fast, and are also reused in monster dens that will make it even more repetitive and a chore to go through, ultimately feeling like going through the same maps over and over again.About the snow region being worse storywise and gameplaywise, this region have alot of sub-areas, or can be called dungeons, that are very bland and are needed to go through to progress the main story. Storywise, the narrative suddenly treats you like a toddler in the snow region. It's not just family friendly now, its a kids show all of a sudden. Lorewise, there are alot of inconsistencies with how the MH world works. There are alot of monsters roaming that don't belong there, like Tobi Kadachi and Barroth. This ultimately just gave me a bad time playing through the snow region.All of these negatives are mainly personal because I am a fan of open world games so I expected some semblances of reward in exploration. Also, admittedly, I am comparing MH Stories 2 world map and design to its predescessor, to me is very much superior and unique design. That's pretty much my very personal rant that I hope MH Stories 3 can avoid.With the negatives out of the way, I really love this game. Despite some missteps, this game is pretty much a very solid followup from MH Stories 1. Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a Turn Based RPG, monster collecting game where you collect monsters from the Monster Hunter franchise. A pretty great alternative if you never play a Pokemon game. Unlike the mainline MH games, the story takes center stage and gameplay is turn-based, unlike the mainline real time combat and gameplay focus.The story is okay and takes a more light-hearted tone but sometimes can get dark in places like the great old Pixar films. The story is also very simple and not a whole lot of twists and depth. Kinda like the usual mainline MH foray, monster goes bad, fight gets bad, but our friendship can beat it, letter A goes to the letter B. Very simple story that gets the job done. Ultimately I like MH Stories 1 more with more memorable characters. The characters in MH Stories 2 do feel like they are there just because they are there.Monster collecting is where the gameplay is at. Combat is played with turn-based where attacks are executed in a rock-papper-scissors kind of manner. Each monsters have a type and you can collect them by harvesting eggs from the dens. After hatching the eggs, you can assemble a six monster team called Monsties. This is pretty much the gameplay. I have a very enjoyable time assembling a team of the mainline flagships like Tigrex and Zinogre. Hell, Nergigante is in this game too.The combat is simple and can get repetitive if you memorise what type the monster is. For example, the Velocidrome is Speed Type, which is weak to Technical Types. That means Velocidrome will always use Speed Type attacks that can be countered by Technical Types. It ultimately boils down to how well you can memorise the monsters moveset since the monsters attacks can change depends on their state like raging or flying. I do think it is a bit of a downgrade from MH Stories 1's combat where its more unpredictable and monsters only mostly use their type attacks. MH Stories 2 omits the unpredictability aspect of MH Stories 1 and uses more AOE attacks or double attacks per turn in difficulty. For me, I much prefer MH Stories 1 unpredictability used for difficulty since that reflects some qualities of the mainline MH games.Other positives, the soundtrack is great. Hunting with NPCs are fun too. I finished the main campaign in 50 hours, and as per usual Monster Hunter tradition, the real game starts after beating the story. There's whole bunch of things unlocked after the main campaign, adding my playtime until 70 hours.Overall, an amazing Monster Hunter experience.4/5

_childDocuments_.review: MHS2 is a great addition to a wonderful series of games. It may not attract the same audience as Monster Hunter: World did, but it’s still a great game on its own. If you can look past the childish story and characters, subpar graphics and lack of returning monsters, you’ll still have lots of fun here. As others have said, Pokémon can take some notes here, this game makes taking eggs and hatching them fun, almost addicting. The combat system is your typical turn-based combat but with a rock, paper scissor-esque system. I liked it but I can see why others prefer combat in games like Ni No Kuni or the other monster hunter games. In combat you can switch out your weapons and your “monsties” to gain an edge on your opponent or break objects the opposing enemy is holding. The exploration is also a little less exciting than World and very typical of other JRPG’s. Exploring caves, taking down the monster, then it runs away to a cave where you can go in and kill them for good or take their eggs whilst they sleep.Gathering ingredients makes a comeback as well. You can create potions, bring items to a smithy to make weapons and armour or bring Bottle Caps to a felyne to get special weapons, armour and upgrades that increase the amount of monsties you can hold at one time in your farm. I don’t recommend this game to everyone but it you enjoy Ni No Kuni mixed with Pokémon and Monster Hunter all rolled into one, you’ll get some good fun out of this!

_childDocuments_.review: I am someone who adores the Monster Hunter setting, but is downright terrible playing any of the mainline games, so Stories was always an interesting game to me. My friend brought it up again recently and showed it to me, so I took a proper try; a week or so later I played barely anything else, and finished its main story.It's a very charming and easy to get into RPG, with a more traditional party and turn-based combat system, except it adds the easy to grasp rock-paper-scissors mechanic to vary it up, and enough wiggle room for you to get used to it thoroughly. You can add a ton of Monsters to your roster, finetune their abilities and skills, and kit yourself out the same way as you always did; crafting your gear from monster materials. Side missions are present to give you things to do, but the general gameplay loop of going out, fighting monsters, and clearing out minidungeons is kept fresh for a long time due to all the variety.Storywise it is nothing out of the ordinary - a pleasant, simple, but endearing tale about companionship and growing as a person.You got arenas, you got multiplayer, you got the real hard-hitting hunts later on that the franchise's always kept around.It was a game well-worth getting, and I am still having a lot of fun with it. If you like Monster Hunter, Pokémon-like monster collecting games and the turn-based RPG gameplay that comes with it, you'll love this - I say this as someone who only really likes the first of those three, and is having a blast with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: With only 14 hours of gameplay, I can say that this game is worth the time and money I put into it. It's like the Pokemon and Final Fantasy game I've always wanted in one. I love the Monster Hunter series, and this is really enjoyable for how much this game provides with not many hours of gameplay as a typical MH game. This isn't a game where you can just roll your face into the keyboard or controller; you gotta know what you're doing. It has some easy moments, but when faced with tougher monsters, you can't rely on random button mashing. You have to know how to build up your team as each monster, even of the same kind, has their own abilities and effects. You can't just throw together a random team and punch your way through the game without dying a lot, oh no no no. You got to pick the right monsters to help you not only in battle, but in the environment as well, to get to places and things you can't usually get on your own. The game itself is a bit "kiddish" in the sense of having some rather silly moments, but it's really cute in the end. You can equip up to 3 different weapons to take with you so you don't feel stuck with just one.Pros:- Beautiful music and ambiance- Very anime-esque graphics.- Open world- Really cute and touching storyline- Battles aren't quick and you have the option to Run Away!- You get to create your own character the way you want!- Store content isn't mandatory, but you do get a free starter pack! - Not as difficult or frustrating as MHW, but still has its tough moments- Team building is a thing! - You don't have the useless and annoying Handler with you, always getting herself into trouble and danger, forcing you to always save her. - You can change your gear out in the wild!Cons:-  No pet Palico to join you; instead you get an annoying Felyne who won't shut TF up, and you just want to punt him into a Rathalos' mouth. - Your character doesn't talk :( - The battle cut scenes do tend to get annoying and repetitive, but there's a skip button for that!- The talking Felyne won't. Stop. Talking.- Some items are confusing. The fact you're given a grill and raw meat, but don't have the option to cook baffles me. - Crafting has return but is limited along the way.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very satisfied with this adorable roller coaster. A true delight for children, adults, and Monster Hunter fans.It started off not being the sort of turn based rpg I think I would get used to, but it quickly began to grow on me and I ended up getting obsess with it. I'll try to articulate why i've enjoyed this.First off, you start off as a young teen of your creation (Male or Female - For my playthrough I chose Female), and you are a Rider of your tropical tribal village called Mahana, on a small island. You're the grandchild of a legendary rider called Red, who has recently passed. His dragon Guardian Ratha makes residence there, and a mysterious girl has met in secret with him while being persued, and Ratha grants this girl an egg. However, things are not as they seem. A strange red light is driving all these dragons to somewhere unknown, and it's making all the monsters overly aggressive. And once you become a rider? It's your job to help explore these lights and stop whatever is the cause of it. It's only a simple summary as it's not an especially clever story, but it's still fun to go through. Let's get to the main meal of this then, shall we? No, it's not oven ready.Now combat works revolves around a Rock Paper Scissors style. You get 3 main attack types: Power, Speed, and Technical. While you can still attack however you like, you need to choose correctly in order to win a head-to-head clash with your opponent, to deal high damage and take less.Power beats Technical; Technical beats Speed; Speed beats PowerYour monster (referred to as a monstie), if not directly told to used certain skills, will attack at their own discretion. Each monster has their own specified attack type (For example, Speed), however they will still used different ones regardless of their main type. You can have 5 (later 6) accompany you at one time. Each has a different attack type, element, and weakness. You get to switch out a monster once per turn, should the monster you're fighting have an attack type yours has a disadvantage to. You can kind of see the similarities to an extent with Pokemon can't you?  You also have 3 weapon types. You have slashes, pierces, and crushes (basically hammers, bows, and swords) - All big monsters will have different parts you can attack seperately, and breaking them will give you more materials from said monster. These parts are all weak to a different weapon type, so you should be ready to swap out your weapons during combat to maximize damage on these parts, as breaking parts will have the additional benefit of weakening the monster's capabilities.Monsties will also have unique interactions with the big hunchos depending on their traits. You have your charge clashes by default (which involves mashing the space bar. Sorry pal...), but if it's flying monsters they can have an Air Showdown (alternate Q/E), and finally if they both have a elemental breath attack, those will clash (circle strafe your arrow keys, son!).You also have several other factors here. You have a standard health system, but you also have hearts. This is jointly shared between you and your monsite: If one of you reaches 0 HP, a heart is consumed and they are restored to full. You essentially have 3 lives in any given combat, and you will be sent back to the closest town should you, or your ally, lose all 3 hearts in a fight. Next is your Kinship gauge. This is a circle that will fill up overtime during battle, and is how you and your monstie will use skills. You, like hearts, will jointly share this pool, and not both of you will be able to use a skill on occasion due to not have enough points for the task. And speaking of joining, it also applies to attacking: When an ally, or you, is the target of a head to head, and one of your monsites (or your companion's) also targets that monster with the same attack type it's weak to, you will conduct a duel attack which will deal much more damage to the target than normal. You also have unique Kinship Skills to use which are mega flashy attacks (and the double attack mentioned earlier will also apply to these as well, though it will only be unique with specific combinations). Outside of combat you've got open areas to roam (areas can be inaccessible until you have certain monsties in your party, who have unique traversal traits,, such as climbing vines), and in these you'll have monsters, dens, and materials and items scattered everywhere. Next, you have settlements that act as hubs where you can pick up quests from the questboard and npcs, buy/sell items and upgrade and forge armour and weapons. You also get a house in each of these to save and customize the look of yourself and the outfits you and your companions wear. Simple, and gets the job done. Maybe there's something hiding there? I dunno, but you also have a shady felyne (the bipedal cat creatures in the series) selling you equipment in exchange for bottle caps. Har har har, I know. Please leave your Fallout jokes at my desk.Now, let's finish with a brief summarry Monster Dens. Dens are where you'll find monster eggs waiting for you (and mostly, other monsters to fight as well, usually with a sleeping one in the nest area). Though, I will mention that this also means touching on the one MAJOR criticism with the game: You WILL see den layouts repeat (A LOT) due to the nature of the game. I won't hold this too much against the game as they are hand-crafted and no procedural, but you will also see this in the actual areas. Like, the dens I get, but unique zones? The only difference in these areas are the monsters you find there. Limitations for the game don't really matter when it can be labelled lazy that you recycle your Rare Monster Den maps to use for later game areas. It won't be as egregious as i'm making it out, but I definitely remember being at places with the same look as Dens.-----But this is mostly a nitpick and I do have others (including the lack of unique combos for Duel Kinship Skils) that mean nothing in the grand scheme of things. This is an adorable, engaging, Pokemon-like Roleplaying Game that's kept my interest far longer than I ever expected. Well worth the money and then some, and will be a fun time killer as an adult or child. ^.^

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic turn based monster battler! Might be best in the genre-interesting and engaging battle system (you'd never get tired of it since you can speed battles up to times 3 and skip battles you are engaged in if you are higher level than the enemies)-NO GRIND (other than skipping battles, exp share is on and there's a system that allows you to passively level a group of monsters up; you can also find monster with better stats easier as the game will indicate it to you)-extremely malleable monsters (can basically give a Ratata Charizard moves)-cool monsters, armor and weapons (as expected from Monster Hunter)-cool landscapes (open areas you can fly in on your favorite monster)-aesthetically pleasing graphics (great color pallette at all times, very dynamic animations)-stand-alone game (despite its title, you do not need to play the first game to enjoy this one)RAMBLE BELOWTL;DR 80% perfect Pokemon gameNitpicks I have with the game:-cut features from the original (mini games, even more customization with the monsters via changing their colors up to 6 variantions, monster saddles changing colors according to bingos, character specific side quests that gives them more depth, easier to use side quest tracker)-no true relation to the first game (story doesn't follow up the previous; with all the returning characters and a similar story it's basically a reboot, would of worked better that way) -characters are nolonger endearing nor memorable (for example the Pikachu of the series went from dorky and lovable in the original to simply obnoxious)-not every large monster is ridable (cannot hip check my enemies :c)-terrible story in a game with "Stories" in the title (the story is stereotypical and boring; where the first at least kept you hooked with its characters, this game just drags on with you feeling inferior as no one would shut up about someone better than you)-isn't entirely polished (UI at the stables, the PC of this game, has very basic designs and functions compared to the first game, missing ability to skip pages with 1 click for example, nor does your cursor and button prompts have customized overlay unlike other PC Monster Hunter games, where the first game has monster special attack animations match the area you are in this game doesn't, some cut scenes are slideshows)Wishful thinking for probably unrealistic things that can be added in the next entry:-selection of starters (Ratha has run his course being the default for these 2 titles; wished he would turn into a Silver Rathalos in the end of the first game)-return of the color changing system (more personalized monsters)-monsters are born according to their ecology  (e.g. Great Jaggi would be born as a Jaggi or at least without scars)-add a "evolution system" (putting subspecies and deviants in the same tree; e.g. Dreadqueen Rathian needs a regular Rathian use the default poison move a number of times; Great Jaggi needs to defeat a number of Jaggis to "grow up"; giving a Yian Kut-Ku the Rathian "poison tail gene" yields a Yian Garuga)-a better story (please either make it completely seperated to everything else to attract more new comers or make it coherently related to the previous, at least add a Red in Pokemon Gold thing; maybe even have multiple endings so players actually have a choice in the story)-full multiplayer  (can play the story in multiplayer)-monster interaction minigames (e.g. Pokemon Amie; the "Pet" ability is a nice touch already though)-monster dress up (very small things like decorating the saddle, give the monsters a small head dress like a bow, could just be within a minigame)-story boss monster loot (equipment made from them)-ridable version of previous final bosses (just something cool to have)In any case still highly recommend anyone who likes turn based RPG and Pokemon games!!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Combat becomes quite luck based removing the usefulness of tactics. Monsters health pools get way too big, making them damage sponges. Combat is a big part of the game so this is incredibly tedious.The game gets very repetitive and at a certain point the monster fights start to become "unfair" in a sense that you play the fight correctly by understanding what the monsters do, but they are given multiple attacks in a single turn and have completely hidden actions so it's really difficult for you to counter anything. So you playing correctly doesn't mean anything, when this starts happening. This happened even when I spent time looking for monsters with good genes, upgrading my weapons and armor + using everything in my power to avoid losing any head to heads (a mechanic in the game, which massively lowers enemy damage to you, if you win it) and using double attacks as much as possible which completely cancel enemy attacks. So at this point the fights are mostly just hoping the monster does something stupid and doesn't actually target you. The fights start becoming needlessly long too and at the same time tedious. The monsters become incredible damage sponges and the fights don't feel rewarding anymore, especially because for some reason the devs decided that it's a good idea to hide an unknown monsters health bar the first time you fight them (Most fights in the story). These things together made me stop playing the game, even when the story interested me.On the other hand if things like this are not a problem to you, by all means get the game. It's a fun monster collector in it's base and the story at least kept me interested.Additional note:This dumb cat that keeps talking is annoying enough that I had to get mods to even try to remove him. Unbearable looking character with terrible and annoying dialogue + voice. Not only that but the game gets paused every 4 seconds because of some unnecessary thing he has to say. _childDocuments_.review: This is, by no means, a  game, but a game that feels it falls short. This mainly has to do with the expectations I had when getting this game and  the price tag. Due to how it disappointed me and its pricetag, I would not recommend the game. It's a game, one of the games of all time. Creature collector with lots of fun creatures to collect, but lacking gameplay in every other way, while also lacking overall polish. If you get it, get it on sale because boy does the base 60 USD price feel bad for the amount you get. Not a great alternative to Pokemon (less interesting combat, less discovery, exploration, etc...) nor a great way to expand on Monster Hunter in my experience (lack of monster behaviors, little information and interaction with monsters). Would not recommend to most. I love Pokemon. Played every mainline game until Sword and Shield. I love being able to discover all these creatures, try and use them in my team, experiment with their movesets and abilities, and learn about their backgrounds and behaviors. The fun of discovery, experimentation, and learning are what makes Pokemon fun for me. The core turn-based combat of Pokemon, while OK, may be considered to be a bit basic and dated among turn-based combat games these days, but that never bothered me, so I did not come in with huge expectations for a sparkling new turn-based combat experience. So, given my experiences with Pokemon, how did this game fare for me? It was okay.There are a lot of monsters, plenty of familiar faces from the earliest games to the newest ones, from monsters that have been in almost every game to ones only present in a single game or two. The monsters come in all sorts of different flavors, from your various wyverns (fanged, beast, bird, etc...) to crabs and spiders, to beasts, and more. Monster Hunter has plenty of monsters to pull from to fill its roster in this creature collector. I found the overall roster fantastic, even with the usual Monster Hunter set of variants (aka, "X monster but a different color and/or element"). What is not as fantastic is how this roster plays into the experimentation and learning portions of Pokemon I enjoy and came in looking for. Without going into too much detail for the game mechanics, there is the elemental types from the mainline games, and there is an added Rock-Paper-Scissors system for attack types and what monsters tend to use what of that RPS system. The elemental types and the RPS system feel like a step down from Pokemon's type system for strategic diversity. While there is some fun customization in the way monsters can inherent "genes" from another monster to create specific builds, it ultimately feels lacking to me when comparing it to what I've come to be used to in Pokemon. The amount of customization available via genes feels much shallower than the combination of movepools, abilities, natures, EVs, IVs, etc... that Pokemon has, for better or for worse. For me, it was for worse, but maybe for you that is not the case. On the other, non-combat side, there's learning about the Monsters. While there is a "Pokedex" of sorts that conveys some basic info about the Monsters, that's generally where all the information stops. Monsters do not have any unique behaviors in the overworld and you cannot interact with them outside combat except for riding on them. This leads to the monsters feeling very same-y outside of their visual design and combat performance. This, to me, is a major step down from both Pokemon -- which had different ways to interact with Pokemon outside combat, depending on the game -- and Monster Hunter itself -- especially from Monster Hunter: World, which had huge amounts of out-of-combat behaviors that made the monsters extremely expressive and interesting to observe even when not hunting. On the combat side, the game is not particularly interesting or revolutionary for turn-based combat. I did not come in looking for much new in a combat system, but the "meh" feeling combat combined with the shallow strategic depth, lacking customization options, and the totally missing interactivity with the monsters combines to make the combat feel particularly dull on repeat encounters. I want to emphasize , as the first fight with a given monster tends to be relatively fun, having to learn its moveset and figure out how to beat it best, but all of the above tends to leave repeat encounters feel lacking. Overall, as a Pokemon alternative, based on what I was looking for, I would say, despite the large roster to collect, this creature collector failed to give me what I was looking for as an alternative to Pokemon. The creature collecting is fun, however.This game is a turn-based creature collector, a big difference from the mainline games. So when I am comparing this game to the mainline games, the main thing I am interested in is how it handles the Monsters themselves, as well as other small elements. In the earlier section, I mentioned the game as lacking in the behavioral diversity of the monsters. In Monster Hunter: World in particular, I had so much fun just donning the Ghillie Mantle and just... following monsters to see what they are up to. There are so many fun little things the monsters do that you just wouldn't see when hunting them, which is precisely what drew me to this game. No monster has any unique behaviors in this game, just the same cut-and-paste walk, run, look around, turn, and sometimes flying animations out of combat. In combat, you will see very familiar attacks from the mainline games. Legiana is my favorite monster, and so imagine my disappointment when the only things I could do with it were fighting it, fighting with it, and riding it, and otherwise it was just the same generic overworld monster as any other, just with a Legiana appearance. While it is cool to ride the monsters (unlike mounting or wyvern riding in the main games), it is not enough given the lack of... everything else. It's not like this game is a horribly glitchy mess that lacks finish, but, it feels disappointing.The story and characters are generally bland and generic. Not horrible, and the voice acting is reasonable, but entirely skippable and forgettable. Do NOT come to this game looking for a rich story or interesting characters, although that would probably be fine if coming from mainline Pokemon and/or Monster Hunter games. Graphics are good enough, but feels like a downgrade coming from Monster Hunter, especially in its environmental design. Dungeon layouts get samey and boring very quickly. Port quality is questionable, with crashes, frame drops, slowdowns, etc.... I have a beefy computer, so it is likely not an issue of minimum specs.In the binary recommend/don't recommend Steam system, I would not recommend the game. This game has that usual triple-A pricing of 60 USD, but for that price, you get a shallow experience that lacks polish. It's not an awful game, I put in about 100 hours, and I'll probably continue to play it to keep collecting Monsters, genes, etc... I just find it difficult to say, "Yeah, this is a generally worthwhile experience", and especially not with such a large upfront price. If you are fine with an OK creature collector with a large roster, then this isn't bad, especially if all you want is to have the monsters and not hunt them. But, if you are looking for fun customization options for your creatures, great strategic depth, cool ways to interact with your creatures, fights that are fun on repeat encounters, then I would recommend skipping this game. If you are to get this game, highly recommend only getting it on a steep sale, like 50% or more.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a cat in this game called Navirou...dude is a whole trip. Everything he does is hilarious. All his scenes make me laugh, heck I smile just seeing his face on-screen lmao. He has some of the funniest run scenes ever, rivaling run scenes of legends such as Tom Cruise and Steven Seagal. The game itself is alright, but he makes everything better by a long shot. He's one of the main reasons I kept booting this game back up, cuz it has its share of problems, but my boy Navirou made it bearable. I'll get into some of the issues below:- There's a game breaking bug regarding multiplayer, you'll see several people explaining what it is in other reviews- The game randomly bugs out of full screen mode into windowed mode & becomes choppy & you need to reboot the game to fix it. It's extremely annoying and shocking knowing Capcom's record for solid PC ports.- The battle system was not well thought out. The flow of battle is ridiculously slow, and the slightest attacks have the biggest, coolest animations. It's amazing at first but gets very old, very quickly. They tried to help by letting you speed up battles by X3 speed but honestly, that doesn't help. You can beat far weaker enemies by pressing a single button to end the fight quickly, but in the grand scheme of things it doesn't help either. Battles become a BORING slog through the mud after some time, and the game is long. If they could have figured out a way to make battles flow better it'd be perfect. The way it is now, you can tell they knew how bad it was with all these patchwork features like speed ups that come after the fact.In the end I wouldn't pay full price for this game. At $19.99 it's pretty solid if you like JRPGS, Monster Breeding, or Monster Hunter. The story is ok, the characters are ok, the comedy is actually pretty good, the overall tone of the game is a bit too juvenile for my taste but that was too be expected just by the looks of the game, and the battles are a love/hate affair. I didn't bother with the post game content because honestly after 75 hours with this battle system, I really had all I could take. A grindy post game is the last thing I want out of this. It's not a bad game, but it could have been a lot better. Gonna miss Navirou though lol.

_childDocuments_.review: I kind of forgot that JRPGs can be fun. Maybe I've been playing the wrong stuff most of the time for a long, long time, but most JRPGs don't my attention anymore. Octopath Traveler is an exception; its in-depth battle mechanics held my attention for double-digits of hours - that's more than I can say for most games in this genre that I've played in recent years.But this game helped me remember that turn-based battles don't have to be stale. The rock-paper-scissors mechanics work extremely well. Picking the right monster to fight the monster(s) in the current encounter didn't get old. I know, I know, Pokémon incorporates a lot of RPS mechanics, but this doesn't ask me to remember a slew of sometimes arbitrary strengths and weaknesses. There are three attack types and their opposites are fairly obvious. (Please keep in mind that I haven't gotten to the point that elemental strengths/weaknesses have become very important.)The story so far is… fine. That's it; it's fine.I don't know if I'll return to this game any time soon, but I'm sure I will at some point. Please know that that is not a statement the game’s quality (see above), it's really a statement about adulthood etc., etc.; I get the feeling that this will be a pretty long game and I don't have the time or attention span to play a long JRPG at the moment. Still, if you do have such an attention span and free time, give this a try. You probably won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - Good game.I'm a fan of Monster Hunter franchise, and this is a love-letter from Capcom to the likes of me. Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a great turn based strategy game with a heartwarming yet cruel story, great gameplay that does not feel far from home and many improvements over the previous game especially a multiplayer mode.  You start the game as the grandkid of a legendary rider, who aims to follow the path of your grandfather. The gameplay mechanics are beautifully explained by the tutorial missions and make some things clear so you don't feel like you are mission out on anything. Your companions -Navirou and Ena- can get pretty annnoying or bothersome at times but they're helpful. Monsters are well designed (especially the final boss) and are kept faithful to the mainline Monster Hunter games. This game also includes Elder Dragon monsties as well as Deviant monsties, which were not present in the previous game and considering they're mostly fan favourite monsters, this is an amazing feature. Soundtrack is beautiful and surgically induces you with emotions you were meant to feel during the key moments of the story. It's an overall amazing experience with very generous post-game content, making you want to play for the hours to come.This does not mean it is perfect though. There are some important downsides. Although the music is great, only ambience can be heard whilst exploring the world or a den, this does make exploring feel tedious and boring. The story is also not very adult-like either despite taking some bog steps from the first game, it ultimately falls short of maturity except for some key instances which I cannot spoil for anyone. Yet, in my opinion, the game is amazing and polished enough.Monster Hunter Stories 2 was an amazing experience for me and I would recommend it to anyone that is or willing to be into Monster Hunter. This was the first game I pre-ordered and I was not disappointed in the slightest.

_childDocuments_.review: Going in as an entirely new player to this game and the world setting, I was pleasantly surprised at just how enjoyable this game is. It has a very ‘pokemon-esk’ feel to it with just the right amount of story, dialogue and dreadful cat related puns (pawdaceous - really?) that kept me entertained.I liked the play style even though I’m not a fan of turn based games myself and soon forgot I was playing a turn-based game thanks to the animations and the engaging nature of the fight scenes themselves.If you have a penchant for collecting, improving and ‘gene splicing’ your monsties this game has this aplenty and is also a significant part of the game play itself.My only minor complaints are:•	I thought the story was too short for the game (max level in this game is 99, I finished the story around the level 45 mark).•	Some of the interface elements are very clunky to use. Having to escape out of the game every time to use the quest tracker, map or inventory / equipment menus was tedious and could easily be replaced by just having clickable icons in the game itself.•	The excellent layered armour feature (which allows the fashionistas amongst you to wear other sets as a skin over the set you are using) only extends to armour and not weapons.I don’t think the deluxe version provides any significant value for money over the regular version and if you want to try the game before buying go for the demo first (you will be able to import game play from that into the full game if you buy it later).Overall a very good game and recommended accordingly

Nonetheless I gave it chance and it blew my mind, the game was pretty good. I had more fun with that game than I had with any other game of that same style. So I completed it and some time later Monster Hunter Stories 2 was announced. It greatly surprised me that the developers decided to make another game, because I knew that the first one wasn't exactly the greatest hit in terms of sales, although it had a solid fan base. Now that I had the opportunity to play this game I appreciate the developers even more, they improved upon the first game in many ways and added many quality of life features. _childDocuments_.review: I have such a hard time putting this game down to go do literally anything else and am grinding so much I am OP going into new regions just because I enjoy the grind, I am LOVING this game and all of it's mechanics. It seems like every "Pokemon-like" game I have played in recent history makes Pokemon look bad, this game is no exception, and in fact improves upon the Rock-Paper-Scissors combat in simple yet very cool ways. One nice addition is being able to swap a monster out during battle and STILL being allowed to make a combat move. This game also has a lot of quality of life that just makes it enjoyable to play and easy to farm monsters, including rare ones. The Bingo system for outfitting monster abilities is fun and adds another layer of depth that lets you build them for custom roles in your party between making them specialioze or turning them into a jack of all trades, also for PVE vs PVP setups, so there is reasons to have more than one for party purposes beyond using duplicates for Gene properties. The story is pretty standard fare for an RPG but it's been enjoyable and makes me excited for each new region I get to explore. Looking forward to MUCH more! Haven't encountered many bugs, one time I was swapping between monsters and the stats from one overlayed to another, but backing out and then back into the menu fixed that, and there are some weird textures in the 3rd chapter town logs.This game is highly accessible to newbies and vets alike and offers a lot of meat to bite into, with a hefty helping of veggies should you choose to partake and extend your play time. I'm on Chapter 3 of however many there are and over 30 hours in as of this review and and hungry for more!If you like RPGs/Pokemon/Turnbased combat with depth/General MH fan I can't recommend this enough. _childDocuments_.review: Already dropped about 220 or so hours on my Switch version, getting all the best Monsters and maxing out their bingo-sheets fully optimized and 2-stared on every gene. Now I'm finally wrapping up the PC version  and caught up now. I'm basing my review content-wise on what I've already done on the Switch version (pretty much everything bar a few irrelevant subquests) and the performance is based on what I've seen so far with my own eyes starting at launch day (made it to the second Anjanath sighting) and then today (Made it to the end of Rutoh Village so far). Content:The game is, really good! Simple and easy at first but eventually the difficulty doesn't come from playing RPS, but rather kinship management, gene placement (so you can actually WIN those HtHs often and deal damage), and the timing for healing (not healing at the right time if you need another heart or to top off CAN get you wiped). The story I really couldn't personally care for. It's not bad by any measure (the plot "twist" kinda sucked and was unpredictable for bad reasons but, it's not TERRIBLE at least), I'm just saying I didn't care for it since its not why I bought this game. For fans of the first game, the story is probably amazing to you since it's filled with characters from the previous title and a few cheeky references. As much as I can appreciate the love and care done, it's not why I bought this time. For someone taking their time and grinding monsters out, and getting average and acceptable genes for the sake of progress, I finished the main story in about 60 hours (10+ hours were from the demo alone). I bought this game knowing the majority of my time playing this game would be in the post-game and its content. I was correct. I love the gameplay loop, I love the Super Rare tickets I can do with friends, I like the trials MUCH MORE than the Tower from the first game, and the overall gene editing as well. Even if I couldn't appreciate the QoL improvements made in this game coming out of the first game (causing me to NEVER look back), I'd still wind up in love this with game enough to play through it (and pay for it) two separate times. I do miss being able to easily change monster elements, but I don't mind it as much as I was expecting. The monster selection in this game is pretty neat, and the future roadmap is 100% going to keep me coming back monthly to catch up and try out all the new stuff (although I'm expecting one of the things to kinda suck I'm ngl). It's nothing 900IQ or anything but, it's not dumb either. It's just nice casual fun, which I think I've needed after playing a ton of minmaxy and hardcore games I've been diving into for thousands of hours the past few years. The attention to detail and the love put into this game is NOT unnoticed (example: using the Ice Armor move on Velkhana gives it it's ice armor form from Iceborne when it enrages). It's not perfect, and it doesn't actually have to be. It's pretty damn close though.Performance:This game was raided with negative reviews on the launch day this game had. I have zero exaggeration when I say this: none of it was even correct lmao. Like cumon, if you're gonna exaggerate stuff to try and make this game look bad, at least base it in truth to make it LOOK honest. People were claiming they were using top of the line specs and they were encountering stuttering, frame dips, the works. I'm running this game on a Rysen 3600 and a 1660 Super and I can play this game at MAX settings and at 144fps smoothly with zero problems, even when a lot is happening on the screen at once. There's ZERO way people were having this many issues with the game. Really now? Keyboard controls were maybe KINDA awkward? Man, using KBM on a Monster Hunter game? That sounds like a goooood idea. This is like lambasting a Souls game in its entirety for not feeling as good on KBM as it does on controller. And to top it off, it was people complaining about the simple character creation when it came to these controls. You can run this game on a potato, and as long as you know where you W, A, S, and D keys are on your keyboard you can figure out how to play this game. This thing is optimized insanely well, and the controls.... well if you can't afford a controller then you better get used to using right click to rotate that camera, bc it really ain't THAT bad. TLDR: Anyone complaining about performance with GOOD hardware 100% has issues with their PC that are not related to the game, and they should get that stuff checked out ASAP because this game is optimized insanely well. Please check your parts if you claim your 2070 Super cant hit 60 fps because something is VERY wrong and it is NOT on the game's end. TL;DR: Bulldrome rarely drops its own parts in 144fps, good game. Worth at full price, which means on sale it's even more worth getting.
