_childDocuments_.review: This is a perfectly fine alternative to Pokemon. The combat's unique levels of unpredictability make it pretty engaging, and the excellent animation makes it feel very satisfying. The monster progression system is a bit strange but it works pretty well, and gives you an interesting way of customizing your monsters. The art style is very nice. The Monster Hunter monsters look great here, with a much more cutesy look than in the mainline games, but still a bit weirdly realistic compared to the very chibi-styled human characters. I didn't really check out the multiplayer. It seems dead?The story is a lot more intricate than I'd expect from a Monster Hunter game, but it is still very flawed. As someone who did not play the first game, I was kinda hoping that the story would be standalone like the mainline games, but that was really not the case here. You meet many returning characters from the first Monster Hunter Stories, with many references to those events as well. This isn't really a big deal, but it did feel like I missed out on a lot of callbacks and jokes because I didn't play the first game.My biggest problem with the story is the player character's grandfather, Red. He is a legendary hero who died many years before the events of the game. For some reason, the game's story focuses on him to the point of obsession. Many of the characters you meet throughout the game were either good friends with Red or have heard about him, and so he is mentioned in nearly every cutscene of the game, even going as far as to show flashbacks of him when he was younger. This makes the player character seem so insignificant and irrelevant to the plot of the game, that every thing they accomplish is all thanks to how cool Red was. It's just not very inspiring.Still though, the final boss was cool as hell, and the ending of the game was pretty satisfying. I'm sure there's a ton of content to be had in the postgame, but I stopped after the credits. If you're ever in the mood for a Pokemon-like monster-collecting RPG, totally check this out! Or maybe the first game if you can? I don't know!

_childDocuments_.review: MHS2 is a fantastic experience for those seeking a story-driven Pokemon experience in the world of Monster Hunter. Instead of adding an absurd amount of monster designs and attack moves like the Pokemon series, the game points towards refining what it already does by adding additional fun mechanics and quality-of-life features. Unlike Pokemon, you have a method of speeding up battles and combat. You also get rewarded each battle you play based on your performance and how well you do. You also fight alongside your own monsties and unlock special moves for working together. While MHS2 is certainly part of the monster-catching genre, it's not just another clone of Pokemon like other games of the same genre try to be. It stands on its own. For players who come from the world of Monster Hunter, you'll notice settle nods to the series through monster references and more.A lot of the current bad reviews of the game haven't given it much effort. I'm going to try to acknowledge each of the major things said to give you an idea about what's actually going on there and you can see if the game is for you.  - The controls are a little janky at first, but they're pretty easy to understand once you know what you're doing. I'll admit the original key layout is questionable, but it doesn't really affect you too much in a meaningful way because the game is a turn-based RPG. Fortunately, you can rebind every key in the game which remedies any issue you could ever have. - This is far from a bad console port. As stated above you can rebind every key in the game. A controller is not required and the game supports the mouse for camera viewing and clicking. Bad console ports don't offer either of these things. - This is a lie. While I'll admit you can't save while on the go and messing around, there's definitely a manual save found in your "home" which is located in every town. - I'm running a normal 1070 with a i5 6600k and the game works flawlessly for me. I maxed out my graphics too. If you're having issues with something better than this, you should check your end first before mindlessly blaming the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played Monster Hunter, as slow action combat without any real exploration isn't really my thing. Nor are enemy sponges, which Hunting games seem to specialize on. Stories is quite a different game, for starters it's turn-based and you actually have a fairly normal jrpg in your hands. And as far as I played so far, it could be one of the best of recent times.Good music, some really well done cutscenes, and a reasonable enough character creation for you to have fun with designing who you want to go into this world with. On top of that, every armor and weapon is visually seen, and can be quite varied. So in that department, this game is well done. It's also running quite well, so even the biggest toaster can probably play this at 1080p/30fps. That said, visuals and music wouldn't cover bad gameplay. Luckily it's not bad:Generally speaking, the game's battles combine paying attention to your enemies with RNG elements to spice things up. Every enemy has very specific types of attacks they do, but who they aim at is random, just like all actions of party members that are not yourself are random-ish. Your job is to know what type of attacks an enemy does when, and choose your attack types (power, speed or technical) accordingly, as well as your monster. Allied monsters prefer a type of attack, though it's not guaranteed. This generally means, you pay attention to what you fight, and how you fight. That said, this only comes into play, when there's a clash of an ally and an enemy. (as in they attack each other) The winner gets a huge advantage through this, but if there's no confrontation, it doesn't matter what type you use. Buffs, heals and the likes never lead to a confrontation. Typical weaknesses to elements also exist, and those work as you'd think. There's slash, blunt and pierce, as well as several elements like fire or water. Ailments also exist.There's more to the battle system, but I think I wrote enough to make clear: You should pay some attention to things. That said, the game isn't particularly difficult so far, as levels give fairly huge bonuses early on, so bad play can be covered by doing the side-quest and upgrading equipment, as well as actively fighting. At least as far as I've played. That said, bad play will tank your battle rewards, so even though the game is on the easier side, you still are encouraged to play well and use the mechanics given to you. Even if dying is probably not something you will do for quite a bit in this game, you probably don't want to get bad battle ranks, which are actually surprisingly well done given the mechanics of the battles. Often battle ratings are more artificial than anything else, here they feel very accurate.As a final note I'd like to mention the areas. Jrpgs started to have more and more uninteresting areas without much to find around. MHS2  seems to be slightly different, and there's a little more to the world. A good example is that environmental skills exist, that you get as you progress and get different monsters, to reach formerly unreachable points and treasures. I'm very happy about the designers actually caring a little about the world design. I will update again later on how it keeps up.edit: It doesn't. On the surface it's good, but the inner workings aren't. I still had my fun for some hours, and I wouldn't call it a good game, but also not a bad game. The more casual your approach it, the better the game probably performs. For how much mechanics there are, it's really demotivating to realize how little all of it matters. Different weapons? Whatever, you gotta dual attack anyway. Hundreds of different genes? Whatever, only bingos matter. Random stat bonuses for new born monsters? Flat, and not base stats, so they don't matter. A game that truly wasted its immense potential like few other games manage to do.edit august 5th.: Capcom still hasn't fixed the multiplayer bug with corrupted character data because a (usually) non preset skin color being chosen. This is not acceptable, as such I can no longer recommend this game. All things considered, the product has too many issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a great sequel and a great game on it's own. Everybody compares the gameplay to Pokemon, and that's probably the best comparison i can think of. So, the game has you playing as a "Rider," and as a Rider, you form bonds with monsters as opposed to slaying them. Near the beginning, you are given a Rathalos egg, and this Rathalos is known as Razewing Ratha; the Wings of Ruin. Ratha is a permanent party member for the entire story and then you can switch him out of your party in post game. So the combat is not too complex, and not too simple, the main battle mechanic is sort of a "rock, paper, scissors" game; you have Power Attacks which are colored red, Technical Attacks which are colored green, and Speed Attacks which are colored blue. Now to get the advantage, Red Power Attacks beat Green Technical Attacks, Green Technical Attacks beat Blue Speed Attacks, and Blue Speed Attacks beat Red Power Attacks. Now, when attacking monsters, most monsters have different body parts that you can target, and each body part may resist the 3 different types of weapons, Slash, Pierce, and Blunt. at the end of the day, Monster Hunter Stories 2; Wings of Ruin is a great game for fans who already have knowledge of the Monster Hunter universe, and great to help players who don't know Monster Hunter get some knowledge about the universe.

And even those missions are practically limited till you complete the story. Which by that point you've already invested practically 30hrs into the game if you played through without rushing. So be aware that you're in for a RNG grind.The game is brand new, and there's going to be plenty of updates to the game to make it even more inviting. _childDocuments_.review: Probably the most engaging turn based combat loop I've ever seen. Most turn based rpgs like these usually involve buff/debuffing then using the best possible move at your disposal. In this game it doesn't matter if you use your best move if you use at at the wrong moment, meanwhile even your simplest moves can benefit from being used at just the right time. The game rewards you for reading the enemy monster's moves and using the correct counter action alongside your monster buddies. Once you get into the flow of "okay this move is coming, nailed it. Now switch this and switch that, nailed it" you'll feel like you have full control of the fight and come out with just a few scratches.I come from a general distaste of dice roll-ish type of turn base games where maybe you just get an unlucky move that screws you over and you resort to turtling up or brute forcing until you beat whatever it is you're fighting. but In stories, if I happen to take a bad hit, it's usually because I forget what move a monster is about to make or perhaps I just spaced out and used the wrong attack. More often than not, as long as you learn the monsters you fight while understanding the buildup and finales of your own weapons and skills, you're golden~Almost everything has a counter or proper response, learn them and you'll be (almost) untouchable.

_childDocuments_.review: A must play game for fans of Monster Hunter. As a JRPG it stands on its own merits for gameplay and mechanics, and combined with the setting and faithful recreation of monster attacks and unique attributes, it makes for very enjoyable and nostalgic experience. Stories 2 has a mix of light-hearted simplicity and just-enough complexity to make it addicting and make you want to finish it. The main campaign is 30-50 hours long, with a wide range of time you can spend stopping to smell the roses and mess around with the monster breeding system. The actual structured content for post-game is about 10-20 hours long once you have assembled a team capable of taking it on. I won't spoil what the post-game consists of, but I will say that it an interesting and welcome, and thematically consistent PvE challange that is not tacked on as an afterthought. There are potentially hundreds of hours of time you can spend in post-game creating and editing monster genes, and this is a casual gameplay type of activity that is relaxing and simple and goal oriented. The multiplayer has problems right now, but the developers are working on it. I can't comment on that section because I didn't want to risk my save being corrupted.In terms of content, there is good value for your $60 here, though much of it is a bit 'samey' after you figure out the gameplay. It's no MMO, but it's a very strong entry in the single player monster breeding genre, even without taking into account the franchise. Overall 8/10.All the DLC is cosmetic garbage you will never even notice. I don't understand why it exists or what capcom is thinking. I cannot imagine that anybody cares about their stupid mascot navirou character enough to spend money on dressing him up. I will never buy DLC of this type.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. _childDocuments_.review: Capcom’s answer to Pokémon, Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a Turn-Based RPG which allows players to tame and develop many of the most iconic monsters found throughout the franchise. Beneath a candy coated façade is a fleshed out game that far exceeds the sum of its parts, but unlike many games of the genre it takes its time before introducing the full experience.The core gameplay loop tasks players with hunting down Monster Dens to acquire Eggs. Each Den provides a small handful of chances to acquire an egg of varied quality related to the Den of origin; the rarer the egg, the better the “Genes” for a specific monster and type. After a certain point in the story, roughly about level 18, players will be able to sacrifice monsters to transfer their “Genes” to another.In layman’s terms; when hatched, monsters generate a random assortment of traits, abilities, and empty slots. Some of which are level locked. Each is related to the species and type, some of which are even unique. Players can then transfer a single one of these so-called “Genes” to a monster of their choice as many times as they like, therefore gradually creating a fully customized monster to fight with.The combat is the traditional turn-based fair with a Rock, Paper, Scissors twist that is deceptively simple on the surface. However, there is little in the way of randomness. Enemies have a pre-scripted set of potential attack types they’ll favor, which means that they can be easily read and memorized. Later in the game, familiarizing yourself with these patterns is essential to victory.Along the way you can gear up your hunter, but weapons are less about play style in this game and more about exploiting a target’s weaknesses. There are three flavors of weapon: Slashing, Blunt, and Piercing. All of which can be switched out every turn without penalty, which allows the player to adjust for every situation on the fly.Monsters can also be switched out mid combat, and in fact that is the primary flow of the combat system overall. The game rewards the player for having a wide variety of weapons and monsters at their disposal at any time. This can make combat feel very trivial and easy, especially in the early game. This sense of ease is further reinforced by the game providing the player with a number of extremely powerful companions early on.These companions do a high amount of damage and even heal the player and their monster, which may give players the feeling that the game is on autopilot. However, as the game progresses further into the story, the aid provided by the AI companions has far less impact on the outcome of the battle. The difficulty spike is there, and it may come as a surprise for many players who haven’t been properly preparing for it. But that spike rears its head around level 20 or so.Multiplayer features are not unlocked until a certain point in the story; once unlocked, players can team up and take on side quests via the quest board. Since the game provides an Open World that gradually gets bigger the further a player progresses, there is plenty to explore and interact with; not to mention a great many quest boards. Although each region is essentially the same in the overall progression: unlock the region; do a few story quests to unlock Monster Dens; hunt and tame monsters unique to that region; complete the story section and move on. Rinse and repeat.There is plenty to do overall, and like its predecessor the game offers a robust post-game experience once the Story has reached a conclusion. From that point on monsters become a lot tougher, armor gets a variety of upgrades and new abilities, and more Genes become available. Any progression beyond the story's conclusion is often related to the game’s PVP Arena, where players strive to rear the most overpowered monster they can and try to annihilate the competition as swiftly as possible.Do not be fooled, this game has a surprising amount of staying power. After all, it is a Monster Hunter title. So there are a great number of personal challenges you can achieve in this game, especially during the expansive post-game. But that being said, there is no doubt the game’s longevity will vary wildly based on how many people a player has to engage with. At launch there is already a robust community of dedicated fans that congregate on Discord; offering up advice, team mates, and even periodic tournaments for PVP.Yet there is either no, or very little in the way of a solid in-game infrastructure that makes finding friends easy. Worse, there doesn’t appear to be any Crossplay, further fragmenting an already niche community.The game is the polar opposite of grim and gritty: the story is cliché, the characters are cartoonish, the protagonist is silent, and there is a certain level of cuteness to a lot of the designs. Yet that is all just a candy shell concealing a truly deep and engaging RPG. The only real gripe I have is that that the early game is deceptive in its simplicity. There is a lot of hand holding and withholding of core mechanics. Much of which the Trial Version doesn’t even bother to brush on.The game opens up very late into the story and doesn’t truly reveal itself until after the credits have rolled; which is as much a blessing as it is a burden upon the player. Ultimately I recommend this game if you’re already a big fan of the Monster Hunter franchise, it rewards players with foreknowledge of the series by allowing them to translate their experience into this unique combat system. While there is a huge variety of Monsters within the roster, sadly not all are present. But many series favorites are there.This game is especially appealing to those who have a taste for Min-Maxing, allowing for hours upon hours of grinding for the perfect Monster, the perfect Genes, and the perfect team composition. As a fan of JRPGs and Monster Hunter, I find this to be a perfect combination of the two; which isn’t as easy as it sounds._____________

_childDocuments_.review: With deeper mechanics and vastly improved gameplay from the first game, MHS2: WoR delivers a satisfying sequel with only a few major gripes. Pros:- fully implemented co-op expeditions- rainbow gene allows for better min/maxing- full controller support with compatible button layouts- weapon loadouts and instant switching in combat- has become something closer to an RPG, more so than its predecessor- monsties added from MHW for fans of the more recent game- Deviants! (and more on their way!)- a MASSIVE roster allowing for a crazy amount of varying team compositions- a beautiful and more mature art and character design (Chibi didn't work as intended in MHS1, since 90% of the Monster Hunter consumer and fan base is made up of adults)Cons:- armour crafting is still as basic as the first game's (Seriously? We crafting jumpsuits/onesies? No one has ever said "I wish RPGs would remove individual armour pieces." NO RPG FAN/MONSTER HUNTER VETERAN HAS EVER WANTED THIS)- too many mainline weapons have been excluded (rip switch axe and charge blade)- the implementation of low-level monstie XP catch-ups ruins the point of this franchise being an RPG (levelling new monsties from scratch was perfectly fine in MHS1, so why change it?)- no customization/player freedom in armour crafting (can't mix sets for unique set bonuses - see first con)- co-op excludes playing the campaign with a friend (limited to expeditions and PvP battles)Regardless of its flaws, the pros vastly outweigh them and there is always room for improvement. Perhaps CAPCOM can release a hotfix or a patch that fixes the armour crafting and low-level monstie leveling issues later this week.For real though, pick this game up if you're a Monster Hunter vet, or even a newbie to the franchise, looking for a high quality Monster (Hunter) capture game!P.S. Unrelated to the game itself; I propose we all rise up against CAPCOM's greedy "DLC" offers. No one should ever have to purchase aesthetics and MMO services (character edit services) in a [somewhat] single-player game. This isn't an MMORPG, nor a mobile game. So why are CAPCOM selling outfits and MMO services to be used in a single-player RPG?? It's predatory and absolutely unacceptable! They should be rewards for end-game content or achievements! Enough is enough.

_childDocuments_.review: My first introduction to the Monster Hunter series was through World and its Iceborne DLC, and I really enjoyed both of those games when I bought it on a whim after a friend recommended it to me the day World released. I played that game for well over 100 hours and really enjoyed the combat and graphics, as well as laughing as all of my friends who endlessly got killed by the monster we were hunting. But, Monster Hunter Stories 2 is not World, in the sense that its combat, story and multiplayer are different. Monster Hunter Stories 2 is the definition of an RPG. You get to customize your own character and team and play in their story, and like most RPGs you do this through turn based combat. If you really liked the combat of the World or Rise games, then this combat format is going to be a big change. There is still a lot of planning and strategy in Stories' combat but it isn't thinking on the fly combat, more of a careful planning of what moves the enemy uses and what weapon breaks their parts fast enough to stop the big attacks. I, for one, really enjoyed the combat, it isn't stale and repetitive like some RPG become in the late game, because the combat against every monster is different and how you build your team to respond to them is different as well. So a solid 10/10 from me on the combat, even if it isn't real time combat like most of the previous titles.The story in Stories is also very good in my opinion, with it being a surprisingly emotional and serious story. I laughed at a lot of the jokes (mostly the ones making fun of Navirou, your pawnter) and cheered at the triumphant moments in the story, but also I almost cried at a very dramatic scene at the end. The game takes itself seriously, and so I took it seriously and gave it a chance to really shine in the story aspects. I will admit that some of the story is more childish and fairly obivious twists in some parts, but that doesn't mean that every part of the story is bad. If you like a story that clearly has love and care written all over it, give this game a shot. (Also a fair bit of characters in the last Stories show up, so if you played that and want the nostalgia, go ahead)

The combat is simple and easy to learn. In some ways, the combat is too simple because you're not given a lot of choices and it feels kind of like "rinse and repeat." However, I'm thinking this will change as I progress through the game more. There seems to be a good amount of content in the game so far. I've played for 5 hours and only made it through the opening area. I'm certain that I explored less than half of the available "monster dens" and solved only about 10 side quests (of which there are many). In retrospect, I should have done more but I was in a hurry to continue the story. Oh, and I should mention that this entire opening area is what you can play in the demo. Download the demo and try it for free. You've nothing to lose.

_childDocuments_.review: a fairly enjoyable game.it exists in the same overall category as Pokemon and digimon, and yet does not try and BE those games. it is not trying to be a knockoff.MHS2 has it's own identity, and while many might compare the game to others in the monster raising genre, this game is decidedly its own entity.so yes, i strongly recommend playing this.however, do not go into this expecting yet another pokemon clone, as many games in the genre of raising monsters and creatures to fight alongside you, tend to be.also do not expect a traditional Monster Hunter game. while the game is OBVIOUSLY part of the franchise, the turn based combat system alone sets this entry apart from the more traditional Action RPG roots of the core Monster hunter games.now, the downside is that this game was clearly aimed at a younger audience, made obvious by the more cartoony graphics, and the honestly cringe worthy dialogue in some places.despite this, the game remains enjoyable. and the blending of the "parts break" system from the core monster hunter games, combined with the more traditional turn based combat of most JRPG's make for a surprisingly simple yet complex system that takes a surprising amount of strategy and tactics in places.so overall? yes, i strongly reccomend the game.just do not bother with the DLC. most of it is cosmetics that have zero impact on the game, other then giving your characters some new clothes to wear. clothes that have zero impact on your stats.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Monster Hunter in JRPG form. It has a lot of quality of life improvements that take away some of the worst parts of grinding JRPGs. Combat can be sped up so battles don't take forever and if you are a high enough level you can just auto-win the fight and skip it completely. You can fast travel from anywhere at any time too. Enjoying the story and the art style is fun. Combat is a more technical rock, paper, scissors format and it's fun. Collecting different 'monties' is fun too. I'd recommend this game to JRPG fans and Monster Hunter fans who like JRPGs. The only downside is that it makes me want to play Monster Hunter World again.

_childDocuments_.review: Turn-based triangle combat in a style similar to Pokemon but in the Monster Hunter universe? Works really well, I'm thoroughly enjoying it.First impressions after clocking 8 hours in a row, it's a cute little game (though the "little" is pending, the world map is HUGE and I feel like there's plenty of story and grinding to be had). I won't comment too much on the story since it seems pretty simple, but the cast of characters covers it definitely.Mechanics are essentially a combination of turn-based RPGs, triangle-efficiency combat, Pokemon-style monstie gathering (through egg collection), and the Monster Hunter trademark "let's go fight this monster a bunch of times to get all its gear." It's been enjoyable enough to keep me playing for 8 hours right after I installed it, so I think that speaks for itself. Don't expect anything super deep or difficult though, it really is just "are you high level enough and is your gear good enough" in usual JRPG fashion. There is room for skill though, and I'm assuming even more late game, as you can set up teams of 5 monsties, equip elemental weapons and armor with their own unique skills, and play combat smart.Only two negatives that stick out to me are that 1. the controls can be a little wonky at times. The Switch port deal doesn't have anything to really do with it though, I'm just not a fan of how the camera handles outside of combat. Doesn't make overworld travel unenjoyable, but I spent more time fine-tuning camera controls than I really should have. Second, the progression seems awfully linear (at least early on). I expected this coming in especially with your MC's gear, but only 8 hours in and I'm noticing the first monsties I've gotten are simply being outclassed by the newer ones I can hatch. Not a major downside though, just a bit of a shame if there's an early monstie you're really fond of (looking at you, Yian Kut-Ku I named Cirno for about nine different reasons).Overall? 8.5/10, it's the kind of game you could give to a younger sibling and they'd get the hang of it pretty quickly too. A lot of the more advanced stuff (like genes) kicks in later in the game, but the story/characters, the art, and the core gameplay loop keep it enjoyable all the way throughout.

_childDocuments_.review: Wondering if the price tag for this game is worth it? Yes!I've been a Pokemon fan since the old days of red and blue, played a lot of competitive Pokemon in generation 5 only. From generation 6 onwards the series lost its charm (for me).This game gets compared a lot to Pokemon due to a few similarities. The similarities I've seen so far in my 7 hours are mostly coming from battles. The game has the same "rock, paper, scissors" combat system (don't deny it, Pokemon is mostly that) with less RNG factors and takes a more tactical approach to battles.One of the things I love about this game is fighting along side your monster. Your character doesn't feel weak and has a nice selection of weapons. Did I mention you can switch out monsters AND weapons during battle if you feel you don't have an advantage? Each weapons have their strengths and weaknesses, learn to use them wisely.As for the story of the game itself. Pretty cheesy so to say. But to be expected since it seems like this game was aimed towards a younger audience. You have a "guide" like the main franchise and he's a bit on the annoying side, but you learn to love him in the end.Other than that, the graphics are pretty. You don't need a big computer to run this smoothly (compared to the main franchise of course). There is a few slight issues with framedrops if you don't enable steam controller in the options, hopefully this will be fixed in a future update.The music is average at most. Battle music is catchy and changes from area to area. So you are not stuck listening to the same song from start to end. There is no music during hunts, like any Monster hunter game really. Voice acting is top notch. Though some characters don't really match their voices. And some of the lines would of needed a bit more work. I mean... come on duuuuude.Honestly, give the demo a try first. You'll get the feel of the game and from there on out you can judge if this is for you or not. For myself, it's the type of game I've been waiting for from Gamefreak. But knowing Gamefreak, they won't ever change their little "recipe".!

_childDocuments_.review: Having played 1 before, my first impression of 2 is pretty good so far. Same rock-paper-scissors mechanics for battles, with a few added features to make things more interesting. Flashier moves and a wider range of monsters to command is great, with an addition of an ai partner as well.I enjoy the graphics, I think its pretty refreshing, although it does feel kinda weird if you're used to playing the main mh series. It feels like rune factory without the farming. You collect eggs and raise them to fight alongside you, collect parts to upgrade, and slowly take your time exploring, gathering materials. Mouse controls feels really weird though, tried giving it a chance but it just doesn't work out, ended up just using the keyboard. Game is pretty chill, and still retains much of what monster hunter really is, which is predicting your enemies' moves and reacting to it. Overall, it's a great game. Recommended for anyone who enjoy monster collection games such as pokemon or digimon, or those who really like monster hunter in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a very enjoyable game. I've just beaten the main story and loved it all the way through. The game uses a simplistic rock paper scissors combat system but spices it up by adding elemental weaknesses and weapon damage types (I.E. slash, pierce, blunt). The most fun parts of MHS2 is going into den's and fighting monsters you know and love and stealing their eggs after murdering them, unfortunately going through the caves/dens/ever-dens can feel pretty long but luckily if you run into monsters you can just run away from them (not the nest monsters they can't be avoided that way). The story starts off very cliche and bland but picks up about halfway through and by the end I was genuinely invested in it pushing me to finish the game. My biggest grievance with the game would have to be how slow things can feel but even so it's not a big problem.If you like the Monster Hunter series and don't mind turn based RPG's I'd recommend this game to you. (It's basically a good pokemon game but for monster hunter, which I hate to compare it to that but it do be like that)

_childDocuments_.review: This is what Pokémon Sword & Shield should've been like LMFAOThe story is your generic Friendship Is Magic (tm) kinda shebang with kids being the hero. The game has a cartoon-y style where characters & monsters don't have as ginormous heads, compared to the first Stories. It's tolerable to me, although it personally gets a bit annoying to see: 1) kids fulfilling important roles & being the saviour of the day and 2) your monsters are always way smaller than the enemies/wild ones. Personally not my finest cup of tea, but it's tolerable because I just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this franchise.The first Stories isn't needed to play & understand the sequel. As far as it goes, there's only some characters that have appeared in the previous game (and the anime I think?), but there's not much reference-throwing to that. Combat & gameplay as a whole can get a bit same-y same-y once you know what you're doing. Luckily, there's some QoL features for that, such as speeding up the animation/battles & you can always run away if you ain't feeling it. The most exciting thing for me is to explore dens & collect monsters. However, if you're already familiar with the Monster Hunter franchise, it makes guessing which eggs you found a lot easier & less surprising at some point. There also seems to be a multiplayer bug according to other reviews, but I can't say much on that as my experience's been fine.The gist is, if you like Pokémon and always dreamed of collecting Monster Hunter beasts, THIS IS YOUR GAME FELLAS! _childDocuments_.review: 10/10 Best memories playing a game. As a rule of thumb, anything they set out to do, they nailed. But they didn't set out to do everything, or even close to it. I think they understood that too much can often have bad effects on the impact of a game like this, and only chose a specific scope they wanted to pursue, and they crushed it. LOVE this gameStory:- doesn't rely on the first game's stories, but refers to them a good deal and reuses a number of characters. Get the story easily with the anime "Monster Hunter Stories: Ride On", 48 episodes like good Pokemon episodes.- the new story in this game follows a very similar structure to the first, which can make it a little predictable at a glance, but the story still has it's own way of going about it that was very fun to be part of.- the story isn't meant to be overly dramatic, full of deep and convoluted mystery, or anything too groundbreaking. But it's simple focus on love, values, and relationships is perfectly presented in ways you can easily enjoy and appreciate. - the characters are so fun and distinct that you can easily fall in love with any and all of them, though you might not relate so much to your own character till late in the story. Like many games, your character doesn't really talk. - Navirou is your partner felyne who is fundamentally tasked to be your voice. The only problem with this is it takes a while to appreciate Navirou's character and voice acting, I do, and many do, but most don't. Please give my boy a good chance.Gameplay:- I am not a nitpicky person so you may not get the good guide you're looking for from me.- feels a lot like an older gen game because the landscape is not made of complex details and textures, but the monsters are excellently modeled to the style.- some dungeons are specific locations, but the generic randomly generated ones can get repetitive as they use a selection of pre-made layouts and piece them together more or less randomly. I wouldn't ask for more, but it becomes a little obvious shortly into each location what the dungeons will be like.- Battling is a big game of rock-paper-scissors with special abilities, trump cards, and usually multiple opponents and teammates, making for a unique and learnable battle system that is approachable to anyone but rewards those who can crack the codes and form solid strategies. Honestly took me some notable mistakes to really grasp the secondary rules they use, but the game is not punishing for one or two major mistakes in battle till nearly the end of the game. - difficulty wise, you can deliberately chose how difficult you want it to be by giving yourself a set of rules, but the game makes winning almost inevitable for those well-enough prepared. You are given three hearts between you and your monster partner, and any time you or your monster runs out of health you lose a heart (and then get your health back). Losing all three hearts ends the fight in defeat. This difficulty is normal, and actually more than challenging at a few points in the game. However, there are some items that can restore a heart during a battle to basically keep your team in the fight forever (unless you are horribly under leveled, in which monsters can take out multiple hearts at once with multi hit attacks that you cant keep up with. So anyway, not a souls-like, but not impossible to lose like PokemonSw/Sh- Any monster can ultimately learn any move (Nergigante can learn elemental attacks, Velocidromes can learn Nergigante moves) which is honestly really weird to me in the main story but when it comes to PvP its a definite win. If this feature is your focus, look it up to learn all its technicalities from people more qualified.Replayability:- The main story is on set tracks you can't derail, so there aren't second endings to find (that I know of. nothing major at least).- I think the average person could play it twice happily, but its always been fun for me to watch people play the game for the first time to go through the story again that way and see how they take it. - There is end game content I haven't really pursued yet, but there are things to do after the main story- The main reason to keep playing after the story would be PvP and making the perfect team of monsties, if that's what you're into

_childDocuments_.review: Im going to be honest. I thought this was going to be similar to Monster Hunter World, but done in a more cartoonish style. I was not expecting a turn based RPG style game, but I am enjoying it. The gameplay and mechanics are simply enough to figure out, and the depth is there if you want to really get into stats/skills.Im about 35 hours in and I would say that this is worth the $60. Monster Hunter Stories 2 has the traditional monster farming for upgrades to gear and farming environmental materials for crafting. What I found to be lacking was how much they simplified the armor sets. In previous MH titles, you had the standard RPG equipment slots: head/shoulders/chest/legs/etc. In Stories 2 however, they cut all that out and essentially gave you an amour onesie. It feels like they took a lot of the creativity out of creating builds and tailoring skills to your play style. The party system is really well done and offers a lot of creativity/customization. I can tell that the end game is going to be a time pit for me though, because Im a bit of a stat ♥♥♥♥♥ in these kinds of games.If youre a fan of older party based RPGs, I would definitely suggest giving Monster Hunter Stories 2 a shot. If youre on the fence about it, throw it on your wish list and see if it goes on sale at some point.

My only criticism is that it was clearly designed to be played on a gamepad since mouse doesn't even move the camera by default, arrows do that. But if you can get around the controls, give this game a fair shot. In fact, you can do so for free because there's a free Demo of the game from which you can transfer data over to the main game if you decide to buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun! Nothing like the usual monster hunter experience in terms of combat, not a bad thing but worth noting, but the grind and story is still there. Nearly 180 hours in and I've still got things to do in game when I want. I personally don't play much multi-player but that is for sure one of this games downsides compared to the main series. You can still do dens with friends but its nothing like the range of hunting to the same degree of difficulty and coordination you can do in a main game. Artstyle is very well stylized and I expect it to hold up as an enjoyable experience for a long while. Free content updates currently keep adding things to do and the potential of a paid DLC later on!

_childDocuments_.review: While it's quite different from those that came before it, it's fun, cute, and surprisingly, kind of difficult. It's a heart-warming story that will take you across a diverse and beautiful land -- full of creatures to encounter and friends to meet. Pretty much THE reason you would want this game. The characters have noticeable differences in the way they talk and perceive the world, and pretty good voice acting to boot. If you like cute games, but also want some challenge, this is a must. (although I do prefer it when my character is an adult) I leave it as a 6 not because it's bad, but because I personally do not like turn-based combat. it has some cool looking combos that make it interesting - and even exciting - to go out of your way to do some battles. I LOVE this style, it's vibrant, simple -- but full of character and well fitting to the story and game-play. It runs flawlessly, noting else to say really. I think there is, but I never used it, and in my opinion -- it doesn't need it.

_childDocuments_.review: A great sequel that improves on everything that made the first game great. It’s basically Pokemon, but in the Monster Hunter World. But here, the monsters can be your friend. While players can’t tame the monsters, they can follow them to their nest and steal their eggs to raise tame so-called Monsties! The game features a connected world that is separated into smaller areas that can be freely explored. Exploration features some very light metroid-vania elements where the player needs certain Monsties to reach new locations. For example you need a Tigrex to climb ranks or a Velicoprey to jump over chasms. Just like in the main series, most of the time is spent on fighting wild monsters. But in Monster Hunter Stories a classic turn based JRPG-battle system takes over. It still features most of the mechanics of the main line series with elemental weaknesses and different weapon types doing different kinds of damages. It also adds a stone, rock, paper like system where fast attacks trump strength attack, strength attacks trump tech attacks and tech attacks again trump fast attacks. Learning the patterns of all the enemies and finding out their weak spots is a big part of the fun.Where there is a JRPG battle system there is also a level up system. Contrary to the mainline series the main character, NPC followers and all Monsties can be leveled up to improve their stats. Later in the game, Monsties can even be fused to transfer skills between them. The system is quite deep and gives a lot of room to build your dream Monstie team. And of course killed monsters drop tons of items and parts that can be crafted into new armors and weapons that can also be improved further. While I’ve only played the single-player, the game also features an extensive online mode where players can go on co-op hunts or even battle each other in an arena. So this can be enjoyed as a single player narrative JRPG and/or as a PvP/Coop game equally. Because it was mainly developed for the Nintendo Switch, Monster Hunter Stories 2 isn’t the most technically advanced game. The graphics are even more stylized then in Monster Hunter Rise. But in my opinion it is still a mighty fine looking game with a strong artstyle. Especially the care and craftsmanship that was put into all the battle animations deserves extra praise. This game looks spectacular in battles and I’d wish Pokemon games could finally keep up with that. It also features nicely rendered and voiced cutscenes that are never too long but also not too sparse. The game is just neatly paced and the mix between exploring, fighting and story segments with funny characters just works. Last but not least a word to Steam Deck compatibility. The game is marked as “not compatible” but it ran without tinkering for me. The game runs pretty good, but not as good as I’d expect from a Switch port. It also makes the Steam Deck fans go “bzzzzzzz!” and the battery drain quickly. So best use some good headphones while playing it and have a power source nearby.

_childDocuments_.review: Log #127: The Barroth have begun migrating to Loloska in an attempt to regroup and get away from my wrath. And yet, not even this has prevented the slaughter. Prantic (my Pukei-Pukei) and I have been getting rid of the stragglers and letting the others escape.Log #181: Apparently, this migration wasn't just an attempt to regroup and survive... it was to increase their numbers. Much to their (probable) dismay, they've revealed the location of the Jade Barroths. This shall prove more fruitful then I thought.Log #205: Barroth kill count was only 43 today, down from yesterday's 49. Either I'm getting rusty, or the population's thinning. Let's hope it's the latter.Log #220: Against my better judgement, Prantic convinced me to keep a Barroth egg we found in one of their dens. Perhaps making a bond with it when it hatches and convincing it to kill it's brethren will be more useful then simply making the mother of all omelets, Jack. (Side notes: Don't ask how Prantic convinced me, you know how the bond between Monstie and Rider works. As for Jack, if you somehow find this... good on you, you finally stopped drinking those so-called "electrolytes.")Log #256: Klepoth (the Barroth that hatched from the egg) has been incredibly helpful in finding Barroths in hiding. Kill count has been steadily increasing, up from 52 to 70. And to be honest... I'm growing somewhat fond of the muddy guy. Prantic will still be my right-hand Monstie, and Noggin my Palico, but Klepoth may be sticking around for a little longer.Log #276: This may be the last log for those finding these in the fields. Pits have started opening up everywhere, with bright red lights shooting out from them. Monsters, including the Barroths, have been getting much more aggressive around these pits. I've heard passing words that these are being called rage-rays (the Guild is apparently horrible at naming things), and it's affecting everything. I may need to head back home, because as this helps bring the Barroths out of hiding, it also brings out the more terrifying things, and in herds I never thought possible. Hopefully this dies down soon, so the slaughter may continue. - Fortel, signing off9/10, still can't get over why the Barroths are in the ice area when they like mud, like, what the f* Capcom?

_childDocuments_.review: T:L:D:R = Great game with a lot to love for new and old fans. 8/10As a huge MH fan i had to pick this up at launch even if going in I wasn't expecting much. What i found however was a very well made turn based RPG with a classic rock, paper, scissors battle system that was way better than it has any right to be. You can tell almost immediately that this game was made with so much love.Its a very open and accessible RPG to people unfamiliar with the franchise but it also rewards veterans with a lot of subtle nods. A seasoned hunter can make an educated guess what types each monster is based on their move set and ecology within the main line games. While the game is also forgiving enough to allow new players to not be punished so severely for not knowing and messing up an opening attack. I currently have 58 hours played in this game and I'm not finished with the high rank content so there is a lot of game to be played here and its well worth the price point especially for any MH fan. The occasional tedious action or quest and the fact that multiplayer isn't really accessible till about 4-8 hours in depending on your grind is the only thing really keeping me from giving this game a higher rating.

_childDocuments_.review: Even as a standalone game, Monster Hunter Stories 2 is phenomenal. It took everything that the first Monster Hunter Stories did right and expanded on it. More Monsters/Monsties, more weapon types, better multiplayer functionality, and of course it's also not exclusive to handheld consoles (Stories 1 could only be played on either mobile devices or the 3DS). The fact that it's a Monster Hunter game and a sequel to an already decent game is just icing on the cake. Like, jeez. Capcom really knocked it outta the park with this one. And the game's still not finished yet given all the free Title Updates that are already on the way!I do have a few complaints, though. For one, JUST like in the first game, Water and Dragon are kinda the ugly ducklings of the elements, though in this game Water is less so (a welcome change from the first game) thanks to Mizutsune existing and being a good Monstie (plus the upcoming Soulseer Mizutsune). Dragon, though? It literally only has TWO Monsties of that particular element (Stygian Zinogre and the pickle) in the base game, and even worse, the Dragon-element Palamute doesn't even get any Speed-type skills... because Speed-type Dragon Element Skills don't exist. Hopefully this gets fixed in a later update.Also, you can pet the doggos.

_childDocuments_.review: (Have about 60-70 hours on the Switch version, liked it enough to want it on my main steam library for use on my Steam Deck - and yes it absolutely DOES run great on Deck, I don't know why it's listed as not-supported. It launches in windowed mode which you can change in the first-launch settings to full screen and then it runs perfect)This game is a must-play for two kinds of people - anybody who has ever felt bad for going "IT'S THE BEST BOY!!!" during a regular Monster Hunter game after their favorite monster shows up and then proceeding to beat it to death and carve its body apart, and people who like Pokemon alternatives.The story is like a family-friendly saturday morning adventure that does a great job at pace setting and moving the player around the world and has enough intrigue and emotional beats to leave you wanting to see more, the turn-based combat has a surprising amount of depth to it and a TON of character with beautifully animated moves and abilities unique to weapon types and different monsters, and the monster taming system, while not over-the-top, has a lot of nuance to it that's fun to engage with.My one and only gripe with the game is the fact that in spite of having a beautiful 10/10 experience, they decided at some point that the game was too good and had to be worse, so they added Navirou - the single worst character I have ever encountered in any video game I have ever played. He's meant to be the comic relief helper but he serves functionally no purpose. He's not funny, he's not charming, he does nothing besides make annoying quips during battles, act as your character's voice in cutscenes, make utterly meaningless additions to conversations, and ruins emotional tension with his mere presence. I want you to imagine for a moment your most beloved family member - a partner, a parent, a sibling, whoever you hold closest to your hear - was just shot. You hear the sirens from the ambulence approaching and your desperately trying to get them to not close their eyes, to just hold on a little bit longer because help is so close...and then you hear in a squeaky out-of-place voice: "MEOW-ZA!!!! THIS SURE IS A REAL PAW-DICAMENT, HUH BUDDY????"And for that reason, I think you should buy this game even more. As much as I despise Navirou, he is so unfathomably bad that he is an experience all on his own. I mean that sincerely, you have GOT to see this ♥♥♥♥. The sheer audacity of putting him in to a game that he just makes worse for no reason is to be respected and feared. They want to make a Monster Hunter Stories 3. The WILL do it again.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying the game but I don't think I could recommend it to anyone. I literally can't use the monsters I want because I'm stuck balancing types and "movement abilities" and only have so many slots. Velocidrome is the only damn thing that has jump until mid-late game and it's replaced with just another one of the great jaggi types. If I want my beefy tigrex, I can't make room for the nercylla I want because they both have climb. It's so stupid, my team is full of monsters I don't care about. I thought it would all be fixed when I unlocked fly but it's not even usable once you enter a dungeon area. It's the exact same with the weapons. If I use hammer, I can't have hunting horn because I have to cover the three damage types. And each weapon only does one damage type it's assigned. You know what's cool about great sword in the actual monster hunter games? It can do slash AND BLUNT damage depending on what combos you use. You even learn the charge rush maneuver WHICH IS A BLUNT ATTACK. But in this game it still does slash despite that. And then since each individual part has different weapon type resistances that also change depending on what state the monster is in, you gotta constantly swap what weapon your using. It would be a cool system honestly if it didn't completely gimp weapons that rely on stockpiling to use their abilities. The gunlance generally gets one bullet loaded with each attack, two on a won head-to-head I think. But you know what happens by the time I get it fully charged for it's ultimate ability? The part breaks or the monster becomes enraged or what have you and now I have to switch weapons or do no damage. That sucks.And to top it off, a lot of the cooler monsters, you can't actually have on your team for what seems like no real reason. I can have Nercylla (bug) but not Seltas or Seltas Queen (also bugs). I can have Popo or Anklyo (trash mob) but I can't have Hermitaur (cool crab).The gameplay is pretty much the same as the first game. Rock-paper-scissors with memorization. The buddy system is cool, there are more monsties, still forced to have Rathalos in your party, etc. The UI and the game as a whole feels extremely un-polished. There aren't simple things like being able to sort your quests by ONES YOU HAVEN'T ALREADY COMPLETED. Why would I want to even look at un-repeatable quests I've finished? Much less have them randomly mixed together with the ones I'm actively tracking. The quick travel map is just kind of a list of names without any indicator of where exactly they take you. The villages aren't marked with anything different to indicate that they are villages. You can't mark your own map for things to come back to or view areas you aren't in to figure out where you want to go. The villages are designed to make it take as long as possible to get to everything. But by far, the most infuriating thing in this entire game is Navirou. There are no options to tell him to shut the heck up and every single damn time he pops up dialogue, you have to click a button to dismiss it. Which of course leads to stuff like not picking up items because dismissing the dialogue ate your button click as you were walking by. Not getting back on your monstie to run away in time. Not being able to click the catstand to activate it as you walk by because FOR SOME GOD FORSAKEN REASON, HE WAITS UNTIL YOU ARE ALREADY ON TOP OF IT TO TELL YOU IT'S NEARBY. Not to mention EVERYTHING HE SAYS IS INSANELY BASIC AND UNHELPFUL. "The monster is asleep! Here's your chance!"I CAN SEE IT. THERE ARE GIANT BUBBLES COMING OUT ITS NOSE AND EVERYTHING."There's a catstand nearby"YES AND I MISSED IT THANKS TO YOU, STUPID. "I think you've collected all the bottle caps buddy"Yeah that's great, I'm currently next to an egg running from a monster and you've prevented me from picking it up and now I'm stuck in a fight thanks.And he repeats all of this dialogue, every. single. time. without fail. I hate him, I wish he would die.*ahem* So to summarize, the game is fun and a good addition to the monster hunter franchise generally but it misses the mark on creature collecting, gameplay, quality/polish and is just generally annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my most anticipated games of 2021, and it paid off pretty well. The story was more engaging to follow than the first game's, seeing monsters from Generations and World was a delight, the combat feels more complex with new mechanics to involve more than just Head-to-Heads, and the presentation in scenes is overall just more pleasant to see compared to the first.My favorite additions are the mechanics between using the right weapon and hitting the right body part. Not only does it add more consideration on what to use and how to stop certain attacks, but much like reading monster patterns in the mainline games, Monster Hunter veterans will immediately know what to use against monsters and hit wherever depending on the situation. Of course, the game makes sure to remember which parts are resistant against which weapons, so newcomers aren't discouraged for not knowing every bit of a monster.There are some problems I have, mainly that monster dens can feel tedious to go through since there is too little variety in room layouts (consider having a Nargacuga if you want to avoid fights, and you're better off only checking golden dens anyway for the sake of rare eggs), and most dungeons involved in the story are also using these same layouts when they should be unique. Still, the pros outweigh the cons for me, and I'll just hope the next Stories game can generate a better variety of den rooms.Overall, I really like this game, and it is such a step up from what the first game introduced. I look forward to more of this series, it is such a unique perspective on Monster Hunter while also making several mechanics from the mainline games translate into a turn-based RPG to still feel familiar to mainline players. Highly recommended for turn-based RPG, Pokemon, and Monster Hunter fans alike.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is probably the most fun I've had in a long time.If you haven't played Stories 1, that's perfectly fine. There are recurring characters in this, but you don't need to know the story of 1 to enjoy the story of 2. That said, I heavily recommend the original Stories as well. I cannot speak enough praise about this series.I had such an enjoyable experience playing this game in every way. Pros:- Monster CollectionCapcom just has this way of taking monster collection and turning it into something that's unique beyond just "hey this is a new monster, catch it :)." Not to bag on pokemon or anything like that, but in most games like pokemon, what makes your team usually comes down to you finding new monsters to put on your team and them overall being stronger just based on progression. There's nothing wrong with that, but Stories takes that concept and while not immediately disregarding it by making every monster do the same thing, it gives you an opportunity to build your monster in any way you want due to the genetics system. While the genes can be frustrating in the sense of you can get screwed over by rng a lot of the time, it's never really a slog to get those genes. By hunting for new genes, you're exploring new dens, finding new items, possibly even discovering new monsters. Every monster is unique in whatever ways you can make it unique, and that's fascinating for me being a long time pokemon player.-CombatWhile there are some frustrations around the combat mechanics such as monsties sometimes being just really stupid (why is my nargacuga just SPIKE BOMBING), overall it's very straightforward and honestly fun. They manage to keep it simple with a RPS style combat, but it's not completely random or based on weapons like in FE (more on weapons later). Kinship skills are a super cool way to have an interaction with your monsties that isn't just directly controlling them like a traditional JRPG, and basically every skill in the game *has a use* which is a complaint I had with a lot of RPGs and JRPGs, as a lot of them just have some moves that just make no sense.-Story and charactersThe characters are phenomenal. Every character has a clear personality. You can tell what they're thinking. You can see how they're meant to be and that's amazing. There's twists that I genuinely didn't expect, and that's just a rarity at this point for me. They put a lot of effort into it.-Animations:My god the attack animations are so good. That's literally all I can say. Watch every kinship skill at least once, you won't regret it.-WeaponsYou have 3 types of weapons, with 2 weapons in each type. Slice, Pierce and Blunt. Weapons do different damage to parts based on that part's weakness to said type of weapon. Classic monster hunter. The weapon pool is limited, but it makes sense for stories and that's fine. They still all have their unique uses and give you the opportunities to use each one whenever you see fit.Con:-DensThe only issue I have with the game is repetitive den layouts. Every den comes down to a random number of rooms, which is fine, and I understand why they made this decision, but after a while you are just going through the same rooms over and over and over again. The random monsters and items in the den definitely make up for it though.Overall, this game is absolutely incredible. I wanted to wait until I had completed the game just to see if my opinion changed at all, but it didn't. I loved it from start to finish. I just started the endgame content, and I haven't messed with multiplayer much so I won't comment on those, but overall this game is a great time. If you're even remotely a fan of either pokemon-esque games or monster hunter. Please try this game.(Redeemed via steam key. Preordered on the 23rd through a different site that I always use, for clarity.)

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, really good. If you've played the first you know what to expect, as this game builds on the previous game's foundation with a variety of QOL changes and so many new areas/monsters. If you haven't, think Pokemon mixed only your trainer fights too and the Pokemon all want to beat you up. The battles have quite a bit of substance to them; you'll have to learn each enemy's patterns and what damage types they're weak to if you want all the drop rate bonuses, but thankfully the game tracks everything you've learned about enemy weaknesses and stores that information for you permanently. The story's tacky but it works well enough, and the writing has a surprising amount of charm behind it. It's good enough that you won't feel the need to skip it, and that's all it has to be.My only gripes with the game so far are the co-op being locked 10 hours in and the relatively low number of co-op quests so far, but they've already announced more co-op content and the wait to unlock the mode is well worth it.Oh, and the PVP is fantastic - other than the questionable decision to make elder dragons/deviants immune to traps, the item sets are well balanced and let you make just about any playstyle viable in both solo and duo battles. Learning elemental weaknesses and trying to predict bluffs makes it consistently fun and challenging, and the option of automatic level balancing means that you don't have to grind your monster levels up just to compete.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, and I'm so glad it came out on PC on launch day. The amount of care from the devs for the game is very apparent.For those who played the first MHST game on 3DS/android/ios, it basically takes it and really refines and improves upon it! If you loved the first, you WILL love this sequel. The only thing that MHST2 dropped the ball on vs the first game is that currently elemental atk up genes & the visual effects on your monsties are bugged, but that will probably be fixed soon enough, since the game only just came out and its one of just 2 bugs I've encountered, the other being a texture glitch on a wooden pole in one of the villages where the texture gets replaced with random pixels.For those who love the mainline MH games, this is still a great game to try - there is a demo, though it only gives a taste of the basics (the fights will get MUCH harder, think of the demo as basically just the first few 1* and 2* hunt quests in a mainline game, but with another hunter there to help you out) - even if JRPG game mechanics are less of your thing. It really pays a lot of respect and attention to detail in translating the mainline games into the format, with its own take on it, and I've generally seen people who are lukewarm or ambivalent on JRPGs in general but do like the mainline MH games really enjoy this game. Its also get some of the most quality of life features in any MH game, so theres that too.For everyone else, who probably thinks of this as a pokemon game, while yes theres superficial similarities, the similarities are only skin deep. Due to a lack of real competition in the genre, you only really end up with a handful of small-name games, with maybe temtem being the outlier, and then theres this and pokemon itself, so theres not a whole lot to compare to. The combat system is substantially different, and honestly I feel it gets a lot deeper, particularly in late game. It also gives you way more control over your monsties' (the playable rider versions of the monster species in the game, distinct from the wild NPC/boss versions which are just called monsters) stats, and you dont' have all this baked-in EV/IV nonsense - the early monsties you get you can keep through the game, upgrading them with new genes you get from eggs you find along the way, unlike with pokemon where getting better EV/IV values on a new pokemon results in the old one having no purpose other than to be boxed or train up their replacement. Oh right, and speaking of that, the XP gain in this game is so much better than in pokemon. MHST2 always gives everyone in the party the same base XP, and anyone who is below the highest leveled party member gets substantial bonus XP, so low level monsties will very quickly catch up to high level ones, even if they just sit safely in the back not actually fighting. You also dont need to buy the game twice to get everyone - one version has all the content, and thats all you need, none of this forced-trading/buy-twice mechanics. And dont get me started on the um, ahem, stories - MHST2, for a game with the name 'stories' in the title does live up to that name and actually delivers a story (yes, some parts of the beginning are a bit relaxed, but the intent is for you to go explore, build up your team, and all that, because ), and even though it may play some tropes dead straight without bothering to subvert them honestly that doesnt really matter because it does such a good job building up to and earning its moments. Meanwhile pokemon sword & shield basically decided to forgo the  whole concept of even pretending to have a real plot half of the way through (the first half it was simply pretending to have a plot), with increasingly inane and pointless tasks thrown in your way that make no sense as to why you would have to do them and eventually leads up to phoning it in by the time you go fight the enemy team in their "base" (for all you know, its actually just an elevator) with self-aware jokes - about the very lack of plot and how bad this segment of the game is - so bad that they would make navirou look like a comedic mastermind by comparison. I will say, the plots of both games made me feel strong emotions: for MHST2 I felt it about the events & characters in the plot, while for S&S it was about how infuriatingly pathetic the excuse for a plot itself was. Argh, I've worked myself up over that stupid game again.Anyways, enough about how pokemon has crashed into the ground in a burning wreck and more about 'go buy this game' instead.Go buy this game!

_childDocuments_.review: + Beautiful open world and overall graphics+ Detailed ability animations+ Lots of Monsties to capture+ Lots of gear+ Decent voice acting+ Option to insta-win encounters when you're over-levelled+/- Combat is simplistic+/- Lots of endgame content, but not much point to play through unless you have someone to play co-op with you- Some Monstie capture requirements are poorly designed as they don't actually work. Eg. Telling you to trap an enraged Monster even though enraged monsters can't be trapped- Combat can get really repetitive thanks to the overall design- Online multiplayer is dead- Several consumables serve little to no purpose, due to how the turn based combat is designed.There are a lot of comparisons to Pokemon. But other than the ability to "capture" monsters and the turn-based combat, there really isn't much of a similarity. MHS2 is mainly story-focused with a simplistic battle system, while Pokemon is focused on "catching em all" and its deep "easy to learn, hard to master" battle system.While the battle system in MHS2 isn't "bad" per se, the biggest problem with it is the rock-paper-scissors system, and how optimal gameplay is centered around not taking damage at all. When your Rider and Monstie use the same type of move and beat a monster at rock-paper-scissors, you attack together, denying the enemy from taking an action. This style of play is essential to get you through the game, as monsters can potentially one shot you or your monstie if they land a blow.And unfortunately, this can also get extremely repetitive, as you'll be doing the same thing for pretty much every monster. Because you don't have a lot of HP, you can't really play any other way. For example, you can't really afford to take a turn to use a whetstone to increase your crit rate, as a monster landing a hit on you or your monstie can potentially one shot either of you. Every turn is valuable and cannot be wasted.But despite the mediocre combat system, I'd say the main strengths of MHS2 are the gorgeous open world and animations, large number of capturable monsters, and its lighthearted story and humour. The colours throughout the game always looked vibrant, and were a treat to look at. Because of that, I enjoyed most of the game.As for the endgame content, MHS2 stays true to the Monster Hunter tradition with the game being packed with endgame content. There is a lot of depth to optimising your gear and Monsties, but because I found the combat system kinda boring, I didn't see any point in going through the trouble of doing all that.Overall, I'd say this is definitely worth a play, but only really worth the buy at half off or more.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game for children. I am complaining regardless.The plot: interesting enough, unfortunately littered with sequences dominated by social ineptitude usually found in *quirky* anime. Example: centuries old wyverian woman trapped in a 14 year-old's body jumps onto your character on-sight, mistaking you for your own grizzled old grandpa. She constantly grabs your hands and follows your character around, making a burden of herself because she's *ahem* "the one who gave you the egg so she should follow you because she gave you an egg once." You can also change her outfit. How great is that. My theory: Capcom has been funding an experimental science program. This program uses a specialized team of shadow operatives to capture and confine wild bonobos, holding them within pens. Taking a look around, the bonobos will find a single control panel with a "cringe dialogue" button. Which, once pressed, sends a string of commands to an advanced A.I., while simultaneously rewarding the bonobo with a fruit, and the power cord to their ipad. On which they may watch one markiplier episode. As you can probably imagine, the button gets pressed very frequently. The gameplay: when you aren't walking around(the ying) the combat(the yang) sits comfortably at above average, but is satisfying to play. It has some similarities to fossil fighters. No real complaints here.The world: empty and without any interest or majesty. An impressive feat for a monster hunter inspired game. When you ride monsters the game plays and feels no differently than when your character walks around on-foot. I would say you move faster while riding but they somehow managed to fine tune that to feel slow as well. Side note: Yian Kut Ku and Yian Garuga cannot fly. This is quite interesting when you consider that they can in fact fly. The cAT.I made the mistake of playing with english dub on, and as a consequence Navirou's voice is an assault on the senses. He constantly repeats information just explained to the main characters in a confused and incessant manner that I can only imagine is a result of his wickedly misshapen brain. He eliminates any possibility of subtlety by idiotically blurting out obvious plot connections, lengthening dialogue sequences as a by-product of his cognitive disfigurement. This would be tolerable if he was a side character played for laughs. But he isn't. He is quite literally the main character of this game. He has no purpose other than be the silent protagonists' "voice," and injecting his cringe anime-tier dialogue between every single sentence spoken by other characters. It is as if the writers were so afraid that their other characters might be compelling enough to illicit some kind of intrigue from the player and they added this fiend in post.Another thing about this cat. His gameplay "purpose" is that he can "sense," with his level 100 myticisim whether a monster egg has a good or average monster within it. He uses the forbidden and arcane magic of "smelling" and "holding" the egg, to see how stinky or heavy the thing is. Incredible I know. It seems our protagonist is not only mute, but was struck by lightning shortly after being born. Like the victim of some Greek tragedy, our hero is unable to experience the smells, tastes, and textures of their world. Overall, disappointing game. Any listing over 10 dollars is overpriced. I enjoy parts of this game, but they wrote Scrappy-do into the main cast of characters, and all the tolerable or fun parts take a backseat to his screeching.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter is known for its fun, real time, fast action paced gameplay. Stories 2 offers a unique take on the series, this time with a focus on turn based combat and monster collecting. For people who might not be a huge fan of the mainline Monster Hunter series whether because they find it too difficult or because they don't enjoy the gameplay, MHS 2 offers a new and simpler entry point for people to get into the franchise so they too can experience the thrill of what makes Monster Hunter so fun. Despite not being a part of the main series, a lot of effort went into this game and it's shown in its presentation. There are tons of monsters to discover and raise, many locations to explore, and a vast array of gear and weapons that Monster Hunter is so well known for. Collecting and upgrading gear is just as addictive in this as with the previous games, this time with the added mechanic of capturing and raising monsters as well. The combat in this game starts off very easy in the beginning, but later on the difficulty picks up and monsters gain new attack patterns and will punish you if you aren't paying attention. It's a simple rock-paper-scissors style gameplay, but it's done so well here that even if you aren't the biggest fan of turn based gameplay (myself included), you might actually enjoy it. I really enjoyed the stunning visuals and animations when monsters perform attacks or unique moves, the kinship skills are honestly such a treat to watch and they're all done with care and style. The only complaints are things that have already been mentioned before. There is some pretty bad pop-in at times and there is this weird issue where if you alt tab while in full screen the game goes back into windowed mode, so you either have to ALT+Enter again to fullscreen or go into the options each time. Also the graphics are obviously not as amazing as something like World, which would be unreasonable to expect since this game was made primarily for the Switch in mind. Regardless, it didn't really bother me because the aesthetics and art style offer its own unique look to the game that is just as pretty to look at. I'm always excited to see what the Stories 2 rendition of a monster I saw in World would look like and it's always done well. All their quirks and traits have been transferred to this game perfectly with a stylized look, yet still retaining its core features. All in all the game is excellent and I highly recommend it. It ran flawlessly for me, not a single crash the entire time playing and frame drops were an extremely rare occurrence. The main game took me about 45~ hours to complete, but there is still post game content that I haven't even touched yet and still more things I want to discover and do. Not to mention that this game has a roadmap and will be getting updates for the next few months to come (maybe even longer), keeping the game alive for the foreseeable future. If you're still undecided, you can always just try the demo they've put out for free. It gives you a chance to see whether you like it or not. If you do get it, I hope you enjoy it.Happy Hunting!
