_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game for anybody that enjoys monster collection games or even just turn-based RPGs in general. There's a lot of content, good enemy variety, and a large selection of monsters. The mechanics are simple enough that a kid could probably pick it up, but there is still some depth to engage with in predicting enemy behavior and memorizing what monsters do, much like the mainline games. The game does a good job of translating mechanics from the mainline Monster Hunter games into a new format, so fans of the series will have fun with that. In an era where Pokemon is frequently criticized for being phoned-in, this game shows love, care, and respect for the genre and series. If you've ever wanted to ride around on your monsters or fight alongside them in battles, this game's the chance to do it.Beyond gameplay, the music is good, the story is fun, and the visuals are nice, especially if you're fond of cute baby monsters. The controls for keyboard take some fiddling to get comfortable, but they can be set up so they're not too clunky and the game has controller support.The game is clearly made for kids, but, like all good children's media, it can still be enjoyed by adults. So long as you like cheesy cat puns and the fact that they're called 'monsties'. Even the annoying sidekick critter grows on you.

That rock, paper, scissors game play has additional rock, paper, scissors elements mixed in so you can rock, paper, scissors while you rock, paper, scissors directly into a Tigrex's stupid face.The Story is alright, nothing AMAZING but it is serviceable enough to keep you going, voice acting is great, animations are fantastic.Graphically it is not the most mind blowing game out there but remember this came from the Switch and it does a decent job at beefing up the visuals for PC. Unlocked frame rate, 4k monitor support, controllers or Keyboard and mouse work great and are able to be completely re-bound to any keys(or buttons) you wish.Sound is great, there is even a totally pointless slider to adjust the pitch of monster battle cries. hearing a whiny Tigrex is funny I guess?There is an "endless" endgame here which is basically running randomly generated dungeons with either online cooperative play or an AI partner. The point being to find good "genes" for your "Monsties" to fully kit them out, a system not too dissimilar from Final Fantasy's Materia system only it's like Connect 4, but with nine slots in a grid, so maybe more like Tic-Tac-Toe or "Connect 3x3x3"... anyways, lining up matching elements(colors) and types(symbols) provides exponential gains to that element or skill's buff and some genes can provide your Monstie with new moves to use in combat. Essentially you can make a "Fire Type" Mizutsune for example or a Anjanath that uses water attacks. It's engaging enough and if you enjoy the core loop of collecting monsters, battling monsters and running, somewhat repetitive dungeons to min-max your party then the game will be PERFECT for you!There IS a PvP online element to the game where you battle your friends parties and can test your builds and test your mettle, but It is pretty dead at this point so you might want to consider scheduling that with them instead of hoping to find a match naturally, Maybe check out the game's DISCORD server for other players to party up with and what have you.It's a great game, I spent close to 120 hours with it on Switch and couldn't help but start over on PC (finally) because I just missed that core loop.As a long time Monster Hunter fan and someone who fell off Pokemon at a young age once there was like 500+ monsters to remember this scratches all those itches while being charming, funny and moderately addicting.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to love with this game, but I'm not gonna lie when I say there's also a lot to hate. But I will say that the demo does a good job of exemplifying both the good and the bad of it, so if you're interested in the title but not sure if it's for you, give it a shot and you'll see what I mean. But if you're still on the fence then let me just share, in more depth, why I say this game is good, but probably not for everyone.I started my journey in the Monster Hunter series with World on the PS4, and I've gotta say that the idea of taming and fighting alongside monsters in a pokemon-esce turn-based battle system wasn't exactly what I was expecting from a branch-off of the series, but it's actually really a lot of fun. Collecting and hunting new monsters is a lot of fun, being able to customize their entire selection of actions and abilities feels rewarding, and being able to bond with them by even just riding around the world feels really good.So let me be clear, with this game I have no problems at all with the gameplay, in fact the gameplay is the best part of this game. What I have the most problems with in this game is all related to writing, dialogue, and the story.Now I will say this: I've never played the first Monster Hunter Stories game on 3DS, but I have friends that have. And if what they've told me holds water, I'm probably betting that the first game has WAY better storytelling than this one does. And I really... really hope it does. Because wowie this game's writing is the worst I've ever experienced, especially considering the price tag and the fact that the word "stories" is literally in the title of the game. SOME of the characters are tolerable and fairly written, especially the first two characters that accompany you on your journey, but 90% of the other characters are the most intolerable cretins I've ever been tasked with tolerating.And don't even get me started on Navirou. Never before have I ever thought "man I would love to kick a cat" and had other people actually agree with me until it came to Navirou. He is by far the most arrogant, irritating, narcissistic, and obnoxious character I've ever experienced in any video game EVER. And the worst part is that he's with you for the ENTIRE game. You don't get a single moment without Navirou, and every time he reminds you he's there he's going to make you want to break something. But hey, at least with DLC you can put him in a silly little costume that makes him look like just as much of a clown as he acts.But of course, the candle on the cake, your character doesn't speak for themself. They're a silent protagonist that can only be heard when taking damage or shouting cheers like Link from Legend of Zelda, and the only direct opinions they give are given through actions rather than words. Which honestly is fine in most cases, but in this game it doesn't work all that well considering your character does a lot of things that I would NEVER want my character to do, and I don't get any agency to alter their opinion or decisions when it comes to how they behave around others. Add on top of the fact that Navirou, the previously stated Worst Character Ever, is always talking in your place and voicing what I assume the writers thought would be "your opinion" to other characters, and you end up feeling less like you're a person that's playing a role in this game's story and more like you're being held prisoner in your own body, with no ability to speak or act for yourself until it's time to fight. Which is a really unenjoyable experience that had me and even some of my friends skipping a lot of cutscenes and dialogue simply because it was too punishing to sit through it.Now I'm sure some could say that the story is meant to be for younger audiences, especially considering it feels so much like a pokemon clone what with the collecting and training monsters and using them to fight other monsters aspect, but I don't think even kids would enjoy having zero agency over how their character interacts so obnoxiously with others, or having an arrogant feline talking over them the entire time while your character stares at him with the saddest look of pity you'd ever seen a character give to a cartoonishly rendered 3D feline. Really, I'm just gobsmacked to think that adults actually let this story get published when it feels like it wasn't even crowd tested once for presentability.But basically in a TLDR; The game is good, and the gameplay is a lot of fun, but the story and writing here REALLY becomes intolerable for pretty much the entire game. Try the demo first before buying the full game and you'll see what I mean right out the gate.

_childDocuments_.review: The game shines with its engaging narrative, featuring a compelling plot filled with emotional depth and interesting character arcs. The story of a world threatened by the mysterious Wings of Ruin keeps players hooked and eager to uncover the truth.The game’s charming, anime-inspired art style stands out with its colorful, detailed visuals and expressive character designs, creating an inviting and immersive world.The turn-based combat system is refreshing and strategic, offering a break from the real-time action of mainline Monster Hunter games. The addition of “Kinship” skills and monster alliances adds more depth to battles.The ability to collect, hatch, and train various monsters provides a satisfying yet strategic element to gameplay. With every monster having different skills, advantages and disadvantages. Pick your monsters wisely for battles! The customization options for both the player’s character and their monsters enhance the overall experience.The game features a diverse range of environments and regions to explore, each with its own unique creatures and resources, encouraging thorough exploration and discovery.Players may find the pacing to be slow at times, particularly during the early stages of the game. The story and gameplay can feel a bit drawn-out, with cutscenes, dialogue-heavy sections and frequent back and forth moving.While the combat system is innovative, it can become repetitive very easily. The reliance on similar strategies and tactics for various battles may lead to a sense of monotony for some players.The behavior of AI-controlled allies in battles can sometimes be inconsistent, leading to less effective strategies and occasional frustration during key fights as the AI pulls some random garbage on you.Personally I had a extremely smooth experience from start to finish but there have been reports of occasional performance issues and technical glitches, such as frame rate drops and minor bugs, your mileage may vary here depending on your hardware combination.For players who have completed the main story, the endgame content may feel somewhat lacking. While there are post-game activities, they might not be as engaging or varied as some players would hope for.Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a delightful and engaging RPG that successfully expands the Monster Hunter universe with its unique turn-based combat and rich storytelling. While it may excel in creating an immersive world and offering strategic gameplay, it is not without its challenges. Slow pacing, repetitive elements, and technical issues are aspects to consider before purchasing. Nonetheless, for hardcore fans of the series and newcomers alike, the game provides a memorable and enjoyable adventure that is well worth experiencing.

The battle system is rather simple at first, but a joy to dig into. I just can't imagine what the decision was for your party member's to be controlled by AI, but alas, most of the time it works. The game has traditional Monster Hunter features, such as forging weapons, upgrades, armors, crafting and of course, the series' staple Monsters. The game length took me around 26 hours to complete. Anyways, if you're looking for a fun RPG set in the Monster Hunter setting, you cannot go wrong with this. It is a love letter to series fans, though with some minor flaws, but don't let that stop you from playing and enjoying this game. Hopeful to see a sequel with my minor flaws corrected. In short, Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a joy to play, with a simple but deep battle system, with a simple, charming story, and an easy to adore game, especially for series' fans!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a really tough one to score. This is one of those games where you need to sit down and way the pros and cons before you get into it. So here’s what you need to know:The gameplay is fairly simple, being made up of two parts. The wandering/exploration, and the combat. The exploration part consists of you running around on a miniature monster, usually collecting resources while looking for your next objective.The combat is basically a flashy game of rock-paper-scissors. It's alright, but it does have a long-term problem. In its design, it is not simple enough to just turn your brain off to and enjoy, but it is also not interesting enough to warrant an enjoyable challenge. It exists in this bland middle ground where you can quickly get bored of it, and if bored, it still demands enough attention that you can’t just go into it while multitasking something else.While the two main parts of the gameplay  fairly simple, they are also what’s advertised, and to that extent, they are just fine. A major issue of the game, as well as the main reason for most of its negative reviews is the fact that you can’t play Co-op through the main campagin. This would be tolerable, if it wasn’t for the fact that the main campagin is around 8-20 hours long. There is also PvP, though I can’t say anything about it since I couldn’t find a single person playing it.The Story, is petty much the weakest part of the game. While Munster Hunter games generally don’t have much of a story, I have to say that I expected a game with “Stories” in the title to have at least some semblance of sense. The story is your usual excuse to go fight monsters, most details are overlooked for convenience, and the plot eventually hinges on a random MacGuffin so miniscule that I can freely spoil it knowing that you will never remember it come the point where it's needed.As far as the general appeal of the game goes, it’s a mixed bag. On one side, most people who get this game likely do it because they are fans of the franchise, and are entertaining the idea of having the monsters be on your side for once. On the other hand, this is a game aimed at kids, and that is apparent as some parts of it can make you cringe so hard that it hurts. And I am talking about the Kinship attacks. In my personal case, I came into the game because I liked the idea of getting to control the monsters, and I certainly wasn’t disappointed, even if it was in a turn-based game.Something that is quite worthy of praise in this game is the upgrade system. This game is one that can easily be compared to Pokemon on basic premise alone. To that extent, it is worth praising the fact that this game does not copy some of the major flaws of some Pokemon games. I am specifically talking about the artificial time bloat, that is making every creature spawn with random, unchangeable power levels. In fact, one of the worst things that some Pokemon games do is giving you a starter Pokemon that has horrible stats that you can’t change, making you have to replace it later down the line with the same, better Pokemon. This game doesn’t have that. Your starting monster is as good as any other monster of that species, any skills it lacks, you can later add. There is no bs 0-100% quality system like in games such as Pokemon Go.Now, if you put the upgrade system aside, the gameplay loop is still just wandering around and collecting monsters. BUT, that is what the game advertises, and it does it well enough.Ehhh… $60 is a bit steep for what it is, especially considering the multiplayer issue. Now to be fair, you could pull quite a lot of hours out of it as there is a lengthy end-game after the initial story. However, most of the gameplay can be brushed off by the common definition of being repetitive, so I would probably recommend that you get it at a sale if the general idea of what I listed so far doesn’t seem particularly appealing.======================================================As a whole, this game has enough ups and downs to the point where I wouldn’t normally write a review on it, simply because its too far in the dead center of quality where its not so bad as to be bad, but not so good as to be worth recommending.The gameplay is a slow-burner, though it is decent.The story is, -well, dumb. But it is entertaining enough.The multiplayer is absent throughout the most lengthy and interesting part of the game. Making anyone who bought this to play it with a friend likely feel ripped off for having to go 10+ hours just to unlock proper multiplayer.And the aesthetics are quite nice.Altogether, this game certainly has some shortcomings. But it also has some generally good aspects. Small details such as continued quest board tasks remembering your progress from the previous quest, the fact that your character doesn’t have the turn rate of a buss, the fact that multiplayer is  quite alright if you find a soul interested in playing through the game just to get to it. It has issues, but it strives to deliver a good experience. Also, it didn’t rip off the horrible Pokemon CP system. So props there.So, if you like solo, turn based games that vaguely resemble Pokemon, then you might like this one.======================================================

_childDocuments_.review: I started out quite liking this game.It looks great, it sounds fanstastic and it plays well.The main strengths of this game are definitely the combat and monster collecting.I originally thought that the combat would feel dull because of the rock paper scissor system.But this actually adds extra complexity on top of the usual turn based combat.You still have skills that you can use, you can also order your monster to its skills.Every monster has its own way of attacking, which the game doesn't actually keep track of, and encourages you to remember the patterns of each monster that you face.Some monsters are very predictable, but are very strong - While others are very unpredictable, but not necessarily life threatening.The monster collecting system is done quite well in my opinion.Each monster has a certain rarity, which is also represents how good a monster is.Monsters with high rarity will have better stats an a low rarity monster.Everytime you enter a new area, new monsters are available for collecting.They are also usually better than the ones you've faced in the past, which incentivizes you to go out of your way to recruit them into your team.What I didn't quite like, was the progression of the gene system (transferring genes from one monster to another by sacrificing them). It felt quite overwhelming, and I never really felt like I could commit to sacrificing a monster for another one, since I would replace them anyway with another stronger monster.To me the story and how it was told is quite average.The story takes a while to pick up, which is unfortunate because early/mid game it feels like you're just running around without an actual story. Eventually the story does pick up at the end.The cutscenes and voice acting were done well.The biggest flaw in my opinion is the dungeon design, it felt like there were 3 dungeons that were used 100x over. And it's not just the randomly generated dens, the actual main dungeons are also mainly copies of eachother. This is ultimately what lead me to rushing through the mid/end of the game, since I couldn't be bothered with the same dungeons over and over again.All in all, not a bad game.Better dungeon design, better story pacing and a better monster progression system would have taken it from a 7 to a 9 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: MHS2 is a game with a lot of promise and that provides a decently enjoyable time. But in the end it usually falls flat and feels like its over ambitious for what it wants to be. Its a game I recommend but with quite a bit of hesitation. Run of the mill Monster hunter style story. Overall really boring and predictable. A lot of the characters, animations and interactions are really adorable, but most of the characters and things happening are just extreme tropes, to the point you could guess what they would do and you would 90 % of the time be correct. There are a lot of small interesting details sprinkled into the story but nothing ever happens with it. Talking about nothing ever happening with it, the over world and locations you go through have a lot of potential to be expanded upon, but none of that ever happens.  Its a common rock paper scissors style battle system that can be found in a lot of different RPG's, especially in collect them all style RPG's. Its done ok here but nothing spectacular or fantastic. Its usually pretty predictable and most of the time doesn't provide much of a challenge until you get to the end game. Pretty much the entire game boils around entering a monsters den to get an egg which you can hatch to get a monstie, this loop is incredibly fun and really addicting. Dens are randomly generated but usually look and play almost all the same. It is really repetitive, and while executed good enough it can still very quickly become a drag to go through, I would have loved to see more hand crafted original dens instead of the  constant like 5 room layouts you have go through in each dungeon/den. Thankfully when you get a new monstie it seems like the game gives them an EXP boost to get them near your level faster, You can also run from most non CO OP fights, this helps alleviate the grind quite a bit. The monstie diversity here is really great. There are a LOT of reskins but you still get to see, fight and ride a lot of really iconic and fun monsters. The animations here are seriously fantastic, all monsters that aren't reskins have unique animations and sounds. Their moveset are usually pretty unique even for the reskins. The main complaint I have here is that there are field skills which allow you to interact with the world, however these field skills barely matter usually and honestly feel more like a pain in the ass and limit you in exploring the world or choosing between your favorite monsters.  If you thought monster hunter worlds co op could have used work then wait until you experience MHS2's co op. You can't do ANY story related thing together. Instead you can create online lobbies and go through dens or arena fights. Its extremely boring, and for some reason there is barely anybody online at any timestip. Not only that but to create online lobbies for a lot of quests you will need vouchers, if you want to do the fun stuff that actually matters you will need to grind for a SR ticket. This usually isn't THAT bad, just by playing SR ticket dens and finding all the chests you can usually find or farm enough for 1 or 2 tickets. Now this would be the case if people online actually allowed you to. The actual player base can be insanely friendly and patient or extremely frustrating, purely focusing on themselves. People can just skip every fight, egg and chest purely to get to the end to get the coveted egg that actually has a good combat monstie. If they manage to beat the monster you will have 1 minute to get to the end and get the egg and leave, making it so you barely get to actually get more tickets or actually have fun even if you used the SR ticket yourself. The only ways to deal with this is to reset the game and load up a save or disconnect during the quest/start the online quest solo, but this gives you an AI companion and can take a very long time as well as potentially meaning you lose the last fight because your AI doesn't perform good enough.Lastly there are is also PvP, however because of how important the rock paper scissors mechanic is, the pvp ends up feeling more like an extra and in the end pretty unbalanced. Its a nice extra but could have used a bit more work to feel fleshed out. The online itself seems to be ok. The fights can drag on a bit more since you can't skip/speed up a lot of animations and the game is constantly syncing up your attack constantly creating a bit of lag. But most of the everything was pretty much seamless. I only had 1 case where someone's online was SO bad that I just had to quit, 1 fight took around 20 minutes + just with how ridicliously bad my connection to them was. And like I said earlier, its REALLY hard to play with random people online because even though this game has a decent playerbase it still seems to have trouble to actually show available lobbies to you, often showing you none at all. All of my complaints relating to co op and online stuff can honestly be ignored if you have a friend who has this game and wants to play together, otherwise you are stuck gambling on having a decent time or not. My god has the ball dropped here. Remember all my complaints about co op earlier? Well I hope you enjoy being forced to deal with that dumb stuff because if you wanna get the end game monsters you will have to use co op to grind for them, you could do it solo but it takes a LOT more time. Remember all the cool stuff I said about monster diversity? Well sorry to say, but if you want to actually experience the end game normally without grinding a stupid amount you will have to stick to a very limited amount of monsters. And you WILL need to get those good monsters, the end game monsters can have a ridiculous amount of health if you do not have their specific weakness and to get that weakness you will probably have to grind for a specific monstie, level them back up and give them proper genetics. Its a lot of grinding for more grinding. There is some single player related stuff but that mainly for people who REALLY just want to test their monstie lineup. Its nothing fresh or original with few exceptions, to actually get the monstie's and upgrade your team you will probably have to stick to co op end game. After 70 hours I felt like I had a good enough feel of the game to write this review, but there is still a lot of monstie's farming and other random end game content that I could have done and most likely over time will. Its a big game with a lot to offer, but a lot of what is being offered is not completely fleshed out or has some serious mistakes. When the game works its fun and great, if you don't mind cliche's the story is good enough and the end game has a lot to explore and is constantly getting updated right now. However getting to that end game can be a drag, and basic things like co op and farming for late game monsters should be way simpler then it is right now. If you have the patience to go through this game its absolutely a recommend, through all the earlier mentioned negatives there is still a great game with a lot of positives. But if you expected the next Pokemon or a master piece RPG you will probably be disappointed. It does not have the story telling, or extremely deep and fun combat that a lot of RPG's have. And in terms of being a collect em all style game I would still say Pokemon does it better in terms of interactions with your partners (Why is there pretty much no out of combat things you can do with your monstie?), online functionality and having a more balanced and competitive end game. MHS2 is a really big and in general a really enjoyable experience. The game is so big that I wish I could talk about it a lot more, but steam does sadly have a character limit on reviews and I think I already wrote about most of the main problems and strengths this game has.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is an incredibly fun title. It offers turn-based combat, merges with a rock-paper-scissors mechanic to create some truly challenging combat.True to Monster Hunter in a traditional sense, monsters have patterns and behaviours that if you invest yourself into learning you'll find the combat is a lot less random than it initially seems, with certain monsters preferring specific types of attacks.On top of that, there's a complicated breeding system that will have you learning to recognise monster eggs by sight alone, and interpreting your aide's lines to know the quality of the egg. If you want the best monsties, there's plenty of time to be spent here too!The story isn't... amazing, but it's also not terrible! It's interesting enough to warrant a play-through and the collectathon achievements warrant plenty of time spent in the game, if that's something you're into. There are no annoying hard-to-get achievements, and even the multiplayer achievements can be completed by yourself.All in all if you like RPGs, and Turn Based battle systems, this system will give you plenty of enjoyment, lace that with an incredible monster-hunter worthy soundtrack and a beautiful world filled with monsters you know and love, and you will have a great time with this title.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game on both the Nintendo Switch, and on PC since the free trial was available on the Switch. I can 100% say I absolutely adore this game. It really scratches the itch that Pokémon has failed to satisfy in recent years. The story, while nothing too special, is still solid, and I've thoroughly got my money's worth out of the game, even buying it twice. I would definitely recommend, although like any game there are some cons, which I've outlined below:Pros:-----* Large range of monsters available for riding, and within the game in general.* The boss at the end of the main story is absolutely gorgeous.* Riding around on your monsters (and later flying around) is really fun.* Some of the Kinship Skill animations for some of the monsters are hilarious and amazing.* Once you reach a certain location in the game, you can purchase a layered armour version of any armour you have with you you've forged for only 700 each. Way better than having to gather parts to craft layered armours like in the mainline Monster Hunter games.* A good selection of monsters, with plenty of monsters returning who weren't in World or Rise.* The step up from normal rank in the main story to high rank in the post-game isn't too jarring and doesn't leave you struggling to gear up or grind.* The game doesn't stop you from running away from a battle, except if you are attacked while taking an egg from a nest, in multiplayer dens, or in main story fights. The only penalty for running away is you don't get any monster parts or rewards you would have obtained.* The Switch version has a lot of framerate problems, but the game runs smoothly on PC.* The Right of Channeling system to boost/change/add to your monsties' abilities by moving in genes from other eggs you've hatched is a fantastic, flexible, and highly customisable system.* Multiplayer is smooth and easy to use.* Voice acting, even in English, matches the lip sync.* The areas in the game are fun to explore and for the most part well-designed.* While your character doesn't speak, they do have some semblance of a personality and character development arc.Cons:----* Tetsucabra is in this game, but you can't ride it or hatch one.* In fact, there are quite a few monsters that are in this game, but you can't ride, which is quite sad.* Sometimes the AI for your monstie and NPCs fighting with you can be downright idiotic and get both themselves and yourself killed.* You can't run away from a battle in multiplayer, even if nobody else joined you.* You have to have a specific monster in your party for all of the main story (except for certain sections, when you have a forced empty party slot instead). While the story reasons for it are understandable, it does limit the selection of monsties you can bring along if you want a balanced party.* There are some small graphical bugs at times.* Navirou.* You have to wait for an NPC to finish their animation and turn back around before you can talk to them again.*You can't skip Kinship Skill animations in multiplayer, even if every player wants to. Animation speed is also fixed for multiplayer at 1x speed while selecting actions, and 2x speed for battle animations once everyone is locked in. This means if you get a double Kinship Skill activation with a friend, you can't properly enjoy it because it's forced into 2x speed.* Dens & dungeons can get a little repetitive as you end up with the same pool of sections grouped together in different combinations to auto-generate them, which can lead to jump/climbing/dig points that don't lead to anything.* NAVIROU.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a sequel to the first game by a similar name, and a good iteration on it at that. However, the chances are if you're looking at this game, you probably didn't play the first, so I'll keep this review focused on the game by its own merit.1. You do not need to have played the first Stories to be able to play this game. That said, if you have played the first, you'll see some familiar faces in this game. (And to be fair, it might... make you a little bit angry.)2. Similar to Pokemon, this game is easily accessible and has a low skill floor, but has a higher skill ceiling and a lot of room for customisation and optimisation. (And, unlike Pokemon, you probably won't need to waste hours of your life trying to breed for perfect IVs and special moves just for one single creature.)3. If you're familiar with typical cartoon stories or anime/manga, the story isn't particularly mind-blowing in any regard. It's fairly average at best; good enough to follow along, but not really enough to get you on the edge of your seat.The basic gameplay of Stories involves combat that focuses on a Rock/Paper/Scissors system - or in this case, Power/Speed/Tech. All monsters in the game have a preference for the type of move they like to use, and this preference might change as the battle goes on and the monster becomes enraged, or maybe charges itself up with a special move. The basic goal of the game as you progress is to learn these monsters' different preferences, and then counter them with the corresponding correct type. So, if you're fighting a Power monster, you'll want to use Speed moves.From there the game builds on this system outwards: you can have three weapons equipped at a time, and can swap between those weapons once . There are six weapons in the game, two of which that deal Slash damage, two that deal Pierce, and two that deal Blunt. Like in the mainline game, different monster parts are weak to different kinds of damage, and so the game encourages you to make use of the once-per-turn weapon swap to switch to a strong weapon to break a part off a monster. Similarly, monsters have a variety of elemental defences, in this game all streamlined so that they are resistant to one, and then particularly weak to another. (So, for example, the titular Rathalos of the game is more resistant to Fire, but is weak to Lightning.) Weapons can also deal elemental damage, meaning that you can truly capitalise on monster weaknesses by using the right type of weapon with the right type of element to deal large damage each turn.Throughout all the game, you'll also be playing together alongside your AI monsters, known as Monsties. There are over 100 to choose from, some of them being variants of others, and many all have a unique gene of their own while also potentially carrying several "cross species" genes. The goal is to go out and raid Monster Dens to get eggs, hatch these eggs, and then slowly build up monsters with good gene boards - aiming to align their elemental genes or their move type genes in a row or column of three within the 3x3 gene board to get bingo bonuses. Bingo bonuses will ultimately dictate the strength of your monster, as they can increase the power of an element or a specific type of move (power/speed/tech) by 10% each per the first two bonuses, and then an extra 5% for every bonus after.And... that's it! The game takes a very simple idea, like rock/paper/scissors, and then rather masterfully elaborates on that idea to create a game around it while interweaving more familiar aspects of the mainline Monster Hunter games. The core game isn't particularly challenging, but the post-game challenges in the Elder's Lair can require incredibly specific strategies if you want to beat them. The game is easy to start playing, but offers a lot for those who also want to try and be more optimised in their builds, and unlike similar games such as Pokemon, Stories 2 is respectful of your time and doesn't require hours upon hours of monster breeding just to get decent base stats. (Bingo bonuses make the initial base stats generally irrelevant unless you're looking to be as optimised as physically possible.)• Excellent gameplay that's gotten me to sink in 120+ hours on the Switch and nearly 50+ hours on PC.• Beautiful graphics that, when you think about it, put Sword and Shield to absolute shame.• Great soundtrack with some real bops, though sadly a lot of the overworld doesn't have a soundtrack and I... don't know why. It's actually a huge shame.• Easy to learn combat with a lot of potential for customising builds and monsters, where I've never found grinding for monsters or genes to be unreasonable.• Huge variety of monsters to ride around on and be your friend! That said, the movement skills in this game are a holdover from the first, and kind of a disappointment. The game should really allow you to teach monsters certain viable movement skills that are, within reason, things they could learn to do. As it stands, movement skills can leave you feeling hamstrung on what monsters to take to certain areas, which is a real negative.• The base vanilla game was honestly not too challenging for me even on my first playthrough, outside of a couple of snags. Replaying the base game my second time around was even easier. Thankfully, post-game content is challenging and there's many hours of it to enjoy, much of it that will really push you and your Monsties to the test.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Hunter Stories 2 (MHS2)… another Monster Hunter game on Steam? Don’t mind if I do! I always had a soft spot for turn-based RPGs, which makes MHS2 definitely right up my alley. Capcom took a different approach to the series and made a story-driven Monster Hunter entry with anime-esque visuals. In addition to that, I’m amazed at how they turned the humble “rock, paper, and scissors'' into an interesting combat mechanic. While some parts of it could’ve been better, I thoroughly enjoyed MHS2!The story begins with what was supposed to be a time for festivities turning grim as an eerie pillar of light bursts out of the ground, causing the guardian of Hakolo island to run amok and disappear, leaving but an egg that could very well be key to our salvation… or destruction. Journey through the beautiful world of Monster Hunter not as a hunter, but as a tamer tasked with unraveling the mystery surrounding the egg, while trying to make sense of what is the meaning behind the eerie pillars of light scattered throughout the continent. Unlike the other entries, MHS2's main selling point is that it focuses on the narrative aspect, so storytelling is a lot more enjoyable. Granted, the story caters to a younger audience, but it’s still enjoyable overall. There are two things I don’t particularly like about the story, the first one would be, everytime a new character is introduced, they seem to know and praise the main character’s late grandfather a lot; they just can’t stop mentioning how great he was. The second one is the fact that one of the antagonists was badly written, and by that, I mean horrible. One of them shows up at one point of the story and is never mentioned again until he decides to make a grand reappearance on the final chapter; by that time, I already forgot that he even existed.MHS2 has a distinct visual style that makes it stand out from the rest of the entries. Capcom’s decision to use cel-shaded visuals was right on the money and it works exceptionally well for this particular kind of RPG. The overworld was lush and a wonder to explore. In fact, sometimes I flew around with my monstie just to admire the view. Plus, the flight control was done exceptionally well, which made flying a fun experience.MHS2 took a complete 180 from the regular MH gameplay, from the staple action-oriented to a turn-based RPG. The combat uses three attack types: power, speed, and technical where each one is weak against the type next to it. Frankly speaking, “it’s a rock, paper, and scissors” game; however, it is layered with several other elements that make each fight a unique experience. Learning each enemy behavior can be a make or break during late-game hunts. Preferably, you’d aim for a double attack, which triggers when both you and your monstie exploit the enemy's weakness, but there are fights where the enemy attacks twice or even three times on the same turn, so that’s another element to consider before choosing which move to use. What’s more, during combat, there’s a possibility to trigger a minigame that allows you to deal extra damage and fill up the kinship gauge or skill bar, which can be used to turn the tide in your favor. There are several issues regarding the combat system, the first one would be that the damage your character deals is extremely low, even with exploiting weakness so, you’ll need to rely on switching monsties to get that weakness damage bonus, and the other one is that there are cases where the announcement texts are scrambled, and the last one would be the bots are badly designed. Imagine cornering a boss only to have the table turned because your partner used the wrong move – yes, this happened more than once, and also yes, you don’t have control over your partner. One of the main features of MHS2 is den exploration. One thing I need to point out is that the den layout consists of a random mix of several template sections unique to the specific region you’re currently in. This gives the illusion that each den differs from one another. These dens, ranging from regular to super rare ones, allow the tamer to collect a monstie egg and, if you’re lucky, several rewarding treasure chests. Keep in mind that the RNG is strong on this one, so you will need several runs before you could actually get the egg you’re looking for. These eggs have distinct patterns and colors that help the tamers differentiate which one they’re holding to.Monsties come with several “genes” that you can unlock by leveling them, and at times, one or two random genes. Genes are essentially a skill that each monstie has. These skills can be transferred into others in order to create an abomination to your liking. How the skill system works is rather simple, the goal is to line up three of the same color or pattern, that way you’ll get an additional bonus stat on them. Furthermore, there’s a wildcard skill that allows you to pair it with any other color or pattern called rainbow gene. Ideally, it would be best to put it in the middle, that way you’d have a wider range of options of stat bonus to rake in.MHS2 has several issues regarding the online experience; the first thing you need to know is that it is region-locked, so you would need to apply a mod in order to have a higher chance of finding anyone to play with. The second, and probably most important thing, is that online mode is pretty much deserted – ouch!, even with the mod applied, I still have a hard time finding anyone to play with. The only saving grace of the online features is that it is still doable with bots, so there’s no need to worry about having those online-related achievements locked. While the co-op quests are extremely helpful to get an early start with your monsties collection and filling up the “field guides” (built-in monster database), the PVP is not so much. The combat system works wonders during the single-player mode; however, against other players it backfired, because it boils down to a guessing game, making fights feel cheap and unrewarding since there is hardly any strategy involved.Monster Hunter Stories 2 is a nice change of pace to the highly action-oriented Monster Hunter games. it really wowed me with the visual aspect and combat system. While I enjoyed the story, Capcom could’ve toned down referencing the previous game a little bit so those that didn’t play it wouldn’t be confused. Online features aside, I had a blast playing through this one! If you enjoy JRPGs, this would be a fine addition to your library. Ride on!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say to wait for a sale before pulling the trigger. It is a good game, and I personally feel that it is better than the past few Pokemon games, but with a price tag of S$81 it is a hard sell.Like many others have already put forth, the story is not particularly new nor interesting. If you want to buy this game to continue off the story from the first game, just watch the playthroughs on YouTube. The story appears to be more directed at children, featuring a forgettable cast of characters with no particular unique traits that would make you want to remember them. Each new area plays out in this sequence:For a game with "Stories" in its title, it really does leave a lot more to be desired.Gameplay has been improved from the previous game. The monsters' attacks now predictable (mostly), requiring you to first learn what moves the monster prefers (rock, paper, scissors) to throw out throughout the fight before you can anticipate and appropriately respond. You'd find yourself spending your first turns buffing yourself or your team because making a wrong move (e.g. scissors against rock) can be very costly. The monster will also change its preferences throughout the fight depending on various factors, such as when it buffs itself or when it enters its enraged state.The gameplay at first glance seems very one-dimensional but you will find that it gets deeper as you progress. There will be roadblocks along the way that forces you to understand the game's combat mechanics. You can potentially 'ooga booga' your way through the game, but I can guarantee you won't have a great time. Having come from the previous game, I had prior knowledge of some monster preferences and the gameplay mechanics (there really wasn't much changes, if any), so it was easy to 'ooga booga' my way through the demo. I subsequently found myself stuck at Yian Garuga, forcing me to play around with the combat mechanics a little more before rediscovering 'double attacks'. I won't elaborate any further, play the game yourself to find out more.Your companions, monsties (monster + besties), is what you will be building around. You are able to merge traits from various monsters to make a monster able to control multiple elements at will, if you so desire. Most of the time, if not always, you would have the monster specialize in a certain aspect. As far as the end-game goes, build diversity is sorely lacking in my opinion. There are only so many different ways I can kit out a monster. The roster of viable monsters are really limited to elder dragons and deviants, in both PvE and PvP.If you take your time with the story, you can comfortably expect 30 hours. I couldn't really spare any attention to the lackluster story, so it only took me around 15 to 20 hours. I spent the remainder of my time decking out monsters, having fun testing out builds... and here I am writing this review 70 hours in. I honestly can't see myself spending much more time on this game, as there isn't any harder content that requires me to work harder. I already do enough damage, and there is no incentive for me to do more.

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: This is REALLY my first Monster Hunter game, so MonHun veterans take this review with a grain of salt. I'll also review the game as a Monster Collector RPG game likewise.This is probably the best monster collector game I've played so far, and somehow it's a spin-off.Monster Hunter Stories 2: Wings of Ruin is a game that puts you in a world where you can tame the various monsters from the Monster Hunter franchise and fight alongside them in a JRPG-Styled Combat. I've had 98 Hours in this game and counting (I need to clear the rest of the Postgame content) and I genuinely enjoyed a lot of what the game has to offer.- Monster Design: I guess it's hard to mention monster hunter without mentioning their designs. They range from "Absolutely awe-inspiring" to "Filler, but it's completing an ecological niche", which I like a lot compared to filler that don't contribute much to the immersion. Each Animations also add quirks to certain monsters that is only possible in Stories 2 due to settings differences from the mainline games.- Monster Customization: You can give the powers/attributes of a lategame monster to a route 1 monster should you wish, so go on and play with your favorites!*- The Player Character takes an active and central role in combat: You know how in Pokemon or Digimon JRPGs the Trainer/Tamers don't actually join in combat? Riders do, and in true Monster Hunter fashion you're supposed to gear them up accordingly using materials that drops from monsters.- Quality of Life: All monsters are obtained from level 1, however extra EXP are awarded to underlevelled party members, so you'll find levelling that new member to be way easier compared to other games.- Monster Representation: Take this one with a grain of salt but I heard friends who are Monster Hunter veterans mentioned that there's a good balance of New and Old monsters, and while the tamable monster roster is only barely in the hundreds each comes with a variety of unique animations and their own Ultimate animation (Variations of the same monsters may or may not have unique ultimate animations.)*With base stat limitations- The Story: Story is pretty baseline for Monster Collector RPGs; it's not bringing anything really new to the table but it doesn't mean it is bad or stale. - Multiplayer: Your postgame would mostly be multiplayer content, so it's even more recommended to find a friend to play this with for more playtime longevity.- Difficulty: The game difficulty scales rather well, until the very last leg for some reason.- Combat Details: You can guess a monster's patterns if you're paying attention to what you're facing, no spamming A mid-combat in this game!- Better in Controller: While the game is absolutely playable on keyboard, there are button mashing sequences mid-combat that would favor controller users.This game is absolutely great, though its longevity really depends on whether or not you have friends to play with. Preferably snag this game on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: 50 hours in I realized I just could not care about any of it. The repetitive dungeons, the frustrating combat with unavoidable attacks, the absolutely painful storyline with one-note unlikeable characters.What you have to understand about the game is it is 50% shonen nonsense for kids and 50% rock-paper-scissors style combat. You have a monster companion, or monstie - "monster bestie" - who will attack based on its type, or you can spend points to select a specific attack. These attacks counter each other in an RPS style. Fine. Beat the monster and get materials, or cart 3 times and game over.The problem comes when you're saddled with an AI partner and monster, neither of whom you have any control over, and if they cart 3 times you also game over. And they will often make the wrong choice in terms of attacks, which means effectively the game is a series of escort quests over which you have very little control.It's like the story is for kids but the gameplay mechanics are for the most obsessive grognards so I'm not even sure who this is for.So, while not necessarily a bad game, it is definitely not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: While it is not a bad game, I cannot *truly* recommend it. (I wish there was a neutral or tendency rating-option...) The first hours are fun and entertaining, however half way through the story it gets clear as crystal; The patterns in storytelling, gameloop and locations repeat themselves over and over again with little to no variation, beefed up with a lot of filler content in the form of repetitive sidequests that require you to hunt either monsters, collect stuff, show certain types of eggs or monsters while also conveniently gating both weapon skills and crafting recipes behind them, basically forcing you to do them. A big weakpoint of the game is the protagonist, that is silent and voiced by the sidekick. While not particularly annoying or bad in itself, I think a sidekick should never be the voice of the protagonist. Graphic-wise it looks good in my opinion, but then again I'm not very focused on such things. All in all the game got boring pretty fast and left no opportunity to really bond with any character and leaving no room to really immerse yourself into the main character. On a sidenote, here are some facts about the game;- There are Monsties that can perform field skills like climbing up ivy, swim, go through lava and the like, but there's not enough room to include all those abilities into your team, forcing you to either live with it (What I did) or go back and forth switching them out to gather all there is. Fortunately nothing important seems to be gated behind it aside from flying, which is story relevant.- Also in regards of those field skills, there's no option to switch the active Monstie on the fly, forcing you to open the main menu and select it manually. While this is no problem for things like jumping, climbing, digging or swimming etc, it's a super inconvenient chore for abilities that have no trigger on the field itself. - There are tons of weapons and armour, however I never sticked with any long enough to make upgrading them worthwhile. Keep the upgrading for lategame. - The roadmap shows that they'll probably only add new Monsties, but in my opinion nothing major is planned. Aside from that they plan to gate certain Monsties behind Coop.- Directly on day one the released a ton of DLCs in form of Cosmetics and the ability to change your character (Hairstyle, Haircolour, Armour and Armour Colour as well as facial features like tattoos, freckles etc can be changed at your house for free though. Armour skins are called Layered Armour and can be bought midway into the story).- There is no auto-battle, but quick-fights. This allows you to finish any non-boss battle against already fought enemies (Fought enemies have a revealed health bar, not fought enemies have a greyed out one) with an S rang, allowing you to efficiently farm materials. It requires you to be stronger in levels than the enemy, which has no level indication. - Allies can get you in trouble due to their terrible AI. You have 3 hearts which get refilled either by using certain items or returning to a village, but the AI allies tend to be dumb and get killed occasionally. Be mindful of that and pay attention to their hearts.That's that for noteable side notes for now. Those are no direct pro or cons. In any case it isn't a bad game, as stated above. But the caveats are strong, so I cannot recommend it. This, however, is only my opinion and perspective on the game. Feel free to try it yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILER FREE (you should experience it blind like I did)Also, I am not actually that far in the game, I am trying to complete every subquest, and there's a lot of subquests lol, so I think I'm only in like the midgame maybe? Don't know for sure.Okay this is gonna be kinda long, and it will change over time, but here are my current thoughts on this game:IT SLAPS SO HARD OH MY GOD I LOVE ITBefore I get into why, let me explain my bias:1. I played the 1st stories game for a little over 100 hours and I loved it (though it lacked post game content)2. I went into this game (almost) completely blind. The only things I new are what was in the trailers and that Nergigante was in this game (which was I big reason why I got it bc I loved World). Also, I think I googled like one thing because I didn't want to waste time grinding a specific monster if what I was doing didn't work, so not technically completely blind but almost3. I love Monster Hunter as a franchise. I have 158 hours on base world (just got Iceborne and Rise, super excited) and I have like 500 hours on GU and Gen respectively.So why do I like this game so much?Pretty easy. It's a fun monster collecting RPG with fairly nuanced mechanics and beautiful environments. I love how intricate the designs are, down to textures of fur and scales, it's fantastic.The combat mechanics are something I especially want to highlight. On paper it's kind of like rock, paper, scissors, but you observe your opponent because they have a preference for one, and you have to figure out when that preference changes what it'll change to. Then, there's the items and hitting different monster body parts, which depending on the part you hit, varies the damage from your weapon. For example, blunt weapons are more effective on the head. It's a neat way to combine main series mechanics in this spin off.The game has a mechanic which I LOVE called quick finish. Basically, if a monster is too weak (like your level is way higher), the game will let you quick finish, which just ends the battle in one turn no need for back and forth.While this makes it so that you'll never fight certain monsters again, a lot of the time you can beat them so easily that I completely understand why they implemented this. So much time to save grinding in an RPG.The story (so far, can't tell you how it goes) is honestly pretty weak. Like it's not bad, but it's not good either. The first game had the same problem, in fact, all monster hunter games have this problem so it's not like I came into this expecting something great. It's pretty meh, and the characters (again so far) are fine. Some of the voice actors had a field day with this game, and you can really tell. They're pretty funny sometimes, though I have seen complaints about the VAs being annoying, I don't really see it. I think the game is a little too upfront with cheesy jokes sometimes and it does make you cringe, but I think that's what it's going for. Sometimes I found myself laughing at the dumb jokes because of how stupid they were.The difficulty is pretty meh. For an RPG, the story bosses are actually laughable. Maybe my subquest completion was to blame for this though, as subquests do provide exp. Not too sure. BUT THE SUBQUEST BOSSES, OH BABYThese things will play tennis with you as the ball. They slap you around and almost one shot you, so they require you to turn your brain on and observe their patterns.So what's my conclusion?32 hours in and this game slaps. This review will continue to evolve as I play more, and I intend to play a lot more. Just thought I should share this so more people can enjoy this awesome game.EDIT: Another 55 hours later and my thoughts really haven't changed.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like Monster Hunter, Pokémon and/or turn-based combat JRPGs?  Then you’ll enjoy MHS 2. It has quality turn-based combat mixed in with the Pokémon-like collection of critters set in the world of Monster Hunter.  If you find the main MH games too complicated to get into, this one is the one you want.  It’s on the easy side, but gets more challenging about halfway through it.  It’s filled with plenty of the usual JRPG cliches: lots of cats, one horribly annoying NPC with you for the entire game (with grating voice to go with it), brain-dead Jrpg story, children protagonists, and plenty of fetch quests and grinding.  If you’re ok with all that, there’s a lot to enjoy here…deep combat, lots of rewarding exploration and the monster hunting and collecting is really well done.  Definitely worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing Monster Hunter: World for a pretty solid amount of time, I picked up the second installment of the Stories iterations, and I am everything but disappointed. I genuinely like this game. From its art style, to it's turn based combat, flashy moves, and mechanics (the whole, "Speed beats Power, Technical beats Speed" thing), and even the ability to utilize team skills for big damage with your companions -- I genuinely appreciate all of it. The vast open world allows you to explore to your heart's content, gather items without having to hold a button (thats something I personally found annoying in MHW), and take in whatever scenery you so please. The story to the game, at least from what I've seen so far as I am currently playing through it, is actually something worth paying attention to; it's even got a sense of humor to it, which is really nice. Monster Hunter Stories 2 also stays true to it's style when it comes to crafting items, armors, and various types of weapons. I think my only real gripe about the game is that -- at the time of this review and gameplay -- I can't wear certain pieces of layered armor like I could in World, at least to my knowledge. Outside of that, this game is a very solid experience, and I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys turn based combat style RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Ohhh man.  If you thought Hunters were bloodthirsty, genocidal maniacs, wait until you’ve met a Rider.  Riders make the Research Commission look like PETA, and they conduct experiments on monsters that would make Josef Mengele squeamish.  These psychopaths slaughter monsters and steal eggs from their nests.  After killing the parents, they brainwash the newly-orphaned hatchlings and raise them to kill endangered species.  However, the cycle doesn’t repeat just yet!  In addition to using monster parts to create armor and weapons like their Hunter brethren, Riders also harvest the genes from LIVING monsters.  Riders discard their victims and frequently transplant the genetic material into entirely different species, giving these unfortunate recipients traits that would otherwise never occur naturally.  These mad scientists then use their garish, nightmarish, abominations to decimate entire ecosystems in search of even more desirable characteristics.  All in the pursuit of creating the perfect monster.  Alas, Riders always fall short.  Their dastardly creations end up resembling Victor Frankenstein’s monster.  Undeterred, they continue with their highly immoral and unethical experiments and the process begins again.  To date, Riders are the most sinister and vile of Capcom’s creations.

_childDocuments_.review: In most ways, this is an improvement over Pokemon. The monster design is better, combat is more interesting, and customizing monsters is more intuitive and fun. One of the main ways Monster Hunter Stories 2 falls short is in its length. You probably won't play it much longer than it takes to complete the main story, and obtain your former team in high rank. The last bit feels like an unnecessary grind. The game could really use an expansion that adds a few more areas and activities. So it might be worth waiting for a sale.The main story is aimed at younger teenagers, at most. So adults will find the dialogue a bit grating with its childishness. Otherwise, the voice acting is good. Combat is complex with having to factor in elemental weaknesses, physical damage type, attack technique, and syncing up attacks with your "monstie" in order to be most effective. Each weapon type has different combos and strategies. Armor is equipped as a set, and each set has a unique selection of skills that change how effective various combat strategies are. Armor and weapons can then be upgraded, in order to keep using them, or to maximize their effectiveness in the late game. Monsters can have several skills equipped, but mostly act on their own. Players may spend kinship points to direct them to use specific attacks. Outside of combat, monsters can help the player with mobility, utility, and detection skills.Overall, this is a surprisingly deep monster battler, but it could be fleshed out to make it a top-notch game.

_childDocuments_.review: So I don't review games very often but this one I feel I had to do.So just to start off this game has been so much fun for me and just seeing the love and attention put into making every monster feel alive and unique is a on a whole other level.Monster Hunter Stories 2 is basically not to different from your other sort of monster raising games (Pokemon, Digimon, Tem Tem) However this game as in a low of charm that makes it just shine every time just makes me want to play every time.StorySo the story is very charming and wholesome. Its not really crazy in terms of narrative and it can be predictable. Though that didn't stop me from being engaged. The characters through out the story very much kinda make it punch way above the threshold for me and really help make the story have impact. I was quite satisfied actually.GameplayMonster Hunter Stories 2 does feature turn based combat similar to games in this genre. You and your monster take turns picking different attack types in an effort to beat the attack type the opponent  uses. So much like a rock-paper-scissors idea. Then through out that you get different skills and attacks as well as special combination attacks with partner npcs and there monsties. This keeps the combat unique and makes every fight kinda different in its own way. In the game you obtain monsters in places called dens where you with some rng you can try to get a monstie that you like. Add in the ability to create builds by transferring abilities and attacks to another monstie. If you like kinda of making builds optimizing your play style, preforming crazy experimental joke builds? Then I think you might enjoy this aspect a lot.Play TimeSo I have easily sank 89 hours into the game and I just hit endgame only a week ago. So as far as things to do...it is a long haul and you will get a lot of play time out of this title. I could easily see someone getting more then a 100 hours in this one.In closing! I have been always on the lookout for a monster raising game that would kinda give pokemon a run for its money and really show what zeal and polish could do. Its safe to say that monster hunter stories 2 is one of the best games of the genre to come out in the last few years. So if your a monster hunter fan then I implore you to pick it up. There are so many omages and references to previous games and events that it is just a love letter to the series as a whole.If your not a monster hunter fan...but you enjoy pokemon and felt  burned by the latest pokemon iterations. Then perhaps try this and you might be pleasantly surprised.Totally my game of the year and I think everyone should pick this up if they game. Its well for the price tag in my honesty opinion

_childDocuments_.review: As this is my first review it may not have everything that people are looking for in a review, but because I love this game as much as I do I have decided to write a review for it. First off, at it's core it is a Monster Hunter game and I am judging it off of that instead of as a catch them all kind of game like Pokemon or Shin Megami. Since the word "stories" is in it's name, we will start there. I will warn you now that you should not play this for the story alone. The story carries it through for what it needs and there are cute moments. However, there are also moments that kind seem embarrassing because the story is about kinship (aka friendship with monsters). There is a childlike element to it, but I don't mind because it brings me back. In a way it reminds me of Pokemon Black and White story wise. The lore and world of Monster Hunter is interesting, but the main story itself is what Monster Hunter usually does. The main core of the game is the gameplay loop and the mechanics. The battle system uses the concept of rock, papers, scissors, and that has it's own perks. This is the first time I've personally played with this kind of system so I thought it was fun. Aside from that system there are also elements and weapon types/damage types (pierce, slash, blunt). Each type has 2 weapon types and there are so many different weapons that can be crafted. This system keeps the core of Monster Hunter as a series and I am glad there is a variety of weapons and armors. The game does start off a bit slow as there aren't that many monsters to choose from and you don't get a choice of starters, but it shouldn't matter if you don't stay hung up in the first area. After the first area it opens up a bit more and there is more monster variety for players to choose from. The game is repetitive in a good sense. It emulates the repetitiveness of a true Monster Hunter game with it's gameplay loop of finding the perfect genes and making the perfect setup.  Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who likes turned base games or Monster Hunter in general. If you are only a fan of one then I recommend you try out the demo to see if you will like it. The main story took me about 40 hours of gameplay, and that is due to my habit of semi rushing and going slowly at different intervals. I'm planning to invest much more time into this game because I have yet to see every monster and make any of the end game gear.

_childDocuments_.review: The transition into the third arc of the story goes like this: the strong knights in shining armor come take the little savage from a tiny island, put his friend in chains, and drag him to their big, cultured city. He then has to prove that he's not like other savages. He's a good, strong savage and is worth keeping around in their city full of smart and educated people. They're so much smarter than the little island savage so he needs to do quests to prove that he has value, in spite of his background.If you love seeing strong, intelligent colonizers subjugate simple brutes, you'll love this game. Though it is a surprise that the Japanese development team didn't include comfort women (Japan's favorite colonizer pastime), it's still a great story of how civilized, better races should subdue, imprison, and re-educate the lesser races.

_childDocuments_.review: MH themed creature collectorfull disclosure; i havent finished the game yetobviously the star of the show are the monsters (or monsties if theyre friendly; and im going to use that term going forwards)monsties have base stats, as well as some variance dictated when theyre born (IVs if likening to pokemon)each monstie has a 3x3 gene grid (youll likely have to use consumables to open up the full grid), genes provide passive or active skills (unlike the original; monsties no longer have their own innate movepools; everything they can use is determined completely by genes), they also have an element (or non element) and type (or are typeless; ill get into types when talking about the combat later)... if you match 3 of either element(/non elemental) or type you receive a 'bingo' bonus that provides a damage boost to that respective element or attack type (unlike the previous game you can stack multiple of the same bingo... and unlike the previous game a non elemental bingo increase the damage of non elemental attacks rather than increasing speed)each monstie is hatched with some base genes, theres guaranteed genes but theres also a pool of non guaranteed genes with various rarities that a specific species can hatch with (so dont go hunting kula ya kus for non elemental boost L in the first area because they cant hatch with it)you can move a gene from one monstie to another (the donor gets eaten or runs away or goes to live on a farm... whatever you want thematically; but functionally it gets deleted) using the 'rite of channeling' (this is a feature unlocked in the second village)... if you played the original then theres two key differences; you can move gene locations (previously if a gene was top left on the donor it would only go in the top left slot of the receiver) and you can level up genes by stacking them (up to 3 times; increasing effectiveness)you can trigger an aesthetic change by messing around with genes; you can shift a monsties element if you stack enough to overide its base stats; its colour pallette will shift to reflect the element it was shifted to... functionally however i doubt this will be worth doing, in the original it was only worth doing for non elemental monsties... but with the bingo changes (specifically non elemental bingo) its essentially gimping them for aesthetics (but the option is there if you want it i guess)not every monster in the game is a rideable monstie, theres small monsters like velociprey that arent (because theyre smaller minions of possible monsties; ex velocidrome)... but theres also some 'big' monsters that arent possible monsties (like tetsucabra)... as far as i can tell the whole roster (sans dlc) from the first game made it across to this one, the new additions are mostly monsters that debuted in MH World; the ones that arent are either the fated 4 from generations or variations on the previous roster like bloodbath diablos or dreadqueen rathian); the total count of monsties is supposedly 81 if the monstiepedia is to be believedCombatso theres 4 types of attacksspeed beats powerpower beats technicaltechnical beats speedand then theres typeless attacks that dont interact with that system at allthis rock paper scissors forms a contentious point; and was often used to detract from the first game... which i disagreed with then because monsters (note the terminology; im not talking about monsties) had their own patterns (for example; p.rathian used to have something like 2 speed 1 power 2 speed 1 power pattern; and if you figured that out you could win 100% of head to heads)... monster hunter stories 2 has sort of dumbed that down (atleast as so far as ive gotten)... monsters have a base type (say technical), when they enrage they change their attack type (say to speed)... and rarely monsters have a third change; say inflate into a beach ball (zamtrios) or get charged with electricity where they change to the third type... its a bit simplisticyou have complete control over the protagonist; your monstie on the other hand does what it wants to do... you can wrangle them into using a learned skill on a select target but this will cost some kinship; which is an in battle resource generated through various actions (and when full can be consumed to jump on top of your monstie; which enables powerful kinship attacks); realistically if you know what you're doing then youll essentially have full control at all times thoughfor equipment the player character has a talisman slot (which if you're familiar with mainline monster hunter games; just provides passives), an armour slot (just one; the whole set; which provides defenses as well as more passives... in the first game if your equipment matched your monstie then you received a kinship cost reduction; i havent verified if thats still the case in this one though) and 3 weapon slots (which you can swap to at will in combat)in monster hunter fashion; your equipment is scavenged from the corpses of your enemies (except not really because somehow you can beat a bulldrome; takes its skull... it still gets up and retreats to its den... where you can take its skull again)each weapon is either slashing (greatsword, sword and shield), piercing (bow, gunlance) or blunt (hammer, hunting horn); some monsters/parts are weak/resistant to certain types of weapons... this only extends to riders though and each specific weapon has its own moveset meaning they play a little bit differently; for example hammer and horn are both blunt weapons but where the hammer has skills that benefit from specific ailments on the target or just deal damage; hunting horn has songs in its skills; which provide buffs, debuffs or unique effects (if you're familiar with the mainline monster hunter games the same 'this horn plays these songs' applies) (if you're familiar with the original; hunting horn had a massive rework in that you dont need to 'play' the notes by losing head to heads; you can just play the song outright for kinship cost)you can break monster parts for big monsters; depending on the monster and the part this will have various effects; opening them up for damage, preventing them from using a move, tripping them... but sadly theres no visual indicator of this; if you break pukei pukeis tail it doesnt fall off line in the mainline games; theres no difference in the model; itll just stop it from using a specific attackVisualcharming aesthetic, but graphically lacking, im sure it looks fine on switch but for pc the textures are a bit low quality (some in particular) and theres a very low grass LoDStoryeh, theres some small inconsistencies across the games... also no one seems to bat an eye at the fact that 4 years before this game there was a legendary rider that saved the world from a 'blight' with a rathalos called 'ratha' (MHS1)... but also the MHS2 protags grandfather (called 'Red', which almost seems like a pokemon callout) had a rathalos ALSO called 'ratha' who become a guardian of the starting island (chronologically way before the MHS1 'ratha' but still no connection)... oh and we arent done; for some reason the razewing rathalos the protagonist hatches is also by default called 'ratha'... youd think that one of the multiple characters (including the annoying cat) that spanned both games would atleast mention this... literally no one does (atleast as far as i am in the game)... its not even a placeholder name that you can change; it has to be 'Ratha'... its weird and i cant wrap my head around it... aside from that its a meh story; its not good, its not particularily bad... but its also not why i play these gamesAudiovoice acting is lacklustre at best; it also doesnt help that the english VA doesnt match mouth movements; i switched to japanese VA before eventually turning sound off altogether so i cant really comment on the score other than it wasnt gripping me

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original but I have always wondered what a Pokemon-like game for the franchise would be like and Monster Hunter Stories 2 does not disappoint. The game is a wonderful blend of Metroidvania, Monster Rancher and Pokemon wrapped up in a charming Breath of the Wild aesthetic that I will definitely be playing for weeks to come.That said the game is far from perfect, mostly because it started off as a Switch game so it is pegged to that hardware standard. For one draw distances are terrible; grass will literally grow ten feet in front of you and you won't spot monsters until you are nearly on top of them, and there is noticeable stuttering after loading an area. Moreover there have been some questionable choices in the sound department that while the game has great music you won't hear it most of the time while exploring, total silence save for your monstie's foot steps, which was obviously a battery saving concession for a portable platform.Finally, which really accounts for this negative review, is DENUVO. At this point there is a bad interaction between it and overlays like Discord and NVIDIA Experience that causes a glitch which closes the game on start. You have to switch off some stuff or the game won't start properly. And Navirou... its mother aborted it for reason. Kill it.
