_childDocuments_.review: Perfect revivals. Despite what some people may think, they do happen. Now and then a long forgotten name appears with a great new story that involves both old and new cast. If you're into teen dramas, you probably remember , which revived  and 's legendary show.  and  returned with kids in .  is still fighting . And, of course, there's . A sensational revival of the original  trilogy that brings back  (),  () and pretty much all the rest of the original movies' main cast one way or another. Aside from  () for obvious reasons. The main story, of course, revolves around the new bunch of kids. Which are absolutely great and make perfect characters on their own. The show is done in a less serious tone than the originals, but still, it's a great show and is totally worth your time. Make sure to check it out if you like the original  movies. It looks like together with the old karate story, though,  also revived an old tradition. A tradition to have at least one video game for every major movie / TV show out there. Think 'bout that. How often do we get something like that nowadays? So... Let's take a look, shall we?The guys who were hired to do the job here are  from . And it's important for you to know because of their first game. A game called .  was a pretty unique fighting game, in which there were no health bars. To win against your opponents, you were supposed to rip their limbs off by using unlockabale special attacks. Don't expect anything like that here, in  game (it's much more family-friendly than that), but remember that  guys a) know their fighting games and b) can think outside the box. Now, what  we have in  game?Well, we've got ourselves a beat 'em up game. Pretty old school one too. At least, on the first glance. Naturally, it's based on  show and  takes place somewhere around second season. I mean, this game was released before season three, while 's rocking his  look, so...  don't think 'bout that much. Because instead of following canon, this game takes place in its own alternate reality, in which characters can use battle magic of sorts. The game comes with two story campaigns. One for  and one for  (you'll need to finish both, though, if you want true final boss and real ending).  specializes on damage and fire “magic” (), while  is all about the defense and ice (). Sounds crazy, but it's actually pretty smart and stylish decision. Even the fact that you need to beat the game twice to get real ending is actually pretty smart. I'm trying to avoid spoilers, though, so you'll need to take my word for it. It  make sense.You know what's even better, though? The fact that we've got the original cast. That's right. The game is actually voiced by real actors from  show. Not all of them are here, unfortunately. Major examples would be  replacing  as ,  playing  instead of ,  replacing  as  and so on.  both  and  are here and so are  and , who play  () and  in the show. Personally? I just loved that. I mean, we rarely get any games based on contemporary movies and TV shows nowadays, but with the original cast involved? YUM!The best thing about this game though, is, surprisingly, its gameplay. To be honest, I didn't expect that. What I did expect is yet another one of those ultra-cheap beat 'em ups. Maybe something akin to . I mean, it's hard to expect good from something with such a casual look  the first couple of levels here do feel really,  basic and casual. But. Right after the game introduces its skills mechanics? It begins to shine for real. See, it's one of those smart games that try to use our usual controllers in some pretty unusual ways. Remember what  did with the mouse? There's no way to compare these two games, but in a way  is trying to achieve something like that. With gamepad instead of a mouse. Four buttons on the right side ( if we're talking 'bout ) can be used in our usual beat 'em up way,  at the same exact time they also represent two groups of skills.The first group is personal skills. The ones that are unique for every character (each dojo gives you access to four characters – , ,  and  for  and , ,  and  for ). The second group is so-called dojo skills. Those are shared between all the characters from dojo you chose at the beginning of the game. Each group comes with four different moves for you to perform and level-up (you'll also be able to customize those a bit to fit your own personal preferences in battle, which is really,  good idea).  Four buttons. Eight skills. Plus four regular attacks. How is that possible? The answer is – by holding triggers. Holding the left trigger will bring up dojo skills, while holding the right trigger will bring personal ones. Also, pressing both triggers at once will activate one of those big-ass special attacks (naturally, it's  for -san). Sounds simple? Well, yeah. But that's the beauty of it. I mean, this game? It's surprisingly addictive. Two triggers and four buttons? There's a lot of fun in that. Even grinding for higher skill levels here is fun just because the core mechanics is satisfying. Congrats, , really nice job.Unfortunately, aside from better visuals, polish is something to be desired here. Can't say that this game feels especially cheap, but yeah, it's far from being perfect. Using environment attacks (there's quite a lot of those and they're quite funny) can be more problematic than needed at times, sometimes the reward currency lands in places you can't reach, some attacks have weird hit detection, it's hard to tell which objects can be broken for pickups and which cannot, it's hard to pick up the right item at times (when food lies near the weapon you may want not to risk it if you're aiming for better score and therefore avoid picking up food for healing), etc. The whole package of slightly cheap aftertaste.Does it feel bad, though? Heck, no! Personally, I had a lot of fun with this one. Like, . Way more than I expected. This game is addictive, those moves are simple (not even original if we won't count controls and customization), yet satisfying,  did make characters feel like themselves in battle, it's more challenging than it looks (at least during the early stages, since even one fully leveled character is, like, a one person army) and, well, it's fun. What else can you ask for? You like the show – I'd say go for it. $19.99 does sound like a fair price. Especially if we'll keep those actors in mind. And on sale? It's a bloody steal. By no means what we have here is a perfect or must-have title. But it's a very nice entertainment in the between of  seasons. Dixi.

_childDocuments_.review: To start with, I *LOVE* the Cobra Kai show. I recommend it to everyone I can. It is clearly a show made by people who love the franchise, the characters and it has so much heart and fun. I wanted to love this game. However, this game has some of the worst enemy design and AI I have ever encountered in a Beat 'em up. Just about every enemy has an invincible attack where they flash red and can not be knocked out of the attack. Ok, so that's to stop you from just spamming attacks recklessly. Except, the red flash doesn't properly reflect when they are invincible, as they will frequently start their invincible attack and flash red AFTER you've already started attacking them, and should have been stunning them.Next, the devs idea of challenge is just for the enemies to non-stop spam these attacks. It's pretty much all they do. On top of that, the enemies pretty much never walk anywhere, they just instantly run from where they are to you, then spam their invincible attacks. The chief concept of beat em ups is to beat down waves of enemies, often facing groups of enemies in different combinations. This means that not every single enemy has to be a difficult annoying obstacle. You sometimes need dumb mooks to work on your combos or practice parrying on. Instead, every battle is a CHORE, because you are constantly dodging or parrying because of all the invincibility of the enemies. Seriously, watch any let's play on youtube past the first level and just watch and see how often the enemies are flashing red. It's basically over half the time the enemies are on screen, and they are actually invincible for MORE than that time, due to the bs coding.The combos and attacks are actually pretty cool, and would be fun if the enemies weren't so damned unfun. The best part of playing co-op beat em ups is to play with people of various skill levels, like my kid nephew. This game started with promise then became rapidly unfun for both of us. I bought this game to support the Cobra Kai franchise, but I regret wasting my time and money on this.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice game and totally overlooked by many. I played all side scroll beat em ups since Double Dragon on my commodore 64 and even Streets of Rage pales in comparison to this game combat wise. Miyagi-Do is defence and has ice effects, Cobra Kai excels in offense ( the best form of defence) with fire effects.Each character has access to 4 dojo attacks but also 4 special individual attacks. They can all be rotated onto the battleground on the fly . I found a few combos, chaining special attacks and essentially air juggling groups but I am certain I missed many more. Very deep combat system and fun to boot.The campaign loosely follows the TV series Cobra Kai with both dojo's having different outcomes.Recommended for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: A fascinating case study in how to do a technically competent job of building a game while failing to make it fun.  The pacing is off (it took me over half an hour to finish the tutorial level), the fights are slow, the hit detection is too fiddly, the fanservice inaccurate, the experience as a whole is tedious.I suspect that I'd be less offended if I didn't like the IP as much as I do.  I just the strong feeling that the creators aren't fans of beat 'em up games, and they're not fans of the show.  Which is why it's so disconnected from what makes an enjoyable beat em up, and what I love about the show.

_childDocuments_.review: Streets of Rage 4 this game is not and that's why I like it. I mostly play rpgs, action games, beat 'em ups are not my cup of tea. I'm what you might call a button masher when it comes to fighting games. Or to put it another way I suck at these games and do not usually enjoy them. This on the other hand is very enjoyable for me and I'll explain why. For a beat 'em up game the movement and attack speeds of the game are incredibly slow. For me that lack of hyper speed game play allows me to do more than button mashing and not only learn all the combos but use them in combat. It's fun and I now understand the charm of these kind of games. I still don't think the genre is for me. If this is a kid's beat 'em up I am ok with that because it's just fun.Another aspect I quite like is the outdated cartoony graphics. Sure, it may look like a xbox 360 side scroller or a mobile game but it works. It reminds me of the old beat 'em up arcade games and less like the recent ones released to console and PC. It's very much like the old T.M.N.T. and Simpsons four player arcade beat 'em ups. A lot of the moves remind of the T.M.N.T. game but the speed and wonky hit detection etc. is more akin to the Simpsons game, which was fun because it was the Simpsons but compared to other arcade games of the time was slow, clunky etc. Which brings me to my final point, I liked that old Simpsons arcade game for what it was, as a Simpsons fan. I am also a Cobra Kai fan so the actual voice actors and nods to the series make it a very enjoyable lockdown time waster. If you're a Cobra Kai fan and even casually into beat 'em up games I would give this a 7/10If you're a Cobra Kai fan but totally hate beat 'em ups I'd pass on it.If you could care less about the series and just enjoy beat 'em ups, i'd say as a stand alone beat 'em up it's a 5/10.  Tl;dr - great time waster, beginner level difficulty but great fun to be had for fans of the show.

_childDocuments_.review: this is like something you find in the bargain bin and have a blast with. it's a good game with many flaws. it's your normal beat'm up but here outside your normal move set you have a 4 characters to tag in/out, a super move on a gauge, and 2 sets of 4 power moves (that do not take hp to use). each team will unlock and upgrade 4 moves based on the dojo, the cobra moves are based on fire/burning and the Miyagi ones are based on ice/slow and all 4 of your team can use them. each character also has their own 4 moves. you can use any of the 8 moves at any time they are not on cooldown (after use they can't be used again until a counter ticks down). once a move is unlocked you can upgrade it. if you unlock a moves skill tree to the end each one has a upgrade you need to do something for it but it's free when you do. some are do X damage with it, toss x enemies in the air with it, or kill X enemy Y times with it. this is a pain and very inconsistent as you first need to finish a tree before you can start on unlocking the last upgrade, then you need to have said character out with said move when x enemies are about and hope you can kill them with said move. all this as some move just unlock passively on their own.as for the story it's your normal beat,m up smack talk with a lose predictable story where you need to play through both sides on 1 save for the better ending. levels for both dojos are basically the same with the talking bits being different.the fighting is fine but as the game goes on most of the enemies will just tank your hit as they move in to slap you in the face. they explain it as some "armor" thing but they turn red and will not fall down when hit though some ground specials can knock them down if they are in the right range. i have not run into any glitches like other reviewers so i can't comment on that (yet).like i said it's a good bargain bin game so grab it on sale but if you're not into cheap (flawed) games you may want to give it a pass though i really don't see much better from other beat'm up games on steam so i feel it's a solid buy. if you do get this the first thing you should use points on is unlocking the 4 dojo moves then each characters 4 personal moves before upgrading anything. you'll want to spam these moves whenever they are up so you want all 8.

_childDocuments_.review: The trailers definitely didn't do the game justice. I thought the same about it as everyone else when I saw them; low budget cash-in, etc.Turns out the game is a lot of fun! It won't set the world on fire but if you have a craving for a side-scrolling beat 'em up, it gets the job done. The fighting is fun and the characters feel just different enough to make you want to try each one out. Upgrading each character in different ways is great, so you can focus on damage for one and defense for another. I got this game for free in a giveaway but it's worth the reduced price tag. I've paid more money for worse/shorter games. There are two campaigns in the game (Cobra Kai/Miyagi-Do) and I'm not even done with one of them yet.One downside is the lack of voice actors from the show. There are only about four or five of them. Most do a decent job but Miguel's voice actor sounds nothing like the character and I don't know what's going on with Brucks (one of Kyler's bully friends). The story itself is nothing special. It's like a comic book spin-off of the main show; aimed at a slightly less mature audience, so only light swearing, and some characters are almost like caricatures of the ones on the show (I got so sick of hearing "Tory with a Y" every time I switched to playing as her). Another downside is the game recommends using a controller and I hate having to scroll through menus using the analog stick, rather than the d-pad. My only real complaint about the graphics is that some characters look ugly during close-ups in cutscenes. In-game, it looks nice enough.If you're into Cobra Kai, I recommend it. _childDocuments_.review: Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues tries to piggy back from the popularity of a TV series but fails miserably. While the TV series focuses on passion to a very real sport, that traverses not only generations but also walls of a dojo, the game somehow managed to add fire and ice magic, physics breaking jump kicks, unblockable special moves and temporary invulnerability.If that wasn't enough, it went out of its way to show as many colourful flashes and flares as possible, creating visual clutter that more often than not renders any deliberate strategy useless. Why the flashes and visual cues? Well, because back in a day it wasn't possible to implement an actually decent fighting mechanics. But nowadays we have flow-driven combat gems like Assassin's Creed, Batman, Shadow of Mordor, Mad Max and countless others. Not here. Here you spam B when enemies flash red indicating an unblockable attack and button mash otherwise. That's about 90% of the gameplay.Officially the game tries to pay homage to the retro beat em ups but I still play some of those games and they not only feel responsive but, most importantly, are predictable - when you get hit, you know why, where and how you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. In Cobra Kai it's mostly random. Maybe the hit box glitched or the input didn't register - you won't know. It's just bad implementation. So bad that they had to make the game extremely easy by stretching the health bar to the point it's boring. I really tried to like it but I can't.NOT RECOMMENDED.

_childDocuments_.review: Cobra Kai the television show has made huge waves as it’s now reached its third season.  The first season started by recontextualizing the original Karate Kid movie by giving the villain of the first movie, Johnny Lawrence, a more in-depth backstory and a redemption arc. From there, the second and third seasons have grown the world and gave us interesting stories and a fresh take on the original franchise, though at its core is Johnny Lawrence’s Cobra Kai versus Daniel Larusso’s Miyagi-do. It’s not surprising that someone has finally decided to capitalize on the growing franchise by creating a video game out of it.  It’s just a shame that this is the result because everything feels wrong with Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues. The most glaring issue is that Cobra Kai feels like it exists in a different universe, and yet also feels like it’s the same universe as the show.  Without spoiling anything season three added some massive changes to the television world of Cobra Kai but Cobra Kai the game doesn’t seem to attempt to undertake these changes. At the same time, there are significant issues with the story. <cut for the steam review, see full review at The story doesn’t help much and the fact is, with this being its own story, the game holds a “Final boss” over the players' heads which fans of the show probably will be able to guess easily. Truthfully, there’s not much reason for the characters to fight, but at least that’s not the core of the game.  I don’t think most players are buying for the in-depth story.  They want a fun experience of being a member at either of these dojos, whether it be Cobra Kair or Miyagi-do.  Unfortunately, the game can’t produce a good reason for that either. Both dojos eventually get four characters and conceptually having Joey Lawrence, Miguel, Tory, and Hawk all on one side as they face off with Daniel Larusso, Sam, Robbie, and Dimitri could be good, the fact is they all play very similar to each other.  Each dojo is given four special attacks, and while upgrades can be purchased which change any special attack along two different branches, they mostly remain the same.  Each character gets four unique special attacks and seeing each character have a different moveset feels good at first.  There’s entirely too much game for such a minor change.  You’ll likely spam your special attacks over and over, and with each character having just the eight special moves, as well as a full normal move set sounds good, after a couple of hours the game will feel repetitive. Cobra Kai boasts a “deep moveset” the fact is most of it is unnecessary or uninteresting to use. So players will use their special attacks which costs no energy and recharges in a short time, the pacing is such that players can use a special attack about every 2 seconds without ever running out. Cobra Kai also relies on a combo system, and this too becomes problematic.  In the first few levels, it presents the combo system but the system itself is a flawed mess.  It rewards variety and using different moves.  The problem is it takes almost half the game before the player will have enough moves to use the combo system, and then the system breaks and becomes rather easy to dominate with as long as they use all their special moves once.   There is a parry system that works and is very powerful but enemies attacks become more annoying to predict and the dodge gives you the same level of invincibility but also allows you to move out of the way of other attacks as well, without worrying about timing your parry. The worst part of the combo system is it’s treated like hidden information.  The current level is decided by a point total that’s not shown to the player,  instead, players will suddenly move from a “D” to a “C” up to an “A and then an “NM” for no mercy.  Good concept, but the reason these letters are changed is because of the mysterious score system that’s not shown to the player. The combo system is also based on not getting hit, and while that makes sense, the mysterious scoring and the fact that getting hit while using special moves doesn’t reset the combo makes the player push for more special moves and less unique fighting styles.  Just spam your favorite moves and you’ll do more than fine. Of course most beat ‘em ups aren’t especially deep but have a fun and engaging gameplay loop for a few levels.  In Cobra Kai, there are 11 major levels in the game which is more than most beat ‘em ups.  There are also 16 minor levels, which players will have to fight through to unlock the next major level on a map screen.  These levels are long, and while the minor levels lack a major boss, there’s still a hard enemy at the end of each.  The Major levels usually have a couple of bosses and feel a bit too long, maybe even twice as long as they should be.  By the time the players beat the mid-boss, the level has usually shown the theme off and presented it well, but the level continues until the player gets bored. The bosses in Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues have entirely too much health. And while the early levels have good pacing to it, the levels in the last two-thirds of the game feel like enemies gain too much health, requiring a battle of attrition, either the enemies will wear down your health, you’ll wear down the enemy’s health, or you’ll get bored of Cobra Kai.   Truthfully, I got bored of Cobra Kai a few times while playing it, and yet I wanted to see how the entire playthrough would go before reviewing the game. The game does change.  Early on the game feels very easy and like a typical Beat ‘em Up, but before long the game starts to lavish on cheap enemies that players will have to battle, large life bars, and eventually normal enemies that can summon additional enemies, and all these factors make the game drag on.  I finished my run of the Cobra Kai Dojo in about ten hours.  And then suddenly the game locked me out of the Cobra Kai Dojo and instead gave me the Miyagi-do Dojo, the problem is the Miyagi-do dojo now have to fight through the same 27 levels, and if they reach the end, then there’s a promise of an obvious final boss.   I gave up on this game at least three times while playing through it, I returned to review it but I wish I had stopped.  After beating one level with Miyagi-do and seeing I was being asked to do the same thing I already had completed once before, with slightly different characters, I was finally able to stop. If you remove the Cobra Kai/Karate Kid license, there’s no reason to play this game, but even if you include the license, you really won’t want to play the entire game.  It’s too long, repetitive, and boring.  This feels like an obvious win, but instead, this is a snoozefest of someone going through the motions to cash in on a popular IP, rather than a loving homage to a great franchise. SImply if they had removed about half the content this game would improve.  Just removing the minor levels, and even pairing a few levels exclusively with either dojo could have improved the game a lot.  Instead, we get this.  It’s a shame because I got excited at the concept, but this game is not worthy of the name.  Maybe I’m being too hard on Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues, but in the words of the one true Cobra Kai… “No Mercy”I give this an arbitrary score of 5/10God I wish it was higher, this should have been an easy win, and if you’re a heavy fan of Cobra Kai television show, maybe it’s a 6/10, but it’s not worth a recommendation, but this is a Beat ‘em up based on Cobra Kai, this should have been a slam dunk, not an average game. If you enjoyed this and want to see more from me, you can check out my youtube channel at

_childDocuments_.review: It sure is nice to have a new beat em up to play. They don't make too many of these anymore. I particularly like the tie in to the excellent Cobra Kai netflix series. Unlike the show, don't expect this to have any good writing (save for the genuinely funny one liners that the characters have after winning a fight). This is purely a fighting game, one that is clearly a loving homage specifically to the Streets of Rage series. It's both better and worse than Streets of Rage 4, which I'll get in to later. Everyone you run across in the street from hippies to mothers to emo kids are all inexplicably out for your blood, which is funny in its own regard. Sometimes characters will provide humorous meta commentary on this. Every character of note in the netflix series is either playable or is a boss in some level. Cobra Kai has fire powers while Miyagi Do has ice powers. Tone wise, it's far more light and irreverent than the show; it does not take itself seriously in the slightest. Some might find this off-putting, but subjectively this works quite well.Mechanics wise, this is a stiff game, with a lack of perceived fluidity in the basic combat moves. I found this to only be a problem in the beginning, when your characters have few special moves to utilize. There is an RPG like progression tree for each character, and also a separate tree for dojo skills that are universally accessible. Dojo money drops from opponents in battle, and it all goes in to a general pool. You can then use that money on anyone's development. One common annoyance is that it's easy to get caught in a grapple which I almost always try to avoid because it makes you vulnerable to attack. Same for beating on someones face when they're on the ground. A very rare and minor annoyance was that sometimes opponents would get stuck off screen for a bit which causes you to lose your combo. This game went from being too hard in the latter part of the first hour to very easy afterward. While dodging, you are invincible, same for your special attacks. Importantly, attacks do not use up health like in the SOR series. They are instead on cooldown timers. Once you get all 8 of your special abilities (4 personal, 4 dojo), it's very easy to dodge when you need to (the enemies turn red before an attack), then you can just spam special attacks on rotation. This sidesteps much of the game's stiffness. After I got to this point I noticed that the game-play wasn't off-putting in its flow anymore, but there was absolutely no challenge, even from bosses (and no difficulty levels that I found). Given this, I would say that there are balance issues here (Daniel LaRusso would have a problem with that). I think there was a good reason for SOR to make specials use health for purposes of balance. Still, this doesn't really bother me personally, as I get in to a very zen like state while playing. Nailing the timing of everything is still satisfying, particularly when there are a ton of enemies on the screen and little room.Despite SOR4 being a more balanced, cleaner, much harder, and more traditional beat em up, I have to give high praise for some of the innovations here, particularly in such a well established genre. Instead of having multiple lives, you can tag in other characters that have more health. Even if a character 'dies', if you get a strong enough combo with another character, they'll come back to life and you can tag them back in again. When you get hit, there's a timer that allows you to inflict damage to heal back your recent hit point loss. This makes this game a LOT easier in general. There is also a cool parry system that allows you to automatically counter if you time the parry right (which isn't too hard). Environmental attacks are cool too, you just have to be close to a green glowing object and hit a specific button to slam them in to the object for high damage. There are gi and belt combos that act as power ups. The gi describes a certain condition (such as hitting 3 critical hits). When this condition is met, it will trigger a power from your belt (such as triggering an explosion, or a buff for more damage).  Because of the progression system, this isn't a beat em up that you can beat in a few hours, which is nice to see. The streets of rage games were formulated for arcade play and that shows (somewhat less in 4), but this feels as though it was designed for extended home play. I also like how you can dodge up and down, even if you can't punch up or down, and this gives the game a bit more 3 dimensionality than SOR4. So, despite its flaws, I would say this game is for you if you like beat em ups, are looking for innovations in this genre, can power through the stiff but very short early game, and aren't looking for nut-crunching difficulty. Being a fan of the Cobra Kai series certainly helps as well.One last thing, use a controller. I would say that's very important for beat em ups in general.

_childDocuments_.review: This is no Streets of Rage 4 (which is pretty much the gold standard for this type of game), but it's still a solid beat 'em up and an exception to the rule that licensed games suck donkey balls.+ When it works, the gameplay offers plenty of variety from one character to the other, as well as a surprising amount of different mechanics and stuff to interact with. Once you get used to the game and buy a few upgrades for your characters the combat becomes a lot more satisfying and fun. Enemy variety isn't incredibly high but it gets the job done. - When it doesn't work, the overall clunkiness of the game can be really frustrating. Many attacks and skills go through enemies without connecting if you're too close to them, and quite often you simply can't interact with objects in the way you're supposed to. Some enemies are also flat out stupid in how they hit and throw you around without any telegraphing of their attacks. The story is mostly nonexistent and literally doesn't get anywhere even after finishing the first campaign. + There are plenty of references to the TV series and classic films, as well as attention to detail. Each dojo (Cobra Kai and Myagi-Do) gets a different narrator, loading screen, soundtrack... The soundtrack for the stages is a bit repetitive but it really gets you in the mood to beat up some goons, and the sound effects add a lot of weight to the attacks (some more than others).- Only Johnny, Daniel, Hawk and Demetri are voiced by the actors who play them. Most of the voice talents are good, especially Sam, but some are just... not. Robby in particular is pretty jarring in how he sounds nothing like the character, and Daniel/Ralph Macchio sounds bored out of his mind most of the time. Both enemies and playable characters repeat the same lines quite often too.   Final score: Cobra Kai Never Dies/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the Karate Kid movies when I was young, I did not really follow the Cobra Kai series but I'm guessing it's as cheesy as the movies, if not more. There is no lack of cheesiness in this game, that's for sure. Beat 'em Up games also give me those nostalgic feelings of back in the day when I used to play games like; Golden Axe, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles IV, Fighting Force, Double Dragon and Streets Of Rage to name a few. Graphically, I can't say the game is gorgeous but it also didn't really bother me that much. It actually made me think of another Beat 'Em up "Double Dragon Neon" , a game which I couldn't get into. The gameplay does what a good Beat 'Em Up should do. There are tons of combo's to defeat your enemies which you can unlock after each level, depending on how much points you get. You can also upgrade your dojo to give you an extra edge on the 'battlefield' by gaining more hp or damage etc. Speaking of 'enemies', there are quite a few of them with all kinds of stereotypes like; ♥♥♥♥♥ girl, preppy guy, motorcycle gang guy, American football player etc. not even counting the many different bosses. After a few missions you should have 4 characters to play with. Whenever a character is almost down you can replace him/her with another character which is pretty cool as well. Often in the later missions you could get spammed with opponents though which makes it tough to get out of the fight alive. Because all npc's have different attacks and speed etc. it could get hectic. Luckily if you throw enough punches you can get a special attack which basically knocks them all down. Cobra Kai-The Karate Kid Saga continues may not be the best Beat 'Em Up of all times but I think it's a great game if you are a fan of the genre. Edit: I do have to say that this "Yasmine" character is a huge pain in the ass and you encounter her at least 3 times. Not only does she shoot 'hearts' at you which damage you (somehow) with quite a big AoE and heals/boosts other minions AND herself, she also has also attacks you when you get near which is almost impossible to defend against. This wouldn't be that hard if the minions she's with would not be these annoying kids with their parfume or whatever it may be, just a rediculous bossfight.

_childDocuments_.review: Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues? More like Cobra Cry: The Karate Kid Saga Disappoints. This tie-in game to the popular Cobra Kai series fails to capture the spirit of its source material, delivering a bland and uninspired experience that will leave fans of the franchise feeling more frustrated than satisfied.Let's start with the gameplay—or lack thereof. Cobra Kai attempts to blend beat 'em up action with RPG elements, but the execution falls flat. The combat feels clunky and unresponsive, with repetitive combos and sluggish animations that quickly grow tiresome. The RPG elements, such as character customization and skill trees, add little depth or strategy to the experience, feeling more like tacked-on gimmicks than meaningful gameplay mechanics.But perhaps the biggest disappointment is the presentation. Despite boasting cel-shaded graphics reminiscent of the Cobra Kai series, the game's visuals are lackluster and unpolished, with generic character models and bland environments that lack the charm and personality of the show. The voice acting is equally uninspired, with flat performances that fail to capture the energy and emotion of the Cobra Kai characters.And let's not forget about the story. Cobra Kai attempts to expand upon the events of the series with an original storyline, but it feels like little more than fan fiction, with contrived plot twists and forced references that do a disservice to the source material. Instead of adding depth or nuance to the Cobra Kai universe, the game's story only serves to undermine the credibility of the franchise.In the end, Cobra Kai: The Karate Kid Saga Continues is a forgettable tie-in game that fails to capture the magic of the Cobra Kai series. Fans of the franchise are better off rewatching the show or revisiting the original Karate Kid movies than wasting their time with this uninspired cash grab.

_childDocuments_.review: It's actually kindof sad, because this is a fairly well designed game, and it COULD be a lot of fun.  But the problem is that it's programming for controls are a cheap joke.For one thing, you CAN NOT use keyboard and mouse to control the game.  And while it IS true that PC gamers have the ability to use a large variety of gamepads, this is still a PC we are talking about.  Meaning that if a game has a complete lack of ability to use keyboard/mouse, the way this one does, then it is considered by most users to be a cheap pathetic console port, and not worth spending any money on.Then besides not being able to use keyboard/mouse, it also apparently has a lot of bugs and issues with it's implementation of gamepad input.  I don't know if it's designed to use either Direct-Input or X-Input, but apparently, judging from posts in the game's discussions page, it only uses one and not the other.  To be a WELL BUILT PC game, you need to support BOTH, possibly even with a menu option to manually choose one or the other.And you ALSO need options for manually choosing to have the game display either XBOX or PS buttons for the in-game prompts.  Because on PC, people use gamepad emulators.  Which means quite often, they are using a DIFFERENT physical gamepad, from the one that gets reported to the game.Then the last issue... Again, this the PC platform we are talking about.  Meaning there are far more people who want to play this kind of game with their friend ON ANOTHER COMPUTER, instead of trying to use two gamepads on the same machine.  So a total lack of any kind of network multiplayer just make this seem even more like a cheap pathetic port.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game, but it's not quite as good as I'd hoped. I'm a really big fan of the TV series, the movies not as much.Positives are that it features many characters, and the fighters have different moves to use. I like the map layout for the game. The levels are not short, and there's plenty to pickup throughout. The game looks nice, and runs well on Deck.Negatives counter the positives in places, while there are lots of characters, the story is locked into a specific point in time of the show quite early on. It's neat to be connected to the show, I just wish it would have been a connected differently since the show has progressed so much even since this came out. Though, that's not entirely on the game as the show introduces shifts in character or story quite often.I find the game to be quite difficult, which is surprising and somewhat expected I suppose at my gaming level. All in all, I recommend the game if you're a fan of the show like me. On sale, it's a steal I'd say ($4 right now). But for those who don't watch the show, you might find the frustrations outweigh the delights. Which TBH, if you're not a fan of the show it's pretty run of the mill I'd venture to say... so, do you like karate?

_childDocuments_.review: Despite my short time in the company of Daniel LaRusso and his daughter, Sam, this is what I have:Since this game mixes Karate Kid plot + Cobra Kai characters + Side-Scroll beat'em up + Californian summer vibe, I have absolute no choice other than recommend it. All this together — like a cake recipe, not isolated — make this game far greater than you might foresee right above in the Previews or down here in the Reviews.I see some players complaining about that clunky mechanics, that's true in the beginning, but I'm sure you quickly get used to it. When you figure the combos — punch, kick, special, defense, jump, roll etc — the fun factor comes in and you hop aboard the addiction loop we always look forward in games. That includes punching bullies to death  and upgrading your DOJO + Characters along the way.Other than that, I'm amazed by the soundtrack and voice acting: the icing on a cake Daniel-San hasn't decided to chop with his bare hands yet.  "Oh Little Bran, should I buy this game or not?" — well, that's easy. Fan of Karate-Kid/Cobra Kai + Side-Scrolling Beat'em Up? Look no further. Get it boy! If you don't, Sensei Lawrence will bully you for the rest of your life! If you do, that means you have strong roots, just like a bonsai! BUT KARATE FOR DEFENSE ONLY, REMEMBER?

_childDocuments_.review: I beat this with Cobra Kai, not sure if I'll replay with Miyagi Do. I enjoyed this beat'em up and definitely felt it was a solid homage to the series. The movesets were easy to understand and I think the game helped early on so you weren't overwhelmed by the controls. The game overall can become repetitive but that's more a note on the genre of beat'em ups, not specific to this game - this game did its best to shake things up with different characters and abilities. This game actually had some quality of life features that more games should have like having to hold a button on a menu. The storyline was lacking what the show Cobra Kai has and there were some annoying gameplay issues such as not being able to pick up certain items if they were slightly outside the level boundary following a battle or combos might get dropped cause an enemy was out of bounds. For the most part, excellent beat'em up and definitely suitable for a Karate Kid/Cobra Kai fan.

_childDocuments_.review: For someone who really enjoys the show (William Zabka is freaking great) this game is a real surprise. I expected some half-baked pile of stinking you-know-what, but it turned out to be really fun thing. I am not a big fan of beat'em ups, but (to my surprise) I enjoy this one. The game seems to be quite long for this genre, soundtrack is great and gives this 80s vibe and characters have their own separate skills. Combat is just serviceable, but it is rather acceptable as the game is probably not aimed at master players. However, the game tends to be hard. There is quite wide array of enemies with different skills (also attacking from distance). Sometimes enemies can hit us with something offscreen and it can be annoying when they ruin our combo meter. Also, although the game is pretty long, the levels are clearly divided into main ones (different locations, such as diner, mall or autoshop - they are noticeably longer and include final boss) and secondary ones (different variations of streets - they are much shorter, but still need to be finished in order to reach main locations).Overall, it is really a steal for this price,PS: The game refers few times to the events in the show. It is probably best to play it whenever after watching around half of season 2 (the game takes place right after the events in the mall).

_childDocuments_.review: The game doesn't have the most robust fighting system in a beat 'em up, but it does do some things different from the granddaddies in the genre. The storytelling is kinda campy, but it vibes with that classic 80's/90's cheese, and terrigood dialogue writing and VO.  This is far from the worst TV/movie tie-ins in existence, and if you go into it with laxed expectations you might find yourself having a good time, esp. if you bring a friend along for the ride.

_childDocuments_.review: A classic Beatem up with just enough style and soul to be a WINNER.Love or hate cobra kai, and I love it, but this game is more then just a cash in. It takes the concept and story of the first few seasons, and turns them into a strong, fun, energetic brawler with a Rockin 80s style, solid gameplay, and a retro apeal that, depending on your taste, may or may not work.But lets make it simple. You want to know the good and bad.Good: 2 stories, plus a special ending when both are finished.8 playbale charecters, 4 per dojo, and both Johnny and Daniel lead the charge, but all of them have there own style and feel to them.Solid visuals, nothing super fancy or super detailed, giving it a ps1/ps2 era style. For most games, it wouldn't work, but for this game, it its the markMusic and sound is rock solid, music gets Big props for the composers from the show coming in to handle it. Sound effects are punchy and solid, if not as epic as id like, and the voice work ,while mostly sound alikes, does a solid job and fits the charecters well enough.Bad:Challenge curve. The game gets hard fast, and unless you level up skillfully, you kind find your weaker charecters going down in a few moments, leaving your stronger fighters to handle it.Limited replay value:: While it has 2 campaigns and great gameplay, once beaten, its mostly nostalgia that will bring you back.Visuals. While I like it, it wont be to everyones taste. Overall, I would give this game a B normally, but it gets major points for being a beatem up, and for its fantastic music. A-, not perfect, but still a hella good time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is better than it has any right to be. It’s a classic Beat ‘em Up in the style of Streets of Rage where you can play as either Cobra Kai or Miyagi Do where completing both campaigns will unlock the true ending and the real final boss. The combat in this game feels great and every fighter feels unique with their own special moves you can upgrade. You don’t “level up” but you do collect coins from defeating enemies, finishing levels, and completing special tasks. You’ll use these to purchase upgrades for each individual character and upgrades that carry across all characters at the Dojo. This alone keeps the game from feeling repetitive and getting stale. It’s also a decent length too at 10 or so hours and longer if you want to get all the collectibles and fully level everyone up. You can tell Game Mill had a very limited budget for this game because it doesn’t look great and all the cutscenes are still animated segments. It does have the voice cast of the show and that really goes a long way to making this feel authentic. If you’re a fan of the show and a fan of classic arcade style Beat em’ Up’s then definitely give this game a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Steel Assault is a hearty ode to 16bit action platformers similar to countless classics from that golden gamers era.Gameplay: The game has a unique movement system using a zipline,you will have to shoot this zipline at stable objects to make your way through the level, you can shoot the zipline in any direction but often this will be necessary when you need to go higher.You will also be able to use this zipline to repel certain bullets, but not all.In addition to the boss battles, you will also be able to encounter mini bosses, and these bosses are no easy feat so be wary.You can play the game in two different ways, the regular way is like the most standard mode in which you can play the game to the end with checkpoints and lives, but during the arcade mode you will have to finish the game in 1 life, some steel assault makes an extremely challenging game if you want to do it that way.
_childDocuments_.name: Steel Assault

_childDocuments_.review: Steel Assault is a short, aggressive action-packed platformer that feels like straight out of 80s. It's pretty much like an arcade game that you'd play on a cabinet and the reason for that is, it takes about 45 minutes to beat (could take up to 2 hours if it's your first time) and each level is only a few minutes long. It also has that NES and SNES vibe going on thanks to CRT & bilinear filters, forced 4:3 aspect ratio, kick-ass 80s rock soundtrack, and classic brief story intro that you'd only see in retro games. Speaking of the story... it doesn't play a big role but it's there. I don't think it's worth mentioning so, I'll talk about the gameplay instead. I know this will sound chaotic but if Contra, Mega Man, Castlevania, Shatterhand, and Bionic Commando merged into one game, we'd have Steel Assault or something very close to it. Our main character's Taro Takahashi's weapon of choice is an electric whip and he carries a zipline to get around in his crusade against the dictator called Magnus Pierce. There are only 2 power-ups for the whole game. One of them is Electric which extends the range of your whip and the other one is Shield which gives you two more hit points. There are several difficulty options and a separate Arcade Mode which requires you to beat the whole game without dying and guess what? You don't get to replenish HP between levels, so you're forced to get good if you want to conquer this hardcore game mode. Finally, I would like to give my thanks to the developers for releasing its beautiful soundtrack for free. That's a pretty good gesture for us retro maniacs.
_childDocuments_.name: Steel Assault

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Awesome 16-bit retro pixel art sidescrolling game-Gameplay feels fluid, smooth, and responsive at 60 frames per second-Supports 16:9 aspect ratio -Supports both Keyboard and Gamepad Controller-You can customize Button Prompts including Xbox 360, Xbox One, Playstation 4, Playstation 1-3, and Nintendo Switch-You can select difficulty between Easy, Medium, or HardCons:-Doesn't scale resolution properly which you may need to use Borderless Gaming Software to run the game in Windowed (Borderless) Fullscreen mode to run at native resolution as well as refresh rate-Toggling Framerate Limiter is recommended to run the game at 60fps, otherwise leaving it off forces the game to run at insane speed (1000fps+) which can literally break the game physics.-You can punch, whip, double jump, slide, zipline with 8 different directions, etc.-Game length time feels short. Can be beating under an hour, regardless of your skill.Verdict:I grew up in the 90s and I love 16-bit artstyle sidescrolling game. You can whip, zipline with 8 different directions, and double jump/slide which was so much fun to play with. although it kind of has that Metal Slug vibe. Unfortunately, the game length time felt too short which can be beaten under an hour. Other than that, if you love retro/vintage game with 16-bit artstyle, I recommend this game! 👍

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, the devs have absolutely nailed the aesthetic with the visuals and soundtrack, on that front they've knocked it out of the park. Unfortunately, the game play is dreadful. Your character is limited to a very minor double jump which gives you just enough mobility to avoid all sources of damage, but only if you know where they're coming from. This leads to everything from level progress to boss fights being extreme trial and error. Steel Assault tries a little too hard to be like Contra in terms of difficulty. They've gotten 90% of the formula correct, but just fall short.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is barely 20 minutes long, even if you take your time and beat it on the Expert or Arcade modes it feels like almost every level ends before they have even started properly. I play a lot of arcade run & gun games and in stuff like Contra, Metal Slug, Makaimura, Strider etc. it never feels like the stages are just couple screen props for the bossfight.Not my cup of tea at all, but your mileage may vary, i guess.Edit 2022: A bunch of people who frequent the same arcade gaming discos/forums have noted that this review makes no sense/i'm giving the game bad rep for no reason because all the previously mentioned games are also very short and only take a similar amount of time to clear.Well here's to you;No, it's not the same at all. In those games every section of play feels complete in an absolutely different kind of way as they do in this game, Steel Assault stage sections are like Warioware minigames where you are thrown a gimmick that you can barely interact with and then you move to the next screen, time wise it might be similar i guess (Although i seriously do think each of the games i listed run for longer than this) but the amount of actual gameplay you do with the mechanics is way different. I still don't like this game at all, i think it's horrible.

_childDocuments_.review: I play a lot of these arcade side scrollers, so here’s my quick review for Steel Assault.Steel Assault took me just 55 minutes to clear, and that is with numerous attempts on some of the bosses. It is not a long game by any means, which I guess kinda fits the arcade theme. So, don’t go in expecting this big multi-hour thing.Control-wise, Steel Assault gives you free movement, an attack button, and a zipline – that’s it. However, it uses these to their absolute max, including things like punches instead of your regular weapon when you’re in close range. These punches in turn charge your special meter, which in turn fuels any upgrade you pick up – such as a small scattershot electricity effect that gives your whip some additional range.Nothing too complex here, but what is here works well. The combat is responsive, movement is fluid and doesn’t feel stiff like others in this genre, and the only iffy thing there is the zipline. It can be a bit finicky, so expect to spend some time getting used to how it controls.Level and enemy variety are also solid. I never had that feeling that I was fighting the same thing over and over. If anything, it felt like I was always fighting something new and the game has this really cool trend of throwing this huge enemy at you that LOOKS like a boss, but is actually just some mid-stage thing, leaving the real boss for the end.And the boss fights are really where the challenge comes into play. On one hand, they have some pretty cool designs, but on the other, this is where that “trial and error” difficulty really shines. The kind of difficulty where you won’t know how to deal with a specific situation until you get hit or die to it.This can even be seen a bit in the regular gameplay – like enemies spawning right on top of you or placing ranged units just outside of your screen until you’ve already committed to a jump. It can feel a bit cheap at times, but it never got so bad that I felt outright frustrated.Graphics and music are also fine and there are a number of options you can change to alter how “retro” the game looks, like CRT filters and such. There’s also a bit of a story, but it’s just one of those side things that hardly matters – as expected from an arcade title.All that said, yeah, it’s fun enough to warrant a recommendation. I don’t know about full price, but if you can catch it on deep sale or even in a bundle – it’s at least worth the time.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: FINAL REVIEW: I beat the game on Expert for my first playthrough, so that's where I'm coming from.TLDR: Play on Expert and enjoy getting your face get shoved in the dirt. What if Gunstar Heroes had a baby with a Capcom platformer like Mega Man Zero? And it was on a hybrid of the GBA and Sega Genesis/Megadrive? You get this.Saw reviews complain about how short the game was, so I went to Expert right away. Holy moley, this game is so satisfy to master. It's super hard on Expert, but you can see yourself get better and better and you play the same level again and again. I would compare the experience to trying to get Pacifist in Cuphead. You know it can be done, you just gotta learn how.That said, some lack of polish is bound to show when you keep playing the same levels again and again while learning. The Textbox GUI sometimes covers projectiles and enemies, randomness in attack patterns and spawns that make it seem like damage booster is the only option, the game seems to speed up when your screen is minimized.I implore you, if you like difficult games PLAY ON EXPERT. The devs have even come out and said that is what they wanted people to play on! Maybe I'm bad at video games, but I put about 10 hours trying to beat it on expert. Hell, even if it took me 5 hours I would still be happy. Give this a try!

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I hate to say it, given how flashy and cool this game is, the protagonist echoes my exact same thoughts during the ending: "It doesn't feel like I got much of anything." In short, it is the fun-size Twix bar of action platformers.Beaten in just less than an hour on normal difficulty, and it doesn't look like there is any extra content like branching paths, endings, or significant changes to level structure and boss patterns for higher difficulties. For example, all 'arcade mode' does is just limit you to one life for the entire game, and that's it: it doesn't even add a lives system where you could gain lives by playing well for points.Don't get me wrong, I was looking for a short and sweet action experience, but this just felt incredibly insubstantial compared to other arcade experiences: both levels and especially bosses ended before I could blink, and most of those levels weren't much to sneeze at, mostly just being filled with Ninja Gaiden-esque unfair "gotcha" traps. More so than that, I was really excited at what they might do with the whole zipline mechanic, but in the end it felt incredibly token, only used here and there for certain situations instead of being a core mechanic that you can get very skilled with. It's also missing lots of quality-of-life, like being unable to skip boss intro cutscenes, so get used to seeing them a lot.Shame because as said, the game is gorgeous and cool, and clearly a lot of love went into it, but compared to other arcade games like Fight n Rage, Gravity Circuit, Blazing Chrome, Super Cyborg, and so on which had satisfying campaigns and strong replayability, this feels paltry. It's a nice experience if you're really in love with the genre, but I'd only recommend it on sale, if that.

_childDocuments_.review: As it stands, this game feels a more like a proof-of-concept with its brief levels and sparse mechanics. The difficulty that others have mentioned is mostly due to the games simple design logic where you'll occasionally run into an area with infinitely spawning enemies that sometimes take cheap shots. The answer to most scenarios is to just rush to the exit - exploring gets you killed and really isn't worth it since there are no secrets. Boss fights are only tricky until you've figured out their patterns, but the controls aren't the best either. I found it better doing a custom map for the slide onto the trigger buttons. The slide is used just as often as the grapple and really should have a dedicated button with how often the game expects you to use it to avoid damage. If the Developers have a sequel planned than I would probably be interested if they can build more into this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna tell you right now, flat out, up front, this game takes about an hour, if that. If you think that's not enough for the price, there is no convincing you - it is not. Move along, consider this a thumbs down. But if the thing that attracted you to this game is the arcade look, like some forgotten GBA remaster of a long lost Treasure game on Genesis, you should know that's pretty much precisely what this is. It's clear at a certain point, judging by the variety of difficulty options and the one credit Arcade selection available from the start, that this was developed in the same mold as those old games - 45 to 60 minutes of game that would be stretched into hours by demanding mastery from the player, learning a little more and making it a little further every time as you master the earlier levels.This isn't how we play games anymore and if the developers had gone with that approach, these reviews would instead have people noting how artificially lengthened the game is.For me, the combination of simple mechanics, gorgeous animation, excellent music, and a run-time that doesn't overstay its welcome made this well worth the price of entry. It's not gonna change your life, it's not the most startlingly original and inventive arction platformer this side of Contra, but it's a whole bunch of pretty fun.(Only one criticism - an unskippable cutscene before the very difficult final boss almost beat me!)

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews for games I play on Steam, but this is one of the rare games that has me continuously coming back for more. Every portion of this game is lovingly crafted, and it pays a fantastic homage to the retro games that taught you how to get your butt kicked and learn from it. If you think this is a bygone era, you're wrong, and the quality of games like this proves it in spades.I'm a pretty seasoned vet when it comes to games of this genre, but this game started off kicking me in the keister, as well. It'll probably do the same to you, especially if you delve into the Expert or Arcade modes (Expert: checkpoints only after each chapter mark; Arcade: no checkpoints, one life). However, despite its challenge, it never derails into unfair territory, and you almost always have a way to keep yourself safe, despite your overall limited action. This game, like the past it gives homage to, is all about practice and basic execution, using the simple control to fluently control your character and fend off enemies and bosses.Speaking of bosses, they are easily the best aspect of the gameplay itself. Taking a note from legacy franchises like Mega Man, they have simple to understand patterns that, at times, require specific actions to best avoid. Expert mode will also add a new move to some of these bosses, making them that much harder in those already difficult runs. All bosses in this game are unique and, as a result, require unique approaches to effectively destroy.The presentation of this game also sells it extremely well. The pixel-art and spritework of this game is detailed and expressive, while the music blows me away every time I listen to any of these tracks. On top of the existing audio, there is an FM remix version if you want a truly old-school vibe while playing this game. Chiptunes are an acquired taste, I admit, so I appreciate the extra effort the devs here made to allow a choice between a more modern soundtrack and a synthesized/chiptune soundtrack.In general, I recommend this game to those who like the short, sweet and challenging experiences. The difficulty modes help somewhat for accessibility, but this is a game best enjoyed when it is trying to serve you on a silver platter, and that experience is for those who want to get frustrated from time to time. Much like the best legacy franchises, your mistakes will be your fault, and it is up to you to get better and learn. Mastery of this game has felt extremely liberating, and only makes the game more fun as you attempt to pursue the next difficulty up in the chain and continue to perfect your control. If you want an arcade-like experience that'll keep you coming back to get better and better at, then this is the game for you.Overall, I love this game, and it has become a rare sweetheart in a library of games I have bought and forgotten after the initial hype. The price might look steep for such a short experience, but I firmly believe it is well worth the money. If you like fun, fast, challenging games, take a shot with this game; you might really come to love it!

_childDocuments_.review: This review takes place after 100% completion of the game's achievements, which would include the 1CC run on Arcade.Steel Assault is a SNES-like old school action-platformer where you play as Taro Takahashi, a dude who carries an electric whip, has an infinitely regenerating two-way grappling hook, and closes his eyes dramatically after destroying robots. Your objective is to stop General Magnus Pierce because nobody likes him. Or something.It doesn't matter. Well, it didn't for me anyway.The point is that Steel Assault feels like a combination of Super Castlevania IV and Contra. Let me tell you. It's a great feeling.Graphics:Gameplay:Soundtrack:Difficulty:Have no fear though. It's doable with practice: In any case, I strongly recommend the game. I'd say that my only gripes are a lack of stage select for practice, particularly with Arcade and the fact that it's too short at 5 levels. I need more. If you're concerned about the length, then I'd still recommend grabbing it even on sale. It was absolutely worth the playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I did enjoy it, I can't help but feel like I got robbed. It is a very trial and error kind of game where you will die multiple times before you figure out what you have to do. Majority of the time, you wont know that you have to use the zipline as it cancel out on majority of the area. For $13+, it was waaaay too short. Once I finished the game, I was like wait, that was it? No new weapons, no new abilities, no unlockables, no bonus modes. After playing the game on normal, why the hell would I punish myself doing arcade mode XD. Some bosses hitboxes are so crazy that there would be no legit way to do it safely so I had to cheese some bosses. Theres literally no reason to continue playing the game. It is hard to recommend this game the way it is.  I'm sure a lot of work went into this, but i cant justify $13 for an hour of gameplay unless you see yourself doing no hit runs for the internet.5/10 -  it was pretty fun and chaotic but over time and especially at the end, you'll probably start to regret your purchase

_childDocuments_.review: I'm so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tired of getting baited into buying games of this type. The pixel art always looks great and the reviews are always glowing and somehow no one manages to mention the glaring flaws that are present from the very first moment of gameplay that would have been ironed out in five seconds with any kind of real Q&A.The default difficulty on this game sucks. This is never a case of 'bad cuz mad git gud'--there are difficulty options, I can make things easier on myself if I want. But I picked 'normal' as the difficulty, not 'super masochist go ♥♥♥♥ yourself' mode. There is a huge difference between something that is difficult but challenging and something that is difficult only because it's designed to be stupidly unplayable. The health total in this game is so low that you will die before you get to the thing you actually want to practice, you will be put into OHKO situations against bosses, giant configs of terrain will be packed with enemies positioned just such that they are guaranteed to hit you before you can reach them... all this type of ♥♥♥♥.Level design in this game is egregiously terrible. Any human being could tell you that after playing only five minutes of it, that somehow that designers don't understand the difference between 'fun challenge' and 'pure annoyance'. There's a default bat-style enemy that loves to respawn infinitely any time you're climbing something or near a pit, and it not only fires a spread shot at you, but if the pellets hit the ground, they cause small AOE. The bat over pits is bad enough, infinitely respawning is even worse, and the shot type being extra annoying is the icing on the cake.Why would you design a super difficult arcade-style game with super punishing damage values but then not optimize your restarts to be within the same scene, rather than transitioning to a clunky 'retry' screen every time? Why not just give me lives and respawn me instantly? Again, something that could have been ironed out in five seconds of playtesting but clearly wasn't.The last straw for me is the grappling hook mechanic--it's one of the least fun to use grappling hooks I've encountered in any game, and it's not only mandatory from the rip, but it's required in such ways that the placement won't be obvious until you manage to clink on to either end of the geometry that looks identical to background dressing and has no clear line work to distinguish it. Sometimes it works like Spiderman and you feel like you can just grab onto thin air, other times you can't make a simple slightly elevated jump because the solid objects around you have decided they hate you. The worst part of this implementation is that every time you're required to use the grappling hook, in an already obtuse and frustrating fashion, you'll also be harassed by the aforementioned endlessly respawning flying enemies, who will delight in knocking you off and bloating your damage total for what initially feels like totally unreactable and unavoidable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.There is such a night and day difference in the proper way to design a difficult game and whatever this is. I quit out on the third level because of how bad the gameplay is. This is tragic because the core moveset is genuinely cool and fun, but the level design is some of the worst I've ever experienced in a game bar none. And the health and damage values... if you want me to enjoy your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game on the default difficulty, give me enough health that I can make more than three mistakes in a boss fight before going back to your stupid retry screen.Holy cow this game pissed me off. Only buy it if you hate yourself. I got it on sale and I still wish I could get my money back.

_childDocuments_.review: Steel Assault is a unique take on the side-scrolling, action-platformer genre. Zenovia Interactive set out to make a fun, fast-paced, arcade-style game inspired by similar games like Castlevania, Contra, Bionic Commando, Mega Man X and Metal Slug and overall succeeded in their first attempt at the genre. The game isn’t perfect and can be quite challenging to new players even on an easier difficulty. It is also lacking in terms of length and story, but fast-paced gameplay, amazing soundtrack and phenomenal pixel artistry make the game an enjoyable experience for both newcomers (on lower difficulties) and fans of the action-platforming genre.Players traverse through 5 different stages while fighting a boss at the end of each stage with gradual difficulty. There are 4 levels of difficulty to select between very easy to expert along with an “Arcade Mode” which is expert mode without the use of continues. The differences between the modes have nothing to do with level, enemy or boss design and are limited to Taro’s stats: Taro’s health bar is doubled, receives a single unit of damage per hit, enemies occasionally drop health and health is restored when starting a new area or stage. Taro has 1 health bar, receives a single unit of damage per hit, enemies will occasionally drop health and health is restored when starting a new area or stage. Taro has 1 health bar, receives 2 units of damage per hit, enemies won’t drop health, but health is restored when starting a new area or stage. Taro has 1 health bar, receives 2 units of damage per hit, enemies won’t drop health and all damage taken is carried over when starting a new area or stage. This game can be difficult and is one of those “easy to learn, hard to master” games. Newcomers should start with “very easy” (easy mode of the game) as it is a great introduction to the game’s mechanics. As the player progresses through harder difficulties (easy being normal and normal being hard), the game forces the player to adapt a stricter strategy to overcome the various obstacles especially on normal and expert where health conservation becomes critical. Here are the pros of Steel Assault: – This game has great level design with excellent platforming sections that require the player to creatively use the zipline mechanic, a good amount of enemy variety, smooth controls and fun gimmicks that provide a progressive difficulty that while challenging isn’t unfair. In addition, these have been designed so that it allows the player to instinctively utilize what is taught in the tutorial to overcome each obstacle without holding the player’s hand. Even though there are only 5 levels, all of them are unique and offer fun nods to other games (examples include: a turret section inspired by Contra, bosses are a nod to Mega Man X, whip is a nod to Castlevania and Taro’s movement feels similar to Metal Slug) while still providing players with a fresh take on the genre. – Along with excellent level design, the game really shines with its boss fights. Each boss has their own unique pattern and combined with an epic score are all great. The only downside to them is that their fights are short and they use the same attacks on all difficulties rather than having a varied move-set. – Graphically and musically, Steel Assault is an amazing experience and Zenovia hit it out of the ball park when it came to the visuals and score. The beautiful pixel art combined with a fast-paced, heart-pumping soundtrack, created the perfect feel for a classic, side-scrolling, arcade game. While Steel Assault is a fun game, it is not without its faults: – Players will be thrown off by how short the levels are. Just as players are getting into the feel for a stage, it just suddenly ends with a quick boss fight. As a result, this doesn’t give the player enough time to get accustomed to core mechanics due to how frequently it fluctuates between sections. I understand why they did this since arcade mode is already an endurance test on its own, but it still doesn’t make it a good thing. The entire game can easily be beaten within 30 minutes and by the end of the game, I definitely felt like I wanted to experience more as Zenovia is very competent with their level design.  – There is a right way to design difficulty in a game and a wrong way to do it. As mentioned above, the levels themselves are the same on all difficulties and the only thing that changes are Taro’s stats between each difficulty. This doesn’t encourage the player to utilize different tactics within the levels themselves, rather it forces them to adopt a specific strategy to conserve health to make it all the way through the game on higher difficulties. On top of this, the game actively punishes the player by forcing repetition of multiple sections of a stage (or an entire stage) all over again making this a tedious chore to complete (made even worse with Arcade mode since there are no continues). Not only is this not welcoming for new players, but to get all the achievements, the player has to be flawless at the game. Repetition should never be the reason why a game’s length is stretched out as it quickly overstays its welcome and becomes frustrating to play. The game’s difficulty should be based on the level design itself, not what affects the player’s stats. – As per the official website, Steel Assault takes place in the late 2030s during the Second Pacific War where radiological warfare saw the debut of the thorium bomb: a radiation bomb that while it caused no visible destruction, left entire cities uninhabitable. This allowed robotic units to pick off resources and humans either died off or fled. The main antagonist of the game, Magnus Von Pierce, an inventor turned army general, rose from the ashes as a dictator of a post-apocalyptic America. Magnus began a regime to kill off all real and suspected enemies including the main protagonist, Taro Takahashi’s parents. Taro becomes a member of the Daybreak Resistance movement and by early 2046 just as Pierce is deploying old nuclear, military and robotic tech, Taro embarks on a mission to investigate the cities they now occupy and to get his own personal revenge on the man that killed his parents. Stories like this, while cliché, are a great addition to side-scroller platformers and compliment the adventure. Steel Assault, however, really doesn’t explain any of this in the entirety of the game and all it amounts to is the player taking control of Taro to defeat Magnus. Having a background story properly implemented creates the world. While it isn’t necessary for games like these and this is just a minor nitpick, it’s something that would’ve been nice to have properly implemented to pad out the game’s length and make the game’s characters and gameplay feel more memorable instead of having a game whose length is built on repetition. Zenovia Interactive did an amazing job for their first attempt in the side-scrolling, action-platforming genre. From smooth gameplay to great level designs complimented perfectly with an amazing soundtrack and beautiful pixel art, Steel Assault is an overall enjoyable game for fans of the genre who will enjoy the call-backs to other famous games while experiencing a unique take on a classic formula. The only real downsides to this game are that this game is incredibly short and the length is padded by repetition on harder difficulties which can make the game tedious and frustrating. This game is challenging, but it isn’t unfair and it still is a great game to get if it goes on sale. After everything, I give Steel Assault a rating of 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Steel Assault manages to be an amazing game, both in gameplay and presentation. It will be a frustrating path the first copuple of times, because this game is very hard but don't give up, the more you play it, you'll get better and better! Some clever use of the chain mechanic on all stages, but there are better parts than others. The music by Qwesta is simply OUTSTANDING!!! and I mean it. Every composition is top notch, with beautiful melodic tunes that fit excellent in the action and also as stand alone music for your playlist! It is a very hard game that demands good reflexes and practice to learn the boss patterns, but there are different modes to play casually or if you are a hardcore and experienced player there's always Arcade mode to beat the game with a single life (Still working on that lol)Overall, an amazing game. Buy it if you love old school platformers like Bionic Comando, Castlevania and Treasure games. And if you don't this game will change your mind ;)

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to say this after how long the game was in development and how many kickstarter status update e-mails kept coming, but it feels half-baked. Gameplay is kind of trial-and-error which doesn't work for me. Early death pits aren't very clear until you accidentally fall into one, then you can watch for them. Boss patterns are very bullet-hell and it's more tiring than fun.The grapple rope thing is neat when the game uses it, but for most situations activating it does nothing at all. This makes it harder to recognize when the game does want you to use it, aside from a few spots where it's made blatantly obvious. It feels like a waste of a face button to have this function available all of the time when it doesn't do much of anything outside of these areas.I still don't comprehend how I'm winning against most bosses; it's "dodge a few attacks and this time you randomly managed to do enough damage for it to die before you did" which doesn't feel rewarding. I don't know if I could reproduce these wins, it feels more like I'm throwing myself against a wall until I get lucky enough to win instead of increasing my skills enough to win.
