_childDocuments_.review: The technical issues I had seem to have been resolved in the recent patch, so I got some space to explain where I was going with this review. After seeing so many people struggle with the new mechanics, I mostly talk about everything that constitutes the backbone of the sequel's gameplay. It's useful to understand how and why Hard West 2 shines if you don't skim on learning its inner workings.Hard West is exactly what I wanted from a game in this setting. With all the well-paced cutscenes, set pieces, badass characters, weapon designs, and impeccable style, it's evident that the budget was put to good use. The art is positively metal, one-liners land perfectly, the music and ambience are just right, creating a rich, distinctive Western atmosphere. Notice how they didn't add any subtitle. No Hard West 2: Mammon's Curse or Hard West: Ghost Train. Some devs seem to feel naked when they don't put at least anything after a colon. Here, Hard West is the name of the game, its setting, and the difficulty I self-inflicted. It speaks for itself.Namely, with its concise writing, which always manages to give a vivid characterisation to a person or a place at hand, and delivers the plot in a compelling manner. The setting begs to go batsh*t insane with it, but things were kept clear-cut. Your party needs to kill a devil, Mammon, who cheated them out of their souls in a game of poker and, what's worse, looks like a hipster. They'll do it with the help of freshly acquired demonic abilities and larger-than-life characters met along the way. To flesh out its lineup of desperados, the game resorts to amusing vignettes where you get to make various choices as a part of a simple reputational mechanic. Studying your posse is a reward in itself, but it's nice to have.Scandalously, the sequel has shed its roguelite elements. You still roam the plains, doing your missions, shopping your heart out, taking sides, and enjoying the results of your choices. The major difference is the switch from bite-sized scenarios with everchanging characters and barely any continuity to linear storytelling and big chapters, facilitating fairly expansive maps. Your posse goes through them while keeping their loot intact. I liked the gimmicky approach of the original, it added replayability, but permanence is a better investment. Oh, there's plenty to invest in! Like pistols, rifles, shotguns, melee weapons, trinkets, several types of explosives, and a wide array of consumables.The sheer amount of items with contrasting properties can be confusing. A word of advice: always carry a fistful of dynamite into battle and some coagulant on the ones who still have blood in them. It would also help to pay attention to the involved card system. Solitary cards don't give abilities anymore, only stats. You get to assign your poker hands depending on what skills from a character's personal list you need to unlock. The only way to get the cards is by completing as many secondary objectives on the missions as you can. I usually went for all of them since they were fun and intense. Like picking up optional loot or killing enemies in a certain way. The objectives added variety to an already diverse tactical feast.There are a few heists with similar premises, but no mission feels the same. The game even jokingly teases it once when it pretends to make you rob a bank twice in a row. Thankfully, things went awry, as always, giving me something fresh and exciting to wade through by the skin of my teeth. Savescum is allowed, but I still ended half of my missions on the last possible turn with most of my party dead, including its already dead members. And I didn't mind, given the stellar encounter design. Not all missions are equally hard, some are about having fun rather than overcoming the overwhelming odds. The game loosens its reigns periodically, giving you a chance to enjoy yourself, to then pull the rug, sending your smug ass face-first into the manure. I call it good pacing.See, Hard West went to great lengths to unchain itself from XCOM, but only this instalment was equipped to outpace it. Let's unravel the peculiarities step by step. There are no dedicated move or attack actions, everyone gets 3 indiscriminate Action Points per turn. Like weapons, abilities don't use luck and instead cost AP. Gone is the apparent Heat system, this game's aggro is hidden but still exists. While permadeath got buried completely. Fallen people get up after a fight and healing is cheap. These features allowed for, say, Old Man Bill, who seems to inherently attract more bullets, to be extremely effective with his AoE ability, which scales with lost health and acts as a perfect initiator. Place him in the right spot, endure, then cash in the damage and say: this turn, everybody dies. Worked for me!Said damage is set in stone, so it's like solving a complex determinate puzzle. Getting lucky crits comes as a bonus, not a crutch. I never took a single <75% shot, there's always a way. Although, sometimes it can be helpful to miss or get hurt since suffering provides Luck Points, which now can be used to raise the hit chance by 25% and trigger certain passive abilities. Normally, the hit chance is counted in 25% increments, and it's always 100% if you flank an enemy yourself or with a well-ricochet bullet. Now, ricochets are a property of guns, not cards. As before, you can bounce bullets off the highlighted objects, nullifying your target's cover bonus. It's also available to some enemies... and isn't it a pain in the ass.It is! And the bastards are swarming. But you have the upper hand this time. The biggest distinctive feature of this game's combat is the Bravado! kill streaks. After killing an enemy, a party member enters the mode, fully recovers their AP and, depending on who's the perpetrator and what skills they have unlocked, also achieve bonuses to crit and damage. For this to work, the ammo limit and reloads had to go. Don't mourn them, for Bravado! is the prized crux of Hard West 2. Setting up the grim fandango is your immediate goal on every turn. To boot, moving doesn't break combos, so it's Blitzkrieg all the way - kill, advance, kill. This creates powerful combinations, allowing to cut through the levels like a knife through butter.Don't fret, no hurried rampaging is typically required. Being crap at math and prone to embarrassing mistakes, I mixed my strategies, playing it safe and going all out interchangeably. Yet, even if you're a mathematician, don't expect an easy ride. Mere basic riflemen and shotgunners have something nasty up their sleeves. Wendigos can tear your guys like paper, but what can they do when their legs are broken? Duelists and their cursed counter-attacks make you remember the ricochet. Ghastly grenadiers make you mind your distance and fear the status effects. Revenants and Witch Doctors fully heal if left alive. At your expense, too! They are but your DPS check. If you can't melt one in a turn, you need to go back to your squad screen.People complain. And it's okay, but remember - every predicament can be outsmarted or outscummed. With all the tools and a telling UI at your disposal, you can accurately anticipate the results of your actions. To me, the game is a pure tactical delight, untainted by everything we begrudgingly consider the norm in this genre. Ice Code have made the boldest of changes and they paid off. Hard West 2 looks and plays fantastically, driving a great bargain by being cheap as dirt. I liked it a lot. But especially Old Man Bill. He could've been a character in The Dark Tower books.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I am really enjoying the game. I feel like most of the negative reviews are from people expecting a western clone of XCOM. but it's not... Grid style movement does not equal XCOM. The combat is fun, and somewhat challenging, its like a puzzle figuring out who to take out first. there is a decent amount of strategy involved. The luck system is useful {mostly for purposely missing shots}. each character has their own special skill, which can be upgraded and unlocked within the card system. Trick shots are useful and very satisfying. one of my favorite mechanics is the Bravado system, which isn't traditional for most TRPG's. it feels nice and fluent, which sets the game apart from most games of the same genre. Overall I'm having a lot of fun with the game , and I plan on beating it on hard and nightmare difficulties.That being said, there are obviously a few cons... the guns are pretty cool, but they get stale, there isn't enough of a difference between most weapons {besides damage} to make them interesting enough. trying to complete optional objectives on a harder difficulty with time limits is tedious. The AI sometimes acts really dumbfounded, and my last minor gripe is that I really wish environments or some obstacles were destructible with explosives or other means.Overall Hard West 2 is a really solid and fun Turn-based game, It's worth the price tag, and if you're expecting a western XCOM clone, then this game isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit after finishing the game: totally worth it! The game combines turn-based combat sections real time map exploring ingame cutscenes and more like comic dialogues. There are few mecanics that will help you doing that - its your decision which one of those you will like the most. A lot of special skills on your characters will give you even more fun if you like to combine and try-hard the game. If you dont you will also manage to and the combat sections but remember that the game will give you more money and items when you make it 100/100.Real time map exploring (like the battles too) also have animation speed management so that exploring of map will never be boring. There are also secondary options that can help you with collectiong eq or getting better with lore of the game.Cutscenes are really dynamic and more like comic dialogues - with really fine dubbing - have seriously good sense of humor. You cannot be bored with that.The story itself is something hard to imagine in this "wild west" typ of game. Demons, devils, animals (so spoilers) that you dont expect are just great. I simply recommend this game. If you're more like HOMM3 person than RDR person you need to try it. Otherwise - just try it not expecting typical real time RPG game, you will probably not regret it. The game and mecanics are "fresh" and surprising. I loved it!

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr Nice game with not such a nice _gameplay_ interface. Pros. 1. Aesthetically this game is very appealing. I like the art style, I pretty much like main characters' stories, overall plot and art style is almost flawless. The war cries of the Laughing Deer during his wild runs are very uplifting. You do feel that it is a "Hard" West around you. This game is good if you LOOK at it, no doubts here. I liked its' visuals and sound design.2. Bravado system - well, I'll take it. It is an interesting stuff, no doubts here. Make the right moves and you'll get an ability to make even more right moves and dominate the battlefield. It is motivating, I do feel myself daredevil.Cons. The gameplay UI is just not finished. It is almost here, but it is not. And this is just irritating. I've visited all of the locations of all of the chapters and I have the corresponding achievement. But I haven't finished the game. Irritating is the word. And here goes whining (spoilers alert). 1. You have 6 posse members with different skillsets - tank, sniper, brawler etc (which you should develop and hone via trinkets, weapons and cards) and you can get only 4 of them to the mission. And there are no level descriptions before the mission. Slight hints in the mission goals - but they are slight. So how do you select this 4 of out 6? Based on what? So you try to guess, you miss - and try to finish the mission without 1 or 2 ill-judged characters. And it is your fault, right? So you end up on the fixed 4 guys that you are used to and use another 2 only if they are required. 2 out of 6 - it is wasted 1/3 of the posse, if my math is correct.2. Bravado system. Game is balanced (via health values, weapon damage values, skills etc) to push you to exploit this Bravado system - otherwise you'll be just literally covered with enemies. And Steam achievements convert this pushing into forcing - "finish level in 8 turns". So gamedesigners definitely wanted us to CALCULATE our actions and its' consequences during the turn. It is expectable there will be at least some planning tools availalble. You know - will you be able to see an enemy if you'll move here. But. There is a visibility system that prevents you from shot if you don't see an enemy - but there is no display of it AT ALL. There is a weapon range restriction that prevents you from shot if enemy is out of range - but there is no display of it AT ALL. Oh, and ricochet system. What the hell is "invalid angle" fot the ricochet - why there is display of the correct ones at least on hover? Summing up - the game should be rebalanced to be more forgiving or some visual tools of planning should be added.3. Other irritaitng UI mischiefs. *Handguns and rifles can fire at any direction, but shotguns can only be shot in the same height level with the owner. "Reusable" means it can be used ONCE per MISSION, not every time you want. How do you know that? Well, because I've just wrote it (game doesn't tell it to you). *Some weapons can only shot one per turn (remember the Bravado, right?). It IS mentioned in the weapon description - by a usual size label "Countdown: 1" in the most lower right corner. So you buy this expensive elephant rifle, you adjust the sniper built respectively, then you ride around the map for an half of hour talking with everyone, then you engage, then you do the move and in the middle of this move you shoot this rifle, you get the kill and you get this "Countdown in progress" message. And you look for the previous save and do the same thing without this crappy elephant rifle. The list is quite long. It ends up in the constant save scumming. It is irritating.

_childDocuments_.review: The story, the art, the UI, the mechanics, the writing, the voice-overs, the music, the cards, the little things, and above all the vibe! When I started playing this game, it was so shiny, so fresh, and cozy I felt like a freshly carved-out Pinocchio screaming “I love it, I love it, I love it… what is it?”I am not a Western fan nor a horror fan for that matter, though it only has a tinge of that, and yet I’ve simply fallen head over heels with this game. I love games made with lots of love, and this one is so well polished it’s worth a try even if you’re not Polish and it falls out slightly of your realm of interests. You just may acquire the taste.If you already enjoy tactical role-playing games you don’t want to miss this title as it has it all. The Polish developers at Creative Forge that brought us Phantom Doctrine a few years back have outdone themselves - brawo! This game was executed with some serious bravado. So much so that I lost myself in it for almost 300 hours and can’t wait for more.At first glance, it can be easily mistaken for a classic Western gig. You shoot through a rich, well-told story, complete some scenarios, score new gear, evolve your character, and face off against a well known enemy. Well yes, but with a twist. Death is out there, yeah the guy that’s always open to striking some kind of a fishy deal with us mortals, he’s out there in full force, and he sure makes this fun.If someone asked me what I love the most about this game, I’d have a hard time nailing it down as it is all so well meshed together. The shooting is so satisfying it could be enough, but so is the writing. Typically, these kinds of turn-based tactical games are all about the tactics, and the story is just there, kind of plopped in like a squished bun on a burger — often stale. This is not the case here. It goes west, and then it goes hard. It’s bleak, it’s against all odds, but you got your companions, and they’re in it with you, for better or worse, and it’s hard to let go until Death himself gets what he deserves, ha!, and when do you get to do that?These close encounters (and conversations) with Death made Hard West 1 fresh and interesting. Hiding behind those corners, and coming up with the best approaches to get that 100% shot lined up, and suddenly facing an otherworldly demon was already great fun.Hard West 2 is even better, with chess-like transparency of targeting mechanics you can turn it into a puzzle-like engagement on higher settings where every shot must count. If you get into a tight spot, and I assure you, you will, just turn down that difficulty setting for a bit and get on with the story, because it’s sweet and juicy and wrapped in the most gorgeous, eye-and-ear-pleasing wrapper. You can almost smell the gunpowder.When you hit 100+ hours into a title it’s rare not to get annoyed by the ever-repeating music, but this is not the case here, the score is so good I let it sit in the background as I trail off to do something else. The high-quality sound effects round off the ambiance. Sometimes, I just want to hear that cling of the revolver and Flynn’s almost French-sounding exclamation “Whoohoo, just warmin’ up boys” one more time after she goes on a shooting spree. There are a few things out there as satisfying as going on a bravado run when your character gets all action points back after downing a foe. If executed well, you can go on a true rampage, and potentially finish some scenarios in a single turn! Not easy that, unless you’re playing on easy.Equipping your posse or party with new gear and beautifully drawn cards that unlock a variety of bonuses and unique character abilities allowing you to customize your party’s boosts is equally satisfying. It’s the little things that make this game tick. It’s like a little gadgety box that you sometimes take out just to tinker with it — it’s so damn cute and fun to play with.Did I mention train heists and a full strategy map where the bigger story unfolds? Yeah, I won’t spoil it all, this game has most unexpectedly compelled me to spend almost 300 hours on it and I can’t wait to jump back right into it. I will be following CreativeForge closely as they sure know how to polish a game.This is the first of the Magnificent 7 Strategy Games worth playing that will be featured in this series.It’s all about the feeling and I will be showcasing more Feel of the Game in an ongoing series.Read the full article here: For more gaming reviews and articles follow me at:

_childDocuments_.review: Huge improvement from the HardWest 1 in all aspects: story*, gameplay in turn-based combats** and on the map***.*Great western story with some mystic stuff: bank robbery, trains hijacking, a lot of shootouts with very bad guys and not good sheriffs :D Interesting to follow, a lot of deep and cool characters, good dialogs. Every fan of western games will find something special for him\her. Great cocktail of different western tropes, I would say.** For me huge plus that there are not so many fights in turn-based mode. The battles themselves eventually turn out to be more important for the storytelling and they are not annoying after 20h in game (hello Gears Tactics). *** A big part of the game is on the huge map (like Wasteland 2-3, if you're new for these kinda games), you can find quests on the map and solve them via dialogs\items in your inventory. Some variants of dialogs will give reputations with your teammates, so they will tell their story in HardWast world. As I said, dialogs and characters are well written, so all activities on the map, all main and side quests help to understand lore of the HW (and of course you will find eastereggs from first game) and rest before next fight, which is really great. PS - To be honest, I didn't expect something special from HW2, because I couldn't go through the first one (I started 3-4 times, it's too boring after several chapters). As western-games fan, I gave this HW2 a chance and as you can see from the review, game is great! Already waiting for a third part. Hope 3rd Hard West will continue the story of some characters from this game ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Right, first off the bat: This is AA game, don't expect the levels of polish or depth of X-COM and its ilk.Now, the pros:- A very different experience to your traditional tactics games, it's much faster paced- To facilitate the faster pace the game features the bravado system, essentially you'll get all your AP back if you score a kill. This leads to ridiculous amounts of chain killing if you play your cards right- As such, planning and precision are key- Like the name suggests, the game is rather difficult. Despite being a veteran in this genre I had to bump down the difficulty down about halfway thru- Some weapons can ricochet their shots which leads to some rather fun and interesting interactions- The story can be skipped in its entirety if you so desire- There is a gameplay speed button, ranging from x,5 to x4- The graphics and art are on point for this genreCons:- The VA is about what you'd expect for a AA game- There appears to be a memory leak leading to longer and longer load times the longer you play. Fortunately it's easily solved by a restart- There is a massive difficulty spike in act 2- There is very little gear progression- Shotguns are terrible - characters are apparently unable to aim up- The card loadout system, which governs what skills and passives character have, lacks depth- The soundtrack is entirely forgettable- The story is a little basic and doesn't run the advertised 25-35 hours. My estimations put it at about 15-18.In conclusion, the game is worth its asking price. It's a fun enough experience for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: More of a "shoot things in the right order" puzzle game than an actual strategy game. Combat is pretty basic and more or less limited to shoot things or shoot ricochet of a few select objects. You have your standard cover-system, however without the ability to vault over objects it seems you should be able to, or the almost industry standard option of an overwatch-system. Moreover, it doesn't seem to innovate the genre in any way to compensate for this. Story seems fine and the voice-acting is solid. RPG-wise however, it is sorely lacking, with mostly linear non-meaningful dialogue options and no options for customization other than swapping weapons and a basic talent system. Can't recommend this title as an Turn-based RPG strategy game, but if you are looking for a story-driven puzzlegame, this might be some bang for your buck - I do however suggest you try the demo first.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, Hard West 2 is a sequel that utilises the same core concepts, the base formula, but alters their expression: enhancing certain factors whilst placing a lower priority on others. A lamentable fate that is destined to please some, yet disappoint others - including myself and forcing the hand of this review, as I see it as an imitation which doesn't advance in quality from what came before it.Despite any heavy criticisms, it's still a fun romp, the primary conclusion here is that distinct developers had a target product to produce with certain and perhaps different goals to achieve, and their execution likely accomplished them. Though there is still some overlap, the target audience is simply different. The main body here is therefore primarily a comparison, focused on offering returning customers some ability to contend whether or not the experience the product provides is suited to them relative to what is available in the original.As a quick summary, in my opinion the player who is most accommodated is the one seeking a simple yet enjoyable combat based experience in the X-Com style who doesn't care to pay much attention, who requires only a tenuous and vapid story to loosely tie everything together will still find a worthwhile experience.In order to attempt to demonstrate a sense for the differentiation of the experiences a few examples must be cited. Hard West One and Two have very present abilities or skills present in one way or another, whose acquisition or presentation affects the general strategy. Many perks that were previously locked behind playing cards are now available elsewhere. For instance, the system of replenishing actions points on kills is now available to all party members by default as bravado, some are moved to certain weapon or character traits such as transfusion, ricochet, or cripple, whilst others such as cannibalism or shadow salve are no longer present. Instead, the cards focus on increasing base stats. While this certainly allows for a sense of progression throughout the campaign and optimisation of each member as more cards are acquired and equipped, it comes at the cost of potentially removing character specialisation, identity, and player expression. That is to say, there is only really one way in which Laughing Deer is most effectively used, so each player is likely to be rather similar. In Hard West 1, a sense of randomisation courtesy of acquired injuries and few passive character abilities made the utilisation of available trinkets, cards, and weapons varying by chapter more meaningful. Or at the very least, it attempted to encourage a variety of play throughout.As far as can be determined, the player has fewer overall options at their disposal, but has more available to them at any given time. In this way it creates a more dynamic and fast paced experience at the expense of difficulty.Speaking of, there are numerous difficulty settings to accommodate various skill levels. By my judgement the overall design tends to favour the less experienced. Unlike Hard West 1, the retention of player inventory between chapters and the posse of playable characters through the continued adventure increases player familiarity, allowing the more inexperienced to feel more comfortable as they continue to increase their overall party strength and knowledge of the mechanics.Those more hardened in the genre may find the experience less rewarding however, even on the harder difficulty settings. Once an observant player has become familiar with the particular gimmicks of the game, combat becomes rather trivial, one dimensional, and unrewarding. Even on the Nightmare difficulties, in many instances it suffices to perform a cursory assessment and lead with area of effect abilities, and clean up all enemies on screen by following with a barrage of continually replenishing melee assaults. The player need then only proceed onto the next trigger point which loads the next wave of assailants in the upcoming area, and repeat. In combination with the aforementioned in addition to the lack of any ironman mode, with the player party composition being made up of entirely critical members, a negligent player is very seldom punished for their mistakes in decision making; losing party members during fights, or lack of foresight and planning multiple turns in advance.The manner of execution significantly alters the over mood and tone of the piece. Hard West 1 opted for a narrated and inferred style, as if the player were an onlooker to a tale, of which they became the protagonist - allowing the player to manifest as the protagonist and envisage the traits they find most appealing. Hard West 2 is more direct, light-hearted, and easy going with its first person presentation style. Each party member speaks with voiced lines towards the protagonist's character, Gin Carter. The player is instead told their motivations and reason for being through their direct speech. The writing is not sufficiently strong to maintain nuanced character development, but for the genre it may not be so necessary. As someone who liked Hard West one for its lack of constraint, depiction of the potentially unpleasant, and sombre atmosphere, the replacement of stereotypical "rootin'-tootin'" cowboys was disappointing.Hard West 1 has the potential of grit and nuance, where Hard West 2 does not. The former has the player become familiar with the personal motivations of different individuals as each becomes the protagonist of his own chapter, only for them to be brutally hunted later on; or to force the player to choose one group over another. Such is the unforgiving nature of the Wild West. The latter follows a linear and uninspired plot, where the protagonists embody the bold and just seeking to overcome evil in a matter of personal and moral vengeance.Furthermore, because no party member is capable of perishing and that the game's ending is singular, the story is unable to be compelling. All apparent choices given in campaign events are never meaningful, the outcomes identical.That is to say, there is little impact of player choice upon the environment and on how events unfold. Either a wanted criminal is killed and brought to justice, or they are captured for the local sheriff to do so. In comparison to Hard West 1, it typically provided the player with a moral decision to be considered and the difference in reward being worthy of that consideration. As each chapter is story linked gameplay wise, but still are mutually exclusive, it can warrant the continuance of the vying of immediate personal power with personal morality, and such like, whereas Hard West 2 cannot.In terms of performance, it runs smoothly enough, but players on lower end systems may find mild annoyance from the lengthy loading times and significant memory consumption, which is a greater amount than one would expect from a turn based combat game. In fact, the experience is in many ways more clunky than its predecessor. Minor compounding grievances such as the locking camera when selecting an enemy making it difficult to select a far enemy directly opposite, every input being a single left click leading to an inevitability of an accidental selection, and length ability animations can mar the experience. The saving grace here is the option to adjust the game speed.Concluding, Hard West 2 has some redeeming qualities, but considering the amount of positive reviews is remarkably unconvincing and uncompelling. Standing on its own feet and relative to its predecessor it possesses considerable flaws, bearing the hallmarks of its status as a product outsourced to another developer. In a word, Hard West 2 is the very definition of the concept of a visionary undergoing a reductive replication by another - a poor interpretation of another man's work that loses nuance and certain praiseworthy qualities in favour of pleasure and gratification.

_childDocuments_.review: If your looking at this game, buy it. Don't pay any attention to the negative reviews, its just people nit picking. I can't wait to sink however many more hours into it. The only thing I would have wanted in it, that isn't; is a leveling system.Edit: (Spoilers) After playing a little longer, I do have some criticisms. This game is exceptionally short, is one of them. I went to look up a side quest, and discovered that there are only three chapters; and I was most of the way through chapter 2 when I did this, and it really surprised me that I was already that far into it. A game like this really needs a leveling system, and a way to fight random/non story battles. The Poker hand system is really cool, but that and the weapon upgrades is not enough to get me engaged enough. I hate linear games, and while this isn't 100% linear; it might as well be. If I had the ability to grind and sink time into leveling, it would be perfect to me. It has an awesome story and characters, and some really cool mechanics in and out of combat; but just not enough to keep me interested long enough. I still suggest that you buy it, if these things dont bother you though. But if your looking for something to be playing for weeks, this is not it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really perplexed by the negative reviews. Some say that there is "only one way to solve each mission", but I deliberately replayed a few (while playing on hard), and that's patently false, even just the choice of characters and upgrades opens up new and various solutions.The Bravado mechanic is one of the most innovative I've yet seen in this type of game. It completely changes the way you have to approach turn-based tactics (which perhaps accounts for some of the disappointment in the reviews). Instead of creating choke points, taking the high ground & all the usual X-Com stuff, here it's all about figuring out the right order in which to hit enemies and use powers. This results in the puzzle-ish feel that many have remarked on, which admittedly may not be for everyone, but which I found really engrossing.And gameplay aside, everything else about this production is top notch - the design and artwork are excellent, the exploration is compelling, the attention to detail impressive. This really is one of the best and most innovative variations on the X-Com formula to date.

If you are a TBS/TBT fan, I would seriously recommend giving this one a good, hard look.

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid turn based strategy game. Bravado system allows you to chain kills into more actions, which is great for speeding up combats, allowing for more varied and interesting encounter design where you can truly feel like the odds are stacked against you but you make it out by the skin of your teeth. If you've played Gears Tactics this will feel familiar to you.Luck system is great for mitigating RNG, gaining a better chance to hit whenever you miss or take damage. Bouncing bullets off of the terrain is flavourful and fun to do. The Card system for skills is very interesting, lots of build diversity and decisions to make about your party composition and how you want to divvy out cards between your posse. Overall great game!

_childDocuments_.review: As almost all turn-based strategy games, this is one more in which developers think will be fun to make things overdifficult. I was willing to live with things like face 50 vs 4 (FIFTHY enemies against FOUR, as in the witches cave), but reaching the mission 'Lady Shrike' the game makes a character, whose survival is mandatory to win the battle, lose 1 health point per turn, even untouched. This is the kind of thing that's make me sick about turn-based games, a genre I so used to love. So they want me to pass through all the (long) battle map (with 4 against more or less 25 enemies) keeping alive a character with 20 health points which loses compulsorily 1 health point per turn, not couting any eventual damage (and there will be, because the enemies focus on him)??? Come on, guys! Get real! Too bad I had played more than two hours, so I can't ask for a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is made by a different developer than the prequel, and it shows. The tone in the writing is very different, and the combat system has been turned on its head through the introduction of a new system.We'll start with the narrative. Hard West 1 was told as a series of connected vignettes, with a single narrator (Death himself) providing commentary and indirect dialogue. [spoilers for HW1] The whole game is a sort of proxy war between Death and the Devil, with both of them choosing to influence a group of determined mortals caught in a series of violent events spurred by greed, faith, anger, and a need to set things straight. As a result, the whole game feels like a grim framework for a story thick with evil, and the people tempted towards it in a world fraught with cruelty.Hard West II is more straightforward, but a bit less mature. The story is a singular tale with a single protagonist (Gin Carter) working to get his soul back from a devil named Mammon, taking him on a journey across the Old West. The characters are relatively simplistic and simply written: Gin is a smooth-talking gambler that rarely changes his tune, Flynn is a loudmouthed mystic that complains constantly, Bill is a revenant that reminds you that he's dead with every single voice line, and every Native American you run into runs the gamut of stereotypes that you could imagine. Laughing Deer sounds like an orc. They even call the setting the "Hard West" without any irony. The only character I have come around to liking so far is Lazarus, as his aggressive preaching feels perfect for the setting.The gameplay simplifies the luck system that was central to the previous game, and instead focuses on a new system called Bravado. Bravado refreshes your action points when a character gets a kill, and it rapidly becomes the center piece of any viable strategy. Most encounters feature a deluge of enemies, which boil down to "killable in one hit" and "killable in two/three hits". It emerges that there's a clear difference between a good turn and a bad turn, in that a good turn has a character knock down all of the dominoes you set by systematically killing whole swaths of weakened enemies, and a bad turn has you leaving several alive to surround you and gun you down. It's extremely binary, and it takes the game away from the more RPG feel of the previous game towards more of a strange puzzle-esque experience. There are also more mission timers, some of which don't make a lot of sense (why do I have to find the machine in Boomtown within 7 turns? It was here before, what's going to happen to it besides me failing for not meeting an arbitrary objective?).I'd give this game a mixed recommendation if I could. It isn't a bad game, but the fact that it carries the same name as a game I liked quite a bit while being so aggressively different leaves me more than a little upset.One major positive is the art. Whoever did all of the mystical comic-book style art, especially for the cards, you did an amazing job.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a RTS/Turn Based Veteran this game feels bad to play. The bravado system would be a lot of fun if the game didn't seem solely built around it. I've noticed the devs keep pointing toward other strats one can use, but at the end of the day that doesn't really change the fact the entire game is set up to use that one mechanic. _childDocuments_.review: When I first heard of Hard West II I tried the demmo. Although it was the kind of game I was looking for I found the game too difficult to play. I still kept it on my wishlist for the future. When I saw the game on sale at a price too good to pass up, I bought it. I have found that the full game is challenging but enjoyable. The game is more than a simple hack 'n' slash kill all the bad guys to get the loot. I've had to think to change and adapt my tactics with each encounter, even to choosing the weapons and equipment to suit different problems and try different approaches to each encounter. There is no 'one size fits all' approach to every situation. I heartily recommend this game to all who like tactics-based adventures, especially those with physical challenges. I only have one hand but the simple mouse-only controlling provides me with a game that is easy to play, while the game itself still provides thought-provoking problem solving. I think that anyone who enjoys action, adventure and RPG games will enjoy this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard west 2 is an impressive improvement over its predecessor as well as a fresh take on turn based games, it offers unique mechanics that makes it stand out to your average turn based combat, and man is it so fun to play.What exactly makes it different? - Killing an enemy in this game will give you a "Bravado" state where your action points get refilled, which you can use in combination with other skills or items to have one insane turn where one or two party members would end up killing a ton enemies in a single turn. It is so damn satisfying planning an encounter and setting up your strategy and then finally having one character casually murder an entire group of enemies.- "Luck" is a resource in the game that can be gained by missing shots or by certain consumables, items, and skills. it allows you to increase your hit chances for a certain character which in combination of ricochet attacks are brilliant ideas that eliminates the need to flank enemies to bypass their cover bonuses, or having to be ALWAYS in the mercy of RNG to land you shots.- Character progression in this game is also unique in that there is no XP bars or levels or anything of the sort. You improve your party by combining a different set of poker cards that you find the world to have the most optimal hand which in turn unlock different skills and passives depending on the hand you have.This game demands that you exploit its bravado mechanic in combination with party synergies and skills to progress. I've seen some comparisons to XCOM (because they're both turn based I guess?) and that couldn't be further away from the truth. If you play it like it's XCOM you will most likely suffer and be punished by the game for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great tactical rpg. I really enjoyed the fantasy/wild west setting. The game looks pretty good as far as shooter tactical rpg's go. The main selling points of this game are the progression systems and the minute to minute play. The basic gameplay loop feels really great. Each character has 3 action points per round, but if they get a kill, they get all of their points back. This mechanic along with the individual character powers leads to some really amazing combos where you can take out 10+ enemies in a single round. The progression system is equally compelling. As you play through missions and complete side quests you get playing cards (standard 4 suits, 9 - Ace + a few jokers). You can assign these cards to your party members for the stat bonuses of the cards, but also to make hands. Each character has a specific set of traits and abilities that get unlocked as you equip better hands of cards to them.The story is alright. The overall plot is fine but the individual story/character beats are mediocre at best. It's not really why I played this game but I did want to note it.Overall, I like this game and I would recommend it to anyone who like tactical  rpg's, especially if, like me, they're just waiting for Xcom 3 to finally get announced.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:  The 'trick shot' ability that you can do with certain guns is really fun and inventive.Cons:  The game has no RNG. Everything in every encounter, is predetermined. Even if the game displays a 99% hit chance, it COULD in reality, be a  0% hit chance. I've conducted multiple tests and have confirmed this to a 99.9% certainty. Example: In one encounter, I had a 75% chance to hit my target, and yet I missed it 100% of the time, in over 20 encounter reloads. This is the biggest issue with the game by far. The game literally lies to you by displaying 95% hit chance or whatever, and yet in reality you have a 0% hit chance. It reminds me of ANTHEM where the DPS of the guns, are completely fake and in reality don't actually do what is shown... this game does exactly the same with the hit chances. You cannot issue multiple orders simultaneously (like you can in XCOM2 or DOS2) Characters cannot move diagonally (but they can melee attack diagonally, which makes little sense) You can't see whether or not your characters are in cover. This is a MASSIVE issue, since being in  or not, literally means life or death in the game (just like it does in XCOM2 for example). You cannot choose your characters, they get chosen for you... so there's very little "rpg-ness" with regards to your party, since you get given a cookie-cutter set of characters and that's it. I much prefer to create my own party, like in XCOM2 or DOS2. Only about a quarter of the game is voiced. The vast majority of the game isn't voiced, so you're gonna have to do a buttload of reading if you want to follow the story at all. Combat gives NO experience. You gain NO experience from killing enemies. And the game has no levels for characters, which means the character progression in this game is FAR inferior to XCOM2 or DOS2. It is exceptionally difficult to see where enemies are if they're in a building. The 'see through highlight' mechanic is rather poor... contrast this to XCOM2 or DOS2 where you can see EXACTLY where enemies are, if they're in a building. The game has a  tutorial, during which, you have zero freedom. You HAVE TO do  what it says. Cannot set the frame rate of the game at all After each kill, the game automatically targets a random enemy to attack. This is really irritating and should NOT be happening. They use the "animated still frame" method for cinematics, which imo is a cheap/lazy method of doing cinematics. I'd honestly rather prefer if cinematics were done with the in-game engine, rather than using this 'still animation' method. You can't quit from the game to desktop. You can only quit from in-game to the main menu, and then from there to desktop (this wastes time and means you have an unnecessary loading screen each time you want to quit the game) You can't rotate the camera away from your character... as soon as you rotate the camera, it immediately snaps back to your currently selected character. You can't damage the environment . So unlike in XCOM2 or other TRPGs where you can destroy the cover of your enemies with a grenade/dynamite, in this game you simply aren't given that tactical option at all. This is a massive downgrade from XCOM2 and provides a gameplay experience with WAY less tactical options or inventivenessIs this game BAD? No, and it could even possibly have been GOOD, if the completely bizarre design choices of cons #1, 2, 3, 4, & 11 weren't made by the devs. Honestly all this game did, was make me want to play more XCOM2, DOS2 or Wasteland3, and I would play those games a hundred more hours, before I play another hour of this game. It has WAY less RPG-ness than XCOM2, DOS2 and Wasteland3 due to point #5 & 7 and also less tactical-ness due to cons #1, 3 & 15. I really wanted to like this game, since I'm a big fan of the genre and have over 500hours in the above mentioned TRPGs, but this game simply isn't worth being mentioned in the same breath as those games.Here's my first hour or so of the game: For more reviews, visit my curator page: For my full recommended list of games:

_childDocuments_.review: Did you like games such as XCOM 2 and Wasteland 3? Then you will definitely enjoy Hard West 2! It's a tactical turn-based combat game in a western setting with fantasy elements and it's a hard and very rewarding challenge!Made in Unity, the graphics aren't amazing, but it does the job well enough. The combat is hard, even in the easy setting, before you get a grasp on it. It has an interesting approach where an aggressive style is rewarded well. You don't get to create your own characters, which has its upsides and downsides. There's still some room for managing them as you can choose their weapons and who gets to have the limited available playing cards, which dictates which skills you unlock.The game also rewards exploring and completing every mission to 100%, as you get special weapons and buffs, which will make the very challenging combat _slightly_ easier.I recommend playing your first play-through on Easy, to not ruin the fun and give up before you try it or Hard (there's no Normal setting). _childDocuments_.review: This was an enjoyable game.  I saw ChristopherOdd and Splattercat play this, and caught it on a steam sale.  Well worth the money, and it doesn't overstay it's welcome.   My 43 hours were probably on the long side but mostly because I was replaying some combat.   Unlike Xcom 2 there's a set number of encounters, so replaying some and trying out different actions felt ok to me. I never experienced any bugs and I enjoyed the overland interactions that let you use your companions outside of combat.   There's no random encounters, so you can expect to be able to navigate all the overland scenarios optimally without really missing anything.  The order you do them however is your choice.   Although there are choices you can make, there's no real RPG and no slides at the end to show you how your choices impact the world.   Without any random encounters, or ways to lose companions this game feels a bit more like a story punctuated by tactical combat.   I haven't tested it, so maybe it's possible to not take a companion but I don't think the game is made that way. Mechanics wise, I would say this game handles much better than Weird West by being tactical turn based.  It creates an interesting world to experience, if not really explore since all encounters are laid out from the beginning.    I suspect adding in a few unique but unessential random encounters and a few random skipable fights, would have made the world feel a little more worth the exploration.I think I paid about 12 bucks for this and very well worth that money.  A purchase at regular price would have been fine.    I don't know that it has quite the same replayability of Xcom but if you want to scratch that itch it would be easy to hop back into this and rerun it without getting sucked in to a protracted game.

_childDocuments_.review: A great isometric turn-based tactics game in the style we've all come to love that both stays faithful to what made these games so enjoyable while also offering some of its own neat tricks and mechanics.We follow a story of a group of mercenaries/hired hands/social outcasts that do questionable jobs for money when they end up dealing with the devil himself. After being cheated by the devil and losing their souls, they now have to find a way to track him down and win their souls back, or rather beat their souls out of the devil by force.In some ways, the game feels like a story-driven RPG with main quest objectives, as well as side-objectives in a rich, well-developed wild west world. Each of our posse members has inventory slots for where we can equip them with two weapons, two items, a trinket, and a bunch of cards. The cards offer bonuses, and when equipped in combinations straight out of poker, they unlock special abilities.The combat is a familiar turn-based tactics encounter with its own set of objectives that requires us to move through the map, face off enemies, and complete the mission. Each of these combat missions also has side objectives, completing which offers us bonuses and also gives us something harder to aim for in case we're finding the mission a bit too easy. The luck system from the first Hard West makes a return, though it's less intrusive now, acting more as an extra little bonus each time a player character misses a shot or gets hit. What's new and quite prominent this time round is the bravado mechanic. With this mechanic, each time one of our posse members finishes off an enemy, all of their action points replenish and they can act again. This allows for a strategic approach to each fight, opening up possibilities for chain combo kills by the same character within the same turn. You could be surrounded by more than a dozen of enemies, but by playing your moves right, you could take out more than half of them in a single turn!When outside of combat, on the map, we can move between towns and settlements, complete sidequests, buy gear, and interact with points of interest, which often throw some situation our way with some dialogue between our characters. During these moments, some of our posse members might disagree and we need to choose how to respond and who to agree with. This gets us to develop trust with them, which is useful as it unlocks combat bonuses for those teammates and also unlocks some special choices during crucial story dialogues. I like that all the consequences of our choices are clearly shown (e.g. if you gain trust with a certain teammate or what the item reward might be), because for a game such as this, where story encounters are text-based and surrounding details aren't clear, having to guess what a bonus might be isn't fun at all. So kudos to the devs for executing this aspect in a way that keeps it fun and doesn't punish the player based on guesswork.There are 5 different difficulty levels, so just about anyone should find the level of difficulty that they need. The 'Hard' difficulty, which is the middle one, felt perfectly challenging enough if you're already familiar with these type of games.Presentation is great. Combat visuals are as you'd expect in other similar games, isometric perspective, clearly shown grid and cover, good icons and UI. The outside of combat visuals are more simplistic and most of the time you'd just be moving between the maps. The dialogue is sufficient enough to convey the story events but without turning into a book that you'd be reading for aeons. Music is pretty good, especially during combat encounters, and voice acting by each character is VERY good and of high quality. It really brought to life the personalities of these characters. I also really enjoyed how some of the combat missions were executed in motion, like on horseback or aboard a train (often a combination of both!). So we still have the grid that determines where and how much we can move, but everything is moving, creating a more action-like and cinematic feel of those combat missions.I enjoyed Hard West 2 a lot. The first game was pretty good already, but this one feels like a tighter, more focused experience with more consistent gameplay mechanics and story. An improvement in all regards really and one of the better games in the isometric turn-based tactics style. I've not come across any bugs or glitches, so any that might've been present, have likely been fixed by now.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 got on my radar during Steam Fest when it was recommended by several Steam curators and Youtube content creators. I checked the demo and really liked what I saw there.Full game builds on the demo, adding more playable characters and host of equipment to deck out your posse with. Hard West 2 has two main layers to its gameplay, strategic over-world map you explore and tactical turn-based combat. The game has XCOM-lite tactical combat, maybe a bit simplified compared to similar games in genre, that introduces few new ideas to the formula--most importantly its Bravado system.  The Bravado system allows you to continue your offensive efforts as long as your character is able to finish its target. It is very interesting modification of "Overwatch" system that is  more offensive-focused.One minor disappointment for me was card system that looked promising at start but it became stale towards the end. I quickly found suitable card combinations for my characters and there was very little need or even opportunities to try new card combos. I found that some of those character skills locked behind high-value card combinations were lackluster or their card costs too restrictive.All in all, Hard West 2 was fun experience that lasted solid 25+ hours of fun for very reasonable price. I did not encounter any major bugs during my time with the game either. I can easily recommend this game to anyone who likes tactical turn-based combat with interesting twist to standard XCOM-like formula.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the extremely annoying timed side mission during battle, like the "defeat all enemies in 1 turn" kind, in fact I assume this would be the theme for the whole game, because other than the tutorial battle, the first actual battle (boomtown) and the next side battle you can get (vs bandit camp) has this. It's not just that, the whole bravado mechanic means the whole game is about chaining kills, with or without reposition, basically it's just a puzzle game, think like those puzzle game and thinking ahead for the next turn and such. It is very predictable, like chess, and this timed missions are essentially those chess puzzles with a video game skin.This means this game feels more like a puzzle game than an rpg, especially with easy way to get 100% hit with fixed damage (rather than damage range). Essentially this game gives an Into the Breach experience, something I don't like. I was looking for something in the vein of Wastelands or Xcom series, Knights Arthur Knight's Tale, or all those turn based fantasy crpg, which are turn based rpg, and this game is not it. It's just another puzzle game disguised as a turn based rpg game, and therefore it gets a resounding thumbs down from me.Some people might wonder what's the difference between the predictable gameplay in this game vs Xcom for example and why I prefer xcom. Xcom is all about taking calculated risk, knowing that your 99% shot can miss, or that your gun deals 4-7 damage and the target has 5 hp left, and unexpected things can happen, that is why it is exciting to ironman the game. But this game is not, you just look at the map situation then solve the puzzle and play it out like Into the Breach basically, if you've solved the puzzle then you clear it. There is no excitement of the unknown whatsoever. Even the luck mechanic essentially ensures that your "rng luck" breaks even. It's literally turn based tactics with a crutch, made for those whiny kids that complained about rigged dice roll when their 90% shot miss twice in a row. Well, to be fair, completion of statistics 101 should be a prerequisite to play any game with rng factor anyway.Edit: I played many more stage after that and all I can say is the game just gets worse and more annoying. I'm at the Calla Calla stage and that stage is just extremely annoying. Like the mission design is just annoying and designed to frustrate players with regenerating enemies camping in elevated full cover building that lobs bleeding grenade every turn (bleeding in this game is way more debilitating than the usual).Another important thing I need to mention is that there are many extremely annoying side mission in the battles. I'm talking about things like, kill x with y skill, kill x enemies 10 times with posse skill (it's actually really annoying because then you need a specific playstyle to do the mission) basically the whole thing just gets more puzzle like. Overall the game have the tendency to railroad you to complete mission in a specific way, and the rpg element, aka card system and such basically mean unlimited respec designed to facilitate this puzzle-like approach.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very early review after playing about 45 minutes of the HW2.  I enjoyed the first game, while I own it both on Steam and the Switch, I played HARD WEST primarily on the Switch.  It wasn't a perfect game, but it was unique and enjoyable enough to lead me to by HW2 on Day 1, that and a friends fair critic of the game.   Look up  Bluesuit's review below or above or just find it over on YT  he points out the good and the bad.   But if you liked the first I believe just like Bluesuit said, you will most likely enjoy the second one as it does add very nice mechanics to the game.  There are a few QoL things that Bluesuit points out that I forsee the developers fixing pretty quickly.  If those are addressed then every people who weren't fans of the first game or by nature fans of turn-based games may indeed find that Hard West 2 is well worth their time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! Never felt unfair. I would go as far as to say it is actually relatively easy for X-COM-like veterans, even on nightmare difficulty.It has a lot of great mechanichs I personally enjoyed:- Luck system makes the game less random, as you have some kind of compensation when missing a shot- Cards stats boosters are great- No wrong answers in dialoges (unlike The Banner Saga, but with the notable exception of the most powerful card in the game, that can only be obtained by making a counterintuitive dialogue choice)- No real penalties if posse members are injured or downed during a mission (unlike XCOM)- Bravado system works well- Train + horses missions feel super cool
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to give this game a recommendation. But it's been a struggle. There are so many good things in this game, improvements from the first. But the level design is what tips it toward a thumbs down for me. Allow me to explain my reasoning, starting with the good first.There atmosphere, narrative and the graphics are really good for an indie title like this. The amount of game you get for the price puts a lot of competitors to shame. The characters are entertaining, and even though it certainly does not reach the depths of AAA-title in character development, it's still great value for the money.But, the level design is what really breaks the fun-factor for me. Many encounters have been done in a way so that there's essentially a linear way of completing them. Being able to fight a more difficult route to deal with some fortified positions, or providing tunnel access, or any alternate routes would've provided with much needed variety in dealing with some encounters. Furthermore, many of the challenges start with the enemies already upon you, so you basically have one single turn to do some very specific moves, or you will immediately be at such a great disadvantage that you just shouldn't do that.This makes you feel less in control about what you can do, especially when you have time-based challenges, where you have a limited amount of rounds to be able to accomplish a certain task. Everything is about finding one optimal way of doing things, and doing anything else will slow you down and your characters will get so much damage it's borderline impossible to complete. Unless of course you play the game on easy-mode. Which instead makes it less about your skillset at all.Hard West 2 does not reward me for trying alternate routes. Instead it wants me to do everything in a specific way. The map, the missions, almost everything is setup to teach me how to do exactly what the designers wanted me to do it. "If you use this power here, you will kill all of these characters in time to get to there... if you do it ANY other way, you will fail that task".The game was very fun until I got disillusioned and discovered that. And everything unfortunately went downhill from there. Which is really REALLY sad. Because before I discovered that, it felt like one of the better games in the genre.Hoping for Hard West 3.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly? It's a really fun and thrilling game if you play it on one of the harder difficulties. I breeze through the content in maybe sixteen hours of actual play-time. So... this was on the second difficulty mind you, not the third: Nightmare. Now there are some noticeable but mostly cosmetic bugs (which I've reported) and I find the lack of voice acting during certain times to be... a bit detracting. The core gameplay though? Very solid. I think the characters are fairly rich but that the enemies you face are a bit more one dimensional; I would have liked to see more levels that were longer or more varied and I am hoping that they do this in later release perhaps.So yes, if you enjoy xcom you will probably enjoy this. I will say that I didn't have to SCUM anything except for Kestral's Hacineda; that was an extremely trying mission and I did have to save many times to solve 'the puzzle' although I do believe there were different paths for me to take to accomplish that mission -- so -- don't be fooled into thinking there is only one path in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent turn based strategy. Played it to the end with no real issues. AI isnt a slouch and it was tough to try and cheese them, especially with all the ricochet items littered around the maps designed to pop you from around your cover. It can seem a bit overwhelming at times, but it forces you to be more efficient with your tactics and special moves. Played for 35 hours and completed all side quests, but it kinda seemed like it was over too soon. Maybe just me. Its like you finally get all the cards to unlock your main 4 character's abilities and its already time for the end game. Definitely worth the money if you love games like xcom. Laughing Deer is OP
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I tried to like this game, it's nothing more than a puzzle game disguised as a modern turned based strategy game. If the level are not played with the correct sequence of actions, you will get stuck. Even on easy I could not get past levels that are chained together where your characters keep the same health between episodes. Enemies seem to appear randomly as you advance. Do not recommend if you are looking for a modern strategy game experience. This is the first game I attempted to refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: This kinda flew under the radar for me until I actually went looking for reviews. In essence it's not dissimilar to the tactical battle part of XCOM 2, and is very enjoyable as such. I've seen some reviews saying it encourages save-scumming, and certainly the setup of many missions is such that you may take more than one go to really nail all the objectives. But as long as you don't mind playing in that way it's really engaging, fun, challenging without being a complete brick wall, and well worth buying if you see it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 is a tactical strategy game / RPG set in a supernatural version of the Wild West. You will assemble a crew of interesting characters, each with a unique supernatural ability, and set on a hunt of the Ghost Train. The combat is very good. It’s quite a bit different from XCOM and the like, but not in a bad way. There is no overwatch here and you’re often heavily outnumbered, so your best bet is to try to take out as many enemies as you can on your turn, before they get the chance to do damage to you. To help you with that, there’s a “Bravado” mechanic that restores all of the character’s action points when they get a kill. You can also bounce the bullets off metal objects to hit targets behind cover. And when you miss or get hit, you get “Luck” that you can spend to improve your chance to hit in the future.Some of the fights take place on and around a moving train, and I don’t believe I’ve seen anything like it in other games of this genre. Looks very cool.Hard West 2's combat is fun and engaging, and overall it's a solid and well-made game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: X-Com style game with Cowboys?  Hell yeah.  Had lots of fun, good mechanics, loved the individual abilities each character had.  The playing card system is also another layer of strategy that you can play with.  My only issue was that the last chapter was very short.  It seemed like chapter 1 had a lot going on, side quests, main quests, finding companions.  Chapter 2 had less but still felt like there was a good amount to do.  Chapter 3 seemed very barren with only a few main quests to finish out the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's alright for fans of the tactics genre, and it could have been great, but it         is          so         slow.Maps are broken down in different areas with fights, but you stay in turn-based mode to get from one to the next. So you crawl painfully, character by character.Even when fighting, it takes forever to move.You need to wait until a character is done moving to start moving the next.You get an unskippable pause on each character at the start of each round displaying their bonus.When mobs enter the area, they come one by one, and at the end a lot of them come.As a comparison, Showgunners made combat feel a lot more dynamic, and xcom2 had a lot of qol features missing here like queuing characters movements.It's a shame, apart from the snail pace there are great features in the game: trick shots are fun, story is good, environment is beautiful, voices are alright, level design is interesting.It's a missed opportunity but it can easily be fixed if they make another sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from solid XCOM-style gameplay with a cool theme (honestly, sometimes all you need) Hard West 2's out-of-combat gameplay loop is simple but with events, tasks, and purchase choices in the in-game stores that let you be both chill but have to think at the same time. Are you going to buy that quest item that so conveniently is in the shop, or a new gun? Should you complete this dialogue now or wait until someone's loyalty is higher and you have more options? These are the kinds of elements you'll find matter with time as you go through the game, and it, along with the card system, helps set it apart from a game where the combat might be good but then the rest is junk. Even the story works well enough, with enough changes and thematic elements that it doesn't just feel like the same thing over and over again. Personally, I've really enjoyed it. I'm near the end (I think) and I've played 57 hours of it in total, so it ain't terribly short. And I could see super gameplay-focused people playing it again solely based on doing different builds. Absolutely recommended - ESPECIALLY for the price, no brainer.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Glad i got it on sale - only wish i stopped sticking the fork in my eye before i could return it but I'll give it a shot anyway. There just isn't enough here to make this anything other than an extremely watered down version of X-com that actually (unbelievably) rolls more misses. I really never thought I'd ever see a game where you miss more than X-com but here it is! It's artificially hard and I hate games that are this lazy.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you liked Hard West 1, you'll love Hard West 2.  But it's currently very short and doesn't feel like a complete game. I loved the first game and this one has got entirely different characters, but the same great atmosphere, music, and nailbitingly tense tactical battles where you're constantly one frustrating damage or action point short of what you need to be able to keep the Bravado chair going to massacre the bad guys before they massacre you. It's a very different focus that sets this series aside from most other X-COM style tactical battlers. The only real downside is that the game is incredibly short and ends rather abruptly. The game just left Beta, so I'm assuming there's going to be more content added in the following months, but it's basically an early access release without officially saying it's an early access release. If you've played the first game, you'll be expecting the game to shift between different characters (with entirely different equipment, cards, and skills) every other act, forcing you to relearn an entirely new set of tactics every so often. A lot of people apparently hated that mechanic, so this time around the action is pretty linear and you've got 6 characters (four of which you can play as at any given time) that you can build up your trust level with to occasionally unlock different rewards or action choices along the way. It seems like there should be an entire parallel game track where you play as the seventh character... Kestrel, your missing brother/partner who more or less disappears after the tutorial, but pops up occasionally to taunt you and talk about how he's off pursuing his own path of revenge... but that's never actually happens, even though there appear to be clear story beats where that's supposed to happen. It also doesn't look like you can get the last two cards (jokers) in this version of the game, though I've seen them in review screenshots. Presumably that's also content that will show up in a later release.   So my review is:  Buy it on sale if you enjoyed the first one or just want to play a cool stripped-down undead cowboy version of X-COM. You'll beat it over a couple of days, and you'll love every second of it, but it's probably not worth paying the full $30 for in its current state. It certainly looks like they're setting it up to have additional content though, including possibly a 4th or 5th act, which I'm eagerly anticipating... provided this doesn't turn into one of those games where they DLC you to death with content that always should have been part of the original game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 = XCOM (turn-based tactics) + Desperados 2/3 (similar setting and storyline).Highly recommended. "Bravada" mechanics is refreshing and satisfying. I often found myself thinking for a few minutes after pack spooling and then completing the pack in one round.Pros:- "Bravada"- "Train" missions with horses gave the feeling of true wild west- Music- Overall game designCritics:- AI is good, but enemies are too repetitive. I'd like to see more creature variety.- I wish there were more at least 2 places for member amulets (1 is too restrictive).
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Please play this game. You won't regret it. Story is excellent. Graphics are crisp. Sound creates great atmosphere. Level design is epic. Characters have character. Flipping between turn based mode and the story explore mode is good too. Different speed levels mean you do not get frustrated. This game tickles the feel guds. Have not had a single issue on hard level yet. Gameplay is challenging enough. The bravado system or the lay back and redeploy - it all works. Please play it. Please.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: This was a real treat - Take the X-Com style game, improve on it in a bunch of ways, add ricocheting with new mechanics and a fun supernatural story of revenge and apparently you get this game. Notably better than the original, this was a joy to finish. And hard mode does end up being quite hard. I ended switching to normal towards the end because I kept failing in a mission. Not sure what I was doing wrong, but I'm confident it was simply something I overlooked in the setup.Totally worth playing and completing and it worked flawlessly in linux. Never a crash, glitch, nor error the entire time.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, yes, yes and YESSS!!! Probably the best purchase I recently made on Steam. Last year I played Wasteland 3 and I thought I won't have another turn based tactical game that lives up to that for a while, but I was pelasently surprised. This game is a solid 9/10 for me if I count Wasteland 3 a 10/10 which I cannot not. The dark fantasy western asthetic just seeping from every bit of this game, the characters are interesting and you want to see and hear more of them on every turn of events. The fighting is creative and lets you mess around with insane combos. I recommend playing this game on Hard if you are an experienced turn based tactical player as the whole Bravado system might turn lower difficulty fights a tad too easy. I have to say on Hard I face challenges that doesn't make me want to rip my hair out from frustration but makes me sweat for success. The world is rich and makes me want to discover every dark corner of every area I set my foot in. And the game rewards you for your curiosity again and again which makes the world map just as interesting part of the game, as the fighting encounters. I also need to highlight the art style that improved sooooo much compared to the first game. And no, I am not trying to compare 2015 graphics to 2022 graphics. I am talking about the quality of the art and how much more it gives to those who are interested in this twisted world. Weapons, characters, locations, even the cards that gives you the skills are just gorgeous and makes me excited for every new piece I encounter. (Sidenote: The company NEEDS to sell deck of poker cards with the arts seen in the game. I need that in my life)I want more of this game so I can only hope for a DLC soon where I will throw my money at the devs within a heartbeat.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of people comparing this game to Xcom, which makes no sense and this game shouldn't even be an Xcom copy. The game is great but a bit short. I wasn't sure if I should buy it at first, but in the end it was a good decision. The art style is western good, as is the music. The characters are interesting as well as the card system. Fans of turn-based games should not miss this game, especially if it is on sale. Good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hard West 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hard West 2 is a journey to the heart of darkness in the American West. Take control of a supernatural posse and catch the mysterious Ghost Train. Outsmart, outcheat and outgun your enemies in this turn-based tactics game set in a Wild West world where nothing is as it seems.

name: Loop Hero
detailed_description: The Lich has thrown the world into a timeless loop and plunged its inhabitants into never ending chaos. Wield an expanding deck of mystical cards to place enemies, buildings, and terrain along each unique expedition loop for the brave hero. Recover and equip powerful loot for each class of hero for their battles and expand the survivors' camp to reinforce each adventure through the loop. Unlock new classes, new cards, and devious guardians on your quest to shatter the endless cycle of despair. Infinite Adventure: Select from unlockable character classes and deck cards before setting out on each expedition along a randomly generated loop path. No expedition is ever the same as the ones before it. Plan Your Struggle: Strategically place building, terrain, and enemy cards along each loop to create your own dangerous path. Find balance between the cards to increase your chances of survival while recovering valuable loot and resources for your camp. Loot and Upgrade: Strike down menacing creatures, recover stronger loot to equip on the fly and unlock new perks along the way. Expand Your Camp: Turn hard-earned resources into campsite upgrades and gain valuable reinforcements with each completed loop along the expedition path. Save the Lost World: Overcome a series of unholy guardian bosses over a grand saga to save the world and break the time loop of the Lich!
