_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Novel gameplay idea. Good-looking NES-style pixel art, good music, somewhat interesting story. First few hours are fun. However, gameplay grows stale quickly: You are, in fact, optimizing HP loss and damage through small, grindy upgrades until you beat the game. Tactics or strategy are neither necessary nor possible, because the few options you have for interacting with the game do not have all that much effect.You can build a deck of cards, place cards in a run, choose hero equipment, and manage your camp.Choosing cards has little actual consequences: Cards primarily determine monsters, but despite different monster abilities (e. g. life steal, item steal), all encounters play out the same. Even if you pick slightly more dangerous foes, there isn't any particular reward for doing so. Utility cards, on the other hand, balance their advantages with similar downsides (e. g. fasten flow of time causes faster healing but also faster enemy respawn). Apart from a few hard-coded combinations (e. g. place card X next to Y), there is hardly any emergent interaction between card effects. In the end, even a very basic deck is more than sufficient to complete the game.Placing cards in the core game loop quickly becomes cumbersome. There are a few, very obvious placing patterns that work well on every run and there is little incentive to use any other than these default patterns. Since monster spawns take a few in-game days to have their effect, there is hardly any chance for reacting to the current state of affairs (e. g. by placing more or less monster spawns). Choosing equipment is an exercise in futility: On the one hand, the heavy RNG kills any intentional builds - on the other hand, just picking items with higher level once available works just fine in most cases. Equipment seems somewhat self-balancing (e. g. if a sword has additional magic damage, it has less normal damage), which just makes equipment management even more futile.Camp management is a grindfest for most of the game. You need to farm resources over many runs just to collect a myriad of miniscule, stacking bonus effects. In contrast, certain upgrades (i. e. attack speed card, archers, magic HP shield for rogue, alchemy) are drastically overpowered and break the entire game. Finally, a usability glitch: some buildings need to be placed next to specific other buildings - which the game does not tell you beforehand, so with a little bad luck you need to raze half your camp for upgrades. Suggestions for improvement:- Add interacting monsters (e. g. goblins combining with ratwolves to goblin rider)- Add minimum and maximum levels for monsters (i. e. make card choice matter)- Have loot differ by monster strength (e. g. skeletons drop better loot than ratwolves)- Have loot differ by monster type (e. g. vampires drop items with life steal, allows targeted builds)- Add opportunities to interact with the game (e. g. cards that damage monsters with specific attributes)- Add mechanics apart from optimizing HP loss vs. damage (e. g. status effects on enemies)
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a game that on the surface seems really simple and boring when in reality it is a more nuanced game that is incredibly addicting.  You can cater it to what you want to achieve in each expedition and I think that is a key to the game that is easily overlooked.  Do you want to just loop a bunch, collect resources and build up your encampment?  You can do that!  Do you want to see how hard you can push yourself before you face the boss or have to retreat?  You can do that too!  The ability to dynamically change the focus and difficulty of the game by how you stack your deck in the beginning is really the backbone I think of the game design.Is it a game that will require twitch reactions and have incredibly hard content right from the start to make you grind a ton before you even reach the first real boss?  Not exactly; but if that is the sort of game you are looking for than Loop Hero is not for you.  If you want a nice mix between Idle and Rougelite that lets you customize your experience based on what sort of gaming mood you are in than buy Loop Hero.  I promise you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I only played it at launch and have not seen the content from any of the releases. It benefits from offering a really unique and cool world/gameplay loop (no pun intended). The ultimate issue I had with it is that it gets too repetitive . . . there is not much the game can do to diversify its content offering as there is very little randomness to the game, the player controls pretty much everything that happens with a high degree of reliability. As a result, once you've tried out all the cards, and pieced together strategies that work for you . . . the magic kind of goes away.However, the 20 hours were great. Enjoyed them thoroughly and was an awesome little experience. Not every game has to overstay its welcome.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: It is a busy working game, I didnt find the game loop interesting. The game feels like a lot of repetition with the decisions being resumed to just stats maximization. After defeating the last boss a first time it does not seems to be any reason to do it again. The idle aspect makes the gameplay feel monotonous.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Great - old school good looks with a winning combination of roguelike dungeon, base building, deck construction, and idle style movement - into a single gameplay loop. And loop you will...But for the more prosaic, a non-permadeath roguelike game of character progression with gradual permanent unlockable bonuses, three classes, three chapters with a different boss (and probably a final 4th boss), lots of different terrain, monster types, monster skills, equipment etc.For the price, a solid title to soak up the pandemic hours quite happily. Excellent. I recommend it if you like this kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: One of the greatest games made in the last decade. I grew up as a kid during the MSDOS era, and this game nails that vibe. The soundtrack is a masterpiece too. It's the perfect game if you work at your computer, and you want to take a quick coffee break to play a loop, it's super easy to get back to work after a run. Worth every cent. Have not seen anything this innovative or unique in a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Unique gameplay, great aesthetic. Try it out if you are on the fence, it will not disappoint.Much like slay the spire this is a game that other devs will try to vainly copy in the years to come. Unlike Slay The Spire it doesn't make any vain attempts to be and endless roguelite, you will get a solid 30-50hours and then the game will come to a fulfilling end.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Intense strategy RPG with deckbuilding and combat that requires luck.PROS:-Gorgeous art-Brutal placements of enemies but if defeated its a risk/reward deal-Addictive gameplay with lots of cards that can be utilized for building  your own loop world-Random generated loops each playthrough offers replayability-Quick and to the point storyline with charming dialougeCONS:-The game can be quite difficult, not that thats a bad thing but it requires you multiple long playthroughs and you will find yourself dying multiple times trying to gain resources only for you to die fast and only gain 30% of what you made most of the time -Bosses are brutal and you need great loot in order to compete with them otherwise they will annihilate you fast.-The game and how you gain loot is completely random, you could either get amazing loot as well as cards that support your world, or the opposite can happen and you get screwed over by the random number generator gods.In short, if you are looking for a challenging RPG with strategy and a side of world building, check this game out, it definitely wont dissappoint. I got it on sale so its very much worth the price its at right now.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a unique rogue-like experience that uses elements of base building that enhances your combat. During expeditions you gain armor, weapons, and field cards that you can use that will both change your stats and playing field. Such as a rogue-like, the field is laid out differently each time you begin an expedition.As for looks, they mastered the retro feel of it perfectly, they even added a CRT tv graphics option. The soundtrack is also really good, so much so that I was actually willing to buy it.In summary, this game is really good and was worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely addicting game.The music is superb, the sprites are beautiful and the story is good, though hard to understand imo.A few minor complaints for the UI and the late game:By the time of this review, you cannot see how many tiles you have placed on the field and how much exactly your and the enemy's stats are influenced by them.In the late game, the scaling of some equipment just stops at some point e.g when playing as the necromancer some rings give between +25% at level 1 and +32% summon quality at level 12ish. That's the highest it will get. On loop 48 I still had my level 12 ring equipped.Other than that my remaining complaints are that the 2x speed is not enough for the long farming runs in level 4, that there is no way out of a battle where you and the enemy just outheal each other in an infinite loop(haha) and that after defeating the bosses in level 4 there are only the normal enemies left. I would suggest adding a boss every 5th loop or something like that.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Solid deckbuilding roguelike with a lot of customizationGets a little grindy as you progress, currently I'm just working on farming resources to increase my maximum supply threshold, so I can stack as many vampirism boosts as possibleAll three classes are good options but it seems like the swordsman falls behind a bit if only because you need to focus so heavily on defensive options, and he has no vampirism boosts on his equipment despite it meshing the best with his playstyleThe ways environments affect each other is endlessly interesting, and a lot of fun on their own
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero has excellent music, visuals and a gameplay loop that hooked me way harder than I thought it would. The fact that it's basically a fleshed-out version of the location-placing mechanic in Final Fantasy Tactics Advance is pretty cool, and the fact that the visuals remind me of Crystalis for GBC doesn't hurt either.Would recommend for anyone who's a fan of tactics games or RPGs.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is such a great game! It sounds strange at first, that it has deckbuilding elements and automatic battles, but dont worry about that. The game has a very great motivation loop and a lot of unique ideas and a quite interesting story. Even if you dont like deckbuilding games(like me) this game worth a look. You use the cards to create the game world arround the path, the player character loops through, so its quite interesting and gets very challenging over time. Random loot and a intersting town-building mechanic completes the motivation loop. I really can recommend this game! :)
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool concept and very well executed. The UI is clean, every mechanic works smoothly and feeds into the others, failure never feels cheap, the music is good background stuff... There is quite a lot of depth to the gameplay as you strive to discover card combos that fit your strategy. This game is challenging, rewarding and fun in that "one more run" sort of way.Your character moves around the loop and fights automatically, the only thing that you can do is place down tiles and swap equipment pieces. The tiles that you place around the circuit will spawn combat encounters that reward exp or will provide some form of bonus to your character. Some tiles seem completely negative at a glance but combined with certain others turn out to be a huge boon. The trick to winning is finding the right balance of difficulty to allow your character to grow strong enough to kill the boss without creating a deadly circuit.There is also a meta-progression element with base development. As you play, you collect resources that allow you to construct and upgrade buildings. Those building provide stat increases, new equipment, new cards, new classes... All sorts of things.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This game was unimaginably cool and deep for me. The mechanics, the story, the characters, I felt very connected to it all, I wanted to know their story, I wanted to help them, I wanted to end that oppressive system. It was great to play Loop Hero, a very rewarding experience, even though you needed to finish the game over and over again, I always wanted to finish it more and more to see more of the story, build the city more, get to know more about this world that was being rebuilt over time few.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Barely played and I'm hooked! I like my roguelites to have a good balance in all things. Progression, difficulty and goals! This seems to have it so far. Not one run has been useless. If I don't try for the boss which is my current newbie goal, then I have plennnnnnnty of stuff to upgrade.The one downside that I could imagine so far is that, the bosses kind of low-key require you to progress the camp enough to be able to build enough power to kill them in a run. Now, that's typical roguelite ♥♥♥♥. HERE, however, you don't feel like you're grinding for very little. *ahem* Something-something Legacy.The game's more of a strategy game too, so it's much more relaxed. Very easy to just go for expedition after expedition and notice that a few hours went by.I really love this game and can't wait for the week-end!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely overrated.There's not a lot to do except cheer for your guy as he runs around in a circle.Gameplay (generous term) gets stale after a few hours as the progression doesn't change much. You discover new combinations of things and feel the boon or bane of rng. Thats about it.Of the tags "Tactical, Choices Matter, Deckbuilding, Indie, 2D" only those last two are accurate.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Some might look at the gameplay and quickly put it off as boring and predictable, but a lot is going on under the surface. It's not 100% RNG, and thanks to that, placing your cards correctly can sometimes save you from an early death thanks to bad RNG. I still haven't unlocked everything yet, but every single run is different, and I really do like that. If you like progression rouglikes with permanent unlocks along the way, then this is a pretty good game to get into. The cards are awkward to use at first, but they really do grow on you. Just be careful with the vampire manor's, they can really ruin your day fast, and try not to stack too many monsters on a single grid. I learned that the hard way...
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really cool. It combines reverse-tower-defense, deckbuilding and RPG mechanics with an old-school/rogue-lite gameplay loop. The pixel art is top notch - it is both readable and "retro" during gameplay; outside the action, all the splash screens and character portraits are stunning.The game has a mystical aesthetic, and I recommend not looking at guides (at least immediately) as self-discovery is a fun aspect of this game.While it seems like there isn't an end, there is, and it reasonable amount of time to reach (40ish hours or so?). But the devs just put out new tiles and enemies that are hidden! I'm not looking at any guides this time because I did last time and I read all the *SPOILERSSPOILERSSPOILERS* and I'm not doing that again! This game is really cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely review games.. Call it laziness. This game is absolutely amazing. Really fun core gameplay enhanced by every additional structure and task. All of the classes are viable and fun in their own way. Part empire building, part RPG, part roguelike.. It really takes the best of these genres and turns them into something truly amazing. I can not wait for the DLC/sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: What a little gem huh.So you craft your own perils, and they come with their (great) rewards, or your death, your quite saddening death. When you learn to taylor your way through things start to progress, so enjoy while at firest you build completely obnoxious cramp of monsters that'll kill you.would mix vampire mansions + groves + goblins + cocoons  in the same spot again.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A fun "little" addictive game. The devs distilled the care game-play of roguelites into a very addictive game-loop which is rewarding albeit grindy at times. Progress can feel slow at times, but that is only because one has not yet mastered different combinations that really speed up progression of some aspects. Finding out good combinations is very rewarding, and late game becomes an entertaining challenge.The game shines with its very appealing art and a surprisingly well written tiny lore and dialogues, which made me quite keen on finishing it to understand the "plot".The quality of life additions in later patches, like speed ups for battles and walk, etc, really made it even more enjoyable.In the end I can highly recommend this charming time-waster.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game a lot because of the retro fantasy aesthetic. The idea of building the world around you and having these realistic interactions that affect stats/gameplay is fascinating and definitely got me hyped in my early hours. There is some pretty great world building to go along with this too, and I love the dialogues because they help set all that up.Where the game falls apart for me is in the actual rouge-like elements. Specifically in how repetitive it gets so quickly. I found myself doing the same things over and over again, getting bored of using the same cards and builds because it was what worked without much feeling of forward progress. For example, the only class that I've been able to complete runs with any degree of regularity is the warrior. Despite unlocking two other classes, it just seems way more powerful, reliable, and easy to use. Maybe there are cards I would have been able to get later on that work better with the rogue and necromancer, but I don't really know that for sure because you can't view specific details about the tech tree unlocks later down the line. Perhaps I might be able to see that one of the next buildings I can build unlocks the "forest" card. Great, what does it do? Does it synergize with one of the other classes somehow? Don't know. I don't even know how to unlock that building, because the game shows me little symbols without names or tooltips for the resources needed to unlock it. I've never seen those symbols before though and they don't seem to correspond to any of the types of resources I've been picking up. None of my cards are capable of making a resource with that symbol and I don't even know what that symbol means because I can't scroll over it to view a tooltip of some kind telling me how I can get it. Even when I spend a lot of hours grinding to unlock a building that supposedly allows me to trade books to unlock codex entries, all it does is unlock flavor text for already discovered things, not new information. The opaqueness of these mechanics really kills my motivation to make forward progress because I'm bored of doing the same thing for 10 hours and I have no idea when its going to get better. It also sucks loosing a run, and therefore a bunch of resources, because you suddenly died. Without being able to control the battles directly, the only control you have is in what cards you place, what gear you equip, and what talents you take. But all of that is subject to both RNG (in terms of what you get) and also varies wildly in balance. Some cards/stats/talents are total garbage while others are auto-takes. There just isn't enough variety, and a lot of these systems are pretty shallow. Like you're just getting +7% more attack speed or something most of the time. It doesn't make decisions interesting and tactical. Like obviously I'm going to take +7% attack speed over +5% attack speed every time. Its very Diablo-esque in that its about scaling your numbers to get bigger without really making very interesting moment-to-moment decisions. For example, maybe I could get an item that adds possibility of lightning damage to my weapon, and also a talent that says whenever I deal lightning damage, it stuns the enemy for 1 second. An environmental card effect could then say stunned enemies take extra damage or something. This is how you do synergy in an interesting way, but its more complex to implement, and it feels like the developers kinda just didn't want to do all that. I think what they wanted to make was an idle mobile game where you really don't do much and don't have much control over anything, because that's what this game is. Its repetitive and the RPG systems are very shallow, even for an RPG lite. It has painfully slow progression and a major lack of variety. If you like an endless grind of collecting random resources because I said so and making numbers bigger then this game might be interesting for you, but I like something with more depth. And sure, maybe it gets better later, but I've already played 10 hours. I beat a boss and I'm just bored now because the prospect of doing it all over again with the same setup but harder just isn't appealing to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable game.I haven't beaten it yet, but so far it's a fun rogue-like game where you enter battle, and then return to your "main base of operations" in order to upgrade your character slightly so that your next battle has a higher chance of getting your farther. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. May look a bit confusing at first, but if you just start playing the game explains everything pretty well.I really like how its pretty much up to the player how they want to play the game - taking it slow and steady or trying to escalate things as quickly as possible. If you're struggling you can always just decide to return, and use resources to improve your campsite to make future runs a bit easier. Or challenge yourself to beat the game with as few upgrades or as few runs as possible. I got the game two weeks ago and spent just over 100 hours playing it. Got every achievement and seen everything the game currently has to offer (as far as I'm aware). _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The game is cool and made with care for sure, but it has a verry monotonous and unengaging gameplay that barelly varies at all from run to run.Even though its really cheap I would not say it was worth the money because of extremely limited content and near irrelevance of player decisionmaking.On the upside it looks good and the sountrack is fire.

_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a fairly good game, BUT be warned: it may not be what you think it is at first glance.After having played it, Loop Hero is an idle/grinder game first, strategy game second. So if you, like me, saw the description of the game include things like "Deckbuilding elements" and "Strategy roguelite" and mentally jumped to the likes of Slay the Spire or Dicey Dungeons you would not be alone, but this isn't quite what Loop Hero is.Loop Hero is instead built to be more of an all-star second monitor game. Something you can take a few minutes to set up, leave running for 5-10 while you do something else, and come back to check in on later , adjust and repeat; Collecting resources to upgrade a home-base of global buffs to "level up" while looking ahead to the next boss and next "loop".Pressing moment to moment decisions there are few of; and the strategic decisions and synergies you'll be making while setting up are mostly small and fixed in payoff. Short of loading your loop with so many monsters you die instantly there are few things you can do to make or break an individual run. Most strategic payoffs are on the scale of plus or minus 20% overall effectiveness, rather than creating self sustaining engines. In other words you won't be going infinite with any unique and brilliant stratagems within the framework of Loop Hero; but you WILL be interested in gathering infinite resources to afford that next perk, building, and class to help you out on the next run, which will be a much greater predictor of success than your exact monster placements will be.Loop Hero is meant to be a game you invest in WITHOUT actually actively investing in it. A game of building up power and options through meaningful but not monumental decision-making, all of which is dwarfed by the inevitable march of Father Time around your Loops.As long as you understand that, you'll have a good time with this game. If you don't though, you'll be waiting a very, very long time for a second strategic depth shoe that never truly drops.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game with a huge amount of replayability, there are countless strategies to try out with lots of enemies that you can meet as well as a bunch of secret combinations for even more interesting strategies. the progression is steady and lets you get into the game while at the same time making the experience hard but rewarding. Overall i would give this game an 8.5/10 as I enjoye the hell out of it and am still playing.

_childDocuments_.review: There's little to no build diversity once you figure out "THE" build for each of the 3 classes. Toss in a little grind and bam, the game is done. That being said it was an enjoyable 50 hours for $5.Now imagine if cards populated the map randomly then you had to build your character around that to survive. Add more builds and classes, add more stat variety and balance. Would be an amazing and TRUE Roguelike. Make it happen

_childDocuments_.review: Very chill game, imagine it as a reverse tower defense. You build the enemy spawners and terrain for passive buffs while your loopy pal loops! Highly recommended, had a lot of fun going for all achievements - landed just under 80 hours. Now for some secret challenges though! Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Is it possible to give the player too much choice? In Loop Hero, you get to choose which terrain and structures that dot the landscape and give character to each expedition, as well as where to place them. You also get to pick your enemies and, for the most part, can choose when and where to fight them. You cannot, however, control the battles when they happen; you are forced to spectate while your hero duels the monsters you selected. This is an intriguing turnabout from how strategy and role-playing games usually work, but it also put an unexpected damper on my enthusiasm to push to the end of the game. In many games, particularly roguelites and roguelikes, seeing 'what's around the next turn' is a big part of the thrill. But in Loop Hero, once I was familiar with the various tiles I could choose from, that sense of discovery faded away; the game rarely surprises you. You get so much choice about what challenges you face that playing frequently feels like packaging up a wonderful present... only to give that immaculate gift box to yourself.That's not to say Loop Hero isn't fun or engaging; it is. And the biggest surprise is how clever the plot and writing are; thoughtful-provoking and funny in equal measure. But having reached the end credits, I feel no compulsion to play on towards 100%. This was not a difficult loop to break out of.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun game Overall! It took me around 45 hours to get all Steam achievements, but if you really want to you could do it faster. In the beginning the game was really hard for me and it took a while before I fully understood everything. But after a while I found a good tactic and beat the game easily. If people tell you this game has too much RNG don't listen to them, they just don't know a good tactic.The game speed is too slow, but the developers promised that they will increase it in a future update, so it will hopefully get better soon. After reaching the endgame it sadly gets too easy with the stuff you have in your village, so there is nothing left than farming materials with no challenge at all. Will play again if another boss comes around!Great chill game while watching something and doing other stuff as it really does not need your full attention, especially later on.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! Those moments you get when you have to take a minute or two and decide do I play and try to survive another loop or retreat to camp and start over to save all of you supplies are intense. Fun gameplay the only problem is the game is really loose with explaining how certain things work and you have to experiment quite a bit. Still once you get a few runs in and get the hang of things its very addicting. You get to that first boss and the theme music kicks in, you know this is one of those games you can't forget.you can also play this game with one hand on your mouse and left hand holding your beer
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is really interesting and original. Its fun trying out different the different card combinations and unlocks. Just be prepared for a grind, this game can get really slow and tedious sometimes. I wasn't able to complete the game, the grind became too much for me to keep interest, but overall it was a really enjoyable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is one of a kind IMO.The more you play, the more you learn all the mechanics and min-max-strategies to progress until the final stages of the game. The basic RPG-elements are satisfying to experiment with.Also, the story is pretty good and it motivates you to discover all the possible dialogues between the hero, NPC's and even enemies.By far the best part is the soundtrack. Really, really good 8-bit/chiptune tracks and it seems the author is a big fan of JoJo.Highly recommended. My favourite game of the year 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't gotten far in this game, but I will keep coming back to it. I could be playing it wrong, but I only feel up for one or two rounds at a time. There's just enough indication of progress to feel like even a "failed" run isn't a waste of time. As a casual gamer most of the time, the learning curve isn't too steep and the time commitment isn't either.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I found the game boring (despite the overwhelming positive reviews). I appreciate the art style and its game design simplicity. But unfortunately this game is not for me: I expect to collect cards with powerful abilities and max my battle damage, not increase resource collection by xx%. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to give this one a down vote, but my reasoning is why create a great premise and then just toss out a small mobile game? I know devolver doesn't do 40 hour AAA games but there was so much more in this game that they didn't do. Right now i have 3 hours but maybe after finishing it I'll change my review. However, looking a guides on card combos there's just not that many. For a deck builder there's like 35 cards and 20 combos. while the core play is fun and a good concept it could have been expanded on big time.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game that revolves around your character making a loop around a stage.  You dont really control the character in the regular sense.  You build the world around them and manage the gear.  You start small, and manage a camp site, and start growing to be really powerful.  Its gonna take a few tries to get it right, but thats all part of the fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Long, boring, grind.You slowly gain resources to build your home base which provides small bonuses until you have enough to win. Most of the time you watch your guy walk in circles and fight monsters. You place terrain that gives bonuses or spawns monsters. All you do is pick items, level up bonuses, and optimise where to place terrain. The best part is discovering terrain that interacts with other terrain (and it doesn't tell you).Winning strategy: Thickets, winding rivers, suburbs. At base pump up your vampirism and pick the best vampirism equipment. Gift of blood is optional.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a roguelite card-driven game that is  a Slay the Spire clone!  Can you believe it?  It should be commended on that alone!  Of course, that probably leaves you asking just what the heck it is in the first place.At a very high level, your hero travels around a looped path that, at first, only has a campfire on it that will heal you as you pass through it.  The path will spawn basic monsters that will drop gear that you can equip to boost your stats and HP, but more importantly, they will start dropping cards from a deck that you build over time.  These cards aren't played, per se, in the traditional sense, but rather they create features on the map on-demand.  Not all of these features are positives, but the negative ones tend to give you access to tougher mobs that drop better loot.The lite side of things, then, is whenever you decide to stop at camp (or you're forced to it because you risked too much), you can spend resources that you've gathered by bashing mobs and placing tiles to build structures that give you benefits on the field.  Whether you stop voluntarily or not, the world outside resets and you start back at loop level 1, ready to go around again.  However, as you build structures, you will also unlock different cards that you can add to your deck for various benefits, making it easier to farm resources for your next pit stop.Narratively, your hero is trying to remember what the world looked like and therefore is rebuilding it piece by piece, but the trick of the game is that every time you stop at camp to beef up your long-term progression, you reset the world again.  As such, resetting is a strategic decision like in most idle games rather than one caused by error as in most roguelikes/lites.  In fact, you really have no agency over how combat or travel works.  You make no decisions on who the hero fights or how they fight at all.Player agency on the field is entirely about equipping gear (mob drops) and placing tiles by playing cards (also mob drops).  As such, while you could compare Loop Hero to a clicker/idler, it requires a lot of attention because you will need to constantly drop tiles onto the map and swap gear if you are to survive long enough to even see the first boss.  Of course this means that the grind is as real as they come, but at least you can survive for quite a long time each run, even on your very first play, so it doesn't feel like the game is stacked against you in that regard.Oh, and that tile-laying thing?  That's not just for show.  Yes, each of the cards/tiles tells you what they do and how to place them, but what you don't know up front is that laying stuff out in a certain way will actually spawn stuff that isn't found on a card.  Experimentation and discovery are key to this aspect of the game, as is your deckbuilding which you can do when you stop at camp.  It might be tempting to remove the annoying mob nests from your deck, but doing so could severely hinder your progress in more ways than one.  However, playing around with the cards is as fun as any other deckbuilder without bogging you down with combos or memorizing keywords.  You don't even have to count copies or figure out frequency or anything like that - you may have only one meadow listed in your deck, but you can bet you're going to get 10 copies of it in no time.Four Quarters have done a terrific job here making Loop Hero an engaging and fun experience, even if you never see it to its end.  There's something compelling in the way that they brought together elements of roguelites and idlers together and I'm sure that this will be the start of the new clone season to come.  At this point, I'd buy ten more copies of Loop Hero rather than spend a dime on yet another Spire clone.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop hero is one of those games which at first you think will be mundane and repetitive. But, this game does a good job of subverting expectations with excellent game design around scope and presentation. The basic loop traversal and turn-based combat are bolstered by the world and base-building aspect. You are choosing which enemies to fight; as well as when and for what resources.You are the protagonist in every sense of the word.  The story is seen through your eyes, and the world unfolds by your actions. It's a relaxing game that doesn't insult the viewer and takes plot and story design seriously. The loop is not just a workaround for having a small development team, the loop is an integral part of this world's story and mission.  It isn't a passive setting, but a plot point that you are unraveling with the character and their adventures. The game is so innovative and ingenious that it would probably rival any AAA studio on the market if these developers scaled up.I can not actually compare this game to anything else I have ever played. Sure it has deck building, like other games. But the card's purpose in this game's presentation is nowhere near the same. Sure it has world-building like other games, but this also isn't comparable to any genre I can place my finger on. In 2021 when most games are looking to copy and retread genres,(looking at you CrowSworn) this game came up with a very original idea and aesthetic.  I look forward to seeing what developer Four Quarters does with their own genre, and as a studio. Do they reiterate what they did and scale up the quality. Or do they move on to do something entirely new and different from what they have presented here? Either way Loop Her deserves a highly endorsed recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a maybe option for reviews, but I still overall like the game despite some of the glaring issues I've started to notice. First off, the game is insanely addictive and fun, a strange deck building rouge like mashed up with a reverse tower defense game that makes it too easy to say one more loop until 4am. The first few hours are amazing, learning new card combos, unlocking new characters, and unlocking new cards. This is when the biggest issue with the game begins to show. Around when you unlock the second chapter, the new cards and upgrades slow down and the runs stop feeling like you are making progress due to the sheer amount of resources needed for new campground tiles and their upgrades. The main issue with this is that resource accumulation is incredibly slow as you only pick up anywhere from 1/10 to 1/20 of a resource at a time, and most of these resources are tied to placing cards. This creates an issue as placing enough cards spawns the boss of the chapter at the end of the loop, which you do not have the resources for upon unlocking the second chapter. The result of this is throwing away multiple runs to resource farming, scared to take on the boss as a death causes you to lose 60% of the resources you gained. This is incredibly unsatisfying, especially when it feels like this has been the majority of my experience after starting fresh after the demo.Overall, the game is well worth the price and incredibly fun and addictive, but the grind the game requires at around the mid point can be very hard to overcome and may not be for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: In Loop Hero, you observe as a small dude traverses a perilous path. It’s a game that plays itself, almost. Only delegating some very specific tasks to you, architect of adventure; tailor of heroes.First of all, you get to equip the hero as he works his way through his adventure. It’s the only reason Loop Hero needs your input to begin with. Because as time flies, his environment develops and grows more fierce. He, however, does not, unless you nudge him in the right direction and don the wonderful trinkets he gathers along the way. It’s where all the juicy RPG-stats and terms come into play. Like strength, evasion, and critical chance. And where you have to juggle equipment with disparate types of benefits. Do you want a warrior with a penchant for damage dealing, or a more defensive one that regenerates lost health? Secondly, as an architect, you’re tasked with developing the world. This is where you specify the different locations the hero has to pass through in order to progress, and the surrounding landscape. Oftentimes, placing these have pros and cons -- giving him specific resources or equipment in exchange for an area that now generates monsters he has to defeat first.You might have guessed it already, but the path he’s on is on a constant loop. Meaning that once he finally reaches camp, his travel starts anew -- same road, same conditions. Therefore, all the things you place for him, the environments you form, serve as immortal landmarks until he retires. Whether that’s because of death or otherwise. It’s also where you’re most likely to overindulge in Loop Hero; where hubris can take over and really make for an impossible mission. Overengineering is actually a classic pitfall. More often than not, you want to be smart. Play environmental tiles and effects that have synergies and added bonuses. Sure, a scary forest is a must-have in any fantasy adventure. But place it next to a magical grove, and suddenly mother nature chips in with killer vines and an occasional golem for you to fight.Most of what’s going on under the hood here is outside of your realm as a player. In fact, the flow of information almost necessitates a lot of guesswork and goodwill on your part, deciphering how it all works. It’s a slow churn, for sure. But if there’s one thing you should remember playing Loop Hero, is that it’s all about the process. Thinking you can force your way to the end credits is a sure-fire way to frustration. So remember to enjoy watching the ebb and flow of his adventures. Advancement will come automatically -- more or less.Recommended if you have a tinkering nature and enjoy engine-building in 8-bit.

_childDocuments_.review: The game consists of two elements. Expedition, which is a mix of auto-battling, looting/gear sorting, and card placing.And there is a base building/upgrading part.The expeditions are the core part of the gameplay. Your character start going in a loop and you obtain cards and gear from monsters slain. The player character fights them in an auto-battler element.Most cards are to be placed on the field. Some of them will become monster spawners, some will benefit the player. The former mechanic works really well, because the more spawners you make, the more loot you get, so you must determine how much your character fights.There are also special tiles that you can make by placing specific tiles beside each other.The camp is fun in early-game and useful in late-game.Here you can place tiles that unlock new cards/features and benefit your runs passively.It is extremely broken late-game, but that is not a problem, since the runs can go infinitely.The only annoying part is that you must place some building next to other specific ones.There are four bosses in the game.He is my personal favourite. His design is really good and  a great mechanic.There are three classes in the game.The default class, you can beat the entire game with just him. The other classes are just for flavour/variety.The story of the game is not anything special in my opinion, but it aligns really well with the gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I almost can't believe I'm giving this a negative review, because I think the concept is really interesting, and there are some parts of the game that I enjoy a lot. I think what kept me playing for 30 hours was the game's theme, I just wanted to uncover more layers of the world, and I respect this game despite not recommending it so I'll write some words about why.The core gameplay loop, most of the time, is not very fun for me. Even when everything is going well, it isn't very fascinating or enjoyable to watch your character go round and round while you sit there and do nothing except occasionally swap out this or that piece of equipment. It takes a very long time to farm the more advanced resources, so if you want 3 more of some particular orb you have to spend 30 minutes to get them, while accomplishing nothing else. You can't leave the game unattended while it farms away for you, however, because enemies are constantly scaling, so you have to keep an attentive eye on the nothing that's happening. I felt bored in my 5th run, and I felt bored in my 50th run.Part of why I think this game is boring is that the meta progression doesn't feel very impactful. Broadly speaking, I have very little idea why I'm expanding the village or what I'm working towards in that regard, even after 30 hours. I know the effects of each building and what they do, but I don't feel a cohesive goal to any of it. I have almost every structure built, and it doesn't seem as though I'll be unlocking more, so shouldn't I feel some kind of accomplishment, or feel like I did something good and worthwhile by making all these buildings? I don't really feel any purpose about any of it, and the development is kind of incidental to me. I don't feel as though I've built anything significant. I think this is both because expanding the village didn't help me in any very significant way or change my runs in any very significant way, with exception of the buildings that unlock new classes. I think it's also partly because I was given very little information about what I was working towards, or how each new structure or upgrade fit into the bigger picture.The way they present information hasn't really worked for me. There's an encyclopedia with most of the information you'll need about the things that you've discovered, but within a run you're given very little info about how enemies and effects interact with one another or how to get a resource, and it feels disconnected. My instinct is always to just do things and see what happens, so it was only bit by bit that uncovered information like which enemies drop what, and what their abilities are, and so on. Uncovering that information ended up feeling tedious, and yet was also one of the only things that gave me any sense of purpose, since I felt I had something to discover. I think if I had relied on the encyclopedia, I would have just stopped playing immediately.Part of why uncovering that information was boring and unsatisfying was because the meta loop, village progression, felt mostly pointless. Once or twice I got a new resource and felt excited because I could finally build a new thing in the village that I'd been waiting to build. And then I built it, and nothing much changed, and I wondered why I had bothered.Another part of why it was unsatisfying is that, at least for me, the feedback you're given about why a run is succeeding or failing is not very useful or reliable. One morning, I did a few runs, and they were all very successful. I scaled very well and reached some nice stat breakpoints, and it was quite a satisfying result if not terribly exciting along the way. My long toil paid off when I took down a couple bosses and claimed some large bounties. Later in the day, without changing anything, I started losing horribly and couldn't scale to save my life. I couldn't tell you why there was a difference between them or what the difference even really was.I don't think the game gives you a good sense of what is working and what isn't, and it sometimes blindsides you, like when you run into the bandit's hidden 5% chance to destroy your equipment, which will almost certainly get you killed on the spot. (Try going from 75% dodge to 0% dodge because your boots disappeared without notice and you died before you realized, it's not an interesting way to lose a run. Keep in mind you'll always be playing at 4x speed because nothing happens for long periods of time, so tragedy can strike in the blink of an eye.)Anyway, if I keep writing more I'll probably just be complaining about random things, and I think covered the broad strokes. I will probably keep playing this game a bit more, and hopefully it gets better and I change my mind about it, but right now this game feels like it should be in early access and is missing a lot of polishing. I wish I had liked it more.Edit: After around 40 hours, I had unlocked and fully upgraded almost everything, and finally noticed real changes in gameplay. At this point the game finally became fun. Not super fun, just standard fun. If it takes that long for a game to get anywhere, I am never going to recommend other people play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was surprised by this game.  I am not typically a fan of the pixel art style but it works with this one.  While the Ai does the fighting for you it isn't an idle game.  You are constantly getting new abilities, equipment and cards to design your loop.  You can overwhelm yourself and fill your loop with too many baddies, or you can leave it empty only fighting slimes.  Every loop raises the difficulty of the critters on your path, so ideally you want to have enough to beat so you're lucky enough to get good enough loot and survive a few more loops.  The RNG nature of the game makes it take longer then it should sometimes, having to abandon some runs because you've made too many loops without enough key cards or gear.  But it is rewarding when you get a key item or card at the right time and are able to spawn and defeat the boss.There are several secrets to discover in this game, some fascinating others convoluted.  Most are intuitive or offered by clues in the encyclopedia in game which I appreciate as it doesn't force you to use a wiki to play.  If you want to relax with a show on in the background and play a game requires enough brain power to keep you awake but not so much that you need total focus this is a great play!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Relatively simple yet quite satisfying rogue-like autobattler/deckbuilder that includes city building mechanics and loot-based gear/resources.Basically you go around in a "loop" traveling this road where enemies spawn both by default and based on the tiles you apply to the map area (either adjacent to, on, or far from the road) from the cards in your deck.  You collect loot in the process that can be equipped on your character to improve their performance as well as collect resources to further develop your settlement after the run.  The kicker is that you can only escape with all the resources you collect if you retreat from your camp tile on the road, otherwise you only get to keep 30% (randomly chosen) at the start.  This makes for an interesting risk vs. reward decision on when to "extract".What's interesting is that you can build more than what's in your cards on the map by placing the tiles in a certain configuration (i.e. a big mountain that spawns harpies when you place 3x3 worth of stone/mountain cards).   In addition, the configuration can have impacts on the stats/resources you obtain from placing tiles.I'll end by noting that unlike some games, the title for this one doesn't lie.  You are a hero and you are traveling a loop to progress through the game.  11/10 for telling the truth.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so, here we go. I usually like games by Devolver Digital. They're a great developer. Props to them for making great indie games.I've never liked idler games, and this is one such example. It comes off as almost as a smartphone game, which I can get off the iOS (since I have an iPhone) App Store. Now, it's far better than the likes of games such as AFK Arena, because obviously this game isn't an attempt at a cheap gacha cashgrab, but I couldn't bring myself to enjoy it nearly as much as other titles Devolver Digital is known for.Music is good, I'll say that. And being born in the 90s, I do like the pixellated art style this game has, as it's reminiscent of that era, in certain ways. But the fact that you have no real direct control, that the game does everything for you (save the camp part and a few commands), feels extremely cheap on Devolver Digital's part. I get that it's a choice, it's what they were going for. And while the execution works and the idea is interesting, this game fails to maintain my attention for any notable periods of time.So, writing this, a thought struck me. I'm on Chapter 1, and I only have 2.5 hours clocked into the game total. Maybe I'm not giving it enough of a chance? The first impressions I got were kind of weak, but maybe there's something I just don't know about. Some mechanics I haven't unlocked. That's why I'm allowing comments. Not to get bashed on, but to receive input from those who think the game is good. I WANT to like the game; maybe you all can convince me to.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero's elevator pitch must have happened while the lift was stuck. It really is one of those games that is exactly what it is described as on the box, but without playing it you can't really get a good sense of what that actually means. In some ways I think that uniqueness is enough to justify buying it and trying it, but let's talk about the game anyway.Before anything else though, I'm going to be clear and say I liked Loop Hero and I would recommend it.Fundamentally, Loop Hero is a high stakes idle game which sounds weird because it is. You have no direct control over your character, only the map and world around him which he gormlessly walks through. In town you build structures which power you, and the map, up while looping. While looping you put down tiles which spawn resources, enemies and eventually progression. It's a game with a very round shape.What makes the game interesting is the variance in loops. It is fun to create a map that is just hostile enough to your little guy without killing him, and seeing all the different ways you can put together a system for your guy to cut through is satisfying in a sort of marble tower sort of way.That said, I wouldn't pay $15 for a marble tower. What pushes the game over though is the writing, for an idle game about a universe that doesn't exist anymore there's a rich world and tons of dialogue and flavor text. It's a nice mixture of intrigue and humor. It's hard to talk about without spoiling, but it is a fascinating story and I was invested by the end.All in all Loop Hero is a game that's very well tied together, while there are strange quibbles that come with the gameplay and you may find the story a bit weird, everything about it tied to the central theme and idea in a way that shows a solid understanding of the medium as a whole that is seldom seen.If you like idle games you should try Loop Hero. If you like experimental or artsy games you should try Loop Hero. If you look at Loop Hero and the idea doesn't interest you, don't play Loop Hero, because it really is all about that central core.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is as difficult to complete as it is to put down. _childDocuments_.review: On paper, Loop Hero sounds like it shouldn't work: a deckbuilding roguelike when you don't actually control the combat. And yet it's one of the best deckbuilder roguelikes out there. It's a balance of risk vs reward: keep the path easy enough to complete a loop, but difficult enough to scale with the increasing strength of the enemies. The meta progression with building your base allowing you to make it further through the loops and later chapters is steady and really feels like the work that you put in has likewise results. The tools that you are provided are provided at a perfect pacing to master them, earning a new one just as you feel like they are necessary; the game is also set up so that not only in the very very end game, overpowered and straight up broken builds are 1) possible 2) necessary and 3) don't feel cheap because you really have to earn getting to that point. It strikes the perfect balance of a game you kind mindlessly play while watching Netflix and smoking weed and one that needs your full attention, where one bad decision about a card placement or changing equipment could spell doom. But if you fail, that's OK; you can always try another loop with a different strategy or with the new upgrades you've spent your hard earned resources on. This is all to say nothing of the amazing old school aesthetics that ooze atmosphere. I do really hope we get DLC for this game, and I know I'm not alone in saying that despite the Devs originally saying it would be free, myself and many others would be more than happy to pay for it. Or going the Team Cherry route and turning what was intended to be DLC into a sequel. What I really mean to say is that Loop Hero is just so good and original that it would be a shame to not see more of it in some capacity. I've bought it for PC, recently for the Switch, and before long I'll be buying it for Mobile too. Really great job Four Quarters, thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit:  Originally gave this a thumbs down but since my review they have added a save and 8x speed increase.  I still stand by the rest but this definitely gets a recommend now.Loop Hero is an amazing concept with a great retro art and music vibe.  My first loop I was riding the hype wave full force with my windows down.  This game is brilliant and im sure there will be many renditions of it.  After one day of digging in my heart sank and i was overwhelmed with utter disappointment.  Lets be real, Loop Hero is hands down an early access game.  I am already simply waiting for more content to be released, maybe a DLC, or waiting for another company to copy the format and do it proper.  There is no content here, and the content that is available is completely optional.  You dont have to farm materials to upgrade your camp other then wanting to see the content.  Which makes the experience very boring.  There are only 3 bosses, and once you easily progress thru them theres nothing left.  You can run them over again to get materials to unlock new "cards" but at this point youve basically cleared all content and now your just unlocking more options to run the same loops again just because. Now lets talk about the loops themselves.  For starters the Necro is so OP there is no reason to play the other 2 classes other then to give yourself a hard mode.  The shape of new loops slightly change but it doesnt change much, its still the same experience with slight advantages or disadvantages.  But for the most part, unless your using a new "card" you havnt used before, you know the placements already.  You have about 20 minutes of gameplay where you wait for the "cards" your looking for and place them, you defeat the boss then decide to quit or just keep going around to see how high you can get.  Which is where Loop Hero falls flat on its face.Lets talk about gameplay.  After your 20 minute investment there is none.  Gameplay consists of constantly mousing over items that will disappear after a few encounters looking for upgrades.  Theres no theory crafting, you just want items with all desired stats.  And that is what you will be doing for HOURS!  There is no save.  And the loops themselves are crazy slow.  Theres a 2x speed feature which needs to be 3x and 4x.  Sometimes I will look at that lonely Loop Hero icon on my desktop and ill want to click it.  And then i think of what ill actually be doing and how much time ill be doing it for and it remains lonely.  I get the no save thing.  It makes running the loops more exciting, wondering if you can make it just one more loop.  A save feature would take that away and make this game more boring then it already is.  But just give it up.  There isnt enough going on here to warrant it.  I have nowhere near 200 hours of gameplay, thats me pausing to continue at a later time.  Sometimes for days cause i wanted to see how many loops i could get but thinking of just sitting there with my hand on my chin mousing over items and i couldnt do it.  Never in my life has a game invoked such feelings of "why am i wasting my time doing this."  Loot hunting couldnt be more boring.  I recommend adding another tier that is very hard to complete a full set of.  Something when you see it drop you immediately get excited.  Thrill of the hunt.For everything I enjoyed in Loop Hero I was met with two things that disappointed me.  The camp you upgrade isnt appealing or exciting to upgrade.  It looks like a garbage pile.  The cards themselves dont feel like cards or a card mechanic.  As great as the sound is, it gets stale real quick.  There isnt much variety there.  The classes are a facepalm.  Id like to see more balancing.  My first heartsink came after i killed the first boss.  I was expecting that to be the first in the loop and things were about to get crazier.  Instead the loop ends but you can continue, if you want.  With 3 bosses total which are not difficult.  And for a game that nails atmosphere and vibe, the worst thing about Loop Hero are the characters and story.  Ill give you a hint, there is none.  All character and dialogue in this game is equivalent to a dollar h-game.  "Hello durka durka durka durka."  None of it even makes sense.  Its flat out nonsense talk that you X out as fast as possible.  Which kills the whole atmosphere and immersion.  Its also a huge part of what the camp is missing.  If you want to see an empty but new and cool game with no expectations then this is the one for you.  Not marketing as early access kills it for me tho.  Is more content coming?  Is this a work in progress?  DLC in the future or whats going on here?

_childDocuments_.review: "Just... One... More... Loop..."The second thing that you'll notice about Loop Hero is how the wonderful graphics (which you'll notice first) are slightly curved to recreate the experience of gaming on a CRT TV. You might think that this will be distracting, but soon you won't notice it anymore, which is a great example of how much thought went into this game: The creators recreated a CRT TV's curved display—probably because they grew up gaming on CRT TVs—and then they made sure you wouldn't really notice their design decision; after all, if you grew up gaming on CRT TVs, you remember the games, not the curved displays. And a similar intentionality flows through the entire game, from the story (which is fantastic) to the gameplay (which is ranges from deceptively simple to rewardingly complex). I don't want to spoil anything about the game, but I'll say this: The third thing you'll notice about Loop Hero is the way the game just drops you into a pile of gameplay mechanics and concepts that you won't understand after your first or tenth loop. There really isn't a tutorial, and that's by design: The creators trust players to figure out how things work, and the game rewards players not only at the end of that process but throughout that process, which is why it doesn't feel like a process; you just feel like you're playing a great game—and you are. However, it's hard to categorize Loop Hero. I've heard people compare it to Slay the Spire (one of my favorite games) because it's a roguelike with deck-building elements, but you're going to be disappointed if you're expecting Slay the Spire. There are also TRPG elements, but it's not a TRPG simulator. Loop Hero is its own game, and it's one of the best games I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is probably the biggest love/hate relationship I have ever had with a game...I usually don't like doing this, but this is a case where I feel I should give this game the thumbs down, despite the fact I do play and... sort of enjoy this game - mostly to balance out the fact it's already currently very positively received.To try to put my very conflicted feelings towards this game in as few words as possible, my issue with this game is that it is an amazing and unique idea in theory - but when you actually sit down and play the game it's very dull, repetitive, and slow paced. You'll still find some enjoyment from the pure satisfaction of growing a little bit stronger with each run every time, but honestly, I think the flaw I cannot get past with this game is the absurdly grindy nature of it.---| GRINDING---The most fun part of this game is just the satisfaction you get from making progress, but the progression is slower than most microtransaction-ridden mobile games, which is especially confusing for a game that doesn't even have microtransactions. It would often take about 8-10 full runs each lasting around half an hour just to get ONE more damn building, and ultimately after all that effort, the benefits would often be as trivial as "oh, now your health potions heal 7% of your health instead of 6%". I can only guess the developers were worried the game isn't long enough? It technically does only have 4 "levels" (unless there's some secret post-game content I'm not aware of), but I honestly feel this would have been much better off as a short and replayable experience, than the absolute slog it is right now to inflate the playtime required to beat it.---| RESOURCES---Beyond the grinding being ridiculously tedious, every resource in the game required to make any permanent progress has its own special conditions for acquiring them. This is a fine idea, and most resources are obtained through reasonable enough methods - defeat these kinds of enemies to get this, walk through these kinds of tiles to get that - that sort of thing. One very important material needed for most buildings and upgrades in the game though, are orbs of expansion, and the game never tells you how to get them. I checked the encyclopedia and found that no enemies or tiles in the game would give you them, and when looking at the material itself it told me all I had to do was fight multiple enemies at once to obtain it. I then proceeded to do about 5 runs spamming as many enemies as possible into single fights, and at the end of all of them I had gotten 0 orbs of expansion. That's because the limit to the amount of enemies on a tile is 4, and to get orbs of expansion you need to fight groups of 5 enemies (game says 4 works, but I never got one orb from 4-enemy fights, and even with 5 you only have a % chance of getting ONE orb). So how the hell does that work? You have to get a tile with 4 enemies, and then have a nearby building which has some sort of gimmick to add enemies onto an already existing fight to get the fifth enemy. I had to look up guides to figure this out, and even once I started using the best strategy the community had found for grinding these orbs, it still took hours just to get enough for the tiniest of incremental upgrades. This is both extremely unintuitive to figure out, and extremely unfun to do - but you need those incremental upgrades to have a chance at the later boss fights, so get grinding.---| GAMEPLAY---I like the idea that because you are building the world, you control the enemies that spawn, the resources you'll earn, and to some extent the equipment you'll get throughout a run - however, other than that, the game plays itself entirely. No targetting options for attacks, no movesets for your character, and not even any activated abilities - I can understand maybe wanting the battles to go mostly automatically, but I'm honestly kind of baffled that as far as I've played, this game just doesn't have any way to interact with a battle as it is happening at all.Of course, the equipment you choose over the course of a run, and the cards you build your Deck with are going to have an effect on the outcome of your battles, but if say you realise "oh I'm a little low on health, and before the next loop I have one more big fight coming up" you genuinely can't do anything most of the time but just watch your character walk blindly into their death. Health potions? You're not allowed to use them manually, the game decides when to use them automatically. Activate some kind of ability to help you? As I said, you don't get any, the only effects you get in this game are passives or one-time use abilities that trigger automatically when the game decides. Play a Card in your Hand? What are you going to play? The vast majority of cards have little to no impact on their own, and also often take a long period of time to give their benefits. The only Card in the entire game that can really save you there I have seen is Oblivion, the one that just deletes everything including enemies on a tile - but you can only get so many of those.It feels like most runs of this game are just rolling the dice, seeing if the game randomly decides to give you the equipment you need to win this game, and if not - tough luck, go again for the 783rd attempt of doing the exact same thing. It feels to me that for the point in the game I'm at, the only viable strategies are:1. Attack speed spam with Rogue until you kill so fast nothing gets a chance to hit you (I went infinite twice with this strategy, but you gotta get lucky with equipment for it to work, unfortunately)2. Attack speed spam with Necromancer to summon a ludicrous amount of skeletons (more consistent, but less likely to scale well into late-game in my experience)And while these strategies were fun at first, it feels like they're the only strategies in the game that really work even over 50 hours into it. Every time I've thought of trying out a different Deck, the new Deck has been vastly inferior to those 2 Decks, so every game ends up being the same. If I was at least progressing at a reasonable rate, I may have been able to stomach that, but that's just it - I'm not progressing at reasonable rate. I'm spending hours and hours just to get 1% bonuses to certain stats and it just feels like... Why am I playing this game anymore?---| CONCLUSION---I realised that I spent more of my time playing this game feeling bored or frustrated with all the grinding than actually enjoying it, but that I kept pushing through that for a long time because the initial idea had captivated me so much that I felt like I couldn't write this game off until I'd completed it. I kept thinking this will get better soon, I kept thinking I'll probably like it by the end - and maybe I still will, I still plan to at least finish this game at some point, but I'm no longer in a rush to do it. Taking a moment to step back and realise that I have now spent over 50 hours on this game, and that I only really enjoyed the first 5 or so hours of that, and spent the rest of those hours pushing through because "surely it gets better, right?" has really put in perspective for me why I think I have to give this game the thumbs down despite how much I love the concept - and despite how much I want this to be good.All that being said, I did say I don't think this is an outright bad game, and believe it or not, I do still stand by that - I just think if you want to play this game to completion, you have to go into it with a certain mindset to enjoy it. Since every run drags on for so long while you have very little control over the outcome of it, this game is much more enjoyable as a sort of "background game" to play while listening to something else or just trying to unwind while doing something to keep you a little busy.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a highly experimental, highly rewarding breakout indie hit that is well worth your time. It’s fully worth the asking price, and if you’re at all curious about the game, it should be a no-brainer to grab on sale.I love it, and while I may be biased, I broke everything down into what I think are fair pros and cons. In addition, I start with some more subjective genre preferences you might want to know before going in, especially since Loop Hero currently has so few comparisons. Above all, it’s a Roguelite, but the moment-to-moment gameplay is an even split between Idle Game, RPG, and even Tower Defense. It’s mostly in the aesthetics. The Idle Game takes over when the battles start, making them short and breezy. Your strategy is fully dependent on the macro decisions you’ve made across the map, all of which will determine in-battle stat checks and survivability. In a successful run, you’re never truly hands off. Think of it as driving through a yellow light, then lucking out and missing all the reds. The pace matches the speed of your planning remarkably well, between adjusting your character’s walk speed, and even more crucially, having a dedicated button to fully pause and resume the game’s automation. Well… maybe Loop Hero isn’t for you. It might be the weakest literal comparison, but the flow of the game is remarkably similar. The crux of your gameplay is filling out the map with unique features, each of which control enemy spawns, stat modifiers, loot drops, and even optional challenge modes. You’ll need to make something challenging enough to earn your character stronger resources and loot, but not too overwhelming where you’ll end your run before it starts. In short, rather than keeping out danger, like a traditional Tower Defense, you’re inviting it.• Prepare in the village! While not as polished as the titular loop, it’s an excellent complement to the overall flow of the game. The progression loop of the Roguelite truly comes alive here, where base building, deck building, resource management, and lore collection all come alive to round out the experience. If you’re interested in highly experimental games, this is a must buy. That experiment was a success! You don’t have to buy into any of Loop Hero’s bold ideas and imagine what could have been. Everything’s here, and everything’s rewarding. This game has plenty of complicated and overlapping systems, but you’re given plenty of time to learn them. Your first hour of gameplay will feel radically different from your tenth hour, and even your twentieth. Before I knew anything else about the game, the lavish throwback pixel art caught my eye. Rest assured, that level of quality is maintained across the entire game. The music is excellent. You’ll still be hearing new tracks the further you progress, but even hearing those tracks multiple time never dampens their impact. Runs are kept fresh long-term with new tile interactions, new cards, new village pieces, and new character perks. When you first start the game, the bulk of this excitement will come from new character classes. While there are only three classes in the game, each plays radically differently. Plenty of gameplay variety comes from switching between these classes frequently, but there is zero punishment for sticking to a single, favorite class. I love playing indies on Switch, but it's hard to beat Loop Hero on Steam, where all you need is a single mouse. For me, this perfectly complimented the more leisurely pace of the game, making it easier to relax into each new loop. While Loop Hero generally does a great job overall of keeping each new run engaging, you’ll still need to embark on multiple farming runs if you want to maintain upgrades in the hub world. For a game that enjoys such a leisurely pace, it doesn’t feel too out of step with the overall experience, but everyone will enjoy this aspect. More than anything, several other systems in the game can make the grind feel worse when you fall behind. While this isn’t 100% true, it’s apparent enough where your progress can feel stifled without a new major upgrade. No upgrade in Loop Hero will automatically win you the game, but you won’t reach the final boss without a full town, either. While this claim is a bit hyperbolic, it also exaggerates the grinding problem. If you lose, 70% of all accrued resources are lost. The game’s upgrades aren’t cheap, so returning to your hub without the ability to make anything can make that loss sting quite a bit more. If you’re still excited about the game, skip this paragraph! You won’t encounter any of this until about twenty hours in, at a minimum. Once you have all the right upgrades, as well as a deeper understanding of the game’s systems, you can nearly break it. For some people, this might be the goal of playing systems driven game, finding the cracks and exploiting them. For some, like me, it’s fun the first few times, but having that knowledge can dampen the impact of future runs that simply aren’t optimized. Even if you don’t crack the game wide open like this, you’ll eventually find patterns for tile layouts that are simply better than others. I still had an excellent time playing Loop Hero, but this brought the whole experience to a definitive end for me.Above all, I stand by what I said in my very first sentence, that the game is well worth a try if you’re at all curious about this novel standout indie title. I’m eagerly keeping an eye out on Four Quarters!
