_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The game has an interesting concept.  However there are just too many flaws in it to be fun to me.Gameplay is mostly placing tiles and equipping items, but its constant so its not an idler.  However like an idler it requires a lot of time investment to gather resources. There is only one time on the loop where you can keep all your resources, else you lose 30% of your invested time.If you get a good build and do too well? It just summons a Lich that you cannot beat and thus you cannot take our anything safely, you just lose 30 or 60% of your invested time.Its clearly not an idler, so why not pause at the camp each run automatically? Why give a penalty to leaving anywhere but the one campfire tile?  The whole game is already push your luck, penalty should be dying in a fight, it would still occur.Upgrades that provide meager gameplay changes through new tiles have pretty extravagant costs.This means that to get a small change you need to grind a lot of time gathering items.I think small changes would make the game more enjoyable, maybe allowing people to quit before the Lich with all their gathered resources?  Maybe reducing some resource cost for unlocking items?
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: so simple, yet so engaging. I love how much I discover when playing this. It really takes me back to when I was a child and didn't have all the answers at my fingertips. "Wait... why is this town filled with ghouls?!" a few hours later "OOOH! If I put it next to the *** it's ransacked and I need to cleanse it, then it lives in prosperity." _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept of a game, and then you hit the super grind wall where you won't make any progress for a long time, or just Act 2.  Will be fine one loop, then instantly dead the next.  That kind of scaling makes wasting 30+ minutes on a run, as you only get to keep 30% and it always throws away all the good items and all artifacts.  Wouldn't be so bad if there was some sort of consistency between loop difficulty increases, as it will go up on a curve then suddenly spike.  That being said, with some balance changes the game will be pretty good, as until getting nowhere after 6 hours at all it was a fun gameplay loop.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10. Very addictive game. It's like a card game which you can build your own deck for each expedition. Also love the "Trial and error" elements  as you have to try out the combinations of different cards/buildings. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but there are a few glaring problems.The first is that it's extremely grindy with very little sense of progression. I might do a run that takes over half an hour, and not get enough resources for any upgrade. This means that I need to spend hours grinding for a single upgrade, which makes the game frustrating.The second is how ludicrously RNG-based the game is. Sometimes, I'll go 2 or even 3 loops without getting an improvement in my weapon, meaning that monsters that should be manageable end up killing me.And the third is the lack of control. For example, if I'm fighting three opponents and one of them has a quest HP buff, then I'll often get torn apart for a long time while I slowly whittle down the tough opponent; I should at least have the ability to choose who I'm attacking, and that's not even considering the times my character switches targets mid-combat.These three issues are pretty glaring. This game would be an 8 or 9 out of 10 if these issues were resolved, but right now, I can't justify putting any more time in.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This game is weird. By the name it's pretty obvious it's going to be repetitive, but the first two acts of the game (of which there are four) don't feel too repetitive - you unlock new tiles to place pretty fast, usually a new character to play as, still seeing a fair amount of new dialogue, etc. It felt a little cut and dry, but it was relaxing and I didn't feel like I was wasting my time (more than I would playing any other game, anyway). But I'm on Act 3 now, and I've hit what could be best referred to as a difficulty *wall* rather than a spike, and the repetitiveness is starting to set in. There's a few reasons for this:- There is a specific resource you start needing to upgrade camp structures and build new ones that can only be acquired by fighting 4 or more enemies in one fight. The "more" is pretty tricky since the number of enemies you can fight (directly) is capped at 4 anyway, and the chance for the resource to drop scales with how many enemies you are fighting, so it's tough to get. I've spent a few hours trying to farm it across multiple runs and even with fighting as many as 8 enemies on a tile, and it just doesn't drop enough to justify how necessary it is to progress.- by now, I have unlocked like 80% of all the lore and dialogue, and the rest is hidden behind making arbitrary combinations of tiles to synergize new ones and then farming *another* resource to unlock the encyclopedia entry (which isn't all that special anyway in many cases - stuff like the lore on a generic rock could really be left unwritten).- the difficulty of a given fight scales with both what loop you are on (enemies get a certain percent stronger per loop) and what act you are on (which changes that percentage and gives enemies new abilities). The thing is, you pretty much start from 0 strength-wise every run - you have more healing but your DPS is pretty much entirely controlled by what equipment you get. You don't get better weapon or armor draws, and you can only increase your strength with a specific camp building and by a small amount (unless you want to farm the resource from the first point and not use it on other things).- one of the game's best points is trying to optimize the geometry of where you place different tiles to enable synergies and maximize the value you get - but I've stopped unlocking tiles (at least, tiles that are any good), so it's basically just repeating the same geometric patterns every run.- there is a cap on how many resources you can farm of *any* type (both the useful ones and the ones you get a lot of anyway) for each act, so you can't even farm infinitely on one run if you wanted to.So I'm at the point where, in order to add variety and progression back into the game, the easiest thing to do is to just farm up a bunch of resources and upgrade/unlock everything - which involves doing like an hour of boring map setup with patterns I already know, then just sitting and staring at the screen, only pausing to change equipment as it comes in. The game has a lot of strong points to balance out the inherent repetitiveness but I can't recommend a game that turns into full-on Cookie Clicker halfway through.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Version 2.0Loop Hero is another game that I want to like due to its novel concept, but in the final analysis it can't make up for its flaws. The core concept of the game as a 'reverse' tower defense is the highlight. Unfortunately the mechanisms surrounding this prove to be limited in complexity, and external systems are implemented in an effort to round out the game. None of these systems are fun, and indeed it quickly paints the game to feel like a painfully dull resource grind.

_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game, I bought it first on Nintendo Switch because the cover art captured me, and fell in love with the gameplay. The aesthetics and art direction are top notch, but what got me actually hooked was the gameplay. The characters and dialogue are some of the most charming I've experienced in a good while!The balancing of the tiles, the slow upgrading of the camp and seeing your work slowly pay off is so satisfying! Even more so, everything is so gorgeous to look at, the characters are a joy to behold and the dialogue has made me do much more than silent amused huff at my screen. And the plot itself is a mystery I'm intrigued to solve!Speaking of which, the game becomes a little grindy after chapter 3, but for me that's not a negative thing. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A professional reviewer called this an idle game. I suspect he never actually touched the game, because it really, really isn't. Neither is it a rogue-like game (you know exactly where you will go and what enemies you'll meet). If anything, this game is a tableau-builder where you add and substract set-pieces to both support and challenge a hero running in a loop. Build too much setting and you will pop the boss too early. Build too many enemies and you will die. Build too little and the enemies will level up faster than you do and you die. Only you don't. The loop resets but every time you leave it, either volunatry or on a stretcher, you find yourself back at a camp where you can unlock buildings that will support you. All this is suprisingly intense without actually feeling like it is. It's an auto-battler, right? Only, it needs constant tweaking and adjusting and suddenly the clock tells you you lost another hour.I'm not fond of the very plain overland graphics. And I would have liked a little more insight into how set pieces work together to build into more than the sum of their parts. But on a whole, it's a nice new genre in-between the RPGs, FPSes and MOBAs that publisher seemingly want to drown us in.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine I suppose, some of the artwork is great(splash page, portraits) while some is ugly as sin(the rest of the game), which is a shame.It's an idle game but i find the grind to be a little too much to make me care about playing it more.It's in my list of "games to play while the toddler has nursery rhymes playing in another window".I think its overpriced for what it is hence the thumbs down.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a good example of why a large portion of rogue(like/lites) are terrible. These RNG based progression games are extremely frustrating for the first 10+ hours. And then only fun after that if you enjoy the tedium of doing the same thing over and over. Loop Hero is especially bad because very little on the players end can effect the general outcome of the "loop". Nearly everything is based on luck. Whether that be getting the gear you want for a build, or the correct card "tiles" to keep from bashing your head into a wall because your 'hero' is great at picking the worst targets to focus on in a battle you have no control over.The general premise of Loop Hero is this; It's a reverse tower defense, where your hero is the monster making rounds along a chain. You place down 'towers' that spawn enemies your hero has to fight along the way. You want to do this in a way that minimizes the risk your hero has to face when they run into enemies, but not to the point that your progress stagnates. So, say~ The problem is you have absolutely no control over the course of battle, outside making sure your hero has a good enough 'build' to survive. Which is determined by gear you have equipped on the hero. Which is determined by an RNG chance of dropping as you defeat enemies along the path. A vast majority of the gear you find in the early part of the game is just straight up garbage, even after making it through 6-7 loops. Which is desperately needed because by the time you reach the third or fourth loops, you'll likely have your hero facing off against enemies like vampires and bandits, whom all have a stupidly high evade chance. Which, so far as I can tell, there is no counter to. There is no 'hit success' stat modifier on any item. So even in battles, you're left to just watching and hoping RNG doesn't screw you by letting the enemy evade EVERY DAMN TIME.I could have spent more time playing... but the whole premise of just idly watching a pixel avatar loop around the screen doing a pissant job at being a 'hero' gets boring. And the fact that the game does as much as possible to delay progress while being everything but completely blatant about your lack of control over how the game wants to play out. Like an idle clicker without the clicking. The only thing that makes this game interesting is the soundtrack. Which is amazing. I would have rather purchased that over wasting my money on the game, if the option was available to me at the time.Also, as a final note. The game is very unstable at the moment. At the time of writing, they've patched the game five times, and there are still a fairly large amount of crashes that can occur, usually within an hour or two of playtime. Before, you would lose all the resources you've aquired on the run that crashed, but that has since been patched... not the crashing, but you at least get to save all the resources back at camp. Which I'm sure in no way will be exploited, now./s
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of idle/incremental games, so I thought this would be up my ally, but all this time later I still can't really get it to click. Building a good run feels nice, and the progression that's here is really pleasant, but it's entirely too much work and grinding to get just a few resources that are used for a lot of stuff, namely expansion orbs. You essentially have to build an entire run around grinding these damn things, or most other special crafting resources, rather than trying to win a run. The first two "parts" of the game weren't like that so much, but by the third I felt I didn't really have a choice. Things curved up in difficulty enough that it was either I wait out for a good run with good loot, or I make myself stronger in a meta way, which is horrible grinding. A loop implies at least the illusion of progression, but I kinda just felt like I never went anywhere to begin with.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Spent a good 8 hours on the demo and now put in about 40 hours into the main game.PROS:Style:  The game oozes it and has a very strong sense of the early 8 bit RPG days.Game-play: Great combination of Rogue-lite, RPG, Auto-battler and card game, with a dash of Dungeon Keeper thrown in too!Game-length: Addictive and quite fast, each loop takes maybe 20 to 30 minutes.CONS:Pacing - Trying to level up some of the camp buildings requires you to grind for resources. It does pad the game a little bit, but I feel that some of the upgrades could have been cut in half and I'd still played for the same amount of time as I'd be using those resources on other buildings, not just one.Balance - The Necromancer class seems by and large the easiest to play, while the Rogue seems the hardest. There seems to be an "optimal" set of cards too, which for me became a little bit stale. QOL Improvements:You can't see what cards you've brought into your current loop and you can't save your current loop either. If you quit the game, you're forced to start over. The book resources has no use once the encyclopedia is completed, along with the plant matter and vampire remains.It can also be quite hard to see where your hero is on the loop too.The ability to speed up, or skip the combat animations would be a nice bonus as well.Not without it's faults, but Loop Hero combines card game, idle battler and dungeon keeper into it's very own, unique genre with an almost philosophical and strangely upbeat atmosphere. You use a deck of cards to build the world that your walk around in a loop. Each card can give a different effect and sometimes when placed next to other cards can evolve .Each loop makes the monsters level up but they also drop stronger loot. Battling is all automatic and with no input from the player. Upon placing a certain amount of cards (depending on which chapter is being played), the boss appears. Each is fairly unique with mechanics that the regular monsters do not possess.With three different classes, a Rogue-lite town hub that you can level up, along with about 50 or so different cards and combinations Loop Hero quickly becomes another "just one more go..." kind of game. If you want to feel a weird sense of meloncholy and optimism while reading about bridges, then this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this is the perfect game for anyone that wants to play something, but will have to be constantly getting up to check on something or otherwise be interrupted. The pixel art is fantastic and the music is great. The game takes concepts from a few differing genres and melds them together perfectly. I would love to see this game (new genre?) expanded upon in the future through either updates, DLC, or a new game entirely. A solid 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Meh. Not bad but generally feels incomplete (like having inventory slots that are never unlocked and generally balance doesn't feel right), grindy and repetitive. Visuals and soundtrack are quite charming though. Has a little bit of dialogues and story which are okay so far.First you need to learn what cards (tiles) you can place and what are their interactions with other cards and what kind of enemies they may spawn. Once you got that, you create some strategy. Gameplay becomes just placing cards (tiles) according to the strategy (there isn't that much to think about placement) and filtering the items you obtain. That's it. Filtering items becomes pretty tedious very quickly because you just get flooded with items and need to figure out if it's better to have 0.25 X stat or 0.3 Y stat while there isn't any kind of in-game preview calculator and unequipped items are trashed. Oh, and about 2-4 times per run you choose a skill from random selection. I suppose that's the worst part of RNG because these skills really define your run. Then you repeat that while trying to stop yourself from placing too many enemies on the map.Basically the game has wedged itself in the dangerous gap between idle games and interactive games where it isn't idle because you can't just leave the hero alone but the gameplay isn't really engaging and becomes tedious.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a game about a lone survivor who walks around a looped path and attempts to rebuild the world. (I simply call him Hero, myself.) It looks much like a standard RPG with building elements, although it is heavily focused on indirectly influencing Hero's expeditions by equipping him with items and - more importantly - using the game's literal world-building. (As somebody who's working on their own novel, I found the world-building aspect to be especially fascinating. You can focus strictly on boosting Hero so that he can fight bosses, or get creative with the landscape to make things interesting - especially once you're powerful enough already throughout the course of the game.)As previously mentioned, the gameplay is incredibly unique, focusing on building Hero's stats and the surrounding landscapes instead of being the one to fight the enemies directly. This aspect of the gameplay suffers from a slight level of disengagement from the game, and a potentially substantial amount of repetition. Given how varied the enemies are meant to be, more mechanics that allow Hero to approach the enemies differently would be an excellent way to improve on this approach to the battle system. Otherwise, the concept is overall unique and interesting, as previously mentioned.The camp can also be laid out more-or-less freely. This alone was what interested me in the game. Additionally, the story is straightforward, yet has a fascinating amount of depth for those who wish to read further into it.The soundtrack is very pleasant to listen to. It has a variety of songs for different scenarios. My only issue with them was that there were not quite enough songs that played in standard expeditions, which ended up feeling slightly repetitive for those who aim for 100% completion and easter eggs (as I did). (As another, very minor issue, certain boss songs not playing in the final chapter came off as a missed opportunity, although it doesn't detract from the experience!) Individually, however, each song is very, very well-made! As for the graphics, they can be adjusted as needed, and the art style reminds me of the simple yet elegant pixel style that retro games often have.To summarize, I highly recommend Loop Hero for its literal world-building, the unique gameplay that focuses on building stats and landscapes (plus town-building), and the interesting graphics and soundtrack that all contribute greatly to the straightforward yet fascinating story of Loop Hero's world.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, beat the last boss yesterday. Would recommendly dearly to everyone who enjoys roguelikeish games.Pros:- Varying options to approach your runs with.- Difficulty ( on the harder side )- Visual style is great, fits perfectly- Amazing OST, probably the best part about the game for me next to gameplayCons:- Due to its difficulty, you have only few viable options available in the endgame.- Classes should be changed to have even powerevel.As you can see, the only downsides are related to balance, which can be easily changed in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: There's very few indie games that have ever made themselves distinguished from the rest. Games like Binding of Isaac, or Super Meat Boy. Games that not execute a concept well, but re-envision the concept and build it into their game from the ground up. Truly owning the concept through their execution.Loop Hero has done that, and although not as loudly or brazenly as Super Meat Boy or the Binding of Isaac, still just as well. Loop Hero used multiple concepts as building blocks, but didn't just implement a concept you've seen before and leave it there. It's not just about getting broken cards, it's not just about running a certain setup, the game is honestly difficult and built around a probable chance at failure.It's honestly unlike anything you've booted up in the past year or two, I'd almost promise you that. There's so much fine tuning and balance to do within your runs, saving cards in case of emergencies, or trying to build that perfect path. There's so much to hope for, and everything to lose. It's refreshing that I can be invested and care about a run but not be edge of my seat button-mashing for the next 15 min as I play a run. It's a slow burn. Am I doing well? What equipment am I hoping for? I need to hold out for XYZ...Just be aware it's a slow game. It's not nail-biting action for the next 15 min as soon as you start a run. There's time to invest and work on your character. Long as you keep your adrenaline expectations in check, I don't think this game will fail to deliver a solid time for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Calling it a twist on tower defense doesn't convey just how much there is to it, but it's a good starting point for a frame of reference. It also taps into that "one more round" vibe in both the loop and the need for one more expedition. Even the story is kinda fun so far.It's also nice to have an engaging game that's not so hard on the wrists -- a lot of the game is automated, but this doesn't detract from the fun in anyway. (Which it normally would, imho!)
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a polished and spectacularly innovative genre-mashup, combining elements of everything from deckbuilding roguelites to auto-battlers into a system that is both cohesive and accessible. The best part of this strange gameplay is how well-tuned it is-- I found myself mastering the deckbuilding mechanics without ever really thinking about it, and it's a great feeling.The game is absolute gorgeous, going for a classic CRT-Amiga aesthetic, has an absolutely banger chiptune soundtrack, and has half-decent writing for its dialogue and lore entries that's engaging enough that I was actually excited to unlock and read many of them.It's a game I can't recommend enough to anyone even remotely interested by the art or gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting take on the RPG/Rogue-lite genre. Eschews combat choice completely (fights are all automatic) in favour of emphasising resource management and equipment optimisation. This does put it dangerously close to idle game territory, but the fast pace of each expedition keeps the player active and entertained.The main drawback is that after while, the game begins to feel like a grind. Earning some of the rarer materials required to expand your camp (a fairly linear task taking place between each expedition) can take quite a long time. Certain rare orbs may only drop once in a 20 minute round, and when 10 or more are required to build a new structure or upgrade an existing structure, the game begins to feel rather tedious.There are three distinct classes which keep things varied, but all three are unlocked fairly quickly, and once you have identified optimal builds for each class not much changes from run to run. Rogue-lites are all about repetition, and this is where Loop Hero starts to fall down. By removing combat from the equation, each new run ends up a scavenger hunt, waiting and hoping that the ideal loot will drop.That said, it took me a good 25 hours to get to the point where things started to feel tedious. I enjoyed the game, and although I doubt I will ever finish it I reckon it's fun enough to be worth a play.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily one of my favorite games in the rogue genre.  I love the concept of the game despite the learning curve.  One thing I would like to see though is an in game explanation of the stats.  It can be a little difficult to choose gear sometimes when you're not sure if one stat is more beneficial than another.

_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game, but I just found myself putting it down to play something else to get a sense of satisfaction.  Part of the mechanic of the looping path is that if you end the loop (retreat) before you are back to your camp tile, you only keep 60% of collected materials, but lose all items.  Well, once the have made 7-8 loops and all the tiles have encounters, its very easy to pass the camp and not be able to "retreat" with all your stuff.  It's ruined the game for me, its like I need SHMUP reaction for this ONE thing in a game thats mostly idle gameplay.  Needs to either prompt you to stay or retreat when you hit the camp tile, or be more lenient on the conditions.  Why shouldn't I keep everything if I am 3 tiles away if those tiles are empty?  Suddenly my character can't carry all the stuff he's already been carrying?Its a shame.  I have a decent amount of time in the game, I love literally every other part of the game, but I can't stand one more time of losing half my progress because I didn't have twitch reflex in an idle game.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Which is what these 4 guys had. And then they followed it up with a bunch of great, smaller ideas.You can easily tell they went with "Lets make a cool game! How can we make this fresh, fun and interesting?," instead of, "Oh, God, I hate my job! How can I make some quick money out of this s**t?"You set out on "Expeditions." Your hero will start moving around a random, empty looped path, reaching the Village at the end of each cycle, which heals you a little bit, in case you want to keep going, or allows you to Retreat, keeping everything you've found, ending your current run.Some Slimes will randomly appear on your path, at first. When you kill them, you'll receive cards representing structures that can be laid down over or around the path. These structures can spawn new monsters, give you stacking bonuses, or buff/debuff an area around them.Fights are fought automatically, you just watch (but don't worry -- you'll be busy often, laying down structures and equipping new items). Each monster you kill will give you either new cards, items, or materials.Items can be equipped by your hero, increasing his attributes. There are 3 different heroes to play with, each with their own particular attributes, and each item affects some of these. Meaning: there's room for creating strategies on how to build your characters.Materials can be used later, in between runs, to build or upgrade structures in your camp which, in turn, unlocks new cards, characters, bonuses.Every creature you kill also yields you some experience. When you level up, you get to pick 1 out of 3 perks, which strongly influence your character's fighting capabilities.Stronger creatures yield better items and more experience. And they're also the ones that usually kill you.Structures can generate combos. Combos can give more/different bonuses and . The game doesn't quite tell you this, so you have to experiment to find out what interacts with what.Items have 4 different rarities, with each giving one more type of attribute bonus than the previous tier.You die often, losing 70% of everything you gathered during that run. That's very important, otherwise you don't care to do things right.Some creatures can join fights in adjacent tiles, range-attacking you. A good deal of strategy goes into deciding what structure to lay down, where and when. Too much too soon will screw you, and too little too late will as well. The cards you want may take a while to get drawn, and the items you need may need even longer to show up.Before each run, you get to change your deck, selecting anything between 7 and 15 different cards to take with you.You can also find items during your loops (besides materials) that can be assigned in your camp to give you some small, extra bonuses. You can focus on one thing or another, so that those small bonus end up actually making quite a difference.Each kind of enemy drops only one or two different types of material. One of these only drop when you fight 5 monsters at once, another one is particularly hard to acquire. You can read the details on the in-game Encyclopedia.If you think you'll be just staring at the screen, because movement and fight are done automatically in Loop Hero, don't worry. It requires your constant attention, and you're putting structures down all the time. You do need to  it.If you think the game is too simple, don't worry. They put a lot of thought into it, and there are many things that combine with each other for interesting results. And you'll have to figure out many of these on your own.If you think you'll get tired of it, or finish the game very quickly, don't worry. It took me about 30 hours to do so, and I enjoyed all of it.The only reason I stopped playing this thing is because I beat it and saw everything there is to be seen. I'd keep playing it for 30 more hours, maybe even more, if there was more to discover. If a second installment comes out one day, it'll be an instant buy for me.So yeah, it's a great game, very innovative, very well thought-out, very well executed. And  bug-free, BTW. And also extraordinarily well balanced.If you find Loop Hero's premise intriguing, or you  it's something you  enjoy, buy it. You will.Congratulations to the guys who made this. That's how you make a good game -- by putting some love and a whole lot of thought into it.

_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A nice spin on the roguelite genre, the main focus of the game is managing the hero's path, where he walks in a loop, and his inventory, full of different (procedural) weapons; it will all build up towards the boss, which will spawn after a certain amount of tiles has been set. The camp part of the game is also fun, making you choose which buildings, and thus special abilities or new cards, to unlock first. It never really gets repetitive or boring, in the sense that every expedition always requires your attention and it will never become an idle game, but it might become repetitive if you're not into rng statistics part of the roguelites, since Loop Hero's gameplay rotates heavily around basically raising the most useful stat in that particular expedition and chapter. All around, a very fun game which i would recommend if you don't mind a simple, yet effective experience, and yet again another Devolver Digital published game that amazes me from the indie scene
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a billion well deserved "Recommended" reviews, so it's unlikely anyone will ever read this. If you are, and you like roguelites: Get this. It's fantastic. It's a boardgame where you control the board instead of your piece. The harder you make it for yourself without dying, the greater the rewards.This game also does an amazing job of evolving gameplay as you upgrade your persistent camp/town between runs. Many roguelites have fairly consistent gameplay and mechanics - this one changes things up in very interesting and different ways, keeping things fresh and compelling, whether it be new classes with very different gear, bonuses, and blay/build styles to new objects which confer entirely new gameplay systems and bonuses, to different cards, which you use to change the "board" of the game - many of which can synergize with each other. All of these things can be utilised to alter the resources you're collecting to upgrade your camp, difficulty, and overall flavor of your run.It's an incredibly unique game with a great amount of depth, for those willing to explore it. If you want a simple game, it can be that, too - though it may take you longer to progress. It's like poker. Easy to learn, difficult to master.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so many things...deck builder, rogue-lite, strategy, rpg...it does all of things very well yet seems like a genre all on it's own. It's meditative and also exciting. completely playable with just mouse clicks, yet the music, animations, and art style still make this feel like an action game and keeps my attention constantly invested. A great game for a quick 30 minute looping session around the randomly-generated "loop dungeon/adventure path" or for spending an entire day getting 'lost in the loop' as you gather resources, build up and expand your camp and abilities, and try for just that one more loop to see if you can beat that boss. I'll admit this game looked really unassuming when i saw it appear on Steam, but after watching the dev stream and playing the demo, it's my new favorite time killer.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: it has the aesthetic of an autoplay-dragon warrior with nice pixel art, but gameplay is more of a calmly paced deck building rogue-lite where your card-actions aren't fight-actions. instead, your card-actions are to build terrain(for buffs) & buildings (enemy spawns), or as map/hand-utility.this could be a new subgenre as it often feels too different from other similar genre comparisons. it's not an arpg (like most rogue-lites). it's only as rpg like most rogue-lites with stories are rpgs. it's not a card-actions-are-attacks-or-creature-placements game (like most deck building games). if you don't like "deck building games" ...i didn't even know it had a deck involved for my first couple hours of the demo, and i was still enjoying it.it's well worth the $12.74 sale price (or a non-sale $15). hope to see more of this 'loop-hero' genre to come from this & other developers

_childDocuments_.review: Not so fun.This is an interesting and fresh idea at least. I did get my $5 of enjoyment out of this game but I'm pretty much done now. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a randomly generated looping rogue-like with pixel graphics following a single protagonist as they regain their memory after the destruction of the planet by a god-like being. A small settlement is rebuilt by the player unlocking more tiles/cards to use to populate the map. There is a small equipment panel where equipment can be dragged and dropped, though some squares are greyed out dependent on your player class. The point of the game is to beat the final boss which spawns at your camp by filling in the bar each time you put a tile down. The character designs are really incredible and the detailed character portraits are just amazing. As the loops progress, the enemies get stronger but so does the equipment you find. It's an interesting game with a dark backstory with unlockable "encyclopedia" entries about each monster, equipment, terrain and resource. It really fleshes out the world a little more and is quite funny at times.Unfortunately, it does get boring seeing as you are going around and around and is very subject to RNG in which tiles you get. There's not too much strategy involved, just really trying to blank out the tiles where the boss buff tiles would generate and then going into battle (that's how I won in the first loop for that achievement).You can adjust the movement and battle speed. Pause using right click or space bar and change the settings to pause at the end of loops or after each battle, which is kind of clutch when youre getting close to filling the bar. Each class plays a little different; the necromancer is good for the early loops but the output of damage from the rogue plus their attack speed is just insane. The music and battle sounds follow a 8? 16? bit format to match with the game. There's no voice acting, just beeps. I did enjoy it, it's good if you like dungeon crawling in a sense. I just really like the character designs designs. Give it a go on sale. I played this game for 50 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a very interesting Roguelike game that takes a fascinating narrative to a game with Card and Idle mechanics. Is very good at what it does, and the feeling of the world is impressivly deep. I highly suggest giving it a try if you like RPG games or Rougelikes, and if you have a sweetspot for "retro games", this may be a jewel in your collection.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game where you wake up in a world reduced to a void and you go around a series of procedurally generated loops, 'reclaiming' memories and fighting monsters. In the process, there is the build-your-own-obstacle-coarse and temporary character level-up mechanics and a more permanent base building mechanic. I tip my hat to the effort that's gone into this game - it's well made and well packaged. However, that is where my list of positives for this game ends.Once you move past the novelty of the game's premise, you realize that it's essentially a glorified idle clicker with a nice RNG engine. There is a lack of depth in the game's mechanics, rendering any need for planning and strategy unnecessary. Even the premise, which initially promises to be interesting turns out to be underutilized and mostly aesthetic. The story here is, sadly, shallow and doesn't really matter to the enjoyment of the game.However, the greatest failure of this game is the fact that it fails to provide a purpose. Yes, there is always the goal of 'beating the game' and earning achievements, but this is not a particularly difficult game - you just have to be patient and wait for the RNG gods to bless you for your devotion. Achieving in-game milestones is not really satisfying in a way that, say, Darkest Dungeon is. Bottomline, it's a good game if you're just looking to kill some time without investing too much mental bandwidth.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop hero is one of those special games that has the magical ability to bend and distort time. I downloaded the game and started playing. and before I knew it five hours had gone by and I still couldn't pt it down. This game's premise, on paper, is so simple. Go on rogue-lite adventures around a mini dungeon circuit that you get to customize and create to your exact specification. But it's so much more. The mechanics during an "expedition" are so compelling and create surprisingly tense moments where I'm weighing every single decision on the outcome of how many resources I will take back to my camp to upgrade it, meet new denizens, and keep pushing the cryptic, but engaging narrative in the right direction. Great game 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This is by no means a bad game. I bought it as I was swayed by the reviews. I came in expecting greatness when in reality it is at best decent. Although this is not a negative review per se, I felt the need to balance the overwhelming positivity with grounded criticism.The combat is lacking in depth. It is entirely automated, you only have control over the gear your hero equips, and you tend to equip whatever has a higher level (with the exception of rare cases)Your strategy in the buildings you construct is also limited, there is an optimal path to success and minimal creativity involved. You will always build villages near mansions, you will always place blood groves near groves, etc.I can see how the gameplay loop can be entertaining in the short term, and progression can certainly be addictive, but a few hours in and it bored me to ♥♥♥♥.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't consider myself one for retro-looking puzzle-esque games, but this one is a real gem and I absolutely love it. The gameplay is complex, unique and captivating, there is actually and interesting story here, the world feels well crafted, the music and art style are both amazing and complement each other well and make for an all together cohesive feel for the game. This game is masterfully crafted and well worth the full prize.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolute banger!!!! I was more than pleasantly surprised. I cant stop playing this its literally the game I needed to scratch my looting/rpg/progression itch I've had. If you're on the fence don't be this is easily the best money I've spent on a game EVER.Then there's the music..........TALK ABOUT GREAT!!! anyways Im excited for my days off work so I can sink 10 hours each day into this.

There's also enough variance in your cards once everything is unlocked to be able to experiment with combinations for quite some time, though I assume most everyone will eventually find the combination per character that just breaks the difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

It took me a minute to get the hang of the mechanics and I would usually not survive past Loop 6 or so. I was rushing myself. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Goodbye real world, my life is officially stuck in a 'loop' now!I bought this game a couple days ago and already I'm close to 50 hours. When I bought it I figured I'd play an hour or two and move on to the next game which normally is the case. Not with Loop Hero though! That hour managed to fly by quick! _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Totally unique and highly addicting. "Just one more run" is often my thought. It gives me clear satisfaction, but isn't so gripping that I forget to go to bed. I do find myself wanting to come back for more and more. I look forward to a couple of loops as often as I can make time. Great game for me, especially since I find myself getting hooked on certain games (in an unhealthy way). Loop Hero doesn't hold on to me too hard, and it allows me sleep and a life.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome.I love how the rules of the game incentivize you to build a world that feels thematically appropriate, while being consummately rewarding, and challenging. At about 9 hours, I've unlocked two classes, and beaten the first of [what appears to be] 3 bosses. The music is so good I find myself nodding or whistling along to it constantly. The pixel art is insanely good. The restraint used in the palette results in some some really sublime visuals.So far I haven't figured out how to make the Rogue class viable, but the other two are both quite fun and different from one another. Looking forward to playing more!UPDATE:I did finish Loop Hero, primarily using the third class that I unlocked. I believe it has the most potential to snowball into being "broken" by focusing on a couple primary stats as it concerns looting during a run. IDK that it's a problem. I did manage to get some wins against other bosses using the Rogue finally, but I did find him to be the most difficult class to playI thought the story was well-thought out, each of the characters are very well illustrated and written, though story is a pretty minimal part of the game, it does make a big impact. There is a bit of a roguelite style progression that essentially makes your character just more and more powerful.The thing that impresses me most about Loop Hero is how dynamic the world can feel, despite being based on very simple relationships between different tiles and monsters. It's an elegantly designed game that I'm very glad I played.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I had been gas lighted by the reviews... for about 15 minutes.  Then the game gripped me and hasn't let go since!  This is the game I had hoped 'Book of Demons' would be.Only negative (so far): Taking the retro/pixel approach is fine, but it still needs to be done well.  The graphics are ropey and unhelpfully obscure/similar at times.  C'mon devs - give it a lick of paint and some tlc!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A superior RPG with a lot of depth that on the surface it looks like it may not have. Well that is far from the truth. Settlement development, deck building, trait picking, classes and world building are all here in a fresh original idea. Cannot beat the price while it is on sale for the holidays either. Check out my tutorial here
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I'll recommend because it's a classic 'great-jewel-of-an-idea' game that's worth playing around with for a while (especially true at this price point), but sometimes your library gets stuffed with these $5 cool ideas and you start to find out which ones really have legs, and which ones you might not stick with. My limit with Loop Hero seems to be the second of 3(?) major bosses. I've found that I'll be enjoying a run, accruing power through the fun roguelite synergy mechanics, and then not standing a chance against the boss. This is, of course, a skill issue, but I've gone looking for tips and found that my struggle is largely based on neglecting the meta-progression (you build up a little village between runs). "Ok, cool, a roguelite where it's actually necessary to consider your meta progression, that could be fun," I thought to myself. Unfortunately, in this case, I simply find those mechanics dense (again, skill issue), and more importantly: time consuming. Basically, it seems to me that you're supposed to be bailing on runs to bring home 100% of your supplies. You don't actually try the boss every time, and instead you build out this town, and gather boons for future runs. To me, that's a huge flaw vs other roguelites, in which the whole fun is scraping your way towards an unlikely victory, run after run. Maybe I'm dead wrong, and the skill issue is worse than I thought, but that premise really hurts the game for me, and I'm not sure I'll find myself returning to grind out the W. Had fun, won't finish. The $5 cool idea graveyard (not to be dramatic).

_childDocuments_.review: Today when I walked into my economics class I saw something I dread every time I close my eyes. Someone had brought their new gaming laptop to class. The Forklift he used to bring it was still running idle at the back. I started sweating as I sat down and gazed over at the 700lb beast that was his laptop. He had already reinforced his desk with steel support beams and was in the process of finding an outlet for a power cable thicker than Amy Schumer's thigh. I start shaking. I keep telling myself I'm going to be alright and that there's nothing to worry about. He somehow finds a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ outlet. Tears are running down my cheeks as I send my last texts to my family saying I love them. The teacher starts the lecture, and the student turns his laptop on. The colored lights on his RGB Backlit keyboard flare to life like a nuclear flash, and a deep humming fills my ears and shakes my very soul. The entire city power grid goes dark. The classroom begins to shake as the massive fans begin to spin. In mere seconds my world has gone from vibrant life, to a dark, earth shattering void where my body is getting torn apart by the 150mph gale force winds and the 500 decibel groan of the cooling fans. As my body finally surrenders, I weep, as my school and my city go under. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate gaming laptops.

_childDocuments_.review: Love the art style and setting but it didn't feel like a deckbuilding or roguelike game to me.You don't build the deck as you go - instead you unlock cards and design a deck in a menu like a collectable card game. Okay for people that want a game like that but I'm more a fan of Slay the Spire and board games like TFM. Grinding to unlock things and then experimenting like a sandbox game wasn't for me. You could argue that the deck building is really the environment, as you do chose how to build that, but the synergies you get are all decided before the game begins in the deck building menu.The loop of the game is strange - whilst other games like Slay the Spire have a clear goal (to reach the top and defeat the boss), this game makes you constantly question if you are doing the right thing. Do I actually want to place structures and get to the boss? Do I retreat before fighting the boss? After a while I discovered that placing 9 rocks can create a mountain which spawns a new enemy - is that a good thing? I don't know. You might kill some of the new enemy for a while, and then be overwhelmed later. Figuring out the cause of your problems is tricky. Whereas if you pick up a card like Normality in Slay The Spire, you will quickly discover if it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: By far the most fun I've ever had in a rogue-lite. Only Enter the Gungeon or Slay the Spire come close to beating it out for my #1 spot but they aren't close enough. The amount of enemy variation, tactics, decision making, and countless other things surprised me and I gotta say, this is probably the best designed game I've played in a long time. If you like rogue-lites at all you should 100% pick this game up. This is the first game I've ever 100% completed on steam, and I have almost 200 games. That pretty much sums up how much I love it.With all that praise out of the way, I have a couple things I think they could do a little better. Now that I've finished the game, each run feels like an automatic win and there isn't a huge amount of replay value now since I've unlocked everything and filled my camp up. I'd love to see them add something else to the end game to spice things up a little (apart from the secret boss which is a great addition but I hate most of the cards you need to spawn it). I'd also like mountains to be reworked as in the endgame theyre pretty much useless. They give max hp but even if you have the whole place filled up with mountains it doesn't give you nearly as much as some of the other methods of getting max hp (not gonna spoil those sry). I'd also like a buff to the beacon as its fairly useless even in the late game when it finally gets a slight use.But yeah, apart from that and a few other issues with balance, its almost a perfect game. I can easily recommend this game to anyone who likes rogue-lites (and anyone else tbh) and I cant wait for future updates to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: okay so first of all: the artstyle, character designs, pixel art, are insanely good. Genius level pixel art, 5/5. I really liked the universe theme. Soundtrack is also pretty lit and fitting so that's nice. For the gameplay: it's a nice simple concept that can have a decent amount of depth and strategy, but for some reason the balancing in some aspects is way off. When a player plays the game, they naturally get better as they gain more game knowledge, when you have rogueLITE elements such as buffs that persist between runs, you have to be very careful not to create huge double whammy effect that allows the player to steamroll through the rest of the game. That's exactly what happens here with the supply feature, some items are ridiculously good and you can stack tens or even hundreds or them, trivializing the whole game in the process. They ought to make them give diminishing returns, have drawbacks to them, or limit the number of single item the player can have, if they wish the game to remain challenging.I mean of course I could just not use the supply at all, but at that point it makes me wonder why the hell does it even exist in the first place, it's like a cheat code that's not hidden away.Also is it just me or do the watchtower archers really screw with necro, like they are so bad compared to necro's own skeleton archers. Would me nice if skeletons replaced them as they get summoned.The supply thing should be fairly easy to fix if the devs wish to, or you can just ignore it for your own sake. If you do it's overall a pretty great game, would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: TL/DR: NOT a roguelike; more of an idle game than anything else. Looks promising but turns out very shallow and grindy.Bought this because a friend recommended it to me and watching some gameplay videos it seemed like it might be interesting. Was very disappointed.The game at its core is an idle game of the sort where your hero auto-fights and loots mobs and you get to choose how to upgrade their equipment as new loot becomes available. The only novelty compared to the dozens of free games of this type is the map isn't something random created by the developer. Instead, you as the player create the map for your character starting from a looping path.There are 4 main types of loot- artefacts, used to equip your hero- cards, that can be placed on the map to create monster spawners or add various area status effects- resources, used to build your settlement- items, that can be added to your settlement to provide passive bonuses to your heroArtefacts add to your main stats (damage, defence, hp) as well as a handful of other typical RPG abilities like vampirism % or counterattack %. There aren't many of these and they don't really allow for very focused builds, especially given the perpetually increasing monster/equipment levels and random nature of the drops. Bottom line, this is mostly a spreadsheet simulator with barely any tactics involved.The terrain cards and map building - arguably the main draw of the game - are definitely an interesting concept with some potential. Especially interesting is the idea that some cards can interact with others - the least spoiling example being that mountains bunched together will eventually create a larger mountain that spawns harpies. This obviously has the potential to create an interesting game and was one of the things that made me buy it. Unfortunately the interactions are relatively few and mostly simple, so you'll only get so much excitement out of them. At the end of the day they all boil down to either cannon fodder with specific loot types or some "highly exciting" bonus like a heal when passing through.This also relates to the much-touted "deck building" aspect of the game. As I mentioned before you build your map from cards randomly looted from enemies. The cards are randomly selected from a configurable pool of card types. At the start you can put pretty much all land types into the pool and your number of choices does not grow all that much bigger. Much like everything else in the game, I see how this has potential, but the delivery is sub-par.Lastly, there's the camp-building aspect, a type of persistent rogue-lite progression of the worst sort: grinding. Building things in the camp requires a lot of resources and the only way to get them is to grind runs. There's no skill-based unlocks like in other games; the only thing skill-based is it introduces a risk/reward mechanic where quitting when you're at the fireplace (start of the loop) gives you 100% resources; quitting anywhere else out of combat gives 50% and death leaves you with only 30%. Although for those last two cases you have an option to loot all the resources anyway at the cost of a special item you can get from boss fights. To make things worse, your maximum loot you can carry has a per-resource type cap, so it's not like super deep runs will net you extreme rewards either. Just grind grind grind grind grind. And the reward you get for it? You unlock two new character classes and some new card types; but mostly it's a bunch of passive buffs.Overall, my impression of the game is it's a rehash of a bunch of ideas from indie games - and especially idle games - that ends up creating something moderately novel, but profoundly mediocre.

_childDocuments_.review: presents itself as an interesting and quirky idea for a rogue-like, but that's all it really remains. The novelty runs dry quickly due to a heavy grind throughout, as well as a vast lack of variety, pacing and balancing of difficulty that make each run feel more like a chore than it needs to be.• Manipulating the map to control what enemies spawn is a fresh and interesting mechanic, even though it never gets developed much further• Three diverse character classes, though the Necromancer feels like the superior class by far, offering a very different playstyle compared to the rest• The general concept gets run into the ground and becomes monotonous quickly• Lack of variety between runs severely damages any sort of replayability• Lack of player engagement• Lack of depth to mechanics makes the game feel extremely dull• Slow-paced and extremely grindy• Poor difficulty balancing between chapters forcing players to do resource-grinding runs• Hard to stay invested for long play sessionsIn , you'll be running around in a randomly generated loop with barely anything on it besides a few slimes. Each run you'll be able to manipulate the surrounding area with cards that you collect from killing enemies as well as gear that you can equip to survive the loop. These card effects range from spawning enemies, granting additional HP, restricting the number of enemies that can be on a single tile etc. You’ll receive specific resources when you walk over cards that you place on the path rather than the surrounding area. These are used to build new structures inside your camp.Each chapter tasks you to defeat the boss in order to progress, in order to spawn the boss in the first place you’ll need to fill up a bar. Everytime you use a card the bar will slowly fill up, once it’s full, the boss will spawn and you’ll have a choice of fighting or retreating back to camp with all the resources you’ve gathered. If you are unsuccessful in this attempt then you’ll only receive 30% of the resources you’ve gathered.Upon experiencing your first few runs, you'll probably get into the swing of how things work. The main problem that persists for  is that the player engagement and mechanics never evolve or have much depth. One half of the game is deciding on what gear to equip and where to place your cards, the other half is brainlessly watching the character run around and slay enemies. It would be an insult to call  an 'idle game,' but I couldn't help but think this when I was only half paying attention to what was happening. Simply watching battles play out, with your only influence being the stats on your equipment, doesn't call for much engagement.Unlike other roguelites,  seemingly pads out the playtime by making the bosses you fight extremely difficult. This not only forces players to grind for resources in order to build structures in their camp, but also causes a lot of frustration. The first boss was fine, took a few tries, but after that it gets viciously difficult, which begs the question of whether there is skill to this game. They've stripped away battle mechanics so what influence do you actually have? You decide which stats to prioritize (evading, regen, defense, counter-attack, etc.), how many enemies to spawn and which terrain cards will benefit you the most. When the entire game boils down to these decisions, it's hard to feel like you're having much of an influence on the game at all.Manipulating the loop with cards is probably the most interesting mechanic that this game has to offer. You'll discover, through experimentation, that putting together specific cards on the map will cause new things to happen. A basic example of this would be if you place nine rock or mountain cards in a 3x3 grid, then would turn into a Mountain Peak that gives you +48% max HP but spawns a Harpy every two days. All of the terrain cards act in a similar way, spawning enemy encampments on your path. Even if some of the other beneficial structures can also spawn new enemies that you'll have to deal with.It's safe to say that the variety is severely lacking in this game which is a major issue for a title that focuses on repetition. Unlike other roguelites, this one doesn't add enough random elements to the table to make each run feel different and to warrant playing it over and over again. Yet, the game encourages you to do exactly that, grinding over and over again to gather enough resources for building new structures in the camp to make the next loop more bearable. The only way of making a run feel different is by changing the cards that you bring to each loop, however, this contradicts with how brutally difficult the bosses are. If you have a good set of cards that you know work well together, then why would you bother changing up your entire deck for the sake of making it more 'varied' in exchange for making the game even more difficult?The only variety the game has to offer is found in the character classes that all play slightly differently from one another. The Warrior, the Rogue and the Necromancer with the latter being my personal favorite. These characters can only equip specific items making you focus on different stats depending on your class, but if you boil these down you're literally just focusing on different stats and haven't got much influence on the battle— aside from the Necromancer where you can manipulate how many skeletons you can spawn at what level and the quality of the summon.The resources that you collect during your runs, via placing terrain and traversing through road cards, are used to build new structures of the camp that will aid you in future runs. These can range from giving you healing potions, friendly archers fighting alongside you, to reviving your character once per loop etc. These structures make each chapter more bearable to tackle, however some of these structures are just too pricey. You might grind for a few runs, build the new facility and then stop because of how tremendously dull it is to collect those resources.That being said, I still appreciate the few unique structures you can build and upgrade inside the camp. It's a shame that the build tree is so linear and doesn't branch off into different directions for more diversity with structures. provides an interesting concept for a game, but drags it through the mud and then runs it over multiple times before you can even get halfway through. The need for constant grinding is laughable at times, the balancing for bosses seems purposely over the top to pad out playtime, the lack of variety makes every run feel monotonous and almost exactly the same.  is simply a good idea, executed poorly over and over again with each progressive chapter feeling too repetitive. Rather fitting, given the name.
