_childDocuments_.review: The first couple hours of this game were fantastic and I was very excited, but any semblance of depth falls away after you beat the first boss and the initial mystique wears off. There is very little to this game. I enjoyed my first 5 or 6 hours but after building about 2/3rds of the buildings and trying out all three classes, I realized that the gameplay was extremely binary and honestly, balance did not feel very good. I found myself going Lifesteal Warrior over and over again because it was the only thing that seemed even remotely successful for me.  (I have not replayed but they did add in speed sliders after I made this review which probably fix this), which only adds to the tedium, even when you aren't going Lifesteal. The card variety is pretty scarce as well, with something in the ballpark of 30 available excluding the combos, of which there are about ten. Many of them were very uninteresting, however, and many had drawbacks that didn't really seem necessary, such as buffing enemies with the same buff you get, or applying the same debuffs to you as enemies. Because of the drawbacks all the "good" things have, nothing is/feels rare because you can always have everything. Initially, it appeared there were 11 gear slots (which was exciting because I only had access to four initially), but I found out through researching the wiki that I can only get a fifth slot per character, and getting that slot applies a penalty to all of my other pieces of gear? This actually disincentivized me from building the structure you unlock this from, as I didn't want to gimp my base gear for a helmet slot that always had retaliation damage (for the warrior). Why show them all for each character, then? Not sure if it was a deliberate misrepresentation of depth or what? Maybe I'm just dumb and someone will comment and correct me, if this is also important to you. Overall, I did enjoy my time with this, but I don't think it's worth $15. I don't usually buy things not on sale, but got sucked into the hype on this one. Rookie mistake. Should additional (probably free because honestly I feel like I already over-invested) content come that fleshes out the core loop of the game or introduces new variables or things to pursue that are interesting, I'll gladly swing back in, check them out, and update this review. If not, I'd say wait until you can get this guy at least 50% off before you pick it up, Otherwise, I'd say play NGU Idle if you want to play an Idle game, or Slay the Spire/OverDungeon if you want a card based  RPG, as I enjoyed both of them more than this overall. For any 20+ hours conquerors of this game who are prowling reviews for some reason, if anything I said is incorrect please let me and others know as I don't have any intentions to mislead. EDIT: Wasn't allowing comments initially. Whoops. EDIT 2: I tried the  and it didn't blow my socks off.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This is MUCH grindier, slower, and more unexciting than I think it could be while still fulfilling what the audience wants from it. The mechanics are very dry, the runs are incredibly repetitive, and it involves waaay too much interaction to even play like the idle game that it probably should be for how shallow the mechanics are.I gave it 20+ runs while playing as an attention-keeper while playing D&D online (easily distracted from the game otherwise), and it was a decent way to keep my hands mindlessly occupied, but it really wasn't anything more than that. Honestly, I'm astounded to see I played it for 12 hours, I feel like I made no "progress" at all in that time.The "town as skill tree" system is incredibly incremental, there are no meaningful power spikes or rewarding moments, everything you get just feels like a tiny drop in the bucket of an endless grind. There is also *very little* you can do to control a run or opt into any specific build. You basically just HAVE to equip the best items you find, you almost NEVER have choices in which ones to equip because the levels/rarities are so inconsistent, and there's no clear way to control the variability there or what you get. Even for what it's trying to do, it's failing to do it well.Gameplay Design: 4/10User Experience: 7/10Aesthetic: 7/10Narrative Design: 2/10Story/Writing: 0/10
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A weird combination of an idle/auto battler and strategy card game - neither of which I would normally play - controlled entirely with the mouse.You go on an 'expedition' where your hero character just walks around the path in a loop, fighting any monsters on the way and stopping at the campfire after each full loop to heal. Monsters drop gear like weapons and armour to equip and increase your stats, because after each loop of the path the monsters get stronger. Killing monsters also drops cards, which you can place in tiles on different parts of the 'map.' Some go on the road, some next to it, and some around the edge of the level. Each one changes something, some spawn new monsters, some affect other tiles, some have some sort of interaction when you walk over them.You also collect resources in every expedition by killing stuff, walking over certain tiles, or filling your bag/card deck which automatically scraps stuff, and when you finish and return to your base you can build permanent tiles there to unlock new cards/perks etc.A nice chill game where you don't really have to do anything. You can customise how fast your character walks and how fast combat, so if it feels too slow or too quick you can change it to your preference and you can pause at any time or change when the game automatically pauses(eg when looking at equipment or combat units).Probably not something just anyone would like, it would probably have to really appeal or you just have to be into lots of different genres.Really cool concept and definitely worth trying at the least.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The idea is great and execution is interesting but this game has a MASSIVE issue : Victory is obtained by farming.You can place your cards the best way possible, be lucky with your loot and gear and you will absolutely fail that level because you were supposed to unlock a building in your town that give you access to some new cards that give you what you need to win.Building are obtained by spending ressources. You gain some in levels and you ONLY retain 30% of these if you fail the level. So you just start levels, farm ressources, leave before you get killed, upgrade your base when you can, rinse and repeat until you obtain the building that will unlock that one card to help you. You realize that far after the refund timer.As a result, the game is padded massively with boring grind. For the comparison's sake, imagine Slay the Spire: but you need to lose 30 runs on purpose to obtain the basic cards you need to win your first run with.It's like the devs realized the game was only 5 hours long, so instead of having some interesting 5 hours, they padded it with a 40 hours long grindfest.It's quite a shame, the idea of the game is great and quite addictive, but I can't recommend it due to that.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: There's no denying that this game is ffffiiiiiine? It's fine, it's well-priced, but you'll pay with your time rather than your wallet, and be left feeling like you wasted most of it. I've no idea why it took off as hard as it did: it's got lovely visuals and a great moody soundtrack, but its entire premise is barely built upon, and instead stretched out into monotony.So you have a lil guy who walks around a pre-built path in a loop and you place objects around in each others' proximity to create enemies and loot and whatnot for them to pick up. It's a good idea for an almost-idle game, but chapter 1 is the same as chapter 4, and the bonuses you get from placing anything other than monster spawners is just negligible.It sounds lovely, the idea of building a landscape in a void out of a hand of cards, improvising as you go, but none of it really does anything, other than increase your health by 1 point, taking you from 2098 to 2099, or giving you 23 health per day instead of 22. The persistent town building is exactly the same, meaning what is meant to be the big reward for your grinding away is instead just kind of mandatory to progress, but wishy washy and minor. So the aesthetic board building aspect is gone, so is the pay-off with the city building, fine, I guess that's not what they were going for. But what about monsters? Gameplay? Well, there aren't very many types, and their numbers just go up the longer you play. Well... loot? Nope, maybe 5 or 6 sets that don't really work well with one another, so you sit there waiting for a full vampirism set or riposte or whatever, basically just playing snap with the game.As I said, chapter 1 = chapter 4: you place things as you get them, concentrate it all on the bendiest section of the loop, and watch it unfold. You can't quite switch off though, or you'll die, so you have to keep swapping out equipment, arbitrarily switching out builds depending on what drops. It's not really satisfying; there's very little strategy, which would work as a minimalistic idle game, but this falls somewhere in between where it just ended up feeling like a lacklustre chore with great ambience. By the end I was running the game in 10x speed and wanting it over just because I'd already sunk a bit of time into it.It's fine, I'm just not sure what it was meant to be, nor why it's been spoken about so much: I finished it and wouldn't recommend it to anyone, because it's not quite easy or simple enough to be a fun throwaway afternoon mobile game, but nor is it any more engaging than your average skinner box.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Unique gameplay style that's part city management, part deck builder, part retro RPG.  Gameplay focuses largely on drawing cards from the deck you've built, and placing tiles on a loop board.  Tile placement is crucial and can mean the difference between life and death for your hero.  It's clear that a lot of thought went into creating this system and balancing the mechanics.  It's a great time-sink, and I look forward to future updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game.It's not going to be the best roguelike you ever play, but it's also going to surprise you with depth at times you won't expect it. While I only got 20 or so hours out of this game, I could certainly see somebody else getting 200 if they really get into it.The price is reasonable, the gameplay has surprising depth, and it's an interesting blend of previous concepts.8/10side note: if you like the universe of Darkest Dungeon, you'll probably find enjoyment out of this universe. They have similarities, but different aesthetics.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: If you would have told me years ago that I would be addicted to a game where I watch a tiny little pixelated friend run in a big circle over and over, I probably wouldn't have believed you.Trying out different strategies with cards/classes/stats has been quite fun, and the game has a 10/10 art style and 500/10 soundtrack. (Seriously worth the separate purchase, I love it so much!)Definitely worth paying full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I think this needs more gameplay polish. I don't feel like my decisions in the game make a huge difference on me making progress, as once you figured out where to place what and what stats are good (which isn't all too hard), it becomes a mechanical gambling grind against the RNG. You're so dendent on getting the right stuff at the right time to the point i feel like i'm playing a gambling machine.The outcomes of battles are very random and usually i fail to survive past loop 4 even with a full HP bar. Most often some monster is getting super lucky on the last squares evading everything. Or a group of monsters drained my HP massively at the start so even a measly goblin stands a chance against my fully tanked out warrior. That makes it hard to judge wether another loop is worth it, as even with a full health bar you might get screwed royally by the RNG and lose 70% of your ressources again.Some of the card description are simply not clear, f. e. i don't have a clue what the crystals really do... Give me double HP from day's passing? And as far as i can tell vampirism is the OP stat to have.Don't get me wrong, it's a well designed game. And i really love the graphics and the story! But those don't calm me down when i see my 10-minutes-run wasted because another unlucky dice roll. A 2/5 game with a 5/5 potential. But for the price it's okay.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: + Nice lore / worldbuilding+ Nice pixel graphics+ Nice music and sound design* Requires some repetitive grinding to progress, which isn't too bad unless you don't expect it.* I think some gameplay elements can only be discovered through accident / blind trial and error (or reading wikis).Recommended, but don't expect to beat it in one sitting. More of a game to play once an evening.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I sure do love a good devolver game, and Loop Hero has that quintessential indie goodness at it's heart. The concept for the game is very engaging - an RPG that plays automatically on a loop and while your character levels up and collects loot, you collect cards which you can use to build structures on and around the track which add enemies, villages, and events.It's a cool idea so it's disappointing that it exhausts itself quickly. The game is intended to be played many times in order to collect resources which you use to build a town in a micro reflection of the main game, placing structures to unlock permanent upgrades, character classes, and special features like resurrections.As you unlock structures you also unlock new cards and you can customise your 'deck' to access different combos and synergies between the structures in-game. Unfortunately there's a very limited number of cards overall and their actual impact is pretty minimal just affecting some monster spawns. There's also only a handful of strategies that will actually result in a winning game and that is still dependent on the luck of equipment drops. Features like the alchemist, power-up crafting, and farms just feel like they exist to ease the grind a bit but it all feels mathematical, not substantive in gameplay.The story is interesting but very short with the game only having 3 levels that are effectively identical beyond some stricter rules and number changes. Most of the game will be spent grinding resources to build your home town up. The environmental card combinations were fun to discover, and some of the structure interactions were fun, but in the end it felt like too little to really support the game long term. I imagine that's why there's only 3 levels.Creative, interesting new ideas being explored, but not very deep.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give this a thumbs down because of how original and charming it is, but unfortunately, this is one of those games where it doesn't matter how good you are, how well you build your deck or how good your placements are. You only win when RNG lets you, and in a game where you can't even control what your character attacks, RNG will very rarely let you win.In a good roguelike, you should be able to win on skill alone. In Hades, you can win even with garbage boons. In Isaac, you can win on a bad run with enough skill. In Slay the Spire, if you play your cards right, you can win. Regardless of how bad those cards may be.In Loop Hero, the *only* way to win is to pray that you get an amazing run with great loot drops and cards OR spend hours grinding materials to upgrade your camp. Once you do that you can *somewhat* offset the terrible RNG, but not entirely. At the end of the day there is no skill involved, and almost none of what you do with your deck matters. Once I realized that all the fun I was having just stopped. It's just not fun to lose over and over again from things entirely out of my control.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This grinding-the videogame.Not a bad game but keep in mind that grinding is very much the core gameplay here. It's autocombat and movement, the thing the player has influence on is the map which you can edit.It also does not play like a standard deckbuilder at all-even though the steam tag says so. I went into this thinking its a card game, it is not. The game presents you a choice of which cards you want to be able to draw during your run. Enemies drop these cards and you use them to place tiles on the map. Tiles are either monster spawns or pieces of envrioment that have some sort of effect on your hero or the surroundings. Your goal is to balance the map so your hero is able to level up, gather resources but not be in risk of dying. Eventually you'll fight a boss. -Grinding might be the core idea of the game but I disliked basic features like exp and level up systems being hidden behind a resource barrier. No reason not to have these things from the get go. Overall the game is a nice timesink but it's just not what I expected. It gets pretty repetitive after a while so it's not really my thing. I still recommend it because I think it can def be enjoyable if you feel like laid back grinding.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Roguelike auto-battler with a focus on resource collection for progression. Challenging until you figure out how the game mechanics / character builds works and then its pretty trivial, with the capability to consistently steamroll bosses. The progression is not really satisfying, and once you finish it there is no endgame. Nonetheless, it is still an interesting and fun game to play through.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's beautiful! Difficult! Feels likes no other game while also feeling retro. I'm so impressed and I only want more.I can't understate how beautiful this game is. The character art when they talk to you are amazing! I found myself screencapping so many of them so I can look at them later since you usually only see them the first time you meet them. Especially the secret characters!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A mix between idle games and tower defence. Two genres I really don't like put together to make something brilliant. This is the perfect game to 'waste' time on. You'll be going round and round and lose track of time very easily. Before you know it an hour has gone by, where does the time go? Well, apparently some ass hat is making it disappear. Good thing your trusty hero plans to put a stop to that.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A rather grindy tower defense-ish game where YOU are the mob and the towers don't shoot you. I'm conflicted on this one, it makes a very good first impression but then gets quite repetitive as you are expected to grind for resources. Great sprite art (when it's not minimalistic), nice music and doesn't demand any real agility, reflexes or quick thinking (fights are always resolved automatically), so you can run a loop or two after work easily.I'd recommend to watch a bit of the gameplay first and then take into account that unlocking new features goes at a very mediocre pace.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Very compelling gameplay loop - combines a few genres in a very simple way, but with enough depth to really carry a player through. The story is somewhat thought provoking, but what you stay for is the gameplay. Very satisfying and makes you want to come back for more, searching for the perfect loop.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not quite sure how to feel about Loop Hero. I enjoyed the art style of it very much and think it's the most beautiful aspect of the game, but the same cannot be said about much else. Before I even got acclimated to the gameplay, the first thing I noticed, and as the more I played, was that the writing and dialogues were just not very good; Characters talk as if they're in a Marvel movie, and the writers were clearly out of their depth when choosing existentialism as one of the underlying themes of their story. The writing is lukewarm, to put it mildly, and since Four Quarters is a studio based in Russia, I'm unsure whether it was the fault of the weak translation or if the writing itself is just that forgettable. Thankfully, the gameplay is somewhat redeemable. I said "somewhat" because, frankly, it can also be boring at times due to its minimalistic approach to combat. In short, there's none. The act of walking and killing monsters is automated and done entirely by the computer, and your responsibility as the player mainly focuses on resource management. Unfortunately, I didn't find this aspect of the gameplay all that fun or engaging either, and I often wished I could do more than stare at my screen while the computer did most of the work for me. Moreover, the game is a lot more grindy than I expected. Trust me, the gameplay won't be that interesting by the time you get to your 100 runs, but that's precisely how much you can expect to do if not more if you want to unlock and upgrade everything. And by the end, much of it feels like a chore, and the game could've benefited greatly had the developer not made it so grindy as if you're playing a mobile game. Overall, I would say Loop Hero is just an average game. One that manages to introduce a novel gameplay structure but overstayed its welcome by the ten-hour mark, whose playtime got padded out by grind, and with a story that left me mostly unimpressed. I have mixed opinions, and it's moments such as these where I wish Steam would provide reviewers with more options than just a binary choice between a simple yes or no. It's for this reason that I'm forced to give Loop Hero a thumbs down, but if bought on sale, I think the purchase can be somewhat justified as a worthwhile experience for casual players. But, personally, it's not my cup of tea, and I feel like I could've gone without playing it and not missed out much.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The game-loop is addictive, and this game is good to play while doing something else. However, at some point (when you reached level 4), the game gets really grindy. I do not mind much normally and like grinding, but Loop Hero becomes boring as not much new is added after that. Nevertheless a clear recommendation for any rogue-lite fans, and good entertainment for many hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly good concept but boring execution. Game gets stale after a few runs. Even when you push through the HUB area (village) and items are just stat grinder randomized pickups which although common in most Roguelikes. in this iteration just make you feel like you have little control over your success and as such decreases your sense of accomplishment when you do succeed
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting game that completely embodies the idea of risk vs reward. Killing enemies gives you gear which is always nice, but it also gives you cards you can use to add extra hazards to the map. Placing extra enemy spawners makes things harder but all those extra enemies mean more chances for upgraded gear. It's a tough thing to balance as greed can quickly outpace preparedness and leave you overrun. Will also run on a potato and feels super nostalgic.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little deck-building idle/macro game. Its actually challenging the further in the story you get and you have actually pay attention to mechanics of both your cards and the enemies to give better synergy with your heroes. 10/10 love this tiny game and there is always fixes/updates and even some new content drops!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game to near-100%, which is more than I can say for much of my library.Other reviews sum up the gameplay better than I could, but the gameplay loop is addictive and the replayability is fantastic. I almost want to start up a new save file-levels of fantastic. I definitely consider myself the type that avoids getting games if they aren't on sale, but I made an exception for Loop Hero and the price was well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite of this year so far! Its combining so much genres that I love with aesthetics from the old SNES days :) Its a mix between Deckbuilder, Auto-Battler, RPG, Roguelite and even has some strategy/building aspects to it. You create your own world and dive loop for loop deeper into it while your character but also the monsters get stronger. Its a simple concept, but its very deep with lots of synergies and theory behind it, everyone should give it a try :) An amazing experience, Devolver released a Masterpiece with this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: I initially liked it, but it got boring real fast. I think it has promise, but the execution seems a bit flawed. I'll stick to the cons since it has such a positive rating. 1) Graphics. I don't mind the pixel art style, but late run, it can be hard to differentiate tiles and find your character on the board.2) Boring. After the initial glut of upgrades, it seems like things slow down a lot. Then you are just repeating runs with the same optimized set of cards over and over. Once you start a run, There's not a lot to do. You place tiles and watch your guy run in a loop fighting. 3) Gear. The gear is not interesting. You can stack certain traits and go for a "build" but that just means you likely will not be upgrading much. And in general, I found myself using the same gear and getting frustrated that I was getting stuff levels above what I was using but not with stats I was looking for. I feel like there needs to be some tweaking there.4) Classes. They are all pretty boring. I found my self using the fighter just because it's easier to get usable gear for him, it doesn't rely so much on stacking a particular stat. The necromancer in particular means slow fights and usually struggles to find gear that won't gimp your build.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: A charming wonderful game with an interesting gameplay, though an idle rpg there's a lot of things you need to take into consideration when building up your character during the loops. A lot of care went into this game, and you can see it from every pixel to the well done music. Its a very nice game to play a loop or two.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: So immensely sloppy.  There is no balance, synergy between the cards is nonexistant, or at most surface level synergies owing to the inherent traits of the card and not any smart design.  The biggest issue that completely ruins the game is how awful of a system they created to 'scale' your equipment.  For classes like necromancer, He has multiple stats that physically don't scale with level, which means the majority of the time you will be using a piece of gear level 4 or below well into levels 11 and beyond because of how awful the stat system is.  The majority of cards are strictly negative and give nothing from choosing them, and there are some you strictly cannot live with using, especially on the later worlds where 'traits' break any semblance of balance between enemies, as some enemies are simply irrefutably more dangerous than others.  Scaling of the base camp is inconsistent, with some upgrades being useful and cheap, while useless ones are exorbitantly expensive requiring substantial grind to achieve.  The game has a great concept that was executed horribly, the best part about this game is the store page.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Why can't I stop playing??!This game is absolutely brilliant and like nothing I've ever played. It evokes old school RPG nostalgia with it's pixelated art and music but in the most unexpected format/medium: a deck building auto-resolve RPG (how is that even a thing??!). Finishing each loop just feels so satisfying and the game keeps surprising me with all the added layers/complexities as I unlock more stuff in the village after each run. Seriously blown away and haven't been addicted to a game like this since I was a teen and discovered Heroes of Might & Magic III

_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: If you like playing as a dungeon master in D&D, resource management, and humor in games, this game is for you. There's a bit of a learning curve, which I like, and I'm looking forward to more content and updates. I think once new content is added, the semi-tedious, grindy nature of certain aspects of the game will probably still be grindy (that's kinda hard to avoid outright, I guess), but likely less tedious. So far I've had a lot of fun exploring this game, and I'd give it a solid 8/10 at launch.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: When the game is observed the first time, it appears to be slightly daunting and complicated. But when getting a closer look and playing around with it, it opens up and the main idea of placing items on the map and their effects are easily grasped. It is quite fun to try to figure out the synergies between the cards and the skills, and the game is not too complicated, but not too easy either.Nonetheless, some of the descriptions and skills make no sense to me as someone who often plays games with stats and numbers. For example, even after 40 hours I still have no idea what are the differences between "summon quality" and "summon level". Additionally, some of the talent descriptions are extremely vague, and there is no way to tell what is the best pick without sometimes hours of trial and error, which for me personally has been frustrating.When we are talking about these small indie games, I often ask myself whether a game has enough depth to be worth to put the time in. This one definitely does, but eventually the game turns into a heavy grind. Retreating from expedition is encouraged because death is heavily penalized - dying to a boss ends up being potentially up to one hour of wasted time. This could discourage people who dislike this sort of gameplay, but it ends up also feeling rewarding to finally figure out what set of cards beats that chapter you have been stuck on.TLDR; game is good, addictive but also extensively repetitive, as roguelikes often are.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: This game resembles life in prison. During the day, you walk endless rounds on the yard, brawling with fellow inmates. During the night, you dream about building a new, better world.Edit - recommendation changed to negative after finding the game is riddled with serious bugs that will be probably never corrected. Also, game is very obviously unfinished, and proper endgame content is replaced with a grind barrier.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Hello, other fans of roguelikes. I come to you today as a Binding of Isaac and RoR2 vet with bad news; this game is not very engaging. I had high hopes coming into the game, and for the first three hours or so considered it to be one of my instant favorites, but now that I've beat the Lich for the first time, I'm not so sure.For those of you who haven't gathered it yet, this is an idle game. There is no skill in playing this game, but there is a lot of "choice." Choices you can make include your equipment, how you play cards to gather resources, and other things that might be spoilers... But. This game does not incentivize making those choices.There is a lot of freedom to roam around in this game, to experiment and whatnot, but this element is incredibly shallow, as trying for a build rarely increases your likelihood of winning. Essentially what I'm saying is... This game is mindless. When I say it's an idle game, I mean it. Having beat the first boss after 8 hours I can say I've failed multiple times, and finally got the bright idea to say 'hey, why don't I just place my tiles as fast as possible, and equip the highest rarity of highest level items and see if I win or not?'Low and behold I did. I am quite disappointed that I did, as I quickly came to realize that this game can be played on autopilot, and incentivizes doing so. Pick the flashy tools with big numbers, don't go for a build, don't farm resources, just play as fast as possible with the strongest tools. That's the intended way.Something like a Binding of Isaac and Risk of Rain 2 teaches the player to work with what little they have and incentivizes skilled gameplay, rewarding it with god tier runs. Every run of this game is a god tier run, but not in a fun way. Your character won't begin to struggle unless you've dragged your run out, or you've decided to go with anything other than high damage and defense, but don't worry, your choices don't matter, as nearly every enemy drops you one, two, maybe three new items every kill, items that are almost always better than the ones you have. Think Binding of Isaac, but after every kill you got a 1% boost to every stat you wanted. It's not fun when the skill and thinking is completely diluted by an over abundance of good items. Think Borderlands, but your character played for you. Its almost exactly like that, now that I think about it. Borderlands, but you sit and watch your character run around a loop killing every enemy with ease, rewarding itself every time with a bigger and better gun. It's not engaging, there's no skill, and there's literally no gameplay outside of placing tiles and equipping weapons.TLDR; This game is fun, but ultimately mindless, and incentivizes unskilled gameplay and can pretty much be played with little thinking or interaction. Think Borderlands, but instead of Borderlands, you watch somebody else play Borderlands and occasionally give them weapons and upgrades.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: The game is extremely shallow in strategy and requires high amounts of grinding to progress. The choices when building your deck are few and mostly obvious or irrelevant, and tile placement has very little impact other than to avoid doing stupid things like dumping all the enemies together. You can also pick which gear to equip but you will end up just equipping the highest level stuff and maybe looking to maximize one stat. Gear drop is totally RNG so it can easily make or break a run, often being the biggest factor. Every run is exactly the same so it gets old very fast. To change things up you could try with different cards, but there's not much point given that the interactions between cards are few and obvious, and different enemies don't drop different loot or have any meaningful impact.In every run you get resources to upgrade your base for marginal buffs. If you die in a run you lose 70% of what you had gathered, but you can retire at any point an keep everything. This sounds cool but given the huge difficulty hike between the normal enemies and the boss, it usually means that you leave just before the boss, which to me is disappointing. I would prefer at least getting to fight the boss every time to reduce repetition and also gauge my power.  This said, I could defeat the first two bosses in a few hours with more or less the starting resources and classes but then the grind becomes necessary. The starting portion of a run is very slow and boring so I couldn't bring myself to keep playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I too can only recommend Loop Hero to any friend of fresh and interesting game design.It has very minimalistic retro-styled visuals, with an unique gamedesign revolving around not actively playing the hero but watching him run in circles in an (initialy) empty world.You are filling this world by setting landscape tiles which you draw randomly from a Card-Deck you prepared before the match. Some of those tiles will passively affect the heroes (or monsters) stats while others decide which monsters spawn or which special effects are active near them.The most interesting part of the game for me in the beginning was figuring things out. Slowly gaining new tile cards to use and finding hidden combinations which "morph" those landscapes if you place them in a certain way. Even hours into the game I still stumbled upon some hidden interaction, giving me new variants to create the world with.Sadly, except for a few exclusions, many of those secrets are simple "tile A will change to tile B if placed next to tile C"-situations. I was secretly hoping in the beginning that there would be more complex tile interaction, possibly hidden in the lore entries of the game, which trigger if you build the world in a certain way ... so I feel that there is some wasted potential here.You also have a random loot drop system, where you have to decide which of the equipment with randomly generated stats the hero should wear. From my experience there are quite a few approaches to focus on different stats in combination with different landscape decks.As others stated before: Both Landscape Cards as well as loot drops are random, so you have to be fine with a very random game environment (Confined in the constraints of the Deck you built and the class you decided to play). I for one think that such an environment makes Card Games interesting though, so you wont hear me complain. ;)The game has increasing difficulties with unique bosses waiting at the end of each. And while you will want a big deck with many tile cards to find out those secret landscape interactions during the early difficulties/bosses, you will most certainly start to develop a strategy with a minimal card deck for the challenging final bosses.All is connected by a city you build between those matches with the ressources you gathered, adding new cards to your repertoire or giving other permanent bonuses for future runs.The story is also quite noteworthy as I believe that it is well executed. The dialogues are worthwhile, while being quite funny once in a while, and the game world has some interesting unique ideas, which is further deepened by well written lore entries which you can unlock in the cities lore library.So to summarize: Nice little pearl of a game which you should definitly play if you look for interesting games with unique game design choices. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a half idle/half time management with pseudo rogue-lite and deck building elements.+ First hour of the game is intriguing.+ A nice try to combine genres to develop an original concept.+ Even somewhat short and revolves around a single idea, story is good.~ Pixel art style has its charm (nothing superb and looks somewhat mediocre)~ Combined genre mechanics works well but half-baked- Repetitive, bleak, grind-fest  gameplay.- Not enough variety to keep you invested.- Bleak, repetitive soundtrack and sfx. _childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is a game about playing your heros memories, not the hero.It therefor acts as a strategy game with light RPG mechanics.You use cards that give you a tile to place on the map. Every tile has effects like spawning monsters or increasing health.Combining tiles can form new unique tiles that cause new effects, like palcing 9 rocks in a square formation forming a mountain that spawns harpies.You are equally playing against and for your hero, as your sole task is to balance out the threat on the map caused by monsters and the support from other beneficial tiles to increase your heros strength.In short, you are defining the framework around your heros expedition but you arent playing the expedition yourself.Loop Hero is basically the Dungeon Master Role of a Pen and Paper RPG, while the hero is played by an automated system.When you return to camp, you can expand it to increase your options for new tiles and other supportive items.Visually it provides a really nice pixelated look that feels superb.You have the option to tweak the menu fonts and you get a CCTV filter to turn on or off.Thats basically it regarding visual options/graphical settings.What stands out is probably the music. Its insanely good chiptune. In this industry you have games with good music and games with ok music but once in a while there is a game that has this one epic soundtrack that just has you instantly getting goosebumps.Loop Hero is that game.Rarely i recommend to buy a soundtrack but here i do.Content:You are unlocking new classes at the camp that come with their own boni and advantages.There are i think three chapters with bossfights and i have seen at least 2 dozen cards to use.So i would say there is content for easily 10 hours but i have seen people playing the limited demo for much much longer.For the price asked its an insanely good title and absolute recommendation.The quality regarding gamedesign, presentation and accompaniment of music make this a no brainer.There are games coming once in a while that end up being highly regarded top tier class games that make their name in the industry for being instant classics.Shovelknight was one such game, or Celeste.Loop Hero is another.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is one of those games I picked up after some persistent word of mouth from both the gaming press and some of my friends. I was therefore not surprised to find out that it is indeed a pretty good game. No, what surprised me was how invested in it I actually became over time, to the point that this little pixel artsy world started occupying my thoughts even when I wasn't playing it, and I started actively looking forward to future sessions.The best way to describe Loop Hero is that it puts you in the role of the Dungeon Master of a pen and paper RPG campaign, and you get to influence all of the elements surrounding your party of one, aside from their direct actions. The main character is placed onto a board consisting of a main road that loops onto itself, a base camp that restores some health at the start of every loop, and a black void that shall serve as your canvas to influence the success of the expedition. You cannot control your character directly, as he walks and fights on his own, but that's where Loop Hero's whole schtick comes into play. As your character battles the foes in his path, you'll acquire cards that can be placed on the board and gear that you can equip. The cards allow you to generate new encounters for your character, giving you access to better gear, materials and cards, but also to trigger beneficial effects such as increasing their health or setting traps for enemies. Some cards can even form combinations that lead to new board tiles with unique effects. I'm being serious when I say that this mechanic is absolutely brilliant and was probably the main reason that kept me coming back for more, as there is a lot of room to experiment based on your character's class and the goal of your current expedition.When you finish an expedition, through either victory or death, you'll return to your village, a safe haven populated by some colorful townsfolk, their numbers growing as you build new structures and homes, which in turn give you benefits on your expeditions, such as better health regeneration when passing the campfire, or even archers on tiles surrounding your starting point. This creates a very engaging gameplay loop where you grow both through sheer numerical increases, but also your own understanding of the game's mechanics, and it feels very rewarding.Beyond its great gameplay experience, Loop Hero offers a somewhat unique pixel art style deliberately emulating the 8-bit era, with its limited color palettes and black void backgrounds which, when combined with its great character designs, makes the game a treat for the eyes. The soundtrack is pretty neat as well, tho I'll fully admit to eventually muting it to replace it with a podcast when grinding for some of the last achievements. The writing isn't half bad and sets up an intriguing enough plot that'll keep pushing until the end to find out the truth about these characters and the dying world they find themselves in.Loop Hero is a great game that's well worth your time, as it sets itself apart from most titles on the market with its unique approach of allowing you to control everything except for the main character, while still making you feel in complete control of your runs. Buy it, play it, and beat it; you owe it to yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Read this review and others Loop Hero is a Roguelike, but also a Dungeon Crawler built from scratch by the player himself, with aspects of an Idle and Deckbuilding title, which has a graphical look reminiscent of titles from the old NES.The player plays the role of a Knight who embarked on the adventure of discovering what happened to the place where he once lived. Everything around him is under a dark film, filled with a haze of vague memories of small notes of what once existed and now does not. Behind this cataclysm is a figure full of bones, embraced by a magical mantle and unimaginable powers that decided to erase every corner of the vast universe.The protagonist aims to clear the bare paths of a road full of nothing, randomly generated and presented in a circular shape that makes it possible to complete a full circle of the map.. The player aims to add elements to the map, in a kind of "tower defense" on the contrary, where the cards played are distributed among small portions of land that help in a way to complete the Loop, or portions of the map that contain enemies. Each pass through a location can generate resource capture and encounters against enemies generate resource capture as well as equipment used in combat itself.But what is the purpose of this Loop? The truth is that there is really much more to it than just a simple Loop.Each Loop starts in a  little campfire and with each successful loop there is the possibility of returning to the main camp with all the resources, so far, collected. If you want, for some reason, to escape halfway, you will only take 60% of the collected resources. Whereas if the Hero loses all his life bar, he only takes 30% of the collected resources.With each new placement of the different cards on the map, there is an increase in the Boss Spawn bar of the chapter in question. It is therefore necessary to pay attention and adjust the use of cards with what is happening on the game board. This bar is present in the upper left corner side by side with the time of day bar. However, only with the confrontation and consequent destruction of the Boss is it possible to advance to a new chapter.Adventure progression equates to capturing new resources, new enemies, and new encounters against Chapter Ending Bosses. The resources are used in the construction of new areas, or the possibility of upgrading existing areas in the camp used between each new "Run". This upgrade mechanic generates new variables for the Loop itself. For example with the construction of the "Herbalist" there is access to passive skills, such as potions, used automatically and when necessary, during the adventure. Or more active skills, such as new cards for the player's deck, or access to new player classes, in the construction of new buildings.Each class has different equipment and mechanics, which directly equates to a different approach to enemy encounters and a learning path that is mostly based on trial and error. However, for the most part, I only used the highest level material and didn't get too attached to the skills attached to them. This is not to say that the abilities of each piece of equipment are not important, because they really are. I found the Necromancer Class particularly interesting and reborn my battalion of "undeads" to fight all the adversities created by me.The complexity of the gameplay itself is truly remarkable. It takes some time to fully understand the combinations that each card can make, to proceed with the construction of the perfect road or corner. This work is done in the creation of the "deck" and applied to the game board, according to each player's style of play.The use of the Nintendo Switch controller is fluid but it is natural to find some frustration due to the need to use too many buttons to select the different options. The simplest is to use the console's touch screen. Still, everything looks a little small to be clicked or dragged across the monitor.Everything about this title fits like a glove. From its simple but very appealing graphic style, through the soundtracks that change its beat depending on the situation you're in, to its addictive game style. With each new Loop, with each new card, there was only one song in his head... Should I Stay or Should I Go.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting idea poorly implemented (maybe pick up deeply discounted, or after A LOT of patches);- Massive lack of basic "quality of life" features.- Information on what basic systems do, what icons mean, and what some things even are/ do is not available in game.10+ hours in, I still have no idea what some of the icons mean, what the point of a couple of systems are, etc.- Trying to keep track of the information that is available is hampered by frustrating design choices (UI rearranges itself)- Has a fast-forward feature which is nice, but is more a patch over the player only needing to be there for 10% of the game. _childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is going to end up as my GOTY for 2021- its an extremely compelling rogue-(like/lite) that feels nostalgic and modern at the same time. The inter-relationships and synergies between the various tiles make planning a run very interesting and strategic. The soundtrack is so good that you'd think the game was developed by Supergiant and the boss music alone is worth the price of admission. There is a bit of a lull in the early mid game but if you can get passed that it's good for at least 40-50+ hours. Definitely recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop Hero

_childDocuments_.review: Loop Hero is simple to play. It's also pretty unique, at least to me. I've not played any games like it. Game play is watching the hero loop around a randomly generated track fighting what ever monsters you place down. If you place too many the hero gets overwhelmed and can't clear the loop efficiently, eventually leading to death. If you don't place enough, the hero falls behind in gear and XP, as mobs level up with each loop the hero completes, eventually leading to death. The challenge is deciding which tiles to include in your deck, what and how much to place down, and what gear to equip on the hero. When the hero dies, resources are taken back to the camp which you build up for various bonuses in future runs. The game has many secrets, especially with the tile placements. Certain tiles when placed near each other create combos. I highly recommend discovering these things for yourself rather than looking at a guide. It's pretty rewarding to discover the combos on your own.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of game you wish was in early access, because after playing for about 5 hours you realize a few things:a. The balance is pretty off. There are dominant strategies (which is okay), but they are easy to adhere to, and there isn't punishment for always going for the same thing (with the exception of resources, some decks are better at getting wood, for example). This also plays out in tile placement, which is easy to optimize after just a few games.b. The class gameplay is too similar. I was hoping the rogue would feel different or open new strategies, but the gameplay was fundamentally the same.c. The permanent effects detract. Many are weak or pointless; they are easily outshadowed by other options. Mostly they act as a gate for beating subsequent bosses, just adding more hours to a game that already requires a decent bit of grinding.All this to say, I had a lot of fun for the first 3 hours, and then after grinding for a bit and seeing it wasn't worth it, I tried to refund with no avail. Fair enough, I did enjoy the game for a while and I do want to encourage this style of game development. I think that another developer may come along and improve on this model. This is why I wish that it was still in early access, so that it could be improved in its current iteration. Loop Hero II might just be the best game I can't wait to play.

Try and keep your hero alive while helping him gear grind for the level's boss (if you don't retreat back to camp) I like to watch anime and play it, since it plays itself mostly. _childDocuments_.review: Before i begin its important that this is made clear: Loop Hero is very much genetically identifiable with Incremental Games and Idle Games, however it does not stick to the gameplay loops of mobile games or casual focused games. You can't permanently lose in Loop Hero but you can lose a run and have to start over, yet even then you get to keep 30% of what you gained in a run and if you retreat before you die this is at 60%. In that way its close to rougelites with space available for experimentation because the loss condition is bearable. But because you only really use a very small and confined pool of cards and items its entirely focused down to optimization be it your tile synergies or your item stats.I beat this game at 46 hours and i dont feel like all of those 46 hours were solid fun, but the ratio was pretty high because i enjoy optimizing stats or discovering and experimenting. And the game ini file does have a variable in plain text to change game speed though setting it to high causes the game to break, so if you feel the game is to slow to reach conclusion you can increase speed that way.The price also is pretty alright as long as you are aware of the general gameloop beforehand and know what to expect. It wont change much but just get harder.I would say this game is lacking a little in variety with the cards, classes, enemies and later the perks. Its important that its this way so you can reliably repeat a strategy and try to improve on it like in slay the spire but since you can decide on your cards before you start a run (and therefore on your enemies) i do feel like it came just a tad short there.But honestly i dont think i can find many major issues with this game and can recommend it

_childDocuments_.review: The world is gone, rendered to dust. The entire universe was wiped from existence by an unknown force. Nothing is left,... nothing but a man. A single man clings to his reality by will alone. With the little remaining memory he has left, he can bring fragments of his world back to life, little by little rebuilding it. Will he gain the resources he needs to grow his whole universe from the seeds of his own mind? Will he find and defeat the shadowy creature that stole all of reality from him? Or, is he destined to fight in an endless loop for the rest of eternity in the small whisp of the world he left behind?Loop Hero, a deck building roguelike with idle elements, is about a man fighting to regain the world he lost by rebuilding it piece by piece and surviving by the tip of his sword. Place tiles to make his journey more fruitful, but beware the consequences. Every boon has a bane, and the greatest resources can end his quest in death.Your quest is to build a thriving town out of the void with the resources you find fighting in the loop. Placing tiles on that loop might gain you health, better gear, or a valued resource, but it could also unleash ancient monsters.You can choose the tile you are able to place before starting out on your adventure, and you get them at random when you defeat monsters. There is a limit to the amount of tiles, or cards, you can choose from before each adventure, and you get a wider selection as you progress through the game.Stopping by a village will gain you some health back, and a new quest to defeat a boss. A boss is essentially a very beefy monster, far stronger than others of its kind. Returning to that village gains you a nice piece of gear. Adding fields to that village boosts the amount of health you will receive from it, but also risks spawning scarecrows. Too many villages and they'll spawn rogues who try and steal your best gear.Most of the game is centered around a track. Your character travels this track, and fights anything that gets in his way. The player has no control of his fighting but can equip him with the best gear, which is Diablo-ish randomized loot. You can find anything from a sword that hits every enemy at once, to a vampiric shield that sucks the life out of your victims. Progression unlocks character types like a thief or a skeleton-raising necromancer as well. Experience will also gain you traits like having a wolf companion, or the ability to stash half your loot every time you pass camp so you don't lose as much if you die.Never think you're safe. The stronger you get the closer you are to death. As you gain power, so does the hoard. A couple of wolves or spiders sound easy enough, but make one of them a quest-boss, and add a flesh golem, and you could be in your last battle.The graphics are in true Devolver fashion, an old-school pixelated piece of art that when coupled with the music that sounds like something out of an old RPG like Ultima feels very nostalgic for a retro gamer like myself.I've found this game quite enjoyable, and certainly able to spend countless hours in. For those of us with less than stellar patience, you can speed up time. Different types of warrior are unlocked as you progress, as well as new tiles you can place. The price of $14.99 is well worth it, as it's a game you may never tire of. I highly recommend it, as I've played it over and over. It never seems to get old because your strategy is constantly changing.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very fun game and it's got a genuinely unique concept, something you don't see often in games just because it's very difficult to do. Writing is decent, although sparse and I wish there were a lot more lines to flesh out the world a bit.  I also noticed some slight editing oversights with the writing.  It also can be difficult to make a build do what you want, since you basically have to upgrade whenever a new piece of gear that is good enough comes along.  I really hope they add content in the future.  Placing cards is fun and strategic although I do find myself following similar patterns that seem to work well again and again. On the downside, gameplay can become somewhat repetitive over time, but that is kind of the nature of the format they've created here.  Overall a good fun game that I am glad I bought.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Props for accessibility options. Art style is good JRPG-derived pixel fun.The rest: I don't really get what's unique or special about this game to merit the glowing reviews. It's okay, but I would rather have my money back than have it in my library, where I'll never touch it again. It's a tower defense game, but with one moving tower (player character) and stationary enemies you place. I always found Dungeon Keeper a little aesthetically aggro, but it was certainly a superior game experience to this non-interactive grind. I guess that's harsh, but so is paying money for what feels like the "premium version" of a free flash game on Kongregate.It has some little differences between sessions because of the mildly random nature of the card system used to build up the "loop," aka dungeon, but the game as a whole is completely linear. The choices you make don't end up mattering at all: for example, the order in which you construct buildings has no lasting effect because there isn't enough class specialization for it to matter, and you are forced to construct buildings in a specific order to advance up the tree. Because the branches of the tree frequently intersect, you can't go very long without having to go back and build the missing buildings.The expedition gameplay isn't interesting to me. Others may group this under the "relaxing" category, I guess, but to me, it's just repetitive. You do an expedition to collect resources. If you luck out and collect the right resources (your control over this is limited), you can upgrade your camp. You repeat that loop. You know, like from the name! You can only go up to 2x speed, so I found myself just sitting there, waiting for fights to be over to see if I needed to do anything. Often, I didn't. Unless you get a couple pieces of high-level equipment in a row that buff the same stat, the equipment choices really don't matter in the aggregate. Some stats are just mathematically superior to others. Once you feel out how to judge, say, regeneration vs. evasion, then all choices involving equipment with those stats become sort of rote. In one run, I got my attack speed very, very high. It felt like maxing out DPS in an MMO, a genre I have no interest in. I tried forcing different strategies, but the game doesn't actually feel any different. You get stronger and gain buffs, many of them being small stat increases for each loop you complete. If you take one of the strong ones early on, you will breeze through the mid-game.Enemies get stronger and drop better equipment as you do more loops. Getting toward the end of a run, you gauge whether you are tough enough to fight the boss. No? Save your stuff, go back to camp, upgrade if possible. Okay, do that whole thing again. And again. Again. Again. Hey, you can upgrade a thing at your camp/unlock a new building! Again. Again. Again. The new card that came with your new building hasn't really changed your strategy. Just replace it with the thing you were doing before that earned more resources. Repeat. It's a hard pass from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop hero is an excellent example of modern day Roguelikes that are fantastically designed but outstay their welcome extremely easily. The presentation is fantastic, the game mechanics are solid (although a bit barebones), the story is extremely gripping at first, and the game puts a ton of effort into giving its world some character. And I can't overstate just how well made those parts of the game are, when you meet a new enemy they get their own dialogue box sprite and they will talk to you about how they perceive the broken world that you the hero are trying to repair. The deck building aspect can be a ton of fun and you can mix and match cards that you maybe would never have thought of. It can be very addicting to do a run and reset. Those are just some of the many examples of the great potential this game has.So what makes this game drag on if so many things are so good? Currently I have 10,2 hours into the game according to steam. In about 2 hours you will see most of the important and interesting mechanics the game has to offer, after that it uses the same horrible system that a lot of modern roguelikes employ where you have a base that you upgrade, and upgrading that base makes you more powerful. However in loop heroes case this becomes even more important because you barely have any control over the game. If you want to avoid RNG your options are to grind a ton or to abuse certain builds to make it through the harder levels.So how difficult is this game? Up until what I assume is the final level, I haven't had much trouble at all. But the final level is what made me give up on this game. Its exactly everything I hated about the game combined. This is technically also a deck builder, but your freedom in creating a deck feels like it doesn't exist. The final level is so hard that its hard to win even with using really strong strategies, if you haven't been grinding a bunch like me then your base also isn't strong enough to make use of a lot of these strategies. So not only am I not playing the game the way I want to play it, I also have to pray that it all ends up working out. It completely drains any and all fun that I had with this game and feels overly punishing as a result.It sucks because I wanted to experience the ending of the story myself. It starts off pretty strong and while it does start getting pretty monotonous, it still is pretty unique and fun. I wanted my time in this game to matter more. But I am not willing to put in another 10 + hours just to see that ending, this game does not have enough depth for that to be the case.I give Loop hero a very disappointed negative review. I think there is a lot to love here, but to me it absolutely wasn't enough to keep me going until the end. I would rather have spent my time playing something else.

name: Autopsy Simulator
detailed_description: In Autopsy Simulator: Dead Memories, you play a middle-aged pathologist whose life has taken a turn for the worse. After a career downfall and the loss of your beloved wife, you live each day shattered and exhausted. One day during a routine post-mortem, you find a relic of your past hidden inside a body. Now, it feels like something just won’t let go… FEATURES Examine the bodies and study the files to get all the answers Every case has its own story and each victim has their secrets. Uncover them to solve the puzzles and learn the truth about your subjects... and yourself. Cases prepared and analyzed by specialists Each case is designed with the help of real life pathomorphologists and forensic doctors, ensuring the feel of being involved in an authentic autopsy process. Down to even the most gruesome details. Detailed depiction of organs and autopsy cases In-game bodies, organs and injuries are crafted with unprecedented attention to detail. While this makes it easy to create immersion, it's also not for the faint hearted. A unique mix of simulation and horror A combination of engrossing gameplay mechanics and spine-chilling moments will keep you on your toes throughout all of the story's chapters.

_childDocuments_.review: In the process of refunding this now. For anyone looking for a simulator in which you are a coroner or mortician and dissecting bodies, this isn't it. This is just an even more hand holdy version of mortuary assistant with a worse story, worse voice acting and no components of a simulator at all. As someone who absolutely enjoys immersive life/job sims, this is false advertisement and honestly it truly upsets me because this game was on my wishlist for years and to see what it is on release is a massive disappointment. My gripe isn't with price, or even the content. I'm sure if it was labeled as a horror game visual novel, SOMEONE would have enjoyed it. But labeling this as a simulator is just false advertisement and misrepresenting itself.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to say - I've been excited for this game for months and followed a majority of the updates and releases. That being said, I have to give this game a pass. I beat it in one sitting, and I was let down. I'll start with the positives, first.-Medical Accuracy I love forensic science, it's been a special interest of mine since I was a teen and it was very cool to see an accurate medical autopsy. Obviously it's a game so not everything is super accurate, but the devil is in the details and I enjoyed that. -AtmosphereThe game does a pretty good job of making itself creepy - though with the subject matter, I feel that 's a given. However, there are parts that just...don't make sense and are there for the sake of being creepy. Like the bathroom, what's up with that? Why is it so dingy and broken, why is there a shack outside? Why did we put a saw in the basement after "cleaning" it when that would be a massive hazard? We gotta move the story along, I know, but it breaks some of the immersion. Dunno, maybe I'm too picky. That's where the positives end. -GameplayMaybe it's on me, but I didn't like how hand-holdy this game was. I assumed we would learn everything we needed in the tutorial (which I did like how it was structured) and then we would perform autopsies on our own to uncover the story based on how thorough and accurate we were (with help tips, if necessary). Instead, this is a hand-hold simulator for each autopsy and you cannot do anything that deviates from what the game wants. This was a massive let down. I understand that not everyone has in depth medical knowledge, but allowing players to make mistakes or give guidance when asked would be better. I've seen what other people say, and it feels like it falls just shy of being a true simulation game. -StoryI can't say much because I don't want to give spoilers, but I'll say this.I hated the story. I completely understand that this is narrative driven, but the story is so weak that the gameplay can't back it up. It's cliche, uninvolved and I honestly could not care less about our protagonist, if you could even call him that. If more time had been put into how we engage with our surroundings, I'm sure it could be really cool. There's also an entire plot point that seems to be missing (or I didn't find it) that involves two bodies we autopsy involving a bite mark, but I guess Jack is too busy trying to not go insane, or I'm connecting dots that aren't anywhere related. -UnfinishedThis game was delayed several times and honestly, I wish it was delayed further. The end of the game, it's very clear where corners were cut to avoid animating certain things and the final conflict resolves and does nothing for the story, which also gets largely revealed in the same instances as the conclusion. There's a secret ending that I'm not entirely sure how to get, but the other thing is, I kind of don't care about getting it.I'm not sure if there was a bug, but I sat there for about 3 minutes straight just downing pills and nothing happened. Not sure if that's intentional but I feel like something should happen if I just horf down the entire bottle.  Overall, I'm pretty disappointed in the game. If you enjoy medical stuff, you'll like it for that. Maybe they can update it in the future and clean up some loose ends.
_childDocuments_.name: Autopsy Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Summary: A very intelligent, but buggy and boring slog through a 4-hour long tutorial with what could have been an interesting story and concept.Pros:* Game looks great. A few graphical bugs here and there when I was speeding through a 2nd time (more on that later)* Impressive in terms of research, topical knowledge, and information. I'll be honest, I learned stuff from this experience....but that's about itCons:* Let's get the big one out of the way first: this is barely a game. When "simulator" is tagged on a title, you expect a lot of freedom in playing that role, but you will not get that here. Even though it's labeled as "horror", the scares are cheap and minimal. This is a "psychological trauma interactive narrative". Don't expect much more than that.* Confused scares. While few in number, the scares in here feel like they don't really know what they want to be. They come with the cliche stinger sound and blurry vision, but aren't jump scares? Imagine someone yelling "Boo!" while slowly walking around a corner. I don't know how else to explain it, but they just didn't work for me.* Far too "hand-holdy". I felt like I never left the tutorial phase. You are always presented with a single action you can perform, and that's about it. It would have been nice to have 1 or 2 "tutorial" bodies, then given the player a chance to figure out what to do next. It even teaches you some cool mechanics and scientific studies, just to never see it happen again. The only choice I got was taking pills too early and it soft-locked me. * Buggy (NOT broken). There were more than a few instances where I was soft-locked: got stuck, couldn't perform the "next step", etc. There are also some features that don't appear to be working consistently, one example being the "secret ending" being broken for a lot of people (me included).* Weak story. Pretty cliche, "person deals with trauma of a lost loved one with drugs and alcohol" trope. There's a buildup to the mystery of what happened, but the conclusion falls extremely flat.* Wasted potential. Look, some of the "cases" presented are genuinely interesting. There was a single moment were I had a revelation of cases being linked and it felt genuinely great. But there was no way to even acknowledge that in game. Like most things, it fell to the wayside and was gone in an instant. I know you're the pathologist, not the police...but it felt like nothing existed outside those four walls.* Annoying main character. Talks WAY too much. Self-narration isn't a bad thing, but jeezus christ this pole-vaults over the line of obnoxious. Speaking of...* I've heard worse, but the voice acting in this is rough, at best. I can't really blame the directing, because some va's are genuinely believable. But again, the main character (which is ALWAYS talking) over-acts way too hard at times and comes off like a really bad anime dub.Like others, I let myself get too excited for this, hoping for something closer to The Mortuary Assistant. IT IS NOT THE DEV TEAMS FAULT THAT I EXPECTED IT TO BE SOMETHING IT WAS NOT. They have stated that they are working on a "Autopsy Only" mode that I feel will be more what people were hoping to get for the $25 price tag. But for many, it'll probably be too little too late.

_childDocuments_.review: Autopsy Only Mode is now in an alpha stage and it is a bigger joke than I thought, it is literally just tutorials with no freedom to choose. A total scam.Woodland Games has abandoned the game, not surprising as they have a record of doing that. The new developers taking over have announced there will only be 3 bodies in Autopsy Only Mode, with 8 causes of death each. Bringing in new developers and they are not even going to perform less than what we were expecting for AOM, don't even bother making it. Not only was criticism not listened to, they literally don't care. Avoid this game at all costs, don't buy, don't view, don't pirate, let it die.Original reviewI'm going to post probably the longest, most in depth review I have ever posted. Autopsy Simulator contains neither simulation and barely any autopsies. In development for nearly 5 years with a 2 year delay I am still scratching the epidermis off my scalpel wondering how anyone on the development team managed to not realize how far off the rails this went. It's barely a game, contains a recycled story to every morgue related setting ever, and dialog. Oh my Lord does it have dialog. The character has so much dialog that the game actually will overlap itself while examining something making you miss up to 10% of the lines spoken. Let's break this down, let's actually tell the development team where to go and then let's see if anything is done. Autopsy Simulator is composed two things. Doing an autopsy, and maintaining your character's mental state with fetch quests. The best parts of the game are when you're examining an organ and finding clues. The worst parts, is literally everything else. Listening to your character groan and sigh constantly to having to fetch everything with boring horror elements while uncovering a back story about your character's trauma. Unlike real life, the best time is in the morgue. Look morgues and horror go hand in hand an it never gets old, but this is the first time where it has been so far off the mark that it makes you wonder why this thing was even made. Morgues and funeral homes are generally where people experience some of the most negative memories they will ever have in their life, so that is naturally scary. What's not scary is making it boring. With almost no interaction at all and the entire game is a tutorial giving you no freedom at all, it just makes you beg to hurry up. There are only 6 bodies, broken down from Prologue to Chapter 5. It's not until chapter 3 that we actually get our first interesting case, and I will now quote John Carpenter. "Death by natural causes, I hate natural causes! Give me a big old stab wound to poke around in, then I'm happy. Ahhh, here we are, body bags! See if it's murder suicide or a nasty accident, they put 'em in these bags." Yes folks chapter 3 gets interesting fast. Each body after 3 heavily progresses in the decay and mutilation that it's in creating a sense of deep investigation and wonder of what happened. It's actually the last 3 corpses that are the most interesting, and they are sadly dampened down by the non stop droning of the character and trauma elements. It's not until we get to the last body that I was full blown horrified. The condition of the last body is so grotesque and the horror only increases the more you find out about it. This is easily the best body of the game, and you don't even get to begin to start it before the game just abruptly ends. I don't mind anti-climax endings, but everyone hates endings with no explanation. To make it worse, there is supposedly a second secret ending with no way to unlock it and the people who have figured it out, the ending doesn't unlock for most making it a bugged ending. Making the player get to sign their own name on paper was a nice touch but a lot is missing. A corpse is not carelessly thrown in the same drawer. It's prepped, tagged, re-bagged or covered before the drawer. There's plenty of drawers here, and only one is used. What is this the public bathroom? Need to knock to see if it's occupied? However, this is a tool that the devs can expand upon. The devs now have two directions they can go:1: Listen to all criticism, update the game to be more interactive in the story mode and put in new details 2: Ignore everyone and fail I think I'm the only one staying around for autopsy mode to be released but you need to do work. A lot of work. The main story needs to have some more details put in. Such as actually hanging your apron up and throwing your gloves away. The characters mental state could be influenced by actions and not guessing at taking pills. For example, Jack doesn't sign in. How about letting us sign in the time sheet, this can be an influence to a positive mental state. Getting rest, getting coffee instead of alcohol, small things like this could have been done for a more classic ending A or ending B set up. Autopsy only mode needs to have way more corpse models than the six, and it needs to have nothing scripted. Make this thing completely random, make some cases sad, some normal, some utterly nightmare fuel (hence body 6, and actually let us finish that) Let us actually properly store a body. In fact, make an interactive style of us opening a drawer of the several so we don't know what to expect, or a mode where we have to unpack and do everything. There's so much you can do with this mode that it's insane. As the game sits now it is not even worth a glance, but the autopsy only mode, some additions and patches to the story and all done properly could save this game. Overall rating 2 (ironically the same amount we actually get to interact with) body bags out of 10.
