_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron - Where I Set Out to Be a Heroic Rat King but Ended Up as the King of Fleeing (After 11 Hours of Furry Frustration)Rating: ★★★☆☆Tails of Iron, the game where I embarked on a noble quest to save the rodent kingdom but mostly just ran away from colossal frogs (after 11 hours of whisker-twisting excitement).Pros:- I've mastered the art of swift retreat. When you're up against foes like sword-wielding frogs twice your size, the tactical retreat becomes your best friend.- The game's world is like a medieval mouse fairy tale. Roaming through tiny villages, battling enormous foes, and doing quests for fellow rodents is as charming as it is chaotic.- I've learned that sometimes you just need a bigger hammer. Upgrading my mouse hero's weaponry and armor is like that satisfying moment when you finally get your dream gadget.Cons:- My mouse hero should probably consider a career change to professional sprinting. I've run away from more foes than I've slain, and the frogs' croaking taunts me in my sleep.- I've developed an irrational fear of tongues. Frog tongues are like elastic death traps, and their unpredictable strikes have made me jump in real life more times than I'd like to admit.- The game's humor is like a cheesy but lovable animated film. The banter between characters often had me chuckling, even while fleeing for my life.Tails of Iron is a game that invites you to be the hero of a rodent kingdom but doesn't mind if you sprint away from danger. It's the kind of game where you'll start with dreams of epic battles and end up laughing at the sight of a mouse with an oversized hammer outrunning massive frogs.To those contemplating a whiskered adventure: Embrace the retreat, face your frog fears, and remember that in Tails of Iron, it's not about the battles you win; it's about the entertaining run you have while trying.In conclusion, Tails of Iron is where I've learned that when life gives you frogs, rodents, and a really big hammer, you run, you explore, and you laugh at the petite pandemonium.Overall rating: ★★★☆☆

_childDocuments_.review: It's honestly just an OK game.  Simply put, it's a 2D souls-like but not really good or bad.The story is pretty much linear despite having a map that looks like it encourages going off the rails and exploring, and be prepared for a lot of backtracking as every main quest will force you to return to the throne before telling you where to go next without an option to instantly return, so you end up having to run back and forth usually for no reason and with no new quests showing up so it seems the game is artificially being prolonged.  One quirk I didn't like was having a board full of sidequests, but you are only allowed to accept and work on them one at a time, meaning you have to backtrack to the board each time to accept another available sidequest (again, backtracking for the sake of prolonging the game).As for the combat...  I had a lot of issues with it.  I found some enemies having some hidden quick move (with no tells) that knocks you down attached to the end of their combos which inconsistently shows up, so after successfully evading their combo and moving in for a damage phase you'll find the enemy just randomly knocking you down when you're not even in the hitbox and losing your damage phase altogether.  So that just results in you having to wait a second more to prevent these random knockdowns which decreases the number of hits you can get in per damage phase, needlessly prolonging fights.Another thing is that enemies can and will chain stun lock you into a corner with knockdowns, so it gets super frustrating unless you try to stay relatively in the center of the screen.Overall, I still think the game is worth trying out, but more of a game you place in your backlog for a rainy day.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is like a table with one short leg. The art is amazing and it is the best aspect of the game by far. The narrative is simple, but a tale the player feels invested in immediately. The music and sound design fits the setting and does its job well. The gameplay, however, leaves much to be desired. While I was not dissatisfied with my experience, I cannot recommend the game. If the combat, quest system, and travel had some improvements, this game would be a very solid indie experience, and I would gladly change this to a recommended title.The combat is not "punishingly brutal" in terms of gameplay, it is actually quite easy if you play very safe and defensively. However, if you drop your controller, mess up too many times in a row, or try to play aggressively, you die really fast. Combat looks and sounds brutal and weighty, but is essentially a game of "rock, paper, scissors" with some occasional mix-ups. To break it down, enemies have attacks that are telegraphed (practically shouted at you) with different colors, symbols and sounds, which the player then responds by taking the appropriate counter action. Red line attacks mean an enemy is performing an attack you can only dodge. Red circle attacks mean the enemy is doing an area attack, and you must double dodge (or so the tutorial tells you, you can also elect to just walk away from where the attack will land). Yellow line attacks can be blocked, parried, and dodged, but it is taught in the tutorial to parry these attacks for a window to deal damage. White line attacks are ranged attacks, which must be blocked. The only other attack an enemy may throw out is an attack telegraphed by animation only (I'll call them light attacks), which can be blocked or parried. Attacks are telegraphed way too hard. The enemy winds up, shakes, then attacks. Enemies are practically geriatric when it comes to speed, giving you massive windows to read the next attack.  I have many complaints about the combat system. For one, the attacks are often very slow and easy to counter. Enemies will often charge, stop in front of Redgi, then attack (enemies stopping before attacking makes it far too easy to dodge. Simply see the red attack, run at the enemy and press dodge). Someone who plays Souls-like games defensively will find no trouble with this game. Tails of Iron seems to be designed to the defensive playstyle (it is established that Redgi is small and not particularly at an advantage in the prologue), as aggression is heavily punished in this game by most enemies. Spamming light attack should not be rewarded, but you should be able to exploit more openings than yellow attack parries and red attack dodges (very few light attacks, like the spear frog's downward slash, can be parried for a large attack window). Fights will often drag out when not necessary, with enemies having only one attack out of many to actually punish. Some bosses are rather annoying to fight. Shield bosses come to mind, as the AI plays defensively and you can't be aggressive, you have to wait or trigger the AI into making a mistake. For instance, Moleberg, the mole arena boss with the shield, can practically be exploited by repeatedly running to the edge of the arena to bait the attack with the biggest opening. Other enemies with shields have light attacks, which you can parry with a timed block. Parrying those attacks give you one free hit at best, and the enemy often counters the attack by throwing out a shield bash that is very difficult to dodge. It simply takes too long to kill enemies at times, and it makes encounters take longer than necessary. Some other things that take longer than necessary is progression and travel time. The quest system is a stonewall to plot progression. The game has "side quests" which are not optional. Sometimes you need gold to continue the story, and gold is only gained from side quests. I would prefer if I could either gather gold naturally along the main story or if the main story didn't require Redgi to go on fetch quests in a linear game. Tails of Iron has a Metroid-like layout, with rooms on the map all being connected via a square grid and freely allowing travel between them. However, the game is not seamless in its level transitions, and loading every single room is frustrating at times. It takes ages to leave the sewer or make a pit stop at The Crimson Keep. For example, The Crimson Keep could certainly benefit from being composed of larger rooms. As an example, It would flow better if the cook's room didn't require four loading screens to get to, with no fast travel back out to the courtyard. The problem in general is travel time, with no shortcuts, and some obstructions respawning (such as the vines in the sewer or the frog barricade). People accuse the game of padding, I hope it is just amateur design.Some good things I'd like to note: I love all the rodent characters and their little Don't Starve instrument voices. I really don't like rodents, but the art team made me care for Redgi, his family, and his friends. The little details in the narrative are nice, such as Lans Alat (Lancelot), the frog boss with a lance. Or the Moleshevik Republic, komrat, and auto-mole-bile. Minor but interesting details. I could gush for ages over the art, their team did very good work. The narration (done by Doug Cockle, voice of Geralt of Rivia) really elevates the story. TL;DR Art, writing, and sound design are very well done in this game. Get it if you want to support the amazing work they did. Do not get this game for the Souls-like experience or combat, you will be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game.  The art style and the narration are all fantastic ( I'd like to imagine that the story is being told by Geralt of Rivia himself). The characters are fun and its always nice to have a companion fighting along side you. Even though the characters don't talk directly, everything is clear and easy to understand. The story isn't perfect. There's a bit of  filler throughout the story, forcing the player to do side quests to progress in certain areas. Sometimes the quests can take you out of it by lacking in urgency. The combat in this game is exciting and quite challenging. i played the game in the bloody whiskers difficulty and got my rear handed to me on several occasions. ( this difficulty isn't recommended for new players... my mistake). Most attacks are fair but some will lead to an instant death even at full health, which can be annoying but not game breaking. The bosses vary in difficulty as expected but, so long as you get better gear as you go, they are all beatable. _childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron was recommended as a Metroidvania, but it's more of a linear 2D action lite RPG, if it makes sense. The story itself is nothing complicated, but it's charming and engaging (puns, pop culture references, etc.). As noted, it's pretty linear, with a gaggle of side quests that grant you weapons you probably won't use. There are also discoverable bosses that can grant desirable equipment, so they're not all write offs. That being said, there is a lot of unnecessary filler consisting of going to take on a quest or side quest, completing the quest, trudging back to the throne room/quest board, and then going back right to the same area you were just in. You can only do one side quest at a time, so it can get annoying after a while. With environmental design, Tails is great. Characters pop out at you, and have little details to include getting battered the more you wittle away at them. Speaking of battle, you will need to Git Gud. Combat on paper is pretty fair--you have block, dodge, shield breaks, and and so on, and controls are intuitive. The major thing for Souls vets is that this game does not have i-frames. If you roll towards an enemy expecting i-frames to carry you through, you're in for a nasty surprise with lots of damage. After a few fights you'll get used to this, though, and adjust your rolling according to enemy attacks. Combat itself isn't too difficult--you just need to invest time in learning the enemy move sets and taking it from there. The combination or regular, parry-able, unblockable, and area attacks makes for a good assortment of enemy attacks to keep you engaged.  (There is no face tanking in this game.) The drawback (or bonus) to this is you can't focus on one play type, and sleep on it. I found myself customizing my loadout constantly to adapt to the environment and bosses.What breaks the game for me, though, is the hit boxes, which are really, really bad. I noticed for a lot of bosses and smaller enemies, if you roll through them, and [turn around] for a point blank hit, you will miss a good amount of the time. This is extremely frustrating as some enemies focus on unblockable attacks, so your counter attack options after a roll are limited. I really hope they'll address this should there be a sequel. Besides helmets, armor, and weapons, there are health upgrades and that's about all you get (hence "lite rpg"). The equipment has an interesting mechanic where you can customize your character's weight/burden. This impacts your roll (think fat-rolling when you're too encumbered like in Souls games), which feeds into boss fights and loadout choices.All in all, I recommend Tails of Iron if you're into Souls or Salt and Sanctuary. The combat isn't really brutal (more of a game of patience and learning movesets), inasmuch as it's hit boxes not registering. Given that you have the VA for Geralt from the Witcher series narrating, great animation style, and wonderful environmental design, definitely pick a copy.  8/10

Very much enjoyed this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I reached what I assume is the leadup to the last boss and I don't think I'll bother finishing. The combat is fairly enjoyable but there are no really memorable fights and everything else about the game is a slog. Exploration rewards you with mostly nothing except the need to backtrack back to where you came from. The "side quests" are incredibly tedious, repetitive content clearly designed to pad out the game's length. I put "side quests" in quotes because most of them are mandatory; you need substantial amounts of coins to continue the story at various points and the side quests are the only way to earn coins.I cannot emphasize enough how poorly these side quests are designed. One particularly memorable stretch of the game has you taking several essentially identical quests to kill bugs in the sewers. You can only take one quest at a time, so you need to start one quest, go into the deepest parts of the sewers, kill the enemies, and return to the job board to take the next one, which could very well end up sending you to literally the exact same location to kill another group of generic bug enemies. Rinse and repeat.As a final point, while the writing isn't very good to begin with, it is further hurt by the bizarre tonal shifts as the narration can't decide whether it wants to tell a gritty and dark story about war and strife or a lighthearted children's' story about silly animals.

_childDocuments_.review: I beat Tails of Iron in under 6 hours. It is a fantastic experience, full of outstanding narration, sound effects, animation and art.If you're coming from a 2D platformer background, this game is amazingly difficult. You must - and I mean must - learn that red means dodge, yellow means double block, and there's more, too. A circular red means to avoid. A red with three lines means to avoid backward. On the whole this game is intuitive to an incredible degree. Strife with difficulty, you will feel rewarded for each step in your quest. I will say there is one boss early on, perhaps the third, a frog probably, that is tuned quite difficult. Otherwise the game is doable - just do not get stressed when you encounter difficulty.If there were anything I'd regret, it's a little bit of required walking outside the norm for some quests in sewers early on. And that you aren't required at all to explore the entirety of the game to complete it.You owe yourself and your friends to enjoy Tails of Iron if you enjoy 2D platformers. It is a wonderful story and an excellent game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot of fun. _childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: It's always nice when a game can surprise you and Tails of Iron is a pleasant surprise indeed. This here does everything it is trying to do very well, rather than mediocre like most 'souls-likes' these days.So 'souls-like' might be a bit of a stretch as I didn't find this one overly punishing. Challenging sure! Every time a boss had me against the wall it felt fair and never cheap. This was made possible due to the solid controls and game-play. Similar to 'souls' games there is plenty of rolling and countering, all based on the enemy attack pattern. That, and a light emphasis on exploration made for a free flowing experience where I never felt bogged down.What really kept everything from getting stale was the story and presentation. It was a joy to play as this little mouse slowly take back his kingdom from it's multiple threats. The mix of pictured voice bubbles from the characters and the narrator speaking over the top of everything kept the story rich. Coupled with the unique hand drawn art style, it all comes together to form an engrossing experience.Once I picked this one up I couldn't put it down. Everything the developers set out to do, they have done better than most. It isn't overly long, but I think the price is right for supporting developers who I hope will continue onto great things.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: The experience was like reading a short-novel. I enjoyed the adventure and I am satisfied with the purchase.I liked how the game used text sparingly and, instead, apply pictures and sound together to converse messages to the player. It was an excellent execution of graphics to communicate that was simple, yet, easy to understand.Another thing I liked from the game was the beautiful music. Fantastic soundtrack in the game that help reveal the atmosphere and emotions in the fantasy world.As for the general combat interactions in the game, it felt like a good mix of action, rhythm, and puzzle. Fairly easy to understand right after the combat tutorial. You might fumble with controls in your early encounters, but you will soon become more familiar with how to duel enemies as your adventure progress.

_childDocuments_.review: It gets boring very fast when you travel back and forth again and again. I like the art and the mechanics but it feels clunky. _childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron: A Rat-astrophe of Fun!I'm not sure what's more surprising, the fact that rats can wield swords or that I actually enjoyed getting my furry little butt kicked repeatedly. Tails of Iron is like a medieval cartoon crossed with a hardcore roguelike, and it's absolutely bonkers.You play as a rat prince who's trying to save his kingdom from a bunch of froggy invaders. It's like Bambi meets Game of Thrones, but with more fur and less Bambi. The combat is tough but fair (mostly), and the art style is so charming it's almost criminal.I've died more times than I can count, but every respawn is just another excuse to dive back into this rodent rampage. It's like a never-ending cheese-fueled adrenaline rush. If you're looking for a game that will make you laugh, cry, and scream all at once, Tails of Iron is your oyster. Or should I say, your cheese?10/10, would get eaten by a giant frog again
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Beautiful Environmental Visual- Combat (2D Souls done properly.)- Linear Game Progression (No headache in figuring out where to go. I'm tired of open world games with a million hidden collectibles or quests that require specific guides.)Cons: - Character & Equipment Design: God awful. Almost as if the designer went out of their way to make the equipment ugly and undesirable.- Story & Dialogue: Almost as good as a middle schooler's mid-term project.- System: Basic. There's no weapon arts or any special attributes to the equipment or even the weapon types that separates them apart in a meaningful way.- Backtracking: Lack of better fast travel system and save point makes me feel that my time is not appreciated as the player. Even if you kill a boss, if you didn't save and died due to falling from a 1cm drop, you will have to fight it again.There's definitely more cons than pros in this game but the few pros make me recommend this game and anticipate that they improve/fix all the cons in the sequel. Please, no player wants to wear an ugly piece of armor made of toad skin or have a toothpick or a chipped toothpick as weapon options throughout the ENTIRE GAME. I would not hire the same artist that designed the equipment.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: Basically a good soulslike Metroidvania game, but the fight system does need a lot of tweaking.Difficulty ★★★★★★☆☆☆☆ (add 2 stars for bloody whiskers mode)* visuals and music is nice* music and story is fitting and much better than in other genre alike game* the game does have a lot of savepoints and unlimited consumables around, which is quite fair* picture dialogues ae working out pretty well* there is a health gating system for heavy damages* most bosses need to be trained to beat. You need to learn their patterns and abuse the weaknesses to win* it takes too long for your character to get off a bench after reload (this is annoying if you have a lot of retries on a boss battle)* health doesn't get auto-restored on saving or while filling up your bottle (time-waste)* weight system is not explained properly (benefits and disadvantages)* there is an urgent need of a retry button during fights (especially on bloody whiskers mode)* too many boss fights, they just don't feel special anymore at some point of the game* the method to swap sides of your shield block cannot be changed, I do not like the method the devs have chosen* already adding Steam achievements for a non-released DLC is dumb.  DLC was released finally. The additional achievements were listed about 9 months in total too earlyBasically the whole fight system. The core issue is that the fight system has a lot of flaws, which is fine on story or normal mode, but will get very obvious on bloody whiskers mode:1. during kill animations you are invulnerable, but enemies still alive will time their attacks often right at the moment you come out of it. You cannot evade, block or do anything to prevent the hit then. So this kill animation does work totally against you.2. you cannot cancel most actions once triggered. Often you can predict 1-2 seconds before that you will get hurt and cannot do anything about it anymore. A proper fight system usually lets you do this as long as there is time left.3. enemies may chain their attack even after knocking you down. Those double, triple, quad-strikes will insta-kill you even with good equipement and full health. It is like doing one single mistake and getting punished multiple times. 4. some hitboxes of (especially bigger) enemies are just nasty. I do not like to be hit just by thin air and loose instantly 90% of my health due to that. This is one of the major flaws that makes this fight system not suitable for harder modes.5. enemies have nasty AoE attacks that reach over the full screen in a limited sized arena you get trapped in - not a good idea to do.6. bug: sometimes your blocks are just ignored (especially if you do re-blockings or just stood up). This will lead to visually fully see your shield raised, but ranged fire will still hit you and also the counterattack for the yellow attacks will just be ignored if pressed. This did cost me a lot wins on a boss fight. Really annoying.8. bug: I was killed twice by two different bosses while performing the final blow (actually we double-killed us somehow, although he didn't performed an attack, it was weird. One of them was Ratnor which was pretty annoying loosing the fight due to that).Yet another game that was ruined by over-ambitious devs that do no realise that challenging does not mean to present unfair or unfinished game mechanics to the players. The fighting system is one of the most flawed ones I experienced the last couple of years, unfortunetally.If you are only going for some chilled fun on story and normal mode, you can buy this game. If you are a completionist or do like challenging games that are properly balanced I cannot recommend it. You will get disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I wan to like this game, in fact I do, the only thing that is stopping me from enjoying it is the non-existent switch pro controller support. Fix this, there isn't any excuses when this game is already released on Switch.Edit:None of the suggestion worked, what did work however, was enabling Switch Pro support, but then disabling "Use Nintendo Button Layout" only then did the game actually respect my inputs, then I was able to execute bosses. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. I've grown tired of "difficult" games (Hi, Cave Story+!) and occasionally just want to enjoy a good story with quality game play. _childDocuments_.review: I was worried at first the game was too simple and linear but it gets better as it progresses. At first it seemed like there was a little too much backtracking to the same areas in the side quests which a lot are mandatory to progress but you end up able to explore more content and find other secrets in the game. Also personally, the slide whistle was driving me a little crazy having to listen to it during dialogue lol. Other than the main initial issues, I really enjoyed the art, the boss design, armor/weapon variety, and most of the combat. The one thing a little confusing with the combat was it seemed like if you blocked or parried with a 2H weapon rather then a shield, it made no difference to your health or parry. I ended up just using my 2H for most of the game blocking and parrying attacks. There are one-hand weapons that are faster then using your 2H for certain situations. That's one thing that made it worth swapping out different weapons as even if some did more damage, others would weigh less or have faster attacking speed. Overall I would recommend it if you enjoy souls-like games. The game seems pretty balanced on normal difficulty, a little short but worth it if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended if you're looking for a 2D action "Souls-Like" game that has a short story! *Combat is easy to understand but takes a while to get used to as you get bombarded with enemies left and right of the screen (above sometimes)*Great narration and short story*Nice music*Fantastic art style and animation*Tons of Gear and Equipment for you to pick and choose*Some side quests*Neat level design*Atmospheric background designI think the only difficult part here is learning how to tackle multiple enemies in a single screen, but you don't really lose that much upon defeat and there's plenty of ways for you to restore your HP. You often get companions when exploring areas or progressing storyline and get secret gear if you explore a bit. Pretty Challenging I'd say but it just takes a bit of practice and the story is short so you wouldn't have to worry about playing for long hoursThanks to my awesome noona Gokidtiger for gifting this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: This game definately has some strong points but there's too many annoying things that drag the experience down for me, mainly the objectives. Almost every 'quest' in this game is go there and kill/retrieve something arbitrary. To make this worse though your character will often stop at a supposed clue or hint, kneel down into a lenghty animation that adds nothing to the experience only to get back up without contextualizing/saying anything. These long and drawn out animations, which are also used for EVERY item you pick up, feel like a waste of time. Had they been used sparingly perhaps they would've made sense but as it stands they got really annoying after a few hours. The objectives also felt like busywork without contributing to a cohesive narrative, these adventures feel tagged on to lenghten gametime rather than deliver a good narrative. This is also because most side missions needed to be completed to earn coins so you can continue the main story. The game failed to make me interested or care about the world and it's characters even though they were masterfully voiced by Doug Cockle (Gerald of Rivia VA).Other than running around the place to complete tasks there's also a lot of fighting to be done. Here i once again felt the game came short, with unresponsive controls, sluggish dodging/blocking and boring enemies. Even the bosses failed to make me engaged which is a cardinal sin for 'soulslikes' as far as i'm concerned. There's a large variety of gear and weapons to be found but these are too similar to one another to keep you engaged. At least the level design and visuals were fun to traverse, as well as being accompanied by a fitting soundtrack. Nothing too memorable but enough to atleast somewhat make up for the lackluster gameplay/narrative. I did not encounter any bugs and performance was great so atleast the product is finished, however at this pricepoint it's hard to recommend this game (especially for it's lenght). I'd give it a mid rating if steam would allow it but it's not quite there yet.

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me cry over rats.Otherwise, it's just so-so and I definitely wouldn't pay full price for it (beat the game on a second save in about 10 hours). Living in a world where games like Hollow Knight exist at a lower price point (on which I have over 40 hours), go buy HK. Everything Tails does, HK does better--unless you're a Redwall fanatic (which I'm not)--with the exception of the art style, in which case comparing the two is like apples and oranges EXCEPT for the fact that as far as I can tell, Tails' art style actually impedes its ability to have the crisp, clean game play that makes HK so darn satisfying. The only other thing Tails has that HK doesn't is the narration and--sorry Geralt--Bastion and Hades do THAT better with the crisper gameplay, more hours to burn, and comparable cost to boot like HK.Combat is really where this game suffers (as another review mentioned, it feels a bit like rock, paper, scissors against the enemies at times) and the only element of what I'm accustom to having in something calling itself an "RPG" that I found was a series of side missions that allow you to boost your max HP, otherwise your stats remain the same throughout outside of equipping different armor/weapons to manage a damage/defense/weight bar. Resource gathering seems a bit moot when the shops only sell ammo and the occasional quest item or blueprint for armor and weapons and imo there's absolutely no replay value, so I don't plan on getting that one achievement where you have to beat the final boss on the harder difficulty.EDIT: I did mean to say, however, that I appreciated the game giving an opportunity after the main storyline was through to have a bit of after-story cleanup where you could run around and continue to collect things, and finish up any loose ends you had.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I wouldn't recommend this game. The game is pretty good looking and is somewhat immersive despite having no music. I could get past VERY linear gameplay and generic story. The things which kills it for  are:Reusing game content over and over. There are 3 main biomes which you'll visit dozen of times to clear a Boss who suddenly spawned right on the edge of the map. You can only pick up one quest at the time so you spent about 1/3 game backtracking to pick up the another one and go right back where you been few minutes ago. In the post-game content there is even situation where shorter route to a Boss is conveniently blocked off by NPCs so you have to take the longer one and run longer for sake of running. Why?You spent most of the game figting Bosses and the combat system is VERY bad. Enemies have 3 indicators for upcoming attacks - Block, Dodge, Parry,  Even though you are playing a rat, the character is about as sluggish as it can be. The animations feel slow and always have to be finished and you can't buffer anything. About 70% of my damage taken was from being in attack/dogge animation and being UNABLE to do anything about upcoming indicator which popped up right after me doing a command. As a result the main gameplay is just you waiting for indicator -> Block/Dodge -> hit once -> stand still and repeat. You can also Roll with extra action during Dodge, while it covers more distance it takes about twice as long as Dodge and it's just inferior with how fast the bosses get.I don't think I played any other platformer/2D game which wants you to press less keys. It's just extremely frustrating to see what enemy is about to do, be able to react to it, but the action won't go off because you had the audacity to try to get extra attack (half second stun lock) or you tried to Dodge left | -> | Attack (and now you are Rolling).The end game bosses are completely not compatible with the move set you are offered. You can't be creative ever and every fight plays out the same. I think a lot of things would be so much smoother if only you could block/dodge during animations, but oh well.

_childDocuments_.review: After getting all achievements for this game and finishing it in the hardest difficulty, I have to say: what a ride.Let's begin by saying that using the VA of Geralt for the narrator was a super clever choice. I can picture Geralt telling Redgi's "tail" to Ciri in the Witcher universe.First, I'll point out the negative aspects of the game. The backtracking can get a little bit tedious when doing sidequests or exploring, I wish there were more fast travel options (even if they unlocked after completing some milestones) and benches (the save points) with healing were more frequent.I think that the way you unlock new gear with the blacksmith is okay-ish, you just bring a blueprint to him and that's it. I wish you had to collect some materials or something similar.The main part of the game is the boss fights. I love them, however, sometimes their attacks can be a bit unfair, especially when you get hit once and unavoidably get hit two more times, killing you.Now, the qualities.The artwork is superb. It's charming, the colors are well-chosen, and every tiny aspect of the scenario and the background are detailed and thought out. Especially the , it looks incredible and it's my favorite region of the game. Even the weapons and the armor sets look amazing. I still can't believe that all the art is hand-drawn.The OST is good and is really cool to see that the drums sometimes are little creatures in the background.I enjoy the combat a lot. There are indicators of enemies' attacks and at first, this can be seen as something that would make the game too easy or simple but having played the game on Bloody Whiskers difficulty, I think it would be impossible to play the game if not for those since it's designed to work that way.The core of the story is not original: is a dethroned princess trying to reclaim his title. That said, the characters are unique are have interesting personalities, even without VA, which is a feat in my opinion. The  is my favorite by far. You care about them and what happens to them during your playthrough.Even if the boss battles can be a little unfair, I loved them. They are really hard and require your quickest reflexes, after battling a boss for almost an hour, it felt extremely rewarding when I finally defeated them.I hope the studio can learn from these little mistakes that can be easily fixed and improve upon everything that made this game great and unique.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly lovely game from what looks to be a very small dev team.  Good story line and narration, surprising amount of customization, fun engaging combat (esp. boss fights, of which there are plenty, and some other... special encounters).  Simple controls but satisfying combat mastery requiring patience and careful timing.  Mechanics & items aren't varied or complex but are exactly what the game needs.  Took me a bit under 20 hrs to 100% (some afk time in the hrs listed on Steam); about 1 hr after beating it to tie up loose ends.  I was actually sad when it ended, in the best way; it left me craving more.  Some really cool design decisions like the musical npc dialogue, somehow really menacing frogs with soulless eyes, and my new favorite between-area loading screens.  Love the artwork.  Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is an exquisitely crafted 2D adventure. On the surface, the game can seem like a 2D Dark Souls. In fact, the first hour you will likely spend with the game leans heavily into that aspect. Since I'm actually not a huge fan of Dark Souls, I initially abandoned it until hitting a 2D adventure kick recently. I'm glad I did because the game chills out a bit and reveals itself to be so much more richly inspired. At times TOI felt like I was playing a clever point and click adventure. At others, I had flashbacks to getting my ass kicked repeatedly in Mike Tyson's Punch Out until I knew exactly how to break an enemy. There's also of course a great and straight forward RPG backbone to keep things interesting. While there's obviously a storybook feel to the artwork, it's of the grimmer (and sexier) variety. The main character, Redgi, will become an insanely efficient and skilled killing machine on his quest to restore his kingdom with the green and yellow gore coated fur to prove it.

_childDocuments_.review: In under 15 hours, I have 100%ed this game, and despite the short play time, this was one of the best experiences that I've had this year in gaming.Tails of Iron is beautiful game about a young Rat King restoring his kingdom and seeking justice for its destruction, full of excellent direct and environmental storytelling, fun map exploration and progression, with difficult and satisfying to master combat.As the game starts, with your character, Prince Redji, preparing to take the crown of the rat kingdom from his father and become king himself, yet a dropkick comes down flying in as the coronation happens, as the Vile Frogs come crashing in like a storm and ransacking the kingdom. Within this moment the game grinds you down to zero, spikes the difficulty, and with the destruction of the Rat kingdom with literal burning, murdering and pillaging by the Frogs.After this passes, You have to build yourself back up, thru mastering the combat and exploring every nook and cranny of the world for the best gear, and undertake quests and jobs, so that thru your efforts, you restore the Kingdom back to full power and prosperity, and seek justice for your fellow ratkin.The gameplay, exploration, and storytelling are all harmonious, with every action and quest you take, feeling like the next part of the tale is being told, which, literally narrated by the magnificent Doug Cockle, voice of Geralt of Rivia (from the Witcher Series). The narrator thruout the entire game, keeps us tied to the challenges we and Redji faces, ever present in a style the reminds me of Supergiant's Bastion and Hades.IMO, souls-like is an incorrect tag for this game, although, please don't be fooled by first impressions. Admittedly, the combat in this game many of the souls game tropes, stamina based combat, blocking, shield parrys, dodging, one handed and two handed weapons, an estus flask, grim-dark fantasy environments, brutal violence, and tons of swordplay. , the combat flow has more in line of the Batman: Arkham series and that combat system. Enemy design is excellent, with clear and reliable telegraphing in the animations and design, as well as on screen UI element that displays if the attack can be parried, blocked, or must be avoided. Every single combat encounter is GOOD, and builds upon the last, but the initial combat sequences deceptively show how simple the system is, hiding the complexity of it, as the entirety of the rest of the game will quickly show. I cannot remember the last game that made me so engaged with almost every single combat encounter, having to think strategically and reflexively about each fight. I genuinely came to really love this combat system, but I did struggle with it in the beginning hours.A few gripes: The combat has a great difficulty curve, until you hit the plateau near the end of the game, which is partly due to the enemy variety starting to slightly stagnate, and is partly due to my second gripe; A "Secret" 1-handed weapon, that completely negates every other option for the 1 handed items, unfortunately making every 1 handed item from that point feel like I was only finding all the weapons from that point just to finish the Achievement requiring them; The flute noise for the Rats is cute, and very close the squeaks rats actually make, but they hurt my ears, and unfortunately cause ear ringing for me (A patch for the game, allows for the NPC flute noises to be disabled); the checkpoint benches do not restore health when used, which is a bold choice that I fully respect, but I am still annoyed by. while this is mitigated by many benches having a keg to refill your flask nearby, not all of them do, espicially when you would want them to; Some mild story gate keeping with artificial thresholds for a quest reward item, that require basically doing every side-quest available in an area in order to progress the story more; The weight system is neat, very much a souls-like idea. but it overall makes very little difference, at least as far as i could tell, so its more of just what clothes you want to wear for the journey. Particular resistances did help with certain fights, but whether it was heavy, medium, or light armor, it never made a difference.The artwork is beautiful, the world feels vibrant and full, and is a joy to explore. The procedural restoration of your kingdom from the destruction it suffered, seeing the ruined and burning castle and village brought back, rebuilt and once more, full of denizens, the underground areas are full of dark and creepy caves and strange sewers, murky crypts, and some of the best Moles depicted in fiction outside of Redwall. The sound design is excellent and well thought out, and the score ranges from feeling minimalist at times, to making itself a cornerstone of many boss fights.The pacing is excellent, and despite my own play time being less then 15 hours, I never felt as though the game was rushed, or unwanted in pushing me forward. At the conclusion of the story I was satisfied, and cleaning up for completion only took a few more hours beside that.I fully recommend to anyone to play Tails of Iron. It is challenging, rewarding, gripping, and so satisfying to play, and it never outstays any welcome, if anything, its a fantastic tale of adventure and peril, with Geralt of Rivia as our storyteller, and I wish it didn't end so soon.(EDIT 11/27/21 :FREE DLC DROP AND WE GET THE FINAL SECRET WITH THE LOCKED DOOR?!?!? LETS GOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO)Play this game

_childDocuments_.review: A bore. The combat never changes, the "upgrades" are just reskins with better stats. The only purpose for gold is as a direct continuation for story missions (which also yes btw, none of the side-quests are actually optional)There is no real difference between being  light, medium or heavy weight in this game, or atleast not big enough of a difference to notice or change how well you can fight meaning that there's not really any reason to wear anything but full heavy armour.The gameplay would be fun if it was short enough for the repetitiveness to not truly sink in. The gameplay loop can be roughly followed by "do quest, get new weapons, do sidequests maybe have a bossfight or two" and it all repeats. There's no reason to keep using a weapon once you get a new one as I said they're just reskins with better stats.The story's nothing amazing and hell I'd almost say it feels a little generic in areas. The only real compliment I have for this game is that the animations are satisfying and the art direction is nice, that is it.The game genuinely feels like it'd be much better if it was exclusively the introduction and maybe the first couple of main quests.The game could be improved upon if:the combat evolved or changed at any pointsThe weapons weren't all just direct upgrades of three different types of weaponsA weapon could atleast be upgraded so you can have the excuse of fashion to use an old weapon.It's a shame too, the game clearly had potential with the things it seemed to be trying to advertise. Had it just leaned a little into combat, progression, optional content or ANYTHING then I might have even enjoyed it up to and past the midpoint, but it's just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ repetitive it feels like pulling nails.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely give bad reviews for smaller games like this, but there is a fundamental flaw in the game's combat that frankly destroys the entire experience.To make a long story short, no i-frames =  situations in which the player has no choice but to get hit by an attack that can't be blocked/parried.Example: In a corner vs a big body enemy/boss. They start the wind-up to their "O" (aoe) attack, and your only choice is to dodge through them. The catch? The hitbox of that aoe attack is large enough that you can't get out of the way in time to avoid being hit. So even if your reaction speed is perfectly on-point, you are simply not given enough time to avoid the attack.So what options do you have? Basically just one: foresight/prediction. Don't get cornered to begin with, since the only way to avoid that attack is to dodge  from the enemy, as opposed to through them. Well, good luck with that. Because many arenas are very small, where your opponent's body will already take up a good 20% of that space alone, with their aoe attack taking up nearly 30-40%.It just doesn't work. And it's really unfortunate, because the game is excellent in so many other areas, including the rest of the combat. It's just this one single oversight that makes the whole thing fall apart. If the game simply had i-frames associated with its dodge, I honestly think that everything else could remain completely unchanged and it would potentially be a 10/10 experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Thoroughly enjoyable adventure. Ignore the kids tagging it as a souls-like. there is no similarity, aside from occasionally challenging combat.Some fights are infuriating but none take more than 5 attempts if you are able to handle games beyond button mashing.The worst fights are some of the later waves of enemies. Fighting a single enemy is fun - but it feels like the game was never intended for waves of groups. _childDocuments_.review: It's rare to say I enjoyed every single second of a game, but this time I did. :D - Not a true Souls-like: while the decisions here benefit the game, it does not have a stamina bar and you lose no resources upon death, nor do you level up in the classic way (you find better gear during the game and you get permenant health upgrades by sampling dishes made by the court's Chef), but it does have strategic combat based on pattern memorization and a juice canteen to let you heal). Figured I'd point this out, so people see what they get might not quite fit the label. + Otherwise the game's fantastic: I love the very distinct and clear signals for what to use: a parry (yellow sign) or a dodge (red sign). I'm usually terrible with 2D platforming and my true forte is 3D combat in Souls-likes, so this was very helpful. E.g. I can never, ever in any game get a parry right, but here there were very few I didn't pull off and I didn't lose for it either. + The mouse and keyboard are excellently implamented and very intuative. Many Souls-likes treat M&K controls as a mere afterthught, no such neglect here. I never felt I'd do better or enjoy the game more with a controller. (I also can't rate any controller controls since I played without one.) + The story has the appeal of a small underdog rising and it feels close to the Redwall series in tone since it's a heroic adventure, but not without a touch of gory details (e.g. you will see blood on enemies and some may have their guts exposed), though a certain underground town is more steampunk than pure medival fantasy that is there for the rest of the game.  + As someone with insect phobia I feel this deserves a special mention: none of the insect enemies were triggering for me, some cattle bugs were wacky in design and all of them very heavily stylized and rather cartoonish and didn't make any harrowing bugs sounds that would stop me form playing. The only thing that did make me somewhat uncomfortable was the "Odd Bug" logo as it did have buzzing sounds, but thankfully it was brief. + There's fairly little music and there's a lot of ambinet sound, but it fits the game and its enviroments very well. + The artstyle is unique and very cute and nearly fairytale like and comic-like in style while also not shying away form a bit of grittiness and blood when the story calls for it. I'd say teen and up for an age rating. + There few enemy races in the game, but they various enemy types are numerous and very diverse - I was amazed at just how many different kinds toads I fought to mention one such race. + The huge variety of gear enables any playstlye and you can be a light warrior, a walking fortress or a mix of both. + There are easy. normal and hard modes (not with such mundane names), so there's something for everyone. I finished all the story and extra content on easy mode - 2D isn't my strong suit, so I figured I'd take it easy - aside from maybe one dish and piece of gear I've likely missed somewhere in 9 hours. + While the game is short it doesn't feel dragged out and it's length is just right: it tells its story without cutting corners or overstaying its welcome. + Platforming was there, but it was not difficult. The reason why i can't properly enjoy most 2D Souls-likes is because there's a lot of platforming and while I can nail the combat, there's always some platforming section that bars my way forward (looking at you, Salt and Sanctury), not such dissapointments here. + Looking back at it, easy mode might nearly be enough even for people that have lost most of their reflexes either due to old age or some other reason. Being 25 and in good health, I can't really judge this directly, but it felt relaxed enough that one could get very far in the game even with far less reflexes. But as I'm not in position to directly test this point, take it with a grain of salt. - Edit: the game IS now sold on GOG and will be discounted for 55% until the 11the of June 2024. I'll play with my GOG copy shortly. A huge "Thank you!" to the developers. :D IN SHORT: it's an absolutely amazing game, go play it. :)

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty great souls-adjacent game. The presentation is incredible right out of the gate, the hand drawn art-style evokes a storybook feel and looks amazing in motion. The sound design is great as well, all sounds, and music are high quality and battles erupt in a suitably visceral and punchy exchange. The narration is also top notch, the voice of Doug Cockle (Geralt of Rivia in the Witcher series) is a welcome addition and brings a healthy dose of gravitas to the story beats.Combat largely consists of a dance between yourself and the enemy, as you learn from their choreographed attacks, knowing when you have a gap to strike and when to retract and defend are key. The game gives you three methods of both attack and defense; one handed weapon, two handed weapon, and ranged and dodge, block, and parry respectively. The enemy variety does a good job of making you utilize each of these tools and pulling off the perfect combos to win a boss fight is suitably enjoyable.While the game is on the shorter side; a completionist run is easily obtainable in 10-15 hours, it is time well spent. As I find myself with less and less free time, I have come to appreciate these polished and concise experiences and find that they are among the most rewarding and enjoyable times I have with games. Tails of Iron is a well-crafted game, and I would highly recommend it, especially if you enjoy your side scrollers with a little touch of souls.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron are a 2D soulslike, where a war between rats and frogs have broken out. After his dad, the king, gets killed during a sudden frog invasion. You set out as the youngest prince to take revenge, retake your territory, and honor.The game features a nicely hand drawn art style, with nicely done animation.My biggest criticism with the game, are the moveset. The combat moves in itself are fine as is, but I could never make out the dodge rolling. Several times when I were certain I dodged an attack, I would often take damage. The same could be said about the hitboxes, most often than not, when I thought I were outside the range of an attack, I would still take damage.Would I recommend this game? Maybe. It got some things going for it, and is a decent experience outside my personal gripes, but I would not replay the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth buying if it's on sale for cheap. Fun but very short and becomes kinda repetitive. Early game is the most fun, very linear story and captures a mood of desperation and fighting against foes much more powerful than you. The battle system is pretty exciting and requires strategy, Unfortunately, the game transitions to more open-world gameplay and becomes kinda boring, forcing you to do sidequests (which are exclusively "revisit this area and kill the monsters") in order to advance. Also, there is a lot of equipment but there are very clear winners and losers, to the point where I was often picking up new items that were objectively worse than what I already had. Despite the open world the game still ends up being incredibly short---it took me 10 hours and I think I'm pretty close to 100% of all items etc. I think it would have been a stronger game if they had stuck to a linear format, reduced the equipment options and exploration and focused on combat and a tight storyline.

_childDocuments_.review: While I'm inclined to say I do recommend the game, I've also got a lot of mixed feelings about it. From the Souls-likes I played, it's one of the worst, though I haven't played many of them. Let's start with the good parts: Visually, it looks great. The art style is charming and the environments contain quite the amount of detail. The finishers animations are also superb. In terms of sound, it's clearly an AA game: there isn't much variety and AAA titles, such as Bloodborne, of course, blow it out of the water when it comes to OST. That being said, the few soundtracks which are present are quite nice. It would be remiss of me not to mention the narration, provided by Doug Cockle (Witcher 3). Cockle's wonderful performance significantly enhances the overall experience and does a lot of heavy lifting.Other thing I particularly enjoyed is the changes in the world. As you complete side quests and the main quest, the world around you changes: ruined castle gets rebuilt, destroyed villages are repaired, regular citizens appear on the streets and go about their business, etc. This small feature really made it feel as if the game progressed and the main character actually made a change in the world. Now, to the less pleasant parts of the game. I played it on the hardest difficulty and some of the encounters didn't feel fun at all. I don't mind learning patterns or getting used to a moveset, but I do mind having to dash around and dodge for 10 seconds just to make a single attack. It's not hard to do, really, the majority of bosses have about 3-5 moves, but it's just so tedious. On the other end of the spectrum, there are bosses who posed zero challenge and were killed in 2-3 tries even though technically they were late-game ones. Moreover, the animations are often very stiff and the attacks are not well telegraphed, which means you mostly rely on visual cues the game presents above enemies' heads. It's pretty common for a fight to be similar to a rhythm game, which I personally did not enjoy that much.Next issue is the general game design one: the game absolutely loves to waste your time with weird unnecessary padding. I will list just a couple of examples:1. Your healing flask charges are not restored on rest, but should be refilled separately instead. Is there ever a point in not restoring them? No, so each time you rest you should also spend ~5-10 seconds to restore healing charges. 2. There are consumables in the game, such as arrows. They, again, are not restored on rest. However, there are barrels with arrows inside of them all throughout the map, with an endless supply of arrows. What it means is your "get ready" routine isn't just "go and rest", but rather "fill your flask, then go to the next corner of the screen to grab the arrows, then run to another screen to grab the poison". It would be fine if there was an element of skill involved, e.g. getting arrows is risky, but there isn't. The only thing you have to do, as a player, to get your arrows is simply run. Sometimes I even closed my eyes and held the movement key because there were quite literally no enemies. The list is not exhaustive, there are other examples as well, but I hope I got the point across. This doesn't make the game terrible, it's just extremely baffling to see such questionable design decisions with seemingly no thought put into them. To summarise, as I've already mentioned, it's a mixed bag. Ultimately, I did not regret my time with the game and neither did I regret choosing the highest difficulty. I'm looking forward to seeing the next instalment and I genuinely hope the devs make overall experience smoother. There is clearly a lot of effort put into the game. It's not the best in the genre, but it's still decent enough.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that will require to you less than 2 GB: I'm enjoying it far more (and better) than playing Elden Ring.I think the developers perfectly understood what a soulslike with RPG and open world elements must be.This' what I do liked so far:-Soulslike elements like hard bosses with different attack patterns that keeps you entertained; a dark world that, however, is still vibrant and colorful in some areas (there are villages and safe areas, a thing that I missed much in many other soulslike).-RPG elements like a main quest that is both thrilling and funny; quest boards with the right amount of side quests that makes you feel in a loosely open world environement, without losing yourself around forgotting the main mission; NO levels or stats to manage, you'll acquire equipments that will modify your attack, defense, etc. stats and that is sufficient: you'll still wanna choose between an armour that will protect you from evil froggies rather than another one that will shield you from devilish mosquitos (or else you'll easily die: yes, it's a soulslike).-Fu*king BEAUTIFUL art: every detail seems hand drawn, still it doesn't lack fluidity. I'm just like "WOW" at every corner. I mean: WOW. Uppercase in my mind, you know?-Weapons chians attacks and combos, and the flexibility of the weapons themselves: sometimes you'll have to figure it out which is the best suited (or the only choice) to overcome a foe.I'm absolute loving this title. I hope someday they will try to make a sequel with 3D graphic, with the same kind of art but someway similar to "Ghost of a Tail" for the 3D environment: that would be glorious! All hail King Rattus.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the worst mechanics the 2D souls-like genre has ever seen.  The buttons are unresponsive, you'll mash attack while standing still only for your character to do absolutely nothing.  Dodging has no iframes and is not reliable, so winning fights at all is purely RNG.  Every enemy, even on normal mode, has so much HP that it's absurd and you'll have to tediously hit even the weakest minion many, many times before they die.  Absolutely the worst combat the souls-like genre has ever seen.  The art is gorgeous.  Sound design is a mixed bag.  The Geralt voice actor does an alright job narrating but he's not a skilled voice actor and it shows.  However, the awful noises they use for NPC speech is so offputting that it's kind of confusing, who thought that was a good idea?  Whenever a rat speaks it's some out of tune musical instrument making screeching noises, like WHY in the WORLD would you do this?  Otherwise, it's a bog standard game that cannot even possibly begin to compare to other 2D Souls-likes like Blasphemous or GRIME.  It's not even fit to smell the dried up crusted dog feces from their boots.  It's not in the same conversation entirely.  0 / 10.  Avoid at all costs.  If you want a 2D Souls-like, get literally any other one, they are all dramatically superior to this tripe.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not often that I run into a game that leaves me engaged at every turn, and that pushes me to get all the achievements just because I want more. Tails of Iron hits the mark here through the use of fantastic art direction, simple worldbuilding, and a solid "show don't tell" approach.You play as Redgi, the smallest of the sons of the legendary King Rattus. King Rattus earned his title after pushing back the wicked frog army and securing the land so that all ratkind may prosper. But rats don't live long, and the aged king must bestow his crown to the next generation. Redgi and his kin must band together to push back the newly aggressive frog menace once again.Through use of environmental storytelling, a Tail of Iron will show you the state of the kingdom for better or for worse. You always get the vibe of where you are based on the village folk working in the background, or monsters stalking them--or stalking you.The pacing is fantastic. There is no portion of the game where I thought "man I can't wait to leave this place" because by the time you get your fill of an area, you'll be thrust to the next one. That being said, you will be doing a lot of backtracking, which some may find slightly tedious. But Redgi scampers along quickly enough so that you can cover vast distances in no time. These moments of peace serve as a foil to the intense boss fights.Combat is the perfect balance of fast paced and manageable. While I died a lot, I rarely felt like the fault was anything but my own poor reflexes or mistaken positioning. There are problems with hitboxes when it comes to certain enemies, but learning their move sets will allow for much easier encounters. There is a plethora of armor and weapons, and a weight system that is hardly restrictive unless you want to fully armor up. Axes tend to weigh more and attack slower, but do more damage. Spears don't hit as hard, but they strike much faster. Swords serve as the balance in between. Ranged weapons have similar choices.The platforming is simple enough that it's hardly a factor-- you won't have Hollow Knight or Ori style sections of difficult movement. The game is more focused on the story elements and combat. And before it overstays its welcome, the game ends in a satisfying manner, and still allows you to tie up loose ends.

_childDocuments_.review: So I played through the whole game and a good chunk of the post game now and can happily say this game is is good. I have a few criticisms for the game though. Firstly, The way equipment works in this game is a bit of a let down. You'll basically always want to wear the lightest possible equipment whilst maximising defence and damage. But the game will throw weapons and armour at you that are just plain garbage for this purpose. These loot items will just sit in your inventory all game and never get touched because using them is totally pointless because they are either exactly equivalent to what you are already using, or actually worse despite being found in the late game zones of the game.Secondly; you get three currencies in this game but the options at merchants and vendors are very limited. Gold is mostly used in advancing the story. However you will quickly have a large amount of iron and bug parts that you can't do anything with. There are cosmetics and equipment blue prints you can buy but they are finite and swiftly exhausted. So you wind up with a big stack of currencies that don't get used for anything.  The resource system and the crafting system should have been integrated more thoroughly with the loot system to create a richer experience of purchasing upgrades and customising equipment. As it is, it feels like a missed opportunity for a more dynamic and rewarding game system.Thirdly, and more of a personal game design nitpick, the game has "Side Quests" that are not side quests at all but completely mandatory to complete the game. Side quests in games should just be side quests. The system for accepting them is fine but differentiating the main plot from the sub plots is important and just a design peeve of mine.It's a solid combat/adventure game that has a brutal Dark Souls style approach to combat encounters. You'll die constantly to bosses and enemies as you attempt to work out their attack patterns. But once you master their moves and learn how to fight like a cornered rat; you'll enjoy the thrill of combat just as much as young Rat King Redgi does.I got this game on sale for 23 AUD. The current (as of 16/07/2024) regular posted of 39.95 AUD is probably the upper limit of what I would pay for this game.

My biggest, and maybe only complaint is that the game says that playing with a controller is recommended, and I do understand why seeing as the controls on keyboard are not great, BUT the game doesn't recognize any controllers if you are using macOS. _childDocuments_.review: I had pet rats of my own, however, they passed away recently. They were my whole world, I loved those rats so much, they made me so happy. I was completely destroyed when they passed. But, this game. I fell in love with this game. the soundtrack is fantastic, the gameplay is fun and compelling, the story is simple and sweet, and everything about this game made it such an enjoyable experience. Seeing all the love and effort put into this game by such a small studio is honestly awe-inspiring. all of the thought and love put into the characters, how the little buddies of the developers are forever immortalized in this game, honestly brought tears to my eyes, and it helped me get through my grief, the awful grief of losing a beloved pet. It keeps me optimistic. Just like how the ratdom overcame hardship and rebuilt what was lost, I too will get better and rebuild, and the legacy of my little buddies will live on forever and their tails will be told for ages to come. I strongly support this game and the studio, I urge all of my friends to play this game, and I urge you too. Thank you for reading if you got this far, and I hope you consider giving this game a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron surely looks interesting at first sight with its beautiful visuals and cute rats and frogs. Behind those are nice-looking cities, which are all hand drawn by the way. However, the game can not keep the same quality in the visuals in every area. While the kingdom looks worked on and detailed, the sewers look very undetailed and unimaginative. (Not because the sewers are a filthy place, it just looks boring. Take sewers in Dark Souls as a counter reference.) Geralt as the narrator is cool, but what's the point when you have no story to tell, other than marketing the game? To be honest, that's all Tails of Iron has in its core. Other than those, we have a janky and clunky combat with troublesome hitboxes. Sometimes, enemies won't telegraph their attacks and mess you up. There is weapon and armor variety, but using them never feels different. So its more like a visual variety. Nevertheless, you get the most powerful weapon mid game and never have to change weapons anywhere later. Game design is very problematic. Tails of Iron asks you to do the same side quests over and over again. The game almost has no main quests. In some side quests, you are expected to take the same route again and again to kill the same enemies, talking about enemies, Tails of Iron has no enemy variety. Most enemies are reskins of each other. Their hitboxes are problematic, making combat feel janky. The game tries to show itself as a metroidvania, but I hope the devs aren't defining it as one. Because metroidvanias aren't supposed to be extremely linear and scripted. The story itself is extremely predictable and routine. And the presentation is extremely ordinary. It's not the main focus of the game, but it takes too much of our time even when that's the case.  Sound effects are very repetitive and lacking, adding to the unsatisfactory gameplay. Exploration is not nonexistent, the same with music. There is no atmospheric music or any music at all.To conclude, Tails of Iron is a game with extremely unsatisfying gameplay, repetitive level and encounter design, and a poor game design. Extremely poor game overall. Not recommended even on a sale.Follow My

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game. The story is fun and mildly dark with some political intrigue that's really neat, the characterization and sounds for the characters is cute, and the art style is great. Lots of fun being in the world. The only thing that could be annoying for some people is that you often are backtracking and being sent to the same location over and over to progress the story or get some materials to progress the story. For people not already desensitized by MMO fetch quests, I can see how that can be super annoying, particularly because it slows the pace of the game and storytelling to a crawl. Aside from that, the boss fights are awesome and difficult. Once you get the two-handed weapon, you cannot just mindlessly wind up to break a shield, as you will get counterhit, so be sure to pick a good time to charge up... However, once you get the gun, the game becomes rather easy. All in all, great experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really write reviews but this game absolutely stole my heart the moment I started playing it. It had been on my radar when it was first announced but I completely forgot about it until it showed up in the 2024 Summer Sale.As soon I started the game up I fell in love with the absolutely gorgeous art style and design. The game-play at standard difficulty was challenging in a few places but felt consistently fair and balanced across the entire experience, which is no small feat with game design.The story has this underlying sensation to it... something of a colourful simplicity that I think I've been missing with a lot of games I've played these days. I say simple with no degrading intent; the story has twists, emotional weight, and depth, but doesn't try hard to be some complex narrative that to be honest, I just get tired of. It tells a story straight, lets you enjoy the moments, and immerses you in an experience that feels like you're playing through a picture book brought to life. Quality is NOT anti-theoretical to simplicity, far from it. The story and experience of Tails of Iron thoroughly proves as much, and the past couple days have been made better for it.Thank you, Odd Bug Studio.I eagerly look forward to Tails of Iron II :)

_childDocuments_.review: Watch my 9 minute review here (or read below at your own pace): Tails of Iron has captivated me, not only with its wonderful, progressive world-building, but the story, music, combat, everything is just well-implemented and polished.  In fact, as soon as I started thinking “Man, I wish the combat was a little more difficult”, I started getting my butt handed to me by some of the side-mission bosses.Story-Redgi the Rat, or as he was surely called in grade school, Wedgi, is maybe not the most predictable heir to his old father’s throne, given Redgi’s diminutive stature compared to his brothers BamBam and RemRem, but when tragedy strikes the Crimson Keep, Redgi must not only establish his claim to the throne, but work on rebuilding the kingdom too in order to take down the menacing Frogs.As you venture far and wide, gathering resources and gold to rebuild, you’ll meet friendly faces abroad in places like Long Tail Village and The Rangers Lodge.  And those places are only the tip of the iceberg, as they say, since there is much more to be discovered below the surface.  As you venture and gather resources, you’ll come home every once in a while to advance the main story and essentially level up by eating delicious meals prepared by RemRem, or building new weapons and armor with BamBam the blacksmith.Probably my favorite feature of the game is how the story is told, through the rats you meet.  When I first heard the dialogue, I thought I was listening to a crappy flute cover on YouTube, but the sounds designed around the rats’ dialogue mimic the squeaks and squeals of a rodent in an endearing way without being annoying.  All the while, small animations and drawn pictures are used to convey what the rat is saying.  It’s a beautiful addition, like an instrumental voiceover, and each character even seems to have his own tone.Gameplay-Tails of Iron is described as an epic RPG adventure with brutal souls-like combat, so let’s take a closer look at those claims and see how the game measures up.  Is it epic?  You bet.  It’s not often these days that a game can elicit a reaction from me, but without spoiling anything, I audibly gasped pretty early on, and was buckled in for the rest of the ride.  Redgi seems like such an underdog because he is so small, but he is backed by his brothers and some great friends along his journey to reclaim the Rat Kingdom from the Frogs.I really like the RPG elements and customizable combat, where you can trade out different styles of weapons like swords, hammers, and spears, depending on how you want to play.  The weapons don’t necessarily have stats shown, aside from their damage and weight, but they do handle differently, and you have quick attacks and charged attacks at your disposal as well.  I tried to keep Redgi as light as possible, and focused on one-handed combat, but you also carry a two-handed weapon, a bow later on, a shield, and wear a helmet and armor.  All of these have weight attributed to them, and the heavier Redgi is, the more sluggishly he moves and dodges.  When you’re in an intense fight with a frog warrior or a giant mozi, you’ll have to figure out which strategy is best for that situation, and you may need to change some equipment out before going back in for more.  Most of your armor pieces even have resistances to certain enemies, so they deal less damage to you.Now let’s talk about the souls-like combat, because this is where my only, very minor complaint, comes in.  The combat feels souls-like, with its strong dependence on dodges, rolls, and parries to defeat even some of the smallest enemies early on.  Everyone has their attack patterns that need to be learned, and when you go against a boss for the first time, you’ll likely be hard pressed to recognize his moves early enough to react and win the fight.  But, in addition to the physical tells that a certain attack is coming, the developers have also included color-coded symbols to warn you too.  It’s not often I ask for more difficulty, or more frustration in my case, but in Tails of Iron, sometimes the color-coded symbols just made me too reliant on them, and took my attention away from the enemy and his tendencies that gave his attacks away.  I think this is one of the most accessible souls-like games out there, and perhaps that’s what the developer intended, but I would have preferred a difficulty option or a menu toggle to turn these extra warnings off.Aside from that, the combat feels just right, with your quick attacks poking and prodding, and your charged attacks causing you to leap forward and deliver a crushing blow, but leaving you vulnerable too for a split second.  The balance of attacking and defending is well done, and there were times when I would finish a boss fight with just a sliver of health left, and my hands almost shaking from the excitement.  So the gameplay and mechanics, in my opinion, are just about as perfect as they can be.  Difficult and challenging, with a noticeable increase about halfway through the game, but not hampered by bad controls or laggy inputs.Art and Graphics-As I mentioned earlier, the world and the way in which it is built and established through the story is hands down one of my favorites that I’ve seen this year, and maybe ever.  From the start at the Crimson Keep, you see it prospering in all its glory, and its abrupt downfall as it’s destroyed by the Frog Clan, and then over time, you see the hard work of Redgi and his brothers coming to fruition in the foreground and background as beauty is slowly restored.  And this happens within each location and even the individual map pieces, as you complete more missions and defeat more Frogs.  In Long Tail Village, you can see the city square being rebuilt, you can find a farmer milking these miniature silt-striders or giant fleas, and in all the areas you can see musicians contributing to the glorious fantasy soundtrack, which I’ll talk about in a minute.The art style is truly a spectacle too.  Every aspect features dark outlines and borders, with muted colors filling in the gaps, akin to something you might see in a dark fairy tale.  It’s a melodious mixture of fantasy and medieval styles that plays out wonderfully.  The kind of misshapen forms and buildings throughout the world too actually remind me of the game Creaks.Soundtrack-If you like fantasy soundtracks filled with strings, woodwinds, and some light percussion, you’re in for a treat.  Evolving as you explore and discover more of the map, this score has some pretty memorable tunes, and even as you walk around the map, and the music fades out from where you just left, as you near the next part of the map, you might begin to hear some audio cues as to what area you’ll go through next.  The soundtrack and sound design are so well done, even including just the right amount of ambient and natural noises when the music dies out.  And when I mentioned earlier that you can see the rats performing some of the music when you explore, it doesn’t stop there.  Even in some of the combat sequences, you can see animals in the background performing in an effort to spur on their champion!  It’s fantastic how well the art, world, and story have been melded together.TL;DR - Should you play Tails of Iron?  I give it the highest recommendation!  I think the art is amazing and the worldbuilding, again, is possibly the best I’ve seen this year, with the way it fuses the soundtrack and story, and continues to develop as the story goes on.  The gameplay is just right, and well-polished, giving you a bit of frustration, as a souls-like game should, but also giving plenty of customization so you can take things into your own hands.  Tails of Iron is fresh and funny, and even if you don’t like rats, you may reconsider your opinion by the end.
