_childDocuments_.review: Alright updating my review since i've now beat the game and almost all of its optional content. Still got two optional quests I gotta clean up but other than that, i've done everything. A quick rundown is, this is a soulslike metroidvania game, but the combat honestly reminds me more of the Batman Arkham games than it does Souls. Now its not a flashy beatemup, but the main gameplay loop comes from dodging 4 different types of attacks, and an icon will flash when an enemy is going to roll out a specific attack... kinda like Batman. In the training it teaches you how deal with each attack, but thats pretty much what you'll be doing is reading the enemy, dealing with that specific attack and dealing out punishment in return. So keep that in mind while you're reading this, most of my gripes come from the games' combat.I want to end on a high note here so i'll start by talking about what I don't like about the game. I actually addressed this in a discussion thread, but healing is far too sluggish for how much damage enemies deal. Now enemies in this game hit hard, usually knocking out most of your HP in 1 or 2 quick hits. Yes most damage is avoidable, but a fight can get chaotic fast especially in the later areas. It takes forever to drink the potion, it takes so long I honestly would recommend against using it unless there is a legitimate break in the fight such as a boss revealing its next phase where its invulnerable anyways. The shockwave attack. Now in training you'll learn about the 4 different attacks the enemies use. A ranged attack, a parry, an unblockable, and a shockwave. Now how its supposed to work, is that the shockwave attack can only be avoided by double-tapping out of the way. You would think that only a set amount of enemies would use these kinds of attacks, but really most of the cast just spams the ever living ♥♥♥♥ out of them, including every boss in the game. Now my problem with it, is simply that usually you can't get enough clearance to clear the hitbox before it crashes down on you. I've done some perfectly executed rolls and still got hit simply because I couldn't get far enough away from the sprite before it came crashing down. As you progress different types of shockwaves emerge, and sometimes you'll get a small notification of where its going to land in the form of leaves falling.. but not always, sometimes enemies will have two types, one being a jump in place and the other a jump forward both with the exact same windup making it impossible to tell which its going to use, and i've rolled into a forward one so many times.. Weapons and armor have a very little difference. Even wearing heavy plate, the damage mitigation it does is very little. There is a weight system like Dark Souls however unlike Dark Souls it doesn't seem to effect your dodges just your walk speed. Weapons just have a damage value and thats it. You just kind of stick to the weapon type that you like the moveset for, all two handers handle exactly the same so just pick the most damaging one.. I would've liked more variation there such as different speeds, maybe some crit, but it works. This is a minor gripe. I've encountered a few audio glitches, sometimes the enemies will completely mute themselves, the narrator will cut out, or it'll get so bad you have to restart the game. Its minor but thought i'd mention it.Another minor thing is that the optional bosses don't have boss music. You're just fighting it to complete ambiance which is a weird weird feeling. Would be nice to have some tunes to pump while fighting those, had to turn on my own.Okay, now we'll move on to the positives. The art style is gorgeous, its got a very storybook aesthetic and it all looks really good, the characters look super cute, and to contrast your character will be covered in the blood of your enemies most of the time like Bloodborne its great. Overall the combat is very responsive, and other than the shockwave gripe I had everything worked well, and I had a pretty enjoyable experience. Its not a spammy game, you have to think about your openings and I really like that about it. The story is pretty good, I really liked some of the later areas it was pretty creative. I don't want to spoil anything, of course having everything narrated by Geralt is awesome. There was quite a bit of side content, a lot of stuff to explore, and worth exploring. You could run into treasure bolstering your armory or even a whole secret boss, its pretty awesome. You have bounty boards listed with content you can do as many times as you want, and a lot of it are totally optional bosses that are pretty fun to take down. In conclusion, this is a short but sweet soulslike title that has pretty tight gameplay, a nice aesthetic and good story. Its got a few things that drag it down, but for the price point you get a game you'll enjoy a lot if you like these games. Tails Of Iron gets a solid 8/10 from me.

_childDocuments_.review: A frustrating mess that goes against all the established rules of the souls-like genre.Pros:+ Nice graphics, I guess+ Keyboard customization is an optionCons:- Combat is completely unsatisfactory, rigid, with no fluidity and no rhythm- Combat can be described as a series of QTE actions. To evade one  roll through red attacks and  block yellow / white attacks. Attempting to block red attacks or roll through yellow / white attacks will lead to an immediate interruption and significant health loss- No I-frames during roll, not even when appropriately used against red enemy attacks- There are dead zones right next to your character where enemies and destroyable scenery cannot be touched. In other words you must be a character length away in order for your strike to connect- No energy bar and/or energy management (unlike every souls-like out there)- Extremely short times for enemy attack telegraphing - Generic story in a by-the-numbers, cookie-cutter fantasy world- Completely linear game. No alternate routes, no unlockable shortcuts, no secrets- No fast-travel system (so far). Annoying levels of needless back-tracking- Unskippable dialogue (i.e. floating pictograms). The flute sounds that accompany said 'dialogue' are annoying after the 100th time. You then have to listen to the (again, unskippable) narrator translating the pictograms into English- Annoying running animation- Garbage inventory system. Weapons & armor aren't named and have no stats, only vague bars to distinguish between their quality levels- Loadout customization only possible at 'bonfires'. Ridiculous- No text description or mouseover tooltips for any inventory gear, items or resources- Keyboard cannot be used for menu / inventory navigation

You dodge when the enemy lights up red, block for another, and parry for another. No exceptions, you have to follow the game's script. I find this incredibly tedious and boring. It restricts variety and makes combat a routine. This formula works in other games, but i don't think it fits a soulslike.I'm not into story in games for the most part, but they usually help hook me in and do a little world building before i start the game. Then i start to tune out the story. The whole rats vs frogs thing piqued my interest, but the into cinematic just went on for way too long. And then the voice over and dialog just annoyed me. _childDocuments_.review: The presentation's great, with a good narrator (Geralt of Rivia's voice actor), but from early gameplay (so take this review with a grain of salt), it doesn't seem like the combat will go anywhere special. The gear you can get doesn't seem to have any interesting properties, it's just weight and damage values. The ranged weapon autoaims.The combat's solid, though a bit confusing at first, because the dodge roll doesn't have any invulnerability that I could find, which you'd expect in a Souls-like. Enemies, at first, seemed like they had too much health for how uninteresting it was to attack them, but I started appreciating their higher health. It provides you more opportunities to make mistakes, or to over-commit, and lose health. The difficulty is nice, and it's interesting to figure out when attacking is safe. The only problem I have with the combat is that it has no flair. No Hollow Knight charm system, seemingly no difference between different melee weapons, no special properties that encourage you to attack or play a certain way to do more damage or debuff enemies.Pretty early on you start unlocking sidequests (the game even calls them sidequests). This strikes me as a problem, because exploration isn't interesting at all with such limited mobility and a lack of tools for exploration. Any amount of exploration or backtracking seems guaranteed to be boring.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, as long as you enjoy it's core mechanic - rat-to-foe(s) melee fights.Redgi is a rat. And he is king of the rat kingdom, which has unfortunately been overrun by the brutal army of the frogs. So your task as Redgi is to reclaim your kingdom, killing frogs and their allies on the way. You do this in deadly 2D fights - and when I say deadly, I mean deadly. This is no hack and slash game where you run button mashing though hordes of enemies. Every fight is a lovingly orchestrated deathmatch that can be your end if you are not concentrated.You have no stamina bar, so it is possible to attack, block or dodge quite fast, but button-mashing won't get you far. You have to avoid getting hit, and you have to make sure your attacks count, especially if you are outnumbered. This game requires learning the attack patterns of your enemies, countering their attacks with the correct response - dodging, dodge rolling, using your shield, parrying, jumping, counter-attacking with fast or heavy blows, changing your position, drinking healing juice, or using long range weapons. If you enjoy that, you will love the game. If not, you will die a lot and soon hate the game. It is a soulslike, after all, and there are no difficulty settings.The game consists of 6 worlds with different enemies, from mosquitos to moles or wasps. Apart from that, there are over 200 pieces of equipment to wear, which have an impact on your attack strength, damage resistance and movement speed. Certain weapons are better against certain enemies, so it helps a lot to use the correct weapons or armor. Changing equipment is only possible at special places. When you die, you can restart from your last savepoint without any punishment. Savepoints are frequent, but you have to activate them.Great 2D combat-heavy soulslike action RPG focusing mainly on the battles, in which good timing and observation are required.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks beautiful, plays like a junker with a flat on ice: sure, you can learn to steer it, and it doesn't matter if you get into a few crashes (and you absolutely will crash into some stuff), but is it what you really want to be driving?Less metaphorically: the combat in this game is just not good enough. It's a very functional system in a lot of fights, but it absolutely falls apart when things start getting more interesting. The "double dodge" mechanic just doesn't seem to work and I can't believe that it's been left in the game in the state it's in. The dodge itself has wildly inconsistent rules about what you can and can't dodge through--even attacks that are signposted as dodgeable (red attacks) have a significant failure rate of actually respecting your dodge rolls. Further, even stacking up armor will have bosses dealing 2/3 your health in a hit, requiring you to find the space to heal to avoid dying to their 2nd hit. The 2H weapons seem silly to use in combat--if the foe has a shield up it usually seems better to dodge or block them to create an opening. In fact, the only parts of combat that felt cohesive were the 1h/shield fighting, which feels quite good actually, I just wish the rest of combat felt as polished.None of the mechanics (what is defense? what is resistance?) are actually explained to the player, so it's unclear how to focus your equipment to succeed in combat. I'm not sure if perhaps the weight system betrayed me at some point and perhaps using anything higher than light weight is a mistake? I'd love it if there were any in-game tutorials to explain literally anything about this stuff.I found the world itself to be amazing. I love the story. I like the crafting system and how straightforward it is (but a big downside is that the inventory system needs quite a lot more love). The game also has a ton of saves at convenient points, which feels less like a gift and more like an apology for the fact that combat will randomly murder you sometimes.The quest design is tedious and tested my goodwill towards the world. After rescuing a rat from a tower, you need to go back to your fort to speak with him, only to immediately be sent back to the tower where you just were to continue the main story. This happens several times! It's hard to respect the incredible world that's been constructed and feel like you're in it when the quests feel so gamey and annoying like this--I understand that if I don't travel back and forth I won't see the progression of the backgrounds, which is amazing, but it feels like beautiful wallpaper over a hole.Overall it's a beautiful game that I really want to love, but the combat makes it not worth it for me. Maybe I'll replay the game in their easy mode where the fact that combat is terrible won't matter, but I'll probably just not pick it up again.

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence on getting this game during the Steam summer sale. It looked cool but from past experiences it could go either way. Thank Gaben it was fantastic.* Great art style combined with good audio design and the voice of Geralt as the narrator. * Very tight and satisfying gameplay. Not too easy, not too hard. Loved the different armor types and how you had to adapt to each fight. Would have loved some additional stats for your build, such as stamina. * Controls took me a little to adjust but overall they were very well mapped. * Level design was simple but effective. A little bit Hollow Knight but with way less platforming and metroidvania. Game design was very good as well although I didn't like the grinding quests. They were such a turn off. I would have loved to see them replaced with something actually relevant to the story.* Speaking of which, the story is fine. It serves its purpose and it kept me interested enough to pay attention to it.Overall I had a lot of fun playing this. I feel like there was a lot of potential that wasn't exploited but I can understand also wanting to publish your game already. More meaningful DLC should be a must for this game but I would have preferred a longer story. It didn't feel rushed but it could have had way more meat in it.Kudos to the developers of this game. Keep it up!8.6/10 - Very recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this game and love that the extra content is free. Still have some of that to go. Looking forward to the sequel which is why I finally dove in (been in my library for half a year now). Not going to do the same for the sequel, I'm playing that right on release!Cute style, unique and simplistic presentation and some customization in your gear are all welcomed and unexpected when I first dove in. I'd recommend buying it up especially if it's on sale. The only drawbacks I had were:1. with the UI and it not being quite clear what some gear is doing when I swap to the different weapon types regarding weight. In the gear chest menu, weight decreasing is shown as a green change in the bar while increased defense or damage is also shown in green while the opposite is shown in red. It's not a big deal, just something I had to figure out. 2. In certain environments and when health gets low, the lighting can affect how enemy telegraphs show.  Red unblockables/AoEs are pretty easy to differentiate but the Yellow counterable and white projectile telegraphs look similar and the lighting makes it tougher to register with sight/peripheral vision alone.It's a solid game. _childDocuments_.review: There's frustration, and then there's this game.You are locked in every animation you start, but not in good souls-like way, where the enemies are bound by the same rules as you. In the time it takes to lower your shield and start dodging the enemy will have performed his entire attack combo. Dodging has no invulnerability frames, and hitboxes are often inaccurate, leading to a lot of frustration. The lack of iframes (even after being hit) combined with the slow animations also means you can get stunlocked.All that combined lead to a style of combat where you can never be aggressive, you just wait and react.Movement is stiff and it's hard to even grab ledges on the first try.The hardest difficulty will just overtune every enemy to have a ton of health while you get two-shotted by the smallest ones. And since they don't respawn (most of the time), this encourages you to go back to the save bench every battle. It's a chore. And you can't change it halfway into the game.On top of that, it's one of those games that didn't bother having a decent control scheme for keyboard users (I mean, why would you test your game on an input that's only present in 100% of the platform you are releasing, the nerve of me).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a solid B+ game.  It has nice art, it's not too long or expensive, and there's nothing broken about the game.While it's solid in general, it also isn't doing anything amazing.  The combat is pretty shallow, and while all the enemies will telegraph their attacks, they don't always do it in a manner that actually helps you do avoid damage.The story goes for a darker tone and has some gory moments, but it does this in a manner that doesn't really  nail the tone.  Initially it appears to be a cutesy kind of game, then it leans hard into massacres, blood, and death, yet the game never really feels like it's handles this tonal shift correctly, so the whole game feels a little off.  On top of that, there are some elements to the game that don't ever really get explained, and the setting is a bit confusing.  It seems like a medieval setting, then it appears to be fantasy, than it appears to be post-apocalyptic, and then it goes to steam punk.  Bottom line, you're not likely going to be getting a ton out of this games story.The main draw of this game is the combat, and your mileage will vary.  If you like combat that punishes failure heavily and requires well thought out attacks, then you might like this game.  If you're easily frustrated or want combat with some depth, then this won't really be fun for you.  Even if you're into slow punishing combat, you'll likely find this game to be infuriating at times.  Some times the method of defense that you are forced to use in this game won't work and you'll die to an enemy that you shouldn't have.  In addition, there are many attacks that are given specific methods to avoid damage, and that method won't work because you didn't move the right direction, or at the right time, but the game gives you no method to discover the right direction or timing without dying first.  Essentially, the game has five types of attacks that an enemy can use: Normal (no hint), dodge-able attack (red lines), AoE attacks that must be avoided before they land (Red circle), parry able attacks (yellow lines), and projectiles (white lines).  Some normal attacks cannot be blocked, some dodge-able attacks will hit you when you try to dodge through them, the AoE attacks will come out uniquely to each enemy and many of them cannot be avoided without luck, and some projectile attacks will hit you even when you are defending (which is what you're taught to do to prevent damage).  You can beat the game even with these issues, but certain fights will involve a lot of trial and error until you understand how to avoid each attack and get lucky that you never deal with an attack that you cannot avoid/defend.if you want a shorter Souls-like game that involves anthropomorphic rats and frogs, then this game is great.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR;Short game with trash fights that are mostly a frustrating experience. Mostly depend on knowledge instead of skill and are definitely not souls likeThe game is quite short about 7 hours ( I have about 12 as I let the game run a bit in the background before finishing it) , which would be okay but it is also extremely padded. Meaning you not only have to run around a lot (often to locations you have already been) but also have to suffer through the tedious slow “dialog” of the game. All of the dialog except the narrator  is done via pictures in speech bubbles. Not only is this slow af and repetitive but also often completely unneeded as the narrator will often then put the pictures into words meaning you will see/hear the dialog twice. Overall I would say that about ~2-3 hours is spent not really playing or engaging with the game which is insane given the overall length of the game.The gear system is beyond pointless with 0 depth. They could just remove it, give you 1 of each basic weapon type and let the rest be skins. The game would play the same but you don't have to rebalance your weight every time you picked a new and objectively better weaponHowever, the worst thing are the battles. First off the game forces you to play completely reactionary. You have to wait for the enemy to do his attack -> dodge/parry and then you are allowed to attack. This is insanely tedious and there is no benefit to playing aggressively which makes fights often very very boring.Secondly the way the fights work is simply frustrating and mostly skill less. It's more about knowing than reacting. Which is a problem in a game with high enemy damage as not knowing mostly means death which means you have to redo stuff.Basically enemies can do the following and it comes down to this:(which the tutorial doesn't even tell you that they exist, very fun running into that I thought it was a bug). You can parry, block or dodge this. Which one should you do? Well that depends on the enemy and there's no way to know without experimenting. There are bosses where it is actually better to block than to parry cause the boss will keep doing a pattern that will guarantee you more damage (yes the “more” skillful action can be worse)Sadly many of those are very poorly animated/choreographed and when there are a group of enemies bunched up it's impossible to tell if one is attacking youYou need to parry them. The only type that is consistent mechanical wise but can still be frustrating as there is no uniform timing. Sometime the attack comes fast sometimes slow, sometimes it will contain a feint. You will learn it by mostly eating it or getting lucky.Both needed to be avoided by dodging through/away from them. What do you need to do exactly? Depends on the attack and the enemy. There is no way for you to know except by guessing. Which is really fun when these types of attack often take ½ of your hp.When you encounter an enemy  or boss for the first time you honestly have to guess on what to do there is no rhyme or reason. Some enemies can literally jump from one corner of the arena to the other during their unblockable or jump forwards and then backwards it's madness and a lesson in frustration.In addition the hitboxes are often bigger than the animations and often you will get hit despite dodging in the right directionwhich you have block but often give you nothing. you simply have to take them and wait for the enemy to do something else. Really fun in fights with multiple enemies as this can drag the fight out.Overall the game loop will be this. You encounter a new enemy and you will eat its attack. if its a boss you will die because the damage is just too high. You will learn by trial and error what to do and then first try the boss after you actually know what you are supposed to do. The fights at both boring and annoying knowledge checks and that's pretty much it

_childDocuments_.review: If you took the story of Red Wall and mixed it with the game mechanic and style of Hollow Knight, you would get Tails of Iron. _childDocuments_.review: Similar to Dark Souls as tag?I would give it Metroidvania instead. I mean, it is way much more this than the other tag, seriously.Aside from that mini rant, let's go to the game itself, shall we!?Tails of Iron is quite small for the length of it. But I was expected about it: Got me a bit longer than 8 hours to finish it and I didn't found everythings I need to fully found stuff around, including gears and sidequests items. The game is quite a small Corridor, Metroidvania type. I would consider it as similar as Monster Boy, Wonder Boy 3 in that matter. Yet, the combat system is heavily focused on a Rock-Paper-Scissors melee mechanic: Some attacks can dodge, while others can parry and the last ones can be blocked. Miss one of those and you can receive some sever punishments. As for the story, it is really narrative. With a dark theme of a fantasy world, rebuilding a ravaged kingdom over the course are what I wanted to pinpoint our attentions. Probably that's the reason why the game is more corridor oriented, rather than a labyrinth style like we know from Metroid games, Castlevania: Symphony of the Night or even Axiom Verge (here on Steam). But by doing so, the game offers more a panoramic view with a background being alive and very well represented.A funny thing that I love from that game is about the implantation of the musics against bosses or for some areas. I mean, possibly like in a Dark Souls game, there is no music, except a very few places and against bosses. In this game, to make it interesting, you have the musicians playing in the background to make the music against the bosses and so forth. Heck, you even meet a friendly npc with high tech gears that it has a pocket radio, playing some kind of 8-bit techno, helping you to fight against a boss. Basicly its radio song is the boss song. Quite funny to see these little details going.For a downside and I would agree with some reviewers here, the sidequests in the game can be quite redundant to do while gathering money to progress in the story. I aim more the hunter lodge sidequests where you do need to go in the sewers in almost at the same area, over and over, just to kill beetles. There was no variations at this point and it frustrated me. But after that, I enjoyed the rest.Tails of Iron is a good, short game. I haven't touched the expansion yet, but I will figure it out, soon enough. For about 8h to complete the story at normal difficulty, it worthed my time and my enjoyment to see the path of a little rat, started with nothing, becoming the king of his kingdom. A very well made game.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. What an absolute treasure of a game!From its darkest hours to its shining moments of hope, Tails of Iron is a souls like platformer that guaranteed to please any fan of the genre. As I fan of both the books Redwall and Souls-likes, this game is essentially my bread and butter for games I love. The combat is fast paced, tactical and surprisingly impactful. The music and sound design are incredibly immersive, and the artistic style of the graphics are just a gem to behold.Something I personally love about this game, is unlike some other souls like, the world changes from its grim dark hopeless setting, and is brought back from the brink of destruction by your own hand. When you save a town, you see buildings rebuild, shop keepers re-opening and people slowly coming back to normality. You feel like a true hero in this game, and honestly I find it a breath of fresh air from all the ever dark and depressing souls-like games on the market. I CANNOT recommending this game enough, it is so worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is a very good game that ended up being much better than I thought at first. Just enough of metroidvania and Souls-like mixed in a pot with emphasis on combat and dramatic story of young prince Redgi reclaiming his kingdom from perfidious frogs. With no way to grind for power you must rely on equipment alone to succeed as your journey takes you from rebuilding the castle to underground as you find new allies. Fast and brutal combat where learning how to parry makes a difference, anyone familiar with Souls games will be right at home. Bosses escalating in difficulty will certainly challenge you and I almost wish I played on high difficulty from the get-go. Not because the game was easy otherwise, but because now I'm just one achievement short of 100%-ing a game that deserves it.Sometimes you play a game that checks just enough boxes from multiple genres or schools of design that the end result is familiar, but still more than enjoyable. Taking cues from metroidvanias and Souls-like titles, Tails of Iron achieves precisely that. Does it hold up on its own merits, though?Following a long reign, King Rattus' legacy of having scoured the realm of dirty Pondscum is suddenly cut short when aforementioned frogs besiege his castle, do away with his life and leave only couple of accidental survivors. Young prince Redgi among them as he swears revenge. So begins his quest to not only get his father's vassals to accept him as the rightful heir, since he's so small in stature and many favor his brother, but also to eradicate the frogs everyone thought were gone for many years. There are also other challenges in store taking him beyond and below what any common folk would think possible.Even though characters, rats or otherwise, don't use words but rather pictograms to communicate, Tails of Iron got a chuckle out of me multiple times as Redgi is self-aware enough to acknowledge he's doing everyone's busywork that normally his retainers should be all over instead. If only he had some. Pulling a lot of the weight is Doug Cockle serving as game's narrator and he doesn't fail to deliver a snide or cynical remark while carrying this Game of Thrones meets folk tale atmosphere. Characterization overall is pretty lacking, though. If you ask me I'd point fingers to narrative department as a whole taking the backseat since storytelling isn't the primary focus here so don't the RPG treatment or such. As the story advances and reaches post-game you have a marriage of things become really dire the closer to finale you get... and then various puns on wrestlers, musicians, etc. Who can forgetting squaring up against Molehammad Moli in the arena?It may be an easily overlooked aspect of the game as you're rushing from sidequests to the main quest, but I absolutely loved how the world kept fixing itself. Gradually, a ruined town gets repaired and royal guards are now securing the castle, for example. This is all fluff since the game isn't reactive in a meaningful way, but it's still nice to see even sidequests have visual feedback. Later on you get to spend some gold on castle ornaments bringing it even further to life. This also means you sometimes don't want to fast travel between sign posts, but take a stroll and see the changes.This is, however, an action game so let's get down to some nitty-gritty details and how the entire things works. I was surprised by how much emphasis there is on combat in comparison to very basic platforming or even customary “re-visit areas to progress with new powers” metroidvania design. Being a Souls-like is much close to Tails of Iron's ethos.Despite lacking a dimension compared to Souls titles which took gaming by storm, here we have a game that very much subscribes to many of those tenants while eschewing others. Perhaps to accommodate scaled back format? Providing you go with the recommended gamepad control scheme shoulder buttons will be your light, heavy and block functions, with the last one dedicated to healing. You get one jug of Grub Juice which you use for that purpose, but in a twist it doesn't recharge when you rest on a bench to save progress. Instead, you have to find juice dispensers or butcher grubs for smaller refills. It's good news those, as well as other goodies, are spread out decently across almost ten locations. Travel only becomes a chore when you have a specific sidequest and it's at the very end of a locations where there's no fast travel signpost nearby. Areas re-populate with enemies, but Tails of Iron doesn't subscribe to “every enemy can easily kill you” so it's just more of a hindrance. Such escapades become an easy way to loot for resources you'll rarely use.There's also no concept of experience to speak of as your character progression comes entirely from equipment. What can Regni use then? As far as armor goes you have slots for helmet, armor and shield, but alongside those your have murderous implements with sword & board, two-handed and ranged weapon slots. In my opinion there's too much equipment and it really becomes apparent towards the end when game starts throwing complete sets at you. Maybe there's a purpose to those if you haven't killed couple of side bosses who net you some of the best stuff in the game, but I do appreciate this extensive variety means you can play dress up and go with whatever Regni looks best in. Want a kingly crown? Plenty of those under light helmets. Want a riot shield? It's there. Want to cosplay as a samurai? Well, you get some look-alike armor AND a katana. Keep in mind you want to rotate and replace equipment as you're constantly finding better pieces, need some armor for resistances against frogs or alike, and you need to manage weight.Which pulls me back to combat since that's the bulk of what you'll be doing when you're not completing chores for the townsfolk as, by Thor, someone needs to clear the cellar of monsters. I survived by simple mantra: PARRY IS KING. Dodging also ranks highly for those unavoidable flashing red attacks or AoEs, but dodging is dependent on how heavy Regni is based on your gear whereas that perfect block will do so much more for you. Especially if you get it right for yellow-telegraphed attacks which are made to be parried. Game will also keep surprising you with enemy variety as you can exploit them as well rather than reserving “special moves” just for bosses. My one regret is devs should've pushed the player harder to master parry earlier. Already mentioned Molehammad Moli is one of those optional, post-game arena bosses... yes, there's both an arena and post-game stuff, who will punish you with his bee stings, but that lesson arrives way too late. Since I brought up bosses there is a steady escalation of threats and player performance expectations. Looking at my time played I've probably spent an hour or so repeating boss fights. It's a learning curve and not a learning cliff, is what I'm trying to say here.Presentation I left for last because game looks just plain gorgeous. If you ever wanted a 2D Redwall game this is it and that aesthetic carries the day. Some animations, particularly brutal executions Regni gets to perform, are sometimes wonky because there's a bit too much pushing and pulling to get the actors into correct positions, but that's negligible in the grand scheme of things. Soundtrack is all over the place, but just give me more strings. Frogs sure love their bongos, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Tails of Iron is an excellent game and perfectly sized at around 10-15 hours in length! Full-price is a little steep if you're considering dollar spent vs. hours played but there is a high level of production value here that can justify the full-price if you can't wait for a sale. My favorite element of this game is the dynamic artwork. As you progress through the story, you'll see certain areas develop or change over time which is neat because it makes you feel like your efforts in-game have weight to them. All of the locations are visually interesting and map traversal is a mostly quick and painless affair (a saving grace because there is a fair bit of backtracking in this game). There is so much visual detail packed into a game that could have gotten away with far less so kudos to the dev team for going above and beyond.On a different note, the combat was fun for the most part but could definitely get annoying at times. While I appreciate the 'rock-paper-scissors' aspect to how enemies telegraph attacks vs. how the player should react, the players movement often felt clunky. Dodge-rolling and blocking feels inconsistent/imprecise and enemies can stun-lock you because of how long it takes to recover after hits and how slow your movement is. Despite its minor shortcomings, the combat was never too frustrating or difficult that I couldn't overcome challenging fights after a few tries. Other reviewers seem to blow their load over the in-game narrator being the guy who voices Geralt in Witcher 3. Honestly? Who cares....In my opinion, the narration was one of the weaker elements of the game. There are a few instances of inflection and quality narration but, for the most part, it's just some gravelly sounding man blandly reading lines. That's right - I said it. FIGHT ME, NERDS!:Pros:- Fantastic art- Solid sound design / music- Straightforward story with appropriate amount of side-quests- Character customization- Challenging combat:Cons:- Lots of backtracking- Player movement/attack speed- Lack of variety in finishing moves- Game starts to drag on a bit by the end

_childDocuments_.review: The game offers a combination of a unique artstyle, fun gameplay, and the voice of Geralt from witcher narrating a typical adventure game in which you perform side scrolling, dark souls combat to commit genocide on the  evil Frog Kingdom. The game has does not have a rpg skills mechanic so there is a minimal grind, though it does become slightly repetitive transitioning between stages and areas fighting mobs. The map and world is designed beautifully, which certainly does help but going through the sewers 5x does wear out the novelty a bit. One thing which is a slight critique is the game gives you quests for the sake of having a quest/objective. For example, in the first mission you are told to grab nails to repair the fast travel 'carriage' by the NPC, which just happen to be right next to said NPC in a nearby corpse. Mission accomplished I suppose?The game offers three difficulties, Easy, normal, and 'bloody whiskers'. While the game is fun, this game mode is beatable but becomes deadly infuriating as the game progresses. There are three main reasons for this. The first is that the game does not have I-frames, and dodging becomes as a way to move past a target or move away an enemy attack. This means positioning becomes incredibly important as wrong position will mean death and even correctly performing a dodge can still result in your getting hit. Getting hit also means instant death in many scenarios as the enemy attacks very rapidly, able to follow up immediately to kill you afterwards. The second is that certain attacks *must* be blocked a certain way, however, this is also incorrect due to the previous mentioned flaw. For instance, a 'red' heavy attack indicator means it must be dodged is unblockable- however, your dodges are still able to be hit during the dodge as it does not perform an i-frame and *After* the dodge as the enemy immediately follows up. Certain bosses such as Red Wart also have high mobility/teleport moves which means your attack window is non-existent in some scenarios. It creates a frustrating mental juggling where you must not only dodge a distinctive but somewhat random enemy pattern, you must do so while maintaining positioning in the center of the map as dodging towards the edge of the map means you cannot rely on an i-frame dodge to avoid attacks which must be dodged but provide no invulnerability for performing said dodge.A third note is that unlike games which feature a bosses doing interesting move sets, enemies in this game respond on a color system which is somewhat inaccurate. *Circle* attacks must be dodged away and yet there are bosses which have circle attacks which require you to both dodge away OR towards the enemy, and there is a split second to determine which is the correct position to dodge as they both use the same attack indicators. The enemies are 2d and thus provide no real way to predict or use enemy body language to determine the mode of attack, and it is wholly reliant on having a reaction time equal or great to a CS:GO esports player or being Kirito from SAO.All in all, still a fun game and even playing blood whiskers mode it was enjoyable until up to the midway point where the attacks became too dizzing to follow up. While some people will compare the hardest difficulty level as a dark souls like challenge, its more accurate to call it an Epileptic version of Dance dance revolution where tapping too much to the left/right will kill you and some moves actually require you to hit the opposite step despite what shows up on your screen.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art design, crippled by poor gameplay mechanics, particularly the combat. fights feel more like a chore rather than a challenge you want to overcome, especially when the enemies literally telegraph in various colors what they are about to do. battles also move very slow. a majority of fights just feels like waiting to react to the color the incoming attack. even the roll dodge doesnt facilitate outmaneuvering the enemy, rather being more of a reaction to one of the color coded attacks. you get a choice of weapon types (sword, ax, spear) but they all end up playing the way, with similar damage, range, and speed, without any significant differences in how you approach a fight. Tons of backtracking and pretty unnecessary traveling to do. for example, having three consecutive quests lead me to kill bugs in the same sewer area, and having to travel back and forth each time to complete and start a new one was frustrating. it would also be amazing if they rid of fall damage, or at least change the threshold for it, cause nobody wants to spend the time to climb down every latter. Geralt narrating your adventure is definitely cool as hell, but the unskipable "dialog" with the other rats just get annoying after a while. like yes i know i need a key, i dont need a 15 second slideshow about how a key will open a lock. its a cute idea to tell the rats dialog through pictures, but it would be nice to be able to fast forward it. Cant understand why theres a souls-like tag attached to the game. then again, they say everything is a souls game as long as its got some "dark atmosphere". but with how linear the game is, coupled with the low difficulty level, its a lot more arcade than souls.

_childDocuments_.review: What a conundrum. It's very pretty, there's a lot of attention to detail, combat feels good, and the story is simple but engaging. And yet the latter half is a horrible drag and the difficulty and combat design cause frustration rather than fun. I did beat it in the end, and I'm happy I did; the game really makes you care about little Redgi and his rat people. And now I'm fully equipped to help you figure out if this is something you'd like to play.Let's start with the obvious. It's so pretty. Feels like an old-timey fairy tale picture book. But that's not all - the environments constantly change as you turn the tide against the Frog invaders. Towns get repaired, NPCs come and do stuff, junk gets cleared, new structures show up. It's great, running through a town over and over seeing it look different every time.The story is grim. It might be a game about cute animals, but their plight is not cute at all. I actually respect the devs for the courage to make things as grim as they did, considering the subject matter. But don't worry - it's not TOO grim; it's a story about hardships and perseverance above all else.And finally, you can equip Redgi with so many pieces of gear. Sadly, it mostly feels like just dress-up with some numbers; fighting feels mostly the same no matter the weapon, and armour never really feels like it protects you. As in, you're still going to get your face bashed in by some attacks. I believe I mentioned the combat feels good. Yes, it does, against regular enemies. But as soon as bosses show up... it stops being fun. This one is a little hard to explain, but let me try:All enemies, including bosses, do a little colour-coded telegraph of what they're going to do next. Mainly it shows whether this attack is blockable or not. But most attacks are unblockable, and dodging doesn't really work the way you'd think. And since this IS a soulslike, you'll get hit -hard-. So what are you supposed to do? Can't block, can't dodge?The answer is: constantly watch the distance and simply predict what the boss will do. Sounds fun? Didn't think so. It makes combat frustrating and not enjoyable at all; and if you try to get greedy and get some hits where you're 'not allowed to' you get punished hard, and often have to redo. It's possible to heal, but it's much slower than in, say, Dark Souls, so healing is often just asking for more trouble.And there are a LOT of bosses. So many. At some point you can't continue the story because you need a certain item, and to get the item you need gold, and to get gold you need to fight more bosses. They don't even feel that different, even though they clearly are. This is a huge strike against the game, and since in the latter half the bosses get REALLY hard, you'll be just bashing your little rat head against the same fight, until you learn to predict what the boss does and patiently execute the proper 'dance'.So even though the fighting sucked, exploring the world was interesting enough to keep me hooked. But let's be honest: the main reason why I saw this through is because I understand how the dev felt on a very personal level.You see, this game is a memorial to their passed friends, the rats. In the options menu there is a cute hand-drawn picture of all the 'real' rats that the characters in the game are incarnations of. If you ever bonded with an animal friend, you'll immediately understand how emotionally important this is. Paying my respects to the love between living beings depicted here was the least I could do - that's why I followed Redgi to the very end.That's all I have to say. I didn't cover everything the game has to offer, but I think you should now have a good idea whether you'd like to play this or not. I recommend it in the end, because while the game is deeply flawed, the first half is a -blast-. If you ignored the side quests and just went straight on, chances are the momentum of that blast would carry you all the way to the end. I did the side quests; I don't recommend it. I do recommend the game, though. Enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: Art is simple and stylized but really nice.The game has his own style, a deep voiced narrator who definitely talks too much, an overall rich enough sound department, a complete if unoriginal ost and a marginal lore. Nothing new or legendary under the sun but more than pleasant and game itself quite large and full of challenges, especially with the criminally cheap DLC.The mission system is a bore, you run around one quest at a time through half of this game is going from point A to point B with nothing happening. But the characters are nice and the adventure itself engaging enough for a run or two.Combat system is fast paced and simple, quite challenging but waaay too old-fashioned: almost completely based on trial on error for literally all bosses (of which there are dozens) and overall not rewarding a good player but simply a player who got to know the AoE and teleporting dance of each absurdly moving boss by memory.Then,...then there's hard mode, which I've forced myself through for my 100%.Hard mode is where I look at the developers in the eyes and wish I could throw actual rats at them.This "Mode" means not faster or stronger bosses but simply bosses capable of attacking two three times more with their constant barrage of unblocklables or half-screen AoE and decimate your full bar even by grazing you with an arrow because quite literally almost EVERYTHING IS AN AOE FOR NO REASON.Furthermore, you can't cancel. Which means if you have begun attacking, you're locked until animation completion, if you've initiated dodging or blocking, you're locked until animation completion. In a fast-paced combat game, this is a nightmare.Hard Mode is where, with no possibility to "Git Gud", you'll find yourself either spending a PhD worth of time analysing every boss like I did, or chuck the PC off the balcony like I wanted to do many times.- This doesn't have the complexity of Sekiro, the combat system of DS, this is a 2d side-scroller, if your protagonist is the weakest, slowest, less agile, less capable character on screen, then you should rely on timing, mechanics like timed parry, cancel, etc... to rely solely on gimmicks, cheesing the game and pattern finding has NEVER made a good game, in history, never. It's boring and frustrating for all the wrong reasons.- If in a game where you die constantly, after each death, you character has to stare at the rainy sky pondering about meaning of it all for 4 full seconds each and every time, people will 100% hate your game, physically.Food for thought, Devs.*EDIT: I'm adding close to a full mark, as usual, due to good company behaviour and granting a GREAT DLC and little bonus packs here and there for free or with huge discounts. Well done Odd Bug! Do better with the sequel! More than decent game, buy for casual use. Achievement hunter/completionists? Begin at your own risk! Hard Mode is where the basic Nintendo-level combat system this game has will push you to kill small critters, in real life, possibly frogs.

_childDocuments_.review: i've never left a negative review before, but here goes.  i wanted to like this game, but right away the game was messed up for me because you cannot change the controller options.  this makes no sense, i've never heard of a game that actually didn't let you change your controller layout.  it even suggests playing with a controller, but why suggest a controller if you can't set it the way you want?  anyway after some fiddling around, i managed to change the button inputs in the "controller setup" option through steam, and it worked ... for about five minutes.  literally while i was in the middle of playing (trying to get the food from the basement, i hadn't even started combat yet) the controls randomly switched back to their defaults.  the controls changed in mid-game and even though they were still changed on steam, the game had returned to their defaults and nothing i did could fix it.  it is the most baffling and incomprehensible thing i've ever experienced in a video game.  i've read some other reviews and comments from people have problems with their controllers, so i'm not the only person who had trouble with this.  sadly i'm not wasting anymore time on this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Seriously, I do not get all these positive reviews. For me, this game is mediocre at best. Good things first: The graphics are nice and the narrator does a pretty good job. The not-so-good things: everything else. The story is near to non-existant, sometimes hints at deeper secrets (like in the crypt) but never gets to them. With the kind of tasks you are meant to do this game should be called "errand boy". I mean, they have a whole kingdom destroyed by frogs and you have to rebuild it and avenge your fathers death. What kind of an epic story arc could that provide! And what do the devs do? They send you on all kinds of mediocre and uninteresting side-quests that do not advance the story a bit and if left out, nobody would notice it. Combat is more like a chain of quick-time events: in other games (e.g. Hollow Knight, Grime, Salt and Sanctuary) you study your opponent and act according to his telegraphed attacks. Here, since they could not be bothered to make the attackes to be clearly distinguishable, and icon above above the enemy, and there is one reaction to every of the 3 attack types that you should do to counter it. That's nothing more then QTE, and badly executed. I do not look for the enemies movement, just for the icons. Maybe that could even be funny, but movement feels so unresponsive and squishy, that it is really no fun to either move through the levels nor to fight. Also, the companions that you have some times do, well, it is pretty close to nothing. I played until the last boss to see whether it would get better - spoiler alert - it does not. Could not be bothered to play the DLC. From what I saw it is just reskinned enemies of the maingame with some of their attacks combined. Sorry for the devs, the graphics look really nice, maybe you had the best of intentions, but Hollow Knight and Salt & Sanctuary are a complete different league.
_childDocuments_.name: Tails of Iron

_childDocuments_.review: Starts off with an annoying tutorial, but then becomes very good.Gameplay, atmosphere, and all the details are good and it's easy to get hooked.The first proper boss you meet, does attacks that can only be avoided if you are far away from the enemy. Instead of doing attacks that you can then duck away from, he does 2 or 3 in a row, and so fast that getting away at times is impossible. To make this fight even harder, they added another enemy right next to the boss which let's face it has to die first. Before this, the game was hard but rewarding and fair. At this point, it borderlines what's called false difficulty, which is just annoying. (And this coming from a demon souls/dark souls/sekiro veteran. What From Software manages to do are boss fights that are insanely difficult, which still feels fair without the use of these lazy methods that would make their games annoying or boring.)Because it's safe to assume that the developers have made more of these lazy bosses (Edit: Yes, the other bosses are equally dreadful for various reasons), I can't recommend this game, and will refund before the 2 hour limit has been reached.Edit: There are too many annoyances in this game to mention. The devs have removed some annoyances like having to loot two mobs who are right next to each other individually, but then added a bunch of annoyances instead. It feels like they tried to do something like a souls like, on a low budget, while also using an expensive voice actor for narration (which isn't needed as the story is also told through game play and chat bubbles), and also trying to reinvent the wheel with the health bar system, dodge system and prompt system. Why not just spend the money on making the game better instead of throwing the money away on dumb decisions and then add padding to the game to make it longer? If there is ever a Tails of Iron 2, that's the game to buy. This one is the "could've been" prequel, which could inspire greatness, is itself filled with potential, but ends in disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Goriest non-gore game that I recall. Each fight you end up with at least few splashed of bug\frog\mole "not blood juice" on you. More intense ones have you coloured from head to toes, moreover wounds and splashes are also displayed on your enemies - from average grunts to bosses that got more beat up longer you fight.Also this is just awesome game - especially if you have read\watched Redwall in days of yore. Plot while mostly being typical is supplemented by humour, world design and quirks of population consisting of mice, frogs, moles, grubs etc. with some of their unique lifestyle and food preferences. Besides taking place in medieval fantasy, there is just a touch of magic existing, but not as moving force, just adding tiny bit of spice. There are also some unusual tech things to balance that unscientific hocus pocus.Graphic design is breathtaking - all those cute little mouse whiskers, crude and primal frog weapons, appendages flying away sometimes as enemy is killed are combines in a style that is both very adorable\kid friendly and brutal\rugged.Audio is fitting for whatever is happening and wherever you are walking through, changing depending on location feels and action or calm on screen.Gameplay is similar to adventure game more than rpg - you travel around, doing quests and felling beasts, collecting new armour\weapons. There is almost no character development and no exp, lvling, skills. Combat though is quite unforgiving - you carry only around one full healthbar amount of healing liquid with you and hp regains while you continuously drink your lifejuice, meaning it takes a while, you're slowed while doing it and you're very much vulnerable at that time. There are 4 general types of attacks from enemy - normal hits that you could dodge, block or parry, yellow hits that require parry, red hits that needs to be avoided and white attacks that need some wind-up like parry\avoidance ones, but could be dealt with as normal hits. And I think all mobs have at least 3 of those 4 types of attacks, so even low level schmuck might require combination of defensive moves. Besides bosses with their mostly unique moveset fight with rank and file monsters could be even harder due to sheer number of them and how they combine their attacks, not giving a moment of rest, sometimes practically stunlocking.Developers also did awesome work in supporting the title with free expansions that add quite the amount of new content.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, it's probably my own damn fault for buying a Soulslike when I generally hate Soulslikes. But I  did not enjoy this one, as much as I wanted to. I loved reading Redwall while growing up. It has an interesting art style and so on.Also, I'm a furry, so there's that.These were not enough to salvage a game with truly bewildering hitboxes--a concept utterly crucial to have locked down airtight for Soulslikes. Instead, it was just depressing and sadistic, with interspersed moments that felt actually unfair to the player instead of merely to the protagonist (another cardinal sin, even for the genre).Like any game, there will be people who adore this game, surely. I, however, cannot be one of them. I have put up with Gitting Gud for a number of games better than this at feeling worthwhile (the Monster Hunter series, for instance, which I've expended far too many hours of my life upon), so it is not merely that I am not up to the challenge; indeed, I finished Tales of Iron's campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a soulslike lite for non-hardcore semi-masochists like me. The fights are challenging but manageable and there are save points a plenty. There is quite a bit of nuance beneath the simple looking cover, though. The story itself might be a bit run of the mill, but the presentation...oh, mama. The artwork, the animations, the cuteness of it all. I love the musicians in the background that actually play the boss combat music! And last but not least, the narration. <3Throw in a free expansion together with a very reasonable price and I AM SOLD. Very enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Set in a grim land plagued by war, Tails of Iron is a hand-drawn RPG Adventure with punishingly brutal combat. As Redgi, heir to the Rat Throne, you must restore your broken Kingdom by banishing the merciless Frog Clan and their ferocious leader, Greenwart. As you explore the deceivingly charming world, you'll encounter a cast of unique companions, ready to aid you in your adventure. And you'll need all the help you can get, whether that's new meal recipes, blueprints to forge deadly weapons and armour, or even a land-chugging, armour-plated mole mobile! Overcome your fears. Rescue your brothers. Restore Your Kingdom. Your tail has begun. Master Brutal Combat: From frog zombies to gargantuan grubs - and everything in-between - the Kingdom is awash with danger. To overcome each perilous encounter, you'll need to study your opponent's attacks and react accordingly! Thankfully, there's a range of deadly abilities at your disposal, including parry bashes and fatal executions, not to mention ranged attacks with your nifty bow and arrow. Explore a Treacherous Kingdom: Fully accompanied by the deep, raspy narrations of Doug Cockle (voice of Geralt of Rivia from The Witcher), prepare to embark on an epic adventure across the mediaeval-fantasy Rat Kingdom. Complete side quests and faction hunts for some additional gold-on-the-side, or join forces with a sharp-eyed companion to help even the playing field. Customise your Attack: Adapt Redgi's combat style to the task at hand. Heavy armour may provide better protection but can you really afford to slow down your dodge-roll? And then there's the question of weapon; axes pack a punch, while spears are quick and nimble. Perhaps you'd prefer the all-round performance of a trusty broadsword?

name: Chariots of War
detailed_description: Chariots of War is an operational real-time game where you can play one of 58 different nations on a huge historically accurate and beautiful map covering the entire Middle East! Build up your cities and keep their inhabitants happy by crating temples, entertainment and other building or deal with angry revolters. Control the Cradle of Civilization! 4000 years ago in the Cradle of Civilization, mighty Empires fought for water, resources and the arable land in the Fertile Crescent. Play as the Egyptians, the Babylonians, screaming Nubian warriors, or the Assyrians. Develop your county by producing commodities and selling them to you neighbors. Raise glorious armies and wage wars of conquest. Roll over the plains and seek victory in Chariots of War! Immerse yourself in Chariots of War. Build hundreds of buildings and city improvements, and collect 9 different resources such as Myrrh, Gems and Horses. Put your General in command of your army fighting real-time battles under the fog of war. Protect the inhabitans from roving barbarian tribes bent on attacking anything in their path. The Happiness and welfare of the inhabitants of your cities will depend on overpopulation, recruitment levels, garrisons and food, and by developing temples, entertainment and other buildings you keep revolution at bay. Recruit units from nearly thirty different troop types for you invincible armies. Barbarian tribes will roam the land, attacking anything they encounter. Trade allows you to buy and sell the 9 resources. Different areas of the map have access to different resources so trade is key. Diplomats can be sent out to gather information. You can eject enemy diplomats in a number of gory ways. Build your armies and wage a campaign to control the Cradle of Civilization!

name: The Planet Crafter
detailed_description: Embark on a chill experience alone or with up to 10+ friends in online co-op. Your mission is to survive on a hostile planet and turn a barren land into a lush paradize. Terraforming is the only way! You are sent on a hostile planet with one mission: Make it habitable for Humans. You'll have to survive, collect resources, build your base, produce machines to heat the planet, create an oxygen-rich atmosphere and eventually geo-engineer an entire planet! Gather minerals and resources to survive. Craft all the tools you need to fulfill your mission. Explore old shipwrecks and ruins and discover a planet full of mysteries! You'll need a base and all sorts of machines to make yourself at home, and be able to bring life to this planet! Progress through building tiers to upgrade and expand your base and explore the planet further. See life forms appear on the planet as you terraform it by increasing heat, oxygen and pressure. Witness the first signs of life with moss and insects and unleash the planet's full potential with thick forests and animals. From chill to hardcore, choose the difficulty level that suits you. Play with starting presets to create new games and experience endless possibilities. Multiplayer: survive by yourself or with friends (1-10+ online co-op) Survival: Thirst, Oxygen, Temperature and Health mechanics Base Building: shelter from a hostile environment and expand your exploration Crafting: equipment, tools and food to help you survive Terraformation: turn an entire hostile planet to a habitable paradise! Build machines to create atmospheric pressure and heat the planet Create a biosphere with breathable oxygen See your environment change as your terraformation progresses Creatures: create life by decrypting and mixing DNA extracts and make your own animals Procedurally generated shipwrecks: explore and find infinite rare loot Chill experience with no violence: the only enemy you'll have to fight is the hostile environment Adjustable difficulty to fit your level Adjustable presets for renewed experiences through time Creative mode

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting start to something with great potential.If you've played Subnautica, then imagine a very stripped-down, early prototype of the game. There are a lot of similarities between the two: you're alone on a barren planet and can build structures from the raw materials lying around. However, much of the elements that make Subnautica so memorable are completely absent here. There is nothing on the planet surface but rocks and dirt. No animals, no plants, no thermal vents, no alien artifacts, no aliens, no biomes, no character.In Subnautica, basic resources are plentiful at the beginning, but you soon realize that the more advanced items require materials that are only found in more dangerous areas. This game  has none of that. Resources are strewn about the surface like someone dropped a bag of marbles around your drop pod. There's no rhyme or reason to their placement. Just run about and gather up the highly visible objects on the ground.Crafting is very weak. There are no components to build; you go from raw materials directly to finished product in one go. Some items, like a wind turbine require a single chunk of iron to build. You could have a field of wind turbines within minutes if you wanted. Scarcity is non-existent.The concept of the game is to terraform the planet. There are a handful of variables that go into that, such as pressure and temperature. Within the game mechanics, you raise each of those levels, you get a terraformed planet. These variables correspond to a device; a surface drill raises the pressure. A 'heater' raises the temperature. A water cooler with a plant in it raises the oxygen levels. The thing is, that a single instance of these tiny devices are enough to slowly transform the planet. The more you build of each one, and the more advanced versions you build will get you there faster, but you could set up one of each, and just sit and wait. You would need food and water, but that's it. You could beat the game just finding ice and food packets strewn about the surface. That's not only immersion breaking game mechanics, but it's just poor game design.This has a ton of potential. Maybe they'll retool the mechanics to make some resources harder to find. Maybe they'll redo the terraforming elements to be more believable and more interesting to perform.Maybe they'll figure out a way to work in some kind of story element. Maybe they'll add biomes and realistic placement of resources.That's a lot of maybes standing between this and a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game in its own right. Completely terraforming the planet and then starting a new game really makes you appreciate all of your hard work when you see the contrast. I can't recommend this game enough based on that synthetic feeling of accomplishing something monumentally important with your life that most of us are doomed to never experience for real.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Land on sad planet. Job to make happy. Water plop, grass grow, and I FIRE OFF AS MANY ROCKETS AT ONCE AS POSSIBLE.Visuals: Decent overall. Nothing to complain about, but certainly isn't going to make you think you're on a desert planet.Sound: A bit... buggy isn't quite the right word, but the sounds can cut off at the end randomly, and some feel a bit out of place. There's really only some ambient music, but really nothing to complain about (or write home about)Gameplay: Honestly, very fun when you have things to do. Unfortunately, some of the benchmarks you have to reach are way up there, and it's easier to go AFK than to build anything else/send 30 more rockets up. So while I have 51 hours logged, 15-20 of that is probably AFK. 30 hours for an early access game is purty good though, and it's definitely entertaining.Controls: 10/10, would control again. Especially the flying up walls backwards parts to get over solid objects and clip into the world.Story: Consider it to be the next George R.R. Martin book; unfinished. I won't rate it, because it barely exists at this moment, but there's some intrigue that could come into play. I give it my official not rating rating of 7 out 4 tree spreaders.Overall: As it stands as an early access game; 7.5 to 8 out of 10. A lot of fun things to do for 20-30 hours before you reach the end of what's available and don't feel the need to come back to it until the next update is out.I suggest grabbing it if you like base building sans combat or vehicles in a small to moderate sized world. Just know remember that it's not finished and the devs have some big plans, so once you finish what's available, you might be waiting weeks/months for the next big thing to accomplish. Is good.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give a "meh" review. There are some really neat ideas in this game, and I generally enjoyed the early game exploring, but holy crap, does this ever become a "watch the numbers go up" grindfest to get to the end of it. I got an ending - I suspect there are multiple - after 67 hours, and I would say I enjoyed about half to 2/3 of those hours. I could have done some things more efficiently throughout to speed up progress, but whatever. This is a game that's trying to dip its toes in the Satisfactory/Factorio water, but it's absolutely not one of those, and it doesn't run nearly as well as either of them. I suppose it's a difficult thing to balance, but I wish they had increased the amount of exploring to do and reduced the amount of grinding to do. If I'm not mistaken, that's 0/3 for me on games rated overwhelmingly positive in the last year or so. I'm beginning to not trust you guys.

_childDocuments_.review: Planet Crafter : A Richly Detailed, and Addictive Sandbox ExperiencePlanet Crafter invites players into a richly detailed sandbox where creativity knows no bounds, offering a mesmerizing journey into the depths of creation and exploration. Visually, Planet Crafter is gorgeous, not top of the line graphics gorgeous, but gorgeous nonetheless. What it might lack in shortcomings in flashy effects, it makes up for in almost every other category of the game. This game pulls you in, and pulls you in hard. What truly sets Planet Crafter apart is its addictive gameplay and flawless execution. From the moment you dive into the game, you're greeted with a sense of endless possibilities. Whether you're terraforming lush landscapes, building up your base, or crafting a multitude of different items, every action feels meaningful and rewarding.The fun factor of Planet Crafter is undeniable. There's an inherent thrill in experimenting with different building techniques, exploring new biomes, and pushing the limits of your creativity. Much like Subnautica, Planet Crafter instills a sense of discovery and wonder as you delve deeper into its world, uncovering hidden secrets and unlocking new possibilities. This game also gives you the apprehension that Subnautica created. You all know what I am talking about, we were afraid to move 10 feet away from our pod in that game, and the world seemed so huge and dangerous. It is exactly the same thing here, the player will feel that apprehension, and slowly build confidence as they progress throughout the game. Moreover, Planet Crafter offers a staggering amount of replay value. With a vast array of tools and options at your disposal, no two creations are ever alike. Whether you're a seasoned builder or a newcomer to the genre, there's always something new to discover and create.In conclusion, Planet Crafter is a masterclass in sandbox game design that offers a rich and immersive experience, addictive gameplay, and endless creativity combinations that create a truly unforgettable adventure. If you're a fan of sandbox games, building games, or survival games, well, you've got it all with this one, and on a scale not seen since the likes of Subnautica. Planet Crafter is an absolute must-play. 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Updating my review as of 2024;Yes, I still recommend this game! They added multiplayer and I ended up beating the entire (current) game cycle in 80 hours with my husband. _childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this is addicting. Kind of similar to how Forager was, in terms of always wanting to see what the next build is and stuff, but way more rewarding than games like that, because as you're doing stuff, the world is getting more beautiful around you. There's also a little geological / geographical mystery to uncover that's extremely rewarding when you reach the end of it. It's like three or four games in one! I'm really excited to see how the developer builds this game out in the future. It's already well worth the money. It does have some minor graphical glitches, and if you troll a bit by jetpacking against the terrain in weird ways you can get to places you obviously aren't meant to, but beyond that it's worth it. _childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable, but after exploring everywhere and gathering loads of resources, becomes a bit of a waiting game rather than playing. Not sure if the teleporters will allow goods to be carried, but I'm not close to getting them yet. _childDocuments_.review: So I've invested 51 hour into it. It's marked as 1.0 at the time of this review and here are my thoughts.There might be some minor spoilers. TLDR: if you've finished subnautica and want something more casual for a weekend you can give this one a go. Personally I think it's more like 70% done and as of 1.0 version is still needs some work to be done on it.What I like:- from mid game it's less grindy because of mining possibilities and drones- planet condition changing (wouldn't call it terraforming cause you can't change landscape that much, just "nature" part a bit)- once again, unless you go for a certain ending it's doesn't give an impression of constantly crafting same things manually.What I don't like:- jet pack. The most annoying thing in this game. Other games just use space and control to go up and down. This game forces you to look into direction of where you wish to fly and use "w". It's frustrating, especially if you made some platforms in mid air for your base.- platforms clipping into terrain\rocks. Second most irritating thing. Sometimes it doesn't allow to place a platform, but if you wobble your mouse a bit around it will allow placing at the exact same spot. This inconsistency is kinda bad.- story MAJOR SPOILERS  - wrecks investigation - trading needs some rebalance. Only 3 things  felt worth of selling in late game. - i don't really get why i need to look for more seeds when i already have some growing at my farms.- meteor showers are just irritating from mid game. give me at least a blaster cannon turret to shoot them down. the mess they leave and shaking while i am trying to build something is just pissing me off. Not to mention all the mess from resources lying around EVERYWHERE.- i would love to see some mechanics like sand storms (slow or blow away player) or acid rains (damage health) in early game - building underground or inside terrain in general. Seems like every other person crashed on the planet was able to do that, but not me.- some sort of balancing and dependence on each other for flora and fauna would be nice. Imagine having 1000 koalas and one bamboo. How would an ecosystem survive that? Maybe even degrading biosphere or slowing down at growth least. so overall it's kinda ok and have some potential, but if you haven't played subnautica add 3-4$ more and go for it instead. otherwise it looks way too similar and lagging behind.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the game. Sure, there's some areas in need of improvements, overall, the game is just fun to play. It feels rather realistic in terms of how it would go. _childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I'm taking crazy pills after how good the reviews are for this game. I felt like I was fighting the inventory and short oxygen timer more than enjoying the game. I'm sent on a mission to terraform a planet, but my oxygen tank doesn't even last a minute out of the gate?- You're going to need to bring extra oxygen tanks to top yourself off for the first few hours when you want to go outside for more than a minute or two.- Items/materials do not stack. Everything from a plant seed to large crafted items take 1 inventory slot. This makes having to carry multiple oxygen tanks even more punishing.- When you build something (say, a part for a base), it exits crafting mode so you cannot make multiple without reopening the crafting menu and selected the part again.Maybe it gets way better later on, but I ran into so many annoyances in the first hour that seemed like systemic design issues, I lost interest.Overall, the game design didn't feel like it learned from the quality-of-life improvements that have been standardized by other modern survival games.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels a lot like Subnautica regarding building and exploration. You have to balance oxygen, food and water while continuously exploring to make sure you can advance. _childDocuments_.review: The look on my face when I went back to my initial base camp (still full of useful materials) after starting the march towards 'liquid water' stage, and learning why my buddy Riley advised me to relocate to higher ground. 12/10 would facepalm again. Definitely scratches that Subnautica itch. Still early access, so many things are bare bones, including the story - yes, there is a reason why you are sent down to a barren planet to terraform it armed with nothing more than a sonic shovel, but you have to dig around a bit to get the background and explanations. But it's all good. In fact, it's a bit better than Subnautica's backstory, because there, your aim was to survive and escape. Here, well, you probably won't, but it made me feel very invested in what I was doing to the planet that is my prison and my home, and the changes you see are just breathtaking.The first time you realize the hard orange sky has turned a faint shade of pink... the first raindrop... the first blade of grass I stumbled upon... It's hard to explain just how gripping and immersive the gameplay is, but I'm way past caring about the highly unrealistic terraforming, the physics errors and other minor hiccups. Actually sometimes, they can be very funny, like the massive - MASSIVE - pulsating purple pulsar comet that bore down on my camp like the wrath of a vindictive god, only to crumble like a cookie over my butterfly dome XD  Now, I just can't wait to have frogs! Frogs!!! Next update please :)
