_childDocuments_.review: 43 hours of playing this game and I've pretty much done everything there is to be done at this point in its development.It has a lot going for it, despite very much being an indie game. Progress is rewarding and smooth (at first), mechanics work great, it's insanely engaging (hours legitimately feel like minutes while playing), game looks pretty good despite the obvious shoestring budget.But I can honestly say that I couldn't recommend it to my worst enemy.At about hour 18-20 it essentially feels like it becomes a job. Buzz around, gather resources, come back to base, build machine that will speed up progress by .05%/second until you unlock the second tier machine that will make progress increase by .1%/s.I finally unlocked automation via drone and autocrafters at hour 40 or so, and after a couple hours setting up a logistical system I breezed through the final 2 stages of terraformation. That 20+ hour period though was not fun or engaging, it was just a slog that I was determined to get through out of an obsessive completionist streak. The worst part is, at this point in the development stage, there is no ending, which means there's no sense of accomplishment at the end and I know that I'll need to return after subsequent updates to get the full experience.If I were to give tips to the developers, it would be to allow greater automation earlier on in the game. Spending 90%+ of your time buzzing to one part of the map and then back is NOT fun. Introduce drones at around hour 25-30, and let you upgrade the drone station over time to allow more drones or more complex drones that can carry more or alternative resources. Let the first half of the game revolve around exploring the map, and the latter half be about optimizing your base and manually terraforming the map, IE how it currently is with the T3 tree spreader.

_childDocuments_.review: I've tried survival games before, but none captured my interest like The Planet Crafter. The game is still in Early Access, which usually means you have to forgive bugs or crashes, but so far I have not experienced either. The game does seem a bit incomplete, of course, but that's to be expected, and there is already a lot to do. In other survival games I usually get frustrated with how quickly thirst and hunger set in, or with just how many different survival elements you have to deal with, but not with The Planet Crafter. This game gives you more than enough food to last until you can grow your own, and water is very easy to keep on hand. And those are the only things you have to deal with (other than air) which means you can spend more time exploring and building your base.Eleven hours in to the game and I feel like I've just scratched the surface. _childDocuments_.review: I don't know why this game is so popular or why it has an overwhelmingly positive rating. Playing it I'm getting very strong "bad Subnautica clone" vibes. This is a very mediocre "me-too" survival game IMHO.Fundamentally I think there's 4 main problems with the game:1. No vehicles so exploration and resource gathering is way too tedious in the early game (also O2 drops WAY too fast, something the devs blindly copied from Subnautica that wasn't fun there either).2. No challenge outside of O2 management and very simple hunger/thirst mechanics3. Boring main game loop that feels like an idle game just building stuff to make numbers go up faster4. Unbalanced tech tree progression where stuff just randomly unlocks if you wait long enough and lots of stuff isn't usefulAlso for a game that's supposedly verified on the Steam Deck the performance is pretty bad and the UI lags a lot and frequently misses button inputs. Also on that topic the graphics aren't anything special, they're Subnautica level but that's an old game now.Overall I was really disappointed in this game, there's some fun but overall it just feels like a bad Subnautica clone and a very mediocre open world survival craft game overall.Update:After giving the game a chance I can say that it does get better later with the ore extractors, drones, portals and and speed boosts, although this comes way too late to really mitigate the early game slog and I still think the game desperately needs vehicles.However I still cannot recommend this game as I've found that it's super easy to softlock your game when running out oxygen (and potentially with water/food as well). When you die and respawn, it takes you back to the last base you visited (including your lifepod). If your lifepod is underwater or you deconstructed the last base you were in (for example if you threw it up as a temporary shelter and deconstructed it to continue exploring) you'll be respawned in an unsafe place with no oxygen. When you die due to lack of O2, it respawns you with almost no O2 (maybe 10s if you're lucky) so you can very easily end up in a death loop with no way out other than attempting to load an earlier save or editing your save file. Not Cool, and is especially egregious for a "released" game.Also found another annoyance where the devs took real life mineral/element names and created in-game resources that are absolutely nothing like their RL counterparts. Most survival games do this to some degree unfortunately, but it's especially egregious here with the number and the fact that it's entirely unnecessary since this is a sci-fi planet so fake mineral names would have been completely fine.Overall finding it more fun to explore than expected later in the game as the planet really starts changing, but extremely disappointed by the low production quality with the serious gamebreaking bugs and rough edges and uninspired Subnautica copy/paste.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall an enjoyable experience and it was absolutely worth it's price. For those, who are looking for a relaxed building and resource management game from a first person view with a mild survival character, I can surely recommend this game.If you are looking for a planetary terraforming game, this is also for you. Although it has it's limits, especially regarding the scientific accuracy. More on that later.Also, if you've enjoyed Subnautica, you might also feel drawn to this game as it employs some similar mechanics regarding the progression.It definitely keeps you busy. And the further you get, the less FPS you have.For me, playing solo on standard difficulty, it took me this long to complete the game. (What is it? About 80 hours?) And I didn't really care about progressing fast.The remaining part of this review may contain spoilers. So read at own risk.Your main goal is to terraform the planet and you get different tools to achieve that. As you progress, you also unlock new buildings and tools which can further accelerate your progress.However, I found the pacing too fast in the beginning and too slow at the late endgame. As a newbie in this game, I felt a bit overwhelmed by what you can do and I could barely plan and construct my facilities, because I was are unlocking new blueprints and tools very fast. Then, the last couple of hours of my game was pure grind and waiting. It wasn't fun to scale up the terraforming buildings in order to increase the overall terraforming speed as it wasn't really rewarding. There was nothing new or creative about it. For the last about 2 hours of the game I literally stood at one place, left the game running and did something entirely different meanwhile, such that terraformation completed while I was AFK.So I'd say the devs should really overhaul the pacing.There is some minor story aspect to this game, which basically unfolds by finding some old stone tablets or diaries and reading a little bit of text. Also, you can receive messages from a character named "Riley" from time to time. I started to build up a small one-sided relationship and was intrigued to learn more about them. They also told me that they are wondering whether I am still alive and hoped to see me again. But, about the time you are leaving mid-game, you'll never hear from her again, which was disappointing and I wondered wtf was happening now to her after I was done. The stone tablets, left by some mysterious alien species which inhabited the planet before, are a bit mysterious and the locations you find them are really cool. But it's mainly some lines of text and static scenery, not much to it and not really interesting anymore after the first few minutes.So there is clearly a lot of improvement potential regarding the story aspect and lore of Planet Crafter.At endgame you are able to create your own mammals by creating their specific genes, which are composed of various genetic traits such as species, colour, size and a bunch of other colours and colour effects. That's a great idea and really some nice groundwork was done. But here again, it lacks depth and complexity. There are literally just three different kinds of species. That's it. Also, there is no breeding, and what I also didn't see - contrary to other creatures like frogs and butterflies - is that those animals I created somehow procreate and are found in other parts of the map. There exactly as many as you created and they are walking around the shelter where you placed them. To me, one of the most annoying things regarding gameplay mechanics, is how extremely scientifically incorrect this game is. Of course I don't expect a fully fledged in-depth terraforming simulation. I was very happy with a very simplified approach. But, the terraforming mechanics in Planet Crafter feel like a simplification of a simplification. For a game, who's core is terraforming, I was really disappointed. That is because of the following:On the one hand the presented values are  incorrect and unrealistic. That's not some nit-picky science talk, but should be visible for most. For example, water started to melt at some nano- or micro-Kelvin. That's almost at absolute zero! There is no fluid water under such circumstances as presented on the planet. Why?! I never reached even 1 K towards the end and still got lakes and ponds and waterfalls. Seriously, what were the devs thinking? And it could have been easily avoidable by just shifting some values or changing the magnitude of temperature increments.It's not much better with the other factors like atmospheric pressure or oxygen density.Another thing, which I found unrealistic and disappointing, is the fact that you don't really need to expand different branches of terraforming buildings in order to get an overall terraforming progression. I haven't really tested this, but in theory, you could just pump a lot of heat into the air and still get a breathable atmosphere.It would've been much better to implement at least some milestones like "get X pressure and Y temperature" in order to allow progress towards moss or whatever. But the way they did it, I didn't really saw a point in building all those different kinds of terraforming buildings, despite my own fun with it.What I also find immersion-breaking in this regard is the fact that some forms of life settled on the surface (e.g. trees), before I even began planting trees.As we are at annoying gameplay technicalities:It was difficult to build stuff sometimes, as you only have that first person view. For a lot of, especially larger buildings, it would have been nice to have a specific "build view", which would've made it easier to arrange the placement of your buildings.Also, one building, the foundation, doesn't snap to living compartments, which made precise and aesthetically pleasing constructions difficult and sometimes impossible. This was worsened by a smaller floor area size of the foundations compared to the larger floor area size of compartment buildings.Especially until about mid-game, there is a lot of running around the map involved. Although you have teleporters, I wish those were unlocked earlier, as it was no fun sometimes to be mindlessly running from A to B and back again dozens of times. Having the drones earlier, which relieve you of transporting resources, would've been nice as well.[Review continues in comments]

_childDocuments_.review: I have just under 20 hours played and paid under £15 on sale. Planet Crafter is similar to Subnautica but without the threat of enemies, but you must be wary to keep health (food), water, & oxygen up.Planet Crafter can easily steal hours of your life and immerse yourself on an unknown planet, exploring, discovering, and surviving the challenges set out before you. Gather items, build a base, and start terra forming this barren land into a habitable planet.  However, there are parts of the game that are extremely slow & boring, waiting for a threshold to reach in order to start building again. With the 2023 update announcements news released on 4th January 2023, it looks like the developers are not slowing down and adding even more exciting content to an already amazing game. Edit: Me and my girlfriend sunk almost 300 hrs into Planet Crafter and it's easily one of the best games around. The relaxation of this game is top notch. The fact the world around you terraforms from an arid desert of nothingness to a tropical sensation, I have to tip my hats to the amazing devs for their hard work during Early Access and give props to not giving up. 5If you and your non-gamer type partner wants to sink hours upon hours playing a relaxing game while managing food, oxygen and the tough task of terraforming this planet, THIS. IS. THE. GAME. FOR. YOU.

_childDocuments_.review: What a  of a game, amidst the most  decade for gaming. I cannot believe these TWO amazing devs have managed to craft a gameplay-loop that is more rewarding and addictive, then  the AA and even the AAA industry have managed in the last ~10 years...This game manages to create a JOURNEY, NOT a grind. Too many developers have missed the mark badly, in this delicate dance. But this game sikes the BULLSEYE on the pacing, which makes you almost completely oblivious to the shortcomings of this title.I have my eyes still GLUED to the screen, at ~20 hrs in. Taking my first bites into the games' juicy late mid-game mechanics, and still maintain extremely high engagement level for such a "small" indie title. I CANNOT WAIT for MORE! And I know I will be so sad, when I finally transform this ball of hell, into an Oasis of life, yet I see...Just half a year into the project the devs are coming with MORE ludicrous terraforming goals, now.I can only wonder... How far can we take the idea of what a fully terraformed world will look like...

_childDocuments_.review: This review is Early Access so things will change. The creator of this game are fans of the genera and it shows. They get so much right. I really only have nit picks. If you like crafting, building, base building, exploration, and reaching a goal this is the game for you. Where it really shines are quality of life game aspects. All the things I dislike in other games are fixed here. No batteries or charging, solar panels work at night, reactors do not require more fuel, you can sprint forever, you eventually get a rocket pack and can rocket forever, resource nodes are distinct in color and shape so finding what you need to build is easy, it takes seconds to break down anything you built, you get all the resources back, rebuilding a base is really quick. There are only minor bugs and visual things that need to be fixed. This game is a ton of fun. It would be nice to see in the pop up preview which materials an excavator can extract.

_childDocuments_.review: This game activated my monkey brain of finding stuff on the ground.See it as, ''OH a piece of candy!'' and you look ahead and see another ''Oh another piece of candy!'' and you continue until your bag is full, thus you make a stash, until all the candy is gone in that area...Then you realize, you're hungry, and thirsty, so you find slurpies in chests!Then you realize you can't make food, but monkey brain found food in random candy chests, and that weird object in the distance looks like more candy ahead!But candy is limited, and you have to decide where to spend it for the tech tree, can't have everything!Thus the cycle continues and now I have a horde's stash, build multiple camps, and vantage points.(fall damage is a thing btw…)Also you ''work'' for a company that completely abandoned you, and owns you with DEBT. _childDocuments_.review: So. This is it. Just finished 100% of the game. All 55 steam achievements acquired, everything explored and seen, all endings done. There's no more to do. I could say a lot about this game. Honestly I regret all these 70+ hours put in this game. Why I did it then ? Because I'm a ''completionist gamer'' and when I start a game I must finish it and do everything. I saw the overwhelming good reviews on steam and tell myself a lot of time ''this game must be good at some point'' and then I continue to play again and again waiting for this fun and rewarding moments to show up. But it never did and I feel bored during my playthrought all along. Now I even regret buying the game. What to say about this game then ? There's a lot to say. Well, I guess it is some kind of functional, reasonable and okay game. It work. And most of all I put 70 hours in this game to do everything possible and more. Which for me is a bare minimum. 1$ = 1 hour of gameplay for me. So this game is cost efficient at least. I must give it that. But the question is : does it really was worth it to put 70 hours in this game ? My answer is no. These are some of the reasons I could list, but there could be more : - Most of all, be prepare for a lot, I mean A LOT, of boring grinding. Especially if you want all the three endings. There is a possibility mid and late game to automate the ressource gathering and be more efficient but it is still a lot of managing and the automation system just feel boring and not rewarding at all. - The game is visually, aesthetically and graphicaly unpleasant. This game want to be some kind of Subnautica, maybe with some mixed elements of No Man's Sky and Satisfactory. But this game just can't get the beauty and wonder in the face of Nature that these games have. In Planet Crafter, the world look boring, it look cheap, it look unreal, it look just lame and sad. There's no life in it. When you reach the insect/animals terraformation you do not see animals roaming the land, they are just silent and still in some spot. Butterfly are the only living being that really add somethings. And mammals, there's only 3 species and they must be crafted and put into farm­. The world also feel weirdly terrestrial and not alien at all. I mean there's butterfly, frogs and fish that look like our real animals. The trees do not move, even when you ear some kind of wind or when there's a storm. And again a lot of trees just look like the one we have on earth. I was just unable to recreate the ''wow'' effect that the world of Subnautica and Satisfactory create on me. These worlds really feel alive compare to Planet Crafter.  - The lighting and weather physics are horrible, cheap and so disappointing. When you're inside building or wreck the outside lighting affect the one inside which make no sens. You can hear the rain and wind when far inside Wreck. Lamps and lights feel odd and weird, unatural. There's no shadows, darkness is only in wreck. The sky is standing still with three ugly planets that will never move. There's no stars, no sun and the clouds are horrible. When you change spot, the lighting drastically change, which is so unrealistic. Imagine walking in dunes under full lighting, then because you enter some kind of crystal biome out of nowhere the sky become black and the lighting become cold and grey. But you are outside. This make no sens. - Sound design is inadequate and unsatisfying. Machines only emit sounds when you are very - I mean very - close to them. Animals do not emit a lot of sound if not none at all and again you must be almost directly on them to hear them. Fauna and flora feels silent and uncanny. Even water feel silent and emit no sounds. The soundtrack is very repetitive and become annoying fast. - The meteors storm system is so annoying. The camera shake during the storm, the sound is destroying your ear. Some meteor move so slowly in the sky and take so much time before ground impact it is so strange, and when it hit the ground it does only spawn a lot of rocks that will block you from harvesting the precious ressources the meteors bring so you will have to wait that the rocks magically disappear. - The base building is way too insufficient and poor, there's not much to do and you quickly discover everything to do. This do not encourage you to make good and well looking base. I dont understand why I can make such simple thing like tree pot only in the end game when base building do not interest me anymore. - The story is cliche, boring and the ending is soooo disappointing. Ending the game leave no feeling alike the one after finishing Subnautica. - The game is not well optimize. Mid to late game in my base I was dropping to 40-50 FPS while I was 100-120 in the wilderness. There was some bugs everywhere, props floating in the air, floor that overlap, hit boxes that make no sens, invisible walls, places where you can go threw walls of grounds, etc. I will stop there. But I could say a lot more. Please consider that this is an opinion review. It is personal, it is subjective. You could enjoy this game while I did not. After all, this game still as overwhelming review on steam. But me I was disappointed. I know that graphics and story do not make goods games and that gameplay is more important. But I do not feel that gameplay was really rewarding here. I did not see anything special about gameplay. I mean, after all it is just some king of clones of Subnautica. If you want my opinion, just grab Subnautica 1 and 2. Play No Man's Sky. Play Satisfactory. These are way more pleasant and immersive games in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Additive and a challenge, however it's a resource grab game. Has potential, but it's missing things.  For me, I wish there was an ability to have some sort of sled/cart, because all the back and forth will make one go insane.  It fells like a running simulator back and forth to resources and your living quarters.  There needs to be something, because I feel a lot of players will hate this part of the game... which IS the game.  Run, collect, run back, craft something new, then run back for more.  Repeat.  Playing with others will make it a bit less of a complete fill your backpack 8 billion times game, but that's exactly what you do.  There needs to be more, a whole lot more content for me to give this a thumbs up.  And yes, I know there are portals, but that later in game.  Even WITH portals, it's a back and forth headache.  Not until Drones are unlocked is when things finally become enjoyable.  What do we do until then?  Run back and forth.It's too bad some blueprints are locked for so long.  By the time you unlock them, there's almost no point in using them... like the T3 Ore Extractor.  Sure, it's nice and no more worries, but why bother cause you're almost done and off the planet.  Some of these blueprints need to be unlocked way before they are now is all I'm saying to make it feel worthy and have them be very useful when the struggle has been back and forth all day.     Only buy this if it's under $15, only buy if you love to run back and forth for resources over and over, and if you're bored of other games.Really really need a Player Icon for multiplayer to see each others location. This should have been done when co-op was introduced.  Now since the Rover Update:   Use the vehicle for portable storage.  That's your best option since you drive into every boulder, tree, and coral on the planet.  If the vehicle was a hovercraft, being able to float over obstacles, then I see it being used as intended.  Currently, just use it for storage, jetpack or teleport back home, and then recall your vehicle back into the station.If it was a spaceship... then fly off the planet lol.

_childDocuments_.review: If you ever liked Subnautica, or have a fancy for the sciences, this is 100% for you! I keep finding new secrets, new portals, new hidden bases, new cave systems, and shortcuts. There is always something to progress towards, and I can't wait to see what animals I will create, and how my decisions effected the terrain! What is predetermined? If I plant a certain tree, will the environment be changed? Will new animals appear? I love that it isn't a straight dive into the horror, like in subnautica, you start with nothing, in nothing, with no future. The horror is the abyss, the will to live, is seen in every blade of grass, every flower, every tree. I feel like I have created a whole new world, discovered ancient beings, new mechanisms, causes behind catastrophe, and how many prisoners have come before. I purposefully spread my bases out, to the four corners of the world, where each has it's own specialety. It gives that area a purpose, and keeps me on my toes! You can come to the same place, and suddenly there is something completely new to discover! Whether it be from ice melting, new plants growing, or sudden appearance of crystals hidden behind every handful of rocks. As soon as you find a new material, and don't know where to find it, it is there, on the map, it just appeared, go find it! Remember little nuances, what can this little puddle become? Did that sky light always have a vine stalk? Wait, I can CLIMB that?! I have been living on a new world for a few days now, and I am only excited to see more! I recommend playing with a podcast, or music in the background. I have a little pop-out window from youtube, so I can create a whole playlist to watch, like a little tv in my suit! and make sure that you make the game the highest priority in the details section of your task manager for optimal results! (and if you have trouble launching the game, yes, every time you launch the game)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm updating this for the 1.0 release. I feel like $25 is rather high for what's here. You know some of those old "Tycoon" games, like, Flash-era old? Where you're just getting more of a thing that makes a number go up until you unlock new things that makes numbers go up quicker, on a loop, to try to hit simple levels of dopamine? That's this.There's very little in the way of logistics management here, nor much change in how you place your buildings. Interconnectivity is sparse and power/energy is literally global. There's a ton of time spent just running around and ferrying things with your very restrictive inventory, even with backpack upgrades, just due to how the volume of what you need to build better things tends to scale alongside how big your backpack gets. The most novel thing the game has to offer are the visuals and workload consequences of you turning a barren, lifeless planet into a lush and primordial haven, which is certainly quite cool conceptually, but the process of getting there can be a little tedious, as the game doesn't offer much for intermittent thrill. Thrill is not something the game is trying to provide, but at the pace you go, it is definitely still something for those with an above average amount of patience to spare.I just don't feel like there's enough depth to it to warrant $25. I'd put it down at somewhere between $15 to $20, but either way, if the game's concept appeals to you (and you don't care for sophisticated logistics), then don't pass it up, but don't necessarily pay full price either if you can help it.

_childDocuments_.review: By far one of my favorite survival games. Big titles always talk about how everything you do effects the environment, well this time its greater than you know. As you progress you'll notice that your drills, reactors, plants, all change the environment. This change can be as small as the color of the ground turning green and full of life, to a giant waterfall bursting from the high rocks. At a first glance, it doesn't look like much, but there's more than just a cover to this book. The story is minuscule, but certainly engaging when you really understand the purpose of it all, and where your character fits in the story. I highly recommend this game for survival lovers. Just a quick tip though, make sure you build your base higher up than the pod ;)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fun crafting survival game, exactly what I wanted. I'd prefer a bit more guidance on how to achieve your teraforming goals, and more of a quest tracker (as the game only gives you a tracker for your first couple of things, then disappears). It'd also be nice to have a glossary of terms or something, as I have no idea what all the different measurements mean or how to affect any specific one. But all of this is just personal preference, because I've continued to progress the milestones just by doing my own thing, exploring and basebuilding and building new technologies as I can.I definitely recommend starting on the easiest mode though, as you can barely explore before running out of oxygen for a good chunk of time in the early game, and I personally hate losing items upon death - especially when some of your early-game resources like food, until you can grow your own, are finite finds.I do hate how limited your inventory and storage options are though - especially later in the game, even with upgrades, some crafts take many different items so you have to go back and forth a lot. I also soon gave up on building chests and just left piles of ores around my base for a while in early game, because it just got ridiculous. Also, I wish I could scan for the rarer materials or something - without looking it up, seems to be  based on pure luck of where your exploring takes you.

_childDocuments_.review: Planet crafter where to begin? Well I got this game in early access and from what I remembered loaded it up for 10 mins never gave it a chance and forgot about it, fast forward to about a month ago now when the game went to full release and I suddenly thought I would give it another try, 100 hours later and I’m about to complete my 3rd playthrough, so let me tell you why it’s actually my favourite game of 2024 so far, it’s a simple concept although your terraforming a planet, start off with basic items get better items replace the old with the new, but it’s more of a cosy game then a survival game, there’s no combat, you go at your own pace the game doesn’t direct you after a short tutorial on where to go or what to do, just explore the map in whatever direction you want and build a base and get to changing the planet, and let’s say the planet starts off looking very much like mars orange skys red everywhere it never gets called mars but it sure as heck looks like it, but this is the thing with this game you see the world terraforming before your very eyes starting off with blue skies then lakes and so on… the exploration discovering old ship wrecks finding crates you can loot, it’s just so satisfying, I haven’t tried co op but the game even has that if you have friends to play with, honestly the only thing I would say is disappointing for a game that’s out in 2024 is the graphics aren’t like AAA graphics even on maximum and also the optimisation isn’t the best I don’t have the most high end of systems but I would expect my 4070 to run a game that looks like it’s 10 years old to perform much better and the bad part the performance gets worse as you progress the game, literally my frames half by the time I’m close to end game from what they are at the start of the game, but even with those two “issues” honestly this game is fantastic and I love it!! Recommend buy but again I got it during early access when it was cheaper then it is now

_childDocuments_.review: The biggest problem with this game is that for the first 20 hours, my brain preferred it to food, water, and sleep. Discipline is needed to play it safely.Starting out, I thought this would be a high-tension survival game... and I was wrong. After the first hour or two, you should have basic needs in hand, and it turns into this slow, cozy gaming experience where you watch the barren red dustball develop rain, then plants, then animals, and each step feels remarkably rewarding. It took ages to find a way to die (meteor strikes), and there's no sudden action sequences lurking around to catch you out. There is a slightly strange plot line running under the surface, which you can completely ignore if it's not gripping you. After 80 hours, I have reached the point where I can choose one of the 3 available endings; I didn't like it much, but that's fine because reload last save, and go for a more advanced ending which demands a bit more work from the player. No problem, I'm having fun here, automating my farming and manufacturing operation.Not ready to play the DLC yet, but bought it without any questions or research. Basic Planet Crafter has convinced me that I want more of this.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty nice and relaxing game from what I believe is a two person team.Be warned though, the game struggles late game when you've got a lot of flora growing and/or build a big base. It gets severely CPU limited at this point.If you don't mind low framerates then this is not an issue.There seem to be a CPU scheduler issue for Ryzen 5000 series at least, where the load is so spread out over available cores that the core clock speed never goes up much, and this reduces overall performance.Disabling one or more cores for the exe (CPU affinity) seem to help force the clockspeeds up and also help overall performance.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the game - It was a little challenging at first - working out what needed to happen to achieve the next goal, but it is worth it.  I did find a little confusion when some build options, or material was unlocked, but the item to make or create that material was not unlocked till much later.I like the idea of the previous civilisation and settlers/colonists - I am really hoping their is some sort of technological advantage to be discovered to allow you to escape the world instead of waiting for your sentence to mature.  When everything in the game has been finalised, I will probably start a new game to get the full progressive experience.sep 2024 additional review - I did start this game in the 2022 free early access - i have enjoyed the updates and yes, would start a new game with each update.  I have played it through to the end, and seen all 3 endingsI have read quite a few other review comments, most of the complaints seem to be about the ship wrecks, and their lack of signage and layout inside - the few in your world area are small enough to navigate without any issues.  The big wrecks you access via the portal can be a little confusing.  But I use the maze technique of following the left wall at every turn,  I also dropped non useful items, such as the iron you get from barriers, or seeds, plants etc that you don't really need anymore, at junctions that I have cleared.  I use the flares to mark the exit junction.  The portal wrecks are a extremely useful way of getting otherwise rare items early.BUT - don't do the portal wrecks until you have unlocked the trade ship - otherwise you might not get the trade credits and you'll miss out on a lot later.you can choose what level of maze you want, so either practise on the small ones to find what system works for you, or take oxygen, food and water if you think you will get lost inside.other issues were about progress - use the terraforming and other info screens.  If some option, pressue, heat, biomass, etc is moving slow -  then you build what ever machine, drill, heaters, etc to impove that option - or if you have the rocket platform- then fire off the appropriate rocket to add the multiplier it.yes, it sometimes is just rocket science

_childDocuments_.review: This game fills a niche I didn't even know I wanted. I have apparently always wanted to terraform a planet directly, rather than an automated cut scene with a ship from orbit. I love how this game allows me to see the world around me progress as I put in the work.      The graphics are beautiful, the game play is crisp, I've not run into any bugs, glitches, or crashes. Its definitely one of the better designed from a technical standpoint that I've seen in awhile. I'm very suprised it has not already been flooded with positive reviews as the community seems very supportive as well.     The demo as released has had the most content I have seen in a demo, to the point I kinda wondered at first if the devs had released the full game by mistake. It took many hours to complete and gives a very real picture of what the complete game could be.     While I think combat can make many games better I believe that at least in this case the chill laid back game play is complemented by a peaceful planet. I find it extremely relaxing to play this game.     The only minor negative I can come up with is as far as I can tell ATM it is impossible to die, you simply get a blackout and a teleport to the last place you were in a breathable atmosphere. This is good and bad. Good because it fits the laid back style of the game, but bad because it decreases the stakes of staying out in the world just that little bit longer. When you know that running out of air, water or food isn't important it makes you wonder why its added to the game at all. When you play games like Minecraft for example and you look for diamonds, but you are low on health and your pick is almost broken and you really should head back, but you push on and hey diamonds! It gives you a sense of risk/reward that I think is missing here.     That said I fully appreciate the efforts of the devs to listen to the community and stick as close to their vision as they have. I wish them luck in their endeavors and hope that as they finish this game it lives up to what they have already released.TL;DR Buy this game its good!

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. This is one of the only games I've ever played that really captures the essence of being stranded on a barren planet. _childDocuments_.review: Planet Crafter is okay. It's not great, but I'd be lying if I said that I didn't enjoy some of the grind. I think that the terraforming became too bulky by the end of it. _childDocuments_.review: Slow-burn game focused heavily on exploration and crafting. Played on a Steam Deck and it was a very smooth experience. IMO, worth the price, even at full cost.I personally got to late game, then things started to feel slow and I felt I'd mostly finished the exploration parts of the game and just had tedious gathering and crafting left. Probably would have finished the game in another ~10hr or so, but lost interest.Room for improvement:(1) Inventory management gets annoying mid- to late-game. Just too many clicks and it feels like a chore. Ideas for the dev(s) include:- a "transfer all items of this type" (as opposed to the existing "transfer all items"), - scrolling once left to get to the other container instead of needing to repeatedly go right- a later-game storage system that links storage directly in with crafting systems, getting you out of minutiae of digging around different storage containers and working through the whole crafting tree. Improving your storage system (i.e. one container per item) helps, but just feels like you're trading it for another kind of monotony.Admittedly, I know one or two things later game exist to improve this that I didn't unlock (I think drones are a thing?), but I feel like they become available way later than the problem they actually solve surfaces.(2) Items aren't always self-documenting and I needed to resort to the wiki a few timesThe role or importance of an item often isn't clear until you actually put the effort in to craft it. I realize discovery and exploration is important, but an in-game "manual" or something with more in-depth explanations of items (likely tied to the unlock system) would be nice. Of note:- The biomass system (which becomes more involved late game) felt like it was missing a "why" for me to look into it- Getting through things that requires explosions is confusing, because you unlock the powder *way* sooner than an actual means to use it in that way, and it's unclear that you can't just use the powder(3) Building could use some quality of life tweaksYou often need to entire tear down things before you can replace them. You should really be able to do things like switch four single rooms for a larger room without having to remove everything from it, especially with containers.The ability to simply move something instead of having to deconstruct then reconstruct it would also be nice. This is particularly annoying with storage containers.(4) Vehicles don't really feel worth itI unlocked the Jetpack and kinda just used it the rest of the game. I realize some upgrades exist for the vehicle, and the oxygen one in particular seemed worthwhile, but I don't think I would have ended up using the vehicle unless it started flying or something. Just felt - too slow- too limited with respects to water and being able to climb up mountains (like you can do to an extent with the jetpack)

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't going to give this a negative review, but after writing it, I realized that there's almost nothing positive I can say about it. It's not just about ultra low budget production, but the quality of release, amount of bugs, artificially stretched grind and plain negligence.A lot of the meshes clash and go into each other. There are gaps in the world EVERYWHERE. Insane amount of textures aren't solid, and you can go through them. Even rockets do not have any sort of physics to them, and can literally fall down, clip onto each other and fly around the base if you push them. None of the wrecks on the map appear... wrecked, it's just stock parts kitbashed together without much care. I was also almost sure that it was made by a non-English speaking persons, because of the really weird almost childish-like texts inside the game, but twitter of the dev implies otherwise. Comparing this to Subnautica would be extremely unfair to both games. Subnautica is a polished experience, complete with some characters, voices, proper graphics, actual semi-realistic biomes, lighting (it's atrocious here, it just pops in and out). This game can almost be considered a sophisticated asset flip, with just how badly things are strewn together. Sudden environment changes, cartoonish asteroid barrages, janky tile borders which you can clearly distinguish, poor meshes and overall generic "vibe" - I am extremely confused at all the positive reviews and comparisons it got to Subnautica.The worst part is the grind. For me, this game is unplayable without mods. Inventory at the start of the game is restrictive beyond any reason, you can't stack anything, and you would spend hundreds of hours just lugging resources. Progress is way too slow. Moving back and forth around the map would've probably made me bash the monitor if I didn't speed things up. Unless you really want to torture yourself - just go on nexus and install akarnokd mod bundle, which fixes literally every single neglected issue, oversight and some bugs. You'll be able to stack items (shocking, I know), automate depositing resources, highlight nodes, get minimap (my god, the in-game is the worst I have ever seen, you can't even control or zoom in and out with mouse), quicksave, craft from containers, see a lot of useful information and get automation early.The only reason I would've given this a positive review is that I like the idea of terraforming, you can manage some nice screenshots occasionally, and I don't want to punish indie developers too much, but there are certainly much better games for a similar price out there. For god’s sake - they left the "unstuck" button which allows you to literally fly around and noclip through anything, that's how bad the release is, and how uncertain they are in their creation. Also note, that in 30 hours with mods, you can accomplish (I got all achievements and finished it) what people are doing in 400 hours without mods, simply because of inventory and stacking restrictions, and very late game automation, this is just a bad game design, and very clear attempt at stretching what amounts to few dozen hours of gameplay otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: Numbers going up should not be this relaxing.Its a game all about going through the stages of ecological succession to turn a desert planet into a thriving biological paradise.  Yes, there's also a breadcrumbs story about survivors and aliens trying to get away from humans and a big meteor and all that, but that's not what the game is ABOUT.  Its about watching the sky turn blue and lakes form from rain.  Its about worms crawling out of the muck to greet a new breathable atmosphere.  Its about building a huge base just the way you want it with lots of scenic vistas nearby.  Its about exploring and finding weird treasures in every nook and cranny.But mostly, its about numbers going up.  And those numbers lead to something special.

_childDocuments_.review: I recently found myself needing something to scratch my survival game itch.  I saw Planet Crafter bundled with another game I like, Medieval Dynasty, and figured, why not?  Well, I can say that that was well worth the $20 I spent.  It is hard to explain why I like this game so much without making it sound dull.  It really isn't dull at all.You land on a planet that you have to make liveable.  That's the game.  No enemies (there don't need to be, the whole planet can kill you), no bosses, just you and a big bleak wasteland that you somehow have to make survivable.  The game is oddly relaxing, but still keeps me engaged.  There's always a new resource to get, new area to explore, or new machine or structure to build. I guess the biggest thing I like about this game is that it really is freedom.  Just you and your empty planet, and you decide what to build and where.  If you like games involving a lot of violence, constant blasts and gore, this may not be the game for you.If you enjoy open world survival games like Subnautica, or Ark, this game may just be what you're looking for.To the developer team:  thanks for this game, please keep making content for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd really recommend this game with a small caveat.The game starts off slow, but with a steady rate of progression. Lots of things in the distance which seem like they could at first just be far off background dressing that turn out to be places to visit and explore. The exploration also gives a satisfying stream of new things as time goes on that make collecting resources, movement and transforming the planet easier and smoother. Comparing how well you're doing to a couple hours previous is a great feeling.The transformation of the planet is incredibly satisfying as well. Starting off with a desert planet, each stage of transformation makes everything look more beautiful, and the fact it's all due to you makes it feel very earned. When butterflies, fish and trees start sprouting in once barren lands, it's a really awesome sight. The areas themselves are fun to explore and find some of the story areas to find were fantastic.The only issue I found with the game was in the last 5-10 hours in the mammal stage of the game. The first 20 hours were a blast and breezed by, but after automating resource collecting and gathering, it seems like the last stage takes an incredibly long time to finish with very little to unlock. This is after launching dozens of boosting rockets, which each give a +1000% multiplier to each of the variables you're increasing (heat/pressure ect). After putting down dozens of butterfly spawners, tree spawners, and animal pens with the terraforming rate only increasing very slightly, I had to look up why it was going so slow. I found that even after completing the heat, pressure, and oxygen goals, they are still counted to the terraforming rate. Despite having reached the needed heat/pressure, spending 5 minutes making a bunch more made me finish the last part of the game in around 10/20 minutes compared to the hours i was spending on increasing the animals which was the given goal. The other frustration is one of the endings to unlock requires a crazy amount of money. Even automating everything, it felt a slog to get that last little part.Despite the last 3 paragraphs, I loved this game. Everything from the progression to the exploration was awesome while it was going strong. Playing this whilst recovering from an illness has just made the time breeze by and almost every moment was enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: This probably was the best invested money in an EA title in quite a while. I thoroughly enjoyed this game so far and still do come back with every major update. Particularly for an EA title I like the fact, that I don't have to start the game from scratch, world updates are integrated into the current game. I don't understand why others can't do that as well. The game is quite enjoyable, it's one of these... "oooooh, what's there"-games where you want to find all little corners and see what's behind the next rock. It can get quite tough sometimes, but not frustratingly tough.There are quite a few graphical glitches, here and there rocks that are see-through or resources mid-air, but little things, no major fun killer. Particularly as you get a jet pack at some point, you will be able to reach places, which you are probably not meant to reach and therefore you'll come across graphical glitches a bit more often - obviously, since you're not meant to be there. :DGenerally I highly recommend this game. I wished it had a bit more lore, the currently implemented lore is curious and interesting, but not sure it's quite there. Technically it doesn't need lore, it's a nice bonus to have. Also... I think the "ancient" buildings and the "sci-fi" lore are not quite... compatible. But again... it's a nice bonus to have.I wished there'd be more inventory space. There is so much to discover and yet I have to run there 20x because there are so many items to find and take back. But that's just my high-level moaning.Learning curve (read: survival curve) is quite steep (and difficult) and it gets quite easy once you have established the basics (water and air) and it feels a bit too easy then (I don't want to say boring, though that might be more applicable). So maybe a bit more end-game stuff would be good. Otherwise it's a really nice "watch the fruition of your efforts" game. I thoroughly enjoy(ed) this. Thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: If crafting and survival is your thing, then this is most definitely the game for you. And when I say crafting, you will be doing A LOT of it (hint - it's in the name!). Just about everything you need will require some crafting in one form or another, ranging from basic equipment up to DNA sequencing for animals (insects, frogs, etc). There is also a small trading part of the game, which will give you more options to unlock other crafting materials, which you won't normally get in-game. I'm about 90 hours in, and I still look at what I can refine, build, trade, and trying to get to the next terraforming level. There are loads of hidden places to explore and a couple of underlying stories. Explore, craft, terraform! It's brilliant!
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me of a landlocked Subnautica, without any hostile creatures and with a greater emphasis on base building. It's meditative and satisfying, provided you aren't put off by its slow pace.  Watching life gradually spread over the surface of the planet is a great joy. You are a lonely homesteader, nurturing your own slice of isolated paradise. I love it.A few minor cons: Like Subnautica, the base building can be a little janky. It's hard to place buildings without a corner hovering precariously in mid air, even if you do use foundations. Most of the furniture is cosmetic only - as of July 2023, you cannot even sit in the chairs. After 16 hours of (admittedly relaxed) play, I haven't unlocked any automation yet. Some degree of automation and smart inventory management for your base should definitely be available sooner.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect for a beta. Achieves everything I wanted out of this game, and more! First of all I love the aspect of you slowly turning a barren desert into a beautiful, lush, and relaxing paradise! And second the Aspect of slowly gaining new things over time gives you something new to work toward all the time!
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: #1 relaxing. Plays alot like SUBNAUTICA. If you have played SUBNAUTICA you'll have zero problem picking up this games inventory, material collection, or building mechanics. You are stranded on this Planet as a 'criminal' living our their sentence by building up the infrastructure needed to begin the process of terraforming a relatively small area of a planet to an EARTH LIKE climate with similar weather patterns, water, plant life, ect...all the basic building materials are scattered around in the open due to the planets frequent meteor storms which leave all your basic building materials after they hit and explode. (you can be killed by these meteors) There are several different biomes in the area, were certain more rare materials can be found and constantly mined by machines you build. As oxygen, heat and air pressure increase, you will SLOWLY begin to see changes in weather and patterns. Rain will begin to occur. Eventually, you will see lakes form. The sky turn blue. rudimentary plant life begin to form. For the Price it's a good investment, and you can play with up to 9 friends, working together to gather, build, and plan the terraforming outcome. Its fun, engaging, has some very unique and interesting scenery. Weather is done well, particularly from an AUDIO standpoint, and the background music goes great with 420 time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems very simple at first, and you find it amusing, but at a certain point, it grabs you and you get increasingly drawn into the game by various mysterious things and tasks. _childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I am not sure I can continue at this point.This game has a great premise. I love games like Subnautica, Satisfactory, Factorio and, similar to a lesser extent, Stardew Valley, Terraria and the evergreen that is FTB modded Minecraft 12.something with an environmental Sounds mod. I collectively have probably, thanks to Minecraft several thousands of hours in these games.The point is i like to collect, craft, built, farm, and that for hours upon hours preferably with a podcast or something on the side.But at roughly 14 hours into Planet Crafter the game gets really tedious in a deadly boring way.First off I want to say that I will not deduct any points from this game for its obviously rather low budget in its presentation or even in how game systems are presented and constructed. I will bring examples of this though because while they are not the main reason why I stopped playing they are contributing to it. There is a giant spaceship, half buried in one of the dessert areas. But the massive outside of the ship has less polygons then ships from Homeworld, a strategy game from 1999 where you are mostly supposed to see them from far away while you direct an entire mixed fleet of them. Then there is a smaller Space Fighter jet whose cockpit alone has more polygons then the previously mentioned massive spaceship. This disconnect between assets is kind of all over the place. Some assets seem delicately crafted and placed and others are just copy pasted and sometimes enlarged far above what the assets should have been in size, ever, with holes in the terrain in quite a few places.Whatever structures you place in the world also feels quite foreign to the world you place it in, though I have to admit that this actually works in the games favor. Most notably is that you do not need to connect for example power structures to power using structures. It doesn't matter if you placed a generator on the other side of the world. If you have placed a power user on the opposite side it will still get power from it to use. No power connections needed. Now I get that they did probably not have the budget to implement power lines like Satisfactory has but just having antennas and maybe require them to have a "line of sight" each other would already have sufficed.

_childDocuments_.review: As of now (January 2023) the game is still a bit rough around the edges but it has great potential. _childDocuments_.review: Its like first person cookie clicker.That's how I would describe this game. That is not a bad thing! in fact, it's a selling point for me. You spend your time clicking on resources and then using those resources to make machines to increase oxygen, pressure, or heat.  then as you obtain more "cookies", you unlock machines that provide more cookies passively. so far, that's describing any other resource management game. So how is this like cookie clicker? After clicking enough, you can sit in your mini base and just die repeatedly from hunger and thirst as the world progressively terraforms. Leave it open for 24 hours and I'm sure you could beat the game.Now for the reason why I wouldn't recommend it:-animations are unfinished (and sometimes just aren't there)- "mining" resources consists of looking at the horizon for the right shape sitting on the ground like trash littered all over the place. --or like someone took an over-sized brush of "iron" and painted the landscape. then did the same for the rest of the resources. there are no "nodes", and mining individual resources consists of a laser streaming from your gun to a - for lack of a better word - dancing resource.- you don't get direction on what to do unless you are already doing what you should be doing and you've unlocked the communications satellite and the monitor for reading emails. overall not worth it unless you get it on deep sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A great terraforming single player survival/base-building game.=== Original Review during Early Access: ===+ Difficulty selection -- from "Relaxing" (Death is inconsequential -- you merely respawn in your base with everything you were carrying) all the way to "Hardcore" (Death is a game over).+ Tutorial portion called "First steps" guides you with objectives in the upper left corner and simple gameplay.+ Once you finish the tutorial, the game opens up and it is up to you to figure out how to accelerate the different elements of the terraforming process. Thanks to the tutorial, you should have no trouble figuring this out, and the challenge here is basically finding the sources of the different resources you will need. At this point, there is no more a "List of objectives", because there are different paths towards the goal, and it's up to you how to achieve it. As an example: Will you cover your lake with Algae to produce a lot of "base" Biomass -- or will you have fewer Algae producers, but instead use space rockets to get a massive "times X" bonus for them? The latter requires you to construct rocket engines and collect tree bark, while the former requires growing eggplants and collecting algae. Similarly, you can go for the raw pressure boost of Drills, or you can use the weaker Ore extractors, which however yield useful ores as a byproduct.+ Simple survival metrics: All you have to watch is your Oxygen level (replenishes upon entering any of your bases), Hydration level (initially, you get water from melted ice, but quickly gain access to Atmospheric water catchers, and eventually, you'll gain a filtration system for safely drinking from lakes), and Food (this one depletes the slowest, and also doubles as your "Health", so if you fall from a deadly height, you don't actually die -- you just enter a "Critical hunger" condition, and if you quickly eat anything, you will be healed). You can carry portable oxygen and water tanks with you to quickly replenish O2 and hydration, and food is also transportable, although I eventually stopped carrying it.+ Anti-frustration measures:> > If you misplace ANY structure, you can demolish it and you will get ALL the resources back, so you can experiment with placement as much as you want.> >  Base elements can be placed in the air, they won't fall, and external staircases will attach to airlock doors to create nice access ramps.> > Base extensions can be added either from inside or from outside, and a helpful color-coded outline shows you whether the placement is valid.> > You don't have a minimap that would be accessible at all times; instead, you can place Beacons (I typically place them at major bases and at "ruins"), each given a color of your choice (16 million options), and these beacons that broadcast a useful symbol into your hud at all times, making navigation simple. It's also possible to carry the components needed for a Map Screen, and plop it down during your exploration to get a satellite view of your area - and then dismantle that screen to get resources back.> > Jetpack! This amazing transportation mode makes traversal easy and allows you to jump off high cliffs with no problem. The controls take a while to get used to, but then you'll love it.=== Addendum for full release: ===> Developers have added multiplayer, which I am unlikely to utilize, but it's still a plus.> So many new things have been added, new biomes, Endgame content, off-planet trading, automation... Very cool!

_childDocuments_.review: to start, i've played about 40 hours of the game before the massive update in November 2022 and a few hours after the update. Pros:-No learning curve to game mechanics and controls, so you quickly catch on. -In the beginning, you're eager to build up since the terraforming goes quickly, and you can visibly see your progress. You want to explore further, so you want to "level up" so you can hold more oxygen. -Seeing all the work you've put into terraforming is fascinating! I think the devs put in some real thought about each part that goes into an ecosystem.-No threats/enemies, so you can explore at your leisure without worrying about being attacked. -Base building is always fun (if you're into that). You have many options, whether you're into several small bases, or a mega base. -deconstruction does not eat your resources! Many games give a penalty for deconstruction and won't give back the resources used to build, but not Planet Crafter! -The ancient lore that came with the update is awesome! It makes you feel less alone, and its rather intriguing to find the next Warden Key to explore further. Cons:-Some of the controls seem a bit clunky. Using a jetpack in particular. My dude always stutters when I try to fly and I find myself spamming the space bar to get him up and going. -The collision needs to be addressed. I thought this would have been addressed with the update, but i clipped my way right through an entire mountain to get to that underground mushroom area. Didn't even realize I was in the mountain until I saw the textures around me. As nice as this can be when you're just about out of oxygen and your base is on the other side of a mountain, this completely breaks immersion. -Terraforming progress comes to a grinding halt when numbers hit terabytes. They slowly tick away, and it almost seems like nothing is happening at all.-Water. Water fills up EVERYWHERE. In places you would not expect. This is mostly a beginning stage issue, but there is no way to know where water will fill. I know starting place may vary, but do not get too comfortable in that ditch. Anything that uses energy does not work underwater, and your oxygen depletes underwater. I wish an elevation mechanic was implemented (other than the coordinates), at least when placing a building, etc. -Map seems huge when you can barely breathe, but quickly shrinks when you've hit the tree phase. Once you upgrade your oxygen abilities, it seems as though there is barely anywhere to explore anymore. -I know some might think this is a positive because of the realism, but materials do not regenerate. If you found a cave filled with uranium, you better be diligent on what you're using it on, as resources are finite. -Traveling is time consuming. Makes the game drag when the only ability you have to teleport becomes much later in the game, and uses a rare material to build. As much as I love a walking/flying simulator, this gets cumbersome after a while, especially after the update. Much running back and forth to one side of the map to the other. -SPOILER! - after finding the city behind the rock, my FPS died. I adjusted all my settings to low, and my game still slugged...so much so that I had to stop playing. Anytime I looked remotely in the direction of the palace, the lag overtook any beauty to behold. Not sure if this is just my experience, but I don't find this game anywhere near difficult to run besides this area. -The random survival elements seems dramatic and weirdly implemented. I feel like the pace that you need food and water is way too often. It just becomes a burden late game. i feel like if they're going for survival, sleep should also be required. You can't use/interact with the beds or furniture you create, which makes creating a beautiful living space feel pointless. Overall, I'm understanding that this is not a finished game, still has its bugs and a lot more development needed. I think it's a great game to play if you're looking for open world, survival feels without the stress. I think given it's early stage, it's a well put together game. I pop in to play every once in a while, and I look forward to future updates.

_childDocuments_.review: How can just two individuals surpass expansive games that took years and way more people to create? It's a combination of talent and passion! Even in its early access stage, the game stands out as an impressive achievement. One of its notable features is the excellent progression through stages. Witnessing the gradual transformation of the planet as you unlock new elements is exceptionally gratifying. The game has been designed to keep you engaged, offering a slow-paced experience that I find appealing. Every unlocked object holds significance, adding to the overall satisfaction.While the game excels in many aspects, there are areas that could be refined:-Optimization becomes an issue in areas where flora is abundant.-The aesthetic quality of the game falters due to low-quality textures.-Some textures allow characters to pass through them.-The jetpack's unlimited usage, while convenient, results in constant activation during movement.-I would have loved to see more natural growth of trees, grass, algae, butterflies, and fish after completing the respective stages.-The intriguing ruins discovered in the game could offer more than just keys to unlock new locations. (Note: The last ruins encountered had notable optimization issues, but their visual impact was still impressive.)Despite these minor concerns, they do not interfere with my enjoyment of the game. I see them as opportunities for improvement. It's encouraging to identify areas where enhancements can be made, especially considering the game already has a strong foundation with solid mechanics and gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: English isn't my first language, so please excuse errors.Cannot recommend, as it gets boring really fast. I played a single session for about 10 hours now on "Intense" and don't intend to continue playing it. When reading this feedback please bear in mind that this game is tagged as a survival game and that's what I bought it for.In contrast to what people post here this is, however, NOT a survival game, at least not if you have any meaningful amount of experience with other survival games. Here's why:- Global energy. Very stupid idea, because it allows you to spread your base across the whole map, defeating danger. If you want to avoid micromanagement of cables, at least restrict the energy to an area around the generators.- Living compartments can generate oxygen out of thin air (pun intended). Combined with the global energy this means you can just place single living compartments everywhere on the map and you won't have to worry about oxygen anymore. And it's illogical, considering that you otherwise have to create oxygen manually.- Generally NO upkeep necessary. Nothing decays, so whatever you build is there forever. Energy, water, food, living compartments ... everything. You build it, you keep it.- Similarly, neither your suit nor your flashlight or the JetPack consume energy/fuel. Again: You build it, you keep it.- Reagents required for survival are scattered everywhere. Food, water, etc. can always be found in the DOZENS of crates.- Food. Seeds are 100% guaranteed to return, so you only need three or four food generators and you'll be fine.- No danger. Ok, you can probably die from falling if you're stupid, but beyond that you only need to make sure that you have enough resources with you (of which there are always plenty) and you won't die. I realize the "no fighting" thing is intentional and I really like that, but you need to offset that through something else.- The meteorites don't cause damage. This may be intentional but just adds to the "not dangerous at ll" feeling- There are occasional dust storms, but they don't seem to cause any harm either.- Health bar seems underutilisedAll of the aspects above make this game VERY boring after an hour or two. Planet Crafter gives me zero incentive to keep playing, because I know "playing" in this case means waiting hours and hours for more "green" without any meaningful gameplay in between.And yes, I've already found three golden crates, found multiple underground bases, melted various pathways (shortcuts) and found the base of the previous planet crafter. It's still boring.On the positive side, I've had no crashes or any other game breaking bugs.To summarize: If you just want to terraform a planet somewhat similar to Minecraft creative mode, Planet Crafter might be your thing. Otherwise play a real survival game.Edit: Typo and fix "meteors" (they're meteorites, not meteors)

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A fun game with some high highs and very low lows, suitable for fans of base-building, exploration and a small degree of automation.So, The Planet Crafter took me and 2 other friends a few days to finish, we saw one of the 3 possible endings (the other two would require a level of grinding that we could not be interested in doing).We came into this game with the expectation of a mix of Satisfactory (one of our favorite games) and Valheim, given the survival elements. The game delivered partially on some of the promises, but not all.First, this is  a game about automation, until you're really close to finishing it, when it suddenly is. This transition is quite jarring, and it's a bummer that the process of automating things with drones makes the game a lot more interesting and dynamic, and yet the game thinks it's a good idea to gate it into the later parts of progression.For the majority of the game, however, this is a game about exploration, with a very light dose of base building (particularly early, where trying to establish a "home base" might hinder your progress way more than simply wandering around the map crafting small rooms to get some oxygen and then go back exploring). The shtick is: you need to terraform the planet, and that happens when you increase 4 factors: Pressure, Heat, Oxygen and Biomass. The first three are available from the start, and you get them by exploring, finding resources to turn into buildings that increase those numbers. As you progress, you unlock blueprints for different, better machines to increase those numbers, and some quality of life for the survival aspect of the game. Biomass comes in the second half of the game, when the planet is stable enough to start gaining plant life, and it's a little different, with you needing to do things like build animal feeders, aquariums and cultivating life forms for the planet. The game features a survival aspect that involves Hunger, Thirst and Oxygen. Hunger depletes the slowest of them all, but it's also one of the only ones that you will never 100% be able to ignore, since oxygen eventually becomes obsolete (the planet will have a breathable atmosphere, and all internal areas give oxygen, so as long as you carry enough materials to build a room and a door, you will never ever lose oxygen), and thirst, while still being something you need to deal with, is so trivially easy after a while that you will never die to it after the very start of the game. As for hunger, you will grow your own seeds and eat a lot of eggplant, but on the very start, there is a very real need to explore to keep finding food.There is no combat element, no enemies and no NPCs to interact with, save for written messages that you get once in a while. It makes exploring easy, with the challenge coming from the game's inventory system and the choices they made regarding it, which are as follows:1)You have a very limited inventory space, which has six levels of upgrading available, all of them adding more slots.2)No item in the game stacks, so EVERY SINGLE UNIT occupies a slot. If you want to carry 5 water bottles, 3 oxygen capsules and 3 pieces of food, that's a total of 11 slots of your backpack occupied only with survival. Need to bring Aluminum back? Every single unit of aluminum occupies a slot.While OF COURSE that is deliberate and intentional, it doesn't make it any less annoying, given a lot of the game's playtime is basically inflated via the fact you have to make several trips and build impromptu lockers in many spots to hold all the loot you need to carry back, which makes this game ideal to play with friends, since more people can carry more stuff around. The same logic also applies to any machines and storage units you make, every single item occupies a slot.Now I'll give a basic panorama of the base building and automation aspects of the game.As said before, there is, in the beginning, a very big incentive to building many small bases all around the map, because every base gives oxygen (so you get lots of places to stop and catch some air without dying), and because resources are all spaced out around the map. The base building is simple and functional, you build rooms one "compartment" at a time, and that compartment automatically links to adjacent ones, including vertically with the use of indoor stairs, so you will not have a lot of issues while building. It's important to note that part of the terraforming process entails the coming of lakes, waterfalls and rivers to the planet, so depending on the altitude you build, one or more of your bases might end up submerged in water (you lose no items, but all production for machines underwater ceases working), so it's smart to check the altitude coordinate and build planning for floods.After a while, you start building ore extractors, the first half of the  part of the game. Basically, Extractors come in 3 tiers, with each tier increasing your control over which ore you get. With tier 1, you can only place the extractor and get an assortment of all the available metals (plus a special metal if you place it in the correct spot), and you have to manually empty the machine (remember the 1-item-per-slot inventory? Yeah, that's an issue here) and do with the ore what you will. Given that all the important special materials are in specific spots in the map, that means for a while, you will have to build extractors spread around the map, and have people constantly walking around, bouncing from one to the next to keep the machines empty and running and depositing the products on a growing assortment of storage lockers (by the end of my save, I'm pretty sure I had over two-hundred lockers). You will then use these ores to progress by building more machines and etc.The next stage of automation the game allows, which I will call stage 1.5, is the ability to unlock Teleporters, that work beautifully and are well-done. Build a teleporter on every extractor you have, build the energy necessary to support it, and now instead of walking everywhere, you're teleporting everywhere. It doesn't really  anything, but not needing to walk makes the process a lot less painful, especially since by that point you still need to walk to find things other than ores, like all the many biomass parts.The final, and true stage of automation, the part that baffles me in how late it comes into the game are the drones. Drones simply change the game completely and turn it into an automation game through and through. You can get your drones to do the item pickups, deliver them to any item processors or storages, and do all sorts of automated crafting and refining of materials. By the end, you'll be creating automatic Fertilizers, growing and collecting food, making animal food, extracting all sorts of materials AND you'll have all the incentive to build a big central base to store and process all those things. By this point, the game in my opinion becomes really fun, but if you're not into automation games, this part can be really jarring, because if you don't make the best of it, you'll increase your playtime ten times solely based on relying on exploration to get all the important parts for the endgame grind.So, to wrap up my points, who do I recommend this game to?1)People with large friend groups. This game can be a grind sometimes, but it's also a lovely multiplayer experience for you to simply chat with your buddies while dividing tasks, and the game supports up to 10 people on a server at once.2)People who like peaceful exploration. There is no combat, and exploration is SUPER important in the game.3)People who enjoy automation games. There is not a lot of it in the early game, but it becomes important in the end.For me and my friends, it's a 5/10 on its low points (Inventory, some decisions) and a 7.5/10 on the highs (exploration moments, visuals and automation.)If it's for you, get it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pure joy. Don't even think about it, just buy it. The amount of time and effort the developer has put into this game really shows. Compared to the world of when I first got this game, the content has at least doubled and the methods of transforming your planet from a barren sandy rock to a green lush environment is amazing. I've restarted this game a few times now and it's more for fine tuning and trying different locations for my base. Don't get me wrong I've enjoyed every restart I've done as something has changed but maybe it's not a game to play over and over again with the same content unless your just experimenting with different designs.If you pressed me for a negative it would be the ending(s).
