_childDocuments_.review: Really fun, super addictive! I didn't like the complexity of Satisfactory - but I love this game! You can play at your own speed, go as fast or slow as you want. I'm very slow, take my time exploring and slowly build up the world terraforming. The other 2 players I know are playing much faster, and sending up multiple rockets to move faster. It works for all of us, when I need my world pushed forward a bit, I can invite one of them to come bump up my game by building things I hadn't gotten to, or sending off appropriate rockets to move the numbers forward. It's great fun to see grass start growing, flowers growing all over, water starting to acquire as the ice melts, learning to make butterfiies and bees!
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: For an early access, the game is very nice. After 5 hours and 30 minutes of playing, I have only reached stage 3 of the 10 terraforming levels in the game. Exploration is nice, even though you can cheat by regularly placing bases to refuel O2 without using bottles, and I have encountered no bugs.But the game still has big negatives at the moment:-   the basic construction is really not user-friendly and there are far too few crafts to make a base for a solitary terraformer-   The fact that each terraforming action only has bonuses eventually leads to ridiculous situations: currently, I am growing plants on the surface because I have reached the right concentration of O2, even though the atmospheric pressure and temperature are worthy of Pluto. Adding negative interactions between elements like "TerraGenesis" does on Android would prevent this kind of absurdity.The demo gives a very good overview of the game and should be a must-visit before buying the game at the moment. I can't wait to see the evolution of the game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I hate survival and grind games. If ever, I rarely play them. Planet Crafter is something else. You play and watch a piss-filter sky, a barren surfaced planet with boring orange rocks turn into a lush and blue Terran beauty. When I play a survival game, it normally feels like tasks extend the playtime for the sake of it. This game is Chekhov's Gun for PC games. Grinding materials and paying extra attention are rewarded rather than punished with the same repetitive task. It draws an opaque line between fun and challenge, offering something for everyone. I haven't finished the game because I don't want to be done with it immediately. The map is static and there are little bugs here and there. Casting these aside, this is an excellent gem from a humble and hardworking team. Note: More personal, flavour items would be a nice addition.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Been playing this regularly with a friend recently and it has been a ton of fun. All in all, It has been a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: After 121 hrs of play I have finished the game with 100% achievements. I didn't rush and loved every minute. It's a chill game with no pressure (apart from managing food/water) and it was fun to watch your planet go from a barren landscape into a thriving ecosystem. The lore was a nice touch and added further interest along the way. This is one of the few games I have completed (and possibly the only one where I got all achievements) as I tend to get bored after spending too long in a game. Although I have a lot more hours in other games, they are generally sandbox and don't have an ending and I also tend to take breaks with them. Overall if you are looking for a relaxing game to fill your time I can certainly recommend this one. Oh and I'm 65yrs old in case anyone of a similar age (or older) is unsure whether it would be a game for them.Note: I just read a comment about a player not wanting to lose their build and avoided playing any ending. You don't lose your build, that's how I managed to get 100%. You can load up the game after you chose an ending and it puts you back on the evacuation platform just prior to leaving so you are able to choose another option - if you have the correct materials etc.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically a fun game but it still needs a LOT of polish. Resources dot the landscape like rainbow sprinkles on a monochrome cake, with the only diegetic entry being resources dropped by meteors, which I do greatly like. The resource management is otherwise well managed, but be very careful to watch your oxygen supplies. Twenty three minutes in, I ran out of 02 outside a compartment with no door, at which point I was soft locked into and endless loop of suffocating before I can reach the drop pod or gather the resources to make a door. THANKFULLY it wasn't far in so no real loss for me, but I dread to think what would happen to a player in a bad position multiple hours in. The building mechanics are also a bit... odd. You can't *actually* place any of your habitation cubes on the ground, they have to hover ominously a few inches of the ground. You can rotate the cube and the access stairs 90 degrees before building, which makes the fact that the the doors can be rotated by 10 degrees an interesting choice. And be careful when placing a a hab cube on any elevated purpose, because you can't attach stairs until after the cube and door are in, so if the cube is an inch too far in one direction, the stairs clip a tiny rock or a random loot chest and you need to deconstruct and rebuild the entire thing, or just access your base via mad ups.I want to see where this game goes. This looks like a product with a lot of promise, but this release seems too early for even early access.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. It took me months to start playing it even after I bought it. I had seen a couple of videos on it and thought, meh, looks ok but kinda cheesy. I am glad I finally started. The game can use some lore and background but I've read that that is coming in future updates. There is Lots to do and a lot more coming according to the devs. Updates are frequent and impactful. I have only encountered one small graphical bug when mining but that is it and it doesn't affect gameplay at all. Highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Having spent nearly 12 hours immersed in The Planet Crafter, I find it to be an engaging experience. As a player, you’ll explore resource gathering, construct bases, upgrade technology and strive to escape the planet’s confines.Resource Gathering: Scouring the barren landscape for essential materials keeps you on your toes.Base Building: Balancing power and functionality while constructing your refuge becomes an art form.Technological Advancements: Upgrading machinery progresses terraformation and unlocks new possibilities, propelling your journey forward.Around Terraformation 7.0 MTi, the game begins to drag. Yes, there’s a learning curve. The formula tilts toward experienced gamers, encouraging thoughtful decision-making.As we await future patches, I hope the developers address the pacing beyond this point. Perhaps more surprises, new crafting recipes or unexpected encounters will be revealed.For the current price of $16, The Planet Crafter delivers an impressive value. It’s a universe worth exploring, even when the terraforming process tests our patience.In summary, The Planet Crafter isn’t just a game; it’s a canvas where you paint your survival story. Verdict: Worth every cent of those 16 bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: So this is the land locked (at first) version of legally distinct "Subnautica" You start of as a no named convicted criminal who's only way to earn freedom is to terraform a planet that you are not the first criminal sent to fix up...as you start the ball rolling you get points in 1 of the 3 branches that unlock more tech that speeds you along to making the planet ready for habitation.Now the game does not tell ya much of this at the start so your going to be going around blind for at least 30 mins.Another thing the game doesn't tell you is to get to the crashed ships you can find on the map asap as they hold very important blueprints, mats and mission required machinery.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Hard not to recommend this as it is extremely addictive, there is always something to focus on - basically alternating between the crafting side of things to advance the terraforming cycle, to unlock more progress, and then the planet exploration while the numbers tick up, to uncover some of the secrets of where you have ended up - and also pick up some more blueprints that increase quality of life.There were only a few times that I felt a little bit stuck on progress, but often it just came down to me not focusing enough on one side or the other and having to catch up.It is by no means perfect: * The ordering of the terraforming cycle is a bit out of sync with reality (you should really get fish / amphibians first before flowers, trees, and insects?) but still really satisfying to see the world come to life around you from your actions. * Some of the blueprints also unlock in a strange order (I can make T3 mutagen but not yet T2?). * Gathering machines that produce multiple things with random chances would do well to tell you what you _could_ get not just the most likely?  * Lighting is strange in some places, with some really jarring over-saturation. * Weather effects have the chance to happen far too frequently - I had two late-game meteor showers in very quick succession that completely overloaded me with what once were scarce materials. * Token rewards for putting effort into trading are tiny compared to the windfalls you get just from exploring some wrecks, and containers that once may have just had simple resources start to give you hundreds of TT out of nowhere, so it never feels worthwhile to make stuff instead of wreck diving. 9 for a cookie that requires so many resources to make, seriously? And nothing for the cake, not even an achievement? But I find its faults to be fairly minor and forgiveable compared to how much I have enjoyed playing. Not sure how much replayability there may be, the discoverable blueprints unlock in a slightly random order but all that really does is impose some annoying movement restrictions on you if you get unlucky. And the changing starting locations just makes things slightly more tedious at the earliest part of the game until you can move around the map more freely.I think it would also be interesting if the possible endings did not rely on the same underlying condition - feels like one in particular could happen much earlier, possibly two, that would make for some variety.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really unbalanced, there are a TON of glitches, and the rules for a lot of the endings arent clear unless you are going to look it up before you start. To make it all worse the story is really anti-climactic. You spend so much time trying to survive just for two ending cards slides that dont really tie it up. Nothing in the game makes any sense and it doesnt connect together. All in all this is a super poor rip off of Subnautica with an unfinished story and really poor mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: To be completely honest, I wasn't expecting a lot out of this game. _childDocuments_.review: One of the coolest games in its category.The atmosphere of the game is outstanding.We focus on building and construction. _childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great for a casual survival experience. Since this game has no hostile creatures, a player can relax and enjoy making the world habitable. The experience of seeing the world change from barren to lush green is highly satisfying. There is a bit of lag on my old machine as the terraforming advances but since the game is still in development, that is to be expected. Updates are regular and bugs are minimal. This is a great game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Cannot wait for the next update to this excellent game just so that I can watch the land change further from a desolate sand pit to a tree and flower covered planet. _childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: This game is surprising, I started playing it because of the concept of giving life back to a planet and stayed cause I somehow started feeling attached to this world the game allows you to build, finding bits of lore, seeing how much it changes, and when I start thinking I saw everything, a new tech ges added to the list, and each time it's a blast to build it and try it out!TL,DR : A chill farming game where you explore and see how much you can impact the planet and how far you can go, definitely a good one!

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and great game to play with a friend, however it is rough around the edges.The weather effects are awful as it either blinds you or makes everything too dark to see, including indoors, not to mention the shaking which you must turn off.The game feels poorly optimised as even with the minimum graphics, my computer runs as well as Red Dead 2 with the highest graphics. Construction has a lot of issues, a LOT of things align poorly and you cannot place things into the terrain or any FUTURE terrain, i.e. trees. Really annoying placing anything for someone with OCD. HOWEVER, the game is really fun, and would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Dare I say, one of the best games i've played in quite some time.The only problem is, I can't wait for the next developments having played it through. I hope we might see more worlds, more customisation, more challenge i.e. adverse weather damage and what would be the ultimate win...people colonisation!
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: The Planet Crafter offers an exhilarating journey of survival and creativity on an alien world. This indie gem excels in blending the sandbox genre with survival mechanics, tasking players with terraforming a desolate planet into a lush, habitable environment. The game's progression system is deeply satisfying, as players gradually transform barren landscapes through resource gathering, crafting, and strategic planning. The immersive atmosphere, combined with stunning visual effects and a dynamic weather system, keeps players engaged as they witness their efforts visibly altering the planet's ecosystem.What sets The Planet Crafter apart is its meticulous attention to detail and the sense of accomplishment it imparts. The game cleverly balances challenges and rewards, ensuring that each step forward feels hard-earned yet immensely rewarding. From constructing advanced infrastructure to discovering hidden secrets of the planet, every action contributes to a larger, cohesive narrative. Whether you're a fan of survival games or enjoy the creative freedom of sandbox experiences, The Planet Crafter offers an engaging and satisfying adventure that stands out in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: Well, let's see. I've played it 9.5 hours or so... nope... don't like it. ;-DKidding of course!i'm enjoying it so far for early release. _childDocuments_.review: this game is really great. ill start right off the bat saying this game does kind of look like a unity asset flip scam, no offense to the devs. but i guarantee most people looking at this game are wondering if its a good game or going to be a janky game that never gets updated. this game is surprisingly deep! its kind of basic at first, collect a handful or resources, build stuff, replenish stats. but as i have been playing the game just keeps expanding, and expanding and its a lot of fun. its similar to subnautica in a lot of ways, the devs definitely have played subnautica, but i think thats a good thing because that was a great game too. i havent experienced any bugs or stuttering, the game is made by a small dev team but the clearly have a passion project with this game i believe they will keep expanding it. if the trailers look interesting then you will like this game. the game has a unique feel to it, good music and the game knows what it wants to be. and nowadays with so many games just being copies of other successful games its nice to see a game making its own niche
_childDocuments_.name: The Planet Crafter

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure if I would like this game because I'm usually not a fan of first person view games. Maybe I quit too soon before it got good but I should not have to play more than 14 hours for a game to start being good. For me I am not going to force myself to keep playing anymore in the hopes of it getting better.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It is satisfying and quite enjoyable to actually craft certain aspects of the planet and watch it change gradually over time, but it is very tedious. Travelling around takes a long time and gets frustrating even with shortcuts, but you are almost always rewarded for exploring.----------------     There will be spoilers and this review is mostly complaining but trust me when I say that I like the game. It is still in early access so things may get changed in the future.     Planet Crafter has been an enjoyable experience overall. The progression of the tech trees as you make the planet more and more hospitable leads to a somewhat satisfying game-play loop. The progression starts off quick and really gets you excited to discover new materials and recipes so that you can make this desolate wasteland into a livable planet.     Dealing with Oxygen, Water and Health, is stressful and difficult at the beginning, but as you get further along, it slowly becomes easier to manage with new oxygen tanks, bigger backpacks and water collectors. It eventually becomes less of a game mechanic and more of a minor inconvenience that you have to remember and be aware of so that you don't die.      Near the end of the available content, I started to get frustrated having to deal with water and food when I could so easily remedy them with my numerous collectors and farms. It isn't difficult to keep your needs met nearing the end of the game, but in the beginning and throughout, it was crucial that you bring water bottles and oxygen tanks if you intended to be out wandering or gathering for any period of time. Initially you are always searching for ice to make water, but as you heat the planet ice begins to melt and you need collectors to gather from the atmosphere. This was very cool, so you no longer needed to worry about water. It really freed me up to do more interesting things.      After water was managed I still needed to search for cobalt to make oxygen. This never really changes, you need oxygen until very late game when you have successfully made a breathable atmosphere. It gets easier with bigger O2 tanks, and special tech later in the game like the gas collector and air filter. It never stops being tedious though, so I resorted to making a little habitation box with a door whenever I got low on oxygen since it refills when in a player made structure. This felt like cheating, but it is necessary if you want to do anything in the game.     My biggest gripe with the game is the travelling. A lot of the game is travelling around between areas to pickup materials or visit mineral extractors. I am not exaggerating when I say it accounts for half my playtime at the least. As you terraform the world, you unlock alternate routes to explore which end up being shortcuts to far out areas so it cuts that time down. There are several movement speed upgrades which is nice early on, but the explorable area is quite large and even though they increase your speed it's not really noticeable when it still takes a couple minutes to get anywhere. The Jetpack upgrade will let you hover slightly above the ground and go much faster but you will have to constantly hold down the jump button which begins to cause cramping. I ended up taking notes of materials I needed because you can't see recipes while traveling around, and it become endlessly frustrating going out for materials and getting 1 less than you needed so you have to travel all the way back again.     Nearing the end of the game you unlock teleporters. Which are a life saver, but that is about when I realized how much time was spent travelling. The materials to make them are very rare when they get unlocked and so you are lucky to have enough for 3. Even with only 2 it cuts down the travel time immensely and I realized that I didn't really know what to do with myself. I needed materials, but my extractors weren't gathering quickly enough now that I could travel so fast, so I needed more of them, but I needed the extractors to extract the materials to make more extractors and I would end up just tabbing out of the game while everything just chugged away. This was my first time playing and so I didn't really know what I needed and what materials were important. It was definitely poor planning on my part and if I play again, I can definitely optimize my buildings so that I don't need to do that.     The game eventually got to a point where I knew what I needed to do, but I had no idea how to go about doing it. I needed a massive amount of materials for a minimal gain. Unfortunately that massive amount of materials also requires a massive amount of storage. I ended up making dozens of large containers for all of the materials that my extractors were gathering. You are able to make a device that destroys materials so you can trash less valuable materials, but in my experience whenever I would use it, I would end up needing the materials I scrapped, so I would inevitably just end up hoarding all the junk materials that my extractors pulled up.     Something I really think could remedy my issue with late game storage issues is something akin to a massive storage container the size of a building that you can deposit things into manually or will automatically draw stored materials from within a certain range that you can link up to a computer system so that you can connect up your different crafting stations to one big automatically sorted inventory. Having to remember so many recipes is already difficult, and there was a number of times where I looked at a recipe at my crafting station then ran to my storage area and grabbed the materials to a different but similar recipe or maybe 1 extra of something or 1 less of another something. This situation was another reason I ended up having to take notes.     There are a lot of good things that I would like to say as well, but it's hard to pick them out. The game is relaxing and it is very satisfying when you get into the swing of things. There are also lots of logs from previous Planet Crafters and little story telling areas that add a bit of reality to your situation. Coming across secret areas or new and unexpected things is pretty exciting. As the planet develops new areas or routes open up to explore and exploring around was almost always rewarded either with rare materials or a new interesting area.     During the process of terraforming you get to choose where you want different plant, trees, and bugs, which adds a lot of customization that I didn't expect. Nearing the end of the game I decided to make a more interesting spectacle or my world while I waited for my progress to tick up, so I would pick out areas to build massive power plants or wind/solar farms. I started to choose which biomes I wanted certain plants and trees in, which ponds or lakes I wanted algae in, and these things really added a lot to my experience. I ended up expanding several of my emergency oxygen huts into full fledged bases with teleporters in them.     In conclusion, I really enjoyed the beginning and very end of the game, I loved being rewarded for curiosity but I had a lot of problems along the way, some of the issues could be fixed by creating plans for my production. Others though, like the travelling and storage really made it hard to enjoy the mid game. The hunger, oxygen and water system feels necessary early game to give you something to focus on, but late game it feels completely irrelevant and becomes just an annoyance. Overall my experience was positive so I'm happy to recommend the game, but the tedious bits are very tedious and I think they could be improved upon.

name: Guild Wars 2
detailed_description: Guild Wars 2's open world is all about discovery and exploration. Check your content guide for suggestions when you set out on your adventures, consult your compass to find interesting landmarks…or just pick your favorite direction to travel in and let adventure find you. Tyria is full of characters with their own stories and goals, and you'll be rewarded for helping them out—or thwarting their plans—by completing renown hearts and dynamic events. Read our new player guide for more tips! When you meet other players in the open world, you don't need to join their party to lend a helping hand, investigate a secret jumping puzzle, or team up against a deadly world boss. Don't grind; play the way you want to play! Whether you're reviving defeated players, rescuing soldiers from a Risen onslaught, or gathering herbs, you'll earn experience points. Arm your character with an arsenal of new weapons as you play. Every profession wields them differently, and each type has its own playstyle, which you can refine and customize by unlocking and equipping hundreds of skills and traits. If you want to jump straight into structured PvP, go for it—every player competes at the same level, with access to the max-level gear and build options you need to make your mark. If you love fashion, express yourself with the perfect character design! When you equip new weapons and armor, you'll unlock their skins in your wardrobe. Make them truly yours with thousands of possible combinations and a massive selection of collectible dyes. Upgrade your free account with a Guild Wars 2 expansion and get access to log-in rewards, additional character and bag slots, expanded chat features, and more. Visit the Black Lion Trading Company in the game and use your Steam Wallet to upgrade. Expansions and Living World seasons feature unique rewards and new Masteries to expand your character's abilities. Unlock and upgrade your glider in Guild Wars 2: Heart of Thorns, befriend a stable of mounts with powerful movement skills in Guild Wars 2: Path of Fire, and learn to fish and pilot a skiff in Guild Wars 2: End of Dragons. Each expansion grants access to nine elite specializations that unlock new weapon choices, skills, and abilities for your profession. You'll also be able to select the revenant profession at character creation and channel legendary heroes and villains from Tyria's history. Living World seasons continue the Guild Wars 2 story between expansions and must be purchased separately through your Story Journal or in Gem Store bundles. Play Living World episodes to unlock new explorable zones, rewards, and Masteries. *Living World episodes become playable at level 80. Players may need to relaunch the game for the upgrade to take effect. **Please note that existing Guild Wars 2 player accounts cannot be accessed via Steam

_childDocuments_.review: In Guild Wars 2, the gearing process involves an extensive and repetitive grind of acquiring countless stacks of "useless material x" to craft component A. This is followed by farming overwhelming quantities of stacks of y to create component C, then progressing to amass stacks of z for component D. Again and again.All of this effort is ultimately geared towards obtaining an item, but the journey is marred by unengaging and monotonous content.The quality of the content lacks excitement, never presents a challenge, and ultimately feels like a considerable waste of time.When faced with such a grinding experience, it's tempting to opt for a quicker escape by purchasing an attractive outfit from the gem store, allowing for a brief 10-minute appreciation before logging off.The desire for more meaningful and entertaining content becomes evident, especially when the current gameplay feels like a repetitive cycle with minimal satisfaction.The drop rates for prestige items are disappointingly low, to the point where obtaining these items feels almost impossible. It's as if the items practically do not exist, making the pursuit of prestige rewards an excessively challenging and frustrating endeavor.Ultimately, players engage with content in pursuit of rewards rather than for the content itself.When both the rewards and the content prove to be elusive, unattainable, and lacking in entertainment value, players understandably become impatient.The disconnect between effort invested and the satisfaction gained can lead to frustration and a diminished sense of motivation.A more balanced and rewarding system that aligns player efforts with meaningful and attainable rewards would contribute significantly to enhancing the overall gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Pay no mind to my hours logged thru Steam, I've got like about 1,500 to 2K hours in this game regardless of what it says on Steam.  (I only recently discovered how to access my existing  account via Steam.  [Right-click GAME PROPERTIES, and add the line "-provider Portal" in the launch options. Boom.This is one of my favorite games and it respects your time without introducing power/gear-score creep.  This is due to it's horizontal progression system.  You can literally quit playing  this game for a year and come back and be just as effective/powerful as you were when you left without being left behind, so there's no FOMO and no need to keep logging in to stay updated.The base game alone has hundreds of hours of content and the experience system works by using mainly map discovery, combat exp, radial quests, to guide you thru leveled areas, and there's a good level scaling system in place so you can still play your level 80 character in a newbie zone and do the regional quests/hearts there for a worth-while prize in both gear and exp.There are dungeons, raids, world bosses, fractals (dungeon/raid hybrid), seasonal story-lines (re-playable) , seasonalo holidaylevents, and the most fun PvP and WvW I've ever had in a game, and I typically HATE PVP.  If you take part in PvP you are automatically level scaled to max level with all builds and traits unlocked while in the PvP lobby so you can INSTANTLY right off the bat play some PvP and contend with players who have already been playing for ages. This makes PVP about skill and not who grindr'd the most d̶u̶d̶e̶s̶ mythics .There's a good variety of classes and abilities that are learnable or unlocked through specific combinations of gear, you can run as many equipment and trait combos/builds as you want and save them and swap between them.  You can literally play however your playstyle is, be a sneaky ninja mans, or a tanky chad, or a shooty ranger man, or be a mesmer and beat enemies down with 20 of your clones.  you can be tiny gnomish gadget man, a big furry beast, or a necromancer and attack with gross dead things.  Once you go to max level there's a prestige system called "elite specializations" which even opens you up to using weapons that you couldn't typically use before and even more abilitiies to unlock.The professions and crafting system is top teir, and there is so much stuff you can do and experiement with different combinations of random items to try to to build, and you can def have fun cooking, arftificing, jewelry making, alchemy, mining, armor, tanning, clothing and more and more to your hearts content. You can make stuff for your guild, or for other players and trade on the market.The game is super-mega populated with multiple servers being so full that if it were a real building the fire marshal has to be called for a code violation and I have never had any problem finding players for even the old dungeons that came out years ago.  The community is one of the best and most friendly/helpful and least toxic I have ever seen in a game.I have played many games, ESO, FFXIV, WOW, Tarisland, Ember's Adrift, Everquest 1/2, DDO, LOTRO and I have to say that right off the bat, GW2 is by far the best MMORPG I have played hands down.  It is not pay to win although there are EXP skips, but with the way PvP and PVE are progression separated it's merely convenience.  This game is more Pay to DRIP, so of course dope character skins and cool transmogs are the endgame.Aesthetically some of the environments are absolutely jaw dropping and stunning I've EVER seen in an MMORPPG especially one that's been around as long as this one has been, and I personally love the painterly art-style and aesthetic that this game is going for and I hope they keep on brand for GW3. <311/10 highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've got 400 in-game hours on my main character and I've played through all the expansions - I'll try to be as objective as possible. The game is F2P with P2P expansions and there are no subscriptions so you never feel like you're wasting time when you're not playing the game. In PvE gear has no impact, how you perform is only up to your micro play and how well you execute your rotation which can range from 2 spells (power rev) to 50 (condi weaver).In PvP everyone gets equal gear so the entry bar is pretty low compared to other games which require you to farm hundreds of raids for low drop rate BiS items.Instead of tedious quests you level up by doing heart quests(events), random events, killing world bosses, etc.Also, your gear never become obsolete, you can actually come back to the game after 2 years and log in on your max lvl char and do fine in all types of content, meanwhile in other games every new expansion/content-update (FFXIV, WoW, etc.) your gear that you spent hundreds of hours on getting is completely meaningless.Late game consists of PVE(Fractals of the Mists(5 player dungeons with increasing difficulty and insane replayability - much harder than WoW dungeons because you actually have to perma dodge stuff not just stand in place and cast), Raids(10 player boss focused instances with scaling difficulty), Strike Missions(10 player boss focused instances that are meant to be an introduction to raids),  PVP(arenas(2v2), capture points(5v5), World vs World(siege)).A lot of people seem to be into getting all the achievements/transmogs/collectibles which the game has A LOT.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game for quite a bit for the past 2 years before it hit steam and I gotta say.𝙄𝙩'𝙨 𝙖𝙬𝙚𝙨𝙤𝙢𝙚.I've played many mmorpgs over the years but none of them held my interest as long as guild wars 2 has. It's a game that many people will find something to enjoy. Like world exploration and dynamic events, challenging PvE group content, competitive player vs player "king of the hill" type fighting, server vs server wide all out brawls between dozens of players in massive battlegrounds where you can capture enemy camps, siege fortified castle walls with catapults or break down reinforced walls with flame rams in huge groups of players. Fast fluid and fun combat that holds up well after 10 years of it's release, 9 different classes and 3 specializations within each class. All of them with different playstyles and unique abillities that distinguish themselves from each other. Unique mounts that help you traverse the world. Ride your raptor that specializes in broad jumps to traverse over large gaps in terrain. Get on the springer to hop over vertical heights and get to higher places. Use your skimmer to travel fast over large bodies of water. The jackal mount will help cross sand portals in the deserts of Elona. Finally there's flying. You can use your glider to gracefully descend over large amounts of terrain or ride your griffon that can dive bomb from high up in the skies and use it's momentum to glide at extreme speeds.The game sports a cash shop that uses gems as currency which you can buy with real money or turn your in-game gold into gems or vice-versa. The shop sells stuff that ranges from purely cosmetic, to consumables that give you a % boost exp to all or some game modes, antiquated and (quite frankly useless) one-time consumables that summon an npc to allow remote access to your bank for a short while and account unlocks such as more character slots, item bag space slots, bank slots, equipment template slots, skill build template slots, etc. And also the living world seasons which are like mini expansions (that contain tons of content and story) which players can purchase with gems.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who are not a fan of the MMO grind and are looking for a more grind-optional gameplay, then like me, Guild Wars 2 may just be the greatest MMORPG you'll have ever played. I have tried nearly every F2P/B2P MMO out there and personally, nothing comes close to GW2. I've played GW2 before it got to Steam and am yet to explore the wondrous features of the expansions, but even just the base game alone is more than worth your time. Graphics are dated obviously for a more than a decade-old game. But where GW2 stands out is with its kit-based, skill-based, versatile gameplay, wide(and I mean WIDE) range of customization/transmog options, and, like its name suggests, its guild-focused tasks, missions, and community events. Back when I last played, it would take you about two to three weeks to reach end game content(assuming you rushed through the game), and by that I mean be on par with the latest and strongest gear, which is called ascended equipment(after an 11 year hiatus, most of my end game gear is STILL on par with the meta. There is basically NO POWER CREEP. No FOMO bs, just play at your own pace).Then you'd have what I mentioned earlier, the hardcore/grind-optional gameplay. This is where legendary equipment come in. I have 1 of them. And that single gear took me six, SIX(!!!) months to grind! And this is considering that I had to buy one of the materials required with irl money(about 40 USD) because back then, it was either pure RNG to obtain it or buy it from the auction house for a sizeable amount of in-game money. But don't get me wrong, the gold it required to purchase it off the auction house wasn't too bad, it would've taken me about 2-3 hours of grinding daily for about 2 weeks to obtain it, give or take a couple days? But at that point I had just come off a six month grind of the other materials so I was pretty jaded and not up to the task anymore, so I took the shortcut lol(aaaand I was pretty stoked to finally obtain my legendary weapon since it was the LAST remaining material I needed). What exactly is this legendary equipment you might ask? It has the EXACT same stats as the gear tier I mentioned earlier, the ascended equipment, but lookswise, just way, WAY more awesome looking. Pretty much an upgraded version cosmetically. If you wanted to stand out, flex your gear and ♥♥♥♥, legendary equips were the way to go. Looking to just chill with your guildies and log in every other day? Totally fine as well, just put on full ascended gear and you're on an even playing field with the rest of the entire playerbase(although back then there were only ascended accessories but since there are ascended armor and weapons now, I'd say about a month to a month and a half of grinding gets you there? Could be wrong tho). And that is where the beauty of GW2 lies, with how flexible the game is to your preference and taste. Wanna go full PVE? You got it, a couple of tinkering here and there with certain in-game preferences and you're good to go. Or are you more into competitive PVP? Still not a prob, you can even LEVEL UP from PVP. Again, just such a flexible game with a PLETHORA of options, including its classes. GW2 is one of those games that puts up a middle finger to the holy trinity of MMO roles. Are you tired of being restricted into being either a tank, healer, or DPS? Then worry no more, since you can be a tank that heals or a DPS that tanks, or even a versatile ranged class that tanks. You can only have 5 class specific skills and 5 class specific-weapon specific skills(by this I mean a mace wielding warrior will have different weapon skills from a mace wielding guardian), which is what I referred to above as your "kit", which could make a team of 5 players of the same class wholly unique with their individual strengths and weaknesses(for example, you could be a DPS focused warrior, a tanky warrior, a support warrior, a CC focused warrior, or even a a healer warrior! Whatever floats your boat!). You might be wondering next, how EXACTLY would that work with its dungeons? Most of GW2's dungeons are what I'd call... objective based? And, well, a bit of cheese lol, like getting certain bosses to glitch and stuff. But most of the time just good ole knowledge and skill! Whereas most MMORPGs require a recommended set of equipments or "gear score" to be able to take on its dungeons, GW2 shines in this department with its reliance on know-how and preparation. A veteran and skilled dungeoneer who is patient enough with a party full of obedient beginners should be able to walk them through the toughest dungeons without breaking a sweat, you just have to know your role and have the requisite knowledge. And don't even get me started on its in-game guild missions! Two of which are an obstacle race and the other a massive, escape room(escape house?)-esque activity which the ENTIRE guild can partake in. And all of these are just scratching the surface on what makes GW2 just the GOAT MMO in my opinion. Sadly, the playerbase is steadily dwindling tho it still has a decent amount of players... for now. I guess it has to do with GW2 being a sort of niche game, as it may very well not be everyone's cup of tea what with the fondness of mandatory grinding for next best gear of the MMO community. But if you're looking for something new as a seasoned MMO veteran who's played mostly grindy games, then I suggest you try GW2. Tho I highly recommend joining an active guild ASAP, as this is where one of the game's strength lies. Or maybe you're someone who hasn't tried any MMO yet, in which case I'd say GW2 would be a solid introduction to the genre because of how versatile it is. All in all, one of my very few 10/10 games. There's a reason why it's still the second highest rated game on  and why it's consistently mentioned as one of the best MMORPGs on most MMO sites after more than a decade of release.

_childDocuments_.review: 10 years with the game, 17 with the series. I certainly haven't lost interest since I started playing all those years ago and have never felt left behind when I've taken breaks to do other things in my life. It's always been available. Even their first game Guild Wars 1 is still running and I sometimes still log onto that game just for nostalgic purposes. I would say try the game out. See if it fits for you. It's plentiful in offering a variety things to do and the story, lore, and world of Tyria can be a mesmerizing fantasy experience. It's definitely a game I'll put more years into.To new players: 1. Soak in your surroundings, explore the environment. Talk to NPC's with a heart above them.  Heart quests aren't 1 dimensional, they offer different avenues for completion. They also don't reset in the core game. So if you want to stop mid way through a heart completion and do something else (maybe another heart NPC) you can do that. Events are also sprinkled about throughout the map each with their own mini stories. Some events are even chained, so a completion or a failure of one event might spawn a new chain of events that are a result of the outcome of that. This was Anet's selling point when they first released the game. As they wanted the game world to feel alive and that player choice mattered. Events will also attract other players so you won't feel so alone in the game world should you choose to participate. 2. Don't feel like you have to play "catch-up" to players that have more years on their belt. Play at your own pace. The game will still be here 10 years from now. I mentioned earlier that their first game Guild Wars 1 is still being maintained. Guild Wars 2 isn't going anywhere anytime soon. 3. Have fun. The Guild Wars 2 community is helpful and chomps at the bit to help new players any chance that pops up. Yes some do look strange (especially the glowing multi-colored giants that look like they jumped into a pool of radioactive nuclear rainbow ooze) but they're extremely friendly (maybe too friendly). Don't hesitate to reach out for help if you get stuck on something. Anyways that's all I have. I guess. I don't know. Good luck!

_childDocuments_.review: An MMORPG with a focus on exploration and cooperation with other players - often times complete strangers.In my experience, I've only had one bad encounter with another player, and that was in PvP (which, yeah, that's where you're bound to find it).I've spent hours just exploring the areas, getting all the little advancements per zone, and then going on to the next place to see what's there until I progress through my personal story. So far haven't spent a dime and I've had a ton of fun.That being said: the game *does* feel very grindy if you don't have XP boosters. This is to encourage exploration and doing other things than the main story, but it does take a long while if you're mostly on your own. However, events are plentiful, there's always something to do to earn XP, and even the dungeons are repeatable (and they give huge amounts of XP in my runs, I leveled up like 5 times each in the first two dungeons lol).All in all, 9/10 game. Good community, good gameplay that doesn't require you to have advanced keybinds (just 1-9 and you're good to go), and a very good art style.... even if some of the female outfits are... questionable.

_childDocuments_.review: Guild Wars 2 has truly become my digital home away from home, and after clocking in a whopping 1000 hours of gameplay, I can confidently say it's a masterpiece in the world of MMORPGs.One of the standout features of Guild Wars 2 is its breathtakingly beautiful and diverse world. From the sprawling landscapes of Tyria to the meticulously crafted cities, every corner is a visual treat. The attention to detail is evident in every nook and cranny, making exploration an absolute joy.The dynamic events system keeps the game world feeling alive and ever-changing. Whether it's rallying to defend a village from a sudden attack or embarking on an epic boss battle, the unpredictability of events adds an immersive layer to the gameplay. No two moments are the same, keeping me on my toes and making every hour feel fresh.The character customization in Guild Wars 2 is nothing short of exceptional. The variety of races, professions, and the ability to mix and match skills allow for a truly unique gaming experience. The flexibility to switch between weapon sets and adapt to different playstyles adds depth and replay value, making each encounter a new opportunity to experiment and refine strategies.The community aspect is another strong point. From dynamic world events to massive world vs. world battles, collaborating with other players is not only encouraged but essential for success. The camaraderie and sense of accomplishment after overcoming challenges together foster a strong sense of community that keeps me coming back for more.The Living World updates have consistently brought fresh content, ensuring that the game stays relevant and exciting. The continuous support from the developers showcases their commitment to delivering a top-notch gaming experience.

For the longest time, I only played these types of games with some exceptions (Any OGs remember Firefall?) until it got old and eventually I stopped completely. A few years later, during high school, I stumbled upon GW2 and my nostalgia got ignited once again. Ever since then I played the F2P version on and off for a couple years whenever I got the MMORPG blues and those were some fond memories. _childDocuments_.review: One of the best MMOs out there.I made a huge mistake years ago, when, burnt out of MMOs due to World of Warcraft, I missed out on playing this gem of a game. Luckily, the game is still running, has a huge community, and is free!-----A few of my favourite things about it:- For the collectors and achievement hunters out there, the achievements you could do at launch are still there. Unlike games like WoW, you're not missing out because you've not been there from the get go. There's some small exceptions, but when you compare it to the massive amounts of content that's forever locked in WoW or Destiny, it's a breath of fresh air. Enjoy the game, knowing that you have time to get all those sweet achievements.- The community is friendly and welcoming; coming from other MMOs in the past, the communities are generally toxic and not beginner friendly. I found that to not be the case in GW2, people will actively try to help you and general chat will answer questions you have, etc.- Shared Trading; If you ever experienced a market crash in New World or early WoW, you know how annoying (or profitable) it can be. And likewise, if you are looking for an exceedingly rare item, it may only be in some high pop servers. Guild Wars uses one trading post\auction house for the entire player base, so if it's not there, it's not anywhere!- Graphically, it's held its own too. It strides a nice middle-ground between the utter cartoonish look of WoW, and the hyper-realism of Black Desert. They update the graphics as they go, though you'll find some older skins for weapons and armour may be lower quality or outdated. Luckily, there's a transmog system to help in those cases!What are you waiting for? Buy this free game, and install it today!

_childDocuments_.review: At well over 3000 hours, I can still say one thing: Arenanet's advertising skills are terrible but the game is the polar opposite.Why should you play Guild Wars 2 over any of the newer MMORPGs out there right now?I won't go over the regular staples - they are all here, gear, quests, dungeons, raids... all the trimmings. There are things here that I have never seen in any other mmo, and they impress me greatly to this day:1. This is an mmo that respects your time and money.This is a game that you can play for a month or two get some exotics (baseline 80 gear), leave for 3 years and come back exactly where you were - able to play all the content available then, and after those years pass. There is no gear treadmill, no reason to feel like you are missing out by not playing constantly. If you choose to play casually, you are not at a disadvantage to raiders or even streamers playing 24/7 - an even playing field in all content. There are rewards for high end content but they are conveniences and cosmetics, bragging rights and the actual fun of raids done right but nothing to say: You are playing the game wrong such as with World of Warcraft or other major players in the space.As for money, Arenanet does not charge a subscription in any way, but counter their other free-to-play competition, there is NOTHING in the store that could in the wildest stretch be considered player power. By picking up and playing the game free, you can play all the content in Tyria, dungeons, fractals (short duration dungeons - more time respect) and even baseline raids. Should you CHOOSE (if you enjoy something why wouldn't you want more of it) to pick up the expansions/living story you get a fair price for incredible amounts of content. I have since purchased all the living story/expansions and consider it a steal without a single regret.2. Gameplay design is skewed to create the least toxic community I have ever seen. While you can't attribute the community as a whole to a developer, at every junction possible ANET has encouraged cooperative play - passive buff sharing, personal loot (no tagging), rewards for assisting and helping fallen allies - skills to assist players with travel/puzzles, I can't even go over each instance but it all contributes over time to creating a positive community that wants to help and be nice to each other. They essentially are dog training players, that they will get experience/loot for helping in any way they can.In my experience this does not carry over to the structured pvp (wvw is still great however)... given the naturally competitive nature of those people - you have been warned.3. Story - This has the biggest caveat. As a whole, Guildwars 2's story is brilliant, fully voice acted, filled with clever twists, has memorable moments and truly gives a feel of being a part of an incredible world. At least it is, after personal story which is the story that follows character creation and culminates at 80 - and as far as I am concerned is the weakest foot forward for GW2. New players will find the style (character cutouts with voice acting) and be middling at best. It is something I am glad to have finished, but ALL of the following living story and expansion story (it happens in-engine, during gameplay) is worlds ahead of it and really where GW2's story shines. I highly recommend playing it in order as it is one continuous storyline with characters and side arcs that last the duration. This requires buying the living story packs (I recommend a sale) - These packs contain not just story instances, but whole massive maps/areas that you can get rewards from and explore/do events in.Guild Wars 2 Personal Story (FREE, just press play above)Living story Season 1 - FREE (depending on how soon you are reading this, it may still be in progress of re-release the last few chapters)Living story Season 2 - Lead-up to Expansion 1, Heart of thorns - helps make the heart of thorns make sense)Heart of thorns (Expansion) - Brilliant, but MUCH harder than base game -  not exactly dark souls but things expect you to dodge once in a while)Living story Season 3 - Separate story that leads to the motivation behind path of fire, just stunningly brilliant storytelling and a must playPath of Fire (Expansion) - I can't even start on this one, too many good memories, Praise Joko!Living story Season 4 - MAJOR plot points, great moments, finishes the path of fire storyline imoIcebrood saga - Mixed reviews regarding its ending, but I loved it - civil war, unique maps, fun mechanics.Cantha (Expansion) - If you make it here in the story, you are are already here to stay as you would have experienced the above - You will buy it and love it3. The gameplay is deeper than it looks.Watching from afar, GW2 combat seems to be standard mmo fare, tab targeting and action bar buttons, however it is somewhere closer to Black Desert than Warcraft, your skills need to connect physically, walls, reflects and dodges (i-frames) turn the combat into a very active real-time game - there will be abilities you need to jump over, hide behind objects and dodge to survive your “HP” is not the whole story.There is almost never a moment that you say: “I couldn’t have done anything to survive that!” buffs such as stability will counter a single stun/cc, but don’t last very long. spells and abilities are tuned to hurt, but not 2 shot you - and always, you decide how much health/damage/mitigation you want to play with - allowing for brick bunker elementalists(mages) and glass cannon warriors or anything between.There’s far more I could say, but really - it's a brilliant game, costs you NOTHING to join a welcoming community and anet is one of the few game companies that hasn’t gone evil yet (ignore NCSOFT as a publisher, they suck but have no say in the game)

_childDocuments_.review: GW2 is a great game. It's got something for everyone. Like personal story quests that take you across several continents? Check. Like the idea of massive World vs. World vs. World pvp seige battles? Check. Like instant, accessible pvp with different modes and play styles? Check. Like building networks and socializing with access to up to five different guilds? Check. Like action platforming and puzzle solving? Check. Like special events with unique content and rewards? Check. Like exploring and games that promote exploration? Check. Like being able to personalize your look with a deep transmog system and massive dye selection? Check. Like account wide progression with no penalties for playing alts? Check. Like Dungeons? Check. Like progressing through increasing difficulty with increasing rewards through an independent dungeon system called Fractals? Check. Like Raids with immersive stories and amazing challenges? Check. Like in-depth crafting systems with real benefits? Check. Like massive in game markets with the potential to make actual profits? Check. Like the idea of a hybrid system with the structure of tab targeting and the fluidity of action combat? Check. Like massive world events and accessible dynamic boss fights? Check. Like mini "raids" for quick rewards and challenge modes? Check. Like an exhaustive achievement panel that provides new and exciting ways to interact with your environment and progression? Check. Like Minis? Like playing music? Like fishing? Like having access to the best mount system and mount skins in any MMO? Check. Like an MMO that actually respects your time and likes you back? Check.Basically, this is only a few of the things GW2 does well. I have another account with roughly 4.5k hours. Pretty sure thats a lot of ROI on fun vs. money spent. The art is amazing, even 10 years on. Tyria is worth a visit.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: 1000+ hours in and not slowing down. Get off your crappy MMO and come play with usRecently wanted an MMO and it came down to Turtle WoW Classic or GW2. GW really does fix many problems typical of MMO worlds so it won my time. So here are my 200 hour thoughts-Dying in Wow is punished by making you run back from far away. GW has enough waypoints to shave this almost completely away in comparison.-Better graphics in GW means the world is actually worth more stop-and-admire moments.-Chat in GW is generally pleasant and helpful. In WoW the chat window must be hidden for fear my IQ will drop.-Questing in WoW consist of walking from: Quest Giver, Area of Quest, Walk Back, Get another quest for the exact same area. In GW the Quest are just areas on a map, go to the area and do the quest, you dont even need to talk to the NPC. Most quest in GW can be solved with killing but most of activities involve some faster way to complete it like reviving NPC, feeding farm animals. splashing drunks with buckets of water, etc. If that sounds boring, well compare it to a 5min walk back before you can even do anything at all.-Have i mentioned walking yet in WoW because everything is so big and far away from each other it just doesn't work for me and the world feels empty considering its size. Who can physically open these 20 story tall doors? Who needs a door that tall?-GW max level isn't hard to achieve, only about 40% of base map completion gets you there so just do the story and the complete the maps it brings you to. I think it took me 4 days, I played a lot but elementalist lives up to being "complex" to play/learn when compared to easier classes-Level scaling here is better than in something like Elder Scroll Online(Level 5 characters killing daedra....). Some people dont like this but consider the fact of your gear never becoming outdated. It might mean you'll have to write a story and add mechanics to keep players involved instead of tricking them into needing bigger level numbers. Remember, Quality>Quantity -I got more Final Fantasy vibes from this than FF14-You can create new characters, complete the 2-5min tutorial, then immediately jump into Structured PvP. Here you are boosted to max level and unlocks all your class skills. Experimenting here on NPC/dummies/Players might help you decide on a main class. Equipment here doesnt matter meaning you dont need to grind gear. You could only play this game for PvP is you wanted(although without DLC Elite Classes your competitive ceiling is limited to a couple "core" classes, Paladin and Necromancer do fine from what I've read).-WvW isn't "fair" like sPvP because your level and gear carry over to this game mode. The good news though is the 2nd best gear in the game (exotic) isn't expensive (1/10 the cost) and the stat lost compared to the best gear is 5-12%. I've read this small difference makes little difference in WvW/PvP and counts more for raids, dungeon, etc. -Crafting Gear you can change the stats of on-the-fly is an endgame goal is you want. Considering the Astral Coin to gold exchange rate, you get a "free" 90 Gold per season. 3 Gold gets you basically endgame cooking skill of 400. Gear is far more expensive so do that later, its like 35g just to hit 400/500 in a craft. Crafting is a decent way to level up another alt-Recommend the expansion bundle with Heart of Thorns and Path of Fire after beating the story. You get mounts, gliders, 18 of 27 Elite classes including 1 new base class, and maybe most important is a Level 80 Token. So now you have 2 Level 80 characters just in case elementalist turned out too complicated for you like it has me (so far). Plus when you read about builds you might want a secondary character to cover a role your main cannot. My alt is Thief so now I have a WvW Roamer/Duelist too. Each of the other 2 (atm) Expansions contain a token too, so if you enjoy the game you won't worry about leveling new character which is another time sink you can avoid.I guess I could go on but my hand is tired and I'm out of spit.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this is the most MMO like MMO, kinda reminds me of EverQuest and early WoW. The entire focus is on horizontal progression. Max level is 80 and it has been since release. Gear isn't that important except for high end stuff which only appeals to the most hardcore players.Story is amazing ngl, I love it although the presentation of the first arc (1-80) is slow. Because the story takes a pause every 10 levels, which makes it feel disconnected and the reason I dropped this game in the beginning and probably the reason many didn't like the story. But there are surprisingly a lot of choices that effect the outcome of certain character stories and give replayability similar to games like Mass Effect. I recommend using the free level boost to get the full story experience and also level your mastery earlier, also before you commit to the boos, you get to play that class at max level in a certain zone to get used to it.The world is the best. I LOVE EXPLORING. Feels similar to games like Legend of Zelda BOTW. The heart quests I love and the rewards stay relevant, in fact all the zones stay relevant all the time, so the game feels alive even now more than a decade later.I love the mastery system that appears after hitting level 80, where you continue to gain xp and levelling. This system allows you to get amazing passive and some active skills. Ranging from things like small xp boost, new merchants, new abilities for your mounts etc. They also appear for alts. Honestly this is the most alt friendly MMO.Mounts are amazing, they feel like mounts and they have their own abilities too, like the raptor is good at jumping long distances, the griffon is like a airplane that needs wind to ascend and gets faster when it descends, the skyscale is like a helicopter albeit slower than the griffon, the jackal is like the raptor but good for short distance jumps for certain puzzlers and I belive generally faster? etc.Combat is also very nice, its a mix of action and tab targetting where you can switch it around. I prefer the action combat.So overall... Good MMO for casual players, and surprisingly PvP players too. I love it! Probably my favourite modern MMO!

_childDocuments_.review: Update: 9/24/2024It's still great, still getting updates and content, has an amazing community and is still one of the most open and welcoming communities I've ever had the pleasure of being involved with. The release of Janthir Wilds is making me reply the story and fall in love with the game all over again. Still a Guardian main but that might change with my first foray into WvW which was super fun, a little terrifying and entirely worthwhile.If you're looking for an MMO that isn't the typical WoW clone or grind-fest this is it 100%.________________________________________________________Gameplay-☐ Exceptional☑ Pretty damn good☐ Nothing special☐ Mediocre☐ Terri-BadThe gameplay is solid and engaging, not difficult but very hard to master. Yet the game doesn't quite force you to engage in ways that you may not want like other titles would. I'm partial to Open World meta events and farming but I might start trying to get into fractals and WvW as our guild grows.Graphics-☐ I saw the face of God☐ Indescribable Beauty☐ Chef's Kiss☑ Average Enough☐ Fridge Crayon DrawingsThey might not have aged well compared to some games but they have a unique charm about them. The engine shows it's limitations and age in densely packed areas like Lion's Arch or similar, but with the right settings and Tekkit's ReShader pack it looks beautiful enough for me to sink almost 1k hours into.THE MESSAGE-☐ None to be found.☑ Player interpretation is key.☐ If you look hard enough you can see it.☐ Typical ideological pandering.☐ Anita Sarkeesian would be proud!I've seen criticism that the game is "woke" because of certain characters and/or relationships within the game and I'll be honest: it's there, but they aren't giving ANY context. When the characters are written well and have depth to them you don't notice little traits like that unless you squint really hard or just hate any and all representation in games.Audio-☑ Immersive and interesting.☐ Like your fave song on repeat.☐ Could you turn that down?☐ I'd rather listen to Nickleback.☐ Dial-Up Connection Noises.I'll be honest, I'm 50/50 with the audio. Sometimes it's awesome and I'll totally lose myself in just wandering, other times I mute the music and jam out to Spotrify. It fits the world and locations well enough but I wish it wasn't quite as High Fantasy trope-y as it is.Audience-☐ Crotch Goblins (Kids)☐ Filthy Parasites (Teens)☐ Regular Meatbags (Adults)☑ All of the Above (Everyone)☐ Unfit for Mortal Consumption. (Nobody)Okay, so maybe don't let younger kids play it due to the complexity, but it's a very average game. No blood, gore or nudity, you get silly cartoon levels of 'intoxication' from alcohol, and the violence is like any other E-rated action title. Chat can get spicy sometimes but by default I keep guild chat as my main channel.Story-☐ GOTY Worthy.☐ It's REALLY good.☑ Decent and engaging.☐ What was happening again?☐ Plot? What Plot?If you want to jump in from Day 1 and expect a coherent story and plot you gotta look real close. It's an MMO so the focus is on leveling, farming and doing end-game. The story, from what I've played so far, is okay but I would heavily recommend grinding the classes you like to 30 or 40 and seeing what sticks then using a L80 boost if you just want the story. Recaps are available but if you hop around you will be lost in regards to characters and plot.Difficulty-☐ Dean Takahashi 100% this game.☑ Just press 'W' and you'll be fine.☐ Easy to learn / Hard to master☐ Comp PvP levels of try-hard.☐ Souls-like.Open World is easy as pie solo if you know your class, minus the odd group event, but when you get into end-game you'll need a solid group to do things like Fractals, Raids, and PvP.Grind-☐ None☐ Ranks/Leaderboards Only☑ It's optional.☐ Risks breaking immersion.☐ No thanks, I choose life.It's as grindy as you want it to be. If you pace yourself and set smaller and managable goals it is super fun and easy to get done. If you sit down and grind out the WHOLE griffon quest in a weekend like I did you'll burn out decently quick.Game Time-☐ Refractory period of CoD players.☐ Less than a day, easy.☐ Avatar wasn't this long...☐ The Spongebob time-card guy died.☑ Oh look, the heat death of the universe.Don't go in expecting to 100% the game or you'll realize it's literally an entire second lifetime worth of content. If you have the time and the drive, sure, but it's a huge game. Just to level to 80, unlock the basic mounts and finish the narrative content of each Xpack will probably take 100-200 hours. Huge game is huge.Price☑ But wait, there's more!☐ Buy one tire, get three for free! ☐ Average Steam sale cost.☐ Check between the couch cushions.☐ Potential money laundering scheme.$100 for the base game, HoT, PoF and EoD isn't a bad bundle. Adding on SotO and JW for an extra $50 puts you at a $150 buy-in for every bit of content in the game, and with gems being able to be bought with gold you can 100% farm your way to any paid items without spending an extra cent. I didn't do that, I might have an addiction. Please send help.MTX-☐ 100% Optional, as all MTX should be.☑ Pay for Convenience type stuff.☐ It's distracting, but optional.☐ Are you sure this isn't Bliz/Acti?☐ Hey EA, hold by BudLite!Like I said above. it's 100% optional if you want to grind the gold, which is decently easy end-game. I've dropped plenty on things I probably shouldn't have, but it's whatever. If you buy ANYTHING I recommend checking YouTube for some good guides on use to value, but I'd start with the Salvage-O-Matics and shared inventory slots to really help you along but wiser minds than mine have covered the topic. I'd recommend Mukluk or Laranity on YT for good new-player coverage of the store and game in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Guild Wars 2 offers one of the best and consumer-friendly experience you could possibly find in the market. The free to play version allows you to play extensively enough to get the idea about how the game is, and you have access to almost every feature of the game without paying a single penny. Although you aren’t able to play other class specialisations rather than the base one without paying for a proper expansion that includes one of these. However, you can purchase some of the content by exchanging in-game currency for premium currency, which results in the possibility of expanding your game content without expending little to no real money. Additionally, there is no subscription fee.The game truly immerses you in a sense of adventure. You can see players constantly flowing through the map zones no matter the level they are or the level these zones are supposed to be covering. This is because there is no vertical progression, and players are constantly incentivised to find their own way through the game squeezing its content and mechanics to an impeccable degree. You never get to feel there are mechanics that serve no purpose, and everyone is encouraged to explore the whole of the map anytime they wish to.The music and the community complement well this feeling. Adventure would not be as epic without a soundtrack that isn’t up to its quality, and you couldn’t enjoy a journey either if everyone is hostile towards you. Thankfully, the two of these factors play a gratifying role that makes unique the stories you make through your experience. I’ll never forget that guy who teamed up with me to get a treasure through a hell of a cavern, when we decided to jump and find glory together or to die as such when we were given three options to choose our fate. We chose right, by the way.However, some players may feel lost at the beginning, and it’s partly due to the extensive amount of content and the way the game wants you to experience the world. It invites the player to do whatever they wish to, but the thing is that they don’t know all of the possibilities, there’s just no way. In that sense, I think the game lacks intuition, and they should work on giving new players clues about the almost infinite opportunities they have before them. Other systems, such as the ability to amplify item/bank slots would feel more gratifying as well if they were obtainable through in-game content and not premium currency. The same applies for appearance change: a hair saloon would feel way more fitting and integrated into the world than a digital store. These restrictions can also confuse new players, as they probably don’t know they can exchange their gold for premium currency.This game is a nice opportunity to try new adventures and a new world full of life and charm. You can try it for free with almost no restrictions. There is so much content that you decide the way you want to spend your spare time in it. Every zone incentivise players to come back anytime and so each zone feels pretty much alive. And there are some improvements to be made, especially oriented towards newcomers, but it is definitely worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Hold onto your helmets, adventurers, because Guild Wars 2 is not just a game – it's a laughter-filled carnival ride through the wacky wonders of Tyria! If you're tired of the usual serious-faced fantasy worlds, prepare to have your funny bone tickled and your expectations hilariously shattered.First things first, the graphics – it's like the game was designed by a team of hyperactive artists on a sugar rush. Tyria is a vibrant, mesmerizing kaleidoscope of colors that'll make you wonder if you accidentally stepped into a Salvador Dali painting. Seriously, who needs realistic landscapes when you can have landscapes that look like they were crafted by the gods of Crayola?Now, let's talk about the characters. Instead of the brooding heroes with a tragic past, Guild Wars 2 gives you a cast of characters that seem to have attended the School of Comedy Arts. From the charismatic norn who thinks he's a stand-up comedian to the asura genius who accidentally turned her lab assistant into a quaggan – you'll be laughing so hard you might miss the next quest marker!The combat system is a comedy show of its own. It's like the developers said, "Why settle for serious strategy when you can have the chaotic charm of a food fight?" Smash those buttons like you're playing a game of whack-a-mole and watch the magic happen. Spoiler alert: It involves a lot of explosions.And the storyline – oh, the storyline. It's a rollercoaster of epic proportions, filled with unexpected twists, hilarious dialogue, and moments that'll make you say, "Did that just happen?" Forget about predicting what comes next – just buckle up and enjoy the comedic chaos.But it's not just the game that's a riot; it's the community too. Guild Wars 2 is home to the friendliest bunch of players this side of the digital realm. From spontaneous dance parties in Lion's Arch to impromptu roleplaying sessions in the most random places, you'll find yourself surrounded by the kind of folks who can turn any situation into a comedy sketch.In conclusion, Guild Wars 2 is the laughter-infused vacation your character deserves. It's a game that doesn't take itself too seriously and invites you to join the party. So, grab your sword, put on your silliest hat, and get ready to LOL your way through Tyria – where dragons are just the coolest neighbors!

_childDocuments_.review: I have always wanted to love this game. The world is big and imaginative. It was always, in my eyes, not the best looking but it's nice. The classes are varied and what you can spec inside them is mind-boggling (too much so for me I suppose). The races are... sort of boring. You have huge cat dogs, humans, green humans, big humans and small baby humans. The small baby humans are the coolest by far, though. Think World of Warcraft gnomes + goblins but without all the annoying parts.I digress.I've played this game for hundreds of hours outside of Steam. I've had periods where I've loved it and played it for a long time. I have zones in the game that are close to my heart. Like, the nightmarish vertical maze of Maguuma, or Kessex Hills, or all of Path of Fire. All zones feel alive with other players. There are few traditional quests, but instead events taking place all the time. Every map has its own lore and you will find other players doing things everywhere and you can without much or any social interaction just join in. No place feels abandoned. There's tons of voiced story where you feel like you're part of something important. This is where the game truly shines.However, for me personally, the game is far too complex. I find my brain closing down after a while. I can learn a class somewhat, do ok in PvE, but I always have this overhanging feeling that I don't really know what I'm doing. Every single stat, more or less, is called something new in this game. The buff and debuff system is filled with these tiny short lived stackable buffs. The advantage is that you can theoretically learn them all and quickly see what's going on to you and enemies. In practise though, you'll see a flickering of tiny icons with long descriptions that you don't have the time to read. I want to learn this game and have tried so many times, but it's just something deeply obtuse with it, You'll look things up outside of the game constantly - things are even so badly explained ingame that there is a /wiki command you can type.The interface isn't great. The painting effect looks nice, but health bars are thin and have this dark red color against black, while the screen is covered in effects during a big battle. You can decrease some effects but that only solves part of it. I have a hard time seeing at a glance whether an enemy is almost dead or at full health.Things aren't explained well in-game. That is just a fact. The game feels like it's teasing you with greatness... if you do weeks of homework. I never feel I'm given enough information by the game to just enjoy things and know what I'm doing.And then there are the archaic design of some things. The inventory management... It's stuck in the stone ages - and of course it will stay there because they sell solutions to it for real money. Highly limited inventory space and tons and tons of unique items. What's this item? Where is it from? Is it a map related thing or is it important? Should I save it? Should I destroy it? Is it rare or common? Is it an ingredient for something? Get ready to do more out-of-game homework. And prepare to forget 90% of it if you have an extended time away from the game.I could rant for a long time but I have kids and its their bedtime.If I were talking to someone like me, I couldn't really recommend this game to them. Many parts of it is just too stale and... old. Too time consuming, too needlessly fiddly and a chore. And personally I think much of the environment designs - while grand - were at the same time ugly and kind of visually barren back when the game was released.
