_childDocuments_.review: Basically a $100 game with a cashshop that let's you straight buy gold from it for USD.The 1-80 story is mostly solo play with zero ways to fail, requiring little player input, that gets injected into you every 10 levels, and can mostly be ignored. The gameplay itself is fast, easy, and mostly comes down to instantly killing 3 enemies at a time while they pose little threat in return. Dying costs you nothing, so there is no risk. There are no quests, you just grind/click random crap on the ground near heart icons on the map, and run around killing things around orange circles that spawn on the map. (Yes all the way from 1-80.) You are always down-scaled to the levels of wherever you are fighting, so progress feels non-rewarding. 1-80 takes around two to three days of play, or you can just buy a handy dandy 1-80 boost, assuming you weren't just given one by buying the expansions. It's fairly pointless really.Post 80 you are given a bunch of needless busy work to fill out the games achievement checkboxes to progress in the story. Want to bounce on mushrooms? Better grind for that achievement. Want to glide? Better grind for that achievement. Want to talk to frogs? Better grind for that achievement. This is the basically the gameplay of every zone past the base game.Every time you think the game is improving, it manages to do something dumb like gate you behind some pointless meta grind, or make you play as a rabbit to progress the story. (I kid you not, there is a main story quest, where you have to escort soldiers in fights against random wolves while playing a freakin bunny.) If the grinding was actually fun, challenging, or even group oriented I could see it. It's not though, it's just mindless.Generally the best way to grind post 80 revolves around running around in a deathball of dozens of people that never talk to each other and killing bosses balanced for 3-10 players with 80+ people for fast/mindless xp. That and run around like a chicken with your head cut off, to be rewarded loot boxes full of items you'll likely never use unless you plan to dive into the crafting system, or care about cosmetics. The crafting system as far as I can see exists only to make legendary items cheaper, or in other words, make you grind more instead of just buying it on the cash shop.The PvE is just bad, all the removal of the trinity of tank/heal/dps really changed was making the content boring. Almost all of the content rewards you an endless stream of loot you'll care nothing about in the form of chests through what amounts to a "participation trophy" reward. You'll earn bronze/silver/gold depending on if you fight for 1, 30, or 60 seconds before you go AFK.The only saving grace I see is the PvP is fairly fun, if a bit pointless. WvW feels a bit like DAoC-lite. The only real way I can recommend this game is if you have a buddy or two, and you want to do some semi casual PvP in an MMO without the time investment many other games of the genre require.

_childDocuments_.review: "Time is money"That's what one player said to me after we wiped on a boss a couple times in a dungeon. He then left the group.But why did we wipe? These dungeons (which the game calls fractals) have an unavoidable damage over time mechanic called agony, and the only way to survive the mechanic is with agony resistance. It takes a long time to acquire the required gear to increase your agony resistance. Had this mechanic not existed, a player could clear the most difficult fractal moments after purchasing the game and boosting a new character.That really sums up what Guild Wars 2 is about. It is an easy game. Very easy. But artificial difficulties are added to pad out your playtime.The artificiality is so deeply ingrained, the game asks you to pay 300 gold for an icon. Without this icon, you cannot start a raid group that people will want to join, as the raid group has no leader. There is nothing stopping the developers from simply designating the leader of a group as the person who started the group. But no. Instead we have a sort of pseudo class structure, where the haves will lord and control the have-nots, and there is nothing you can do about it except spend that gold for your own icon.This is a game of walls. And the gameplay is not that different after you have overcome each wall. The most challenging content, PvP, is available to level 1 characters. Everything else is easy, and usually takes a really really long time.One final note: this game has a massive amount of inventory items. You will be swamped with items. To the point of having to spend what will accumulate to hours of your time merely organizing your bags and bank."Time is money"So says the player that has put thousands of hours into this game. Elitism is all he has left.

_childDocuments_.review: The best action MMO is finally here on Steam! If you're looking for a new MMO to play, don't look for a New World to explore, look for one with a strong track record!Combat - 9/10The Guild Wars franchise is known for it's build craft, & GW2 features many choices to your gameplay. Your weapon & profession defines your skills. 9 professions with 3 specializations in total.As an action game, you have to actually dodge to avoid damage. Combat has tab targeting, but most target skills can be freely activated. Combat is highly co-operative. Skills can bounce off another & create combos using combo fields paired with the combo finisher, giving heals & buffs.Skill animations are grounded in reality. You don't cast ultimate meteor showers of demonic proportions to obliterate the enemy. The ultimate abilities don't feel ultimate, just strong skills on high cooldown. If you like flashy skills, you will be disappointed.Questing - 9/10One thing I miss in new MMOs is the leveling grind where exp comes from to quests, leaving grinding monsters moot. That is not the case with GW2. When combat is good, it’s something you want to do over & over. You play until you find a Dynamic Event, which takes you on a fully voiced action packed journey. Exp is given for participation in these events but feel natural as if it were from combat. Some Dynamic Events are fetch quests, but most involve combat.Meta Dynamic Events are bigger events where background story takes place. They are essential to the open world map progress to unlock gates or world bosses. Without the M in MMO, you will not progress; this design philosophy encourages high levels of co-operation. Unfortunately, some maps feel rather dead as everyone moves to play the newer content.Mounts - 11/10Each mount is unique, like playing Zelda with Epona but more. Each mount improves your ability to navigate through older & newer maps, making something that used to take forever a breeze.The Raptor, Springer, Skimmer & Jackal help you traverse the areas in Path of Fire. These maps have been built to utilize each mount's unique capabilities & incorporate mini puzzles to reach certain areas. The other 4 mounts are only obtainable after completing scavenger hunt/fetch quests.The Griffon plays like Aladdin on the magic carpet. (Cue "A whole new world~"). Revisiting the world from the skies is truly breathtaking, there are no words other than to experience it. The Roller Beetle is a slick motorcycle mount. The Skyscale is a different take on flight, being easier to control but less distance. The Siege Turtle, a returning favorite from GW1, obliterates everything with their cannons.No mount has disappointed except the Warclaw, discussed later.Story - 7/10The game starts you off on a "personal story" which is your origin story. It starts weak & disjointed due to being tied to leveling & dungeons, leaving you with a sense of dissatisfaction when you finish each mission. Elder dragons are a weak point of tension; “big evil” is hollow. If an elder dragon is involved, expect disappointment.The fifth chapter marks a major turning point, taking you on a real epic where the elder dragons become a backdrop to something greater. The latest chapter, "End of Dragons" signals the end of the elder dragon story arc. GW1 has rich lore that are yet to be tapped into. Expect better stories to come.The banter with the cast are very good, like banter from Uncharted 4. There's lots of technobabble used to disguise deus ex machina though. The addition of the communicator earpiece plot device helped drive better pacing & flow compared to previously with characters needing to pop in & out of missions.Economy - 2/10The gathering economy is strong & can be a main source of income for players, but you will be inconvenienced by limited use tools, pushing you to purchase the unlimited tools from the cash shop. One of the better things is the official gold seller service, letting you farm cash shop items with gold. Investing in unlimited tools do eventually help your sanity although it will take many years for that investment to actually pay off.Because of the cash shop, you are never rewarded. When you beat an epic boss, you will not obtain a nice skin for your weapons or armor. You will need to farm the same boss several times to obtain a currency that buy items to craft the skin. This pushes you to the highest gold/hour game loop. If you're looking for great skins you will only find them in the cash shop or after endless grind. When you do finish, the rush of dopamine does not feel satisfying because you worked for it.PvP - 6/10GW2 only takes Conquest mode seriously. There's a DotA-ish mode, we don't talk about that. Who you get matched up with usually matters in whether you will win that round or not. Unfortunately, this leads to player toxicity, as blaming others is made easy & inconsequential.GW2 often receives frequent balance changes, but the game will always have some level of imbalance so you'll have a certain meta to play with if you’re looking to compete. Some professions will not be competitive no matter how good you play. The competitive scene is non-existent, so it’s difficult to gauge if a build is top tier because it is popular or effective.There are only a few maps you will play on repeat. The lack of other modes hurt re-playability of PvP. After every season there is a mini season of TDM that lasts 2 weeks, which is a nice breather.WvW - 4/10WvW is like a game of Risk, defending your territory while invading & taking others, a war simulator complete with siege weaponry for knocking down gates & walls. The mode is addictive, until you play enough to see the flaws.The game mode is designed so that a win is based on points from capture & holding the structure to keep points rolling, so enrolling into the largest World gives you the best results. Many players avoid defense & look for fights when the population supports it. A good fight is a good day, even if you lose every tower & keep along the way. This leads to this game mode being simply a playground for big fights & the game mode itself just a backdrop.Since Heart of Thorns, WvW has no major changes. The last update was the Warclaw mount, which is inconsequential to the game mode.The dedicated WvW player base is the only thing that keeps it all together. Disturbingly, this player base is highly sensitive to content changes, where inclusion of the new Siege Turtle mount needs to be "heavily considered with the community" by the developers before including it into the mode. That's a lot of backward-ism going on.WvW needs the other mounts, period. Change the keeps & towers for better defense, & enable new attack vectors by flight, carpet bombing, etc. New incentives are needed for defense, e.g. economic incentives like gold or items. The mode needs players aligned to the objective.Conclusion - 8/10Ten years ago, this was my 10/10 dream MMO. It had everything; great combat, great PvP & a massive world to call home. The stories get bolder as it moves away from elder dragon lore. The mounts are incredible; all I do for fun is login, fly around a bit, then log out.Unfortunately, the lack of any updates to WvW, one of my favorite game modes, shows the game hasn't evolved all that much either. It's a great MMO that misses a lot of points to continue to become the dream MMO in 2022 standards. Treat it like a single player RPG that happens to have a lot of people playing. It’s best played together with a group of 5 friends, but you can play solo.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm someone with 5k+ hours in BDO and WoW, and I can say that the quote above is how I feel as well. This game is not perfect and def has its problems, but for the price of free (for the base content) and NO MONTHLY SUB, you are screwing yourself for at least not giving it a try. I have almost 200 hours and finally think I understand this game (take what you will from the fact that it took me this long to get a handle on the game). Hard to rate an mmo like this but if I had to in 2023 it would be a 8.5/10[1] thousands of hours of PvE content in the form of story, dungeons / raids, world meta events, gear grinding, mount farming, and much more.[2] The combat is actually fantastic. I remember playing this years ago and not liking it, but I gave it a second chance and I fell in love with it. To me its combat is only second to BDO's. [3] Lots of fresh takes and innovation that you either never seen in a MMO, or you may have seen its derivative cheap copies (dragon riding from WoW). [4] Map design is fantastic. The Heart of Thorns expac is a perfect example of what MMO maps are capable of looking like. [5] The gear grind is pretty much the ideal MMO gear grind. It takes months to get a legendary, but it is basically BIS forever, depending on your build. While the grind takes a long time, it at least mixes up what you are doing a lot, instead of having you just doing the same thing for hundreds of hours (looking at you BDO). [6] The cash shop is actually very tame and I would say its acceptable. [1] While I prefer horizontal progression to vertical progression, its flaws are made very evident in this game. When an expac sucks, you can't pretend that it doesn't exist. That bad content is now more of less relevant to the day the game shuts down. Also the old content is pretty much the worst in the game and the animations /  graphics / story is pretty bad overall so the first impression for people will be sub par to say the least. [2] The inventory is a total mess. Since all expacs are relevant and they all drop their own currencies and items, your inv will fill up with so much trash so fast. [3] To much content and to little explanation. The game has a /wiki command built into the game because it would be unplayable without it. The game needs a kind of adventure log that organizes and keeps track of goals and objectives. [4] The game is a thematic mess with wild inconsistency (aka the game is still finding its identity). Despite being the origins for many innovative mmo designs such as the great mount riding, the devs have been struggling to find what this game is actually supposed to be. They had creative leads come and go, but the latest at least seems to have a good idea of where to take the game. [5] PvP has played second fiddle for a long time, and while they promise they will add more PvP content in the future, the reality is that in summer 2023 there has been almost no new PvP content in many years. [6] This may not be a negative for others but for me its a big one. This game is a high fantasy setting, which means that nothing about it is realistic and it constantly pulls me out of any immersion. A perfect example is the setting of Dragons End in which you are in a massive city where they have working appliances like microwaves, but you fight enemies with wooden sticks...what.

Nearly every five minutes in this game I discover something that surprises me, either through exploration, story, or mechanics, and for this reason I'm comfortable giving the gaming time I have to this one. Guild Wars 2 doesn't hold you ransom with completionist checklists, shinning new items, or new updates to keep playing. The reason to play is far more simple: it's fun. _childDocuments_.review: This is an MMORPG which doesn't make you sweat that you've missed a couple days, or even a couple months of playtime. It also lets you play all day, which is unfortunately quite a rare thing these days in this genre. It also offers some of the best combat gameplay experience in the genre.Compared to other modern MMORPGs, which use the extremely predatory daily/weekly lockouts design, Guild Wars 2 has no such thing. While there are many daily/weekly tasks, they are not required for you to progress in the game. You can safely skip days or even weeks of playtime and not fall behind. This is achieved partly thanks to the horizontal gear progression. Getting best in slot gear in GW2 is quite easy, and can be achieved in couple weeks of playtime. After that any gear grind is completely self imposed - you can progress towards making your legendary items, or whatever else you want - but those items will not have better stats than the easy BiS gear you've already collected, they will only have minor gameplay benefits, like swapping item stats at will or cosmetic effects. Some people will not find this system to their liking, because there is no endless gear ladder that you constantly climb.Personally, what made me love this game is that it lets me play it whenever I want and do whatever I want. There is a massive amount of things you can do all day, every day. The game doesn't lock you out of anything. You want to farm Fractals all day? Go ahead. Dungeons? No problem. Jumping puzzles? Yeah, you can spend your day doing that. Map events? You can spam them all day. Believe or not, an MMORPG which lets you actually play it for however long you wish is a rarity in modern times.This is also one of the only MMORPGs which made me pay attention to the story. It has become this genre's trait that the campaign quests/main storylines are mediocre and rarely worth paying attention to. Well, this game offers a great story, BUT it only starts with the expansions. The base game storyline is not that great, but oh boy, the expansions more than make up for it. Personally I think the story in Guild Wars 2 expansions is much better than in most single player story-based games.The community of this game is also quite friendly and extremely new player welcoming. Seriously it's one of the better MMO communities out there.I thoroughly recommend playing this game if you're an MMORPG fan.

_childDocuments_.review: GW2 is a game with a sea of content, no subscription, and compared to other MMO's has an easier barrier to entry but a similar height of skill that can be attained with a bit of practice without needing to memorize or keybind half a keyboard like classic MMO's (not that I mind, but still it does let you focus on mechanics more than muscle memory for a keyboard which is nice). Without going into too much detail, I'd give this game a 9/10 overall, but I'll go into more detail for those who want it below. Gameplay: Game is fun, and unlike most MMO's, the overworld is actually quite threatening, and a massive part of the games endgame as well, but I'll get to endgame in a second. First and foremost is how the game itself isnt too easy to the point where you can simply hit 1 skill on an enemy and watch them go down, and it isn't too hard to the point where you'll die every three seconds. It also doesn't have the classic MMO concept of Tank/Healer/DPS(Damage), so it's far more individual in how a build affects you, and everyone does a good bit of damage regardless of their role. Your skills are tied to your class and a weapon type. If you're dual wielding daggers as a thief, for example, your skills are different than if you use a sword and a dagger. The way the division works is that the first 3 skills belong to the first weapon (right hand), and the last 2 belong to the left hand, though if you use something like a staff, a bow, or a greatsword, it counts for both so you get all 5 skills at once. This makes the skills far more compact, while also giving you a healing skill (with variety options based on class), multiple utility/damage skills tied to your class directly or your specialization, and an ultimate that can provide incredible support, stellar damage, or a mix of both. Story 8/10The story of this game isn't some stellar masterpiece, and it sure as hell isn't FF14 level of writing for its DLC's, but it does an amazing job of being well written enough to have you care and enjoy the cast while also not being as bad as some other MMO plotlines. The original campaign is good, but it isn't amazing. Like most original mmo plots its serviceable for what it tries to accomplish. The DLC's are good, and get better as they progress, HoT was beginning to spread its wings, and PoF has some stellar story content, with EoD being the culmination of a very long (ten years I think) plotline. SoTo is also amazing, but a very different vibe that is enjoyable, imo. Endgame 9/10While the game only has very few raids, they're enjoyable. Strikes (like bite sized raids), are also fun and at times harder than raids. And fractals are dungeons that scale difficulties. There's also endgame collecting, crafting legendaries, all endgame but a very different and time consuming aspect that is more for fashion and bragging rights, as well as some amazing looking weapons. Music 8/10The music has some stellar moments, others I can't really remember the music, but overall its good, though that is subjective of course.

_childDocuments_.review: There are so many things I love about this game. I come from grind fests so I'm a bit skewed because I don't mind that there's a grind for some of the more luxurious items in the game. that said, there's so much content between the starting of the game and that point, I'm hardly one to talk about what that actually looks like. Instead, I'll mention what I can talk about from first hand experience.Exploring the world of Tyria is what I've always wanted from an MMO. It's rich, textured, stylized, unique, and most importantly, rewarding! Like you actually get experience and progress towards a legendary item by simply exploring all the maps in the game. It always will give you much needed access to waypoints (quick travel locations) all around the game making it easier to collect things in the future (or help out a friend). Along the way, you'll find many vista points (little cutscenes from prime viewpoints basically) and these also give experience. You've got jumping puzzles, completionist content, and just so much to do outside of combat, you can likely get to max level without even touching a single mob.Gathering and crafting is also very broad in this game, I've only just started doing some of these, so I'll be brief here. You'll find plenty of nodes for mats around the open world, but also tons of useful drops from mobs too. You've guessed it, you also get pretty great exp from this as well! I like that you can spend base levels working on this and be rewarded in the end with useful things like gear, but also food that helps buff anyone who eats it!PVP is a little daunting for me still. I'm a noob coming into the arena with people who have 10 years experience, so that's to be expected, but you still can have a rewarding experience here. You also get these level up tomes, so you can also grind your levels here as soon as your toon is level 2. It is a little meta build focused here, but aside from that, it's not pay to win at all from my experience, it's more skill and knowledge based.Combat is really fun, it's a little bit tab target, a little bit action combat, and a lot of classes (if not all) have substantial AOE capabilities. From what little end game content I have played, it's the right amount of challenging and possible to do that scratches the itch of engaging pve/pvm content. You have many options for each class in terms of weapons and specialization combinations, so if you're a classic min-maxer you can tweak until your hearts content, or if you just like a certain playstyle you can make it viable through the talent tree! High-End game content is a little less flexible than the general daily/open world/grindy stuff, but chances are no one will mind as long as you pull you weight and learn the mechanics!Now for the best part, the community is legit the most sincere and amazing bunch of baddies I ever met. I immediately dropped my other games because of this alone. Once you find a solid guild, they are full of friendly people willing to help you grind up skill points and achievements, or simply keep each other company on discord! The toxicity level is so low in my personal experience, I even find when I'm randomly in the world exploring, there's someone who comes along and they're just naturally assisting you in content and answering questions. I haven't yet found many people who want to one-up me constantly or bring me down because I failed a mechanic, so far its been a lot of laughing together at the situation versus laughing at me. It keeps me coming back after work to destress because I know I'm not gonna get stressed out over something that happens in a game and I won't get bullied for being inexperienced unlike some other games (>.> looking at a certain MOBA). I've only played a bit over 50 hours so far, but I definitely see this becoming my next 1k+ hour game. It just fits me, personally, so well. I went ahead and also bought all the expansions so that I have eons of content to explore. On that note, I gotta say that the expansions storyline feels like a built in series of sequels to the game. They're very well done and add enough content to feel worth my money.If you're reading this far, download the game, even the base game is just a great experience to sink your teeth into for a while, and if you feel like it, at least buy the Path of Fire and Heart of Thorns expansion combo for a massive addition to mounts and content .TL;DR: Game good, download, play, support devs by buying expansions for more good game things.

_childDocuments_.review: Big CON for GW2 and hidden value in the Complete Collection Steam package.  GW2 has something called "Living World" DLC. They are about the size of a third of an expansion.  They cost about $55 to get all of them unless you wait for random sales to save $15.  So if you want to play through a coherent story you need to buy them AND the expansions they are for.  They are all added into the $100 Complete Collection on steam.  Otherwise you will be spending $55 in the shop or you can be like me and be extremely confused with the horrible disconnected story between expansions... That is the game I got so its the one this review is for.The story seems pretty good, you are not the chosen one, but you survive and fight an impossible fight, slowly earning you the respect of those around you.  NPCs grow on you and some of them are sacrificed. Then new characters are introduced out of nowhere as current friends.  You have never seen them but your PC says they trust them with their life and they talk about events that happened off screen.  Its a huge drop in writing quality.    These "Living Worlds" are zones, quests, achievements, items, masteries, group dungeons, AND a campaign quest to understand what is going on between the expansions.  I think it is a horrible game design choice to confuse the hell out of your new players who are dumb enough to assume expansion leads into expansion.  Just bundle them with the expansions and charge $10 more. I am pissed specifically because I have been having fun playing it once I got to 80 even though I hated early game.  I don't want to be a combat god with no risk. Then suddenly at 80 you can be one shot if you are not careful.  This is the difficulty I seek in an MMO.  Allow people to be glass cannons.  Allow mobs to punish people for not paying attention.  There are many good things about this game but the people running it insane for ruining their own story like this.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like MMORPGs, give GW2 a try. Important points:* No quota. You only pay for the software.* Easy game to not get outdated easyly. Level cap it's the same as the beginning (80) and the same armor that you could get at the beginning is still valid, being the top stats Ascended/Legendary tier. What they usually do is add different combination of stats or change in how those work instead of increasing the level cap of character and armor.* Buy HoT and PoF Expansions together and the new EoD separately.* Buying the expansions DON'T give you access to the old Living Story Seasons. They were given for free when they went live, but as soon as a new episode launches, the old one can only be accessed via Gem Store Purchase (you can invest real money or in-game gold).* Is it recomended to have the LSs? Yes. I would recommend to start with LS4 to get the Skyscale mount (you need PoF expansion for that), and after that LS3 as in it's the best way to get Ascended trinkets.* With the free game you can access  Core Tyria Maps, Dungeons (really outdated nowadays) and Fractals (good way of making money and high end dungeons).* To access Raids, you need the expansions. To access Wings 1 to 4 Heart of Thorns is needed and for Wings 5 to 7 Path Of  Fire is needed.* To access Strikes, you need Living Season: IceBrood Saga (IBS) for its strikes and End Of Dragons expansion for its Strikes.* Dungeons and fractals are 5 players team instances, while raids and strikes are 10-player squads, being Strikes 'easier' than raids because they were introduced as a 'introduction' to raid content so more people try to get into raids.* From level 80, the progression it's horizontal, with a Mastery System that will allow the player to get different skills normally oriented to map exploration (like gliding and mounts). This system requires two things: Mastery Points (scattered accros the maps and also rewarded with achievements completion) and you need to get experience before to spents those points for each Mastery Track. Once the experience bar is full, one can spent some mastery points to unlock that reward and unlock the next level of the mastery.* Regarding the gameplay, unlike WoW this game is Action oriented. The dogde is an active skill instead of being passive and positioning is really important.* Each expansion increases the Elite Specialization accesible for each class (1 per class and expansion).* The game has Three main game modes. PvE (Open PVE and instances like dungeons, fractals, raids and strikes), PvP (3v3 or 5v5 matches) and WvW (Three servers (or alliances in the future) battling each other through 4 big maps. Each team can have 90+ players in the map with 50 player squads organized by a commander.* Most of the microtransactions are aesthetic or utilities (like increase bank space, material space, shared inventory spaces, infinite recicle tools, etc.) No Pay To Win in this game.* No mission system, outside history missions. The "sidequests" are hearts around the maps that need to be completed.For me, as a "casual" player that don't want to invest too much time playing, it's the easiest MMORPG to keep playing, as I can stop playing for a while, go back and don't have to worry too much to update my character, because normally my build will still be good.

_childDocuments_.review: Tough game, especially the "Living World" story line portions, but it has a little of everything.  AreaNet is always adding more places to it, more features.  It isn't easy, like I said it's tough.  Many have played this for years to get really good at it.  Granted, the original (older) portions don't get updated or changed, so they still look old style.  Most of the players are in the expansion packs.  The base game gives you a chance to get started.  To live long at all you need to watch the enemy, the ground around your character's feet (for area of effect or attack warnings), and you health - a lot to look at in a battle.  Like all MMORPG's you can simply teleport to a waypoint nearby if you die, though.  Crafting is enormous in game.  There are many types of crafting.  Personally, now that I'm on my second character in this, I recommend crafting jewelry as a starter.  I crafted jewelry better than the game was giving me in many cases, and it reaches it's peak at 400 (others go to 500).  You can do 2 kinds of crafting at once, so if you choose to do so I would say do whatever will give you more character storage.  Armor crafting can expand your characters carrying by providing larger (more slot) boxes to carry goods in, but it's only useful if your character uses heavy armor.  Find what does you the most good.  I strongly recommend getting the first two expansion packs at least, but play through the base first.  You can sometimes get through to the new areas (Heart of Thorns, Path of Fire) without playing all the way through the Living World episodes.  Play enough of them to get there, and then use the waypoints & exploration.  Do the Living World when you get better at it.  Those are my recommendations to get a newby started.  From there, you can decide on your own.

_childDocuments_.review: To me, Guild Wars 2 isn't a game, it is a feeling: Nostalgia seeps out of every attack, every dodge roll and every corner of Tyria. That makes it quite difficult to review in truth because I forgive shortcomings where I find them because I am grateful for the thousands of hours the game has given me. That said, I can try to remember why GW2 hooked me all those years long years ago:Chiefly, the game respects your time because it is entirely built around horizontal progression: the first ascended weapon I crafted some 8 years ago is still as strong and relevant now as it was then. Secondly, the developers made exploration and adventure just as much a part of the game as combat and I still regularly run the jumping puzzles and spend hours running around the new zones that are added looking for all the easter eggs and delightful environmental designs. Thirdly, the combat feels responsive and the animations (with a few exceptions) are impactful. The combat doesn't feel 'floaty' and there is a satisfying heft to attacks. It is difficult to really describe but you'll know it when you pick the game up. I suppose, in my mind, the combat never felt cheap. Ultimately, GW2 is free and not just 5 minutes of free but hours of free. Sure you'll need to buy DLC if you want the newer innovations from the past 7 years or so but the entire vanilla base game is free: what really is stopping you finding out if you like it yourself?

This game has ,,dynamic questing'' which means it has events with ,,Hearts'' instead of talking to NPC you do tasks on each part of zone, let's say you help village to take care of storage and defend it from enemies. It was quite refreshing that time doing this, but after time i felt it's more like chore than fun. Plus the walking and no mounts in the game that time made me stop play, as it took quite forever travel somewhere specially for Story. So i gave up that easily. But this year when i saw Janthir Wilds trailer introducing Homesteads, Warclaw reworks and so many QoL changes to whole game i was like...,,I LOVE HOUSING in MMOS, one of my most reasons to stay play'' yes i am that weirdo who LOVES housing. So i bought full collection in June during the Discount on the Website as i heard Steam version does not allow using codes from third party retailers. And boom.... i began my addiction to GW2, as i promised myself this time to give this game ,,proper serious try'' and when i did lvl up to lvl 80 and finished Personal Story to end, the game story, lore, world building got on me in huuge way. The base game might feel bit ,,lacking'' things and can feel as chore for lvling, but if you take lvling as Journey and Explore zones on your OWN PACE. Then it becomes fun and not ,,grind'' just think in this game differently and you will have a lot of fun meeting new players on the maps thanks to megaservers that makes all servers on it¨s continent connected together into more instances, so there is low chance you will see empty zone or places. There is always someone to do events and stuff with which is so refreshing and i must say it forced my Social Anxiety Disorder to fight and overcome my fears of comunicating with other players. Let's talk now about story, first of fall you start as ,,hero'' or more of ,,peasant'' person in each racial zone (depends which race you pick and gender, each gender has different voice actor and race, good to know that first 3-4 chapters are quite like backstory of your own character so its kinda cool thing, reminds me Swtor in this matter a little, which is compliment from me) where you kinda ,,build up'' your reputation to the way of Commander later. Story bits can feel tedious at some part, some parts felt rushed or way too long. It kind of feel like un-balanced but the Personal Story is important to do at least once, so you meet all the most important characters that will be later also in expansions, dlcs and stuff. I must say some of boss mechanisms felt quite easy compare to expansions, but i take it as ArenaNet was kind of experimenting and finding their style for ,,balancing'' out you know smooth way how they want make things up later. The story for me was quite fun, and if you enjoy Personal Story then it GETS better and better later, as each expansion feels like new game, at least to me. So i personally do recommend do the story at least once, so you kind of understand main plot of the whole game. Then there goes Living World Seasons. How to explain this kind of ,,DLC'¨content to you? Well from what i know by players Anet was releasing Living World Seasons as post launch free updates to players who did login that time and got that content for free. So it's like ,,extensions of content after major expansion''. Base Game for example has Living World Season 1 and 2 which kinda extends story of base game to introduction of first expansion Heart of Thorns. You must buy each Living World Season on Gemstore in-game, so good to know that. Except LW1 which is free for all players. Living World Season 1 and 2 feels bit clunky in gameplay department, it can feel frustrating at some parts. but story is quite okayish, for sure i must say LW1 was quite difficult but actually it does teach you your own class and how to use dodges and stuff in story boss fights which i find personally important, as in this game gear does not mean everything but also your skill to fight enemies, as some enemies has different mechanism or weaknesses. Do i recommend the base game? YES i do, i spent over 100 hours in base game, and had fun and do not regret it. It's very casual mmorpg, which does REALLY RESPECT your own time, and does allow your to play on your own pace, and if you feel burned out you can take break for months and your gear afterwards will be still relevant compare to other mmos which has the annoying ,,Gear Treadmill''. Also good and positive things i find, that not many people says about GW2 is that every expansion is relevant in terms of end game, there is no lvl cap increase with each expansion release, instead of that you have a Mastery System, which unlocks stuff for gameplay, or does help boost your mount stats or does unlock other useful gameplay gimmicks for exploration, it's called Horizontal Progression, very casual system that i wish more games finally adapt. + Story is is breathtaking, if you like dragons, world building and the characters+ So many known voice actors from other rpg games, i was suprised!+ Many beautiful locations to explore, on your own pace+ Casual, solo, group friendly, for each type of player + Horizontal Progression, which makes this game so refreshing + Very friendly and helpful community, you will not find in most online games, thanks you veterans being so nice and considerate to newbies ♥ + Graphics does hold up well, in comparison to other mmos, they are slowly updating things, eventually and hopefully they will update older zones with textures, my wish + Customization of armor, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dyes to apply to armor, endless possibilities, if you put your creativity to ,,grind'' more skins. many pets, toys, chairs, emotes + Crafting can be fun, if you put a little more effort it it, quite useful for Ascended gearing and Legendaries, later on + Gemstore is not pay2win! It does sell some gimmicks for time less using things, but i would personally not say it does give others some BIG advantage compare to players who does not buy things ,,Useful QoL tools''. It's more of  time convenient type of gimmicks in terms of gameplay. - Lack of outfit templates, it's mind bugging me that Anet still did not rework the skins to introduce Outfit Templates, you can build up only one kind of outfit, sadly :( , for me who loves fashion and would love to have more type of outfits, it's quite limiting me, i would love to have more templates for exploration, for example for each biome different type of outfit i would fashion up, for like desert exploration either forest exploration, yes i am that wild for outfits ideas :D i am spoiled by FFXIV and Swtor fashion from yeaars back. - Living World Season 1 and 2 can feel tedious, painful at times, wish LW1 gets another reworks in terms of not forcing you to do group public dungeons, which are most of the time empty, and it's quite challenge to find people for it.  - Some zones could use update with visuals, mainly textures, in comparison with expansions that has beautiful views and stuff, but nothing grouond breaking in immersion, just small complain from me - Lvling alts, can be boring, or either tedious, still do not know proper way to lvl up alts, so far using boosts to avoid ,,chores''. - Some story parts in base game, could use update for better improved cut scenes, but nothing too bad- Sad that dungeon system is abandoned and replaced with Fractals, would love to see new dungeons in future, who knows? With Anet you never know if they will bring something old back... we will see!

_childDocuments_.review: I guess it's my turn now to give GW2 a review. It's a love and hate relationship for all of the years. - You buy the expansions to unlock more content. At least core content is free so new players can give the game a try. No subscription payment. Just hop in and enjoy the ride. Everything is obtainable without spending a single money.- Horizontal progression. The highest tier for gear is ascended and has been for many years. And max level is 80. Once you are at that stage, you're pretty much done in terms of gear and levels.- Vertical progression is based on YOU. You decide if you want to improve, learn other classes, achievement hunt, etc.- Can easily play with friends since levels don't matter. A high level will downscale you to the area.- Combat is great and fluids pretty nicely (although there are times that things don't align properly...)- Visuals are awesome.- True endgame: Fashion Wars- Tons of content that you can do from core, HoT, PoF, EoD, raids, strikes, metas, etc.- World vs World (server vs server). a PvPvE environment where you just go smack people as a blob- Best mount system- Balance team is just questionable at times. - Blue class is strong and Anet's favorite child- Anet hates purple class- sPvP is like <1% playerbase and can be super toxic- Bugs can be left in the game for years and becomes the norm. Anet will be like "yeah thats a bug" 10 years later- Leaving old content into the dusts. RIP Dungeons. No new raid wing for a long time since they went down with the Strikes route. The latest strikes for Challenge Mote is very difficult if PUGging. - Light blobs- Too much blob on ground- Absolutely a puke of a mess if you do not have Effect LOD checked but still a messShort answer is... yes. Give it a try if it's your type of MMO. If you do enjoy it, find an awesome community guild preferably small guilds as you can make yourself known there. Big guilds can be very intimidating for new players and may forget who you truly are. But really, it's a matter whether you put yourself forward and make yourself known to others.

_childDocuments_.review: GW2 is, or rather, was a game with great potential ruined by incompetent company. _childDocuments_.review: Ah, Guild Wars 2, where do I begin? It's like entering a fantastical realm where each nook holds a brand new journey. Let's start with the community—it's the coronary heart and soul of the game. Whether you're a seasoned participant or a complete noob, you may find a welcoming bunch geared up to help or embark on epic quests collectively. It's not just a recreation; it's a social enjoyment.Now, let's communicate about our surroundings. Guild Wars 2 boasts some of the most breathtaking landscapes in gaming internationally. From the snowy peaks of the Shiverpeaks to the lush greenery of the Maguuma Jungle, each zone is a visual banquet. And the satisfactory component? They're no longer just pretty to examine; they're full of dynamic activities that keep the world alive and kicking.Mob layout is every other highlight. Gone are the days of mindless button-mashing on well-known foes. The creatures in Guild Wars 2 aren't simply difficult, but fairly numerous. You'll face enemies that require approach and skill, preserving you in your feet and making each come upon feel sparkling.Map design is a masterpiece. The zones aren't simply expansive but intricately designed with hidden nooks and crannies, jumping puzzles, and secret areas that praise the curious explorer. It's a sandbox for adventurers, and each map appears like a residing, respiration entity with its very own stories to inform.And do not even get me started on these occasions. Dynamic occasions can flip a tranquil walk right into a chaotic battlefield or an impromptu dance party. It's this unpredictability that makes the world vibrant and tasty.In a nutshell, Guild Wars 2 isn't only a sport; it's a living, evolving world that invites gamers into its tapestry of stories. The network, the environment, the mobs, the maps—each detail comes together to create an experience that is nothing quick.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the go-to MMO if you play multiple games. Most MMOs try to convince you that they should be your only focus, but here, I feel like I can take all the time I need. I revisit the game often, with breaks lasting up to years, and I never feel like I’ve missed out. This is especially true since you only need to buy expansions (no subscription), which is one of the main reasons I don't play WoW or Final Fantasy. With those games, I’d feel obligated to play if I’m paying for a subscription. Plus, what’s the point of a subscription if there’s an in-game shop, paid convenience, and expansion fees? Seriously, wtf?The game looks decent—nothing too fancy, just MMO standard. However, the areas always feel populated, thanks to systems that give you reasons to come back.I also think this is one of the few MMOs where you can genuinely "theory craft." In most content, you can run the build you enjoy without having to copy from online guides.If you want to play the game, don’t let others tell you what to do. Want to raid? Go for it. Prefer dungeons, exploration, or PvP? Do that! It doesn't matter when or how—everything stays relevant (mostly; some older content gets easier with new mechanics, but it still requires effort). Just have fun. Simple, yet powerful.

_childDocuments_.review: it's f*cking disgusting how they designed this game almost impossible to play solo, especially in the expansion/dlc map. Enemies in the original game are fine and you can just play the game solo. To get to the expansion map, your characters need to be lvl 80 first (max lvl of the original game), but when you enter the expansion map (be it Path of Fire or Heart of Thorns), even enemies in the early map hit like a truck you barely able to survive solo, especially if you're a glass cannon class like elementalist (wizard in this game)There're also mastery points in which you need to collectin each expansion in order to lvl up your skills regarding those expansion. e.g. mostly mount skills for Path of Fire. Problem is, even mastery points in the early expansion map are just designed to annoy you, especially solo players. For example, there're some mastery points that the devs put on top of a high rock pillar, which requires springer (bunny), which is the second mount from PoF expansion. Problem is, to unlock the springer you need third skill of your mount, the raptor, to jump across a ravine and reach area where you can unlock the springer.Is there any mastery point that doesn't require mount to collect? Of course! But of course, not without a cache. There's a sidequest  inside the first city in the expansion, where you need to help a headchef, as his souschef. Most gameplay of the sidequest is running around the kitchen area searching for random ingredients the headchef shouts, and then throw said ingredient to the chef while he's running around the kitchen, all under time limit. I guessed bcs i play solo i just need to throw 5 ingredients at him, but no, the game requires you to throw a set amount of ingredients (i never managed to). Feels like there's no difference in the mission objective no matter you play it solo or in a group. Just a few tries of this sidequest already discouraged me to collect mastery points and play the expansion. Sure it's easy to ask for a group in the early days after PoF was just released in 2017, but now 6 years later? The maps there feels like a deserted server.A good game character, combat gameplay, environment design wise, but feels like it was designed to be very hostile especially to those who try to play the game solo

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, engaging, brings people together and respects players' time. Shines the most in open world content. Instanced content is difficult enough but not to the point it drives player off like other mmos. Graphics are awesome. There's a variety of armor and mount skins to obtain, all of them without paying real money. Nearly all of them can be dyed. And there are A LOT of colors to choose from. The combat system is dynamic and fun and as are the mounts. All of them are useful and have their own abilities. The only issue I find in Guild Wars 2 is the lack of freedom when it comes to key-binds. You cannot drag your skills across the screen like in World of Warcraft. Every weapon type in the game has their own skills and they all share the same keybinds. The same goes for mounts. You can't key-bind your mounts' abilities individually. They all share the same key-binds. ( At least you can change those, just like the weapons' skills ). Some mount abilities are tied to the same key-binds as your weapons, thus making it very frustrating when you get a new mount and have to change the key-binds you're used to in order to be able play properly. Other than that the UI is very clean and well-designed. No clusters of text, meters and icons like other popular mmos. There is an  option play with action camera instead of holding right mouse button as well and it is perfectly viable. The game has horizontal progression and there is no irrelevant content. Each expansion is bought individually and and there is no subscription. You're definitely getting your money's worth and more. Exploration is a very big part of the game and the leveling process is long and fun. There is always something to do even after hitting max level and getting max gear. The game is actively bringing players to more populated maps, thus making it so you always have someone to play with. Despite its major key-binds issue, Guild Wars 2 is by far the best mmo I have ever played.

And as others already mentioned: There's no Pay to Win, the shop has a ton of cosmetics and some quality of life items, which are all accessible by exchanging gold into gems.So, just give it a try! _childDocuments_.review: My favorite MMO of all time, but I do want to break down why a little bit, especially since I've been playing quite a bit of ff14 as well.GW2 has wonderful and combat and movement, it's moment-to-moment gameplay is the best in the MMO industry. The devs are active and responsive, making this game feel loved. The community is genuinely one of the best that I've ever been a part of. The players are so nice and supportive. The grind and loot mechanics and crafting are all fun and not very tedious, which is a big reason why I prefer this game over other MMOs. It's also fun to play on your own, with friends, or with strangers, there's a wide variety of content for pretty much any playstyle.My biggest complaint is that the devs keep changing directions when a system doesn't work as well as they hoped. Dungeons were the original end-game content, but they were too easy, so they invested in fractals, but then decided raids should be the real end-game, but that was too hard for many players so now it's Strike Missions. Also, they originally wanted no expansions and permanent changes to the game world, but that meant that it was hard to market to new players, so they said they'd only make one big expansion. But after that one expansion, they realized they had the same problem of marketing to new players, so they made another one, then another one. Now they say they're going to make one mini-expansion a year. I hope it works out for them, but it's hurt their past content because their projections kept changing. You can especially tell at the end of the Icebrood Saga that they really REALLY rushed the story to prep the game for a new expansion (End of Dragons).FF14 shares a lot of these strengths, great player base and awesome devs, mostly fun grind, fun solo content. But they've also had the benefit of having much more consistent and planned timelines and have added small tweaks that really help with the immersion, which really helps with the community and roleplay. However I don't find the combat, the movement, and open world travel as fun as GW2.If I were to simplify the two experiences, I'd say GW2 feels more "arcadey." It's focus is more on being fast paced and fun with lots of animations and colors and "epic" set pieces. FF14 feels more grounded, slower paced, which helps make each small adrenaline boost from a victory feel more meaningful. It's a better game to relax to and feel immersed. If you want to have fun every moment you're playing, play GW2. If you want to feel incentivized to chill with strangers and sign out in an inn for extra XP, play FF14. Me personally, I do both :~)

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been playing Guild Wars 2 (GW2) for 9 years overall. I took a few extended breaks but always came back. Why? Because it’s an awesome game! GW2 has everything you’d expect from an MMO. Most people are likely familiar with the MMO formula but I’ll try to cover as much as I can.A huge world to explore with quests and events. Most of this content can be done alone but there are certain things that require a group. The events happen on open world maps so there are usually people around who just jump into events to help and then go their separate ways. Each map has points of interest to find and beautiful views to discover. Map completing areas and exploring is fun solo or with friends. GW2 also has optional platforming style mini activities called jumping puzzles. These are on most maps and vary in scale and difficulty but are a nice way to mix it up. There are dungeons which can be completed in a casual story mode or harder modes and there are strikes which are harder again but work as a bridge to top end raiding content. I can’t give any details about strikes or raids as I have never done them (I’m one of those players that’ll be found picking flowers not raiding.) You are never forced it engage in any dungeon content.The mains stories are excellent. The base game story is quite standard fantasy stuff but as time goes on the content becomes much more cinematic and completely voiced.  The music is of an epic standard throughout. Crafting is an optional feature that will allow you to get hold of the best items made through your own hard work. You can completely ignore crafting if it isn’t your thing but there are certain high end items that require it. GW2 has a vibrant PvP scene which has arena  based combat and a world Vs world mode where servers are locked in a perpetual open world war. I’ve not spent a lot of time in these modes but I have dabbled and would say that a certain level of skill is required to really get the most out of PvP and while it can be daunting it is frantic fun. The base game has many hundreds of hours of play time if you aim to map complete each zone. With each expansion adding hundreds more. You definitely won’t run out of things to do.This is not a young game and starting it fresh will be daunting. The game can be a bit bloated with various map currencies and different types of progression but don’t let any of that put you off. Just play the game how you want. You’ll learn as you go, there’s no rush.GW2 is my favourite MMO because it allows me to decide how deep I want to go. From wandering around finding points of interest to trying to gather specific materials for crafting to massive map wide boss events. You can play your way without feeling that you are always chasing better gear. The game does an excellent job of never letting you feel like you’re completely behind everyone else. It respects your time and doesn’t expect you to play 10 hours a day just to keep up.Now for some questions I’d probably ask:Can I use mounts?Yes. GW2 has brilliantly integrated mounts that have uses in combat and in map traversal. But. There is a but. Some of the mounts are locked behind collections which require a lot of work. While I quite like having to work for mounts I find the time and effort needed is a smidge over the top. Ultimately it is worth it because they are the best mounts I have encountered in an MMO to date. Is GW2 grindy?It depends on what you want out of it. If you want to be crafting the best gear then you will need to grind for materials. I’d say I’m a pretty casual player and I’ve never really had to do much grinding. But I don’t craft much or try to get the best of the best items so maybe I’m not best placed to say. What I can say is that for more casual players there isn’t much of a grind.Is GW2 pay to win?Not really. You can use real money to buy in game gold but the items you can buy from the trading post don’t include the most powerful equipment. The things you can buy for gold are largely available to everyone through playing. The only edge buying gold may give you is the ability to buy rare materials for crafting but even then you’d still need the crafting skill to use said items.  Is it free?The base game is free. As stated above it has hundreds of hours of content but if you want the mounts and gliding then you do need expansions which are one time purchases. The game is broken up into main expansions and living world story chapters in between. The living world chapters are free when they come out but usually have to be bought if you miss them on their initial release. There is of course a real money shop in GW2. This is mostly for cosmetics like mount and weapon skins which are all optional. If you want the best experience then I’d say you do need to buy the expansions as they add so much to the base game. Having said that the base game does it stand up in its own right. How is the character creation? You can choose from 5 playable races. All can be male or female and there are enough options for you to make a unique looking character. It isn’t the deepest character creator but it  certainly isn’t lacking. If you’re like me and spend hours in character creators fussing about your nose and forehead you’ll be glad to know that in game you can earn or buy hair styling kits or total makeover kits that let you change your entire look whenever.Give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: I've put off playing this game for years. Why? Because something about it doesn't click with me.  So I actually played it as I had a little time, and my initial response to this game when it was revealed was right on the money - I do not like it. Now, some of the art work in it is great, and a credit to the RPG genre. There are less options on the aesthetics side when making your character than I'd like - because typically they want a bunch of stuff locked behind a paywall, of course - but the stuff that's available is pretty enough. However, the "cut scenes" and conversations in the game are dreadful. The intro to your character is fugly - its more of that "cut, rotate, paste/morph the image points to distort it" style art that makes me want to slap the "artist" that did it. It's LAZY - plain and simple. Now, I'll give GW2 its due credit - they've actually spent the pittance it costs compared to the rest of the games' development to have the majority of it voice acted. It is so refreshing to actually sit in an MMORPG and not have to read through the wall of dialogue, as the character actually has a conversation with an NPC.It's such a forgotten, small thing, that it distresses me to see so many games similar this one but don't have it in order to save a few pennies from their development costs - and yet it's impact to immersion is worth those few bucks every time: and immersion in an RPG is EVERYTHING.So why don't I like it?It's the progression.Like so many other games, calling it a level up progression system seems redundant. You levelled, woo, your stats went up, cor, hey look this level unlocked a new ability, wow. It's all on rails and automatic - the character and it's growth is not truly MINE. When you line up your character to other peoples, there's going to be another that is the same class, and despite the tweaks you made on character creation, will look and play exactly like them, breaking the notion that it is YOUR character - it's not, its just another plain digestive biscuit from the large budget packet from the supermarket. Sure, the first ones alright, but after a few, you tire of the bland taste. And that's what the character "levelling" system is here (and in so many other games of a similar type) - bland. It's all because - for some reason - the dev's of these types of games keep perpetuating this annoying and persistent hand-holding of players, molly-coddling them so that they don't "mess up their character's build" by putting stats in weird places and learning skills that they believe don't fit.That's the player's choice, surely. If they want their wizard to fling a greatsword around, or their warrior to know a healing/buff spell or two or - perish the thought - have some OTHER form of utility that can be quite handy in a pinch - then shouldn't that be their choice, as it's their character and they want to play it that way.Way back in the late 90's, there was this genre defining game. It blew away people that played it because of the way it was done. It was an RPG, but it was isometric rather than 3d (because of system capabilities back them). It had multiplayer, so you could buddy up on your quest if you wanted to. Even PVP of a sorts.Yet it had one small, overlooked thing to it that was pure genius - a little idea that seems to have been long forgotten.You could train your character - which ever class you picked - to use any armour, any weapon, and learn any spell you wanted.That was the original Diablo.Now granted, the higher end spell (apocalypse or armageddon or something - it was a high cost fire spell) only got like one or two casts off when fired by a warrior that used it, but the fact that they still could was their choice to make.Now, we just have this stale rendition of RPG's that has everything on rails, and every choice done for us, that even the stories rarely play out in different ways, and are merely there for the illusion of choice.It's stale, dull and I'm bored of them.Let me make my character MY way. Let me play and develop them how I want - even if it's not "optimal", or doesn't "fit the theme".Go to a group of engineers, heck even a convention for one type of professional vocation, and each and every one of them will have skills, talents physical abilities different to everyone else there: some will be able to cook, others skilled artists, while others will be able to play a freaking guitar or violin - a persons "class" or "vocation" does NOT limit an individual to what they can learn - AND IT'S BEYOND TIME GAMES STARTED REFLECTING THIS.What's the excuse? Development time? Cost? With today's capabilities, this is not beyond the pale, its not impossible, stop hiding behind the wall of hand-holding and countless excuses to make a game over-simplified - just because its cheaper.In fact, I'd challenge that it is. If every skill and/or spell is in a pool of skills and pickable by every class, that actually makes everything way easier to develop, as its then just a matter of tables and related stats - and we've seen from countless other games that it doesn't matter how many stats there are, they can all be "upgraded" at the whims of a player easily.So no, I'm not sold on this game. I'll give it a little more time, just in case the story improves, but it looks a lot like other RPG's that are loaded with pointless busy work (fetch and carry, random murder, more murder to make monsters drop X amount of object Y... blah blah blah SNORE).There are other games out there where your choices matter, and you can build your character how you want - play them instead.

_childDocuments_.review: There is no such thing as a 100% perfect game or gaming community. Just like any MMO, GW2 has its fair share of toxic players and sweaty try-hards. The game itself, while really fun and dynamic, also has plenty of bugs; some of them are so long standing they've become memes, and others are just plain frustrating. That said, GW2 is a really great game. I highly recommend that new players at least give the free account a try. If you like it, get the expansions. If it's not for you, then at least you didn't waste your money.I've got almost 2000 hrs invested into this game. It was the first MMO I tried and the only one I consistently keep up with. In the game, you've got five different races to chose from, each with multiple unique story options (beginning at level 10), 8 different professions (9 if you buy the expansions) with differing levels of complexity, and a ton of different weapon/skill combinations to make your gameplay as button mashy or brain dead as you like.The core game is massive with plenty of places to explore, achievements to get, and gold to earn. The gold you earn in game can also be turned into gems which gives you access to all kinds of cosmetics as well as some account upgrades like storage expansion and general QoL stuff, but these things are completely unnecessary to complete/enjoy the game.On top of all of that, the community is really solid. Almost everyone is willing to give their time to help out new players or returning vets to guide them through story or end game content if needed. Of course, as with any MMO, you get the odd toxic sweatlord now and again. It happens. But overall, the community is really wholesome and helpful which makes the gaming experience that much better.I highly recommend new players get a free account and just see if it's right for you. If you hate it, then I'm sorry it wasn't for you but I'm glad at least you didn't spend anything other than your time. If you like it, then awesome! Welcome to the GW2 family and I'm sure I'll see you around :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is different from about any MMO I have played prior because the classes have unique skills based on what weapons you use. Part of that uniqueness is this game does not follow the holy trinity of tank, healer, dps. Instead, everyone has built in heals and buffs (some classes are better at tanking and healing than others). Like most MMO’s you get overwhelmed with what to do so I stuck to the story quests after I hit 80. As for the pros and cons:Pros:Unique classes: they feel different than other games which is a pleasant change of pace. World: Large world with lots to do, open public events go on everywhere and there seems to be a lot of activity.Subscription: You only need to buy the DLC’s and you can play the game with no sub. The base game is free so I would recommend you try this game if you have an itch for a new MMO.Community: People are friendly, active, and helpful. Feel free to ask your questions Weapon skills: Diverse options of weapons for classes. An example is the hunter can use a one-handed axe but most of those abilities are ranged attacks on main hand but on offhand those abilities change to meleeCons:Weapon options: Every class is mostly melee, with ranged thrown in. I played a hunter as I like ranged classes and found that you mostly would use melee weapons in the later game (especially raids). I can force being ranged by using a long bow and a short bow as a backbar, but this is not ideal in higher end play. Class progression: I went from feeling strong to feeling very weak as I leveled, gear was hard to come by. Felt like I was getting a lot of gear that was not for my class and I out leveled the story quests so the rewards I received from that as mostly junk to me.Monetization: As I said in the pros that there is no subscription for this game but the one problem, I see with it is for quality-of-life things like more inventory requires buying things from the shop using gems. Now its possible to get gems by converting gold to gems, but gold is extremely hard to get. Just leveling from 1 to 80 without selling my mats on the auction house I had around six gold. (my understanding is higher end players can make 5g to 25g an hour but this is based on your knowledge of the game and how invested you gotten with upgrades like mounts already) Either way your spending money to have a better experience or your spending a lot of your time grinding for gold so you can have a better experience in the future.The only game I played that had a similar shop to me was Lost Ark. When I did calculations, you would need to spend $100s to get some basic quality of life stuff to make the game feel better and that is not counting cosmetics. There should be a subscription option that gives you’re a large storage (or unlimited), gems, and some other perks. (Elder Scrolls Online uses this model)Weapon skills: Yes, I listed this one as a pro, but it is also a con because you are forced to use whatever skills are on those assigned slots. You cannot customize what skills go on what button and you get no other options, so this causes issues if you do not like certain abilities. Gold sink: Everything cost gold in this game. Scrapping kits to turn items into mats, fast traveling, and gathering tools. There is gathering tools on the shop that do not break but it is over 2000 gems which is $25 or around 500 gold depending how you get those gems. Even at level 80 “junk” items you vendor you were lucky if you received one silver for it.Overall, I recommend trying this game only because it is free to play the core game. I personally liked the classes uniqueness, but I hate the current monetization model as it reminds me too much of Lost Ark’s approach (minus the pay to win). _childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Guild Wars 2 Since Alpha, Beta and then even pre-ordered the game for myself and 2 others (Whom stopped playing a while) - So my hours far exceed 500 before it came to Steam and my review being valid! I do have some points to cover off below!Graphics: The graphics still to today hold up pretty well. It's a decent game to look at running on a massively outdated engine. The art style is like a paint brush canvas anime art, it's kinda weird but in a way it works pretty well, so overall graphically it's a nice look MMO!There are some real spectacle off fights graphically!Audio: Some great audio from character yelling powers to dragons roaring to animals all around. It is a great audiophile game!Controls: I do not like or use WASD as I am old school arrow key player (Which is what they are designed for) but with this game it kinda forces you to use the WASD due to how many keys for casting abilities are, but super super easy to get used too on this game and character control getting used too will take some time.Game-play and everything else after: So the game is an MMO on a huge scale but locked behind some walls forcing you to purchase.So when I started playing, there was no mounts, gliding etc and the maps where just big enough to run around. Now, they've added mounts, gliders which originally was said they would not and that means the base core maps remained the same but the newer maps are bigger and have less respawn points, meaning more running around for distance with a mount, but you NEED the DLC for these.If you just have the core game, that's fine. You are still going to get a lot of content on the go but you will then need the DLC which massively opens the game up beyond anything seen before and it's a worth wild purchase.ANet do not allow as I write this review veteran players to transfer to Steam at all and their logic/ answers just do not make sense, it's all the same servers, worlds etc... So the way around this is in the launcher adding "provider - Portal" and this then allows you to login on your account, which is great but bare in mind, it's not using fully Steam because you STILL need to make any purchases via their store and website, you cannot purchase the Steam DLC and expect it to work.Some maps I am not a fan off, like the 'Heart of Thorns' DLC, the maps are all over the place, up and down it's to confusing and hate it. The Path of Fire is a lot bigger open maps with less respawn points so you spend 90% of the time running around back and forth.Another issue with the game is the fact, you and your friends are in a party or squad, you go and do a heart (Side missions) on the map, even though their contributing, it does not effect yours, you ALSO have to do your own, the same as the story. It's like all different and they are on the bus for the ride, which I find a massive off put.Amazing features apart from the unique game-play has to be the trading store, it's all cosmetic but you can buy and sell on the go, without having to visit someone.. Unless you collect your items and on the go, you can do pretty much everything, which is great "Grabbing an item, selling, moving on, without going to a vendor"The game has multiple characters, classes etc for you to create and all have their own back story, starting worlds etc but there are TONS of abilities you can unlock and play along the way your way, which is great.The story? I did not pay attention as there is a lot of talking sometimes, so skipping videos for me all the way as I just wanted to play.  You have an option to go off, explore, level, craft, farm, fish, mastery, cosmetic, gear etc, it's a massive game to go off and do your own thing, plenty of vista's, points of interest, collections etc to find and XP is rewarded for everything you do!Would I recommend this gamer? Yes, without a doubt it's a great MMORPG like many others with a unique twist but a great game to hammer hundreds off hours of game time with a friend or solo.
