_childDocuments_.review:
Exoprimal is an online, team-based action game that pits humanity's cutting-edge exosuit technology against history's most ferocious beasts - dinosaurs.  Exosuits are grouped into different roles, and players will pilot these exosuits to hold firm against overwhelming dinosaur swarms in online-only, team-based action game modes. Dino Survival, the main game mode, sees two teams of five players compete in a variety of PvE and PvP missions. Players will be transported to the scene of the latest dinosaur outbreak and follow Leviathan's guidance to complete objectives. The team that completes the mission first will emerge victorious.

Whether players are engaging the other team directly, or fighting alongside them against a common enemy, the aim is to accomplish objectives as quickly as possible. Missions vary depending on player skill and other factors, meaning no two matches will unfold the same way.

name: BPM: BULLETS PER MINUTE
detailed_description: WARNING: BPM contains flashing images. If you experience epileptic seizures or blackouts when exposed to certain light patterns or flashing lights, immediately stop playing BPM and consult your doctor before resuming. Fight as a mighty Valkyrie to repel the forces of the underworld from invading the world of Asgard. Gameplay In BPM, all of your actions and the actions of your enemies are tied to the beat of the music. Your enemies perform a dance-like sequence of attacks to an epic rock opera. BPM is inspired by retro shooters of the 90’s. It is fast, frenetic and rhythmical. You can double jump, dash, rocket jump and bunny hop to evade your opponents. Your goal is to reach the end of randomly generated dungeons, collecting different weapons, abilities and items each time you play. These weapons and abilities can radically alter the way you play, making each playthrough unique. You must defeat 7 bosses to reach the final boss. Each boss moves and attacks in a unique way that you must learn to exploit if you want to succeed. Some attacks require you to jump over fields of lava, some to dodge fast projectiles, some to hold fast for a beat. Features: Shoot, jump and dodge to the beat while battling hordes of enemies. Fight powerful bosses in challenging boss battles that will push you to the edge. Explore randomly generated dungeons. Choose from 10 different characters with unique strengths and weaknesses. Wield a powerful arsenal of weapons, all with different behaviour for firing and reloading to the beat of the soundtrack. Battle a diverse array of enemies, each with unique rhythmic behaviours. Get overpowered and fire shotgun rockets while flying through the air. Utilize abilities that radically alter the way you play the game, from teleport to freezing bolts. Equip over 60 items that buff your character in unique and interesting ways. Experience an epic rock opera soundtrack. Challenge modes for extra gameplay. Add Custom Music into BPM and shoot, dash and dodge to the beat of your own soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: Expect a number of reviews to be from Humble Bundle subscribers (like myself) and while I technically only paid a few dollars for this game, I am reflecting on it as it would be a stand alone, ~$22 purchase, and even for that amount this game is half baked. It has an excellent concept of mashing 1st person shooter, rouge-like, and rhyme game but this game feels like its still in alpha testing. Yes, the aesthetic looks neat, at first. But it gets old and makes it plain difficult to see what's going on (make shrines more visible, every forum on this game has a few threads asking for this. The items and guns are not well planned out. Many have extremely cryptic descriptions or even misleading. Look at the two headwear items, Midgard Bracelet and Loki's Bargain. They are described in-game as "Pure Goodness" and "Sacrifice slot for stats". The two items actually do nearly the exact same thing (Bracelet will sometimes give an extra 25HP but is sometimes bugged/inconsistent for an unknown reason) by giving +1 stats up while worn, plus an additional +1 permanently for each floor cleared. The idea of putting in duplicate items, that occupy the same inventory slot, and never giving any explanation to learn how they operate seems like lazy dev work. Worst is the room to room gameplay. Shooting on beat is very fun actually, which makes the rest of the game even more frustrating. There is a main currency of gold coins that are picked up from enemy and chest drops. There are also keys (to use on unlocking more valuable chests and rooms) that are randomly dropped. As far as I can tell, there is no boundaries or ranges of how many coins, keys, or shops appear. This might be anecdotally but in all of my play throughs I was either swimming in a surplus of keys and opening every chest, or I was starved for keys and had to miss 70% of drops off pure RNG. I was able to complete 2 runs and each time it really only felt because I happened to stumble across one of the game-breaking items/guns and its momentum carried me to maxing out all stats and high tier gear. Anytime I got passed that hurdle it was easy mode but the challenge was getting to a spot where I could get a viable build. I never felt I was playing well, it was just that I was blessed with good loot and RNG. If you can manage to score this game for under $3 like a lot of us, then of course expectations would be much different. But for its current state and full price its a no from me, dawg.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay loop is basically perfect. Super fun. You have to be locked into the beat the entire time to do any good.Some of the presentation also rules. The few tracks in this game (one per level) are all complete bangers.Here's where BPM 2 should focus in order to get Hi-Fi Rush levels of attention:1. Bigger soundtrack. At least double. Song that plays each level is random. This would keep the game feeling fresh longer.2. Songs of noticeably different BPM. Maybe 90, 120 and 200 are good break points. Varies up the challenge and feel from level to level and run to run. Also forces more music variety so keeps it interesting.3. Different art style. There are a billion options that would work. They could go realistic/comic like Doom. They could go cartoon like Hi-Fi Rush. They could even do like an Ashen thing where everything is clear shapes but otherwise not so distinct. The point is that this art style grates on the nerves after 10 minutes of play. Monochromatic AND blurry/indistinct is a drag.4. Some kind of sparse narrative. Quick, high-impact story beats at the starts and ends of each level would rule. Point of it all should be to increase the hype, not challenge the mind or inspire a TV show.5. More interesting character diversity. We have the health-reliant one, the absolute worthless piece of ♥♥♥♥ (looking at you Freyr), the fast one and then from what I can tell a bunch of gimmicks. Geri is just a little guy, for instance. That's all he is. Everyone should feel markedly different to play, even when they aren't upgraded.BONUS POINTS: Let us use local mp4s to create our own soundtracks.EVEN MORE BONUS POINTS: Spotify integration.

_childDocuments_.review: BPM: Beetle Prank Manicure, is a most singular game, that uniquely manages to draw me back in from time to time. The challenge gradually evolves as you gain experience, from merely trying to stay on the beat, to perfectly knowing and evading the attack patterns of every enemy you may encounter.It features a large number of weapons, items, skills and power-ups, and since these are all doled out randomly, getting to know them all requires time and patience. I'm a good sixty hours in, and still frequently encounter new items or abilities whose function eludes me. Getting to know what powerups are effective in which scenario, and how they compare to each other, is a whole hidden sub-curriculum of learning this game. Sure, you may be able to shoot and dodge like a champion, but do you know the difference between Rythmic Chaos Boots and the Boots of Rock? Well, you better learn, because one of these will help you a lot more than the other.One of the most addictive things a game can do for me, is to make me feel like I am getting better at it. And BPM: Brown Potato Mash does it like no other. Foes that would once strike fear into the hearts of the bravest Valkyrie are now shrugged off with disdain. Encounters that would leave me at the brink of death I can now complete without taking a single hit. It's not just that I am getting better at it: it's that I can  myself getting better at it.There are very few games I continue playing. Fewer still I continue playing after completing them. After finishing the campaign in Metal Hellsinger, I felt like I just played through a fun game with great music, but also that it was now done. Not so with BPM: Blasphemous Puny Monsters. I only just completed the game with Odr, and I already know I'll be back to tackle Sanngriðr one day. I'll die a lot, fail a lot, but I know I'll be coming back.To me, there is no higher praise for a game. Buy it, bash your head against the wall for a bit, and keep trying. You'll love it.

_childDocuments_.review: 8.5/10 - Phenomenal game! Regardless of your musical capabilities, BPM is worth your time and money. It firmly delivers on its face-value expectations and experience considering this was a dev team of two people. Challenging and addictive, entertaining and rewarding, this title brings a fresh experience to both the FPS and Rhythm genres.The game is locked in a tempo of around 88bpm (beats per minute, in this case) or 176bpm counting in double time; that's roughly the tempo of "Beverly Hills" by Weezer or "Bulls On Parade" by Rage Against the Machine. There are no options to increase or decrease tempo, but there is a setting for the rhythm requirement if you are struggling to keep the beat.Small difficulty tunings are needed for bosses (general rooms are more difficult than actual bosses are throughout the entire game), as well as some minor graphical issues (screen flashing, dash animation is stuck in place and doesn't move with FOV setting changes); despite BPM's small hiccups, the game is absolutely worth picking up for the price.Personally speaking, I would be willing to participate in crowd-funding for future content of BPM. Some suggestions:- additional tracks, levels, characters, items- tempo adjustment options (preferably slightly faster options for difficulty)

_childDocuments_.review: The game has constant frame drops and stuttering which make it near impossible to keep rhythm. If you miss a beat you mess up firing your gun, reloading, and you lose your multiplier. Given it's the whole point of the game, the fact that this issue has nearly no fix I can find is frustrating. My system is more than capable of running the game, so I can't see what else could be causing it other than poor optimization or something.Outside of that, the game's roguelike mechanics seem basic and a little poor. It feels like a case of a neat game idea and concept that they shoved into the roguelike format just so it would sell better or something. The room layouts are boring, there's little item variety or synergy. The enemies on the first couple floors feel like absolute fodder, so easy to deal with, just a chore and slog to go through so you can get to the more interesting floors of the game.And the new guns that you get can just feel way too unwieldy to even bother with. Why should I mess around with an RPG that's tricky as hell to fire and reload, when I could just take the burst assault rifle which arguably does more damage and is easier to manage? It should also be noted that you can only hold ONE GUN at a time. Unless there's an upgrade that lets you hold two? It seems like a huge missed opportunity for gun chaining to be a synergy option the player could consider.The game almost feels trapped by the roguelike element. This would've been far better if it progressed more like DOOM or something similar. If it allowed you to keep an arsenal of weapons that you could switch between, maybe chain together to the beat? That way progression would make more sense, as you progress further and improve you gain a more complex set of weapons that you can freely switch between and use. The game wouldn't have to have stuffy and samey roguelike rooms, it could have rooms specially catered for what the game truly is: a rhythm based FPS game.It's so disappointing honestly, since the game (when it's not stuttering and dropping frames) feels fantastic to  play. I loved firing and reloading to the beat, dashing to the beat, jumping to the beat. But there's just too many things clashing, plus the stuttering issue, that I can't currently recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I refunded this game.  I would probably have stuck with it if it wasn't for "TOO FAR".  You see, your bullets only work for about 10 meters.  Oh, and the primary enemy in the first level is a flying bat.. and you get 4 hits then your run is over. _childDocuments_.review: Having almost 100% completed this game I feel I can give a review.The GoodRepetitive but fun game play loop. I find myself enjoying the randomness seen through the different rooms, enemies, stats, items and powers I may come across each run. Some runs I breeze through the first few levels to get destroyed down the line and other runs the first boss gains a modifier that makes him stronger or even cloned and I lose immediately or at least struggle through an intense fight. This keeps me constantly on my toes every run. The random rooms is also a key component, I can find the best items for my build and misjudge one room and find myself dead to a swarm of flies. The music beat mechanic never over stays its welcome, I am always reminded of the pure fun that is reloading, shooting and dashing to the games music. It's a fun gimmick albeit one that does feel could have been expanded upon even further such as harder levels having new music that increases or decreases in tempo and as such you must adapt to the increased or decreased amount of bullets you are able to fire and how fast enemies can move/shoot. This feels like a missed opportunity.Different characters are basically the only thing that got me to play this game for as long as I have, the uniqueness is a great extra gimmick to handle such as one character having his health based on coins essentially changing the game into a sonic mode of sorts where managing money is key, instead of buying a great gun I may have to hold off to ensure I have enough health to take a hit or two. Other characters such can come come with hard mode gimmicks such as a constantly draining health that is refilled by doing damage, the game now becomes a speed run in which I cannot take time in shops and in some cases one trip into the wrong room has led to me not having time to get back to the boss room before dying. It's great extra fun, on top of this you have their all unique abilities and super abilities that you unlock by finishing the game in easy and then hard. (One downside was however I started attempting characters on hard straight away as I found the difference between the two not very noticeable so I would finish a character, unlock both their abilities but have no reason to play them anymore other than to attempt a hellish run which offers no achievement for completion so once again, not much reason for it).The BadVisuals are a bit of a mess for me, I could really imagine enjoying this game with a more fleshed out map/enemy design. If you ask me to tell you what the games rooms, enemies and bosses look like I would tell you that off the top of head I can just see orange blurs. The game is bathed in an odd orange mess of highly saturated colours. So bad to the point I really cannot visualise anything other than this mess. The different levels do become apparent with Asgard being orange and the following levels moving through greens to reds and finally a deep dark black and red hell for the final two levels. The last levels are the only ones that I feel match the colour.Bosses are boring. Sad but it is true the bosses for me are easier to kill than the flies in half the rooms. I die more to a random projectile from a fly/bat than I ever have to bosses which all come with very predictable and obvious attacks. The best boss is the first boss and arguably the final one. Why is this? Because usually the first boss you are not that strong yet so you quickly come to respect the mechanics such as dodging to the left and right to avoid a massive attack on one side of the room. Being weak here means I have to take my time and actually dodge and weave through the boss fight. Often by the second/third/fourth boss I end up finding some sort of decent gun/gear that makes the boss a literal bullet sponge that I can clear within 10 seconds. It is so rare that I ever spend longer on these bosses to actually realise what attacks they even have. The last boss is a mix of the same, sometimes it can take me a few minutes and other times 10 seconds all based on how lucky my run has been with guns/gear combinations. On top of that when you do spend any time on these bosses you realise how boring their attacks are, the final boss for example shooting fireballs and an expanding sphere of damage you must pass through when the sphere takes brief pauses in movement. Get that down and the boss is once again just a bullet sponge with little changes even if you pick the hellish difficulty.Ah my least favourite thing. How luck based the game is... So like any other rogue like, you may come across random loot in the form of different armour pieces. A head, Shield, Hand and Boots piece can be worn at the same time. The head pieces can range from gaining explosive shots, damage vamp to the worst such as slight damage when close to enemies (You never want to be close so this is just never worth having). The shield is basically always a search for either the shield that gives double damage or the shield that gives infinite ammo, these two are so essential for an easy win that upon finding one you can almost confirm a run as guaranteed. This is mostly further confirmed by having the right weapon such as the mini gun which makes the game a snooze fest of holding down left click as every enemy in front of you drops dead (the gun is only balanced by its 30 ammo limit and charge up time both of which with infinite ammo you can get rid of). My first ever successful run was with the infinite ammo, mini gun combo and ever since I sometimes force myself not to pair the two just to ensure my run doesn't into a boring mess. Realistically the luck in this game doesn't feel well earned, the use of these amazing items should be to potentially save a dying run, in other words to not give up just because of a bad start when the next room may offer me a double damage shield or new power that gives me healing over time. The issue is that items are so unbalanced that in many instances you can just repeatedly restart the first level until you find the best starting items and secure an easy finish.Finally, my last issue is the game feels way too short. Once I got the game under control I was finishing some runs in 15 minutes. The game boils down to: 2 levels in the first zone, 2 in the next zone, 2 in the zone after and then 1 in the final zone and the last level is just the final boss. If you have ever played a game like Hades or Ultrakill the final boss in this game should realistically be the first major boss of maybe 3-5 more. Or maybe the final boss after being killed should lead to a few more zones. The game feels almost like a play test of sorts when I really begin to think about how basic its rogue like systems are compared to others. I also should mention each level can be cleared in either 1 - 15 minutes. Purely depends how slow you decide to be and how soon you find the boss room as you can fight the boss and move on at any time once found.Ultimately though, I like Bullets Per Minute, it has held my attention for many hours and I have had lots of fun and some moments of major frustration. Completing the game on hard as the character that can only take one hit felt like a major achievement and I cannot really knock this game for what it does. I have plenty of bad points but in comparison to the good the bad feels minor in the long run.I will however suggest to get this game on sale like I did. BPM cost me £3 and to me that's money well spent. For full price I think these minor issues would have felt way more problematic to me.70% out of 100% Orange Juice

_childDocuments_.review: What i really appreciate about this game is how it actuallyacknowledges being a shooter as well as a rhythm game.It does not punish you if you miss the beats and lets you flow with the music whenever you can, and that is great.It could've easily gone the unfun way, jam your guns if you miss the reload, make you take damage if you missed the dodge.But it doesn't, instead it expects you to oblige to the song and not every beat, and thats it. You're not the drummer, this is not Guitar Hero, the song does not go away if you fail.And guns actually make good beats which makes a lot more sense than those gun sync music videos.As a little critique: The first level of the game is the hardest one. With your peashooter in the start, it is a real struggle. And the difficulty slope is a downhill once you get the best items. Like so many other roguelites, you're heavily dependent on luck rather than just skill, which is a usual flaw of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: As a rhythm gamer, oldschool FPS fan and someone who has ascended in Nethack a few times, I thought I could waltz right in and dominate the game. No, oh no.The range mechanic will stop you from sniping everything across the room with a shotgun. The stats matter, the item interactions matter, and few things are really "guaranteed" on your way to the final boss. That said, FPS skills are still very important and will augment your character stats nicely.Rhythm is only important insofar as when you (and enemies!) can take action. But you don't think about it so much when it sets into your subconscious. The soundtrack is outstanding IF you like wailing guitars and electro-industrial metal (and I do.)Its roguelike aspects come from randomized dungeon layouts, fixed bestiary, random loot and character stats. The only things BPM departs from in this respect are the turn-based movement and combat, and random item appearances (a minigun is always a minigun with 30 shots per reload.) But with all the random loot available, you are tasked with making the situation work however you can, and there are multiple superior combinations of weapons and gear to discover. This game is designed to be busted open like that.The starting characters all have different stats, physical properties and starting weapon. Later, they also have special powers- you must unlock these by playing through the game on the associated characters though. It will fool you into thinking you're doing well in the early game. But later levels turn up the heat fast and the penultimate Hellheim readily makes you its ♥♥♥♥♥.If the challenge is not enough, there are two characters to unlock that will die immediately after receiving any damage. 55 hours in, I'm still trying to master these characters. It doesn't matter that I've failed over a hundred times; I keep coming back to show the game what's what, and it's addictive in that way.I can't set it down. But if you pick this up, be ready for a real challenge- it will not hold your hand and it will punish you for your mistakes.

_childDocuments_.review: The core gameplay mechanics of shooting, reloading, and dashing to the rhythm are great. Even the enemies do the same, though it's less noticeable. I did not find it hard to get used to and felt it was quite intuitive. One thing that could have helped me get into the game easier though, would have been if the easy difficulty was a bit easier since it feels almost the same as hard. And if items an abilities had an actual explanation/description besides one or two cryptic words.The rogue-like structure gives the game some decent replayability with different equipment, abilities, and weapons each round. Each weapon having its unique pattern to reload and shoot is one of my favorite parts of the game. Equipment also manages to change the game in interesting ways and can make for some wild and wacky builds. Where it lacks is by always having the same song for the same stage/floor and having one set boss for each stage. Enemy and room variety is rather small. There are modifiers that can change a stage, but they are often just an annoyance instead of giving something interesting. In the end, I can't say if this game benefited from the rogue-lite formula or not. The aesthetics of the game are not too great. I wouldn't call it ugly but it's not much more than the minimum to make it look serviceable. I don't really mind that much, I just wish some important things (altars) had more visual distinction from the surroundings.It feels like this game had the potential to be something outstanding but ended up being something that falls somewhat short. Maybe I need to look at it from a different angle and see how good of a game they managed to create with a very small team and budget. Either way, it was a quite fun game that I enjoyed but couldn't help but feel a bit disappointed, looking at the unfulfilled potential.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: BPM has some of the most exhilarating gunplay and cool style in the entire roguelike genre, but I think that it could've used some more time in the oven. 8.5/10First off, I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ adore this game. The Norse Mythology backdrop, the metal soundtrack, the incredibly fun guns, it tickles the roguelike bone in a way very few other games have in a long time. However, once you beat the game on hard with a few different characters, you've basically got the full experience.Think of it this way. BPM is a gourmet chef who makes the best ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ steak you've ever had. So you go there, and you eat it - 10/10. You have 176 BPM, 4/4 time, and just enough auto-aim to make the process of aiming and timing to the beat at the same time bearable, but not difficult. You go there again. 10/10. It's even better the second time, now that you're good at it. You go a third time, maybe with a different character, 10/10 again. But eventually you want something else. All the music in the game has the same BPM and same time signature, maybe it's time to try something else?But that's all BPM has to offer. It's an 11/10 game. It's 20 hours that is by far worth your time and money. But if you're coming by expecting the traditional roguelike feel of "I want to do this over and over and over again for hundreds - maybe thousands of hours" then you should look elsewhere.I feel like the game was designed to use different BPM and time signatures, but time and budget constraints forced it into all being the same. There are weapons that subdivide oddly, fun proof of concept items that mess with the way the beat counter works etc. but the full picture isn't there.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a short explanation and exercise to help you decide if you're going to enjoy this game.  Try it out.The Music:  Look up the song "The Rhythm King" off BPM's soundtrack and give it a listen.  You will hear the rhythm of the beat for the first ten seconds and then the beat and off-beat afterward.  Depending on your weapon, you'll want to focus on one or the other.Weapon Mechanics:  The shotgun pistol is an early weapon that holds four shots and has a three-step reload.  It can be fired and reloaded on the offbeat.  What this means is that you fire the weapon four times then press reload three times on both the beat and off-beat of the song.  There is no delay between reloading and firing beyond losing the rhythm.The Exercise:  Now listen to the song and tap your mouse and keyboard to the beat and off-beat: M1, M1, M1, M1, R, R, R.  Repeat without missing a beat and that's basically the gunplay in this game.  Do this for the first minute of the song and that's basically the gunplay in this game.  Now, when the song picks up, imagine 12 flies zipping around a room shooting fireballs at you and that you'll die if you stop moving for a single beat.  Congratulations, you're probably already stressed out and that's basically the game itself.Tips:  1. Don't rush to unlock the extra characters - somehow powerful skills but they tend to just make the game even harder.  Hildr is my current unlocked favorite, she starts with the shotty pistol and a key but has lower HP.  2. The boss and mini-boss always drop a key unless a level modifier prevents it, so you always get two keys per stage.  3. A 'secret' stage exit can spawn only on the first stage of the game, it'll be a set of stairs.  ALWAYS take it if you want to be OP.  4. If you're having trouble finding the rhythm, pause the game and just listen to the song.  It's much easier to do when stuff isn't trying to kill you.  5. Save your money and check the shops before you spend, missing out on infinite ammo because you spent your coins on subjectively bad weapon upgrade really sucks.Verdict:  I've played 23.5 hours and beaten the game 6 times.  I've died  ~20 times between each win.  On easy.  I love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing this for a few hours. Great soundtrack, fresh game mashup, and you want to keep coming back. Shooting and reloading are the only real rhythm mechanics in the game. So once you get a hang of that all that's left to learn is how to dodge projectiles really. It's unfortunate that it feels like there's so much potential to improve here. After beating the game a couple times you mainly just click on the beat and play a pretty mediocre shooter.There are also some major balance issues. After beating the first 2- 4 levels you may become completely overpowered because of an item or gun you find. After that you walk all over the game, its bosses, and even its end boss. This feels really cheesy, and robs you of any conception that the way to beat this game is to get good at it.This game is a great proof of concept. This genre definitely works and I hope either the devs or another company expand on the concept. I think the next iteration of this type of game will be much better. Still, I'd recommend playing it for the great soundtrack and interesting concept. Just don't expect to be hooked on it if you're looking for something with a bit more substance.

_childDocuments_.review: I have so much to say about this game, but it can be summed up in one word. WOW!This game is not easy. You (usually) have to do everything except move and jump on the beat, including dashing. I can't keep a beat, but it is a lot of fun. If you're like me in the sense that you too can't keep a beat, you don't even have to perform the actions on the beat if you don't want to. You can enable a setting that lets you hit the buttons off the beat and they still perform on the beat. However, even if you can keep a beat, sometimes you are just in a bad position. Took me 6 hours of playing to finally beat it on easy (mostly because I refuse to take the easy way out). I still haven't beaten it on hard. The game is nice in the sense that it hasn't gotten old like other roguelike games. It has not-so-subtly taken some ideas from Doom, but the game feels remarkably smooth and it still manages to be it's own thing. That actually leads to my ONLY complaint about the game. The whole red saturation filter over most of the levels that makes it feel like Doom is quite distracting at first (The last one is more of a black one that removes a lot of color and I feel the same way). I think that it just makes the game a little hard to look at. However, I've gotten used to it by now. Overall, it's a fun game. Takes a lot of getting used to. Helps to get into the music, but not too into the music. That's when you start making gameplay errors like running into enemy projectiles.

_childDocuments_.review: This is objectively one of the worst rogue-likes I've ever played; enemy variety doesn't exist and rooms are filled with the same 3 enemies for the entire game practically, this doesn't help that they are the worst enemies to get close to and the game has a short range limit on your weapons to where they flat out do nothing a few steps away from enemies unless you buy per-run range upgrades; this coupled with the small rooms leads to getting hit because you practically have to hug enemies in a essentially a closet to deal damage.Progression elements are next to none besides the coin banking and unlocking a character, there is no sense of returning on your next run stronger than you were before; the items which are supposed to make you stronger are cryptic/overly simplistic in their description of what they even do, I'd rather take a overly long description than the one or two word explanation of what I just picked up or deciding to buy even does; I theorize this is done because many items in the game are exact clones of each other with slightly different explanations to conflate the item pool.To move onto positives the good of this game is it's ost, sfx and creative but poorly executed concept; the soundtrack for this game is extremely good and the weapons sfx add the two to create a gun sync with little difficulty as long as you have a sense of rhythm, it's honestly more fun at times to sit in a room and do nothing but shoot to the music than play the actual game; the idea of a rhythm fps is creative and is ONE of the earliest merges of the two genres.TL;DR bad as a rogue-like, bad as a shooter, ost good; not to be a shill and but Metal:Hellsinger is a more fleshed out and polished evolution of this idea without the rogue-like elements.

_childDocuments_.review: BPM is a roguelike FPS with optional rhythm elements. Yes, exactly optional as you can disable the rhythm thing in options. Is it still a good game without this feature? Yes, it's still good - I've played with and without rhythm requirement and it looks more like an additional challenge rather than an essential feature to enjoy this game. And all the positive and negative aspects in this game are not related to it. Personally, I've played only ~2-3 hours with rhythm requirement after I got used to other mechanics but then I turned it off again - I'm not a huge fan of it and how it's done while I liked most of the other things here.First of all, BPM is a roguelike, with all random stuff that you can expect from it - chests, coins and ways to spend them, randomly generated dungeons, random loot, shops, relics, upgrades, weapons etc. Get lucky and you will be destroying everything. Sometimes it creates weird situations when you know for sure that you will slaughter everyone while you may still be on the first level of Hard difficulty. Almost every time the first 2-3 levels were harder than later ones, because you can kinda faceroll everything after obtaining certain items and a decent HP pool. At the same time, the game would be rather challenging if you didn't get good upgrades/items early.+ Gunplay is mostly enjoyable. It's fun to shoot enemies here.+ Different guns and abilities create relatively unique experiences when using and combining them. Your "rocket launcher" playthrough experience will be different compared to revolver or something else.+ The game is polished really well in every technical aspect. I never experienced lags/bugs or glitches in BPM.+ Soundtrack is actually good but, unfortunately, there're not that many tracks.+- At first I wanted to complain about the amount of content but there's some replayability actually. When you beat the game for the first time on Hard (that you can do in one hour, but more likely in 2-4 hours) - that means that most likely you've seen like 90% on the game content and gameplay experience. But there're 5 Valkyries (heroes) in total and some of those provive slightly different gameplay experience and it's fun to try to beat the game as each of those. There're also some challenges to do. Even though there's not that much of variety - I still wanted to replay this game over and over again. +- Bosses are kinda meh -- only 2 out of 8 bosses require some actual efforts/strategy to kill them, but only when you're unable to annihilate them fast enough (that is often possible to do). But in general bossfights are not that bad.- Probably one of the most annoying reload mechanics in the history of shooters. In short, you have to press the R button two-three times to reload. It's soooo fun when you have 4 (or even less) bullets in your gun. In addition, reloading also goes poorly with other actions. The hardest thing in this game is to constantly think about reloading and it's definitely not a fun way to make your game harder. And yeah, if you have a revolver/rifle then you're welcome to reload each bullet manually, yay! You can get used to it and it's even immersive at times but it's not fun.- Some essential objects are barely visible. For example, altars where you have to donate coins to get upgrades. Honestly, on the last level it looks like bad trolling - I can't imagine that people who tested this game never mentioned it. Not much better on other levels though.- Poor description for several items, bad variety of items and questionable balance between them. I still don't know how exactly some items/mechanics work after 10+ hours in the game (and some of those are impossible to guess for sure, without exact numbers/descriptions). Poor variety/amount of items is another reason why you won't be able to have any "build" that would provide a different gameplay experince that you can often expect in other roguelikes (there's one specific build that you can do around one ability and it'll be rather effective but that's it I believe). All you need is to get an overpowered shield with HP regen + a decent weapon and you're good to go.All in all,  is a fun and somewhat unique game. It's cool as a shooter, it's decent as a roguelike, the rhythm feature fits well enough and you can always disable it if you don't like it. While it's challenging and fun to play, don't expect a huge variety of gameplay experience besides weapons - almost every (successful) playthrough would be very similar here. I have A LOT of questions about balance in this game but I guess balance is not that important if the game is still fun to play. I just managed to beat the game as 5th Valkyrie without taking any damage and it was a really awesome experience, so  for  from me while I understand that it's far from perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very interesting concept, but boy did I bounce off of it. Listen, I'm a fan of roguelikes, and I love rhythm games like Beat Blast and Crypt of the Necrodancer. I went in thinking I'd like this one, but there's some design choices here that really don't gel with me.Let's start easy: the graphics aggressively work against you. I understand that they're an intentional style choice, but the entire screen is an unreadable mess at times. I had to turn down the contrast on all levels by 70% to make this playable. If your "metal artstyle" makes it impossible to distinguish enemy from projectile from scenery, then maybe consider toning it down, eh? Still, at least that can be fixed with the contrast sliders.Great music! But only a single track per level? That got old  quick.There's objectively poor design present too: lads, it's not fun having to traverse half the map to pick up a health potion I left behind. It's downtime that's painfully at odds with the flow and style that the rest of the game tries so desperately to provoke. Enter the Gungeon already solved that problem. The arena topology is also pretty poorly done at times. You want free-flowing movement, but there's sometimes steps in the map that aren't properly telegraphed and just impede your movement by surprise, causing you to get hit. It's not because The Binding of Isaac did it, that you have to do it too, you're allowed to improve upon things. You know what isn't fun? Finding three special cool reward rooms you've never seen before but getting no f*cking keys to open up access to them in the entire floor.There's subjectively bad design too. On easy difficulty, why is the game so demanding of perfection? This should be a game about killing monsters in glorious style. So why can I only get hit like three times? Consider Doom 2016: killing demons in brutal fashion with plenty of opportunities to heal. Doom wants you to have fun, while this game wants you to play a perfect rhythm game. That's a shame, because when you get into the groove this game is genuinely fun.Difficulty curve is a bit wonky too, but that's par for the course for a roguelike. My first 6 runs I couldn't get past the first act, then I picked up a regenerating shield and beat the entire game... Same deal with the grenade and rocket launchers. This game is difficult until it's a cakewalk. The frustrating thing is I thoroughly enjoyed the cakewalks when they occurred, making me wish the devs would've chosen fun over challenge.All in all, this is one of those games feels bad for the simple reason that it could've been perfect. So much of it feels like squandered potential. That said, if you're much better at rhythm games than I am, or enjoying getting punished a whole lot more than I do, then I'm sure you'll find this fun. At its core this game is a true gem, as the overall reviews show. It's just  not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game, obviously, as I've refunded it.If you go into this expecting something like a Necrodancer + Doom hybrid, you'll be very disappointed.First off: Enemies are so, so, so very bland and uninspired. Besides the bosses (which as far as I've seen are recycled Paragon models btw) the height of normal gameplay is having some sort of insect either shoot or jump at you. It's not very fun and super obvious that these are just bought or open source assets. These assets don't even fit together very well, hence the insufferable amount of native filters that bleed everything together (you can lower those).Secondly and most importantly: It's not really a rhythm game at all. I'd call this "a rhythm game for people who want to feel like they are playing a rhythm game without actually playing one".Let me explain: In Crypt of the Necrodancer the fun and hard part is learning to do everything on-beat. In the beginning you'll have a hard time with that and will often be off-beat, ruining your streak. It won't ruin the game because if you panic and spam some buttons to get out of a pinch, the game lets you do that.Now comes this game: You literally, yes literally, can not be off-beat. If you hit a button with the wrong timing, nothing will happen. You just won't shoot that shot or reload your weapon.This is what makes this game very boring, in my opinion. There's no real learning curve and the rhythm feature feels more like a forced limitation and not something to figure out and get good at on your own.Lastly: Item RNG is completely messed up in this game. Worse than in any rogue-like I've ever played. 80% of the time you'll either get no items at all, making the game super tedious, or you'll find a broken item in every corner, making the game way too easy. A run where progression feels well paced and balanced really is a rarity in this game.I'd really wait before getting this game. Or play < 2 hours and get a refund if you don't like it. Tl:dr This game is a messy combination of bland, bought or open source assets that are bled together using weird shaders and filters.The rythm feature feels like an annoying constraint as it forces you to do everything on beat and just ignores every other input. There's really nothing to get good at and the gameplay flow suffers noticeably.Item RNG is messed up beyond belief. If you want a real rhythm game, get something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's be clear and get the negatives out of the way first.  This game is an early access game but got released cause the devs ran out of money.  The balancing is pretty bad; if you make it to level 3 you're likely an unstoppable killing machine and you're gonna have a successful run.  The saturated colors can make it really difficult to see enemies or shrines.  There is a distinct lack of enemy types.All that said, this game is super addicting and fun as hell.  Getting into the right rhythm,  where you're bouncing around, blasting, reloading, dashing, it feels amazing!  The tunes are great and each room is a mostly fun encounter.  If you're a fan of rougelikes, shooting, and music, this is a great game for you.  Having different characters with different stats/abilities gives you some replayability, along with the hard mode.The combat is a lot like Serious Sam combat: strafe around the enemy and keep blasting.  Never get too close.  Don't go into this expecting a Doom like, "push foreward" combat.  Stay as far away from enemies (though not too far, your guns have a set range to them) as you can and you should be fine.A bit of advice, I suggest rebinding the reload button to a mouse button, as it's really hard to strafe(and you'll need to be strafing at all times) while reloading to the beat.

_childDocuments_.review: -Aesthetics are too much in the way of the gameplay. Impossibly dark in too many areas making enemies invisible. -Weapon variations are limited and not very interesting to use. Limited to the guns you see in Doom.-Some of the sound design for the weapons are terrible for a rhythm game. The burst and pump action weapons sound terrible in rhythm with the music, making them difficult to listen to the beat of the game.-Music, while good, doesn't help with the beat of the game. Bass isn't as prominent as it needs to be for a game like this, where the player's rhythm is basically being the drum or bass line.-Very little benefit to shooting on beat, purely a limitation on the player and no reward for combo counter except for pity points.-Upgrades and items are boring. most are just increase in numbers and very few affect the rhythm aspect of the game. -Clip upgrades don't scale to the weapon, making it very weak for some and incredibly powerful on others.Overall, doesn't feel a good rhythm game experience, Doom but with a beat to stop you from shooting. Rhythm aspect feels like it was tacked on later. Better off you play another shooter with a heavy metal aesthetic.Might change my opinion later if I play more of the game, but as it stands, I had an okay time. Spent 5 of the hours stuck on the first 2 levels, and the last hour cleared it in one go just because I got the gauss cannon.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty standard roguelike setup, but the rhythm mechanic paired with some fantastic music makes a hell of a time once you start getting the hang of it. You can turn on a rhythm lock that basically automatically keeps you on the beat if you want an easier time; I find this more satisfying to play with. Also you can turn down the color saturation to a more palatable level in the settings if you like. Beyond that there isn't a whole lot to say—if you like roguelikes or rhythm games, it's fun. My only real complaint is I wish the endgame scaled in difficulty a little harder; usually if you've done well enough to get to a certain point, you're almost certainly coasting an overpowered build to nigh guaranteed win. You'll want to set a custom reload button that doesn't require taking your fingers off WASD.

_childDocuments_.review: This is game is amazing. If you like rhythm games or FPSs then you'll love this game. The music is really good, especially once you get to Svartalfheim. There's only a few things to keep in mind though. Each floor has a color theme to it and it can get a little hard to see, but luckily there's an option to adjust each floor's saturation if it's too much for you. Also, if you have a mechanical keyboard and are using keyboard and mouse you may want to rebind the reload button. It's not so much the delay but rather it gets pretty tiring. Right mouse seemed to work fairly well as an alternative. Be prepared to use the wiki to see what every powerup does. That's not a bad thing necessarily as it's par for the course as far as roguelikes go. Luckily, every negative thing I found about the game can be fixed in-game. Some other reviewers mention that the game can be fairly difficult. As of this review I've beaten the game on the easiest difficulty once after about 4 hours. Speaking of playtime, I still find new items and rooms 5 hours in. TL;DR+great soundtrack+fair difficulty curve+high replayability+accessibility settings-settings may need to be adjusted-wiki use is recommended10/10 probably the best game I've played all year and definitely the best rhythm game of 2020.

_childDocuments_.review: IT'S EXTREMELY GOODThat's it, that's the reviewwhat else do you want from meAlright, alright, fine, I'll talk about itLet me start by saying this: This game has a few quirks. Lemme list it off:Enemies: They always feel like they were simply scattered into the room with no thought put into placement or "enemy combinations" (you know, which enemies to appear alongside which enemies in which positions). Most of the ai is very simple. Some of them use the rhytmn mechanics of the game and those are REALLY COOL, but most of them don't.Mechanics: A LITTLE HARD TO GRASP AT FIRST GRANTED, but once you get the hang of it? There is nothing in the world more satisfying than reloading, dodging and jumping to avoid specific attacks to the beat. Each attack that uses the rhytmn mechanics is always marked on your "rhytmn counter" thing. If you need to dodge a specific way for the rhytmn, a special note will come from the side, if you need to jump to the rhytmn, an upwards note will come. It's very simple once you get a grasp of it! Although it is hard to understand since the game REALLY DOESN'T EXPLAIN A LOT. You basically need to figure things out about it on your own.Levels: THEY FEEL BLAND HONESTLY. Some of them can be cool! But after a while the rooms really start to feel repetitive and "samey". Some of them have a few platforming challenges and interesting tidbits, but most of them are really just "big open space with enemies"Graphics: THE STYLE FEELS COOL HONESTLY. After some time in I started becoming not a huge fan of the graphics and started wishing they were better or more stylistic than just "bright color" but it's not a huge deal for me. The overall vibe almost feels like an early PS2 game honestly!Boss fights: BY FAR THE EASIEST PART OF THIS GAME. Most of them are really easy and quick to get through honestly, it's just getting there that's an issue. There are some things that are odd, certain boss attacks that are really weird and hard to grasp since again, the game doesn't tell you much about itself or it's mechanics and you just need to throw yourself at that wall in different ways until it cracks, but that's really my only gripe with them.Music: YES. WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ DO YOU WANT ME TO SAY, JUST LISTEN TO IT, IT'S SO GOOD. I just wish there was a system like in crypt of the necrodancer where you can import your own songs into the game since after a while they start to become repetitive as, well, there's only 12 tracks in the entire game.Roguelike elements: This is... hard to explain, but by far the worst point of this game. If this game wasn't a roguelike it would be perfect. But it chooses to be a roguelike and that... that's not a thing it succeds in very well. The items are very basic, most of them not being exactly creative. The weapons feel satisfying, yes, but they're all generic, you know? There's nothing creative like "a rocket launcher that fires sharks" or "a bow that fires laser arrows", no, they're all just generic guns. They feel satisfying! more satisfying than in any shooter game I've ever played! But it's nothing to write home about by roguelike standards. And the items that buff you and the overall systems of the game... Even for a roguelike they're luck dependant. What I will give to it is that, this is a game that you can very much get through even with bad luck if you're symply good enough at it's mechanics since that's the main focus of it, but the roguelike elements themselves are very... "scattered", if that makes sense. Dungeon design is simplistic, most items don't really do anything creative, you can carry very little at a time, increasing your stats is entirely dependant on luck, there's things in it that just feel straight up not worth it since the game barely gives you most resources, especially if you're not lucky... There's this one thing in the game where you can throw either your coins or keys into it dependant on which version of it you get, but all it does is give you a stat up. For multiple coins/keys. To put this into perspective, there's another thing in the game that does the exact same thing, for simply 1(one) coin. And these are both just found scattered randomly across rooms and usually hard to spot thanks to the graphics.This is a reeeeaalllly good game, but god, if it wasn't a roguelike it would be so much better. And I like roguelike games! I've played Hades, Binding of Isaac, Wizard of Legend, Risk of rain 1 and 2, Scourgebringer, Gungeon, Necrodancer, Gunfire Reborn, Dead cells, Loop Hero, Dicey Dungeons, you get the gist of it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to love this game. The soundtrack is amazing and the concept is right up my alley. Reloading your weapon is satisfying, but unintuitive at first since it requires multiple presses depending on the weapon. The basic pistol you start with requires you to press it twice, and the revolver up to six times if it's empty. Because of this I highly recommend changing your reload bind to a mouse button if you want to strafe to the right while mashing the reload button to the music.Now on to my gripes with this game. First, the enemies are awful. It's a lot of small flying enemies, and even smaller fast moving spiders. Maybe I should just git gud, but having tiny ass enemies in a FPS is a big no no. There's even a Retro mode that pixelates these enemies so much that you are literally pixel hunting to shoot them.Next you can only have ONE weapon at a time. No weapon switching means you have to stick with one, even if you run into situation where maybe a longer range weapon would work better for the current situation, but you're stuck with a shotgun. Or your right next to a chunky enemy that you need to get rid of now, but you have a longer range weapon.Speaking of ranges, there is a range limit to all your weapons, and it's hard to tell if you're close enough to fire. It does tell you AFTER you fail, but that initial shot could've been a deciding factor if you take out that teeny spider or you get snacked on.The shader really bothers me because everything is washed out in red for the beginning stages. This especially sucks for me since I have some red/green color blindness. Finding shrines that give you oh so important upgrades are hard to find since they blend in with the background.Tuning is all over the place. I have played a bunch of roguelites like Binding of Isaac, but even a run where I have had no keys for the first two floors seems more balanced than what is going on in this game.Like I said, I want to love this game, but it needs to be patched up before I consider picking it back up again.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing a novel here because I want to like this game so bad. the concept rules but is totally spoiled in the execution. First off, BPM absolutely did not need to be a rougelite. Each stage has only one song, and permadeath ensures you'll spend a lot of time listening to the first level. I'm so sick of the first level song. Additionally, all tracks are in a vanilla 4/4 time at 88 BPM. It all runs together and gets really old.  BPM doesn't feel like it was designed for first-person.  Levels are pretty much identical to Binding Of Isaac's grids. You walk in a small room and enemies spawn in all corners. This works with the top-down view of Isaac, but in BPM I'm constantly getting ganked by enemies to my left or right as soon as I walk through a door.  I honestly think this game started development from a top-down view like B.O.I. or Gungeon and was refitted to an FPS at a later stage.Major enemies have sound cues for attacks but for common mobs there's no indication you're getting fired at from behind. It doesn't help that you can only take 4 hits at the start of a run, and health potions are scarce. Most of my runs are just getting whittled down by cheap shots from the rear and not finding enough potions to offset these. It's not a good sign when every death I'm saying "Okay that was BS"What else? There are grotesque bloom and saturation filters covering everything. Most upgrades are just incremental stat buffs. there are maybe a dozen room layouts that get recycled ad nauseum.honestly BPM feels like it's still in early access and even then I'd say it's a fixer-upper.

As a rogue-like it isn't all to remarkable, its fairly unbalanced and the determining factor in most run will be luck, but as a gaming experience it will leave you always wanting to come back for just one more attempt.The best 20 dollars I've spent in a long time

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game at its core, but it has a ton of flaws, and after revisiting this game I unfortunately don't think I can completely forgive it for them.For one it feels like the mouse sensitivity is always changing. This is a pretty large issue for an FPS. It also feels like there's a lot of delay between when you move the mouse and when your view moves. It's likely a part of the calibration, introducing delay in an FPS is usually a recipe for disaster. Could also be the game not playing well with proton, as I have not seen it mentioned in any other reviews.The game is also pretty difficult. Might just be that I suck at it, might also be the inconsistent feeling mouse controls, but my first dozen playthroughs I couldn't even get past the first part. Despite this though it's surprisingly not too enraging, if anything it kept me pretty hooked for a good hour or so.However, some of the times when I've died have felt undeserved, such as getting cornered by a really small enemy, having an enemy spawn right in front of the room entrance, or enemies attacking right as you enter the room. On top of this, there were the aforementioned mouse delays, and the game consistently froze for a second or two upon entering a room for the first time. However, the latter could be a proton issue with compiling shaders.It's ok if you can excuse some of the flaws, but overall feels unpolished. Even then it's a game you'd either play for about an hour then get bored of, I'd say buy it on sale.Addendum: Upon further reading on protondb, it does appear to be a proton issue caused by the steam overlay. I'll test it and update my review accordingly. I'll keep this review positive under the assumption that the game works flawlessly under windows.Addendum 2: While it's certainly better, the problem of the sensitivity constantly changing is still there. It feels like the game is trying to somehow change the sensitivity to match my mouse's DPI, because whenever I increase my mouse's DPI to compensate, it feels like the game's sensitivity decreases a little after that. There ends up being moments where it feels like I can't move my mouse at all, even at full DPI.

_childDocuments_.review: BPM borrows heavily from Binding of Isaac. So much so that BPM isn't just inspired by it, but directly copies many of its mechanical elements including weapons, modifiers, rooms, and enemy types. It does feel like the devs initially thought "hey, what if Isaac had a rhythm mechanic," as a starting point. If you're like me, that combination seems fantastic on paper. But BPM has it's share of issues. The main problem I had is with it's art direction affecting gameplay. Everything shares the same limited color palette in BPM; the walls, the floor, the enemies, projectiles, etc. This creates an effect where all the elements in a dungeon blend together, making it difficult to see enemies telegraphing their attacks, or projectiles coming at you. The projectiles issue might not matter if the game had a top-down perspective, but this is an FPS. Often times you'll get hit by attacks that seem to come out of nowhere.

_childDocuments_.review: How do I put this in words...? BPM is incredible in concept, highly questionable in execution, and bankrupt in creativity. What do I mean? Well;BPM's core idea of shooting-rhythm game is very good. The Idea of having to keep pace with the music and do things like dodge, jump, shoot, and reload is a genuinely brilliant gimmick and not only elevates bland shooting mechanics to interesting, but also elevates interesting shooting mechanics to ones that are outrageously so. Based on my introductory paragraph you can tell what I think of the shooting mechanics without the gimmick.BPM is also a procedural rougelike, allowing for potentially infinite repeatability assisted by a slew of items, guns, and abilities you can unlock for your character upon victory, to make them both stronger and more fun to play on subsequent runs... In theory. Later I will explain the unfortunate reasons why BPM fails at the rougelike aspect too.BPM doesn't use it's interesting baseline idea in a very effective way and in fact actively sabotages it with it's design. While you have to dodge on beat your enemies do not attack on beat themselves, nor does their attack reach you on beat. This leads to situations where you're up close with an enemy and they attack at some random point and you can't dodge it, forcing the hit. The same thing can happen with projectiles, you'll be moving along and turn to see a bat shooting at you from one of your - numerous and punishing - blind spots. Your jump is not on beat, but with everything else being rhythm based the jump being open creates more problems then it solves. coming back to the blind spots, there's about 270 degrees worth, and even if you crank the FOV to a downright displeasing level, you still will be getting shot at by threats you couldn't perceive because you were too busy focusing on the other threats that demanded you look a them or get owned.The choice to make the game a rougelike is one that I have trouble reconciling. On the one hand, it makes for more replay-ability, but on the other, that replay-ability is squandered with repetitious rooms and bland, overly spam-reliant enemy placement. The bosses (after the first and maybe second floor's) either die so fast you don't get to see what they do, or you get ganked by the excessive trash-mobs in the rooms leading up to the boss, because not being able to do the former by floor 3 - at the latest - means that you will definitely suffer the latter. Why is this? Because item collection is not only essential, but also inconsistent and very heavily RNG based, far more than other Rougelike. Here's a few examples of other Rougelikes and how they mitigate RNG in comparison to BPM: -  Easily the second most RNG dependent one I know of, RoR2's controlling factor is the fact that nearly every item you pick up is something that you can definitely use. even if it's not that special you can add it to your kit. When its an item that you can only have one of, in almost all cases you are aware that you are opening a container that will dispense that item before you open said container. Compare that to BPM, you don't know what you will get out of a gold chest until you open it, and beyond that, if you open an item chest, you don't know if that item is boots or a helmet until you spend the key. Sometimes you'll go 2 floors without getting anything other then boots... Then you die on floor 3 because you didn't spike hard enough on the first two floors. -  Wizard of legend is a very hard game just like BPM. Unlike BPM, you are guaranteed the ability to go into a run with the framework of a build. WoL lets you pick 4 abilities, a prebuilt set of traits, and an item. In BPM you get to pick a character, which gives you a starting weapon, and a secondary attack plus an ultimate, but those last two are dependent on you already beating the game with that character on both easy (secondary) AND HARD (ultimate), meaning that as a player you are punished the newer to the game you are, which is the opposite of how it should be. Punishment should be based off of your player not using all of their kit, not based off of that player not getting that part of the kit to begin with. My desire to play a new character is shot by the knowledge that if they have a cool mechanic like a block or coin generation then I need to dig for it. -  Dead Estate is the least RNG reliant game on the list, which is good because its the most like BPM. Even then, it mitigates RNG more than BPM by making the shops predictable and offering many chances for items despite those items not being essential to win. BPM's punishment of new players shines through again, because the shops start off with very few things in stock, most of which are armor or healing, that doesn't help mitigate the rapid resource bleed that runs that are refusing to spike will cause. Runs in BPM are decided by Guns, Items, and Skill Increases. forcing a new player to have only one new weapon choice and one item chance (yeah, because the chicken that runs the shop doesn't even guarantee his stock to have an item) is asinine and tells new players to eat ♥♥♥♥ for multiple runs before they get a decent chance at winning as any of the characters.This section is the most subjective, but also most damning. Let me explain because it might be hard to understand why I would say that at first: The items and guns have a strange, basic look to them, which I find hard to put into words, it's like they're all basic si-fy guns. More concrete is the level design, or rather, the lack thereof. The starting floor is a stone, churchy-area that looks more like a chapel then a place where immortal Norse warriors await Ragnarok. And the characters? They're called Valkyries but not only are some of them men, but they all have halos, and wings, as if these characters are more of a depiction of Modern Christianity's Angel then of a Valkyrie. It's clear from looking at the rooms on each floor that the maps were not inspired by Norse myth in any sense of the word, bearing stone halls and stone undergrounds and stone crypts. On the subject of that test, Reducing the Saturation only worsened the bland look of the rooms. it's clear that the florescent visuals are to hide the rooms rather than accentuate it. And the music? at hour 2 I was going to make a video discussing why this game had an awesome sound track. now I am very much not going to do that. Into Asgard lasts about 5:50, but you will be playing floor 1 over and over again. It just keeps going and there's not enough reprieve.Awe Interactive has a game that could've been good but squandered that opportunity with a messy jumble of poorly executed mechanics trapped in a bland maze of stone.

_childDocuments_.review: -Core gameplay loop is very fun, after the initial fairly steep learning curve it is very satisfying to be slaying out to the beat-Music-Weapons feel good (quick tip: use right-click to reload)-Movement is snappy-Visually underwhelming, the over saturation just covers up already poor assets, and sometimes makes shrines and enemy animations difficult to see.-The level generation poorly balanced and is very feast or famine: I've had some games where I literally killed the first 2 bosses and didn't have a single coin or key drop, and in turn meant I couldn't purchase any upgrades, use any shrines etc. Then I've also had games where from the second level I was one-shotting everything while being able to air-jump endlessly, killing bosses before they had used their first ability.-No audio latency compensation, I was unable to play with my wireless earbuds because they have ~300ms latency, an option to dial this in would be nice.-Many items don't give you any indication what actually they do, and they don't seem to be remotely balanced between each other.-Heroes don't seem balanced, for example one starts with no health, only armour - which means any damage you take is semi-permanent, and it is not uncommon to go multiple levels without finding a way to gain health or armour.-Not much variation in enemies, circle-strafing will get you by most of the time.All in all, BPM has a really great concept and at its core is very fun. However in its current state it's hard to recommend, there are too many issues (particularly balance) which make it frustrating - once you have the core gameplay down, it doesn't feel like you can make meaningful decisions during a run, it's just up to the RNG to decide if you get currency and are offered good or synergistic upgrades.

_childDocuments_.review: This was an instant favorite. The music is catchy. The graphics are simple but evocative. The shooting handles really well. The difficulty is punishing yet fair. There's a great sense of subtle humor and plenty of charm to go around.The learning curve is steep, but since no one run matters, you're free to learn at your pace. Extra options unlock at reasonable intervals for player investment. Even if it feels way too hard, RNG will shine on you eventually, with heal spells or regenerating armor, life steal, or a great damage spell.If you have ever enjoyed a shooter and a rhythm game this is probably for you.  If you enjoyed Crypt of the Necrodancer or Cadence of Hyrule, this is probably for you.I only wish I hadn't let it rot in my backlog for so long.PS. Extra props to the gun designs. This game suffers a little from a common problem in rogue-likes where there's just a huge number of items and no way to look up what they do or make informed decisions in a shop, but the make great use of game culture and affordances to inform the player.  For example, see a pistol with 2 barrels, it probably shoots twice per pull, increasing damage but also decreasing time between reloads, or see a revolver, it probably does more damage at the cost of longer reloads.  This one aspect was absolutely brilliant.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty 50/50 with this game to be honest. There are plenty of elements to like about this game. The movement feels pretty good and the skill requirements of being on beat make this game really fun to master. The various items all feel different enough to make some decisions very difficult. Getting a good run feels amazing, and being all kitted up is a pretty good time. Some of my favourite aspects are the enemy variety and character variety. Each character feels distinct enough to make a run interesting with them. While the first characters may be somewhat similar in some aspects, with each merely starting with a different type of pistol, how you play those early stages of the game and play around their differences might change drastically. And the characters that you tend to attain a little later are fantastic, each offering a unique challenge for how to play the game. The enemies are just as good in my opinion. While there isn't really any thematic cohesion, each enemy seems to have its place. In the opening levels, a lot of the enemies are fairly vanilla. A mobile bat that dies in one shot, various spiders with distinct looks and attack patterns, sneaky worms etc. But then there are guardians. They can only be damaged from their backs, and have 4 charged up shots that track you. Learning to dodge their attacks is crucial and when they're done attacking, they remain still enough for you to go behind them for a counterattack. The scorpion looks like it may be a duplicate of the spider, until you hear its shriek and it charges at you with full speed. Igneous Red switches between various attacks, including an attack which spawns rings on the ground that the player must jump over. And this is before boss fights enter the picture.  This isn't without frustrations however. First of all, flies are my arch nemesis. No enemy is as annoying to deal with as the fly. With 200HP, a small, agile frame that also flies and shoots on every beat from a long range, these enemies feel absolutely busted. The worst part is that they attack in swarms. Early challenge rooms are infested with these blights and depending on your weapon, they can range from minor nuisance to a slow and agonising death. These enemies have no right to be as strong as they are, and often take away from what is an otherwise solid set of enemies with clear strengths and weaknesses. The next thing is that this game is hideous to look at. The filters that they put over each level can be argued as a stylistic choice, but seems like a rather lazy way to avoid extra work. I recommend taking away a lot of the red saturation in the settings.I think the other thing I don't like is that this game requires you to have the wiki open. There is no encyclopaedia or anything within the game that allows the player to learn specific details. Information is very vague in this game. Having multiple tabs open, ideally on a second screen, is strongly recommended. For one example, there is a helmet called "equity". When you are considering whether or not to pick it up, it will just say that it reflects damage. What does this mean? How much damage is reflected? Is it reflected as a projectile that can be blocked? Is it reflected an aoe circle around the player? You have to go to the wiki to find out, and in this case, you'd be disappointed to find out just how dull this item is. The final thing are the challenge rooms. These are great in theory, but due to how numerous flies are in these rooms, these can be the biggest pain to deal with, and are usually tougher than the bosses. Most of the time these rooms are risky chances of getting ahead in the game, but the rewards for completing a challenge room are mediocre considering how difficult they often are. All in all, I'd recommend this game. I have had a lot of fun with it but it could be better.

In this game, players must navigate through a series of procedurally generated levels, all while battling hordes of demonic creatures with a range of powerful weapons.One of the standout features of BPM: Bullets Per Minute is its unique rhythm-based gameplay. Every action in the game, from shooting to reloading, is tied to the beat of the game's rock soundtrack. This creates a fast-paced and frenetic gameplay experience that is unlike anything else out there.Many players have praised the game for its challenging difficulty level, with each level presenting a new set of obstacles and enemies to overcome. The game's boss battles are particularly noteworthy, with each one requiring a combination of quick reflexes and strategic thinking to defeat.Overall, I would highly recommend BPM: Bullets Per Minute to anyone looking for a fast-paced and challenging first-person shooter experience. The game's unique rhythm-based mechanics, challenging difficulty, and engaging soundtrack all come together to create a truly unforgettable gameplay experience. And based on the positive feedback from other players, it's clear that I'm not the only one who feels this way. So if you're a fan of the genre, be sure to check out BPM: Bullets Per Minute for an experience that you won't soon forget.

_childDocuments_.review: A simple arcade shooter with some fun twists. Fire and perform actions on the beat. IT's really fun to sync up kills and reloads with the music. I am not great at syncing so I use an assistance option that syncs my shots for me (so they will delay slightly to sync with the beat if I am off-beat). That option lets me focus less and enjoy more.THE GOOD:- Gunplay is fun. The upgrade systems are fun too -- trying to stack traits, stats, equipment, etc. to synergize can be pretty fun. It lets you break the game is you combine some things, but it's all RNG so some games you'll be desperate, others you will be a god, but it is usually somewhere in the middle.- Music is good enough to rock to while playing but I'd love for them to add some more tracks for diversity.- RNG dungeons encourage minor exploration and offer good risk/reward scenarios.THE BAD:-  If you get lucky enough to combine OP items, you end up playing in godmode. - The color filter is bad. Super saturated dungeons in a pretty lazy attempt to make levels seem distinguishable and disguise assets licensed from other games. It ends up making everything look like a torch lighting a wall in a games from 2005. You lose a lot of detail because of this -- not to say the textures had a ton of detail anyway. On that note, they opted for this coloring over decent lighting. The game just doesn't look like much. It doesn't take away from the game for me, but it is a design choice I wish they made differently. NOTE - this can be edited in the options, but without it the game loses a lot of light too -- it was not meant to be played without the saturation and there's not really a good way around how the game looks.- Very repetitive. That's fine for a few games at a time; but don't expect this game to eat up large chunks. It's a title to be routinely visited, but not played to exhaustion.SUMMARY:- No regrets on my purchase. I have fun with this game.- If you want a FPS that you can get into a rhythm with, similar to a game like DOOM, you'll probably enjoy this.
