_childDocuments_.review: Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands seemed to struggle to truly find its identity and is left feeling as though it desperately leans on the formula that made previous Borderlands titles majorly successful, whilst it does attempts to build on said formula none of it’s new features ever truly seem to shine through as phenomenal additions and even begun to feel jarring towards the games conclusion. With that said it isn’t all bad the games looter shooter design and gunplay mechanics make it undeniably fun to mow down waves of enemies but is never truly enough for Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands to identify as anything more than a carbon copy of all the other entries in the Borderland series.Right from the Opening Credits Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands oozes with the colourful charm and on the nose humour that its predecessors were beloved for, however I couldn't help but feel as though the writers had limited their sense of creativity by binding themselves to the theme of Dungeons and Dragons, this is felt exponentially through it’s main campaign that at times felt stale, uninspired, and as if the writers never truly knew where to go with the games overall story and theme. What started as a very tongue in cheek take on the self proclaimed “Worlds Greatest Roleplaying Game”, pretty quickly became a handful of jokes about the most common tropes and clichés that have been recited to death in other forms of media. On many occasions I found myself pulled from my enjoyment by one of these various clumsily delivered quips that left me wanting for something more that didn’t feel like a second hand joke that had been pulled from the mouth of someone much more charismatic. The main campaign felt rushed and as though the inclusion of side quests was only to extend the average time it takes to reach the story's climax. At the time of review I have spent just under 20 hours in Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands with roughly over half of that spent deviating from the main campaigns path in order to reach the level recommendations for each quest, which resulted in slogging through many forgettable quests that just never truly captured that Borderlands charm. The story is told through the form of an in-universe version of D&D known as Bunkers & Badasses and is rather excellently narrated by the prolific voice over talent in Ashley Burch who returns to reprise her role as Tiny Tina, throughout the main story Tina as the “Bunker Master” guides her players through a wild and haphazardly thrown together Bunkers & Badasses campaign which sees the Player referred to as “Newbie” and the other players at the Table, Frett & Valentine, take on the evil forces of The Dragon Lord. Whilst the voiceover work that is put on display is top notch and the cast boasts names such as Ashley Burch, Andy Samburg and Wanda Sykes their terrific performances are never quite enough to save the campaign from itself and fail to make up for the very apparent rushed and lazy writing. I found myself giving a resounding sigh of relief at the sight of the games end credits and was left with no real desire to continue on with what remained of Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands clearly lazily thrown together side content.For the most part Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands minute to minute gameplay loop is undeniably fun, however it seems to fall apart during the implementation of its new features that mostly feel ill-thought-out and at times tacked on to artificially increase the amount of time Gearbox could keep their players in game. The decision to completely remove vehicular travel and combat in favour for the new Overworld that seemed out of place and better implemented by games akin to Nino Kuni and Final Fantasies of old was a flawed design choice that not only had me feeling detached from the game world but has ensured that Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands has had more loading screens than most modern AAA titles. Unfortunately the cures of the new Overworld feature doesn’t end there, clearly added to the game in order to implement the new “Random Encounters'' that are a blatant design choice to reduce the amount of quality content needed to fill the game world. These random encounters see the player put into a small handful of encounter maps fighting a smaller diversity in enemy types making this new feature a very unwelcome one. My time in Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands was spent on their “balanced” or normal difficulty which was anything but balanced, leaving many of their bosses and minions feeling super easy to mow down and as though I was never in any real threat. My recommendation to anyone choosing to pick up Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands over any of the other entries into the Borderlands series is to play this game on its hardest difficulty in order to have the most enjoyable experience. Despite my harsh criticism the feature that I’d like to commend Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands for is their new class system that sees the player choosing from one of six classes that each are a take on typical character tropes from Dungeons & Dragons, this feature removes the character selection from previous Borderlands games and offers the player more choice in the character they want to play, this feature reaches greater depths once the player unlocks the capability to “Multiclass” giving them the chance to pick up a second one of the six classes. I spent my time playing a combination of the Clawbringer and Spellshot that gave me access to the wyvern companion and later multiclassing into the Spellshot heavily boosted the usefulness of my spells which take the place of grenades from the games of old. This combination of classes really allowed me to feel increasingly stronger the further along each skill tree I found myself going down. Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands gunplay is one of its best features, this however is overshadowed by the fact that it is still the basic combat and gameplay loop that other Borderlands games that in the past were renowned for  and resulted in it once again leaning on that Borderlands crutch in an attempt to fight for relevance.To summarise, Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands never truly manages to find its way out of the shadow of its predecessors and ultimately suffers from its lack of identity, whilst a fun but short experience it struggles under the weight of expectation that comes with the territory of being a spin off of a widely beloved series. After the curtain fell on its lacklustre campaign I couldn’t help but feel as though Gearbox Software never truly gave Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands the love and attention it needed to truly flourish into the game it tried to be. I cannot in good faith recommend this game at its full asking price but do believe it’s a valuable pick up on a hefty discount and believe that despite its glaring flaws there is still a fun experience underneath to be had. During my time with Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands I couldn’t help but feel as though this should have and would have been a great DLC inclusion to a main line Borderlands game instead of the half baked solo release that we received. My harsh criticisms come from a place of wanting Gearbox to recapture the love and attention older Borderlands games had in spades and not succumb in putting out soulless releases that rely heavily on the legacy of older games that other studios have become guilty of mass producing. Ultimately I had fun with Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands but couldn’t shake the unbearable feeling that it could have been so much more.

_childDocuments_.review: It put almost 70 hours into this game playing it in 4 player co-op. This game is not perfect by any means but it improves in previous Borderlands games in a lot of tangible ways. My favourite improvement is the removal of vehicles. I HATED the vehicle sections in literally all the Borderlands games and I suspect I'm not the only one. This game knows the gunplay is the fun part of any BL game and just focuses on it and trims out the chaff. Changing grenades to spells and linking them a cooldown instead of a pickup is another good choice and helps eliminates the compulsion to never use your grenades. I've also found that this game is less annoying then other BL games. The story is kinda meh, but I've never cared about the story in BL games, but what I appreciate is thousands of lines of dialogue that get barked out while you do everything are at least fairly well written and voice acted. You will still get a lot of repeated vocal barks from npcs especially in the main hub city.The dlc seems like a cool idea at first, but I think I understand why everyone is downvoting them. They're too expensive for how short they are (they expect you to repeat them over and over to earn special reward currency but you start getting duplicate rewards after only three runs.)Like any BL game try to rope some friends into playing this with you. The core games lasts a good long time including maybe 10 or more hours after you hit max level. If you're on the fence (or you just need to buy 4 copies of the game so that your crew can play together) this game is an especially good value if you can nab it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Take the review with a bit of caution before buying the game. The Art/Graphics is really great, and world design is done well. Combat with the spells and guns are decently fun as well, although it can get a bit boring if you have bad weapons. But having cool spells/weapons can make the process go smoother. However this is my biggest issue with the game, the story/writing isn't that fun. I was really excited when I saw the trailer a while back, and liked Tiny Tina's over the top humor. But overall, I struggled to make myself progress further in the game. But since I enjoyed the combat, I ignored everything story-related and just went further. I forced myself to continue since I bought the game. If you're looking for something lighthearted, and popcorn-style gaming, and the game is on sale, you can try out this game. I wish Borderlands franchise can improve its writing and storytelling. I know it's supposed to be whacky and goofy and over the top, but even with that, it can be done better. Some jokes are funny. Some are cringy. Some are boring. I feel like Borderlands can do better if they focus more on the writing. Because the looter-shooter parts/ combat can be really fun, and that's where Borderlands shines.

It doesn't fill your pockets with legendaries, but also somehow only gives me a duplicate cosmetic on a nat 20 on dice that don't respawn and don't exist across characters. _childDocuments_.review: Meh. So I’ve put 80-odd hours into this and completed the campaign, so it must be good, right? Err well…yes and no. If you like Borderlands you’ll be OK with TTW. But the campaign is poor, there is little in the way of “Borderlands-style” humour and Tiny Tina is an acquired taste. As time went on, I found her voice increasingly grating. Best in small measures. Very small measures. The maps aren’t great. Some are really difficult to navigate. Not nearly enough fast travel points and/or vending machines – and the few that are there feel badly located. The loot drops are a bit rubbish too. I rarely found anything better than what I already had and - despite making real efforts to increase my “loot luck” score - I found that chests and enemies mostly dropped white, green and blue items – right up to and beyond the endgame. Purple drops were very rare. Orange drops were ridiculously rare. Saying that, the gear didn’t seem to matter that much, as I managed to complete the campaign with little trouble. I did make an awful lot of fast travel jumps back to the hub town of Brighthoof to sell useless loot. This got real tiresome. I also frequently encountered a bug whereby I couldn’t return to the area I had jumped from via the map because the fast travel point in that Zone was not selectable. This meant that I often had to return to an area via the Overworld – this got real tiresome. And on the World Map screen my cursor had a habit of flying way off the map for no apparent reason. Yeah…you guessed it…tiresome. The post-campaign “Chaos Chamber” stuff and the dlcs did nothing for me – tried them; didn’t see the point. They are both just extended inescapable “encounters” where you move through several areas killing bad guys who drop way-more mostly-useless loot than you could ever carry. Overall, I think TTW was a decent idea that was not terribly well implemented. Not enough TLC. Get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Tiny Tina's Wonderlands

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to be enjoyed about Tiny Tina's Wonderlands... unfortunately none of that is actually playing the game. This game backtracks from Borderlands play by introducing a hacky overworld map and a bunch of small arena encounters. It's got an all-star ensemble cast and has some really great moments... again unfortuntely none of them are actually *playing* the game. It feels like a dlc that could have been a side quest extended out into a full featured product by just bogging the game down with really simple mechanics and throwing as many of those simple encounters at you over and over again. I got this as part of Humble Choice which nets me regularly between 6-10 games and benefits charity, and played a few hours intent to watch a Let's play for the cutscenes to see this through to the end. _childDocuments_.review: So far game is fun and enjoyable. From hearing other reviews of the game being "Too short" but I do so where there's more time into the game.Sidequests. This game fleshes out sidequests more, whether you're helping an organization for their freedom with a funny acronym, helping an individual find love, or creating Forgery through... the other forgery... This game puts its emphasis more on exploring different things just as much as it does the main story, and with good rewards no less.As for the gameplay of the characters itself, without too much spoilers, Build flexibility is much more interesting in this game, and using spells instead of grenades feels much more diverse than previous borderland entries. The spells aren't just fun, they're good, and can have more than one purpose. They can do damage, plus heal, or give a damage bonus, or have a lingering effect. The same spell type can also be a variant, and not just because of element either, which is great. This isn't even regarding legendary types which also can be interesting.In the end, Game's great. People who complain about price tag probably forget what the other borderlands were like on immediate release, or don't understand that this game isn't meant to bolt through just the main story to actually enjoy the whole game. _childDocuments_.review: Since Steam forces us to either give a thumbs up or down I am going with the "no". Let me explain. The game looks gorgeous. The artistry on display reinforced by the Unreal engine makes this game the best looking in the Franchise. But (you knew this was coming) that is the best thing about the game. And when the visuals are the best thing in a Looter-Shooter you know something is not right. The "bazillion guns" that drop make it arbitrary if you really want to waste your time comparing stats when you will find one that is ever so slightly better just around the corner. I stopped caring altogether and just sold everything without ever looking at them. Ever so often I would take new one after leveling up a few levels but it was not really enganging wich brings me to my second problem. The enemies are just as arbitrary. The vast majority of enemies don't require you to tackle them differently. Basically all of them can be killed by spamming them with bullets and your special skills. Those could be interesting but they aren't because you just don't have any reason to refine them. And the skill tree is a smoke screen. They split them in multiple parts and sell them as extra classes which might feel like more but if you compare it with BL2 they just split them up and made them smaller and in direct comparison not remotely as interesting. Minor stats changes don't affect your playstyle and major new abilities are very rare and disappointing me more often than not.What made BL2 click for me just is not present here and it is really hard to pin down. Lots of quality of life stuff is missing, odd decisions like the names of your friends being just that bit too large on screen are annoying. The total overload of effects make strategic play absolutely impossible (not that you would need to) and the story is okay. The voice actors do a good job and the writing is okay but a far cry from being memorable like BL2. The tons ob side missions do almost nothing for the main story and you forget what it's all about constantly. The many cameos of characters from the other games are undercooked and feel like lame fan service.All in all, the sum of its parts leave me mostly indifferent. I stopped interacting with most of the systems like skill tree, weapon selection, listening to the story since none of it matters much since the core gameplay loop is just so plain. So, If I could, I would give it a neutral "meh" instead of the thumbs down. It is just not interesting enough for a recommendation and just not bad enough for a "stay away" warning. It is okay if you really do not have anything else which should be impossible these days.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay: 8/10Total Content: 4/10Visuals: 8/10Audio: 8/10Story: 6/10Hilariously overpriced, microscopic DLC that aren't worth your time or money.Very nice visuals and theme, with great voice work, as with the rest of the franchise. Tiny Tina is always a great character to have around, even if I have some issues with how her story plays out. The gunplay is fantastic, borrowing from BL3 and changing up the gameplay with the introduction of "spells" in place of your normal grenades. This combined with the multi-classing feature gives you some room to play around with different setups. The story is also a bit better than that of BL3's base game, especially if you enjoy Tina as a character. Loot is just as fun to find and play with as ever, with a bunch of really unique options on both guns and gear. The main positive for me is the ability for them to pull from any DND or related RPG themes for potential DLC, which gives them freedom to make nearly anything in the future.The game is disappointing for many reasons. To start, there's a completely un-skippable, fairly lengthy tutorial, which is just annoying if you intend to play more than 1 character. You'll immediately notice that while the overworld is a cool idea, there's no point to it existing, and it feels like a clever way of hiding a lack of actual world design. You have tons of Pokemon-esque world encounters that randomly spring on you, but you can just ignore them with a click, so there's not really much point to them. Traversing this overworld is also a pain, as you walk pretty slowly, and the map navigation/fast-travel system in the game is very poorly designed. The map in general needs a lot of work if I'm being honest, as it's clumsy and hard to read at times, and annoying to adjust. You do get some variation in levels, but be prepared to play EXTREMELY similar maps over, and over, and over again throughout the campaign. While the multi-class customization is nice, you only get 1 talent tree per class, as opposed to the 4 per character in BL3, and the 3 per character in the other games. This makes you feel a bit restricted in total variety, as you really only have 1 or 2 viable setups per main class. (STORY SPOILERS) Story-wise, there's literally no reason for us to be tackling the main plot point of Tina's abandonment issues and trauma, as these were addressed in the Dragon Keep DLC for Borderlands 2 and presumably already resolved. It is a touching story and fairly well-written in a vacuum, but it feels like we're re-treading the same story beats for no reason instead of exploring something new, which is a recurring theme in this game. While Tina is my second favorite character in the franchise, just below Handsome Jack, I really don't feel like this game does anything substantial for her character, and it doesn't provide any growth that wasn't already there.There's also an appalling lack off endgame content, and this is my biggest gripe with this game, along with the pricing. The total runtime for the game seems to be between 10-20 hours, possibly more if you really want to go out of your way to get every collectible. This isn't that bad, but considering most of this is filler, it's underwhelming at best for a full-priced game. Once you've beaten the campaign, literally the ONLY thing you will be doing from then on is the Chaos Chamber. The Chaos Chamber is a roguelike mode where you get teleported between levels you've played through in the campaign to clear for rewards, with increasing difficulty and some minor enemy variation. This gets boring very, very quickly, I'd say after about 5-6 runs. Now keep in mind that to max out, you have to clear up to level 50 at the time I'm writing this review, gaining a level every time you successfully clear the challenge run. This is a huge time sink with no real reward except for higher changes for the same loot, only slightly stronger, which is incredibly disappointing. Now we have to talk about the DLCs and pricing, which are nothing short of shameless, embarrassingly bad money-grubbing. There are currently 4 "FLCs", each of which are $10 and can be completed in around 15 minutes. This is a total of $40 for around an hour worth of content. All of these COMBINED would not be worth $10, especially when compared to the quality and quantity of content offered by DLCs in any of the other games. All of these FLCs, plus another small (1-hour-ish) DLC would probably be worth $15 if it was all of decent quality. There simply is nowhere near enough content to justify these having a price tag at all, as they're effectively worse versions of headhunter packs from BL2. The content inside each mirror is effectively the same thing; clear 4 "wings" to open a boss room and kill the boss. Then you're done, just like that. I cannot recommend strongly enough that you save your money and avoid the FLCs/Season Pass at all costs. As a massive fan of the Borderlands franchise, this games deserves to be so much better than it is, with as much support and content as BL2 or BL3 received in their lives. Unfortunately, this is simply not the case, and no amount of pretending will change that. The core of the game is extremely solid, with great gameplay and a decent story, but the lack of content combined with the terrible pricing just drags this game down. Get the base game on sale if you can, but under no circumstances should you ever pay any money for the FLCs or the Season Pass, which is a scam. I initially gave this a tentative positive review, but after ANOTHER FLC which was microscopic AND time-gated, as well as an update that did nothing but give us more boring chaos levels, I'm confidently saying this game is going nowhere, and I cannot recommend it to anyone. Save your money, do not preorder, and wait for reviews to come in before buying another Gearbox title in the future. This has shown a flagrant disregard for the customer's time, money, and love for the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Short: It is not as bad as Borderlands 3 because one can go into the settings and disable all voice and subtitles, completing missions is just a question of following the blue marker.Buy heavily discounted, be aware DLC is worthless.The gameplay itself is mechanically solid (same as in BL3), map design is much better than BL3 IMHO, however it suffers from many of the same flaws as BL3. There so much stuff going on in the screen all at once that you get killed dozens of times and have no clue what is that killed you. You will die many times right after a level has been cleared or a boss defeated because you will step in a pool of some goo that in a second will eat your shield and your health, doesn't matter how high they are.As with every borderlands game one gun category is rendered useless this time around is shotguns, save the ones that fire bombs or swords 99% are useless. I finished the game just using smgs, pistols and assault rifles, bazookas, snipers and as mentioned shotguns are useless. The loot, there is so much of it that is rendered irrelevant, you find a decent gun level 20 and you can carry it to level 30 discarding 1000 guns in the way, eventually you need to replace it because it becomes a peashooter, when you replace it you won't replace it with a better gun, just whatever you find that can make a dent in the enemy's health just because it is a higher level weapon. All the enchantments and status effects, hero trees, etc, all amount to a huge mess that becomes bothersome quickly, I couldn't bother to look at it proper.The sound effects are decent, the music is non-existent, is elevator quality at best.It is a 25/30h mid game buy only heavily discounted. I'm not excited for more Borderlands games anymore, it is clear Gearbox doesn't understand what made BL1 and BL2 fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Something about Borderlands 3 felt hateful. The villains were awful, the story and sidequests felt mean spirited to the point of joylessness and I paradoxically played most of it listening to podcasts as a way to get away from it. The gunplay and gameplay was fun but the only time I actually enjoyed the experience was during DLC2 when I got to explore a cosmic haunted village in the snow with a cast of halfway likable characters.Wonderlands is SUCH an improvement.+ No driving keep the levels tight and fun to explore.+ Fantasy aesthetic and enemies really hit the spot and feel lovingly crafted.+ Overworld was a great idea and improved pacing.+ The tabletop gimmick allowed the Gearbox humor to land. Characters talking about the grizzly twists of their campaign stories is so much more enjoyable than the oppressive negativity of Borderlands 3. I don't think I chuckled once during BL3 and Wonderands had me laugh out loud every couple of hours.+ Sidequests were substantial and I got surprisingly invested in many of them.Endgame is admittedly pretty rough.- DLC 1-4 are pretty awful, essentially just new skins for Chaos Chambers.- Endgame just isn't compelling. It's been said 500 million times but they need to include a repeatable NG+ with random overworld events to give occasional reprieve to the Chaos Chamber grind. The campaign is great and absolutely the most I've ever enjoyed Borderlands and it's shocking they cut you off from it once you finish it.I'll probably play it less hours than BL3 but I actually enjoyed myself this time. Hope they continue at this level.

_childDocuments_.review: For character building, this title has been my favorite entry to the Borderlands games. The Borderlands style RPG elements are greatly enhanced by the dual class system, allowing you to create tons of builds to your own liking. Having spells instead of nades was surprisingly fun, and even then you don't have to use them specifically to feel strong, they're mainly another option you can focus your build on.It's a fun (for me mostly co-op) experience up to a point, and then starts to drop off quickly, mostly because you can't replay the story like in other Borderlands entries, and because raid bosses are locked behind the chaos chamber, a rogue-like mode that is all endgame there is. You can try out all kinds of builds, and as always there's tons of weapons to choose from. With how rewarding the chaos chamber is, you can quickly farm whatever legendary you want. It even allows you to target specific weapon types and accessories. But the only content you can really do is the chaos chamber, and the DLCs, but they aren't really that different to the chaos chamber. I was hoping the DLCs would be a nice addition to the endgame, but they're designed as these mini dungeons you have to progress through to get to a raid boss. None of them add any story, either.Speaking of, the story definitely needed more time. Without spoiling too much, the main story is surprisingly short, and doesn't really explore its possibilities. It's not bad, but it did make me feel like there should be more. The collectible scrolls, and to some degree the poems, added some nice lore at least. As for the side quests, they were in typical Borderlands fashion some hit, some miss, but overall mostly enjoyable.The addition of collectible loot dice to increase loot luck is a really cool idea. In general, having more collectibles made me explore each area more, making me notice some cool details I would've missed otherwise. I should also mention that the loot dice never made me feel like I was missing out on loot when not getting them, so if you don't like hunting collectibles you shouldn't really care too much.One last thing I wanna mention is how nice the areas are. The hub town feels like an actual town, while the shops are still reasonably spaced. Definitely was a step up for me from the other Borderlands hubs. The areas in general felt very in tune with the part of the story (and side stories) they were telling, and were nicely designed. There are always a few secret paths to uncover, almost always rewarding you with either a collectible or a loot chest. The overworld board is neat. Since it's not on the path of the main story I definitely recommend checking out Tangledrift.tl;dr: Character building great. Area design good. Story not bad, but disappointing. Endgame lacking, at least gear grind is fast. Don't buy DLCs unless heavily discounted.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR For a post DLC completed game experience, the amount of bugs and issues present is unacceptable. If I had paid full price for this game I'd want my money back. Buy it on sale and enjoy the gameplay.I'll keep this brief as yeah, I do intend to complete the game but not in the sense I did former Borderlands titles by finding the best gear doing all the quests etc. This game is held up by its gameplay for me. If that wasn't fun, honestly I would have refunded it and tried to find a different game for my buddy and I to play. To put it simply, this game is pretty buggy, even moreso than any Borderlands title I've played in the past. They range from complete game crashes, graphical issues minor and major, sound issues minor and major, desync issues, a few of them requiring complete restarts after booting up the game. The gameplay is fun enough to be willing to tolerate these to a degree. Some of the other issues come with the maps design and the existence of certain invisible walls in places they really shouldn't be and some not being in places they should. The worst bug I found is in the magical bean quest area. There's a completely random spot on the map that if you "superhero slide" into it, you just die. The other part, I'm not one for politics in games, left or right unless it's a proper fit to the overall story and really is setting a deep tone of some kind or whatever the case may be. I will say seeing pronouns on the character creation screen had me a little leery and it was rightfully so. Now it isn't that they push themes too harshly or anything but it's just the writing in this game isn't flavorful or really all that good. The lack of wordplay for innuendo and overly crude humor just for the sake of it gets old really really fast. They just don't land, the characters aren't going to be memorable from this game. It's carried solely by Tina so far. If you just want the combat from Borderlands, it's here 100% and it's good. The rest of the game is most likely going to be forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: Since the end of Battleborn, I've been growing less and less enthused about Gearbox products. I thought BL:TPS was fine(mostly cause it did a decent job of making Jack the villain he would become). But BL3, and now this...I just think Gearbox has lost the ideas it had before. TTWL is a game with a lot of memory for what made Borderlands appealing....but very little of what made it FUN. I'm not gonna touch on the DLC issues, because I'm reviewing the whole product that I got for $40. But I can cerrtainly understand the frustrations others may have had for ponying up $120 for this as a pre-order....which is why I didn't. TECHNICAL DIFFICULTIESFrom a technical standpoint, TTWL is a decent game. There's a fair few visual splendor moments, the game runs....mostly above 60 on my machine, though there are moments where it just stops dead in its tracks and I think the game crashed for about five seconds before it picks back up. And certain locations just drag the game to sub-30 frames. I'm not running a bleeding edge machine, so I can give it some credit, but the two glitches combined, leave me wondering if there's some kind of memory sink that just isn't gonna be fixed in the game. ART STYLEIt's Borderlands. If you know it, you know it's the same style that is just getting up-rezzed more and more. It's not bad, but it's also not memorable. For me personally, I find the abundance of sparkles and glitter a little annoying, but I don't really slam it for that; this is supposed to be an RPG of sorts, so yeah, that should be a part of it. But the game has a tremendous amount of visual noise. It loves to throw light shows into everything, making trying to find the dark green monster against the dark green background, and next to the slightly lighter dark green monster annoying. SOUNDAgain, it's Borderlands. While the story is okay, and Arnett, Burch and the BL voice actors do a good job of narrating it, it's still just a lot of pew-pew, boom-boom sound effects. You're not going to find the next soundscape here. GAMEPLAYAnd we at last come to WHY I'm writing this review....the gameplay is horribly unbalanced. Maybe the game is meant to be played multiplayer. I've played BL1, 2, TPS, 3 and almost all the DLC for all three, and never have I felt so both underpowered, and beholden as a "Fatemaker" playing alone. I'll start with the smallest of sins: you can't really skip the narration when leveling and progressing the main story. You CAN skip the cutscenes(which ironically are better)...but after listening to the same pedantic story told again and again by floating pictures on screen so I can be allowed to see the next checkpoint or push he next button, I got bored REAL fast. Usually when one of the long ones start, I just go get myself a drink or surf online, and let the game run in the background. Dying doesn't really affect you, so you don't lose anything, and the game won't progress until you X the macguffin. But if you're making a story you can't interact with that also gets dull like a chainsaw made out of recycled paper, a skip option would be nice. From what I understand, modding the game by removing the some of the .pak files nixes the story in full. Take that as my commentary on the story's engagement: people found a way to literally tear the story out of the game, so they weren't bored to tears.Combat is again...Borderlands. Nothing you will see here, is new or groundbreaking. If you've played anything prior to TPS...you know what you're getting. The multiclass system really isn't. You know your Moze/Axton/Roland build or your Amara/Maya/Lilith Build. And Critical Damage, of course, is still king of all builds. It's still making numbers change in different ways. The bosses during the story, are pushovers for the most part. Some are nice looking, others just blend into the background. But Chaos Levels basically break the game. After beating the game, you unlock Chaos Mode(Mayhem Mode or UVHM for those who are already yawning about this) You can then run a randomized set of instances, with a few bosses thrown into the mix. But here, the devs decided to swing balance well out of the player's control. SOULSBORNE games don't have the grind of some fights in Chaos Mode. A perfect example is Dry'l. In the game, your damage can outpace his shield healing fairly quickly. It makes him among the toughest fights during the story that you'll face, memorable, but not insanely difficult.....In Chaos Mode, that changes. Dry'l's shield will INSTANTLY regenerate from nothing to almost full, every 45 seconds. So if you don't have a finely tuned lightning damage focused build that can do (infinity x million)^2 damage, you're stuck with a boss you won't ever damage after phase 1. This kind of boss fight is rife throughout Chaos Mode. Another is the Eros Wyvern, who flies around a stage, and shotgun-blasts AoE damage shots that ALSO regen their THREE health bars. If you get hit by one pellet, I'd say it gets 1/6th of a health bar back. You can't freeze them, you can't really poison them, you can't focus on them, and you have to play pillar-peekaboo to avoid the regen effect. There are fights where a main enemy is just wholly immune, or can't be reached by your build(Melee players know this one all too well), or has some insane catchup mechanic. it robs the game of any kind of challenge. To be clear, challenge is setting a clear, understandable goal before you, and providing the means and tools to achieve that goal. This isn't challenge, this is trying to ape the ways of From Software and call it original. I'm not personally a fan of Souls-like games, and when I realized that is what TTWL is ultimately, I stopped playing and started writing. FINAL JUDGEMENTI think Gearbox has become another developer that's trying to ride the coattails of past greatness. So fixated on recreating the magic of BL2,  Gearbox can no longer see anything but ways to repackage that game with more modern visuals or ideas....note that I said more MODERN...not BETTER. TTWL is the game to get if your Borderlands themed bedroom still had three square feet of uncovered wall, and you just couldn't take it anymore. In the broad strokes, it's another Borderlands game....that was new and exciting a decade ago. Today, it's just a relic of big gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: NB: I've been increasingly disappointed with Borderlands games since the first one, so if you generally enjoy them, you might have a completely different perspective.I don't think anyone would be confused by the fact that this game isn't called "Borderlands", but just to be extra sure: yes, this is most definitely a Borderlands game. It has the same basic gameplay, the same structure, the same kind of story, the same brand of humor. The only real differences are that the player characters aren't *actual* characters anymore and are instead fully customizable, that there are no vehicles, the grenades are replaced with magic spells, and there are now different melee weapons and "armor". Otherwise it's pretty much the same game.It doesn't even look all that different visually: despite being fantasy, it still has the same not-quite-cel-shaded appearance, you mostly pick up guns that look almost exactly the same as in other entries to the series (except some of them now have bow parts), and you fight some very familiar-looking and behaving enemies (though in the interest of fairness there are some fresh-ish additions).Since I doubt that a lot of people would expect anything from the story of this game, I'll be brief: the story is a mess. The writers try to go for something meta with the villain, include banter between both the characters in the Borderlands setting and the in-universe Wonderlands setting, and have some fun in the process with the D&D-type setting, but stumbled on pretty much every step to the point that even stuff that you'd think would be basic is unclear. If the "Newbie", i.e., your character, is playing with two other people, where are their characters in-game? Why do they keep talking as if they have any impact on the events? And if they do, why would the villain never address them? What was the villain's plan, anyway? None of this would really be clear by the end.One more thing that is related to writing before I move on: the jokes in this entry make my soul shrivel and die every time. They're the most shallow, often hopelessly outdated kind of referential humor, only sometimes connected with the premise of the game. It often feels like a Friedberg and Seltzer type of movie, not helped by the fact that at least one of the "jokes" in this game actually did appear in the infamous Epic Movie (2007).In terms of gameplay, at least at the time of this review the game feels incredibly unpolished, even compared to the other games in the series. The maps can be hard to navigate (some are three-dimensional, and one has portals to complicate matters even further) and have a lot of invisible walls and odd level geometry, there are some pretty serious buggy interactions between items and skills, etc.Perhaps the biggest issue with the gameplay, however, is the wildly inconsistent difficulty. With the exception of one particular boss, every boss fight in this game was a complete joke, some not even managing to finish their introductory monologue before getting killed. Even the final boss barely lasted two minutes. Meanwhile, battles with normal enemies can be anything from a breeze to a chore to a complete nightmare depending solely on which types of enemies you're fighting and seemingly no other reason.Most of all, this game feels lazy. The credit sequence starts with an apology that the development was difficult due to COVID, but I don't think that can explain every problem this game ended up having and every choice that was made. About half the gameplay is done in the form of "Encounters", fights with enemies spawning out of thin air with no real explanation or reason in small combat arenas (that are repeated for each of the four main areas of the overworld map). The DLC follows the same structure, but even the main game isn't all that much better: one tiny, but illustrative example is that the levels are full of impassable black voids out of which the enemies arrive, when the previous games in the series usually at least had put enough care into this to put doors or something like that there. And this kind of laziness is felt throughout everything.All in all, I would only recommend this if you're really, REALLY jonesing for more Borderlands, no matter the quality.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy a game with first-person shooting, dungeon quest crawling, and item looting—you can get your kick by playing  While I’ve enjoyed watching this  franchise grow, TTW has its flair by incorporating tabletop functions, heavily verbose characters, and a right mix of goth and sparkle themes in its gameplay.It is not best to purchase with its original pricing since other better FPS loot games could offer better gameplay at their original price. But it is best to get a 70% discount—and, at the very least, get the main storyline. If you aim to get a complete Steam Achievement, the four quests are “cash locked” via four separate DLCs.Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands caters to players with varying levels of FPS experience. Whether you prefer rifles, SMGs, grenade launchers, melee weapons, or ward shields, there's a playstyle to suit you. The game offers diverse gameplay options with seven unique classes, including the Brr-Zerker and Clawbringer for melee enthusiasts and the Spellshot for those who enjoy a balance of gun skill and spell barrage. The ultimate goal in TTW is to complete the challenging dungeon quests and acquire better loot. This can be achieved by revisiting previously finished dungeons or exploring the four purchasable DLCs, adding depth and longevity to the game.  You are assigned as the Fatemaker who will change Brighthoof’s fate, as played through the “Bunkers and Badasses” tabletop game. As the game progresses, the tabletop characters (primarily the Dragon Lord) decide to take matters into their own hands, shifting how Tina (the tabletop’s Dungeon Master) plays the game. Tangential side quests also provide leverage on the overall storyline—by unveiling how improper tabletop gaming (in real life) could somehow create a sense of disillusionment on the game’s “pawns” (in this case, the characters build within the imaginary sense of Tina). Tina’s infantile, over-the-top reaction could not be for everyone’s kind of gameplay. It’s one of the drawbacks of this game—you may want to mute the dialogue because Tina and the rest of the tabletop players could talk a lot—like The  franchise heavily inspires the graphics—the dark and sharp black strokes give the 3D animation a cartoon feel. The visuals of the different regions are a sight to behold—there are times that I couldn’t stop using the Photo Mode function because it is just too majestic. The music is fine—I couldn’t appreciate it a lot because of the heavily condensed narration—the music could no longer be heard. However, walking alone in Brighthoof and other Fast Travel areas is excellent. It's not an entirely  moment, but at least the music fits the scenery. The end-game progression, also known as the , is striking but needs to be more varied (especially if you already acquired the Ascended-tier items). You can finally test your character’s acquired gear by fighting higher-tier enemies. It is heavily inspired by Borderland’s looting system (procedurally generated loot), which means a higher-tier enemy can improve the odds of dropping an Ascended gear (the highest quality). TTW’s additional DLCs  are unnecessary. They cost 20 to 30 minutes of new gameplay, which is not worth its hefty price tag. But if you’re a Steam Achievement completionist and want to try out Vesper’s Mirror of Mystery, you can include this in your collection. It's also one of the reasons why I can’t give it a solid 9 out of 10 rating.The  DLC can give you a more comprehensive array of equipment options; it is the only DLC I could recommend. The  is the worst DLC offer, as it could only give you a gold tint to your armor—and TONS of better color options are available within the game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you look at this game as very expansive DLC for Borderlands 3, under the assumption you enjoy Borderlands 3, you'll likely enjoy this game — if you're not sold on the hack n' slash genre but with guns and the camera being first person instead of being isometric, stay very far away form this game.• Melee weapons are now loot, they have weapon manufacturers and are no longer tied to specific characters.• Grenades are replaced by spells and no longer act as a consumable but are rather recharged by a cooldown period.• There's a lot of customization up front for your hero, voice, appearance, class etc. • Guardian Rank is replaced by Mythic Rank.• Your character has an actual stat sheet; dexterity, strength, wisdom, all that good stuff. This is in addition to the traditional skill tree that Borderlands characters have.• There's an overworld map that has dungeons, random encounters that can be explored, as opposed to a HUB city. (Which is still present.)And that's pretty much it. The gun manufacturers, should you have developed a favorite by now, have slightly different names from the mainline Borderlands' games. Jakobs is now Blackpowder and Dahl is now Dahlia for example. All in some vaguely humorous attempt to create a more  setting.The entire game is based on the  popular Borderlands 2 DLC “Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep”. I was never that fond of that DLC: I'm still pondering if that is due to me not liking the  Tiny Tina character, not generally enjoying  fantasy settings or the fact that they tried to jam an ostensibly sci-fi theme into a fantasy setting, just for sake of it. These reviews are for sharing your opinion and whether or not you'd  that someone  purchase and play a specific title. And for that I would say, if you enjoy Borderlands, buy this on sale. There's really nothing worth full price here. Don't get me wrong, there are some  ideas in this game that are just poorly executed. If you're on the fence, just skip it.I do see it as a stepping stone for Borderlands 4 or whatever they call the next mainline Borderlands. More customization is always good, maybe one day they'll make a DLC package that suits everyone's desires but this one leaves a lot to be desired.My other Borderlands reviews:• Borderlands 3 review • Borderlands 1 GOTY Enhanced review • Borderlands: Pre-Sequel review

This is a covid game that was released, and not really expected to do as well as it did. So there hasn't really been updates or extra content beyond the really poor DLC. Character appearance customisation needed extra options because there are literally 16 different hair styles and most of them suck. It feels half-produced in this department.It's still a really fun game. You pick a base class and you can mix and match with another to create an ungodly amount of combinations to customise your character. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - 8/10 - Keeps the gameplay improvements from Borderlands 3 and combines them with a lukewarm story that won't piss you off, but also won't wow you. Not bad. Enjoyable, but not a must play.And now, the longer review you will almost certainly not read...GAMEPLAYJust like Borderlands 3, the actual gameplay in Wonderlands is fantastic. It features all the QOL improvements of the previous title (like damage scaling so that you can play with anyone at any level, sliding, and not getting stuck on every single little piece of map geometry) and combines them with some new D&D-esque mechanics and the chaos chamber, which operates like a randomized dungeon arena.STORYTELLING, CHARACTERS, AND HUMORThe story is an improvement over Borderlands 3, but this is very much not a game to be recommended for its story. Most of the time it feels very lukewarm, not pissing me off, but not wowing me either. Exceptions are any quest involving Mr. Torgue or Claptrap , the Pirate Words scroll, seducing the door, and Peasant-Ass Peasant. Like almost every Borderlands game, the jokes are very much hit or miss. The characters are often referential jokes, and they are also very much hit or miss.GLITCHES AND BUGSHad a bug where the game would freeze for about 20 seconds once after launching and spawning in a map, but that may have been due to my graphics settings. I never did look into trying to fix it. Mildly annoying more than anything. Also had the game crash twice without error message and without warning. Once in the middle of a chaos chamber I had reached the final boss of. Kept my gold and everything I got up to that point, but I was still pissed because I wanted to finish the chamber. That seems to have been due to graphics settings because I lowered them and didn't have a crashing issue after that.SEASON PASSI'm not buying it at this time. It seems overpriced for what you get.OVERALLI did enjoy the game and I do recommend it, especially if there's a sale. I feel like I got my money's worth. Gameplay is great. Story is mostly eh, but it didn't piss me off.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright. Tiny Tina's Wonderlands is done and dusted. This was definitely a step up from the Prequel, BL3, and Assault on Dragon Keep, which were all subpar for various reasons (although I actually did enjoy the Prequel alright).I would like to start by noting that this game doesn't want to let you go. When you finish the story, you immediately begin the epilogue, which features Chaos runs, which are effectively challenge runs with debuffs added to make them more challenging. The game really, really wants you to play these, lol.Anyway, the campaign is an epic run through Tina's tabletop session where she is Gamemaster. But, the antagonist goes rogue, defying Gamemaster Tina; and you, Newbie, run through the campaign helping people out on the way to defeating the antagonist and restoring order to the Wonderlands.This is represented by increasingly unhinged and insane scenarios, lol. Which are by and large a lot of fun. That said, by around hour twenty, I was ready to start skipping side quests and dungeons in favor of wrapping up the main story.If you've played any Borderlands games, you already know the deal. It's immature, with nonstop jokes and meta, has faced paced and incredibly tight battles and gameplay, interesting level design, fantastic graphics, and stellar voice acting.Where this game deviates from the standard BL format is by including an Overland map (think tabletop world map), quick dungeons, and a mix of quests that happen in the Overland map and in the individual areas.It was stellar on the Steam Deck, where the default settings provided a mostly consistent 60 FPS and required no tweaks to play. It was obviously a battery hog, and I found I'd get just a little more than an hour on full charge. I did play plugged in mostly, but be aware that your battery life will be limited.There was an occasional stuttering, but beyond that, there were no issues to report.I don't think I would've actually bought this game given how much I did not enjoy BL3 and AoDK, but since it was in a Humble Choice, I was able to give it a try, and all in all, I'm glad I did. This was a legitimately fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: i'm enjoying this more than BL3. I think the art team in particular were reinvigorated to be working on something that wasn't more post apocalyptic desert landscape. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but as someone who's never been a big BL fan, I think TTW hits the spot in ways the other games fail to. It's world building is fun (and literally world building at some points) and it never gets to be too old or grindy. It's a charming game with a lot of replay value due to the classes and ways to play that feel so different. While Tiny Tina's Wonderlands might not win Game of the Year or create some massively difficult world with bosses you run your face against 100 times, it does create a nostalgia blast that feels... refreshing.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, i loved borderlands 2 and 3, and the gameplay is great in wonderlands too, but the changes to farming were really quite bad. I like the lucky dice thing wonderlands has going for it where you find dice to increase your loot luck but other than that the experience has been pretty negative for me. The class systems were also interesting, compared to playing different characters as in previous titles.But that's really all the good things i can say for Wonderlands:The encounter system was novel and fun for a bit, but considering that you will spend a most percentage of time (especially in the late/end game) just going through encounters, it get really old after a bit.Having no dedicated drops for non-legendary uniques means if you find a good and fun non-legendary unique, you have to start farming vending machines.Having different tiered loot (the Chaotic/Volatile/Primordial/Ascended) loot is nice and handles tier-ing of loot much better than OP levels and Mayhem levels in my opinion. The problem is unlocking each tier of loot, where you have to run through the Chaos Chambers more than 30 times (if i remember correctly) to reach the max chaos level is frustrating.Farming the DLC items is even worse, the content is fine (just fine, not great), but then to just go to the Wheel of Fate and pressing E and praying to get the loot you want is not fun at all. I'd rather be killing bosses and getting loot rather than pressing one button to get loot.It's also disappointing that the best way to farm certain items is just to run through the chaos chambers and pray to the bunnies that you get what you want too. Again its gameplay followed by lull where you just have to press a button for a bit.As someone who spent 1k+ hours in BL2 and 500+ hours in BL3 (would have been more but Epic launcher glitched out my account for a long time), i've reached a 100 hours in this game but i don't see myself playing that much more of this. IMO if you want to play borderlands, go get BL1 or 2 or 3, and only this title if you really are desperate for more borderlands.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, long time Borderlands fan here. I've put over 200 hours into this game on PS5 and completed the main story three times, so I know the story and the end game pretty well. Let me start this review by saying the base game here is really good. The game play and the story are both great - aside from the odd story character I found to be weirdly handled...The story is several steps up from that mess in BL3. Is it on par with BL2? I wouldn't say so, but it's still great in its own right. Definitely a worthy continuation of the Dragon's Keep DLC. The main bad guy is surprisingly well set up. I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone that played BL2 and the Dragon's Keep DLC just for the story.The game play is very similar to BL3, in all the right ways in my opinion. The movement feels good, not like the awkward rigid movement in BL2, and the new spell system makes for a lot of fun. Spells replace grenades in this game, so while you technically have infinite ammo, you are restricted by the cool down (in most cases) so you can't spam all your grenades/spells to instantly clear a zone. The spells do make for much more varied play styles though, so I think they're a great addition.Playable characters now have voice lines and actually interact with the world in unique and interesting ways depending on your character's personality. The character customisation here is far better than any BL game previously, and offers a respectable level of customisation. My only wish would be the ability to transmog armour. Armour replaces Class Mods from previous BL games, Amulets replace Relics/Artifacts, and new Rings (you can equip up to two) also act like additional Relics/Artifacts. This is a decent change, and makes sense. Wards also replace shields, and function exactly the same as shields from BL3, for example. I like all of these changes.I also like the new hero point and myth rank systems. Hero points are like additional skill points you can use to increase crit damage, crit chance, spell cooldown, etc. Myth rank is basically like BAR from BL2. Both are great. The level cap is currently 40, so a little lower than the max level of 50 in BL2's base game. Although you do unlock your action skill at level two, so you don't lose out on as many points as you'd expect. I expect this to get increased in future though.The actual classes you can choose, however, leave something to be desired. Currently, the Spellshot is by far the most powerful class, and there's not really much point going with anything else. Spellshot + Stabbomancer seems to be the meta for most end game builds, and it's easy to see why. It would be nice if the other classes got some buffs to put them on par, or at least close to, the power of the Spellshot - in their own respective ways (I'm not saying Clawbringer should be able to deal as much spell damage as the Spellshot, for example).The new split class system is also a bit of a double edged sword too, I think. On one hand, it means players only have to level up half as many characters, which is great for more casual players that want to try every character. On the other hand, it makes which class you choose less impactful since their short comings can be offset by choosing an appropriate secondary class. Moreover, combining two classes which compliment each other in unique ways makes for an unbalanced end game - like Spellshot + Stabbomancer using Double Knot and From The Shadows. More character balance is definitely needed in my opinion.The guns also leave something to be desired. The vast majority of legendary weapons feel underwhelming, in terms of damage dealt, special effects, and cool factor. BL2 and 3 had some awesome legendaries... The Monarch/Dictator, Unkempt Harold, Slagga, Conference Call, etc. This game doesn't have anything that comes even close to any of those. In fact, a lot of regular (i.e. non-unique) blue/purple weapons outperform many legendaries. That should not be the case. This is made worse by the fact that legendaries are rarer in this game compared to BL3 (although more common than in BL2). So getting legendaries is harder than in BL3, and they also perform worse. That doesn't make for a fun game play experience.Melee weapons have also been added to this game, and they actually add a lot to the experience. Legendary melee weapons (unlike the majority of legendary guns) offer really cool benefits over their lesser rarity counterparts, and can change how you play the game. This is a really fun change. However, don't expect to be running any melee only builds because there are a lot of flying enemies you can't melee - plus a lot of bosses that also can't be melee'd (like... why?). That being said, I'm glad they're in the game, even if the developers seem to forget that sometimes when they're designing bosses.The end game consists of Chaos Chambers - dungeon style encounters which allow you to unlock Chaos Levels (mayhem levels from BL3). This is actually pretty fun at first, but due to lack of variety, tedious farming in the final loot chamber, and over reliance on farming Chaos Chambers for loot, they quickly become uninteresting. Spending 15 minutes doing a run and then another 15 minutes (or probably more) sorting through loot in the final loot room is not my idea of a fun time. They have made efforts to improve this experience by adding vending machines in the final room, but it still feels like a chore to slog through a Chaos Chamber. This is made worse by the fact that they keep raising the maximum Chaos level. I thought 20 was fine. It was pretty hard, but not punishing. Then they upped it to 35, and destroyed build diversity because it was so difficult. Now it's 50. I haven't taken the time to get to Chaos Level 50, but I don't imagine it's going to be fun. There are now more Chaos levels than actual levels... And you don't get skill points for increasing your Chaos level. You don't get anything. You get tougher enemies and a chance for slightly more powerful loot to drop in the form of Chaotic/Volatile/Primordial/Ascended loot. Great...Now for my biggest gripe with this game - aside from the current state of Chaos Chambers. The "first season pass." Firstly, I find the idea of a game having multiple season passes offensive already. Was my £55 initial payment not enough? You need another £50 in the form of two additional season passes? Really? Insulting... Not to mention the fact that the first DLC came out less than a month after the release of the actual game, so they were surely working on it before the game was released and decided not to include it in the base game... and it came out with bugs which they only just recently fixed by the way (shark enemies with missing names, for example). This whole things stinks of corporate greed, and I hate it. As for the DLCs themselves, well, they're trash. They're basically just additional Chaos Chambers you pay extra for. Yes, it's pretty nice that once you complete one of these DLCs their rooms and bosses get added to the Chaos Chamber rotation, but they're still ultimately more monotonous Chaos Chambers.Why no story DLCs? BL2 had some of the best story DLCs ever. This game is literally a spin off from one of BL2's DLCs. It seems like after BL2 you guys forgot how to make good DLC. BL3 had a similar problem with seemingly lazy DLC content churned out. The only reason to buy any BL3 or Wonderlands DLCs is for the powerful loot you guys put in them. Other than that, they hardly deserve to see the light of day, never mind the hard earned money from your player base. It's frankly insulting. And what makes it even worse in this case (compared to BL3) is there's no transparency. TALK TO YOUR PLAYERS. Leaving us in the dark is just disrespectful.In summary, I would recommend playing this game if you liked Dragon's Keep or BL3. Wait for a decent sale (<=£30) and buy the base game. Avoid the first season pass for now, it's nowhere near worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: First, I am not a native English speaker, so please excuse my bad English.  Second, I am not a game developer, everything is based only on my OPINION. I am really disappointed with this game. I played all Borderlands titles up to this date and loved most of them except Borderlands 3.  These are some of my problems I have with this game:You don't have different playable characters, instead you have to make your own. This really took away from the replayability of this game.  I played through Borderlands 2 and 3 with all the characters, and every interaction was different. Now you have the same dialog over and over again. Yes, you can change the voice, but it doesn't feel that different. In Borderlands 2, playing Krieg and Axton was a whole other feeling. The personality of their voice lines were fitted to their skills and overall appearance. The skill and the skill tree got a really hard downgrade from previous Borderlands games. Every class has only one skill tree, and you can have two classes on one character. The skills are, most of the time, really boring. There are some many skills that say: “Damage Type: + X%” or “Reload/Swap Speed: +X%”. The cap stones and kill skills are some of the most interesting skills, but they shouldn't be the only interesting ones. Picking a backstory a besides the class is the second important choice you have to make at the start of the game. The backstory provides bonuses to your Hero Stats that are essentially your crit, health and cooldown stats.  The bad thing about this is that you can't change it. I understand why you can't spontaneously change your backstory, but it feels awful that some class combination have a disadvantage because of your backstory. You have to know what class combo you want to play to be able to pick the right backstory for your character.  Most enemies in this game are melees. They come running and charging at you, and you are surrounded by enemies. They are constantly dodging and with most of the new guns having projectiles with travel time it makes them really hard to hit. Like said in the point above, most enemies are melees, but we have melee weapons too, so why not fight melee enemies with melee weapons? Because melee in this game feels terrible. Every time you melee, the control of the camera is taken away from you, and you lock on to an enemy. That not only feels bad, but it doesn't do anything if you don't build around melee. The worst part about the new melee weapons is that they are clogging up the loot pools, but more about this later. The guns in this game are a mix between the new fantasy approach and ripped straight out of Borderlands 3. The problem with the new weapons is that most of them have projectiles with travel time. There are so many enemies that dodge your shots or run around or in the worst case fly around that hit something with the new weapons is a pain in the butt. The old weapons that got ripped aren't bad, but leave a bitter taste. I really don't want to call Gearbox uninspired or something like that, but it adds to the feeling that this game is more like a DLC for Borderlands 3 than a stand alone.  Bosses in this game are another thing that bugs me. In the base game, we have 8-story bosses and 4 from side quest. That is not a lot of bosses. Especially when you play chaos runs, you see the same bosses over and over again. The bosses we have aren't really special, most of them have mechanics where you have to dodge an incoming wave.  Loot is one of the most important things in all the Borderlands games. But this game has so few legendary items, and a big portion of them are melee weapons. That wouldn't be a big issue if they were all ok and useable, but with the introduction of chaos mode, most of them can't keep up.  Then there is the problem that a lot of the good rings and amulet don't have a dedicated loot source. That means if you want a specific ring that doesn't have a dedicated loot source, you have to get lucky and is just frustrating. Since Borderlands 3 it is impossible to farm for perfect guns and other gear, but it was still possible to farm a nearly perfect class mod. Now class mods or armor are a complete mess. A class mod now has an own effect, two classes, up to 3 skills and bonus stats. The order of the classes on the armor has an effect on the skill that come with it too. The naming scheme for items is just confusing. The name for an item contains, most of the time, a prefix, the name of the item and a suffix. That makes item names way too long and is a pain to keep track of.The last gear specific problem I have with this game are the enchantments. There are too many of them, a lot of them aren't good and the amount of Moon Orbs you need to roll another one is way too high, for the amount of possibilities. One roll starts at a cost of 9 and goes up to 4000 Moon Orbs. You can only have 16,000 Moon Orbs at a time. Farming a specific enchantment is not only time-consuming, but tedious. Farming 16 000 Moon Orbs to roll 4 times when I rolled an item 10 times.Chaos level are now the new form of end game difficulty like mayhem level in Borderlands 3. That wouldn't be bad if there weren't 3 issues. First, there are too many chaos levels, at the time of this review there are 50 level. After a specif milestone, gear of higher quality can be dropped, but the problem is that the enemies get stronger, and you only have a chance of better loot no guarantee. Second, the chaos level's maximum was raised to quick. I can't say if / when they will raise it again, but if it happens, you have to farm everything again. Third, the higher the chaos level is, the higher the chance of you getting killed in one shot. The scaling doesn't feel right, and enemies mutate to bullet sponges. It doesn't make it better that you are constantly getting swarmed by melee enemies. At the end, I want to say that I don't hate this game. I am going to continue playing this game, but I hope they will change some of the points I have talked about.For everyone who is thinking about buying this game, I want to give some advice.If you are looking for a fun looter shooter that you can play with friends or solo, and you don't care about longevity or overall balancing, I can recommend this game. But please buy it when it's on discount you maybe want gear from the DLCs, and they are not worth the $9.99 each. If you are a long time Borderlands fan like me, and you hope this game is a step forward from Borderlands 3 I think this game is not for you. There are too many flaws that hold this game back from being a good Borderlands title. But the game is still being work on, so perhaps it will get there.

_childDocuments_.review: Poorly designed Chaos Chamber mechanics. Very weird applied buffs. If the enemies have targetted you, then rip for the rest of the game for you. Game breaking mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: Tiny Tina's Wonderlands is an absolute blast that takes the Borderlands universe to a whole new level of whimsical mayhem. _childDocuments_.review: Another great Borderlands game, and the game within a game bit is a fun way to make a big detour from previous titles in a fantasy setting like this. Tina is obv hilarious, rest of returning cast was fun too, and Will Arnett did a great job even if the plot felt a bit like a rehash of the Lego movie. Still, you got to kill Smurfs so I'm all for it.The story is basically you are playing D&D (sorry - Bunkers and Badasses!) with Tina, so you are basically in a role playing game inside the Borderlands universe, so in addition to the usual puns and silliness you also have Tina retconning the story as it progresses and having her own motives for not wanting the story to end. It works if you are not expecting a serious story, and was typically pretty funny.Pretty solid and bug free for me, though there have been a couple of looping/locking issues where DX seemed to be looping and stuck for a couple of seconds. Not too often and only once did last more than a couple seconds where I had to alt tab and then come back to get it to advance. Seems to happen when quest dialogue is happening during battles for me.Game play is definitely Borderlands - spells replace grenades, and fuse skeletons replace kamikaze psychos, etc. You get an extra slot now for a melee weapon, and that allows some more choices for melee and less chance that your ranged weapon wastes bonuses on melee bonuses. The overland map allows easy moving from town to town, though I do wish you could fast travel to an explored town.  I like the fast small random encounter maps from encampments/ambushes/overland ruins too, and don't really miss the vehicle travel which got old. There's also a bunch of challenges that give you stat bonuses that can be pretty important - the Lucky Dice can more than double your Loot Luck (aka your chance for loot to be higher rarity) even before getting the final bonus for finding them all.  Lucky Dice is shared among all your characters, while other bonuses are per character though much easier to do. The BL series has done a great job improving the basic game systems and TTW is a step forward there.TTW has more classes than Borderlands, and you can make your character look however you like. BL3 has 4 classes while TTW has 6 and you dual class, so it seems like TTW has more choices. But each BL class has 4 skill trees which mean (4x4x3%2) = 24 skill tree combos, while TTW only has 1 skill tree per class so only has (6x5%2) = 15 skill tree combos. Still, it is fun to be able to take your two favorite skill trees no matter what class they are in.End game is also much improved over BL. Instead of grinding the same boss fights on the same campaign maps, you now have the Chaos Trials. These are like the smaller random encounters with the added twist that you chain a bunch of them together and collect modifiers to make it harder/different and can purchase boosts that help you for that run. Chaos Trials end with a boss fight, and those fights get to be pretty annoying as they are already pretty tanky and the higher Chaos levels make their huge HP pools a real slog to handle.You also now have the ability to modify equipment a bit. The Armorer shows you how to spend Moon Orbs to change or add the special Enchantment bonus on most gear items. That is nice as there are so many different possibilities, and some of them are very powerful in specific builds or with other gear. Its very cheap to add a power or change it the first couple times, but I dislike how the change keeps doubling in price without a cap and eventually you won't be able to change it as your Moon Orb currency is capped. Also, you can only change the special Enchantment, so all the other bonuses/stats including item level are still locked. When you have so many bonus choices you often really want/need one from an item and then get stuck with near wasted ones like "Pistol Mag Size" that is at best going to be wanted for very specific builds. I hope they add at least Item Level later so any DLC to increase level cap won't mean replacing all your gear.There are still some areas to improve on, especially for someone who has played lots of BL over the years. I still find it annoying that a single level can have so many containers and that 99% of them are worth almost nothing. It is great the game auto loots money and ammo, but it is time for the game to auto pickup everything and allow us to setup autosell on most items too. It takes a long time to get enough gold to get all those inventory upgrades, and until then you either waste time selling trash items or handicap your gold income. Even after that you will need to do a lot of spam clicking to pick up the mass quantities of purple+ loot that you will check out as possibly being useful before selling off 99% of it for being garbage. If you need to tweak this based on MP games with comp loot fine, but for coop loot or SP it currently is a major obstacle to the rest of the fun. The game play is fun so let me get back to that please.Overall though - lots of fun and pretty solid, and looking forward to some DLCs and more Bunkers and Baddasses!

_childDocuments_.review: After taking a break from the Borderlands series since Borderlands 3, I finally dived back in with Tiny Tina's Wonderlands, and I must say, it was a delight to return to this universe. With 73 hours of gameplay under my belt, including all the DLCs, I found the core campaign to be a solid experience that rekindled the chaotic fun I’ve always loved about the series.The campaign is a wild ride, filled with the signature humor, over-the-top action, and imaginative settings that you’d expect from a Borderlands spin-off. Tiny Tina as a Dungeon Master adds a unique flavor to the storytelling, and the fantasy theme provides a fresh twist on the usual formula. It was engaging from start to finish, offering just the right mix of exploration, combat, and quirky quests.What really stood out to me, though, was the endgame content. The introduction of Chaos Levels and the Chaos Chamber was a fantastic move. It added layers of replayability and challenge that kept me hooked long after the main story ended. Grinding through the Chaos Chamber to tweak my build and push the limits of my character was incredibly satisfying, and it gave the game that addictive "just one more run" quality.However, not everything was perfect. The in-game economy felt unbalanced, particularly when it came to earning enough money for certain achievements. The need to amass 300 million gold was a bit excessive, and there weren’t many efficient ways to achieve this without a considerable grind, which dampened the experience somewhat.Additionally, the DLCs were a bit of a letdown. They felt more like extended Chaos Chamber runs with minimal story content. The watered-down narrative and lack of substantial new content made them feel like a missed opportunity to expand on the rich world of Wonderlands.Overall, Tiny Tina's Wonderlands is a great game that I thoroughly enjoyed. The core experience is strong, and the endgame content adds a lot of value. That said, given the issues with the in-game economy and the underwhelming DLCs, I would recommend picking it up when it’s on sale. The price-to-content ratio isn’t quite as favourable as in previous Borderlands titles, but it’s still a must-play for fans of the series.
