_childDocuments_.review: Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands is an enchanting and wildly imaginative spin-off from the Borderlands franchise, crafted by Gearbox Software. Released in 2022, the game takes players on a fantastical journey that blends the familiar looter-shooter mechanics of Borderlands with a whimsical, tabletop RPG twist.At its core, Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands is a bold departure from the traditional Borderlands formula, immersing players in a magical fantasy world orchestrated by Tiny Tina, the fan-favorite character known for her chaotic and unpredictable nature. The game is set in a Dungeons & Dragons-inspired universe called "Wonderlands," where players traverse a realm filled with mythical creatures, enchanted loot, and a plethora of fantastical quests.The narrative revolves around Tiny Tina's own version of a tabletop RPG campaign, with players taking on the role of "Fatemakers" who must navigate through Tina’s ever-changing fantasy world. The story is characterized by Tina’s erratic storytelling style, resulting in a blend of comedic absurdity and heartfelt moments. The writing is sharp and full of humor, with Tiny Tina's irreverent commentary and the game’s playful dialogue providing a constant stream of laughs.Gameplay-wise, Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands successfully marries Borderlands’ signature shoot-and-loot mechanics with the fantasy RPG genre. Players can choose from a variety of character classes, each with unique abilities and skill trees that offer extensive customization. The game’s combat is fast-paced and satisfying, with an array of creative weapons and spells that fit seamlessly into the fantasy setting. The loot system remains a highlight, with a wide range of magical and absurdly powerful items to discover.The game's world design is another standout feature. The environments are vibrant and varied, ranging from enchanted forests to eerie dungeons, all rendered in a colorful and engaging art style that echoes the whimsical nature of the narrative. The fantastical creatures and imaginative settings are a feast for the eyes and a testament to the game’s creative design.One area where Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands might fall short for some players is in its pacing. While the game is packed with content and side quests, some of the narrative pacing can feel uneven, with certain segments dragging compared to others. Additionally, while the RPG elements are a refreshing change, they may not fully resonate with players who are more accustomed to the traditional Borderlands experience.In conclusion, Tiny Tina’s Wonderlands is a delightful and imaginative entry into the Borderlands universe that offers a fresh take on the series' gameplay. Its blend of fantasy RPG elements, humor, and engaging combat make it a must-play for fans of the franchise and anyone looking for a whimsical adventure. While it may not appeal to everyone, particularly those seeking a more traditional Borderlands experience, it stands as a testament to the creativity and humor that Gearbox Software brings to their games.

_childDocuments_.review: Though I usually enjoy somewhat the adolescent humor of the Borderlands franchise, this one was veering very close to the edge. The player is within a D&D world with Tiny Tina as the Dungeon Master, barely holding it together. _childDocuments_.review: This is by no means a bad game. It has gorgeous environments, fun characters and dialogue, and interesting weaponry and game mechanics. However there are just too many minor things that drag it down. Each of these issues on there own are, at worst, a minor inconvenience, but together they compound and make this a meh experience. _childDocuments_.review: So much fun.  So over the top and out there <cue Twilight zone music>. Tiny Tina brings an amazing journey through a pretty lax although very enjoyable D&D (Bunkers and Badasses) style play.  I've only played Spore Warden solo, so I have no feedback to give on multiplayer.I personally found no cons to the game, but then I'm not a technical player. I play for (what makes Square Enix shake their fists and yell, you are not contributing, you filth)...FUN!     It's not often I will shell out full price or even 20% off for AAA games but Tiny Tina had me hooked with the leading trailer and I had to see more.   I was worried about it being first person.  FPS games usually make me  sick.  Tiny Tina's Wonderland has a fov( field of view) slider. Ram that sucker all the way to ...nearly the end and you'll have few nausea issues if any.   The game play is fun.  I've not played a borderlands game before.  Now I will definitely purchase one  at the winter sale.  ( call me cheap: I don't care)  I was lucky to score a great pistol at the beginning of the game that shot not only bullets but explosive fairies. 'WhatNot of the Wizard', if memory serves me right.I hated to give it up but now I have a pistol that shoots out fire and explosives.  (So sue me I like pistols)  I don't find my spore companion to be that much help.  It's usually run off to attack a goblin or skeleton so far away that by the time it responds to a ping and arrives to help the mob is already dead. His poison cloud is not bad though and he can tank three at a time, or a boss for a minute before needing resurrecting.  Multiclass is a nice touch. I added clawbringer for the  fire breathing companion. Who doesn't want more than one havoc causing pet you don't have to micromanage creating chaos?  Now I'm not one for looking up builds and messing around, I leave that to others. I can use what I feel would be good for me and it works out well.  Can't say that for many games with all their special builds and leveling builds and how to build a builds.  Therefore even a beginner or someone like me who wants it simple and fun can play this game without worries.  Although I must say if your not a warrior you might want to put some points in strength, (for when they get too close, survive your spells) otherwise you hit them like your giving them a mild fish slapping even with a good melee weapon .  I have to say something about the in game quests. HAHAHAHAHA!   Oh you need more detail?  Some of them are eye poppingly out there and hilarious.  The enemies have some funny lines, that don't, for me at least, get old and annoying.I would have to say this game is a labour of love from some real nerds with a sense of humour that I love.One of my family came in to watch and said WTF?  That's crazy.  No higher praise can be given.  The fight style is fast, furious and full of explosions, so don't expect to see much of what is going on at times.  You would think that would be a drawback.  It isn't.  Keep on the move and It works out.  Not being able to have eyes in the back of your head, usually stresses me out in games: not here, you soon learn when your being shot in the back and can accommodate quickly.   I will tell you, I am old and slow and I never PVP because my reactions times are horrendous and I can't think fast enough.  Sound like you?  Yeah, I know how you feel.  If you're a gaming god go read some other review for this part. I was using pvp for an example of my gaming prowess and didn't mean to give any care bears reading this heart attacks.  Do not be afeared, the vasty world of games for the well co-ordinated does not have to impact you.        TIny Tina's Wonderland has a relaxed setting so you can enjoy the story and  not die so often.  Sounds great right?  It is.   But wait there's more. Do you like puzzles? You don't?  Forget I mentioned them.Jumping puzzles? Annoyingly, brain draining to work out jumping puzzles.  Never fear.  You don't need to be co-ordinated like a monkey, and for the ones you simply cannot work out, some lovely person or  twelve  has posted a video or twenty on how to do each puzzle in the game here on steam, or on You Tube.     The other thing you are encouraged to find are the Lucky dice in each area.  Good luck, ( rummages around the internet looking for helpful videos on finding the last elusive dice or two in every area that I've missed).  You don't have to get them all or do the puzzles;  the game does reward you handsomely if you do.  There are two main areas.  The overworld, the only place that the player appears in  third player mode in the game and the quest areas which are all first person. (Does that answer your mental query on whether you can play third person?)  Do all the side quests.  They are pretty good and sometimes insane.  Leveling up isn't fast, but who wants to race to the end when the journey is so much fun?  It definitely has some replay ability.The way Tiny Tina runs her game reminds me of another Dungeon master I knew in my youth.  Oh those days of Yore, back when dinosaurs roamed the earth and cell phones were just a glimmering spark in the microcosm of an amoebas brain.  I like her style, relaxed and forgiving, not a stickler for rules and if you die in the first minute doesn't kick you from the campaign.Other reviewers will get technical or more in depths and I leave that to them.Only remember this: in Tiny Tina's Wonderland." almost every situation can be solved with violence".<Valentine>

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game, had the highest hopes for another fun filled borderlands experience, and all I got was sick bard jokes. That's basically all. There is literally no real soundtrack, except some generic dnd background music. to the game and no engaging gunplay, which in combination accomplishes some of the most boring boss fights I have ever seen. The open world got cut for stupid random encounters in the same few battle arenas, filled with junk and so sparsley populated enemy wise, that it's not even worth using any AOE weapons/skills. The few enemies that are there sponge bullets like they are straight from bikini bottom and are plain as grassland variation wise. If it weren't for some badass enemies that tend to onehit you on higher difficulty levels you could literally just shoot wooden dummies. For me Tiny Tina as a narrator is not cutting it either, as her voice and hyper energy got boring and even tiring in just the first hour of the game. To charge 60 Bucks for this dumpsterfire is a scam at best.Quest wise and storytelling wise it boils down to being bombarded with dialogue whilst shooting at your bullet sponges and watching your weapon reload animation like the most bland animation movie ever made. If it is not that it forces you to  wait for some unimportant dialogue to finish whilst you are standing around and pondering life.I really don't get it why people recommend this game for i quote "A laugh or two", if I want a laugh i could simply watch a cat video on youtube and that's even free.I would only recommend this game for diehard fans with a high frustration tolerance and ask yourself beforehand if the money isn't worth investing in a actual fun activity, like a boardgame, or catfood, or a tree sapling. Conclusion: Stating that the game isn't cutting it for me would be a bold understatement. I am actually disappointed and bored by the lack of engagement this piece of virtual "Art", that I would really recommend reconsidering your choice twice or even thrice if you consider buying this game.

_childDocuments_.review: "Wonderlands" is a game that reminds me of old parody movies such as "Airplane!", "Young Frankenstein" and "The Holy Grail". I say this because while such movies were spoofs, they still took themselves somewhat seriously in terms of presentation and production, trying to get close to the things they were spoofing.As such, "Wonderlands" too feels like a well-executed spoof of CRPGs, getting close to the real thing sometimes, only for it to remind us it's a "Borderlands" game first and last. Maybe all the "Borderlands" games were spoofs - they surely spoofed a lot of pop culture in their long run (mostly to my disdain). But "Wonderlands" is the one that feels the least serious of all the games - for better and worse. And it may very well be my second favourite in the franchise, behind only "Borderlands 2".For starters, and I do feel like I should start with this, I must address what I believe to be the biggest issue of the game: the dialogues. The "Borderlands" games are known for their fun exchanges between the characters, but in here, it feels like they're dragging the whole experience, halting the flow. Because this game is set as a real tabletop RPG being played by Tina and her friends, the game is pretty much entirely narrated, and characters can yack for long seconds. They mostly stall what is overall an excellent game.With that clarified and out of the way, "Wonderlands" is a wonderful game. It is for "Borderlands 3" what "The Pre-Sequel" was for "Borderlands 2" - a complementary, smaller game that was made with the resources and developer momentum that were still gathered by the completion of the mainline game. But while "The Pre-Sequel" - as great as it was - was more of an expansion pack that got big enough for a standalone release, "Wonderlands" feels like a game on its own right. As it seems, Gearbox "listened to fans" by observing the enduring love for the "Assault on Dragon Keep" expansion for "BL2", so they made a full, proper game that expanded on that idea."Wonderlands" at first can be a bit frustrating, again with the dialogues and all. But after a time, the game really starts to pick up. If you're familiar with the franchise, you'll immediately notice that, perhaps because of the game's medieval fantasy nature, it can be a bit of a horde shooter. Previous games in the franchise did have the Psychos that would run towards players, but in this game, you'll see a lot of such melee-based enemies. I've seen this setup multiple times: enemies that attack you physically while supported by ranged enemies at a distance.Now, guns in this game are a bit iffy. The thing about "Borderlands" games is that most guns are garbage: they're filler you may use for other reasons. But in this game, it really feels like there are very few guns that are worthy: most shotguns are awful. SMGs barely cause any damage, and rifles are particularly poor in accuracy. Some guns have a gimmick about them, and can be of some value. And then there'll be diamonds in the rough: guns that are great, and genuinely feel like great finds. This game being a fantasy means that you'll also have spells, and at a point, you can have two equipped - they remind me a bit of the plasmids in the "BioShock" games, and you should most definitely use and upgrade them.You have armours that impact on your stats, shields in form of necklaces, and melee weapons of different capacities. But the best thing your character will have is this companion that, with the right upgrades, can be of enormous help in combat - even if only by drawing attention towards him. A companion that never lags, and even when he's down, he gets back in a considerable short amount of time. Unfortunately, however, he can't help you when you're down, and I felt this was a missed opportunity.I felt the enemies were a bit spongy, taking several shots to kill. I much prefer games that toss me multiple enemies that can beat me by numbers but are easily disposable than moderately-numbered bullet-sponge enemies that are hard to kill. And to make matters more damning, enemies' levels rise along with yours, rather than being dictated by the world as it usually is in RPGs. Guns didn't do enough damage, and melee weapons even less so. The game however is a RPG, meaning that, with enough levelling up and  upgrading, your character can do some serious damage. The levelling caps out at 40, and after that, you'll move on to a different kind of levelling, in which you invest directly on your stats rather than special perks. And eventually, gameplay will become really fun and addictive.Now, one thing that bothered me a little about the game is the key mapping. You access your spells with F and G, and melee is V. It took me some time for me to change the commands into something more relatable, as I made Q melee, and one of the spells M3.Last but not least, my favourite aspect of the game is the worlds. "Wonderlands" mostly ditches those open-ended sets from the previous games and instead goes for those interconnected paths that you would see in "Dark Souls" - which may very well have been the point. At first I hated it, but then I started respecting it deeply when I realised how well-constructed those levels are. Besides, players can always leave the level on the map menu, and can even teleport to the hub city. Levels also have some fast-travel points that make traversing them much easier - albeit I felt there could have been more per level.Different places have different visual themes: some are medieval, while others are tropical and pirate-themed. Some are Nordic-like and snowy, and others are sand deserts - it really reminded me of those N64 platformers. Levels have their collectables and challenges, and I loved them so much that I would take my time to collect everything they had. But if you want to do so as well, know that parts of some worlds are locked until you beat the world's main objective. Some worlds are massive, but they're not even part of the main campaign: there are side missions that are really side campaigns, taking place in worlds of their own, taking you a lot of time.Levels are held together by that classic isometric-view overworld, with collectables and side missions of its own. The overworld has side dungeons, shrines whose pieces are scattered and must be found, shortcuts in the style of "Dark Souls" (again), and enemies that suddenly appear and can chase you into sudden combats - unless you slap them into a colourful mist, which is hilarious everytime. It's important to notice that the game is sort of a Metroidvania, in that there are places in the overworld that are out of boundaries, until you find a way to access them - usually by following missions.In the end, "Wonderlands" is a great game, slightly marred by some issues. But once it clicks, it's unstoppable.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty fun game in the series albeit a couple drawbacks:Firstly performance. For some reason this game either hogs up too many resources or is poorly optimized. It is pretty hard to have this game run above 45 fps and not have potato quality. Not to mention constant video bugs mainly from lighting or a strange glitch texture in your inventory. I have yet to have a crash but had to restart this game several times just on default settings for the game to run at a decent framerate for first launch.Secondly repetition. The random encounter mechanic was cool, but quickly became old. I would rather just traverse the world like other Borderlands games. Nevertheless the Overworld is a pretty cool concept being this is DnD themed, but random encounters should stay in RPG where you want slower paced games and not fast-paced FPS Borderlands is known for. Especially how half the time in encounters will be chasing enemies around instead of hiding for cover or just shooting them.Lastly would be story. It is definitely a step up from BL3, but still relies on BL1 and 2 for its content and character development instead of standing on its own. The characters are still much better than BLTPS or BL3 because of a large reduction in filler characters here. It still is a pretty chill story though, just not a memorable one.However the game is very fun to play. The combat is on par or better then BL3 with spells making grenades much more fun and viable. Even meelle is useful beyond the first hour of the game on non-meelle characters. The amount of customizability is insane letting characters change their second class tree to having 3 stat boosting items, and the annoinment feature without class-specific skills. There are a ton of ways to play how you want, as a proper RPG should be. The enemies are a fresh change from constant reused bandits and psychos and as you progress so the enemies, meaning you shouldnt have to refight the same enemy the entire game. Not to mention the thematics of most guns from using magic crystals as ammo to shooting arrows instead of bullets and the crazy variety of spells to suit most playstyles.This game is a very fun experience, especially with friends. The only problem would be the combat loop through the Overworld  and replacing end-game Takedowns, which albeit were repetitive but much more fun than rinsing and repeating raid bosses. If you're a fan of the series this game is worth investing into, but without friends you may not play this one as much as the other games in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I enjoyed playing Borderlands 3, as much was I bored when playing Tiny Tina's Wonderlands. It's not a bad game per se, but it just doesn't hold up to its legacy. I wanted to finish it, and I did, but it wasn't much fun most of the time.The writing feels mostly uninspired, with the ratio of laughable jokes being far below its predecessor's, its characters(!) and its DLCs. The gameplay feels sluggish at times, although probably being built upon its predecessor's foundation. The story's highlight, from my point of view, happened quite early in the game. Its DLCs add nearly nothing to the game apart from new loot and multiple, loosely connected series of semi-horde and arena combats.If you liked the previous shooter installments of the franchise, you might like this as well. If you really enjoyed the previous installments though, you might be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: First couple of hours was fun enough, but then!Gameplay: is surprisingly boring.. combat feels bad and there are no good weapons in the game.I played through the game 4 times, and there was always 20-30 levels between finding a small weapon upgrade, which is bad because all enemies are super-powered sponges even on the lowest difficulty (which gives you 15% increased damage).That, mixed with most weapons projectiles having travel time and all enemies constantly dodging(with DarkSouls damage immunity) makes for a bad game in itself in a ''shooter''.But then there's the story.. Which is also super boring and dragged out.. The main ''humour'' in the game is npc's talking for way too long while you just have to wait for them to finish so you can continue.. There are no jokes.Endgame content: Non-existent currently.There is the Chaos Chamber, which allows you to go through about 30 Chaos Trials, to unlock higher Chaos levels. (difficulty/Mayhem levels without modifiers)Said trials are several small levels, small arenas/dungeons filled with traps and enemies that spawn way to slowly and in too few numbers. (one reason combat is really boring)And then there are normal Chaos runs, which are the same but serve no purpose other than boring, unrewarding grinding.Chaos Boss runs which is self-explanatory, except for having to do a Obelisk fight in between ''all'' 2-3 bosses in a RunSo nothing interesting or rewarding after unlocking Difficulty levels which you have to do WITH EACH CHARACTER.. It's insanely boring, even the first time going through that.Farming for gear: Gigantic waste of time and you will not succeed.I spent a couple of days farming a boss at max Chaos level (currently 50) without seeing even one a of the item i was looking for with even one mod on it i was looking for.All items can roll with so many different random things on it, it is literally impossible to find any kind of ''perfect'' gear... So, i tried farming the same boss, but with cheats to increase drop rates a whole lot.. after a couple more days, i got 1 of said item with the right class bonuses and mostly correct bonus skill points, only to find out 30 minutes later the Legendary power was wrong, so even that can be random on some legendaries.This game is in desperate need of a Smart-Loot system, like in Borderlands 3Been farming for 15 more hours now, still haven't found anything close to a good roll on any needed gear.Always only 1 out of 5 things that are good, the rest is useless stuff for other classes, or just plain useless bonusses.So i guess in short, if you are looking for a good Borderlands game, this ain't it.This game is as clunky/bad as the original Borderlands 1, just without redeeming qualities.I hope the game gets a lot of changes and polishing, as i can see the game being good, but it's just not..

_childDocuments_.review: The thing is... very rough. TL;DR: Even 6 months after release it's very buggy, and the "loot" part of "Looter-shooter" isn't funIn long:Within the first 3h of playing it, I already had enemies T-pose me, NPC instances not despawn (which gets funny when you're supposed to find the NPC but they're just chillin in front of you), UI get stuck on screen, and and story-relevant cosmetic changes not apply ("oh look this is a rare dotted goblin" - shows a completely normal goblin)You get spammed with common stuff, which I, loot-goblin that I am, all pick up, and quickly run out of space and need to inventory manage. This was a problem in earlier games, too, but I'm fairly certain in BL2 you could at least complete a single mission and then sell your stuff, while here you ideally need to sell your stuff 2-3x per mission. Which means teleporting to the map start, selling your stuff, and then backtracking to where you just were.In BL2, hovering over any item in the inventory would compare it to your currently equipped one. Not so here, you first need to select it and then hover over the currently equipped item. Or go the other way round and click on the equipped one to see the options for it -- but if you do that it remembers your scrolling position. So if you're 2 pages down in your main inventory, and then filter by, say, shields, you'll still be on the second page. And if you don't have 2 pages worth of shields, you see nothing until you notice you're not actually at the top of the list and scroll back up. And when then switching back to the main menu, you need to scroll back down to continue where you left off.It's infuriating. Aside from that - the story is completely wacky and somewhat meaningless (as is expected), which isn't aided by the constant immersion breaks from the DnD setting. The characters feel like fanfics of themselves, instead of just being insane, they're now insane in a costume. As such they're even shallower than their originals. Shooting is alright, melee is finally interesting. But I won't be finishing it, the looting is just too frustrating. It makes me want to play BL2 again.

_childDocuments_.review: Borderlands has never let me down... much... until now. Okay, I'll take 49% of the blame here because I didn't think to do much research before purchasing TTW. I just figured the content would be mostly similar to the rest of the franchise. It's not. At all. In all the previous Borderlands titles, there is a sort of organic open-world experience, and even though in the other titles there are loading screens between large map sections, there are relative few loading screens outside story boss fight content. TTW, however, serves up loading screens for breakfast, lunch, dinner, and everything in-between. What you end up with is a game that feels like a low-budget film where all the scenes are shot in a single location. Except in this single location they added what everyone loves so much about Pokemon games... high grass encounters! I'm serious... they added this to a Borderlands title... and they're super, super complete with loading screens... and they're pretty damn frequent, too. Oh, and the NPCs chase you and never, ever stop. Ever. So, yeah, that bs along with worst-than-ever inventory management and extremely confusing item descriptions, the non-stop loading screen experience is just not worth it. The ONLY reason I played this past 20 hours was because someone joined my game and hacked my character and gave them max level and skills and then gave me and helped me get a ton of legendaries, which okay, AFTER I had all that crap and I was wayyy OP I DID finally have a TINY amount of fun, but still... no matter how many legendaries I equipped, the loading screen was the final boss I could no longer farm.

U could say that "heyy that's the whole point because the story is made by Tiny Tina!" but let's be honest here. Thats just making excuses for a lazy development team. _childDocuments_.review: The Pros:Beautiful environments and graphics-Spells are fun, replacing your grenades. Depending on the spell, you have to hold to charge, cast multiple, or cast with a simple button press.-Great voice talents involved-Can choose your pronouns (He, She, They)-Can put beards on female bodies and makeup on male bodies, hurray customization-I like the gun play well enough. Smooth and satisfying.-The game really does its best to combine Borderlands with DnD just as it did with the BL2 DLC. It's a "DnD skin", yes, but there is depth and thought put into it with you traveling an Overworld with your character as a miniature, your origin giving you buffs and debuffs to your stats, a little customizable banner, a spell slot, a companion for applicable classes...-Loot is pretty good! If you don't have any luck with drops, the vending machine often has something to make up for it.-Tiny Tina is fun and funny as always-Actually feels like a spiritual successor to the BL2 DLC that inspired this stand-alone. -Smooth, easy-to-navigate interface and menus.Cons:-Pricey af DLC that offers literal minutes of extra gameplay. The BL2 Headhunters DLCs offered twice, maybe three times the content for half the price.-The writing for Claptrap is awful. He is very annoying. I am a big fan of Claptrap, but this was painful, probably because it's not the same voice actor that really sold the character for BL1, BL2, and BL:TPS. Thanks a lot, Randy.-Some graphics bugs (flickering shadows and black patches on the ocean and in the sky, sometimes, as well as insane 'flares'. Those go away if you close out and reboot the game)Neutral:-I do not mind the humor or the dialogue, for the most part. It's a bit basic, a bit obvious, but..oh well. My comments regarding some of the negative reviews:No, this game is not "SJW". A game allowing you to choose your pronouns and features a non-binary NPC isn't "shoving SJW down your throat". LGBT people play games, too, not just you, Tyler. In fact, DnD has been an escape for people other than straight white male nerds, so their stories and fantasies can also be represented. You aren't special cuz you got bullied in high school by Chad for liking dragons and excel more than football. If you want to play a game that "isn't political", go play Tetris. All games are political, boy-o. All art is political. As always, I recommend this game on a big sale, because God knows we're all on a budget. Never pay full price for any game, ever.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon starting a new game, you will have the option to choose the game’s difficulty. You have three options to choose from: Relaxed, Balanced and Intense. Relaxed allows you to play the game a little more chilled, where players deal 15% more damage and enemies deal 15% less damage. Balanced is the difficulty on which the game was intended to be played, and on the Intense difficulty, players deal 15% less damage, enemies deal 15% more damage and you’ll gain 15% bonus in Gold and Moon Orb drops.  After you’ve decided how brave you are, you then have to create a character. First you choose a Class. There are six classes in total: Stabbomancer, Clawbringer, Spellshot, Graveborn, Spore Warden and Brr-Zerker. Each class has its own combat style and focus: the Stabbomancer is a sneaky murderer and has a focus on Critical Hits, the Clawbringers is a Wyvern tamer with a focus on Fire and Lightning Damage, the Spellshot is a magic-user whose focus is on constantly Casting Spells, and the Graveborn is a soul-trapper with a focus on dealing damage in exchange for Health.  Spore Warden is a fungal friend with a focus on Ranged Damage and the Brr-Zerker is an angry smasher with a focus on Frost Damage. Each class also has its own Class Feat and two Action Skills, all of which will help you to decide which class to choose.  After choosing your Class you can customise the look of your character or choose one of the presets. Here you can customise your character’s Body and Personality, Facial Features, and Face and Armour Decoration. There are quite a few customise options for you to create your perfect character. Next you choose your character’s Twist of Fate (their background); this will have an effect on the stats of your character. There are five backgrounds to choose from: the Village Idiot, Raised by Elves, Failed Monk, Recovering Inventory Hoarder and Rogue Alchemist. Once you’ve chosen your background, your next job is to assign some Hero Points to your character’s stats. The points can be applied to either Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Wisdom, Constitution and Attunement. Once you’ve created your character, there’s a small intro with Tina, Frette and Valentine who will help you play through the game of Bunkers & Badasses, after which you’ll head off to the Snoring Valley - Glade of Helpful Tutorials. Here you will go over some basics of the game with Tina playing as Bunker Master throughout the game. She has created the Wonderland and you play as the Fatemaker, it’s up to you to explore, loot and save Tina’s Wonderland from the Dragon Lord who will soon rise again. Defeating the Dragon Lord is the main objective of the game, and the story will unfold as you unlock new campaign quests. There are also plenty of side quests; with each campaign quest you will have a number of objectives to complete. The campaign is divided into chapters and at the end of each chapter you’ll find yourself up against the final boss. Defeating them will then allow you to move on to the next chapter and open up a new location, maybe in the Overworld. After leaving the Valley of Tutorials you find yourself in the Overworld, which is the world map. Here you can move through the Wonderland visiting new locations and their surroundings, find quests, activities and encounters, some of whom may be dangerous although a quick left right can deal with them with ease when they appear, so beware of the tall grass, you never know who’s hiding in it.  Not all locations will be available for you to visit right away, they may need unlocking through either the story or from the collection of certain items. There are shrines which have a number of missing pieces; you’ll have to collect all of the missing pieces to make the shrine whole again. After completing the shrine, you will then receive some sort of reward from the god of the shrine.  You will also find Camp Sites and Dungeons along with the Shrines, and upon entering them you’ll set off an Encounter. This will pit you against whatever creatures reside in the location you’ve just entered. Defeating them will end the encounter, however, you will have multiple rounds of encounters before you finally complete the location. After each round of encounters a chest will appear with some nice goodies for you. After the last round of encounters, you will gain the reward for completing that location, such as a missing piece of a shrine or some other item required elsewhere. When you encounter the enemy throughout the game combat will commence. This will consist of you using a variety of weapons, different types of bladed weapons, hammers, pistol, rifles, grenade launchers and snipers. All weapons will have different stats and some will have added abilities and may also have the added status effects, such as poison, fire, ice and lightning. The weapons come in different qualities: common, uncommon, rare and legendary, which can be easily identified by their different colours. You’ll also have any abilities your character has from their class to help you spank some botty.  Scattered all over the place are chests, safes, wooden boxes and barrels. When opened or smashed, in the case of the wooden boxes and barrels, you may find some gold, ammo, weapons, gear or health vials. Keep your mince pies open for D20 dice, as finding one of these and opening them will also give you some items. Unlike chests, however, they could be hidden or in a place which might be out of reach at first sight. There are other things to find, such as Marbles, Poem Pages, Rune Switches and Obelisks where you can gain some sort of reward. You can also equip your character with new gear: Armour, Ward, Rings, Amulets. Like the weapons, they all come in different rarities, abilities and effects. You may also come across some small satchels mixed in with some of the other items, which will unlock some customisation in the Quick-Change booths. This will allow you to customise your character’s look with more options than those available at the beginning of the game. If you come across any that you already have, then you can sell them for a nice bit of profit to top up your coffers. You can sell any of the gear, weapons or items you find on your journey at some vending machines scattered around in various locations. You’ll be able to buy new equipment and weapons from these vending machines; there’s always a special item on offer so you might want a to keep butchers on what’s regularly available. Although I do find that they can be expensive and they don’t really give me much of a boost over my favourite stuff that I collected from enemies, chests and anywhere else I’m find them. One thing I would say, though, is if you do buy something for, say 50,000 gold, then don’t walk away and come back later trying to recuperate anything like that back because it’s not going to happen.  Positives  + Fantastic graphics + Multiple character classes + Cross-play platforms + Online Co-op and Lan + Crazy characters and story + Has achievements Negatives  - Some stuttering - No cards currently It’s your job as the Fatemaker to go on an adventure, loot dungeons, travel through magical lands, and more importantly, deal with the evil Dragon Lord who’s just been released from his slumber. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: For a brief overview, if you have played any of the Borderlands series you will know what to expect game play wise, and to some extent theme wise if you know Tina.With that said, I wouldn't go much beyond that for an explanation if you have prior exposure. Beyond adding melee weapons, rings, and spell slots (grenades), everything else is consistent for better or worse. The theme is the major sell here, and with a brief understand of Dungeon and Dragons, it does suit it well. There are no vehicles this time around, but rather a over world to which the character moves across with the appearance of a board game. While this matches the theme, it doesn't change anything beyond aesthetic as the story progresses appropriately and with guidance.When it comes down to much of the game, because it is D&D themed, most is just designed to match. Instead of characters, you have slight customization with a blank slate character, and classes to choose from. With that said, while the plot works around the "insert character here" theme, the engagement and characters are not as built.Also to be noted, that classes have skill tree, and while you can "dual class" to unlock more build ideas and potentially more pets, it does feel a tad underwhelming. Further playing into this was items that almost felt unnecessary (rings)/melee weapons. These just played into the idea for more things to grind for, but no substance. And while this is a "fantasy" world, much of the enemies were re-skinned, and the same guns/mechanics existed. While understanding borderlands was themed around guns and the combinations therein, the new spell introduction which replaced grenades, seemed more appropriate and innovative. The environments had the sword and shield, bows, etc, but at most the character had a "crossbow" machine gun. The game would have benefited greater if the emphasis was greater with melee weapons, and removed guns, outside of musket esque items, and replaced them with bow variations, slingshots, etc. This is of course my opinion, but does shine on some greater things the game has.The environments are far more diverse and engaging than in the past, and the universe and theme aloud for it. As stated before, while the universe built was great, some slight alterations that could have been designed would have greatly made the game more engaging or unique.In simplicity, if you ever wanted to shoot guns at dragons, to then loot more guns this is your game. Outside the realm of that, I would recommend other titles in Borderlands if you haven't already played before this.With that in mind, this is a spin off and met the expectations to that extent.

_childDocuments_.review: "Tiny Tina's Wonderlands" is -- what? the fifth installment? -- in the "Borderlands" series (Tales from the Borderlands notwithstanding), and continues in its parent franchise's tradition of crass, stupid, irreverent humour and ridiculous cartoon violence. Something that sets this game apart from the rest is its wealth of heart. Other instalments have had some heart, sure, but it was always in short supply, secondary by far to the humour. This game balances the two more cleanly, with tales of redemption, true love and romantic ambition, to name just a few themes. Also, the aesthetics are gay AF.On the other hand, the graphics are still a bit unstable. Sometimes textures don't load, sometimes buttons stay middle screen far too long. Sometimes your companions's status bars show dead when the companion is fine. The inventory system is bulky and the weapons naming system is somewhere between senseless and hard to decode. A tighter algorithm for single-person play might benefit a good deal, but, hey, at least there's plenty of loot to sell. Also, in-game cut scenes tend to slow the pacing somewhat.A good-ass game, all told. 7.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a Borderlands game, so it's good. It has a much better story than BL3 with very similar game play. The different classes can be fun, but the level cap (40) limits your skill points. The endgame is garbage. After finishing all of the missions and area challenges, the fun died.Unlike Mayhem Mode in BL3, Chaos levels increase enemy HP & Damage, but the  gear doesn't scale. You have to reach Chaos level 20 before there's a chance that 'better' gear can drop. Then again at Chaos level 35, there's a chance for better drops. The increase in gear specs doesn't match the increase in enemy HP/DMG. Basically, the game gets increasingly harder, but you don't get more powerful. Some bosses are challenging, others are so unbalanced that they down you in a few seconds, go into an Immunity phase or straight up vanish - and there are no other enemies present to kill, so you're screwed. (frustrating AF)After thousands of hours playing the Borderlands series, this one is getting old after 180hrs.Buy it on sale to get your money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge borderlands fan. Played all the games through multiple times. I even enjoyed the pre-sequel that gets dumped on a lot. This game isn't like any of the others. It's way worse. It's a fine way to fill some time, but you won't get your mind blown playing it. Even Borderland's trademark "humour" is absent. Do you find "parodies" like Smurfs who replace every third word with "Smurf" and "The Ditcher: Gerard of Trivia" funny? I doubt it. That's the level of writing and humour you're getting here. The voice acting, which Borderlands has rarely excelled at, is an embarrassment. Many of the same voice actors return, Bethesda style, but what's here is just awkward. So many people attempted "accents" and they should never, ever do that again. If you want an English, Scottish or Australian voice, get someone with that accent. The "Scottish" accent in this game is bordering on offensive. It makes Groundskeeper Willie sound like Rabbie Burns and in no way should that have made it out of the studio, let alone into a published game.The levels are huge and vehicles are no longer a thing, so prepare for a lot of walking. Your walking will be interrupted constantly by waves of spawning enemies and it just makes travelling around frustrating. Very easy to get lost on some of the levels, too.The missions and gameplay are beyond lazy. Essentially, some lazy plot device is presented in which they find reason after reason for you to either walk through a level fighting waves of enemies to grab items until you end up at a mini boss, or you fight your way through waves of enemies in an arena style setting. I hope you're up for that, because it's the only gameplay there is. Even the end game, with the choas chamber is just more of the same. The DLC is an embarrassment and, yes, it's just more arena wave spawning.This game has no heart and little to no effort has been put into it. Hell, I played through this on launch on Epic, just bought it on Steam and I'm STILL seeing bugs that I experienced on launch. If Gearbox want to treat fans like crap by lazily cramming this thing together and asking for your money, give them the money it deserves. Don't pay for than 10 bucks for this and even that's pushing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Forced "message" gets tiring quickly as it distracts from the content.  30mins or so into game they take a left turn to introduce paladin mike who just kills entire "sarcastic snarky humour" vibe to force in a political message.  The contrived character is just flat and un-inspriing, added nothing but annoying sound clips you have to wait through.  Maybe they were trying to create their own "jar jar".   Overall its same old borderlands combat with 2 slotted powers; gets a bit grind'y fast and really no changes as you progress.  Grind for better loot, wash and repeat. _childDocuments_.review: Pre-sequel but for the Tiny Tina DLC. If that's a bad thing in your eyes that's you not me.Anyway, fun romp through our favourite bunker masters campaign, scaled up to be a lil bit smaller than a main line game with plenty of fun jokes and a pleasant if a bit thin main story. But you don't really play borderlands for the story you play it for jokes and actually I think this game does quite a good job for dnd nerds, constantly playing off of the frustrations of dm's or the ridiculous actions of players resulting in some great bits to Tina's dismay often as she loses control of a side mission.Anyway what wonderlands changes is usually great, specifically it changes travel, class system and the loadouts. I personally think these changes are fantastic, the travel is now done on an overworld map letting you swiftly get to areas in a unique and charming way with some additional things to see if you want to explore, though sadly there are some repeats on the maps, I imagine that's a result of the turnaround for this game but it still is far better than the other games with constant backtracking in usually boring areas with horrible vehicles this game provides plenty of fast travel and rarely requires much backtracking. The classes have been changed in that instead of playing a character with a selection of three skill trees, you play one character who picks a main class and a second dual spec, each making one skill tree. My main complaint about the classes is how the game explains the classes, sure some are self explanatory but others feel confusing and since you're locked in for the entire first playthrough after selecting one you're mildly gambling on if you'll enjoy it or not. So it kind of incentivises optimization/expression on the players part but changing it after the fact is made difficult for little reason I feel, allowing respeccing from the get would be a huge boon IMO. But that leads well into the loadout changes, so importantly for borderlands players is the class mod, sadly the game seemingly ignores loot distribution (at least for my selection of classes) meaning I spent the entire game usually with mods that weren't meant for my class combos. I think a just loot distribution change to you know the classes I am would help a LOT. But it makes up for it in something REALLY cool. You are blessed with a very interesting spell system, replacing grenades and action skills in my case. And I think they got really quite creative with all the different spell types meaning I was constantly mixing up my spell slots and experimenting with the new mechanic. And my last thing is the rings, which are new and, they are fine enough just more passive mods for your character that are usually pretty minor, but what I don't like is that the second ring slot they held out on for until the end of the game meaning I didn't get to use that ring slot at all seeing as I have little interest in the end game content.Anyway on checking out the reviews there is about one opinion I agree with, that being that this game seems a bit overpriced, I exclusively call out the producers of this in this case. This game is WAY too much for what it realistically is, and that's sad because it leaves people pissed at the fantastic devs who put in a very clear passion to this project. I think the games great but misguided due to corporate greed.Conlcusion, game good, buy it on the cheap and play it with friends if you're fortunate enough and definitely play the sidequests that I should have talked more about in this review.

name: CONSCRIPT
detailed_description: Deluxe & Officer Editions Trench Raider Pack Battle through the trenches with 3 additional uniforms to choose from in the Trench Raider Pack, containing: • Elite Trench Raider • Pilot • English Tommy About the Game ADD TO YOUR WISHLIST! CONSCRIPT is a top-down survival horror game inspired by classics of the genre - set in 1916 during the Great War. CONSCRIPT will blend all the punishing mechanics of older horror games into a cohesive, tense, and unique experience. In CONSCRIPT, you play as a French soldier searching for his missing-in-action brother during the Battle of Verdun. Will you be able to search twisted trenches, navigate overrun forts, and cross no-mans-land to find him, and ensure a home goes unbroken? Experience classic and methodical survival horror gameplay in a unique historical setting: the Battle of Verdun. Highly re-playable with various difficulty settings, multiple endings, unlockable costumes and bonus weapons. Fend off enemy soldiers and combatants with a variety of WW1 melee weapons and firearms. Survive in an intense, harrowing atmosphere boosted by a unique pixel art aesthetic and oppressive sound design. Navigate intricate level design that promotes item management and route planning, whilst solving complex environmental puzzles. Explore distinct WW1 themed areas that intertwine and overlap.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first completed this game after about 12 hours, I discovered that the "true ending" required a second playthrough. I was disappointed because while I really enjoyed the game, I didn't think I wanted to play it all again, so I just watched the ending on youtube and went to bed.And I could not stop thinking about this damn game.Long story short, 50 hours later (I occasionally left it running while paused) I have played it through I think 7 times and gotten all of the achievements, which I very rarely do. In fact I so rarely get invested enough to dedicate the time to mastering games that I've only done it one other time, which was Amnesia the Bunker, amusingly a similar game in many ways (damn rats!). Mastering both of these games is something I'm quite proud of.I'm not going to pretend this game is perfect, and I recommend you read some other reviews if it's important to you to have plenty of details before you buy or not, just keep in mind that the dev put out a couple significant patches after release that helped with most of the significant complaints. Though I'd argue the 94% positive rating speaks for itself. I personally think the first chapter is a poor introduction to what the majority of the game actually is, so just stick with it until chapter 2 and see how you like it from there. The combat gameplay especially is much more fun in the middle and end of the playthrough.I've bought both the cosmetic pack and the soundtrack (and also wrote my first real review lol) because I would love to see the game be expanded and I want to support the dev (that's right, (mostly) just one developer!) because he's done something great, imho.PS: If you are also a huge WW1 buff the historical themeing of this game is obviously cool and the environment and story are very authentic in their own pixellated way lol.

_childDocuments_.review: I was highly anticipating Conscript and it didnt disappoint. This is a hardcore, harrowing and relentlessly bleak game set in the absolute meat grinder of Verdun, where classic survival horror game tropes get masterfully assimilated into a historical setting. By far the most unique aspect of the game is the total lack of supernatural elements, nearly everything you see in this game has this amazing air of plausibility and authenticity that really amps up the grim atmosphere that hangs around every minute of the game. While the game has some welcoming options assisting players who are not as valiant, the game absolutely shines when saves are limited, every injury hurts, and you're resource starved. This makes the stop and pop shooting, the very risky but punchy melee, and those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rats to be as undesirable as possible. Maybe I'm just a masochist, but I really enjoyed how brutal and clunky the combat was, even if I can understand someone being very turned off by how slow and difficult it is.That all said, I have two grievances - the rats can be a bit too punishing (there will be a small nerf soon) and I find the amazing visual style can at times hide essential paths needed to progress due to the murkiness, which got me lost a few times. However, if the idea of surviving the trench warfare sounds interesting to you, or you just want a great game to play, pick this one up right now. Few horror titles have been as unique and engrossing as this one in recent memory.
_childDocuments_.name: CONSCRIPT

_childDocuments_.review: This game was carried by its style, not its gameplay.Would've benefited from less time spent running around due to maze like levels, item running due to restricted inventory space and having enemies die from fewer hits but be otherwise more dangerous. Once you progress opening up new paths in the levels, gain more inventory space and upgrade your guns to require less kiting in battles, things improve, atmosphere shines through and the game is at its best. I don't get why "inventory management" is so romanticized in these games. I've never heard anyone say "Silent Hill would've been so much better with restricted inventory". You can withdraw from almost any situation, so any poor choices of what to carry it will only result in backtracking time, which there is already so much of. It doesn't create impactful choices, only chores. Being able to infinitely reset each encounter by running out of the room and back in nearly kills all of the tension. Gripping and atmospheric to the bitter end despite its shortcomings.

_childDocuments_.review: Scratches both the WW1 and old school survival horror itches! Im actually stunned that a first time developer made this, whatever you were doing before Jordan, ignore that and focus on game development. This is your callingElements that make it stand out from other attempts in the SH genre are things such as its level design and balancing. Both are pretty much spot on, aside from one or two long moments, I felt like it had been meticulously thought out and therefore was worth my time (Which is the biggest commodity these days). Take some of the later SIlent Hill or Resi games and they lost their way on this so its very refreshing to be able to see it again.One other really niche point I liked was that you still interacted with other french soldiers throughout the game, rather than being all by yourself during the "aftermath" of the event like in Resi 2.Also being a fellow WW1 nerd I appreciated all the factual touches and locations. Fort Vaux gave me Battlefield 1 flashbacks so was nice to see!In a nutshell;Positives:Superb atmosphereFaithful WW1 settingGreat resource balancingArt design Creepy soundtrackGreat well thought out level designVery functional combatExcellent pacingSome excellent well used emotional hooks with the photographs on the soldiersGood difficulty management, doesnt do unnecessary spikes or leave you in the cold if you missed an item earlierNegatives;Slightly too long (Seems to want to end and then goes on for another level)Rats (Already discussed, too fast and dont die that easily so are more grief than the soliders)Some long winded backtracking in later chapters (Essentially having to go the LONG way around for something got a bit tedious at times, a few more shortcuts would of been appreciated)Outdoor level design. It wasn't particularly clear what elements of the countryside I could walk around and what I couldnt so spent a lot of time getting stuck or caught by the rats on a puddle that was similar to one I walked over earlierPerformance was largely excellent, aside from a hard crash when repairing an item when your inventory was full and some frame drops in the last few scenes, also this random issue where the game window didnt quite fill the screen properly when first loaded (Resolved when going to a new room or loading a save)Suggestions;No map indicator if there are items left inside a room (This was a later edition to the resi remakes but I always felt like it was an improvement to know whether you had cleared a room or not)Blocked routes not being largely shown on the map. Would of been nice for that blocked marker to appear on areas that were now or temporarily blocked, this appeared sometimes but not all so would of helped with route managementThanks very much Jordan, I look forward to Conscript 2!

_childDocuments_.review: Conscript is a game with very high highs and very low lows. I'll begin by mentioning how a majority of the work seen in Conscript is done by one Jordan Mochi, with help from various others such as in voice acting. This alone is incredibly impressive, especially for a game of such quality, but of such length too. You most definitely get your money's worth with Conscript as it boasts 6 lengthy chapters to fight your way through (with relatively good area variety for quite a limited setting).For the positives: 1. The game is gorgeous. The proficiency in pixel art is on full display the entire time with fluid animation and detailed environments. Actions from both enemy and player character are perfectly clear and readable no matter the circumstances. The game world oozes atmosphere, with the soundtrack and sound design emphasising it in every room of the game2. The level design is top notch. There's a very good flow in gathering key items, using them, and getting new ones. Most if not all areas cannot be completely cleared on first visit, heavily encouraging backtracking and re-exploration of old areas. On this note, general progression is excellent also. You can very clearly feel the power increases when discovering new weapons and the severity of the war itself getting more extreme as the game continues on.3. Speaking of the War, the intensity and horror of war is captured extremely well within Conscript. Soldiers, either French or German, seemingly losing their minds or writhing from pain is an all too common sight. The occasional Soldier dropping a photo of a family member, animal or place consistently reinforces to the player that you are fighting other innocent people - fighting for a cause they may not even understand.4. Finally, the Merchant is well implemented. He never directly sells anything of immediate (effective) use, meaning the player must make critical decisions regarding their purchases and resource management. For most (non-key) items there will be a trade-off to make. Do you craft a Molotov, or do you create a disinfectant with the alcohol?Now for the negatives: 1. Beginning with what may be the most major negative, the Rats. When you kill any German Soldier, Rats will soon spawn and begin to fester around the corpses unless they are burned. Simply put, they are not implemented well. Rats are much faster than the player - though not in running speed. Rats can easily optimise their movement around the (sometimes strange) geography of the map, allowing them to easily catch up to the player.Upon hit, there is a chance for the player to be poisoned by Rats. Poison reduces your maximum health until it is healed with a disinfectant bandage. The status effect on it's own is a good idea (especially since it is applied in different areas of the game under different circumstances) however the Rats do it poorly. Rats will, more often than not, poison the player on the first bite (which may be unavoidable depending on the circumstances they are encountered). Furthermore, sometimes Rats lack the windup to their attack, instantly poisoning the player without a chance to fight back.Lastly, the Rats will not fight the Germans and vice versa. They will ignore each other, instead choosing to gang up on the player. Unless both Rats and Germans have a mutual hatred of the French, this is a serious flaw in the design of the game.2. Combat is generally not very good. It attempts to capture the clunky and slow combat of classic Resident Evil (and other Survival Horror games of the time). There is a severe lack of enemy variety in Conscript, and all the enemies really do is charge straight at the player in an attempt to hit them. With melee combat, this can devolve into a back and forth of running away and getting a single hit in - being more silly than scary. Ranged combat is not much better. It can be extremely hard to tell what exactly you are aiming at because the environment does not communicate well enough if you have line of sight or not. I have had enemies shoot me despite clearly being behind a wall they could not possibly shoot me from, whereas I can't shoot them back from the same position.3. Combat is further hindered by how weak a majority of the weapons are - especially in the beginning. Your beginning weapons might as well be shooting BB Bullets with the exception of the Pump-Action Shotgun. The rifle, which you would expect to pack a punch, takes numerous bullets to take down even a single non-armoured enemy. This is largely solved by chapter 4 where you effectively have the best versions of each weapon, but it is still a problem nonetheless. 4.  The story is incredibly lacking. There isn't much beyond the premise of the game, which is a shame. But I can understand how it would be difficult to write a more intriguing story about a World War.5. Some puzzles are far too obtuse for their own good. The main example of this is in the final area of the game, which the solution is so poorly communicated to the player that most people will not solve it. Granted, it is optional, but this is only one example.6. The inventory is too tight. Conscript feels like how people complained about Signalis' inventory. There is simply too much stuff to carry at all times, meaning inventory fills up fast. This inevitably leads to a lot of backtracking, something that is initially a positive, becoming a chore. The needlessly limited stamina (and how slow sprinting actually is) adds to the ever growing tedium.At the end of the day, Conscript is obviously a passion project. While it has several flaws, some which could be considered deal-breakers to specific players, I could not imagine not recommending it. It blows several modern Survival Horror games out of the water with it's quality of level design and atmosphere. It is definitely an acquired taste, though I believe it is worth a try (especially with the very generous demo) to see if it could become one of your Survival Horror favourites like it has mine.

_childDocuments_.review: For the emotional elements of the story, the theme, art and presentation I can recommend the title. I played on Soldier, which was the highest difficulty I could play by default I think? I can't remember at this point, but it's above easy and normal and there was one higher than it. I found myself compelled to finish the game, most likely because I really love the genre of survival horror. A nice treat that also ends up being a con, is I certainly expected monsters or zombies going into this game blind. The game's theme showing both the pointlessness of this battle AND that humans are monsters is a good one, and they portray this well.Some story beats and secrets don't really make sense at times but that is mostly okay besides an ending being locked behind some things you wouldn't think of and you will get locked out of that ending because of it.The gameplay is middling at best, not particularly impressive. You've got a dodge roll but sometimes your hitbox seems to extend and you'll get hit from a long swing. It doesn't happen that often but when it does you'll just think, "Oh." Enemies can be dodge rolled and kited pretty easily, the danger comes from managing your supplies and reloading.Incredibly low enemy varietyLack of shortcuts resulting in incredibly tedious backtrackingRats are a punishment to the tedious backtrackingInventory will be generally reserved at 50-60% capacity for key items and key equipmentDifficulty is lacking due to no boss fights and poor enemy varietyBizarre pacing throughout the game. You can suddenly find yourself in a loooong puzzle breakSome pretty obtuse puzzles, especially one that locks away the "best" endingI really like this genre a lot, and can appreciate the theme here greatly. A lot could have been improved but as an experience overall it was a net positive, JUST slightly. If you aren't a fan of the survival horror genre, then maybe skip.

_childDocuments_.review: Saw this game in a YouTube video about upcoming survival horror quite a while ago, so it's been on my radar. I have to say, indie devs like this one are absolutely killing it. Conscript, Skald Against The Black Priory, and Faith are probably my favorite games I've played this year.This game feels like a love letter to old-school Resident Evil fans, albeit no tank controls. The setting is perfect for a survival horror game and the mechanics of the game work together very well both in terms of scare factor and narrative. Limited ammo, overwhelming number of enemies, and scarce health items mean you have to pick and choose your battles. Typically in every game I play I end up as a murdering b@stard, but just like in REmake, there are consequences for killing enemies and not burning their bodies. So far I'm only on chapter 2 of 6, but I'm loving it. The art style is charming, the story has me intrigued, the combat is really satisfying once you get the hang of it, and there have been no cheap jump scares thus far, just the right amount of atmospheric tension. Looking forward to seeing what else the game has to offer and I would highly recommend for fans of survival horror

_childDocuments_.review: Conscript is quite clearly a labour of love - both a love of history and a passion for the game itself. So much care has clearly gone into finding ways of balancing accurate historical detail with interesting gameplay. It's quite an achievement, especially when considering this is a solo dev's work, and manages to be respectful of the real lives lost and the emotional impact of the war while also offering a wealth of content and replayability. I have to praise the bold choice to create a survival horror game with absolutely zero supernatural elements in it, and the game succeeds admirably at evoking the real horrors of trench warfare without paranormal aid. It's also incredibly old school in many ways, with all the positives and negatives that come with that as I'll describe below.  The level design is frankly superb, reminding me of classic metroidvanias and early Resident Evil games, with perfectly-paced exploration, backtracking, and shortcut-unlocking making the trenches, forts, and towns a joy to explore. Despite each area being vast I never felt lost - they unfold logically and you're never presented with a blockage for which the solution cannot be easily found with proper exploration. Revisiting old areas is kept interesting by the new possibilities presented by your equipment, as well as ever-present flesh-eating rats chewing on the corpses that you've left behind and the possibility of a German raid sending new threats your way. The puzzle elements are incredibly old school and resistant to the modern tendency to look things up rather than work it out yourself - many of them are randomized and will require you to either keep a pen and paper handy or use the notebook in the steam overlay to work things out and retain codes for doors and lockers. Despite being very lo-fi, the backdrops look excellent too. The whole place is a wet and muddy hell with corpses and rats everywhere, shattered equipment and craters blocking your path. Blood mixes with water, fire flickers, and lethal yellow-green gas haze drifts. There are even moments of desolate beauty, like when you find poppies growing in a swamp or a stained glass window still standing in a bombed-out church. The combat element is much harsher and more skill-based than I expected. It sits somewhere between Resident Evil and Dark Souls (I know, I know, everybody's bored of Dark Souls comparisons. Shhh!); you have to be very active to stay alive and spacing is key to doing so. When aiming a firearm it takes a while to attain accuracy, so you have to time your shots and concentrate on positioning under pressure. This makes the shooting almost feel like drawing a bow - you hold aim for a while before you shoot. Many of the guns require you to pull the bolt, turn the cylinder, or pump the shell before you can fire again, racking up the tension as your foes charge after you with trench shovels and clubs. Your guns also have limited ammunition and you're always scrabbling around for more, which makes missing all the more galling. The majority of your enemies will be melee fighters, so you'll have to make good use of the Souls-style combat roll and manage your stamina carefully to avoid their licks while dishing out your own while staying wary of any ranged attackers. Your melee weapons have a durability bar that is ever-dwindling, and once they break the damage they put out drops off a cliff. I actually thought this was a rare bad design choice - it doesn't really add anything worthwhile and the melee combat is tense enough without your weapon breaking and you having to backtrack to fix it. There are also a few issues with hitboxes, both yours and the enemies, that I noticed - obvious hits going astray while wild swings somehow connect and the like. Some enemies are also bullet sponges, which in such an otherwise realistic game also felt a bit excessive. Despite these quibbles though, it's an engaging and unique setup, and you certainly have to stay focused if you want to live. Some of the background mechanical choices will be divisive. The game has a classic Resi-style inventory management system and although you can expand your bag as time goes on, at times it's very frustrating being unable to pick up an essential item without throwing out precious ammunition or healing items. You're often forced to backtrack extremely long distances to try and find a stashbox so you can swap your items around. The dev has acknowledged this complaint and added more stash boxes to mitigate it, but the unnecessary backtracking still impacted the pacing for me - shuffling stuff around in your bag just isn't much fun as far as I'm concerned. Many modern games have a "Quest Items" tab for just this reason. I can understand the idea behind it - after all lugging around a satchel full of ammunition and artillery shells is hardly realistic, especially in a muddy environment - but I felt it could've been a bit more forgiving given the scarcity of places to rotate items in and out. The default save system is also very traditional, calling back to Resident Evil again with its ink-ribbon-and-typewriter and no autosaves. It's a mixed blessing. On the one hand, it does suit the ambience - war is hell and Verdun is one of the deepest circles therein. Death can come quickly and fairness isn't really a factor. Safety is a rare luxury. There are swarms of trench raiders, gas attacks, shelling, and landmines just waiting to end your life in an instant, so having an unforgiving save system suits the theme perfectly. However, if you're struggling with a particular area and you find yourself repeatedly losing 10-20 minutes progress, you'll quickly tire of it. After a particularly bad loss of progress in which I'd pushed out too far and forgotten to save, I lost half an hour's progress and I had to put the game down for a couple of days before coming back to it. Skill issue, you might reasonably say, but I doubt I'm the only one that will experience this frustration. This system is clearly the way the dev intended you to play the game, and some of the achievements and top rankings are locked behind it. Be that as it may, I'd still recommend that you at least think about what kind of player you are rather than letting desire for hardcore gamer legitimacy and bragging rights impact your playthrough: the option is there at the start of the game to enable checkpointing and/or more frequent saving and you should consider using them if the standard system would annoy you. Tying the whole package together is the replay value, which is excellent. As in some of the classics of survival horror there are outfits to unlock, but there's also multiple endings based on your actions, achievements for challenge runs that will put your skill to the test, and even unlimited ammunition if you manage to upgrade every weapon in the game to its maximum potential. Overall, I was really impressed - this kind of passion project feels rare and special in this day and age. If you're a fan of truly old-school survival horror this is a great place to find it.
