_childDocuments_.review: I bought the deluxe edition off CD Keys for cheaper than the regular version on Steam. I have played through the game on 2 characters and here are my thoughts. The game has a solid premise and is "fun" but I cannot recommend it for the price or length of the game. If you can find it on a crazy good sale or have game pass and can play for free then give it a try, but don't have high expectations.Pros:- Difficulty does not effect achievements or in game drops (from what I can tell)- Fun premise, think Borderlands and Resident Evil 4 had a vampire Psycho baby and let it run wild.- The characters are all unique and their abilities make each one fun in their own way.- A decent story that unfolds through a play through with added bits in "files" you can find and audio collectibles (gravelocks)- Each character has a legendary weapon type specifically for them.Cons:- A multitude of glitches that have yet to be patched. From main story missions glitching on steps until you exit, change difficulty and reload (sometimes multiple times if the quest has several steps that can glitch), side quests showing up that you've already completed, environmental collision, poor enemy AI (even on harder difficulties), sound glitches that make alarms continue going off until you exit the game and reload, - Overall limited weapon selection. Few legendary weapons that are shared between all characters: 4 pistols, 4 shotguns, and 3 assault rifles. All other non legendary weapons have little variety and aren't far off from the legendary in stats- No random match making, you have to have friends lists- Must always be online to play even in single player- Story is fairly short, you can play through the campaign on easiest difficulty in about 8-12 hours depending on if you want to explore some side quests (which are also limited)This game had so much potential but sadly I doubt it will ever get fixed to the point it should have been at launch. Maybe we'll get another No Mans Sky rise to glory but I doubt it.

_childDocuments_.review: I approached Redfall with high hopes, fueled by my love for vampires, open-world games, and looter shooters. Unfortunately, this game turned out to be a crushing disappointment, and no amount of patches can salvage its core issues.Redfall is plagued by a lack of basic features that are essential for any video game. The narrative is virtually non-existent. It fails to deliver on the promise of an immersive experience in every way possible.While the gunplay manages to be enjoyable and responsive, the overall gaming experience is marred by poorly executed combat encounters. The AI, in particular, is the worst AI I have ever experienced in my life, in a video game. Constant glitches, awkward t-poses, erratic behavior and other bugs are not even the main issue. The main issue is core programming of the AI. The coding is uninspired and lazy, showcasing a lack of imagination and a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes games truly enjoyable.Even if the developers miraculously fix the AI issues, fill the game with content, and make it feature-complete, Redfall would still a below average gaming experience. It falls short of the entertainment value expected from games, turning each session into a laborious task that made me feel bored, frustrated, and ultimately disappointed.Even at a discounted price, Redfall makes me feel like I got ripped-off. The game fails to fulfill its primary purpose – providing entertainment. The initial excitement fades quickly, transforming every gaming session into a disheartening experience.Save yourselves the money, there are plenty of good games out there. Unfortunately, Redfall will never be one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok I've now completed this using Jacob as my run character.More out of a sense of stubbornness than anything else just to see where the story went but heres my 2p worth for anyone that cares.This was an AMAZING idea that was poorly executed, I'm sure we'll hear many reasons why the devs didnt do this or that and left things unfinished or unpolished but frankly at this stage, without continued support (that they are unlikely to put in) this was a TERRIBLE execution of what could have been a monumental franchise starter.  Seriously, this could have left Dishonoured and Borderlands et al in the dust for years to come if they had just poured love into it.As with most of the people who have already played this, yes the AI is shocking, the graphics are sub par in many places and the gameplay falls flat.  The echos of Borderlands shooter looter in there that could have been great had they taken the time, but frankly this game really doesn't know what it's supposed to be.I may at some point pick it back up for a run through of another character if there are fixes and updates but as this stands, do not buy this game.  I love Arkane, I loved Dishonoured and Deathloop.  I wanted to love this and I gave it every opportunity to surprise me despite its flaws, but just as the antagonists, the game is without a heartbeat :(

_childDocuments_.review: I will preface with saying that I received a key for free with the purchase of my new GPU. Nvidia ran this for a while, not sure if it still going.**EDIT**Game is fun, but not that challenging. Enemy AI is dumb, Story element is a bit lackluster. After playing a bit more, I realized that for anyone looking at the price and being on the fence about buying it, only for them to experience all of what ive seen from the game, would make me salty.I got this for free, so its whatever for me.Get this on gamepass if you really want something new to play. Else wait for a 50%+ sale.I keep my thumbsup, but lets say this gets a 5/10.**END OF EDIT**Before launch, this game received a lot of hate for various reasons , and from what I've read and seen , it just seems like a hate-train without much to justify it. _childDocuments_.review: A friend gifted me the game and I've been playing both SP and co-op.  Co-op is a buggy mess, but I haven't come across anything game breaking, and it's still a lot of fun. The interaction between the main chars is cute, and sometimes hilarious.The story is interesting - but it requires some leg-work and note-reading if you want to see the full picture. All notes you open are saved in your archive though, so you can pick up fast when your friends are in a hurry looting and read everything later. The world feels quite empty, there aren't enough enemies re-spawning in the streets or buildings (and definitely not enough car or burglary alarms). When you have roamed around and killed everything once there's just the small events (nests and rooks) left. You are forced to continue the main story to find more stuff to do, and I wish there were way more small encounters and more side quests. Pick your character with care, there's only one save... I play Remi on Daylight difficulty - I don't want a challenge, I just want to be entertained -  and random encounters are very easy while most bosses are too hard to be fun solo (in co-op it's just right). I do recommend the game, it's a lot of fun! But the game in it's current state is *not* worth the full price. It really feels like it's in early access. Get it on Game Pass or wait for it to either go on sale or (hopefully) get a massive update.

_childDocuments_.review: FIRST IMPRESSIONS This is one of those games that needs a meh option. Before the review let me talk about performance:Spec - RTX3080ti, 32 Ram, i912900KWith these specs I had no real issues with the game. I understand that some people are having worse issues than that, but it is definitely NOT "one of the worst PC launches ever" that is becoming a mantra now. Last of Us and Jedi Survivor are CLEARLY much more broken launches, so let's not call everything the worst ever.The only real performance issue for me was that It seams that when you move into a new area, sometimes you get a slight pause, but I don't think that is graphics performance issue; I think it is an always on-line loading assets issue like the Diablo 4 beta had and it is a very uncommon occurrence.I played through one neighborhood so far taking it slow and wandering as much as trying to do a mission. So far here are the ups and downs.UPS+ Atmosphere is creepy, but not scary+ The game feels like a town and the aesthetic is overall good.+ Weapons are solid and feel punchy. Despite what I have seen some others say, there are definitely several styles of weapon to play with from your basic shotgun, sniper, and handgun (I have yet to see an assault rifle) to the more specific purpose stake shooters, uv guns and flare guns.+ Weapon levels and quality both are very impactful. Weapon damage seems more level dependent and special modifier quantities are defined by rarity.+ Exploration is rewarded with lots of different things from rare guns to cosmetics.+ There is mob diversity so some fights could be interesting, but see below.+ No inventory concerns. You are frequently picking up items that the civilians can use at hubs and safe houses, but they instantly get converted to cash. So, the only thing you store is guns and even they can be instantly turned into cash.DOWNS- The world is too empty. There are too few roaming mobs so far and I have gone through a few buildings now that had only 3-6 mobs in them and one that had NONE. Perhaps this is how they intended to curb the difficulty for single player. But more would definitely be better.- The AI on most mobs is terrible. I was jumped by a pack of 4 vampires at close range. I should have been dead as I was just starting with mostly crappy weapons, but I killed them because half of them just stood there and they were getting in each others way as they just rushed me.- Small but significant bugs. That may sound contradictory, but what I mean is that there are glaring bugs that don't break the game in any way. There was one house where a vampire seemed to have gotten stuck in the ceiling and just stood there unavailable but not doing anything. In another place, I opened a chest and it displayed nothing, but then I shut it and walked away. When I came back, it was full of stuff. Things like that.- Odd immersive element choices, there are things that are just... odd and disconnected feeling about the game. You are picking up everything from rope to toilet paper for your survivors, but not aspirin or many other obvious and small essentials laying around. You also don't pick up food for them. Food is for small heals. You would think that, if you are full on health and you pick up a food item it would just cash itself for the community but it doesn't. So, I guess you are supposed to just leave it there? There was another place where there was a big deal made about a furnace in the basement and when I got to the place that allowed me to unlock the furnace... nothing happened and nothing was in there.- The graphics, while not terrible are very average and enemy motions are stilted and awkward. Even with fast vampires they are not liquid and menacing. They are marionettes with invisible strings. The cultists move more naturally, but they are pretty brain dead so they seem more like zombies in very small quantities.I would say that this game is pretty half baked, but that would not be fair as it is playable and there was only a bug or two that I saw. The main problem seems to be more design oriented than being launched to early.

_childDocuments_.review: How Does the Zero Trust Exchange Work?The Zero Trust Exchange eliminates the attack surface by making applications invisible to the internet. Plus, because the traffic never touches your network directly, lateral movement is impossible. Ultimately, this approach significantly reduces your organization's risk of falling victim to ransomware and other malware, accidental or malicious data loss, and more.In our hyperconnected, dynamic, and distributed world, the traditional security perimeter is vanishing. Applications are moving into the cloud, and users are connecting from everywhere, on all kinds of devices. IoT and OT traffic are exploding, and apps are communicating with each other across clouds. In effect, the network connecting employees, apps, workloads, and devices today is the internet itself. The cloud and data centers have become destinations, with the internet as the transport layer for traffic.So, how do you secure a network you don’t own and can’t control?The Zero Trust Exchange provides a platform of services for securing all enterprise traffic and routing it intelligently through the fastest channels. It's the foundation for secure digital transformation, delivering the agility, security, automation, and experiences your organization needs to move ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:The game is a ton of fun, provided you manage your expectations. This isn't GOTY material by any means, but I am thoroughly enjoying my time with the game playing solo.It performs decent on my system, traversal stutter notwithstanding. Your mileage *will* vary.The story is intriguing, but nothing amazing yet.The gunplay feels great once you get the controls tweaked. I play with a controller and the default response curve is dreadful. Definitely set it to low and bump your sensitivity to 3.25+ if you're playing with a gamepad.The middling:The visuals can look really good in some aspects, and really poor in others. I like the stylized art style they went with here. There can be a ton of little details in some areas, but then some woefully empty locations by contrast.Not a lot to the game yet. Seems like it maybe needed another six months to flesh out the content.Cutscenes are pretty low budget. Basically still dioramas with spoken dialogue. Good enough for the kind of game they made I suppose, but for the asking price these leave a lot to be desired.The multiplayer centric focus ultimately works against the game as a whole. I would have enjoyed this far better had it been a more typical immersive sim from Arkane. I can't confirm as I haven't played co-op by myself, but it sounds like only the host actually progresses when playing co-op which is not great in my opinion.The bad:The AI, for real. A lot of the time, enemies can't even hit you at close range and their reaction time is hilariously slow between the time they've spotted you to when they start to engage. Then sometimes you'll get absolutely wombo combo'd by a group that seems to have the difficulty knob cranked to 11. The balance needs to be tweaked considerably to have it be more even across the board. At least the checkpoints are gracious and the enemies don't regain their health upon you respawning.Limited stealth options despite the game encouraging it via tutorials. No stealth kill animations either. Just sneak up behind someone and elbow them in the b-hole. Getting stuck on invisible geometry. Or getting pulled into a wall by an enemy with no way to unstick yourself except to fast travel or quit the game.Certain controls becoming unresponsive if you don't manually clear a tutorial popup. Basically crouch and the start buttons refuse to function if this happens. Again, only way to fix is to quit the game, or hope that another tutorial message pops so you can clear it.The summary:Overall, in it's current state I'd give it a solid 6/10 despite the amount of fun I'm having with it. If they can patch it into shape and get some more content in here, it could eventually become something worthy of a higher score. Wait for a sale.

Redfall is an open-world, co-op FPS from Arkane Austin, the award-winning team behind Prey and Dishonored. Continuing Arkane's legacy of carefully crafted worlds and immersive sims, Redfall brings the studio's signature gameplay to this story-driven action shooter.

Until your sight is taken from you, and you must learn to “ feel ” the world anew... — A world of data and lies The Mask of the Oni creates a simulation of the world around you, but tread carefully: old data will show you only deceiving echoes of the past . — Swords sing unseen Even blind, you are unstoppable. _childDocuments_.review: The best way to describe this game: It's a mix of good ideas that aren't mixed well. Combat feels slow and repetitive. Your basic attacks don’t deal a lot of damage and the enemies are tanky. The game mitigates this with its gauge mechanic, in where you can activate a super attack if you hit the enemy X number times within a short amount time. But because of the stamina bar mechanic I found myself backing off and waiting for my stamina to regenerate in full before attempting an attack cycle on each enemy. All the while the enemies’ attack gauge is reset, and I’m stuck doing basic attacks again. I feel like parrying should contribute to enemies’ gauge build up, but I doesn’t.There are late game skills that do put enemies into stun states, in which you can QTE instant kill them; or just kill enemies outright. But until you unlock them, the combat will be slow and boring. The sensory mechanic is meant for exploration, finding items, locating enemies, and initiating the super attacks. I found myself pausing the game constantly switching between each sensory mode. Which you have to in order to detect environmental traps and some enemies can only be detected with a specific sensory mode.  This in and of itself isn’t bad on paper, but because you must pause each time this mechanic just slows the game to a crawl. If switching between the sensory modes were mapped to the d-pad instead of a pause menu, it wouldn’t so bad.Platforming feels stiff and awkward. There is a slight pause before falling and after landing. And for some reason you can’t grab onto ledges after air dashing. These problems are exemplified in the Tatsu boss fight, in which you’re playing the floor is lava game in between platforms over instant kill pits. But the camera is too close, and you can’t see the platforms underneath you nor the rising water that will instantly kill you. And on top of that the game suddenly introduces a ledge grabbing mechanic in which you must use the left stick to manually lift yourself onto the platform or move in between grabbable ledges. This was never present at any point prior to this fight as lifting yourself onto ledges was done automatically. Many of my deaths were contributed to me fumbling to figuring out how the platforming worked, while being hung over instant kill water. I initially assumed that you could press the jump button to move up, but all this did was detach me from the ledge and I couldn’t turn or move midair to grab onto any of the ledges.The early game Kirin boss fight almost broke me and is probably the most poorly designed boss fight I’ve ever done. The first part of the fight is a simple dodge followed by a QTE, then you can attack it while it’s stunned; you do this three times, and it only takes a small portion of its health off. Then the rest of the fight is literally just dodge into the boss’s charge attack then you can hit it once, ONE, 1 time, on its backside. I did this for 10-15 minutes straight with no variations whatsoever. Because it can kill you in two hits and it’s so tanky, I wasn’t incentivized to try anything else, lest I restart the entire boss fight again.I really wanted to love this game. I wanted to have fun playing as a cyborg samurai, but I didn’t.

_childDocuments_.review: Before going on with the review, I would like to appreciate the effort put by the team in this title. It really shows, and thats something most games lack, however, thats almost as far as you'd want to read if you expect positive stuff. I don't know if its the team lack of experience in some aspects of game design, lack of time and polishing, or just weird decisions all around, but the game at its core has some big flaws imo.In today's videogame market, flooded by long-mantained games, early accesses, betas, etc., a full game is supposed to be released in a somewhat bug-free state, however, its not the case. In my playthrough I've had a major bug (making me reset the area as a whole), and multiple minor ones that ended up in me dying in weird situations. Before writing the review, I have directly given some feedback to the devs and I'm sure they will fix some stuff, but still releasing a game like these feels like it was rushed or like no Q&A was carried prior to releasing it. Aside from the bugs, I was expecting some excellent moments driven by the core mechanics, which are very good ideas all around, however, that did not happen. The senses system plays almost no role outside of the combat part where you match them to weak "elements". Sure, there are specific parts planned for each sense to shine, but to me, even in those parts, they did not shine, the visuals for them don't do it for me, the objective of each sense seems meaningless, and it just seems as a system that should be at best a little extra, not a core mechanic.Then theres the combat system. You start the game off strong, with multiple options such as dashing, double jumps, parries, stuns, a build-up meter for extra damage, and the senses system working as elements, cool. Then you progress and you get... nothing. Theres a skill system that seems quite powerful, however as you go on if you dont max it out, most of the enemies are too tanky and ingore most of the skills available (no stun, no parry possibility on many, too many unblockable attacks) so you just stick to good old hackin' and slashin'... or so you would if the stamina system was not as tight as in Dark Souls, so your gameplay gets reduced to getting a couple hits in when you can, falling back, couple hits in, rinse and repeat. If you somehow max it out (it needs repeating levels to get exp for no reason) then the combat becomes a mix of instakilling basic enemies and QTEing your way out of harder ones, resulting in a combat that does not flow at all. This being specially true on minibosses you cant finish or instakill.Finally, Its worth mentioning some other minor design choices of the game:- Level design is very flat, many corridors are too long, puzzles are too basic, transitions are too slow to play and furthermore slow down the pace. The overall game feels too long and too slow.- There are secondary combat systems, being mainly quick-time events, that feel repetitive (same three presses for finishing every enemy), too hard for no reason () or meaningless (). Also boss fights try to bring new ideas to the table but end up not working ().- The character movement feels clunky for a 2022 game. Almost no aerial control, a weird delay on jumping/landing, very weird hitboxes on some enemies attacks (yes hammer guys im looking at you), and a few more oddities.- Checkpoints and progression feels wrong. There are levels (to call them somehow) which are made up of different locations, each location having some combats and some puzzles. If you feel like going back to the dojo at any point in the level, then you have to repeat it whole, even if locations are often times totally detached from one another. Also if you do this you lose all exp earned in the whole level you were in, which makes going to the dojo a total waste of time. Theres checkpoints that seem put at random (sometimes you die you just have to repeat that fight, other times you have to repeat multiple packs of enemies in the location). Some packs in each location are just a couple of enemies while others are multiple waves. If you die in those, you have to repeat all the waves. And to top it off, levels are too long.If you've read this far, i thank you, and would not like you to leave in such a negative note, so there's some pros:- The style is cool. The setting is appealling and the characters are for the most part likeable.- Cutscenes and dialogues are enjoyable and the story and lore are deep enough to be interesing and complex enough to keep you going, without being too obscure or overwhelming.- Art design is on point, animations are fluid, visuals are fitting for the game style, menus, dialogues and such are well presented; the game looks good overall.To me it feels like a game that had some very good ideas and planned them out properly, but then could not manage to wrap them with the basics accordingly.

_childDocuments_.review: Throughout the video game timeline, action platformers have always been popular to create and play,with few who have really tried much new in the genre.But that's not a bad thing at all, as it gives players a sense of instant familiarity with a new game in this genre.Blind Fate: Edo no Yami brings together both a feudal Japan and a postmodern cyberpunk Japanese setting, offering a mix of fast-paced and more strategic action.There is nothing else like this on the market and that is an impressive feat for a genre that has had so many entries in recent years.Check out some gameplay of the game here: While the player generally has a reasonably lit view, there are times when you're in the dark which makes identifying direct enemies not always easy, which is a fascinating approach.The heat sensor allows you to detect areas where you can go back and forth along an enemy's heat trail. Sometimes an enemy doesn't have a heat trace - in which case you may need to use the sense of smell. So where the enemy has left a body trail, you can follow that trail to them and take them out.However, Blind Fate's graphics are also very interesting with the colorful cyberpunk environmentsThe characters all look good and things like neon effects in nighttime environments are amazing. Likewise, woodland areas look beautiful with nice foliage.Blind Fate: Edo no Yami is a good action game with quite a bit of variety in platforming types with a mix of swordplay, platforming and sense-based puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: When I started writing this review, my opinion of the game was essentially positive and I wanted to recommend it. However, my opinion was mixed at the end of my playthrough, and since there's only a "yes or no" choice on Steam… I feel like leaning towards the latter more than the former.I start with the main feature of the game, namely Yami's sensors. For story-related reasons, Yami is blind and cannot directly see the world around him, but he can feel it by using 3 sensors (acoustic, olfactory, thermal). Since only one can be active at a time, exploring levels and fighting enemies results in frequent switching between these sensors. Yami can also turn them off in favor of a visual reconstruction of the environment, but the reconstruction is based on outdated data, so what he sees does not necessarily match reality. This reconstruction can be updated by collecting data released by enemies, but the truth is that you'll spend most of your playtime with sensors enabled (in order to pick up enemies, traps, or items to interact with). Many players criticize this aspect of the game, and perhaps it could have been balanced better (the acoustic sensor is probably the one you will use the most), but I liked it and I don't consider it on the list of "cons".Moving on to the combat system, Yami's move-set consists of: a melee attack, a ranged attack, a stomp attack (while in the air), a parry, and a dodge/dash. There are no complex combos, but it doesn't mean that fights are just a matter of spamming attacks. Each type of enemy has different behavior, and their attacks deal relevant damage: learning enemies' patterns is crucial to avoid losing miserably, which will happen often (especially when facing new enemies). After getting a certain number of hits, enemies expose their "weak point" which can be hit by quickly activating the correct sensor. Also, stunned enemies can be immediately destroyed with a spectacular animation by completing a QTE (but I rarely used it). Since Yami's attacks and moves consume stamina, the player must dose them wisely, or Yami will be defenseless against enemies. The boss fights are not very elaborate, but I found them varied and interesting despite their simplicity.As for exploration, the levels look quite vast at first and they don't even have a map, but their actual "explorable" part is limited so it's not too difficult to get your bearings. New areas and paths become available as the story progresses, with a few ones requiring specific abilities (and a good glance at times). One major detail is that the exploration is "one-way only": when you exit an area, it's never possible to go back. Considering that (1) fast travel is limited to the starting point of each level, and (2) some levels have multiple exits, the player must visit the same areas several times to take all the possible exits/paths. In addition, all exploration progress is saved only when Yami takes an exit to the world map, and it is lost if you return to the Dojo from the pause menu (gained experience is not lost though). At least Yami is fast when he's on the ground, so you can move through the levels very quickly… until you have to jump or grab onto ledges, which is quite difficult because of Yami's extremely reduced mobility in the air. For these reasons, the game is not a good fit for eat-and-go sessions in my opinion.Story, world, and characters are all on the list of "pros". Specifically, the game's post-apocalyptic world mixes Japanese folklore with a slight cyberpunk, and I found the result believable and fascinating. The story is interesting as well (even though predictable at times), it unravels almost completely throughout the game, with some collectibles providing a little more info about the lore. The design of the characters and enemies is very good, they're all detailed and differentiated, with the main characters well-characterized and acted. Unfortunately, stages didn't get the same care: their level design is simple and their appearance does not stand out much, which is mitigated by the fact that the player uses Yami's sensors most of the time. Last but not least, the music is good, it mixes traditional Japanese sounds with cyberpunk/tech sounds, always providing the right tone and emphasis.Unfortunately, the weak point of Blind Fate lies in technical polishing, which I believe was also the main cause of the issues I experienced during my playthrough. Some examples: the exploration percentage of levels was not always precise; in one specific QTE, the game had some problems detecting controller inputs; while exploring the peripheral corners/edges of the levels, I often found myself jumping beyond the boundaries of the stage, without being able to go back "inside the level", thus forcing me to return to the Dojo from the pause menu (and losing all the exploration progress up to that point); a few achievements rely on data released by defeated enemies, but (at the time of writing this review) there's an issue with a specific type of enemy which prevents to unlock the corresponding achievement.In conclusion, I find  to be a divisive game in many respects: either you love it, or you hate it. I enjoyed playing the game and I liked the mix of Japanese folklore and cyberpunk setting, the game also features a fair amount of content without dragging on too much. However, the lack of technical polishing and all the resulting issues lead me not to recommend it, at least not widely: I could recommend it to people who like action side-scroller games featuring slow-paced fights and a bit of exploration, in case they are willing to turn a blind eye to some possible technical problems, but I cannot recommend it to everyone. If there is an update in the future to fix some of the problems, I will be happy to update the review.

_childDocuments_.review: is a story-driven, Souls-like hack and slash side scroller in 2.5D with outstanding visuals and tough-as-nails combat. Initially, this review started with the tag-line: "If you don’t like the Dark Souls iconic difficulty, this game isn’t for you.". While this was painfully true at the moment of playing and reviewing it, things changed considerably with the release of the , which addressed a lot of the complaints regarding the difficulty and the boss fights. In my opinion, this patch  improved substantially the game by making it more accessible to anyone interested in it in the slightest, and thus allowing it to reach a wider range  of players.Set in a fictional Edo period in which Japan has been overtaken by robotic versions of Japanese folklore creatures, you play a cyborg samurai whose main body parts have been replaced by machines. Yami is an experienced warrior who lost not only his limbs, but also his sight. Despite this, he never backs off from a fight, remaining true to the core values of a samurai: honor and bravery.To compensate for his blindness, Yami employs his other senses to explore the world and to detect enemies in combat. The player can switch from normal vision to a “sound”, “smell” and respectively a ”heat” vision, each of them making different aspects of the environment visible. While the “sound” sensor is heavily used, not only because it can highlight traps, enemies approaching you (which are invisible at first and become visible as long as Yami keeps landing hits on them) and collectibles, the other two are fairly rarely used, with the “smell” sensor being the core mechanic in one boss fight only, and the “heat” vision (which is supposed to highlight exits or objects to interact with) being useful only very few times during the whole game, including another boss fight and some enemies and locations. has a rather slow-paced, but precision-based combat system, in which well-timed attacks, parries and dodges are of uttermost importance. Aside from melee-ing the enemies with his Katana, Yami also has a ranged attack in the form of a cannon with 5 bullets plus 5 extra for recharge. He also has 3 medkits that can recover his lost HP, but both the ammo and the med kits are extremely scarce in the game world, therefore you’ll need to be rather stingy with using them. As such, your attacks will mostly be melee, and timing them, together with parrying and building combos will allow Yami to stun the enemies and trigger a charged blow or a finisher, delivered through a short minigame of quickly switching to a certain sensor followed by aiming your mouse / controller in a certain position, or respectively a QTE sequence that instantly kills them.The fights can take several minutes, and normally consist of multiple waves of enemies that attack Yami in mixed ranged and melee groups. There is no way to save the game during these sequences but the levels are split into rooms / sections, with a checkpoint before each of them. Defeating enemies will award XP which can then be used to upgrade Yami’s abilities. The basic attacks do very little damage, but their final forms have considerably more impact, plus the upgraded version of dashing through enemies or stomping them will prove to be extremely useful end-game. However, in order to unlock these, a certain amount of grinding is needed.There are 5 bosses in the game, ranging from decent to being quite frustrating mainly because of the length of the fights. Some take even a dozen minutes (that is, if you manage to survive that long) and are pretty unforgiving to mistakes. The combat mechanic of the game is overall very repetitive but the boss fights are even more so, because they’re designed so that you can place only a couple of hits before a long sequence of enemies spawning follows (or some other event that makes the boss invulnerable), and in order to defeat a boss you’ll need to correctly perform many cycles of “a couple of hits on the boss” followed by “several minutes to kill enemies or continuously dodge various attacks”. On top of that, having a very low amount of heals and an extremely limited number of bullets that you can use makes these fights even more of an endless suffering, even on the easiest of the two possible difficulty modes.The plot is unraveled in a fragmented manner and until the end of the game, when everything is explained in one single sequence, the player is fed only bits, here and there, through dialogues or lore fragments. The story is perhaps even more cryptic prior to the final reveal if you don’t have any knowledge of Japanese mythology or you’re unable to recognize the meaning behind all the Japanese terms mentioned in the dialogues. Without spoiling too much of the plot, I can perhaps only hint at the fact that the story revolves around the idea of making a better world through science, but sacrificing humanity in the process.In order to obtain all the achievements, one has to defeat all the bosses, unlock all the skills, complete all the mini challenges (these act as short tutorial / practice levels), and also acquire all the data and collectibles from the world. The latter two categories require not only a considerable amount of grinding (only certain enemies seem to drop a data fragment) but also constantly switching to the “sound” sensor in order to be able to see the lore fragments. Even though it’s possible to play the entire game with the “sound” sensor on, this ruins the whole experience because the blue layer of this sensor completely covers the beautifully crafted  environments. One other annoying thing is that applying finishers during combat will automatically switch you to normal vision mode, thus you’ll have to repeatedly switch back to the “sound” mode after each finisher. The main story can be completed in around 10 hours (depending on your skills), and all areas can be revisited afterwards in order to gather the missing collectibles or more data about the enemies. Each area has a completion rate that indicates whether you still have things to discover there or not.As a casual player, I initially found the game way past my comfort zone, but after the patch was released it felt much more relaxing in comparison to my prior experience - unfortunately by then I had completed the whole game, with lots of struggles. While playing in its original form, I didn’t even have the bravery to try the “Normal” mode because the “Easy” mode was already pretty much like the “Hard” mode in other games, or even more difficult than that, but then the difficulty was noticeably scaled down. What kept me going until the end was the whole atmosphere and story. The combat is what it is - repetitive and to some extent merciless (although I don’t mind the former), but the Cyberpunk-Edo environments and the whole story line managed to always compensate for my struggles. From a neon-lit replica of Tokyo, to forest pathways, rainy and foggy docks or climbing snowy mountains, the biomes of  are all exquisitely beautiful and well-designed. The visual effects during fights are also very catchy.Underneath the many, many frustrations of a Souls-like mechanics and difficulty,  is a genuinely nice game that deserves to be explored, especially if you’re a fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I received the review key free of charge from the game publisher 101XP. I'm not affiliated with 101XP and I have not received any kind of compensation for my review.Blind Faith: Edo no Yami is what I'd call a soul-lite action game set in a feudal-punk Sengoku-era Japan. You take control of Yami, once a famous demon-hunter samurai faithfully serving the Shogun now reduced to a blind, bionic-warrior that needs to rely on his artificial sensors. While Yami tries to track down his aggressors and the plot unfolds, new secrets comes to light that makes him question his principles, values and actions.Just like most "souls" games the game features a pattern-based combat where you also need to keep an eye to your stamina bar that progressively depletes with every attack, roll, jump or dash you make; unlike traditional souls games though there's no XP penalty upon death. Each enemy has a sort of "exhaustion bar" that fills with every attack you land: when it's full you can land a precisely timed attack to the enemy's weak spot for big damage. Combat feels satisfying despite being pretty basic - no fancy combos whatsoever, just a basic 3-4 hit combo and a ranged shot; swiftly dashing around "dancing like a butterfly, stinging like a bee" is big fun, though.The game's pivotal game mechanics are the sensors: your bionic body can detect heat, movements and life through one of your 3 sensors, and only one sensor can be active at a given time. On the paper each sensors could ne useful to scan the stage for details that couldn't be seen in the standard view - hidden upgrades, doors, interactable objects, even enemies - but in practice these mechanics feels a little underused and you'll probably want stick to your "hearing" sensor for most part of the journey.While hardly stretching any graphical boundaries, Edo no Yami is a good looking game. The graphics are 3D but the game plays out on 2D stages, therefore you can't really fully appreciate the quality (or lack of thereof) of the models. The stages generally aren't filled with a big amount of details, to a point that sometimes they can even feel a little empty, and the level design could really benefit from less linear/more complex layouts from time to time. The total however is greater than the sum of its parts, and the overall aesthetics retain that traditional Japanese allure while nailing a more modern, robotic feel.As a final note, I have to say I TOTALLY fell in love with the hand-drawn sketches that you're shown throughout the game: I must've taken a couple dozens of screens while playing, they're simply stunning. Kudos to the artists!I completed the game in almost 14 hours. I've been playing the whole game on the go on my Steam Deck, it was a match made in Heaven and for the most part a flawless experience, only partially marred by a couple of hard crashes (the devs are running a Discord server and are very helpful when reporting a bug) and some sporadic performance slowdowns in very specific areas that hardly compromised my gaming experience. I definitely enjoyed my time with the game. Of course you could argue that there would be a lot of room for improvement - as I said earlier, the level design could be expanded and the sensor mechanics, while being neat on the paper, unfortunately didn't show their full potential throughout the game. But all in all, I still think that Edo no Yami could be a good fit for those who love some good samurai action, a nice story and some frankly-quite-sick steampunk aesthetics.

_childDocuments_.review: The quality is very polished and has amazing aesthetics. Been looking forward to this game for some time. Can't provide a full review because I just started playing it, but the tutorial seems a bit half-arsed. At times, they don't really provide enough hints to the next steps in the tutorials. The Introduction & training Dojo needs more information provided on what to do, you often find yourself trying everything to trigger the next sequence with very little information. Most selection items you can double click instead of interacting with your keyboard if you're lazy like me.Also the story line has to be triggered per discussion, kind of annoying better to just wait a few seconds and have them exchange words in a timely manner. I sat there wondering why the other guy wouldn't talk until I realized I needed to click the mouse to move forward in the discussion 🙄If you get to the Dojo scene and asked to use your sensor to detect the enemies, switch  between all three sensors, its needed to see all the enemies in separate sensor habitats. I still give it a thumbs up, the game seems pretty sweet and continuity follows through as promised.Edit:So back after a couple hours and there seems to be something missing in this game. As mentioned earlier, its that "Pretty" kind of game, but there's something drab ab out the combat system. There is nothing suave or swift about your attacks/swings, but more of a draw back and hesitation between swings, quite annoying really. The XP system still hasn't identified itself for a purpose, and the talent tree has no explanation. No idea how to unlock skills for that matter.I feel absolutely useless using my sensors and basic swing technique. The second attempt on first boss (as per the story goes) feel like a chore fighting with my hands tied behind my back blindfolded... and my game is on easy mind you. _childDocuments_.review: Blind Fate: Edo no Yami:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ The game takes place in the aftermath of the apocalypse in Japan. Your name is Yami, a Demon Hunter, part of the Shogunate. Now a blind cyber-Samurai equipped with a sharp sword in one hand and an arm that can shoot projectiles, you are sent by your master to retrieve information from the Tengun AI. This is Blind Fate: Edo no Yami!Blind Fate: Edo no Yami is a cyberpunk, hack-and-slash platformer game developed by Troglobytes Games and published by 101XP on the 15th of September 2022 on the Steam platform. The game is also available on PS4/PS5, Xbox One, Xbox One Series X|S and Nintendo switch.What an interesting game with interesting ideas and mechanisms, but I don’t think they gel correctly together. In this game, there are 11 locations to visit, including the Dojo, where you can train, receive upgrades for melee and distance weapons, health, stamina and, of course, unlock new skills. To unlock a skill, you’ll need experience points which you gather by eliminating enemies during a level. There are 6 skills in total, and you can upgrade them 4 times. All the other upgrades will be found as data through the levels and can be implemented at the Dojo through Tengo the AI.As you start the game, you will play the first level until a certain point, and from there, you’ll be able to access the Dojo. From that point, you’ll be able to select any of the available levels that are currently unlocked. You can go back to all unlock levels at any time to try to complete them 100% if you wish. But when you unlock the Palace, you must finish and beat the last boss before returning to the Dojo. The gameplay is interesting in itself, but the combat mechanisms are my biggest complaint! Yes, the game is a bit challenging at first as you get used to the three senses that Yami has, but as you unlock more skills, the challenging aspect of the game diminishes rapidly. So, what are Yami’s senses? Well, as he is blind, he can’t see the world he is in at first, and he will need to rely on his hearing to locate data, upgrades, lore, medick, and bullet kits which all make noises. As he finds data, the world will appear and also change as he moves further into the level. He also uses his hearing to detect enemies. The heat senses will allow him to find new areas with the levels as long as there is heat. And the last sense can detect lives around the levels. But let’s be really fair here, you will probably use the hearing sense at least 95% of your playthrough. The other aspect of the senses is that they activate the super moves, which I found really fun at first but draining after a while as it slows down the combat dramatically. What do I mean by that? Well, all the ground enemies need to be hit several times, and then a sense symbol will appear next to their life bar. You activate the super move by switching to the correct senses for a few seconds. During these few seconds, the image will be static, except for a beam of white light that shoots onto the image at an angle and becomes narrower as you look at it. In the middle of this light, an orange arrow will appear, and you need to move Yami’s arrow onto the orange arrow and press the attack button to activate the kill. It just slows down the combat fluidity far too much. Not only can you stunt enemies and activate another powerful attack, but this time, you have to press the gamepad buttons in sequences shown during the move to execute it. That said, once you unlock the second, third and fourth stomping skills, not the challenging aspect of the game is gone, and you’ll probably use this move instead of the repetitive slow moves. The bosses’ fights are fun, but within the first couple of attempts, you’ll definitely figure out how to defeat them (including the last boss), which is a bit of a shame.In terms of enemies, they are mostly ground robots of different sizes and a couple of aerial robots too. So again, the start of the game is a bit more challenging than after you’ve unlocked some skills.The story is average, but I did enjoy the artistic cutscenes, which refreshed the game. Graphically, the game is sound, and the apocalyptic atmosphere is well portrayed. The fact that there are too many slow-motion attacks, even if you decide not to follow through with them, negatively impacts the gameplay. This title has been translated into 10 languages and has full controller support and Steam cloud. Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Nice graphics+	Interesting concept with the implementation of senses+	Nice hand-drawn cutscenes+	The ability to come back to any level to complete it+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	Not a very challenging game-	Too many slow-motion attacks-	No trading cardsBlind Fate: Edo no Yami is an interesting concept but has far too many slow-motion attacks, which impacts the fluidity of the combat.  6/10 Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

(helps I guess) Cons:- Gets Repetitive VERY FAST!- Some of THE most annoying boss fights, Kirin (devs say they fixed this, I still found it annoying), Tatsu, Amatsumara- Bosses are INCREDIBLY TANKY!!- No Direction, or TIPS of what to do next in some cases and your stuck either looking online or YT to figure out how to progress- Enemies can STILL damage you after your Blade Dash Finish skill (this is really stupid, you should be invincible but that's just my opinion)- There are evident Game Bugs, Lots of them (unobtainable drops, level hangs up and unable to progress, VFX issues)\- Medpacks are dropped VERY rarely, gets annoying fast, every time you uses a finisher you should regain health or at least have the enemies drop a medpack, geeeezBy the end of the game I just wanted it to be over so I can uninstall lol, maybe there are others who will enjoy this but it just wasn't for me. _childDocuments_.review: I was incredibly excited to play this game after watching the trailer. I've always loved combat with a focus on timing and parrying (I mean, just look at my playtime in Sekiro) so to bring it to a 2D platformer seemed like an interesting idea. The senses mechanic is incredibly unique and interesting, and I love the idea of getting more information about the world from potentially outdated sources. The setting is also perfect – I love cyberpunk and I love samurai, so this game seemed PERFECT to me.How disappointed I was when I booted it up and played it. The first hour or so was fun! I enjoyed getting to grips with the combat and learning more about Yami's character. However, once I reached the forest, I got very burnt out very quickly. Zero enemy variety. Encounters every other minute. A constant cycle of the same repetitive attack patterns, over and over again. I haven't got past the forest yet. Its boss, , was the final nail in the coffin for me. The first 10 minutes’ worth of attempts were spent simply trying to figure out what the hell to do, and then the next 40 were spent doing what the game asked me to, and then being killed at the end because it decided it didn’t want to read my input, even though I pressed my F key just as hard as I had the last 20 times. I tried to push through it, hoping that maybe this time it won’t screw me over arbitrarily and I’ll be able to move on to something more interesting. Unfortunately, the slow-paced snooze-fest of a boss fight was just too boring to justify trying again that many times. I closed the game. I don’t know if I’ll return to this game. I want to, because it’s clear that the developers put an immense amount of effort into it. The graphics are impressive, the story is compelling, and their ideas are fantastic. They have all the right ingredients for a perfect game, but unfortunately, it may have been slightly too ambitious for such a new studio. The controls are full to the brim with jank, and the combat is entirely less inspiring and engaging than I had anticipated; the enemies are repetitive and boring to fight. I truly respect the work they’ve done on this game, and I wish it could have been better. It had so much potential – it just needed a little more time in the oven. I want to give it a second, third, fourth chance. I don’t know how long it will take me – I’m aware the game is rather short – but perhaps someday I’ll have a  review to post here. 3.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Its quite an enjoyable game with an interesting concept of using specific senses to be able to interact with certain things as you are playing a blind samurai.Not the best but its decently written, there are some parts which feels rushed or skipped. Narration and dialogue is a little off or missing on some parts. Overall its alright. The game can be completed within 3 - 4 hours or less if you only focus on the main story playthrough.Most time can be spent on exploring all the maps and maxing out the skill tree for specific skills to get the 100% (my current play time is mainly exploring before finishing the story).There is not a lot of controls for combat which makes it simple to play. Once you know the attack patterns, it gets pretty easy and repetitive. There are the mechanics of "critical strikes" and finishers with some QTE action which adds a little spice to the gameplay.Expected since it is a new game but it did not ruin my experience for the most part cause it happens rarely. Going to the main menu and starting back solves it.- After maxing out the health upgrade, health bar becomes bugged and shows full health even when taking damage. _childDocuments_.review: This review is written for version 1.01TL;DR: This was a good game.Pros:- Great aesthetics- Epic takedowns- Pumped bossfight music- Polished combat- VERY useful skills (like you need them to even survive later on)- Small amount of metroid/backtracking- A good story- Dad jokes (your AI companion is a funny one)- Intrigueing concept (blind protagonist has to use other senses to navigate the world and his enemies)- You can go back to earlier levels after you finished the game to clean upCons:- Start of the game is a bit grindy until you get your dodge to a stunlock level- Some bugs will force you to quit the game and reload (there are some crashes too)- Underutilized senses. Most of the game you only need the hearing sense and it kinds forces you to use that more because collectibles are only visible in hearing mode- Platforming is... well... inconsistent. Sometimes your doublejump moves you forward like 1 step, other times it's an entire screen. You can't use jump (nor double jump) from hanging ledges. A bit counterintuitive and it can cause some confusion in a certain bossfight- Playing the "human" version of your character after the bionic hero with zero skills felt bland. The bossfight was okay though.All in all I think this one was definitely worth playing. Will be even better after the first couple of feedbacks and the initial defects getting fixed I guess. I'll be looking forward to later games if they make any.

_childDocuments_.review: This game should really be the standard by which remasters are judged. I got the original on the PS1 ages ago and thoroughly enjoyed it despite its flaws. The remastered version does a lot to iron out the original flaws (the inclusion of the new journal helps immensely in keeping on track with stories and events, which was likely the biggest flaw in the original), restores tons of cut or unfinished content (big-yay here), and gives a new character to play. It also has an in-game artbook, and the ability to change the gamespeed between x1 and x3 (and tracks overworld and combat speeds separately, so if you prefer exploration at x1 and combat at x2-3, it's got your back).Probably the most amazing new feature is the New Game +, which while not an original idea (NG+ was a popular inclusion for a number of games including other Squaresoft titles like Parasite Eve), this remaster's version is hands down the best implementation of a NG+ I've ever seen. Once you have unlocked NG+ (simply clear any hero's main quest) you can then choose NG+ from that point on. When you choose NG+, you may import stuff from any save file you have (it doesn't have to be an end-game file), and it will ask you what information you want to import into your new file, with a checkbox system. This means you get to play your NG+ the way you want. Do you want to breeze through the next main story using end-game characters? Maybe you want to start out pretty normal and level up, but you want to keep your credits and items you spent time grinding before? What if you don't want any of that, but you want to import previously known spells and abilities? You can do all of this and more. The NG+ also adds a layer of replayability for both the completionist and the optimizer. A number of unique items found throughout a playthrough can be carried through to subsequent playthroughs. For example, if during a quest a certain NPC offers to either join you or give you a legendary sword, if you take the sword it can be carried over to a new playthrough, even if in the new playthrough you have the NPC join you instead. If you're a power gamer or completionist, you might make a point to track down multiple copies of the strongest end-game gear to outfit your whole team with, or you might make a point to max every character's stats and learn all the skills and magic they possibly can (a task that would be harrowing on a single file, but relatively do-able if you import your gains from previous games).That's not even including how utterly beautiful the game is compared to the original. The sprites are lovely, and the environments have been touched up and expanded for modern monitors (a lot of the game's art wasn't visible in the original release due to aspect ratio issues). All the characters look wonderful.Honestly, if you are at all a fan of the original you should definitely buy this. Even it's full asking price is cheaper than the original game was when it came out, and it is the original made better in just about every way imaginable. Even if you never played the original, you should play this version if you ever intend to. It is truly what every remaster should be.

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier with missing content restored. The UI is glaringly mobile-like, but the worst offenses can be disabled in the menu (such as the "dash" touchscreen button on the map screen.) Upscaling the pre-rendered backgrounds wasn't going to be perfect no matter what, but the result is pretty good. The sprites look fine. Some useful quality-of-life mechanisms have been added, such as a "Story" menu option that recaps the previous events and hints where to go or what to do now. In one case it even seems to alert you to the possibility of side quests you might otherwise miss, at least in Red's scenario. I haven't seen any censorship in either the graphics or the dialogue yet (at least compared to the PSX original.) So far, this is a faithful remaster.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This may be the best of the remasters on Square's list. Why? 1) It's still relatively true to the original localisation except the skill names, RIP to those. Also dialogue has been sanitised a bit, but that's a minor thing.2) The new sprites are absolutely gorgeous compared to the original slightly pixelated blobs. I actually couldn't see what the characters were doing clearly in the original, but now I can and it's very refreshing.3) Plenty of QoL improvements including unlimited party space (great for a game with a large cast of optional recruitables!), story hints with plenty of warnings before Point of No Return, field AND battle speed-ups, and a New Game+ feature to take the edge off grinding through multiple scenarios.4) They kept certain quirky glitches that were very advantageous to the players. We're very grateful. 5) This game was originally released during Square's infamous 'rush to release' era where a number of their games were released either on the dot or ahead of schedule resulting in plenty of cut content or slightly incoherent plots (due to the cut content). This Remaster adds a good portion of that lost content back in along with the intended 8th route whose protagonist wound up being demoted to extra in the original release. 6) Still one of the best soundtracks out there. Most of the battle music are as earwormy as I remember.If you were a fan of the original and were wondering if it's worth shelling out for a remaster, Then I can heartily recommend a yes. If you're a new player wondering what's the deal with this obscure little title, I can recommend but with a few caveats:1) This isn't your typical RPG. It has a fairly open-world concept and you can more or less get on and off the plot railroad at your leisure. Each route is fairly short, and you can probably expect to clear one between 10 to 12 hours of leisurely gameplay. 2) If you're a grinder, you'll either love or hate the way battle difficulty scales in this game. The more battles you fight, the more difficult the enemies become sometimes to the point of unforgiving. You don't level up so much as grow stats, which are dependent on your choice of action and the RNG. Your skill development is also very dependent on RNG. Expect a good portion of your playtime to be dedicated to trying to get the skills you want. 3) Use a guide for your first route, or save often in different slots. it's entirely possible to be trapped in a place of no return or deep in a dungeon with the battle difficulty having ramped up beyond your character's abilities to manage. There's no shame in this: Most seasoned SF players will still recommend and rely on a guide for the very complex growth mechanics of monster party members.4) Expect to fail a few times (or a lot) as you get to know the world and the mechanics. If you're up to the challenge then welcome to the Frontier and have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so this is a review geared towards people who already played Saga Frontier and just want to know how this runs on PC. I'll flesh out this review fully later on when I'm through a few character routes, because I like to take my time grinding and all.*First update after finishing one route. Check the bottomFor all intents and purposes, it's a great remaster. The UI might put some people off, but you can hide the mobile like interface in Settings. The rest runs well. The game didn't crash on me in about 3-4 hours session. In certain areas I've gotten random hangups but overall it's rare. But I have gotten some slight pause from big flashy combos. You can quick save like in the original. Heck the soft reset you used to be able to do on certain PS1 game? You can do that in this game too. L1 + L2 + R1 + R2 + Start + Select. The load time is quick. The ship transition screen? Those can be skipped with a button press except for that one instance where it's quest related, yes the giant whale one. The Scrap shop bug is still in the game, wink wink. In terms of cut content restoration, since I haven't had time to play through everything since the game literally came out yesterday, I can't tell you. The game was played entirely with a controller. I used two to test: Steelseries Stratus Duo and the 8bitdo SN30 pro+. The Steelseries I had a lot of issues getting it to run properly. The inputs were barely registering. Character was sliding around from a gentle nudge on the analog stick. Controller was continuously dropping in and out the game. Absolutely unplayable when said controller performed well enough for Blaster Master and Bloodstained. After swapping to SN30 pro+, everything's golden. I'm not sure who to blame for wonky controller configuration. Mouse and keyboard works too, but I've played SF on PS1 so I'm more used to controller setup. In settings you can adjust Map Speed and Battle Speed up to 3x the original speed. Personally I wish it can go even faster, but that's just me. My biggest beef with this remaster: Egad the translations. OMG the translations. The skill names. Did they have to change the skill names?! Gale Slash is now called Tornado Slash when its improved version is already Twin Gales in the Remaster. Air Throw is Tumble. The weird name changes go on. I was trying to raise a monster by absorbing skills, only to find a decent amount of names changed into something else. Ugh. Yeah You'll want to have a guide open for this if you are going to raise monsters.Additional Remaster stuff: **Fuse becomes available once you've beaten one route. I picked Lute's first, but it shouldn't be character specific? *They added Gallery and Sound on the main screen. All of that is available immediately and requires no unlocking. Nice if you want to listen to the soundtrack in the background*I already mentioned Battle Speed and Map Speed adjustments.*You can play the game in Japanese or English, but you can't change that in the middle of the run.*They added a Story tab under your usual Menu options so if you are lost, you can look at that to see as hints on how to progress. Much more player friendly to newcomers. (Lute's route still looks a bit skimpy according to this tab though)*There's a Combo tab under Menu that shows the recent Combos that you've performed in battle. You can favorite 3, but does setting them as favorites do anything to increase the chance of combo success at all?**New game + becomes available once you've finished one character route. New Game+ can carry over some of your items, techs, attributes and other stuff: Enemy rank, HP, JP, WP, Attributes, Credits, Items, Skills, Spells, Mystic Abilities, Monster Abilities, Monster Types, and Programs.Bottomline. If you loved Saga Frontier and was on the fence about this Remaster, there's no reason not to get this. This game runs well, plays well and even added in the cut content. If anything changes that's game breaking though, I'll definitely update this review.

_childDocuments_.review: a super clunky and old JRPG near and dear ot my heart that I was convinced nobody in the world knew about except for me. turnms out I was wrong, lol.it's nice seeing ppl reminisce about the game, our old teams, the epic junkyard scrap shortselling exploit, all the good stuff that I thought only I knew of - it wasn't a huge game when it came out. And it is VERy bizare. you play muiltiple characters as the MC, but you often run into the other characters in your runs.every character has their own special skill, bnut for the most part -0 your wep decides what you learn in battle. so you want a suplexing master of a robot? just use martial arts! you won't gain stats from the gear though, the equip system is strange. the skill system is odder ( you learn new moves just in mid battle ) you get these disgaea-like combos of ppl piling into one atytack for these incredible attack sequences ( when you select the right moves, with the right ppl.,.. in the right spots on the field ) oh and did i mention you don't die when your HP runs out? you do " die " in battle, but you come back. you instead lose 1 LP, a LIFE POINT. do you want to know what happens when your un-recoverable LP run out? ( you don't, trust me )why is this game so confusing, complex, and filled ot the brim with arbitrary systems, leveling and end game? bc it's 2nd division, man. they were ahead of their time. tons of wild ideas, most of em land, a few don't - and the ones that don't land are pretty miserable ( lookin at you, riki ) - but generally, this game is pretty great. You will almost always be finding new stuff out. there's tons of end-game content, and post game content. the writing is weird, the characters are weird - it's enjoyably weird. I highly recommend you go in blind. and with that regard, talk to EVERYONE. you might not progress till you talk to X person, for no good reason. And why are they in Y spot now? I just saw them back at X.... that's Saga Frontier for ya, my dude. blind entry, try the chars out, and if you wanna learn on your own, you will get some enjoyment out of it. but if all these mechanics confuse you, or seem daunting - grab a guide online. _childDocuments_.review: It took almost 20 years, but finally the world could enjoy the complete SaGa Frontier. Of course I started Asellus as my first scenario, since her original story was cut down so much, and for decades I could only imagine what her complete story looked like. Based on the Essence of SaGa Frontier and 2nd Div., this game was originally developed only about 1.5 years and they only had a month to do a QA.To think SaGa Frontier is getting a remaster and completed is like a dream come true. This remaster sets a new benchmark of remaster standard. I cannot be more than happy. I played the original game so many times to the point I know this game like the back of my hand. I know this is gonna be GOTY. Thank you very much Square Enix, especially Masanori  Ichikawa to give this game a chance despite being considered obscure in the jrpg scene. Best year ever for SaGa Frontier fans! (please give us SaGa frontier II too if possible)UPDATE:After 53 hours, I finally finished the entire game, along with Fuse's scenario, it is an amazing experience. Why you may be disappointed:- It seems all bad bugs present in the original game are still present, they just didn't bother to fix them. Unfortunately it means Suzaku's form is still buggy, and if you started Emilia's rune quest without getting the pebbles, you can be possibly unable to finish the Rune quest because Tanzer arc will not trigger. However, Fuse's scenarios added a lot of contents based on Fuse's investigation log from the essence of Saga Frontier, the contents from his scenario really enrich the narratives, and solve the narrative gaps that were present in the original PSX. The catch: Fuse's scenario is similar with Lute for the better or worse, you don't need to repeat the dungeons over and over again. You will be automatically watching the cutscenes, and you are free to recruit whomever you want to recruit. 10/10. Thank you for the release of this remaster. Finally SaGa Frontier fans have a proper closure!UPDATE 2:Commentaries on restored contents (spoilers alerts):- Asellus' restored contents were well documented, it is quite fortunate that they managed to restore the most important cutscenes with Nashiira, Furdo, and Dr. Nusakan which you could access after the Dark Labyrinth arc. However, there's one particular disconnect regarding Trinity abduction case: it's like a filler that just added just for the sake being restored. During the escape from Facinaturu arc, Asellus has three options to escape, and one of them is being abducted by Trinity, which crossed her scenario with Emilia's story arc where she infiltrated Trinity lambda base with her dancer costume. Emilia's status is temporary during this story, and you can recruit her permanently when you start the Arcane magic quest. However to my disappointment, they didn't add any additional conversations. Emilia joined Asellus' party and re-introducing her name again even though she already did that during Trinity lambda base arc. That actually created a sense of disconnection. Could have been nicer had they added an extra conversations if Asellus chose this option to escape from Facinaturu.- A similar problem occurred in Fuse's casefiles. So Emelia will not join Fuse until her casefile finished, which made sense given the background story of those two characters where they are in odds with each other. However what doesn't make sense is what happened outside Emilia's casefile: you will notice that Ren can join Fuse's party anytime. Given that Emilia's story started because of what happened to Ren, it means his presence created a paradox, as Emilia's story arc has not happened, and she had no reason to join Gradius and do a covert op as a bunny girl. I understand that cohesive narratives are not really the main point of SaGa Frontier, but it could have been handled better.despite those oddities, Asellus' and Fuse's restored contents will be a great delight to those who have been waiting for two decades for SaGa Frontier to complete. If someday Kawazu add DLCs that restore even more cut contents, I definitely will buy them.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this when I was young, and loved it. I picked this up and played it fresh and, after beating Emilia's scenario, felt pretty bad. It wasn't that fun. I thought that this might be another game ruined by nostalgia goggles.But then I played T260s scenario with New Game+, and everything clicked! It all felt magical again, and weird... in a good way! The SaGa games are unique in that unlike most JRPGs where your exploration is relegated to locations and plot, SaGa has you explore systems. 70% of the systems play out just fine without you understanding them, but once your third eye opens and you start catching glimpses of little mysteries and curious exceptions, it's like a whole new dimension pops into existence.New Game+ is the real charmer here. It is so vital to my experience that I think it must have been planned from the get-go and just didn't make it into the original product because of time management. You gather 15+ characters in every scenario, but you almost always just play with 5. How could you not? New recruits are a bit weaker than your main team. Plus, because battle difficulty scales dynamically with the number of battles you do, it's hard to justify swapping to other teams just to grind them. NG+ fixes that! Suddenly you aren't afraid to experiment. Now you can recruit characters from previous scenarios who have end-game stats, which frees you up to try new combos, or allows you to have one heavy-hitter carry a team of weak hitters until they reach some for of potential. You can get weird and make your best mage learn some kung fu! You can try changing Turnip Monster into a giant Squid! As you barrel through scenarios, you collect new people and old people, and you feel like you're fleshing out your own album of greatest hits!I sat down with a book and pencil for this game. For hours, I catalogued movesets and progress. I never do this with games. Never. Every time a Monster on my team absorbed a new skill, I'd set down my controller and write it on my growing list. I'd experiment, I'd play around.It's not all perfect, though. The biggest shame of the game can be summed up by what my spouse said to me when she walked into the room and saw me fighting a Xeno enemy in Koorong: "Babe... this is the ugliest game I've ever seen you play!"Well, she's not wrong. This is one of those ugly, ratty dogs only its owner could love. I recommend owning it.

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier is my favourite JRPG ever, which is weird, because it's also somewhat flawed.Compared to polished gems like Chrono Trigger and FFVI, SaGa Frontier can look like an uncultured barbarian. There's not that much dialogue, the world is full of dead ends, the difficulty is uneven. However, it compensates it's roughness with style, originality and sheer fun. It also has a lot of tactical depth, and a somewhat arcane stat/leveling system.But the most important part is, SaGa Frontier means FUN.It's good to do a double or triple tech in Chrono Trigger? Yes, but it's not barely as satisfying as managing a 4 or 5-character combo in SF.It's good to release a Limit break in FFVII? Yes, but it's not as good as suddenly learning a powerful new sword or martial arts skill right when you're losing in a desperate boss fight.Also, it has STYLE. All SaGa games I've played have crazily cool sprites (RS2, RS3, SF1 and 2) - I look at them and I just feel I wanna have them on my team. I felt that way since the first time I even laid my eyes on SF, decades ago. Also, the soundtrack!! Blessed be Kenji Ito!SF makes you feel powerful - you're always unleashing amazing fighting moves, learning cool magic and fighting really hard, menacing bosses that force you to the limit. This is no Final Fantasy, you're not babysitted through the game, not even at the beginning. Expect to die a bunch of times, at least when you're still learning. Real power comes with real challenge.Except for Lute, all the characters have interesting stories - and trek through the open world in a particular way. There's a lot of replayability. I really like the open world approach, in all of it's limitations. I get it that a beginner can feel lost, but this is because we've been spoiled by overly linear Final Fantasies. Just get your ♥♥♥♥ together and go do some exploration! You'll probably stumble upon something on the way.Also, I love how robots, swordsmans, magical vampire-elves and monsters get along in this crazy setting. You can have a magician with a bazooka, Or maybe not, if you don't want to. You can build your own team the way you like it, choose the magical schools that you feel akin. Every team behaves differently and that makes it feel more personal.Now, for the downsides. I already mentioned the lack of dialogue - and the frequent dead ends in exploration. It really feels like the game was released before it was ready. Had they given a couple more months to the devs, this game would be the BEST - not only in my nostalgia-tinted perception.I'm ok with the JRPG approach of visuals/music over text, but in SaGa games it sometimes feels a bit extra dry. I'm left thirsting for every bit of personalized dialogue lines and cutscenes. I wish the world would react a bit more differently depending on what is your main character, or your team. I mean, there's a little bit of that here and there, but it falls short of my tastes.I'm ok with the difficulty of the game, but the grind and the easy enemy battles really bore me. Fortunately, the remaster offers a 3x speed option for battles (without distorting the battle music, which is better than any emulator would do!)The game may sometimes lock you into a final dungeon or corner you before a difficult boss fight. So it's good to keep a lot of saves if you don't know where you're threading. Asellus has the best scenario storywise, but I remember being cornered by a boss and having to begin again in the PSX version.All in all, I think all JRPG fans should try this out. Just pick the easier and more linear scenarios (Red, Emelia or T260G) for a starter and enjoy the game in all it's quirkiness.ps. you probably should edit the mobile HUD out of your screen.
