_childDocuments_.review: I have beat the game now with all of the characters and can say I would recommend this game.  Do understand what you are getting.  You are getting seven different characters, each with different stories and then an extra character who will go and recap the character's stories when you beat the game with a character.  The quality of the different characters' stores varies greatly.  Some characters have a branching and interesting story while a couple of characters literally can face their final boss after talking to two characters.  I recommend using Emilia to start with, as she has a developed storyline, because if you use a character like Lute or Blue you may be disappointed by the lack of story or the lack of an ending and think that all characters are like this.  Even for the more developed characters you are not getting lots of dialog, the stories are in many cases left vague and character motivations can be hard to determine.This game is a remaster of a game from the late 90's.  I appreciate what they have added.  You can run from enemies now and there is cut content that has been added, as well as Fuse as a playable character, but he serves mainly to recap a character's story when you have completed the game.  This is nice as it adds and explains things that were left vague in the characters' stories when you first play them.  In the 90's I beat the game with Blue and then quit, as I was not satisfied with the ending.  Here Fuse gives Blue a proper ending.  The remaster also adds a new game plus, and lets you pick what carries over, which is a great feature.Saga Frontier is a difficult game.  There are many hidden or poorly explained systems, which is not a bad thing, but there are bosses that require you to use these systems to beat them.  They are not optional bosses either, so you may need a guide for this game.  I try not to use guides, but for Riki I had to, to beat a boss that required a combo system that I had not used (or needed to) the entire game.  The game does feel like it experiments and tries many things and sometimes it succeeds and sometimes it fails.  The game does not have levels, but instead you gain attributes for humans and mystics, based on what actions they take during battle.  Robots gain strength based on equipment they use and monsters eat other monster's meat to transform.  It is much like the saga games on the Gameboy (released as Final Fantasy Legends over in the West)Graphics look nice, but the option to use the original character sprites would be nice.  The music is also great, I have Time Lord's Domain on my tunes that I listen to in my car.If you can handle the difficulty and sometimes experimental nature of this game and the game's vagueness, then I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10e: whoops turns out ZAUBER is a real game and not a beta SaGa Frontier name. While I'm here, I do appreciate that the devs put in the effort to fix a save bug (albeit in a roundabout way) and add more resolutions to the game. I'm excited to see the old monster system be brought back!I just completed the entire game, including all of Fuse's case files. I haven't gotten Fuse's alternate endings nor have I beaten one of the max leveled final bosses, but I can tell you right now that this is 1000x better than the original game. Every single useful glitch still exists and works just like the original, including Infinite Overdrive via SnakeOil. In fact, they even made Takonomics *better* than the original glitch. The upscaled and redrawn graphics are incredible, the fast forward option is amazing (though I and many others would love the option to rebind it to something other than R3), auto-save is a life-saver, Flee is a glorious meme; every single QoL feature that was added just for the remaster is perfect. And the new music, oh my god it's so good!!! Fuse's scenario is a joy to play, even though it's a little bit weird at first. With that being said, there are still things I'm not entirely happy with:- While the game is much more welcoming to new players, it can still kick their asses way too hard in my opinion. Tutorials for things like Battle Rank, Monsters, Mecs, etc. would greatly help with this- The monster system is easier to use, but still very confusing and still requires a guide from GameFAQs to effectively utilize. I would love for there to be a bestiary that shows you how to transform into monsters you've encountered throughout your playthrough. Another thing to add to the monster system would be for the ability to overwrite a skill even if you're not full on skills. It unfortunately makes it impossible for people to get forms like Skullasaurus and TrisaurJr as Thunder the moment you recruit him, though that's a very minor thing- From a casual perspective, Virgil is still very confusing- The new attack and item names are okay, but there are quite a handful that are either strange or downright bad- Some if not most of the new collision maps are just as bad as the original game, which is a shame- Some animations are weird. When Skullasaurus dies, it just disappears for a moment. With all of that said, I do think this game is very much worth your $25. This version is superior to the PSX version in every single way and you're missing out if you don't at least give the game a try. 9/10 pls give Essence of SaGa Frontier Remastered=====================================I do hope that Ichikawa and Kawazu decide it's worth it to add DLC to this game to actually finish it. That would be amazing. They should call it the Eternal Frontier DLC cuz that'd be funny and also a call back to what the game could have been called back in 1996. I already have several ideas for DLC packs outside of some other more obvious mechanical DLC packs:- Put Itako, the 9th protagonist, back in the game (I know you want to devs I saw the RSRS stream. Also maybe add in a cut title screen BG in the process?)- Flesh out the lore behind Cube and the Rings even more cuz their plot is really cool- Put Nirvana and Golden Gate back in the game- Finish the entirety of Magic Kingdom and add Blue's missing content (including the ability for protagonists to visit the Overt Academy)- Put Santario back in the game and add Red's missing content (maybe even make Alkarl playable?)- Add the rest of Asellus' missing content (yes, there's still wayyy more, though I don't care as much about this since Mystic Visit and the new Facinaturu escape routes are already enough for me)- Add Lute's missing content please he sorely needs more story outside of talking to Captain Hamilton (including Yorkland Lady and maybe Went. Possibly even put in the Golem Ring stuff?)- Finish Nelson (tied to Lute's missing content)- Bring back Joker as Emelia's final boss and restore the rest of her cut content- Bring back the removed Shingrow areas- Make Shuzer Base accessible by everyone again that'd be very cool- Restore Despair's cut content please it existed until 1997 it's so cool please Kawazu please- Restore Sei's Tomb's cut content (very minor thing)- Add in T260G's cut content (very minor thing since her scenario is finished as-is in my opinion)- Add the option to use Fuse's beta design upon beating Fuse's scenario (very minor thing)- Restore MBlack's removed content please his cut attacks are so cool (tied to Red's missing content)- Bring back Limbo that was a cool idea- Bring back cut attacks such as Shocked Stunned Mec and items such as AlkaRing- Release more footage of what the game looked like throughout development, from mid-1996 to release (maybe even playable bits? that'd be really sick)I understand that a lot of this stuff will be impossible since I'm aware that the developers don't have all of the source code for the game, but I do know they have some source code. Even just adding a couple things from this way too extensive list would be enough for me to give the game 11/10 tbh

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite game.If you're familiar with it but curious about the changes, here is a summary of some of the less obvious things you may be wondering about:The item descriptions are improved. Now it is a lot easier to know exactly what each piece of equipment is doing, and a lot of them have hidden skills that were easy to miss. It's easier to know how Mystic and Mech equipment affect their stats as well as what kinds of attacks your shields are guarding against.New Game Plus makes it advantageous to force characters to give up any magics they come with by default. For example, if Mei-Ling learns every Shadow magic, in New Game Plus she will have all of her Shadow magic as well as the two Light spells she starts with- however, the gift doesn't carry over, and such a character can't enter Omble OR the Labyrinth. This also applies to every Mystic: if you purchase Realm magic for them, then (in the next scenario you choose) they can keep those magics as they learn Mystic magic. Unfortunately, this doesn't work with Silence who starts with the gift of Shadow magic (even if he gives up Shadow Magic, he keeps the gift and therefore cannot get the Light magic gift).New Game Plus also lets you accumulate items that you otherwise can only get once:Blue can get Sea Stones from Mesarthim and the Dragon Sword in Abyss ("Hell")Red can get Spriggan Suits, Power Belts from the Black Ray and Black X BaseAsellus can get Golden Lion, Silver Moon, and Light RifleEmelia can get Angel Broach, EMH TagAnyone can get Kusanagi, Asura, Lordstar, Dragon ShieldRotten Meat is fun to collectI have 1 Flash Bomb, but I don't remember where I found it. It's taunting meThe junk shop trick in Scrap is the sameSelling gold for a profit is a little easier (the Koorong gold vendor and max # of gold were modified)Comet Blades cap at 6, even if you're using both Fuse and Rouge to attempt to get moreAsellus can still obtain her Human ending despite using Mystic Glove. Her scenario was also modified to include new events that were planned for the original (two alternative routes out of Chateau Aguille, recruiting Dr. Nusaken, speaking with Furdo in Magic Kingdom, and the Bio Research Lab event)In Red's scenario, losing to Berva gets you captured, and exiting the area before reuniting with the team removes them all from your party. However, NPC's will still interact with you as though that party member were still there (Gen still spooks the skeleton, etc.)Lastly, the Fuse boss rush is straight-forward but I think could use explanation: Fuse's scenario is essentially 7 separate Lute scenarios. They're very short, and you go straight to the last boss of whichever character's scenario he is "following." Before you fight this boss, any of the other six main characters you have recruited will appear in the IRPO conference room. You can fight their last boss by speaking with them, and defeating all six will make the final boss "oppressively difficult" (this is the description in-game)

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa games are some of the most unique RPGs you could possibly experience, with a levelling and progress system unlike any other. As a result, they are one of the most misunderstood JRPGs and while SaGa enjoys great popularity in Japan, in the West it never managed to pick up much of an audience and is often plagued with bad reviews uniquely in the west from said misunderstandings. The game gives you full freedom to explore and do sidequests and whatever you want, but, without questmarkers or much guidance, allowing you to truly feel like on your own adventure, and making discoveries feel like your own. Your main source of income, for example, are not battles but quests. There are no levels, instead, your stats increase directly depending on what kind of moves you use. Every single battle makes you immediately stronger and raises some stats. Your characters learn skills at random during battles, and sometimes you just get the right skill in a hard boss fight that wins you the fight. The right equipment is critical. The world and setting is incredibly unique, but you should not play SaGa for the story alone, but for the adventure. You have more than 30 characters available for recruitment, each of them being unique gameplay-wise.SaGa is challenging. The mechanics are not always clear and you don't have full control over your characters' growth. This is not the typical JRPG where you attack -> heal everyone -> attack ad infinitum until you win. Bosses are much more like puzzles - you have to tweak and change your team's strategy AND get lucky to get past some bosses. This might sound frustrating, but it feels incredibly rewarding once you get that Eureka! moment and find just the right strategy to win. If you misssed the feeling of being relieved when you finally got past a boss, if you miss yelling "YESS!" in your mind once the boss finally falls, this game is for you.Give SaGa, a legendary series by Square, a chance if you love to tinker with systems. If you love a sense of discovery not only for the world but for how the game works on a fundamental level itself, this is for you. If you love huge variety in gameplay in a JRPG with eight different characters to play, this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier is a re-release of the Playstation 1 game of the same name from long, long ago.I first got this game when I was in my early 20s way back during the PS1 days, but I was never really able to get anywhere, due to how difficult this game can be at times, and how easy it is to get lost and not really 'get' what you're supposed to do next, and also technical difficulties such as memory card block usage (this game was terrible on memory cards back in the day!).Lo and behold, SE has chosen this game for its re-release on Steam library, and I jumped at the chance to try it again, now that I'm older and wiser, and now that it is a much easier play without all of the memory card shenanigans.GRAPHICS: 8/10: They touched up the sprites very nicely and seemingly applied an AI upscaler to the backgrounds. Some backgrounds look a little 'off', but the sprites are very nicely done. The only complaint I can come up with here, is the fact they used the same generic font that they always use in their games these days, and it gets a little old. I miss the days when they had stylized fonts that were made for the game, and were unique to each game. But, considering the rest of the pros, I consider this to be a very minor nitpick.SOUND: 9/10: They didn't butcher the music, in fact, they seemingly kept the music pretty much intact! The sounds, music, everything is as I remember it. They might have cleaned the audio up a little, but honestly it's been so long since I've played it, that I can't tell. Every now and then I'd pull out the .PSF tracks of this game and listen to a few of my favorite tracks, but otherwise... I haven't played the game in years. It sounds exactly as I remember it. And that's a good thing. The music in this game, especially the normal battle theme, is catchy AF.DIFFICULTY: 7/10: I feel this game is a bit overly difficult, your characters feel rather weak and can go down in a hit or two and sometimes you just don't know what the frick you're supposed to do or why you are dying so fast to common mooks. This is not a game where you want to just mindlessly mash the Attack command, you will die and die often. Some people may like the difficulty, others might be put off by it a little.STORY: ???/10: I honestly don't know much about the game's story. I've heard it's good. Each character has their own story, and I think they are all inter-twined somehow, if I recall correctly?OTHER (New Features, etc): 10/10: A few things here:1). QUICKSAVE! This game lets you quick-save on the fly anytime you want, as long as you're not in battle. They even gave you a controller shortcut to do so. If you die, reloading your game takes about 5 seconds, so that's awesome too.2). STORY MENU: Another ludicrously awesome addition to the game. You can open your menu, and go to the "Story" option (I am pretty sure this was not present in the original game) and after each plot point, a new entry gets added there. Each entry gives a vague hint of where to go or what to do next, but yet it doesn't hold your hand. Remember how I said earlier, that I could never figure out what I was supposed to do next? This fixes that! Seriously, this is the fix the game sorely needed. 3). D-INPUT SUPPORT: This game recognized my D-Input controller right off the bat. I use a Dualshock->USB adapter with a PS1 Dualshock controller plugged into it. Most games today won't even see it, or if it does see it, there's various problems, such as reading double inputs, and such. This game not only saw the controller, but all of the buttons were mapped properly without even needing to touch the mapping config! I was shocked and amazed in equal measure, and I very much thank SE for doing this.4). STABILITY/PERFORMANCE: I run a 4+ year old rig with a Ryzen 5 1500x and a 1050ti, 1440p native resolution. I ran the game windowed at 1080p with all the default settings, and I did not notice any slowtowns, framerate drops, etc whatsoever.OVERALL: 9/10: I'm very happy with this. I feel they did an excellent job with this remaster. They kept the game true to the original, and gave it a fresh coat of paint, and added an extra feature or two that are largely optional.Let's hope future SE remasters are done in this way.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun free-form JRPG with the multiple playable characters, offering several shorter stories that can be finished in 5-10 hours instead of a single 'epic' story padded across 60 hours or so. The scenarios are fun on their own (except for Lute's scenario, which feels rushed and underdeveloped), and each character plays somewhat differently, making the game feel familiar yet different enough to keep things interesting.That said, don't expect a generic JRPG in a weird setting. This game can be hard and unforgiving at times, and you should be prepared to invest hours to learn how it works before it finally clicks for you. But once it does, you'll have a hard time putting it down.The port is nice, and by no means a 'low effort cashgrab'. While there are some UI leftovers from the mobile version (probably to make the game playable w/ mouse & keyboard), they can be turned off in the settings.Now I'm waiting for Saga Frontier 2 and Unlimited Saga.

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa games are for the hardcore RPG enthusiasts only.  If you walk into this game blind, pick the wrong main character, play it like you do a normal RPG, you will hate the game within the Steam refund timeframe to get your money back.  The remastered version of this game is pretty much tailored to those who played the original back then, and maybe those looking for a little sadism.If you're willing to step up to the plate....well the game still isn't very good.  Of the many different protagonists, only two have any semblance of story (Red and Emilia),  the rest just give you a single goal, open up the world and let you do your thing.  This means SaGa Frontier is a gameplay-first type of RPG.  That's where the real faults of the game lies.  Everything in the game is kept hidden from the player.  How strong are you exactly? How strong are the enemies you face?  Are you up to the task of facing a boss gauntlet?  You have absolutely no idea and run the risks of soft locks unless you make multiple backup saves.  You can go through a dungeon, face nothing but weak mobs, run into the next screen, then fight an enemy that overkills your party before you get an action.How your party gets stronger is entirely up to chance.  Every battle won you have a chance of getting small stat increments.  |Sometimes you get a lot, sometimes you get little.  See ,there's this invisible counter called "Battle Rank" that determines EVERYTHING: how you grow, how difficult enemies are, and it goes up by quantity of battles, NOT quality.  That means you can screw yourself if you fight weak mobs to raise your battle rank without raising your stats.  If not for a easy money glitch (the developers left in the remasters for a reason) the midgame will be unbearably difficult.  This is also ignoring the insanely complex magic system, where you need to do sidequests to unlock "Gifts" to learn advance magics.  But watch out, you can only unlock one type of magic over an another and only people in your party get that gift.  Talk to the wrong NPC and accept the wrong quest and you just locked yourself out of a skillset and potential playable characters.  The game pretty much requires you to have an old GameFAQs guide open at all times, just to understand how to play the game, let alone all the crazy missables and optional content the game offers.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're an avid fan of JRPGs and looking to try your palette out on something different, then pass on Octopath Traveler and pick up this eccentric title instead.- Completely non-linear questing system.- Large world map (divided into zones and hub cities).- Eight different unique protagonist storylines with multiple overlapping elements.- Incredibly interesting race and sub-class system.The Saga Frontier and Romancing Saga series are quite established JRPGs in Japan, during their initial releases they were boxing with some of the renowned heavyweights in the genre, such as Xenogears and Final Fantasy. It never managed to pick up much steam here in the West due to a multitude of different issues: brand confusion, poor marketing, and simply being overall unwelcoming to new players.I was baffled to hear they were releasing this game again with the restored content a while back - but I was more concerned with whether they were bringing any quality of life changes to the table. My memories of playing Saga Frontier as a child have stayed with me for a long time and I can easily say it's one of my all-time favorite games, but there's a lot in the PS1 release that would have aged worse than milk. Thankfully, I can say the remastered version rectifies a handful of the more pronounced blemishes, although it's far from perfect, it's a solid attempt of readopting this cult classic to be more suitable to modern times. I clocked 100s of hours on it back on the original PS1 game, and now with all the new additions in the remastered - I'm ready to dive back in!

_childDocuments_.review: They just don’t make JRPGs like they used to. Either that or maybe I’m just getting old and screaming these words at the kids who are out on my lawn. Whichever it is, the entertainment value that I get out of some of the classics is a high that I can’t seem to get out of any of the modern releases in the genre. Give me a Chrono Trigger or Final Fantasy VI and I’ll blow an entire weekend on it.SaGa Frontier has a throne reserved for it at this table. I remember playing it as a little guy and feeling overwhelmed by the experience and its overwhelmingly open gameplay for the time. Getting my hands on the remaster when I saw announced became a priority to sip on that sweet, sweet nostalgia, and I must say that it’s lived up to the hype even in the Year of Our Lord 2021.SaGa Frontier opens by giving you a choice between eight main characters to choose from. Each has their own story to experience and the variety between them is astonishing. One may be quite linear with clear goals and an in-depth super hero story arc while the next has only one goal, kill the big bad, and it’s up to you to get a lone jobless bum into fighting shape alongside the allies that you find in your completely open-ended travels. The best part is that you’ll be able to play as all of them and you can carry over your progress from one to the next in a persistent legacy save.Characters overall are varied in their goals and personalities while their attributes and skills can be customized as you see fit. Whether you’re that superhero or the jobless bum, there’s plenty of options available for how to specialize them and each of the four species that might end up in your party offer different experiences. Humans gain attributes in nearly every battle based on what they’re doing; punch your enemies and you’ll gain strength, cast spells and you’ll gain intelligence. Skills are learned by change when you’re using related abilities and weapons; punch and kick enough and you’ll learn to start body slamming your foes.Magic works only slightly differently. Basic spells can be purchased from magic vendors, though to get the truly powerful ones you’ll need to learn them by chance once you’ve earned “the gift.” “The gift” is a questline that you have to undertake to master a category of magic so that you can learn spells that are unavailable to gain anywhere other than inside yourself.Monsters absorb their defeated foes and gain their abilities from them. They can only have up to eight of them at a time and newly gained skills will replace one that they already have. Different combinations of skills result in varying forms for your monsters as well and it’s important that you pay attention to these as the lion’s share of their attributes come from whatever form they happen to be in at the time as they don’t organically level like a human. A monster who’s taken the shape of a dragon is a far more useful ally than one that’s taken the shape of a flower. This system lends a “gotta catch ’em all” feel to improving your monster characters, especially since each new enemy that absorb adds a permanent health bonus to all of their forms going forward.Mechs are a combination of their parts. Absorbing programs from defeated enemy mechs is the only way that they improve in battle. These provide useful abilities to them but their attributes are built entirely from the items that they have equipped. The type of item that you’re putting on them alters their statistics in varying ways, a sword will boost their strength while a gun will boost their concentration. This means that decking them out with endgame tier gear will make them beastly at any point, though they’re also nearly useless if you don’t have an inventory to devote to their development.Mystics feel like something of a hybrid between humans and monsters. Though they can increase a few of their attributes, such as hit points and charisma simply by winning battles, they gain most of their abilities and stats from using their mystic weapons to absorb weakened enemies. They don’t transform like monsters do, but they rely heavily on absorption as opposed to the more simplified experience gain of humans.Though stories vary from the linear and objective-based to progressing as you see fit, SaGa Frontier offers a world waiting to be explored at your leisure. Even the most railroaded characters are capable of exploring much of it and encountering many of the same characters that were seen in other stories. Magic academies, Far East-inspired villages, pleasant suburbs, and neon cities are only a few of the memorable places that you can visit, and each offers its own places of interest that are likely to pique your curiosity.It’s a testament to the thoughtful and open-ended gameplay design that your party composition is almost entirely up to you as well. Starting with your choice of a variety of main characters, there are dozens of others to find throughout the world to join you, even the other main characters are out there waiting to be recruited at one time or another. This ends up with having a highly customized and persistent world as the remaster’s new game plus mode allows you to carry over the progress that you’ve made with each of the characters (major or minor) that you’ve used in the past. In the old days, each story required you to build them up again, now they are recruited at the same strength as last you saw them if you so choose.SaGa Frontier lives up to its legacy and is still an impressive and unique experience in 2021. Few RPGs can compete with the raw customization available and the open-ended stories still stand out for letting you truly live in the setting that it lays before you. I highly recommend this title to any who is looking for the nostalgia offered by classic RPGs especially if you're looking for something that stands out from the rest. For the rest, it's certainly worth a try as it's one of the better JRPGs that have been released in the history of the genre. Now all we need is the remaster of SaGa Frontier 2. Here's to hoping!

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, sometimes we have to be honest about the things we love.Saga Frontier is not the BEST Playstation RPG. Parts of it I would consider entirely inscrutable without a walkthrough or guide of some sort. The difficulty is all over the place where you can easily wander into a zone where you'll just get destroyed by monsters, or worse you'll be FORCED into a place where you're more or less incapable of winning fights. The magic system is simultaneously simplistic yet confusing... Saga Frontier lacks a lot of the polish that its contemporaries has. I hesitate to recommend this one to someone who isn't already familiar with it or who doesn't have an innate love for this era of RPGs...And yet it's one of my absolute favorites. I played the hell out of this game in high school, and after playing through one of the stories in full this remaster is absolutely exactly what it needs to be. The world it takes place in is at once under-explained yet totally enthralling with a wonderful ly diverse cast of characters both minor and major, and while the different campaigns have a fair bit of overlap at times with what you have to do (How many times are you willing to go through the gauntlet of unlocking Arcane Magic? I hope it's a lot!), each campaign still has its own unique story, gameplay features, and areas and the way they overlap with each other narratively just hits the good parts of my brain throughout.If you didn't play this game when it came out or are not an established fan of late 90's RPGs, I have a hard time giving Saga Frontier a solid recommend...But if you did or are, I would highly encourage you to pick up one of my personal favorite mediocre-but-beloved games here. I've tried a few times over the years to get into other Saga games and none of them ever really clicked with me, but this one does it.

_childDocuments_.review: its a real monkey's paw. new version of the classic game with new content ... but its a mobile port.thankfully this time you can turn off the mobile control UI hud and the gamepad has no issues this time. so you can play it normally as intended. the graphics are still a little wonky though. its AI upscaled backgrounds with poorly redone sprites. it looks blurry at times and you can really notice the area where the AI freaked out. it really makes me worry about the future possible port for saga frontier 2 as that uses painted backgrounds. the new content is nice, but requires you to beat the game multiple times with all the chracters to unlock everything as the chapters are alternate takes and epilogues of character stories. though the other new thing added is a proper 'new game+'. you can go through the other campaigns real easy now and carry everything over. it all culminates at the end with a bunch of super tough secret bosses to use those acquired levels and loot on.also if you're starting off, this game has no direction and no basic quests (even less than other SaGa games).  go to the town of devin and pick up the arcane gift and runic gift quest lines which will give you something to do early on to gain stats, equipment, and even party members.

_childDocuments_.review: A great adventure between 8 different protagonist but this is not an rpg for beginners of the genre. Saga frontier will absolutely kick your ass and not be afraid to do it. Unlike romancing saga minstral song which i played earlier you can actually flee battles without consequence and it's more encouraged to do so. Battle ranks is still very much a thing as with all saga games the more you fight the tougher the monsters get as they scale with you. Grind too much and you could be absolutely destroyed by bosses or even regular monsters in the field. Saga frontier goes about this a whole lot better as there is healing points every where you just have to seek them out so you can actually level grind until you can stand a chance. However saga frontier does one thing wrong. Saving. how does it mess up saving? Well you can save where you can get soft lock just before a boss fight and not be able to return to areas to grind more so be careful of that. If someone saying this is your last chance to do anything do not save beyond that point.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is its own worse enemy. The experience is incredible, but you have to put up with some frustrating balance issues in the early game to get there. This game seems to be only for those with rose-colored glasses that played it on the Playstation 1 in 1997. The story, music, and gameplay can easily be a 10/10 once you get to NG+ but the early balance is bizarre and worse than I remember as a teenager. I'm glad this remaster exists and everything improved on is beautiful, but I struggle to see how I could recommend it to new players. There is something special here, but you have to be willing to dig for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the original, and I loved the remaster. This is how a game should use eight characters with their own stories (... looking at you Octopath!!! -_- ) . It still has some of the problems of games from the time, mainly that there will be story moments where you don't really know what you are supposed to be doing. The stories themselves vary in linearity and openness as well as what regions you get to visit... but overall it is a very fun world setting with lots of variety in terms of allies, enemies, skills, and gear. I pray they remake Saga Frontier 2 just as well!

_childDocuments_.review: Solid remaster of a solid game.Not much to say here. If you like SaGa games you'll like this one, if you don't like them this probably won't change your mind, if you are new to the series Romancing SaGa 2 is still better starting point.It serves as a nice bridge between retro and more modern games as it contains a bit of mechanics from both, with monsters, robots and mutants/mystics from old games and tech glimmering, battle rank and multiple scenarios from newer ones.There is a lot of soul in this old dog too. One of the character is a Kamen Rider superhero that can only use his alter ego in combat if rest of the party are either robots, unconscious, or blinded since he cannot reveal his secret identity. Other character that is a supermodel can change between multiple costumes that change her appearance in battle and overworld. And of course plenty of obscure SaGa secrets. Clearly the game has been created with lot's of love and I don't feel like remastered ruined any of that.In short: very good entry in the series, just maybe not the best for new timers.

_childDocuments_.review: 2 seconds to, New Players: This is an RNG Save-Scrum JRPG.(not unlike Rogue-likes where you die/repeat or Reset-game before Bosses for that 3% drop)Mostly hand-drawn with gorgeous 2D sprites. Beautifully upscaled and polished.---I'll list Positives specific to this REMASTER, by importance:1. True to the original. (Added without taking away, same art style) New Scenes for Asellus. New playable Character Fuse.(included in gold-Duplicate, "trick" yay! I didn't use it, but it's nice to have a choice.)2. Quality-of-Life: - New info. Interface (I turn it off). - Auto-save every time you enter a new room, you can also manually save ANYWHERE any time (yay Save-Scrum) No Steam Cloud Save (yet Saga 3 for SNES on Steam does?) - Fast-forward, yes! one-press. and Quick/Run feels clean, - 100% combat Flee rate with no penalty. (sometimes you'll want to skip battles until your team mates are Recruited - or when hunting a specific Monster). - Controls are clean (Mobile port is always 'meh' but better than similar games with these complaints.) - Increased Character Roster, 'additional team' slots, so RECRUITING all characters shouldn't be an issue.3. Video, Huge upgrade in sprites and animations. They look clean.The visuals are stellar and my first-play-through I didn't even use the "Fast Forward" much because I loved watching the combat; spells, swords and fists fly.4. Story Guide in-game in case you forget your current Mission/Story Event.5. Library Mode, BG music, SFX, Story/Images.6. Item name or monster name changes, slight dialogue tweaks, nothing that affects the overall gameplay.I'm pretty sure "global icons' and New Game+ were a feature of the original.Complaints? Nothing? Add Steam Cloud Save and Android/iOS Cloud Save please!New Players - what to Expect?- RNG. Its random, but fair. You might get one-shot if you're not prepared, have gear, or have the % Stats. (Incoming DevilSquad Maelstrom, bye team!)- SAVE OFTEN! It's a DIFFICULT game at first, and you should expect to SAVE often. But you'll find the mechanics, characters, story to be a charming and rewarding experience.- No true Leveling, you get stats every few battles.- You learn skills/abilities by USING skills abilities. Fists, Guns, Swords, Magic, etc, if you want to learn new skills... just "punch" or "thrust" and you'll have a chance of learning a new skill!- No perma-death other than your Main character/Game Reset. So no death penalty? When you drop to 0 LP, your characters can not participate in combat until revived at an INN (or rare Item).- Very limited Resources, GOLD, and healing spells, and no true "Healer" (except Mellow Ring), so you'll want to rely on Potions and resources, or swapping-out to a Back-up Party (you can do this Any-time as well).- Not many, "secret items," or "hidden walls," just run through the maps, what you see is what you get.- Quests and What to Do, can be confusing to Newcomers, but hopefully the Story/Event Guide will help with this. and Exploring.I played Saga Frontier on PS1 as a kid, THIS is how a true Remaster needs to be made, the team behind Square who worked on this Project needs to do all the rest of these glorious Retro remakes (not a FF Pixel Remaster fan, super clunky)With zero load-time, fast-forward, and run, even 100% combat Flee rate, you can dart-through areas of the game pretty quickly. I hope this revival spurs on more games like this: branching story, multiple characters, new game+, i love the combat Spark System. All of the latest games are like... 2016/2018 Android/iOS gatcha games.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Game is still incomplete with remastered version, BUT Fuse helps wrap up a LOT of loose ends so that's nice of the developers to do. You get basically to play eight mini storylines, then another **SPOILER SPOILER** ADDITIONAL storylines for each respective character to give backstory. You also get a few "alternate" endings for some characters, so there is a lot of gameplay to be had, but biggest gripe is some of that additional gameplay requires running through a lot of VERY SIMILAR processes to achieve it. Best to play it in a casual basis, then just hop on YT or something like that to watch alternate endings/achievements/etc. It's.. not worth teh extra 15+ hours grinding to get some of the achievements.I would recommend this game to those of a more hardcore RPG variety, there are parts of this game that I would define as.. BROKEN. It's not that the game is inherently hard or easy, it's just that the balance is weird. The game itself has a lot of fun elements to it, but I see it as more of an experimental build game than a "complete" game, mostly those fans of the original "Saga Frontier" pre remastered will appreciate this as Fuse helps to **SPOILER SPOILER DONT READ AHEAD IFFF YOUU DONT WANT SPOILERS....Basically wrap up each and every characters storyline giving a more "complete" feel to the game. A few of the achievements imo are well... broken. There is COUGH COUGH SPOILER AGAINa chance that with the improper boss rush mix you will LITERALLY not be able to beat the last boss for one of the achievements. I mean.. there is a literal achievement for SHOPPING but it doesn't tell you what items you colllected, what areas you colllected them in.. anything, so if you miss an item from.. some obscure store, you have to search ALL the stores just for it.For someone such as myself that's basically a perfectionist, this annoyance bugs me more than it should.I love this game to pieces, but honestly. it's still broken. They do wrap up all the stories to the best of their ability but the more underlying game-play mechanics aren't quite "there" yet, I wouldn't recommend it for a full price, this will DEFINITELY go on sale due to the fact that even after the remastering, it's still riddled with bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved the game when it first came out, read no further, go buy the game. It's a really good remake, with greatly cleaned up sprites, sensible QoL upgrades and restored content.But the game itself, well, nostalgia could only get me so far. 3 characters' stories in, the repetitiveness really bit me, and the game's much-adored "non-linearity" at the time is just that the game doesn't handhold you in letting you figure out where to go (except that there's a "story" section in the menu that WILL tell you where to go, but you can easily ignore it). The combat, once you get into it, really isn't that interesting, and item drops and levelling is too RNG-heavy even for a JRPG. I would have quit it but nostalgia and the desire to play the added content (it wasn't great, to be honest, extremely repetitive) kept me going.Oh, and the story seemed decent to me when I was 10, but it's basically non-existent to adult me. This could be a cool world but you don't get much of it, and you don't get much of the characters, either.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the original SaGa Frontier on PlayStation a heckuva a lot. I really like it, but I'll readily admit it isn't for everyone. It's nonlinear structure and flexible character customization make it feel extremely different from other JRPGs. Every system in this game feels like an experiment. The monster, robot, and mystic party members all operate by their own rules for advancement. The magic system and skill system are unlike any other game (aside from other SaGa games). The sci-fi setting is extremely quirky.I love all the things that make this game unique, but it is quite difficult to get into. There are lots of rules that are not well explained and many of the game's systems just don't work that well. Nonetheless, this is an experimental and highly original game, and if you are jaded with other JRPGs, this is an interesting one.Romancing SaGa: Minstrel Song is a bigger, more refined, and more complex SaGa game. So if that appeals to you, you might try that one first.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, its just as good as I remember, I was expecting it to feel kinda rough.  I got kingdom hearts 1+2 on Epic recently and it's not nearly as fun to play the original as I remember, destiny islands and traverse town are agonizingly slow to get through.In contrast, within 2 minutes each character of Saga Frontier is like "yo lets go, BOOM here's my backstory, BLAM here's what I gotta do whenever you feel like advancing the plot, KAPOW here's my starting zone full of stuff to explore". It expects you'll want to play through each of the 7 routes with sometimes repeating sections, so they made each one feel very different in tone and gameplay, made magic really fun to experiment with, and filled the worlds with rewards that are only available for some characters, or better for some characters than others.

_childDocuments_.review: Great remaster when compared to the other atrocities that are SquareEnix's re-releases/remasters of Squaresoft's Final Fantasy series, Mana series, and Chrono Trigger:+Content not existent in the original has been added+The 2D graphics look better than any of their previous attempts on Squaresoft's titles(look up "Final Fantasy 6" in the Steam store)+No bugs or crashes to report so farAs for the actual game: It has a learning curve, and expects you to read the "Help" section to understand how to play.The story is also half-baked, which is good if you hate reading, but bad if you'd like a coherent story.You will also lose alot depending on what character you choose, as some stories are easier than others(I started with "Blue" and died 5 times without killing a single enemy, then started with "Red" and have rarely died).This game is great, but know what you're getting into.:)

_childDocuments_.review: Great remaster of a great game. It adds a bunch of features that make it much more beginner friendly, such as a quest log that more or less tells you where to go to advance the story, an in-game manual that explains the battle system, autosave in case you accidentally bump into an enemy you shouldn't have, etc. If you've ever been curious about the SaGa franchise, this is a great place to start. Pick a character, get maybe 2 minutes of story, and then go do whatever the hell you want in the game's extremely weird and unique scifi/medieval/??? setting. Great stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: This remaster really remastered my feeling from childhood.This is the most addictive SaGa game I've ever played!Total in-game hour 63 hours.Play till NG+13 cleared!Watched all 7 original endings and 7 remaster endings!If there is something I would like to ask, please release other SaGa series remaster!
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: It's everything I hoped!!This is the way to do a Remaster of an old PSX game. Take note, Square Enix. This is how you do it.New music, restored content, and finally we can play the 8 secret scenario as it was always intended!The UI for mobile can be turned off completely on the Config Menu to make it play just like the original and let you appreciate all the beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds.The character and monster sprites look even better than the original!The new font has less charm but I got used to it in around 4 hours or so. If you ever played this game and liked it, you owe it to yourself to play this definitive version.For fans of the SaGa series, this is a must buy.For fans of JRPGs in general, I strongly recommend you watch some gameplay and if it seems like you could enjoy this, buy it.Every story has it's own theme and let's you experience a different side of the world with some overlap. There's surely a protagonist that will click with you among the original 7 so don't be shy to restart if the one you chose is not really what you expected.You may wait for a sale but honestly, this is the kind of labor of love that we should reward with our wallets, to show Square Enix that when they actually put in the work for a remaster it can become a better version than the original and not just a lazy mobile port.TLDR: If you are a fan of the series or the original, it's a must buy. If you like JRPGs, consider it or maybe wait for  sale. This is the kind of Remasters that are worth the purchase and I have absolutely no regrets and I am enjoying the game like it was the first time I played it.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this mostly for nostalgia's sake, but I was already toying with the idea of doing a replay of the old version, so this coming out now was perfect timing. They should return to the glimmer system, but just expand on it with more hidden conditions, larger selection of moves and maybe a few extra weapon types to keep things fresh. Happy to support this remaster if it helps us get more SF!

_childDocuments_.review: First tried Asellus' story.  After you trigger a certain event, enemy bosses start coming after you, automatically engaging you in areas that would normally be safe upon changing screens.  Is your team not nearly strong enough to face them yet?  They don't care.  Once one has decided to appear, you are stuck with him.  Since there was no possible way for me to beat the third, my attempt with Asellus reached a dead end and I was forced to abandon it.  I have since learned that veterans of the series know which event triggers the pursuit, and know to avoid it until they have spent a good deal of time grinding up stats for their team, but I consider anything that requires information outside of what the game provides you just to proceed normally to be a very poor design choice on part of the developers.Next tried Lute's story.  This time, before triggering even the first story mission, I gathered a team and spent a little time grinding to build them up.  Ok, good!  Now let's try that first story mission!  ...well, it turns out his first is also his last.  You are sent immediately to the final dungeon and the confrontation with the final boss.  Needless to say I was utterly destroyed.  So... Lute doesn't actually have a story.  Just intro, grind, then final boss.  What kind of lazy bull is this?I do love the mechanics of leveling up the different kinds of characters, but there are SO MANY bad design choices with regards to the stories!  Don't even attempt to play this game unless you have looked through a guide beforehand so that you will be able to avoid the various game-ending traps the developers have set for their players.edit:  Completed Emilia's story.  If you are careful to research what you need to know to play this game ahead of time, it can be reasonably fun for those who enjoy grinding.  Just don't expect any wow from the story, no matter which one you pick!
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to something many fans of this game have wanted since it came out on PS1 in 97/98... the game finished.No, I'm not joking. As the selling points point out, there's a bunch of stuff re-added from the cutting room floors, to finish off stuff that was planned in some fashion, to make it a fleshed out version of the original.Is it "the best it could possibly be"? Nah, but it's better than the original I feel. QoL added in many places, including helpful "Point Of No Return" warnings, and some mechanic explanations that were sorely lacking in the original. They decided to update tech names, for the most part, to match other SaGa series games' versions of the techs/spells (most specifically, the Romancing SaGa remaster names), which will be a stumbling block for players who had came to this only experienced with the original... and in the mix, they ruined a word play that admittedly was better in Japanese -- Red's Al-Phoenix X (which was originally Re-Al-Phoenix, which is supposed to basically translate as "True Al-Phoenix", being the ultimate perfection of the Al-Phoenix technique; the new version feels more 80s/90s Anime Protagonist Technique-in-English name, where they couldn't come up with something good and didn't want it to be "Ultimate [move name]" in case of a bigger one later)All in all, though, and the tl;dr -- it's basically the best version of this game, and far easier to find.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: I wish they'd leave out the mobile garbage, but you can turn off most of the mobile UI features. It's nowhere near as nauseating as Square's other mobile ports they dumped on Steam (like Chrono Trigger, FF6, etc.). The reworked sprites remind me of the mobile FF6 sprites, but they're much less offensive. The AI-upscaled backgrounds are decent—better than just slapping higher-res sprites or models on a 240p background, like in the FF9 port. However, characters can still look a bit "flat" against the backgrounds. Some people dislike the game's typeface, but it doesn’t bother me personally.A few downsides include the limited graphical settings: you can only choose between 1280x720, 1600x900, and 1920x1080. I don't understand why so many Japanese developers are so stingy with game settings—Square, in particular, is guilty of this. Also, I may be missing something, but I can’t find an option to display PlayStation button icons. I really wish Xbox didn't win the button icon war.Despite these issues, I think the game is still worth it if you can overlook the cons I mentioned. They've restored some cut content, and that's definitely the biggest plus here. It feels like more care went into this port than their other, bigger IPs for some reason.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier is a brilliant fever dream of ridiculous art design and visual storytelling. It can't really be compared to a game like Final Fantasy VII because they are almost nothing alike, except that both come from the pre-rendered background era of Squaresoft jRPGs. The difference here is that the backgrounds are completely unrestrained and the characters are made up of beautifully drawn sprites. The soundtrack is fantastic, and the story relies more on sprite animations and visual details rather than long dialogue exposition.To new players in particular, it will likely feel a bit overwhelming, but the remaster does a ton to elate the issues with the original. You can set battles to 3x speed, and flee as many as you want, so any grinding is much easier to roll with than it was before. Second, I would encourage the use of the New Game + feature. It feels like this game was made for it. You won't ever get all the games 40 playable characters to endgame power in just one scenario. So take 8 scenarios to build them all up. Of course you have the option to hit the reset switch with each new scenario too, that's all up to you, but I would encourage it.In any case, for such a reasonable asking price, you're getting a game that will last you upwards of 100 hours. Tons of value.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This review is of both the remaster and the original.A very good remaster of a great, but flawed RPG. This game sold over 1 million copies when it first came, and I suspect part of this reason was because the back of the box claimed that there was something around 140 of game play. Impressive, sure, but admittedly a lot of this is repetitive content that you will repeat six or seven times in order to truly experience the entire game. Pros:- Fantastic game music, some of the best on the PS1- Cartoony, quirky graphics. They actually hold up better than most of the full 3D games on the console. - Countless unique enemies, skills, magic, etc., the game is dense and complex, and even after playing for 100 hours you still won't know everything-  Seven main character quests, some who have very interesting (Though shallow) storylines- Tons of things to do on the side, very exploration heavy world- Extremely quirky programming that is fun to mess around with to see how different events play out. I particularly like the combo system because the random nature of it makes it more of an art than a science- Epic final boss fights, which is even more impressive when you consider there are seven final bosses- Extra content in the remaster is a nice touch, and it blends together seamlessly. I really like that the player can speed up the battles to make grinding go faster, a major improvement over the original.- Lots of little puzzles and obstacles to break up the monotony of fighting enemies over and over againCons:- You have to grind to beat the final bosses, and this can take hours- RNG or random probability determines how most skills get developed, so you may spend hours trying to acquire a skill. The DSC skill in the game is the most powerful attack, but very difficult to acquire. It's necessary to obtain unless you want to spend a half hour fighting each final boss. - Game is a little confusing when it comes to character classes. Humans, mechs and monsters all become more powerful differently, and the system isn't intuitive. You really have to research online how to power up your characters.- The additional eighth storyline, Fuse, seems kind of pointless, since it's just adding him to the existing storylines and not really revealing too much, although Blue and Emelia's terrible original endings get expanded to make them at least make sense. - Saving in the wrong place can ruin your save file (This could be considered a pro if you like ultra unforgiving games)Character storylines from best to worst:T260G: His quest is the longest and most diverse, and his final boss fight is the hardest. He can switch to different robot body types. This is probably the only really challenging part of the game.Riki: His (?) storyline feels more like a collection of minigames, but it's a lot of fun trying to get through all of it.Blue: He's got the coolest storyline. It feels reminiscent of Final Fantasy 7, but for some bizarre reason the game just shows "The End" after killing the final boss. Bizarre and disappointing.Red: Superhero character who fights enemies that look like they're from Power Rangers. He has a lengthier storyline and a ton of bosses to fight, but it's not higher on the list because the rules for transforming into Alkaiser are so obtuse that it makes the game annoying.Emelia: She has the easiest storyline, it can be completed in a few hours. The story is interesting, but the "good" ending makes no sense and is a disappointment. The additional content with Fuse's storyline makes it make even less sense.Asellus: She is a half mystic, which is this game's version of a vampire. Interesting story, but the actual game scenario is kind of dull. It's nice that they gave her three different endings.Lute: Lute is for players who want a freeform scenario, since all you do is go straight to the final boss. With that said, the final boss is very difficult, so you have to spend a lot of time building him up all the same.Fuse: This is the new character (He was in the other game but had no scenario). His is the most irritating because you're basically just completing some story scenarios to get to the final boss in one of the other cases. I don't like how this was designed, since I didn't do a constant new game+ I had drastic power differences between the existing and new characters when I ported the save over. Overall, a really good remake, and it plays find using a mouse and keyboard, so definitely worth checking out if you like turn-based RPGs or are a fan of Squaresoft games. Just keep in mind that you are going to be dealing with a lot of repetitive content if you decide to play through all eight scenarios.

_childDocuments_.review: Having this game remastered is truly a dream come true. SaGa Frontier is one of my all time favorite games. I have easily probably dumped thousands of hours in this game. If you played it in the past know that is has some great QoL (Quality of Life) updates. I do not like the name changes of certain moves but there is a mod to switch them back. To me this is a solid 10/10. Give it a try if you never played it.

_childDocuments_.review: The SaGa series isn't for everyone, but there's almost always something worth exploring in them. These games were open-world before "open-world" was coined.Frontier in particular is one of the more approachable ones if you're okay with not understanding every niggling detail of how systems function. It's easy to just mess around and stumble your way into winning, but the skill ceiling is high enough that there's tons of replay value, and the world and concepts in the game are enticing enough that the only issue with them is that even in this extra-material version, you won't have the really cool stuff fleshed out enough to feel satisfied. But if you're good with letting your imagination fill in details, this might be your kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: Many complain that it feels like a RPG fidget spinner of random events and the story are the spark notes of a first draft of a stage play.  The story is minimalist and leaves a lot to the imagination, scenes will transition with no warning, and stuff just kinda happens.  However, these unfamiliar and bizarre elements are its greatest strengths and lead to a well crafted RPG experience full of soul.SaGa frontier is a game that does not waste your time, and the combat and growth of the characters is part the story; at the end of the game you'll remember that time you got ambushed by robots and Gen pulls off a sick series of parries, or when the party almost gets wiped out and Red turned the tables by transforming into a superhero, or when Riki absorbed a monster he shouldn't have and went from being a Dragon to a Slime.  Exploration doesn't just mean navigating the open world either, exploring the mechanics of the game is an endeavor itself. As you puzzle over how something like a combo works you start to "feel" the way it works and intuit a way to exploit it.  Repeated playthroughs offer some new perspectives on the world and setting that subconsciously piece themselves together in the back of your mind, while the game openly encourages you to master the systems or break them completely. Also the music is perfect and any other opinion is factually wrong.If you ever played Final Fantasy 8 and wished everyone would shut up so you could abuse the junction system while listening to Fisherman's Horizon and appreciating how cool the lore for the Lunar Cry is, you're in the right mindset to try this game out.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: Finally 23 years later and no more emulators needed or dusting off that old PS they finally have a release on new Gen and it has been improved!This is definitely an underrated RPG of the past that still is fun and amazing to play now with far improved graphics and better models it is refreshing to relive this game again and not immediately be annoyed.The remaster version adds some interesting and nice QOL improvements that would have been a great help in the past when learning this game so veterans may not need them but new players should help a lot.only small grips I found and it mostly only being you cannot change the menus color anymore or turn it Opaque which i find odd.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: Hoo, boy, do I have to caveat this one.For people that have played the original and want to experience it again, this is a safe buy: the translation and spritework have both been cleaned up, the latter fairly considerably so.  Fuse is a very solid edition to the game's protagonist lineup, The 'Story' section in the menu helps point towards the next story event, and jumping between stories is considerably less grindy and repetitive with the addition of the New Game + Mechanic.   The game's difficulty also feels to have been rebalanced, such that you can get through the main quest fairly easily.For people looking for a PS1-era RPG, SaGa Frontier is worth considering, but only if you have a lot of patience for its idiosyncrasies.  There are three major issues:-The original was  flag-dependent, and the Remaster's only effort to rectify this is to tell you specifically what you have to do next to progress the story.  If you don't make use of the Story feature or know what you need to do already, it can be fairly difficult to bumble into the next major story event.  Mercifully, the game does now warn you when you're about to cross a Point of No Return.-The stories themselves are a bit bare-bones in a lot of cases - the ideas are definitely there, but the storytelling on display is fairly light.  -The game, like most of the entries in this series, is .  Thanks to a difficulty adjustment this particular go-around feels a bit less punishing, but you are still probably going to have to look up how certain concepts work.If none of these are deal-breakers for you, give it a try - for all its faults there is something oddly compelling about it.  The title was clearly very ambitious for its time, and while it's easy for the combat to devolve into just smacking the crap out of enemies, there is a lot of depth under the hood.Kenji Ito was brought back for the remake, and though he's only seemingly provided a couple of Remixes specifically for Fuse's campaign, they're great - although the sudden jump in quality is just a touch jarring.  The rest of the soundtrack hasn't been touched - some of it is definitely an acquired taste, but there are some real stand-outs in the track list too (every final boss has its own theme, and there are multiple tracks for regular bosses).
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: After all these years and several tries, I can honestly say that I still cannot bring myself to do a full playthrough of this game. It's just too off the beaten path of a game for me. In terms of cohesiveness of the story, the crazy amount of backtracking, grinding, imo god-awful enemy design, and boss level enemies appearing around every corner, I just can't bring myself to play this jank. I don't, nor have I ever apparently, have the patience to figure it all out. It's true that I came into the remastered version with a bias against it. But I thought that with being older, and having a different mindframe to look at this game from, that I would be able to progress further and learn the deeper, inner workings of this game. But no. No. If anything, I just realized that I don't have time for it.

_childDocuments_.review: So when people were saying this is one of the weirdest JRPGs ever made – they were not lying. I did not play the original SaGa Frontier when that came out back in 1997, so this remaster was the perfect opportunity to jump in.I should start by saying that you cannot really go into this one expecting a traditional JRPG. This starts before you even get into the game, as you have to select one from a bunch of different characters and that’s whose story you will be playing. Each character’s story plays out in the same world – and you will be visiting a lot of the same locations – but it’s effectively a bunch of mini-JRPGs rolled into one game. This sounds great on paper, but ultimately, this setup is underutilized as there is basically no crossover between the different stories (aside from one).Such a setup can still work, but this only makes the next problem more apparent – that being that the stories by themselves aren’t that great to begin with. In fact – for most of them – they are hardly even there. One of the characters, Lute, quite literally has like one minute of introductory dialogue before just tossing you into the world. Ten minutes later, I had managed to reach the final boss of that route by accident. There was no main questline, no deeper story, just a little introduction, traveling to a couple cities to talk to an NPC, and then bam – final boss. So yeah, this is definitely not a JRPG to play for the story.SaGa Frontier is a very free-form JRPG, with most of the character routes opening up the entire game world early on for exploration. Given that, a lot of your time is going to be spent exploring – which is good, I always love a JRPG with a good sense of exploration. You wonder around, talking with NPCs, and basically learn more about the limited lore behind it all. When it comes time to actually tackle the story, well – that’s where the problems come up again. Even with the introduction of a new “story” UI element to give you hints as to where to go – the game is still very obtuse and a massive chunk of your time is going to be spent trying to figure out where to go.Of course, that is if you go at it without a walkthrough – which honestly, the design choices here basically necessitate it. To give an example. I was playing T260G’s route. There was an NPC I was required to talk to. However, every time I tried, nothing would happen – he would just stare at me. I explored the entire game world and talked with basically everyone I could – with the one hint from a scientist in another location telling me I needed to talk to this guy. Well, upon looking up a walkthrough, I found out that I needed to interact with a computer in a completely unrelated location that looks like its part of the background – not something to be interacted with.I did that, traveled back to the guy, and he STILL wouldn’t talk to me. The walkthrough then indicated that he would not because I had completed the quests out of order and had already upgraded my character – the NPC wanted to speak with my previous form. Fortunately, I was still able to revert to my character’s previous state at another location, so I went back there, reverted, finally talked to that NPC, and then went back and upgraded again. It’s an absolute mess of events that took me an hour to figure out – just to talk with one NPC. The entire game is designed like this and it is just outright frustrating to play at times.This game is extremely hard at some points, but easy at others, oftentimes right next to each other. During Red’s story, for example, I had to face four bosses at four separate locations. I discovered the location of one and then proceeded to go through a gauntlet of 40 or 50 enemy encounters – each where I was just spamming A because my characters did enough damage to one-shot them all. I finally reached the boss – where I had the complete opposite experience and kept getting wiped over and over. I finally managed to beat it after twelve or so attempts only to then uncover that that was actually not the boss – the real boss is immediately after it and does way more damage.There’s no saving, no regenerating your action points, nothing – just thrown right into this boss. I figured – okay, I’ll just leave the dungeon and go grind somewhere, but nope, you can’t leave the dungeon once you enter it – a fact I did not realize until this point and I ultimately ended up reloading a save from a couple hours beforehand.I can understand a game not giving you direction on what to do – and I’m usually one to complain about modern JRPGs giving you too much – but this is the extreme opposite, where you are given nothing and expected to just figure out the game’s bizarre design choices. Like grinding for example. There are no levels in this game and the stats you gain at the end of fights are entirely random. I would go from one-shotting an enemy and getting a bunch of stat increases to fighting a boss and hardly getting any. So not only is this an incredibly grindy game, but the grinding itself is completely random.I know some are going to say “well, that’s just how JRPGs were done back in the day” and yes, to a certain extent they were, but SaGa Frontier is that to the extreme and it’s really telling when I’m able to play through the original Megami Tensei game – released a full 10 years earlier and known for its extreme difficulty – and not have to look at a walkthrough every hour or get softlocked.That’s what ultimately brought down the experience for me. The combat, exploration, music, and design of the world and all of that is great and it can be fun at times, but the frustration brought on by its obtuse game design eventually outweighed that.I gotta knock the game for not having resolution support above 1080p. It doesn’t even stretch if you have a monitor bigger than that – either changing your monitor’s resolution to 1080p when running in fullscreen or just giving you a floating window when running borderless. It does at least run at 144 fps though, so points for that. I also had no issues with crashes, freezes, or actual bugs. The updated graphics are good too, better than the similar upscale we saw with the Grandia HD collection.And the stuff added by the remaster is also nice, including faster battle speed, the ability to run from battles, and map pointers so you know which elements of the background you can walk through. Some nice quality of life stuff that honestly makes me wonder just how much more time-consuming the experience would have been without them. The only other complaint I have here is that the UI has that nasty mobile game look to it – which unsurprisingly is because the game was also ported to mobile. They couldn’t be bothered to give the PC and console versions a better UI I guess.Despite a strong foundation for a good JRPG, SaGa Frontier Remastered makes so many bizarre design choices that it quickly devolves into aimless wandering, plentiful grinding, and even outright frustration. It’s one of those “needs a walkthrough” kind of games taken to the extreme, not even explaining the basics of its own combat system. That, coupled with how easy it is to softlock and all the other minor issues and I just cannot in good faith recommend it – even if the remaster elements help make it more palatable.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!
