_childDocuments_.review: 5/5 Good game. Good remaster.Instead of one protagonist that runs through a very long RPG, SaGa Frontier gives you several characters with short stories that slightly overlap and take place in the same game world. Upon completing one, you keep your money, items and experience and the characters you used retain their development when you start "New Game+". You don't necessarily START with the characters though you have to find or encounter them again.There's a bit of grind to it like doing extra leveling in any RPG but it's somehow not as bad when you know you're going to encounter the same characters again. The remaster also has a welcome "speed stuff up" toggle that roughly doubles spell and attack animation speed and a "flee" button so random encounters are optional. The remaster also conspicuously left in bugs/exploits to get free cash.Just beware old RPG antics like having to fight bosses to leave areas, trapping you if you saved inside and can't get out, or characters you invested in suddenly leaving mid game or even right before final bosses.... after final checkpoints where you can't go back... use a few save slots so you can go back a bit if you need to and browse one of the many guides, but again remember it's an old RPG so watch out for different translations between versions/guides especially with monster ability names.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier is a classic JRPG with a variety of characters and stories to choose from, all taking place in the same world. Some of these stories are more linear, while others open up almost immediately and allow you to explore various areas and search for hidden secrets. The game can be difficult to learn, as many of the systems are never properly explained. So while for the most part the story and world are best discovered and explored at your own pace, I would recommend looking up a guide on how the combat mechanics work so that you don't feel confused and can fully enjoy the interesting and unique elements present in the game.The remaster is acceptable. The graphical improvements are mostly just an automatic upscaling of the original textures by artificial intelligence. The most meaningful improvement over the original is the addition of another character's story that had been planned for the game but was never finished until now. I believe this character can only be accessed after completing all of the other character's stories however, making it mostly a treat for fans of the original game.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: A nice and unexpected remake. The original was one of my favorite PSX RPGs, but I'm not going to pretend it's appealing to everyone. Some of the systems that were mysteries in the original have been explained, and content has been added, but not excessively, so it's a very similar experience to the original PSX game but improved in most ways. The high-res backgrounds are beautiful and the new Fuse scenario has been interesting, although I have only seen two of the stories thus far. My only gripe graphicswise is the appearance of the menus, which have been changed to be more readable. That's fine for most people I'm sure, I just preferred the old PSX look.There were a few changes that surprised me. A couple of lines of dialogue have been changed - Cpt. Hamilton in Owmi used to say she liked eating at the restaurant and that you could eat more because "they don't use crap like MSG". This has been removed to something vague about bad ingredients. In Kyo, when you do the quest for Mind magic, you used to be in a room with a statue of Buddha, and the character would say "A staring contest with Buddha?" This has been altered to a vague statue of a long-haired guy and the message "A staring contest with the gods?" These lines just jumped out at me because they didn't change much else in the dialogue from the original and it seemed unnecessary. The original lines had flavor, the new ones are bland. I guess they wanted to avoid any possible controversy?Still, I can't fault this remake for much, it's really nice to see a game I loved with beautiful graphics that show off details I didn't realize were in the art before, and there's a bit more to Aselleus's quest, who is my favorite character. If you already love the game it'll be great, but SaGa Frontier is an odd game that might not appeal to new players even with somewhat modernized features. They could have added explanations of how the hell monsters worked, or really just changed that mechanic entirely. It's truly obscure and strange, and practically requires the player to read a 100-page FAQ or grind for a dozen hours to beat Riki's quest.My girlfriend bought me this as a surprise gift because she knew I loved Saga Frontier, so I'll always think fondly of it for that reason. Love you, Fiona <3
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: You're either into old school squaresoft RPGs or you aren't. If you are, there's still a chance you missed SaGa, since it was overshadowed by blockbuster games like FF7 and FF tactics that came out around the same time. Which is a shame, because this game was and is a sleeper hit.Significantly less story heavy than other rpgs of the time, the game is much more free form, giving you a goal but more or less allowing you to wander off off in any direction you like to find adventure after choosing a hero from a motley cast of characters including:-A robot-A lesbian tomboy half-vampire-A Power Ranger-An ex-convict supermodel-A useless stoner with a guitar-God, but split in half-A furry r e t a r dOne of the best things about the game is the world, which has an even greater variety than the heroes. Every town/dungeon is it's own encapsulated universe. You can go from a modern suburb, to a European castle, to a futuristic space station, to a mystical spirit world, to totally-not-Hong-Kong, to Hell, to a realm made of giant candy, or to the end of time and more. You get the idea. The way the game mashes incongruous themes together not only somehow works, but actually creates a very unique and memorable world.Battles likewise revolve around patching unique elements together to form a greater whole in the form of linking attacks into elaborate chain combos to add a bit of depth on top of the usual turn base fare. Nothing truly groundbreaking by today's standards, but it's definitely a step above the "mash X to win" vibes you get from a lot of sub-par Jrpgs. So what the game lacks in technical flair or deep story it makes up for in style, is what I'm basically saying.The remaster gives the game a shiny new reskin and restores all the content that was cut from the original PS1 version, which is not an insignificant amount of content, and the horrible mobile style UI they added for some reason can mercifully be turned off. At the time of writing I haven't played for a significant amount of time but I poked around some familiar places and everything seems in order, and I haven't run into any new glitches, so I'm pleased with this remake so far, which isn't something you get to say about square games so often these days, unfortunately.If you're not into fringe weeb RPGs, don't bother, obviously. But if you are, and you missed it in the 90s, now would be a good time to pick it up and give it a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This is how a remaster should be done. I've played Saga Frontier many times since it came out, but I've never been able to complete the game. The remaster fixes most of the problems I had with the original that made me hit a wall in completing it.Pros:- New Game+. A main issue with the original game is having to do basically the same side quests, 7 times. With new game+, you don't need to use the side quests every time to grind/get gear. Grinding is more or less a one time thing, unless you want to use characters unique to a story.- Running away added. No more pointless fighting overpowered enemies and ending up at the boss depleted. Running is AUTOMATIC, no chance of failing. Speeds up the game greatly.- Updated graphics.- No party size limit.- More control of monster skills.- AUTOSAVECons:- New game+ eventually gets overpowered. At about character 5-6 you're just hitting the x button waiting for stuff to die. Not much strategy needed.If you ever liked the original at all its a sure buy.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as a present from my brother. And i could not have asked a better gift.This games is awesome!!! i played it back in the day on the playstation 1. It really helped me through my childhood and kept me busy in sad times. The reason this game is so good is that you can choose your own destiny, and the games has so many extra sidequests. You can choose this time out of 8 characters instead of 7, and every one of them has different storys and can also intertwine with other characters story's if you want. I love the 2d oldskool rpg style and the fact that it still has the old skool turnbased fighting style. There is so much too love about this game, i give it 10 stars. So glad i can play this game again, i hope that they bring more RPG classics back.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier has been a gem when I first played it in 1998. Spent countless hours on it learning techs, maxing out characters and just having a great time with it. It's a Non-Linear RPG that NOW has 8 protagonists (7 were in the original). Some stories intertwine with others. This time around, Fuse is playable after finishing one or more other scenarios. Graphics are more cleaned up now and you can definitely see the details in the game more clearly now than before. On PC, highest resolution is 1080P. You can change the game speed to 2x or 3x, option to play with additional content that didn't make it in the original, view artwork and listen to the soundtrack (which has been updated with NEW tracks). For those that are new to Saga Frontier Remastered, there is a quest log that gives you hints on where to go.I can go on and on, but this is a really an excellent job of Square Enix and Akitoshi Kawazu's to remaster this underrated gem for the current generation. You won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: _Short version_This remake contains the love and care that any classic should get. The soundtrack is playable from the word go in the, the art bumpers are in full HD (both in the gallery), the option to turn off the modernization is present, and overall, it just feel like someone at Square really loved this game specifically - as they should, its amazing.Do you like anime inspired, classic JRPGs?~ Buy this.Do you want Square to remake other classic JRPGs from their library?~ Buy this."Okay, but where is Parasite EVE Remake?"~ Buy this."Okay, but where is the Chrono Cross Remake?"~ BUY THISVote with your dollar, folks.Now as to WHY I love this game. It was a formative part of my childhood and the aesthetic and mechanics stuck with me more than anything else. The sheer variety and speed of the game play makes it a dream to slide into.Back in the day (the 90s) I was a hardcore Square Soft mark. If they released a game there's a good chance I would try it at least once (back when rentals were a more common thing). I have a unique history with this game specifically though. A bit of a pointless story overall, but that history helped make this game one of my all time favorites so when I heard this was getting a Remaster I was over the moon with the presentation.It looked faithful yet new, it looked just as humble as I remember yet it looked like it fixed a LOT of the problems I had with the main game without destroying the limitations. It seemed balanced. It seemed like there was love worked into this Remake. And there is, there's so much care and love baked into ever inch of the game I've played so far with the modern convinces that let you expedite the experience and cut away the chaff from this classic JRPG master work.Now...Do the old bones of the game have its strange as hell quirks?Yes indeed.Does it still feel like the old PS1 era game that it is?Certainly.Did that involve reading a guide book to know exactly where certain aspects would lead or take you?Oh hell yes - but they've also worked a lot of that INTO The game's story chapter section.It is, simply put, a great time if you're down for a slightly janky, different take on how Saturday Morning JRPGs can be.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: I have a lot of nostalgia for this game because I owned it as a kid on Playstation. The remaster adds several quality of life features and cut content from the original. I played through Red's campaign and really enjoyed it, especially the music. However, I couldn't see myself doing all of the other campaigns plus Fuse's cases; so in terms of fun, this game didn't age too well for me.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite game ever. I very much dig the mechanics: No levels, the stats that you use are the stats you improve, human mechanics, mec mechanics. The 8-fold interwoven stories, the magic system. They're all very cool. The playable monster system is a little difficult to grok, but rewarding once you do. And mystics are still basically just weak/useless humans, unfortunately.The Remaster provides an 8th primary character story, a new recruitable character, improved character sprites, and the ability to recruit all available characters per protagonist, not just limited to 15. One of the most game-changing changes is the ability to flee from fights with no penalty; this significantly reduces the game difficulty (though you can just ignore that if you want more challenge). The controller interface works well with an Xbox 360 USB controller.All in all, I feel the remaster is all improvement, nothing is taken away from the original. None of the new content feels "out of place", as it sometimes does in other games. It's my understanding they just finished implementing stories that were written by the original team way back when. The PS1 games was a 10/10 in my book, and the remaster is still 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This game was awesome on PSX and it's even better now. It's all over the place with vampires and robots and superheroes, but it works. The universe it takes place in is cool. There isn't a planet, chunks of reality just float around an endless sky. The New Game + fixes a lot of what made it difficult to finish each character's path. If you are generally a JRPG fan this is really worth crossing off your list.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember renting this as a kid just fresh off playing Final Fantasy VII for a while and I loved every second of it from the different stories and building your characters to the epic fights of having new moves when you are about to lose just to turn the tide and win. I highly recommend this game the graphics are crisp and fresh and I can see details I've never noticed before or had to leave up to my imagination. I love pixel art and sprites but this was done right instead of a dumb filter that tries horribly to improve upon pixel sprites they have scaled it all up and it looks fantastic. I give this game a 9/10 and highly recommend it to anyone who likes JRPGS.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my best-remembered Playstation games, brought to a modern platform with some nice additions.Calling it a JRPG could be misleading, because while the battle mechanics fit in that genre, it's mostly missing the railroad track plot and the accompanying attitude that you are really playing the game for the plot cutscenes, and the rest of the game is makework to earn the next cutscene.But calling it "open world" would be an exaggeration. The world is a network of planets with travel routes between them, and depending on which character you are playing and where you are in their plot, you can generally move around freely and visit locations in any order and multiple times.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: I want to say I'm not clouded by nostalgia, and that this is an amazing remaster. But I have things to say first.This game gives you very little instruction on how to proceed, and sometimes there's not even much of a plot for why you're doing what you're doing. You're given a handful of bills, a knife or a gun. Blindfolded and spun around and dropped off in the vast world and told "Go get 'em kid."There's no explanation of how the character growth system works, how to gain new abilities. It's trial and error, there are exploits that crack the game in half, and the game is still difficult and obtuse.Yep, exactly how I remember it from my childhood. Thanks for not patching out those "exploits", because damn, I don't think I could do this without them.Good job on this one, Squeenix. Now give us SaGa Frontier 2 Remastered.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: Saga Frontier is a classic JRPG, one of my favorites when I first upgraded to the PSX after loving Squaresoft games I'd played on the SNES.It occupies an interesting space that uses the additional power of the PSX to drive the same kinds of mechanics seen in 16-bit. While not at ambitious as FF7 and other contemporaries, it plays to an older style quite well. The Remaster, in particular, has some significant quality of life upgrades on familiar aspects that make for a more fun replay experience if you have enjoyed the game before.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing remaster of the original PSX classic.  Improved in every way.  If you enjoyed the original, you'll definitely enjoy the remaster.  New Game+ is a godsend, and the QoL improvements make it so much more enjoyable to play.If you've never played a SaGa game, be warned that it's much different than your 'typical' JRPG.Major Differences: - Overarching story? Nah.  Each character has a small individual story, there is no 'greater mission' at work here. - Character archetypes? Optional.  Anyone can do just about anything. - Level ups? Nah.  You improve your stats based on what abilities you use.   - Battle Rank - monsters level up as you do, which also makes things harder. - Direction of where to go next? - The Remaster team decided this was worth adding, and thank goodness.A few notes for anyone who hasn't played this game before and wants to pick up the Remaster: - Do not start with Riki/Asellus as your first characters because they're the most complicated. - Do not start with Lute as your first character because his story sucks. - Don't feel bad about 'abusing' the Gold or Junk shop 'exploits'
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: A great followup to the original 90s game. It carries all of the mechanics of the original and even adds scenes and a character that was cut from the original game. A good choice if you are looking for a solid entry into the SaGa series, as it was the first game that introduced me to this series as a whole. Contains moments where you will have to grind, but it is not a grind heavy game, especially if you compare it to Romancing SaGa 2. Fun on all counts, try it if you want to learn about the SaGa series, or want a new take on the RPG genre of games.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: The game is phenomenal and, despite being a relic, still holds up today. The characters are fun and interesting. The universe is insane and unique. The sparking system and abilities in general are fascinating. Admittedly, I am biased as this was my favorite Squaresoft RPG, but SaGa Frontier Remastered is a solid 8/10.Pros:Cut content restoredThe original style wasn't sacrificedAudio player and Character art viewer in the menusGame speed togglesImproved menusImproved LayoutAdded quest log for each character's critical pathCons:Some choppy art (Owmi landing in particular looks...bad)Controllers sometimes require re-entering the system menu to enable, even while in use.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, review of Saga Frontier. Where do I begin with this pile of incoherent mess.....There are 7 stories in the original ( the 8th in this version is basically Fuse investigating the original 7 ) but they are all very shallow, bare bones stories. They almost look like outlines of potential stories for the final product as opposed to being the actual stories that should be in the final game. They are 7 separate stories that barely touch at all.  Red and Blue ( which I swear are just place holders for names they never got around to thinking of ) are the only ones that don't join you. The rest will join someone else's story. If you, as one character, meet a character from another story that joins, the joining character seems to put their entire important quest on hold to join... whatever it is you're doing.  Personally, I believe they should have done one good story that the characters all link to, instead of 7 that have nothing to do with each other. Asellus is the only character with a good story. Emelia, T260, and Red are all "Go after these bad guys that are never fully explained and we never find out reasons for most of the few plot points we get and nothing is explained. Who's Trinity? What is Cube? What is BlackX? What is RB3 and why are we fighting it? I'm not marking that as spoiler because it's never explained.  never explained.   Riki tries to save his homeworld by collecting rings  Blue's quest is to collect magic to kill and absorb his twin brother  Lute.... he literally has almost no story at all. It's like they ran out of time and just packaged the game without putting his full story in. He gets an incomplete. From starting a new game as Lute to final boss is about 20 minutes or so.Furthermore, a complaint I have with how the story is presented is text boxes. Sometimes they will display a smaller text box that types out but scrolls up as it runs out of room and you can't read what was said. It doesn't wait until you press the confirm button... it just scrolls on and on until it gets to the stop point and doesn't let you read what was in the beginning part, forcing some resets or screenshotting to see what it said. Sometimes the game DOES use larger text boxes so we know it's possible. Why let us read text boxes sometimes but not others? In addition, I get the feeling this game was unfinished. There's a ladder in the sewers that seems to lead to somewhere that never got filled. There are parts of dungeons you can't reach. There's this thing called "Draw scared lot" in the region of Devin that you apparently can't do because she always says "SOLD OUT" every time, so no clue what that was even supposed to be. A monolith with writing that you can't interact with, a few rooms exist with no purpose. And so on. Finish the game please or cut these loose ends out.One thing I'm happy for in this version, an 8th character is introduced when you beat a story: Fuse. If you start a new game with Fuse, he will investigate a character you have beaten the game with, and essentially try to explain some of the plot holes the original game had. It's a nice touch to try to explain some things, as a LOT of things were unexplained in the original. They never did explain what Draw Sacred Lot meant, but at least they tried to tie up some loose ends.There's some good things in this game though. Artwork is pretty good. Music is pretty good too, however get used to hearing the battle song a LOT, which brings me to my biggest complaint: Combat. The combat system in this game is pretty good though. There are 4 types of characters: Human, Mystic, Mech, and Monster. Each one learns skills in a different way. Some characters can combo their skills together to make combos for more damage. Nothing wrong with the actual combat system....Instead of random encounters like most RPG's, you have to walk into the enemy sprite to initiate the battle. In some games like Chrono Cross, this system works, allowing you to grind if you want to, or bypass them if you don't want to fight. In Saga Frontier however, as soon as you're on a screen the mobs will charge you at full speed. You step into their line of sight, they all want to fight you. Sometimes you have to clear 3-5 mobs before you're even able to see what the room you're in looks like so you can figure out where to go. Heaven forbid any dungeons where you have to go between more than one screen and have to clear 3-5 mobs each time you go to another screen so you can figure out what you are supposed to do. You move to one screen and by the time you get a chance to see what the room looks like, you forgot why you are there or what you are doing in the first place. Even if you are highly levelled far above where the mobs are leveled to in new game plus, they will all charge to their deaths at full speed the moment you enter. In new game plus you beat the mobs easily but still have to sit through character command inputs being entered one at a time, then after battle you sit through HP Up for Emelia, Vit Up for Emelia, Concentration Up for Emelia, JP up for Roufas, Vit Up for Roufas, WP Up for Annie, HP Up for Annie, Concentration Up for Rouge..... and so on. It's repetitive and boring. I'd rather just have the random battles from the Final Fantasy games or something as opposed to this annoyance. I spent 45 hours to beat all stories, including all the Fuse missions, and I swear I spent AT LEAST 30 hours of that in battle, with I'm sure about 20 hours of it in battles I didn't even want to be in. The remastered version of this game at least has a fast forward button but it doesn't go forward fast enough. The original game was a HUGE HUGE grind fest. Each of the 7 stories in the original, you would have to grind credits to buy the equipment you needed to beat the bosses with ( and that's VERY hard to do if you don't know about the Junk Shop glitch or the Gold Ingot glitch ) and the final bosses for each story are incredibly hard for this reason alone. With new game plus, thankfully you can carry over gold, weapons, items, etc to the new game for a new story. Therefore a LOT of the grinding is reduced so you don't have to do the exact same grind for each individual story.... but still there is a LOT of grinding even with the new game plus and it gets incredibly boring. At least 80% of my game time is doing stuff I have already done in other stories but had to do yet again. With 7 characters, they ALL repeat these same side quests and it's a chore to go through them.In short, Saga Frontier Remastered is a faithful remaster of the original game but the original sucked, was boring and uninteresting, and seems to be unfinished, even after adding Fuse's story and the rest of the cut content. If this game was presented to me as a game somebody is working on, I'd say "It looks great! I can't wait to see the finished product." However, as it is presented as a final game, I'm highly suggesting to play something else.

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier.. ahh.  What a wonderfully wonderful game.  If you need reasons to play this game,  I could list hundreds.  Literally.  I won't here, but here's some pro/cons about this beautifully crafted JRPG.++ Multiple story lines, huge replayability++ New Game+ with a secret dungeon++ Grinding is satisfying due to battle rank system constantly keeping things challenging++ Character roster is more than you can fit in a party!  Literally!  You can't take everyone you see!++ Beautiful OST - I listen to this at night all the time still to this day.++ In this Remaster, there's now a quest log and a cleaned up UI to help with navigation (a serious problem of the PSX classic)++ New character to play as -- FUSE!!!!!++ Combo system is insanely fun, and sparking new skills is an easy to learn, hard to master system.++ Remaster has.. wait for it.. FAST FORWARD!!  No more need for an emulator (sup retroarch) for playing this game at modern speed!++ Remaster has a favorite system for Combos!  This is great for when you have monster's or mechs and need a good way to combo off them without spending all your WP/JP.Now for some cons.-- Stat system can be hard to understand due to no descriptors about stats.-- Battle rank system is hidden, and there is opportunity to completely miss best in slot items due to unfamiliarity of BR.-- Grindy. -- Difficulty scaling means end bosses ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ truck you, trash mobs will be VERY strong creatures (mini-bosses) with multi-hit abilities able to wipe you in 1-2 turns.-- Inability to hear OST during normal gameplay - due to the almost frantic nature of this game, you're dashing with fast forward on and moving through towns so quickly you barely get to hear this beautiful masterpiece.  Definitely take some time to run it in the background to hear those sweet sweet =========If you've made it this far, buy the damn game.  It's superb.  IF you don't like it at first, give it some time.  The game really shines around 3-4 hours into a playthrough.  Don't be afraid to follow a guide, but avoid using Scrap trick or Ingot dupe to get infinite money as it really ruins the feeling of acquiring credits and items.  You should do this after you've beaten the game and want to rush through a character to unlock more of the game.BUY THE DAMN GAME!!!
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This crazy fantasy/sci-fi fusion world is just as imaginative as I remember. Multiple protagonists to choose from to give you a different perspective on the world. Each story taking around 10ish hours to complete, which makes each adventure nice, short, and digestible. Four different races with completely different paths for growth, making party building a big part of the enjoyment. Ridiculous over the top combos to style on your enemies with. And a bunch of quality of life features such as speeding up combat to 3x speed, and a New Game+ option that is highly customizable so that you only carry over the data you want carried over. Not only does SaGa Frontier live up to my nostalgic memories of the game, but it surpasses it, easily crowning this gem as one of the greatest RPGs I've had the pleasure to play.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This was one of my favorite games back on Playstation, and I was ecstatic to see it come out again here, remastered and with restored cut content.Is it grindy?  Is it a little thin?  It's a jrpg from 1997, of course it is.  But it's a lot of fun, with a lot of charm, and a gorgeous aesthetic.  Absolutely beautiful game.It meant a lot to a young me, also, to see a canonically lesbian protagonist back in the 90s.  You just didn't get those in games.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I will put a lot of hours into this game. I would be willing to let a friend try my copy of the game and see if they like it. I would not recommend anyone buying this game without knowing exactly what they're getting themselves into.It is a turn based jRPG with interesting ideas, mechanics, and an early effort at open-world game design. It has a charming asthetic and I'm very fond of many of the stories and characters. But I wouldn't call it well made and I'd definitely warn prospective players that it's best experienced with a lot of guidance from a friend familiar with the title or a walkthrough.And I don't think that's something most people are going to enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Akitoshi Kawazu creates a brilliant marriage of east meets west RPG in the SaGa series.  Filled with adventure and exploration,  SaGa Frontier is unlike your typical JRPG.  Expect to wander and wonder, fight tons of interesting enemies and uncover the secrets of the world without much guidance of "what next"; "what next" is up to you, welcome to SaGa.During development for the Playstation, funding was stripped from the game and given to the Final Fantasy series.  That, along with development crunch times caused the game to have quite a few missing pieces.  Thankfully those have been implemented for the remaster.  The remaster does feature a bit of a jarring UI fit for a mobile game, but otherwise the new sprites and the game look great overall.  Also, huge bonus for adding the option to speed up battle times!SaGa Frontier is my favorite game of all time and I'm glad it gets to finally be finished.  I hope you will enjoy it as much as I do.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the ORIGINAL.I HATE with a passion, what they did with this game.They made everything very LINEAR, and too many explanations.Why did they change the skill's original names? They're AWFUL and don't feel right. I literally want to cry every time I see "Ursine Assault" (used to be Bear Crush, flows/sounds better).They don't have Fuse as a playable character on this steam version it seems? Why?Some of the graphics are a bit nicer and smoother, however whenever you use Phantasm Shot, the art of the beasts summoned look awful...it used to be detailed.This game is the love of my life, along with two others, so I am very disappointed with the remake of this game. They didn't need fixing/changing.I will say I still recommend this game, however, as "confusing" and non-linear the original one was (I actually loved this about the game)...play the original first so you understand what I'm saying.The appeal was taken away in the remastered versions, for which I do not appreciate...Again...I will only recommend it (specifically the original one), since this is one of my absolute favourite games of all time. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, I'd recommend it but this game is like the embodiment of that Homer Simpson meme where he's buying the evil Krusty doll.- It's a cult-classic JRPG previously unavailable on modern systems ("That's good!")- The update is another lazy mobile port from Square Enix with obnoxious UI and an ugly hodgepodge of old, fuzzy 3D assets mixed with new, simplified 2D sprites ("That's bad.")- They added in new story content and characters cut from the original game  ("That's good!")- The game can be unforgivably difficult, with sudden, unpredictable difficulty spikes that can leave your game soft-locked ("That's bad.")- They added a robust autosave feature that prevents hours of lost progress from random difficulty ("That's good!")- When you're in an unwinnable fight, you can't just quit to the title screen and reload.  You either die or have to quit to desktop. ("Can I go now?")

_childDocuments_.review: If you played this back on PS1 and liked it, you'll probably like the remaster. It has some nice aspects here and there, but it's not a good game. If you do play it, use a walkthrough, because without it you will wander around forever trying to figure out what the game wants you to do, and Red's story in particular, I can promise you will not beat it without a guide. It has a section where you have to move through a certain number of rooms before you confront the boss chasing you, but gives absolutely no indication that this is the case. If you confront the boss without moving through the right number of rooms, you go through the entire boss fight, and then when you win, you get a game over. It's not good. Nothing but good music and nostalgia give it any real value.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: Not even 10 hours later, SaGa Frontier's Riki story lays beaten, and.. after seeing how much of an improvement Romancing SaGa 3 was compared to its two Romancing predecessors, I was eager to see what the big step to the PS1 would bring, how much bigger and more complex the game would be.. I didn't expect baby's first JRPGThe game has absolutely no challenge, holds yer hand all the time and constantly reminds you where to go and what to do.  Gone are all the weapon types, character archetypes, and complex weapon/magic leveling systems.  This time, all the (human) characters get OP real fast since they just sorta learn their best attacks within a few battles, without any requirements (since yanno, no more weapon/magic levels), and there's only three real weapon types : Sword, Fist, and Gun.  Magic is super cheap and easy to master, but most of it's useless, when you can just buy the best gun in the game right in the starter hub (in fact, you can buy the best gear in general, right away)Instead of actually being open-world and yer starter character simply affecting where you start, each character in this game has a different goal and characters they can recruit, but they're all very short, have virtually nothing to do with eachother, and they all visit (and revisit) the same areasThere's an extra character in the remaster that sort of counts as a final story since he unlocks extra mini-chapters for every story you beat, but it's more of a recap kinda deal, and his main appeal (relatively) is a boss rush mode, culminating in a boosted version of that mini-chapter's final boss but since you essentially need to beat every single story twice to get the "full experience", it'd just feel like a bunch of fluff to try and justify the ridiculous price tagI have no idea why this was on PS1, and what the hell they did with all the extra storage space and resources, this could have easily been an N64 game
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This game was bad twenty years ago when I played it as a kid and it is still bad today even after this remaster. I was hoping that being grown up would help me appreciate the game more but it sadly has not. I have no attachment to the characters as their stories are shallow and the dialogue is horrible. Just truly awful. Most of the game is wandering around hoping that you stumble onto the next story beat or quest. I shouldn't have to read the story recap every time something happens just to understand what's going on in the story. It's so bad.I want to like the battle system, I really do...but it too is terribad. The majority of the skills you learn are absolutely trash, you learn them completely at random it seems so you sit there spamming either basic attack or one of your other skills hoping that you spark a new skill. So, on some characters you just never spark anything and you're completely worthless in battle. Then, the battle difficulty curve is nonexistant. It dips and spikes however the hell it wants. Like I was exploring one of the first dungeons you can go to in Shrike and got to the end boss which was so over the top powerful that it was literally impossible for me to win. I had to come back later after hours of grinding and it was still a challenge to complete. Like why? Even story bosses spike in difficulty that is so unfair and frustrating that I almost just quit a few times. For example, in Asellus' campaign when you get attacked by the three elemental mages and they are unavoidable encounters that happen when you enter a certain type of screen (?).  The first two mages were manageable but the third was one shotting my entire party.  Again, it took me hours of grinding to beat him and avoiding certain screens because those would trigger the boss fight. It's just trash. It's frustrating, boring, and nothing has improved over the last two years. I'm not sure why it gets called a masterpiece because I certainly don't think it deserves that at all. It's a low tier JRPG at best.

_childDocuments_.review: The number of people reading the negative reviews is...well, it's a pleasure to see.Because it means that people are being smart and they're skeptical about all of the glowing reviews.  As well you should be.Here's the thing.  Every single person that says this is a good game, is suffering from what I refer to as .  A very serious disease that has claimed more casualties than COVID-19 and war put together.It's this idea that, when you liked it as a kid, a remake can simply do no wrong.  Even when the developer goes off the rails.  You're nostalgic about it rather than rightfully criticizing it against the games of the current era that are of a similar make.  And I'm going to cover that in my review because I've seen some whoppers.There are some people who are immune to this terrible disease.  I am one of them.  There are games I couldn't STAND as a kid where they impressed me later (Trials of Mana) and games where I thought they were the ATG as a kid yet older I was able to clearly see the flaws (Skies of Arcadia).  It means I'm not swayed by how I felt as a kid, and I can separate.But here?  SaGa Frontier was garbage when I was a kid and it's garbage now.  But I want you to understand  I say it's garbage, because the same flaws aren't addressed. 🚫 ✅OBJECTION: Improper Characterization.The ONLY similarity here is that you have a bunch of random people with separate events, eventually teaming up.  There is NO similarity beyond that.Octopath actually HAS a story.  SaGa Frontier has a fraction of story for each person then it's "go out and find your destiny" with no direction and no real gameplan until the end of each segment.Octopath doesn't subject you to random stat increases; you actually level up logically and predictably.Octopath doesn't throw you to some boss that one-shots you simply because you were chasing some villain.Octopath has voice acting.  A lot of it.  Which enhances the characters and the story.I could go on and on.  Octopath was inspired by a lot of different games, and there are certainly pieces of SaGa found here, but they're the exception to the rule.🚫 ✅OBJECTION: Assumes Facts Not In Evidence.Dewprism (aka "Threads of Fate" for you 'Muricans) was way deeper than this, as were numerous RPGs of the era.  Vagrant Story, Tales series, any of the Final Fantasies, Dragon Quest VII, any of the Breath of Fires, Magic Knight Rayearth, Lunar, etc etc etc.No, this game is just thin because it was half-assed when it was released and it's still half-assed.🚫 ✅OBJECTION: Hearsay.If you look at Trials of Mana and compare it to this and try to tell me that SaGa is "better" than Trials?You're just being biased at that point.  Come on.Look, there's a reason that Square Enix released this at a very reasonable $25 price point yet felt compelled to release the Mana Collection at $40 despite being a bunch of unoptimized ROMs.SaGa Frontier is arguably one of the worst games to come out of that developer, period, and they knew it wasn't worth spending more than $25 on it.At $25?  Sure, go ahead and try it.  It might be for you if you like to .  But let's be realistic.  It can't lace the boots of ANY RPG out there, past or present.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of the original you're loving this. If you haven't played a romancing saga game befor, I would look it up. There are multiple characters to choose from off the start and tentatively you will complete each of their "scenarios" that are different but in game terms is fairly usual, you go to "towns" buy stuff, fight enemies and get stronger. Instead of experience and levels your characters grow organically based on what they "do" in battle. While characters have "builds" they favor you are not obligated in following them. Depends on the characters race, humans level up by battle, mystiques (espers, mutants etc) level up in battle AND absorbing monsters into their unremoveable gear, half mystique is both, monsters level up by eating meat after battle (make sure it's from a stronger monster.) and robots power up by equipping gear. Humans and mystiques pennultimately are OP by and far since you can just grind fights. Enemy groups do level up alongside player's power level overall but I havent' found that challenging. Game's a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Underrated isn’t a word that I like to just toss around, as I feel like it’s been overused ad nauseam. But I genuinely feel like this game is underrated in the rpg world, and the SaGa games as a whole, At least here in the west I should say. It takes on a drastically different, somewhat ambitious design formula than what most people would be used to from square.Not to mention, it’s punishingly difficult, and can be downright unfair. All that aside though, I feel like there’s enough here to warrant an amazing experience assuming you’re looking for a challenge, not just in gameplay, but also the mechanics. And while they may not be hard to understand, there is a good amount of learning to be done. Particularly when it comes to powering up some of the character types, such as the mystics and the monsters. You can literally find several full spreadsheets online that will help you understand the proper stat spreads, obtainable abilities, as well as monster transformations  from people who’ve meticulously studied every aspect of the game. Obviously you don’t have to do this, but it can save you some time on character progression, especially if you find yourself stuck on a really difficult boss. However, If you’re like me, you take enjoyment in the aspect of not having your hand held, which this game will never do, ever…. If you’re looking for an entirely nonlinear, world building focused rpg. This one is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that brings me back to childhood, I had been meaning to revisit the game for so many years, and the remake seemed like a good opportunity to do so.  If you ever play Saga frontier, go with remastered, it gives such nice QoL improvements like speeding everything up.  Well, that's mostly it, but with oldschool RPGS thats what you need, making combat and walking speed much faster.I love the multiple branching character lines, though my memory clearly comes from mostly playing "Blue", which makes sense, my mind even now playing as an adult will go "Oh yeah I like blue nice color" and pick that each time.   The big thing here for the remake is that they added a new playable character, but it didn't feel super fleshed out so it's one of the weaker storylines, kind of like Lute.  Anyway, the QoL improvements is what makes this game worth playing.  If you played the original, you know its a fun game but the writing is.. not Squares best work. _childDocuments_.review: Childhood favorite that I never got to fully appreciate until I got older. Buying a remastered version was a no brainer for me, but I still recommend this to people who like the older Squaresoft games, or just enjoy games that let you really dig into training characters up. SaGa Frontier is by no means a standard RPG, but it's one that is excellent for when you want to calm down and just relax. The QoL features have made leveling your party even easier, and it's the sort of game that you can take a break from between character stories, then return to when you want to continue.There is lore to be found in the game, but combat and character building takes precedence over story most of the time. There are really only two characters who almost entirely lack a storyline, but that shouldn't stop you from trying this game out.

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier is an interesting SaGa series entry; it has all the usual gameplay mechanics on display but it chose a different direction for the story.You start by choosing one of the eight main characters, each with their own unique story to experience (except Fuse, his involves experiencing other's stories from an outside perspective.)You'll be visiting the same places and doing some of the same side quests as you do each character's story. This might become grating to some but I found it to be rather enjoyable as there are a few different recruitable character between each story. Once you've built up most of the recruits, the last few stories become a breeze thanks to NG+.SaGa Frontier can be quite confusing at first as it tends to not give you much direction at all and this can be especially true depending on the character you choose. For example after Blue's opening cutscene you're dumped in the world and all you have is a general goal, you're left to explore and figure it out for yourself. If you're feeling a bit alienated by the game, your best bet is generally to try another character.Another thing to be mindful of are the different races, Human, Monster, Mystic and Mec. Human is the most common and easy to use race, whereas the other races fight/work differently, which can be really fun once you know what you're doing but overwhelming when you're first getting into the game (so it might be best to avoid Asellus, Riki or T260G on your first playthrough). Monsters, for example, get their moveset by absorbing an enemy they've just defeated in battle, this can also cause them to transform and increase/decrease stats.Personally I found a lot of enjoyment in SaGa Frontier and I believe the individual stories played a big part in that. Some were much better than others, but all around it was a great experience. I played through Romancing SaGa 3 prior to this and absolutely loved that, I wasn't expecting SaGa Frontier to reach as high as Romancing SaGa 3, but for me SaGa Frontier managed to top it. This game isn't going to be for everyone though as it does get repetitive at times.So if you're looking for one cohesive and epic story, Romancing SaGa 3 is probably more for you but if you like the sound of multiple bite sized stories that you can consume at your own leisure, then definitely give SaGa Frontier a try. SaGa Frontier manages to give the player a taste of what the SaGa series is all about.

_childDocuments_.review: SaGa Frontier Remastered is an excellent game that offers a ton of replayability and engaging gameplay. The combat system is deep and strategic, allowing for a variety of approaches to combat. The seven playable characters each have their own unique story arcs, which adds a lot of replayability. The enhanced visuals and music are a welcome addition and the game runs smoothly on modern systems. With all of these features, SaGa Frontier Remastered is a must-have for any RPG fan.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a real SaGa Frontier fan, as in the type to finish all seven characters and the developer room (back on PS1), *and* do autistic playthroughs where I run themed parties (five mages, five mechs, five monsters, five mystics, whatever). This review is more for people who were similar to me from the PS1 era.- Even though the sprite art is a little uglier imo, the overall feel of the game graphically is way better.- The battle/map speed options are great, as I used to have to play it nearly muted on an emulator running at 300% speed (which would obviously make the music unbearable).- Simple quality of life features were added, like how you manually choose which monster ability you want to overwrite rather than having to keep the disposable ability in a specific slot. - Big fat super bosses when playing Fuse- They changed some of the wording unnecessarily, like describing T260 as a "they" and not a "he". That one might just be a minor pet peeve for me and not others, which is fine. Though they also changed a lot of the names for skills, which wasn't exactly an improvement, like "Double Vertical" instead of "Double Slash".- And now the big con... they didn't finish the game. There's still side areas that are incomplete, still dummied-out areas that they could've put back into use. One glaring instance new players might notice is this strange room in the Light Labyrinth that you could redirect light into it, but nothing happens there. It's a room with zero purpose. There's a dummied-out room that you won't see in the game, that is just like that room except it was supposed to be on the left side of the map. In the original game, they were pressed for time and simply buried that left room with the rest of the unused assets, but forgot to do the same with the right room. This time they were *not* pressed for time. Why didn't they fix it? On top of that, if they chose to, they could've added way more content. At least some optional dungeons or something! I mean, it's cool that Fuse has unlockable super bosses, but I definitely feel they could've done more.
_childDocuments_.name: SaGa Frontier Remastered

_childDocuments_.review: This is a faithful remaster of the original game, and for that I enjoyed it. I can't help but feel some disappointment at the new content though. _childDocuments_.review: The Remaster does a good job of addressing some of the quality of life issues present in the original game. The new game content of Fuse's story and the additional content for Asellus' story are engaging and fit organically with the rest of the game. I appreciate that the original version of the game has been preserved and can also be played.The only minor issue I have with this game is that there is no built in vsync option.

_childDocuments_.review: The best remaster SquareEnix has done by far.  The speedup options are a godsend as the default battle speed is incredibly slow by modern standards. There's almost nothing negative I can say about the remaster other than it still has that weird issue all Square Enix japan PC ports have where if a USB bluetooth device reconnects the game freezes or goes to 2 FPS while it reconnects. Some implementation of a library they use is awry.I didn't encounter a single crash in my entire playthrough, according to steam is 200 hrs or so. That's truly high praise as I've played every other SquareEnix remaster and even modern games and they all seem to crash eventually. Originally SaGa Frontier was the victim of marketing blunders back in the 90s. The SaGa trilogy on gameboy was great, but I knew them as Final Fantasy Legend, and didn't pick up the SaGa Frontier at the time because of the naming. The systems are quite similar - 8 slots for equipment/skills, mystics=mutants - though the mystic systems are slightly different from mutants. SaGa Frontier is the last game of its kind SADLY. There is a SaGa Frontier 2, however it is very different. After that only a couple SaGa games got made, and those abandoned the mutant/mystic and recruitable monster systems which I thought were great. I was sad when I finished all the main SaGa Frontier Remastered content.

_childDocuments_.review: I was truly surprised when I found out Square was going to allow this classic unfinished gem to actually be finished.  And they made so many improvements!  All while keeping the experience similar to the old days - albeit the remastered version can be called "easy mode", they still allow for you to pick and choose what new features you want.  Overall this is an amazing remastering and part of a group of PS1 era Square games that are being treated with care.  Well done guys.

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful remaster of a classic Playstation Game. So many fond memories of trying to figure out all the weirdness of this game with my roommates. Specifically this version, the remaster has so many wonderful quality of life improvements, bug fixes, tiny improvements, and bonus content. Well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I still have the original PS1 disc laying around at home somewhere. _childDocuments_.review: I wanted this for a very long time, but I thought it was never going to happen.Until it did. I was very much excited for this rerelease. So excited that I actually pre-ordered the game, and I don't pre-order anything anymore. I'm glad to say I wasn't disappointed by the end product.SaGa Frontier is a rerelease of a PS1 game made by Squaresoft. The SaGa series is a cousin to the Final Fantasy series, and SaGa Frontier in particular was released in the shadow of Final Fantasy VII. It was panned back in the day for being a non-linear RPG experience. Much of the meat of the game comes from exploring dungeons, building your party, grinding for stats and finding loot. THe main quests for each of the characters can be completed in just a few hours.Apparently it has gotten a lot more positive reception in light of games like Elder Scrolls and Dark Souls paving the road for nonlinear RPG experiences.There are some problems with the game's design, for sure, between the imbalance and the many, MANY holes where content was cut due to time and budget constraints, but damn if this game isn't charming and full of interesting content. Character designs (drawn by Saga artist veteran Tomomi Kobayashi) are absolutely insane, and monster designs are even more insane (one sub-boss is a pirate platypus, one of the mec party members is shaped like a fighter jet, and another monster is a floating rodent and is a police officer!). Combat is interesting to watch as the camera shifts around as each character attacks, making the turn-based combat feel a lot more alive and dynamic considering how primitive it is.This remaster port in particular is also top notch (mostly). In a full playthrough, I only had one crash, but because of the autosave function (which autosaves after every battle and screen transition), I basically lost no progress. The remastered sprites were both AI upscaled and redrawn; special props goes to Emilia's redesign, which gives her sprite more voluminous hair. There's some modern, mobile-looking UI that was added to this port, but you can turn it off. The restored content (of which there wasn't much, but whatever; it was what was still on the original disc) gives us an eighth saga and a little bit more information about each of the characters. New Game Plus is now a thing (something I've dreamed about for 23 years!), and you can customize what data you want to bring over to a new game.The one thing I take umbrage with, however, is the edits to the script. A lot of minor things like monster, attack and item names were altered for some baffling reason, which for an OG fan like me, ranges anywhere from slightly annoying (the Easy Rifle is now called Pendragon) to absolutely heretical (the Asura is now called Phantasm, and the Genocide Heart is now called Heretical Heart). But it's an easy thing to look over when the rest of the remaster is smooth as butter, and when you've been fantasizing about this for over twenty years.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is my childhood, but also something new. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's a weird toss-up. The remaster is better than the original. I don't think they did enough to improve the story, but the quality of life additions make it the superior option and it's probably cheaper than buying the original. Give it a try, maybe wait for a sale, refund if you don't like it, but understand you're looking at a niche JRPG from the era of "figure it out or fail". You may not have a good time until you know what you're doing, but you may not figure out what you're doing until it's past the refund period.------As someone who played this game way back in the day, who loves this game and to this very day still occasionally boots it up to complete a character arc or two even before I knew the remaster was a thing, I will say that it's kind of a let down how little they did with the remaster. For how niche this game is? For how far forgotten it was? I was expecting a lot more put into it. This isn't the kind of game that you just brush up the visuals and hope that nostalgia skyrockets your sales like what was attempted with that 3D Secret of Mana remake. The fanbase that still cares about this game is maybe in the lower end of the tens of thousands. Maybe. So when I heard about a remaster I was kind of expecting it to be a remake of love, to restore all the things that got cut out of the original game due to time constraints, resources, etc. But that didn't really happen.Asellus's story got 'finished', Fuse's story got added but not the way it was originally intended, there were some quality of life additions and some minor fixes (some major bugs actually intentionally got left in because they made the intense grinding you would otherwise deal with more bearable), there were some translation corrections, name changes for moves, and that's kind of it. Lute's entire storyline is still, STILL, "Start game, go to Owmi, fight final boss". Literally. Those are the steps you need to take to 'complete' his story, not counting grinding so you aren't one-shot by his literally seven phase back to back uninterrupted boss battle. I'm pretty sure the only reason Lute didn't get cut while Fuse did is because they already had all of Lute's boss assets made, so they just threw them together in one huge fight to make up for other losses. Asellus got touched up. Fuse got kind of added. We got some QoL. The sprites have a new look. That's basically it.So is this game good? I mean, I still love it, despite all its flaws. It definitely isn't an 'everyone' game. It's niche for a reason. And it's hard to compare the original game to the remaster. Part of the original's charm was how broken it was, how blatantly ignorant the player was of all the behind the scenes mechanics, all the trial and error figuring out what did what, how to get X, Y, or Z, discovering and exploiting bugs. The game, mechanically, is better for the remaster. And from a returning player's perspective, it's interesting seeing the additional information the remaster gives, comparing it against what I already knew, if there was something I didn't know or that I misunderstood. But for a new player? I don't know if this game will even hit above 'average'. It's an already niche game from an era notorious for not holding punches, but given some modern day quality of life. It's a weird mixture when you know what you're looking at.Is it worth the price? It's probably cheaper than buying the original disc off of eBay, especially with the remaster causing nostalgia scalpers to ramp up prices, and you have a refund policy if you don't like it. So for a remaster of an old forgotten game? ...Yeah. Sure. $25 isn't a bad asking price. $25 if you know the game and you already know you'll like it, $20 may be more reasonable to someone new, so maybe wait for a sale.Is it a good remaster? I'd say no. It's more of a port than a remaster. A port with 'enhanced visuals' (I put quotations not because I dislike the new visuals but because it's a style change and it's more of a sidegrade than an upgrade), a super speed button, and a help menu where the original game threw you in blind. It isn't a good remaster, but it's better than the original game. So take that how you will.Can I recommend this remaster over the original? I mean, when it's literally just the original game but slightly better, I'd be doing you a disservice recommending the original game. Between buying old controllers, a console that can play PS1 games, and the original disc (assuming you even get it at a reasonable price)? You're saving a lot of money just getting the remaster here on Steam. The only reason to play the original game anymore is if you just really, really miss those old pixel sprites. Which I can understand. I'll probably still boot up my copy to look at them now and again. But for actually playing? I'll probably just stick to the remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: Executive Summary: Excellent throwback for gamers of a certain age, might be a hard sell for younger players.The visual upgrade is quite obvious, but retains (or remains, if you see it that way) the somewhat blobby textures of the prerendered backgrounds that the original iteration had on the PS1. In a way, it seems to possess a somewhat dream-like quality, engaging more of the imagination than a modern fully-rendered game, though that could be the nostalgia talking.Map navigation is the same as it was -- simple, if somewhat under-expressive. The simple geometries of the areas you can move in sometimes causes you to snag on a piece of scenery, and consequently push you into combat.Combat is helped along by the inclusion of 2x and 3x speed modes. Otherwise, the combat mechanics are exactly the same as they were. Combat can be tough, and there is a real chance that any given encounter could be one that is way above what you can reasonably win -- more on this in a bit.Now for the not-so-good stuff. It doesn't hold your hand, and sometimes feels like it relies on its arcaneness, substituting obfuscation for any real complexity. Understandably, that could have been a limitation of the original hardware and expectations of the time, but it could be frustrating for new players who are more used to a little more clarity.One such impenetrable mechanic is the enemy scaling. It feels like the upper bound of the "challenge rating" of mob encounters is significantly higher than it should be, and TPW are common. Fortunately, loading from the title screen takes no more than a few seconds, so you are back and throwing yourself at another potential game over within a few moments. Assuming you quicksave after every few battles, or even after each one.That's one modern QOL issue that the developers could have been kind enough to automate. If the player can quicksave their game (almost) anywhere, then why not include auto-saves, even just between scene changes? (EDIT: Turns out that it does auto-save between scene changes, but you have to manually choose to load and auto-save, as "continue" defaults to your last manual save.) Moving on... The designs in this game are quite unique and memorable, from massive axe-beaked birds to an entire town of wacky fortunetellers, there's much to see that you can't find in any other game. That said, some areas feel unfinished, not having been developed to the extent that they could have been. Again, possibly a limitation of the original hardware and development, but the result is a world that feels fragmented and piecemeal.It's challenging enough that you can't mindlessly grind through it, sometimes frustrating, and in comparison to modern games, feels somewhat shallow and incomplete. All things considered, I am having fun though, and maybe completing it can give me some closure on what were some of my earliest gaming experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent remaster! This game was always a bit of an odd duck but I'd forgotten how much fun it was too. _childDocuments_.review: I adore this game. It's a great blast from the past and this remaster is almost without blemish. With so many crappy ports from Square Enix this is breath of fresh air. There are a few mobile game style additional menus but they aren't too bad. It runs great except for a few small frame drops. My favorite feature is that: THEY LEFT ALL THE FUN EXPLOITS IN!I would recommend this game just because of that decision. With the new content and Fuse character added back in, this is a complete package.This is still a fun JRPG sandbox for you to mess around in just like it was in 1998.The ability to speedup the battles and the game speed is pretty much required due to the grindy nature of the game at times.There are eight characters now and each has their own story. Even though some of these stories are good, there is some overlap with similar events between them.My main problem with the game is that it can get old quick if you've played it in the past and know allthe ins and outs. Each character can be broken down like this.1. Play the intro story campaign.2. Get a team together you want to fight the end boss with.3. Get 300 credits and do the junk shop exploit to get enough money to start the gold exploit. 4. Do the gold exploit and buy the best armor and weapons for your team.5. Grind until you are strong enough to beat the end boss, doing any rune or magic quests that are needed.6. Finish the campaign.7. Repeat 7 more times.The game is bit too repetitive for 8 characters but is fun to play, explore, fight build a strong fighting team, at least for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good <3.  It was my first time playing SaGa Frontier since I missed out on it's PSX release. I think it's a lot easier to get into if you're new to the SaGa series, except the difficulty could come as a bit of a surprise if you come from playing JRPGs like Final Fantasy. Do *not* try to fight every single encounter, the difficulty scales, so the game is easier and more enjoyable when you flee from hard trash mobs. It is a difficult balance in fighting enough to level up your stats, and not being too high that would require you to grind a *lot* more cause you pushed the bosses and trash mobs to the next threshold XD. I believe it is a fun challenge, and even though I have struggled a bit on my first run as Blue, I've really enjoyed myself <3.Although, technically it's my *second* run because I was silly and didn't realise that I would be locked into Despair without the Infrared Scope to complete the dungeon :P. I was just looking to recruit people, Annie spoke to me, and I got sent to Despair :X. Make sure you *always* have multiple saves in this game! ;) I can't wait to spend more hours in this game, I was going to wait to write a review but I wanted to give it another positive review because it's just such an amazing game <3!

_childDocuments_.review: Not an easy one to recommend, since it's not a game for everyone, but I really like a lot this remaster.I discovered this game a few years ago, so I think I'm not blinded by nostalgia when I talk about it. I played on emulator, since the game wasn't available in Europe, unlike SaGa Frontier 2. I played a bit of Asellus' storyline and quitted a few hours in, despite really liking the game. Others games not available in our region such as the first Parasite Eve were calling out to me. I'm taking my second round against this game right now, again with Asellus and I think I'm near the end.First things first, SaGa Frontier is all about its non-linear structure. Don't expect a story full of drama, only a journey full of discoveries and hardships. A lot of, actually. The core of the gameplay is focused around going wherever you feel like it and building a team able to defeat your many opponents along the way before they do. I emphase on this last part, it's not because it's a remaster that they make the game less challenging that it was in 1997.It might be a good idea to check the help options in the config menu in order to grasp the subtleties of the battle system, such as the combination attacks or monsters feeding. The game seems after that a bit less unpredictable and random^^The soundrack from Kenji Ito is a pleasure to the ears.Now for the remaster features, some elements added are welcome, the art and sound gallery for example. But I believe the boost in battle speed up to 3 times and the flee mechanic almost always avalaible are what's making the game really fun to play. It makes the leveling sessions really short! Also this remaster adds all the cut content in the original, including an eighth storyline, Fuse's, which isn't available at first. The game offers a vanilla experience as well for gaming historians.I pre-ordered the game, feeling along the way fear it wouldn't be worth it or disappointing, I was wrong. The game is a really interesting one, but it comes with a warning : it won't be for everyone. Nonetheless it has fully earned a full fledged recommendation on my book.

_childDocuments_.review: Well the SaGa Frontier remaster was everything that I hoped it would be.   The new content fits organically into the game without seeming obtrusive.   The old content is restored and cleaned up visually.   New music tracks are integrated well into the game.   New metagaming options (a robust NG+ feature that lets you toggle what exactly to carry forward into new save files) allow for virtually endless customization choices for your replays.   This is the game that I always fantasized about as a teenager and assumed it would stay as just that, a fantasy.   That Square was able to go back and faithfully remaster the game without adding a lot of garbage, including bringing back content originally cut for time, is amazing.   I don't think I will ever be truly happy with another remaster again.You've granted a childhood wish of mine Square, and I love you for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a little skeptical about this game because Square Enix has a rather checkered past when it comes to their remakes, remasters, and ports of older games.  This one, however, is a straight upgrade of the original PS1 version that retains all of the original's charm, quirks, art styles, and...everything, all while adding some nice QoL upgrades.  It's true to the original in just about every way and is a perfect example of how remasters should be done.They even left in all of the beneficial bugs:- Scrap junk shop trick:  Buy 3 picks, go collect things, sell repair kits, try to sell a Hyperion Bazooka that you don't have to get 7 more picks, repeat until you're loaded up on Cybersuits, Excel Shields,  High-Freq Swords, Lethal  Dragoons, then go all in on the sword pile until you have about 40, sell them at Shrike.- Gold Ingot trick:  Buy Gold Ingots for 500 per in Nelson, sell them in Koorong in large enough quantities to hike the price way up.  Totally bonkers moneymaking trick that they seemingly left in intentionally. <3- Learn opposing spells:  Characters with the gifts for Rune or Mystic magic can learn Realm and Arcane magic, then equip a Rune Sword or Purple Eye and relearn all of their lost spells over time using the spell attached to those items.Anyway, I played this game to death back in the days and bought it on day 1 of its remaster release when I normally never buy games full-price.  I'll admit though, this game isn't for everyone.  If you're looking for a hand holder, you'd better stay away.  Here's a bunch of things I think might not appeal to first-time, would-be players:- Weird difficulty spikes.  You can be trudging along, fighting weak enemies when suddenly, you find yourself in a boss fight that flattens you without mercy.- Annoying missable things.  Certain ares, like the Luminous Labyrinth, Mospriburg Mountain, etc are one-time-only areas you get sent to when on certain quests.  If you miss the goodies there, you're out of luck.  If you attempt the magic gift quests too early, anyone who joins later is going to miss out.- Terrible skill balance.  You can't see them, but each skill has a strength modifier.  While you'd think the cost and strength would go hand in hand, they don't.  It's possible for a skill with a higher cost to be less effective than a skill with a lower cost.- Vague quest objectives.  There's an in-game quest journal, which is a nice addition, but you still might find yourself turning to a guide to figure out where to go next.- Not everyone's quest is created equal.  Characters like Red, T260, Emelia, and Asellus have a lot more story content than characters like Lute.  Do not pick Lute as your first character.If these don't seem like any big deal to you though, give the game a go!  You'll probably know well within the refund period whether or not you like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is as fun as I remember and then some, now I'll come out and say - I do not think this game is for everyone. But if you're a big fan of Octopath Traveller, I'd really recommend this since it's essentially the granddad of that game, the skill learning system is satisfying, the stories are fun in their own right and personally I'm a big fan of the magic system.Mind you I've only just gotten through Blue's story since I remember them being my favourite from childhood.This game has many ways you can minmax it, there's plenty of secrets to find ; the usual JRPG shtick, the scaling enemies keep difficulty interesting to a certain degree and with all the cut content they added I'm sure there's even more secrets to find. I would say maybe wait until this game goes on sale however if you're sceptical.

_childDocuments_.review: For the gamer on the go looking for not an in depth review (there's some great ones here already)- Character designs vary quite a bit and there's gorgeous concept art on loading screens- Interacting with most NPCs is largely a waste of time with the exception of a few times in each protagonist's arc- Story is ok at the absolute best. There's some cool moments. Nothing super riveting here but neat concepts.- The combat is where this game shines, it's engrossing and fun -- although it can be easy to exploit- A fun, light play that you don't have to invest a ton of hours in but has decent replay value and is full of really neat concepts that inspired many RPGs after- Solid 7/10 IMO. Hope to see more of these classics come up.I played this game on PSX when I was 15, so I was very excited from a nostalgic standpoint.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked Asellus first not because she's a favorite; not mine anyway. But she's got the new stuff right? Well... 15 minutes in and I'm already enjoying some new stuff.It's good.If you don't know SaGa this is a good place to start.Edit Update: I've now completed Asellus while totally forgetting to do her new stuff with Dr. Nusakan. Oops! Mostly after this additional playtime I want to point out that the port is excellent. You can turn off the dumb mobile UI garbo (as with the Romancing remasters), and the framerate is uncapped. So even at 3x speed in battles it's still smooth for me. No crashes of any sort. The QoL improvements are huge and very welcome. I won't be touching Fuse until I finish all 7 original characters, but even after just one I can't imagine ever playing the original again.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Octopath Traveler then you will like SaGa Frontier. _childDocuments_.review: The 1998 PlayStation® classic is back: SaGa Frontier is remastered. The team of eight have returned – now with Fuse added as a playable character. Choose your favorite character and embark on your own unique journey. Each of the eight characters have different goals and endings. Your choices will affect how events unfold using the Free-Form Scenario System. This in-depth system will allow you to manipulate and expand a story all your own. Challenge yourself in nail-biting battles by using “glimmer" as well as learning new skills such as the ability to fire consecutive special attacks from multiple team members.
