_childDocuments_.review: Don't pay full price. This game is currently worth about £15 in content. It has all the foundations of a potentially great game, however the devs phoned it in and half assed it. Graphics - Good, not greatMechanics - Lacklustre, very basic compared to X-ComSetting - Amazing, you get a real feel for the Warhammer 40k settingOther Notes -Absolutely zero repercussions for losing squads and don't be surprised to have 1 or 2 men left out of a whole army when the missions are over on high difficulties. Next to no RPG elements. You get a very boring upgrade tree for your named characters which affect the rest of your army. However individual units have zero 'experience tracking' and restart every mission as new. Such a shame, allowing each unit to upgrade on their own and earn new weapons and stat improvements would of gone a long way to making this a solid game worthy of the price tag. This would also give an incentive to 'save' squads as at the moment they may as well all be guardsmen with how replaceable they all are. When this is supposed to be showcasing the blood angels space marines, expecting even half of them to die each mission is completely against the lore and setting.As with all games utilising the Warhammer 40k IP at the moment, this game pulls you in with great graphics and the promise of scratching that 40k itch before letting you down just like the rest. Final verdict:5/10 - Flawed game, great foundationCould be a 8/10 game with more content and a altered progression system.

_childDocuments_.review: Battlesector is a solid game  and a breath of fresh air compared to the usual shovelware games that somehow end up with the 40K license. It has a lot of complexity to it, a reasonably compelling single-player campaign, and a myriad of ways to play online versus your friends.I think it's an excellent foundation and I'm excited to see what the devs intend to add on to it. If you like turn-based strategy and/or enjoy the tabletop game, this is a reasonably faithful recreation of that rendered in good graphics and surprisingly good VA. Whether the online play and 20-mission campaign is worth $40 is up to you, but it has the legs to go wherever it wants from here.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? YES! Turn-based battles do not get much better.Control your squads of Blood Angel Space Marines in a deadly fight against swarms of ugly Tyranids. As Sergeant Carleon says, "Their death is our only option". You can command the Tyranids in multiplayer, other races are not included (yet).The main game consists of squad-level combat on various maps. Your squads use movement points and action points for their attacks or special actions. What I absolutely loved is that you can give orders to the next unit while the first unit still executes it's orders. You can examine the levels from all directions, zoom out or down to a close-up view of your units. Enemy units are of course covered in the fog of war, but there is an overhead map for extra convenience. Between the missions you can buy new units in the army management screen or spend HQ tokens to unlock new abilities and weapons for your hero units - there are large tech trees to unlock.Quite a few of the (often good) strategy titles published by Slitherine are ugly and with a cumbersome user interface. This game looks amazing and has a user interface that even I understood after a few minutes. In addition to the good looks and polished UI, it comes with professional voice-overs between and during the 20 missions of the campaign.The Emperor is always the truth! As long as you don't suffer from a Warhammer 40,000 allergy, this is one of the best squad-level turn-based combat games you can play.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first; if you are a 40k fan, you definitely should buy this game. Further, if you're a Blood Angels fan (like I am) then you NEED to buy this game. This is objectively the best 40k game since Mechanicus, easily among the best 40k games ever, and I personally enjoyed it more than Mechanicus, though that is probably just the Blood Angels fanboy in me talking.Pros:- Very 40k story that was written by 40k fans. You can tell that the developers love the setting and have an understanding of the material they are working with. Nods to Commander Dante and the level of detail that they've put into locations like Angel's Fall show that these people know their ♥♥♥♥ when it comes to their 40k lore.-  Great gameplay. Nothing feels without purpose, and every unit feels like it is point-priced fairly. Force multipliers like Librarians and Sanguinary Priests are expensive, but their buffs are valuable. Units like Intercessors and Sisters of Battle are cheaper, but are great for clearing chaff or just doing that last sliver of damage to take down a big bug.- Variety of gameplay. Lots and lots of options for how you want your Blood Angels to play. Being a Blood Angels purist, I leaned heavily into a highly aggressive, highly mobile force with a focus on close-combat, and bringing one or two iconic heavier Blood Angel units like the Baal Predator and Librarian Dreadnought when I needed the extra firepower. However, it is just as possible to build a gunline army of Intercessors, Battle Sisters, Hellblasters, and Aggressors, or to build an army that leans heavily into Hero units.- Probably the best representation of the tabletop game to date on a digital platform that isn't a mod for Tabletop simulator. Right down to the point values of the units to the additional wargear options.- DEATH COMPANY! Easily my favorite unit in the game, replaced my Assault Marines with them as soon as they were unlocked. Great for clearing out chaff with either their ten attacks or Hand Flamers (when they've been unlocked), which builds up their Black Rage stacks (which buffs melee and makes their shooting less accurate) and their momentum meter, which makes them an enormous threat to even the chunkiest Tyranids. x20 attacks of +30 damage ain't nothing to ♥♥♥♥ with. If you want to absolutely annihilate something, throw a couple melee buffs from your Sang Priest and Sisters of Battle character and watch them go to town.Cons:- The unit limit can be pretty frustrating. It steadily rises through the campaign and then around the middle caps out at 20 units. Further, you HAVE to take all the voiced characters into each battle, which takes up five full slots by the midgame. I understand the balancing concerns, but if I'm going infantry-heavy my Techmarine doesn't really have a whole lot to do except take potshots with his bolt pistol or maybe swing his axe a couple times.- I wish there was a way to see how many points unlockable wargear added to the unit cost before you unlocked it. As it was, on several occasions I unlocked a weapon, equipped it, saw it would send my desired army over the mission point limit, and reloaded a save so I could respend the points. Thankfully, the game autosaves after each mission before you've spent your tokens and the load speed is very quick, so it wasn't a huge issue but seems like it would be an easy fix.- No Chaplains. This was pretty disappointing for me personally, as the Chaplains of the Blood Angels play a pretty important and unique role in their chapter (and successors) compared to other founding chapters as they are tasked with overseeing Blood Angels that have succumbed to the Black Rage. The fact that the Black Rage plays an important role in the story makes this extra disappointing. It would have been awesome to see a Jump Chaplain leading my three+ squads of Death Company and giving them additional buffs.What I want going forward:- More factions. This gameplay system is great. I'd love to see it applied to factions that could be added in the future like Imperial Guard, Chaos Space Marines, Necrons, or Orks.- More campaigns. Kind of goes hand-in-hand with more factions. Having additional campaigns to play such fighting any of the factions I listed above would be great fun. Really, I just want more Battle Sector.

_childDocuments_.review: GRADE A-. So i wasn't expecting much from this game at first glance and i ended up picking it up on sale since i like the IP. What a pleasant surprise to find that this is a much better game than i anticipated. I liked how it really captures the feel of tabletop Warhammer in the 40k universe.Battlesector is a love letter to the tabletop game, capturing its tactical depth and unit variety in stunning digital form. Each squad feels distinct and has a specific tactical purpose. And The RPG-like skill trees add a layer of satisfying customization, letting you forge your own band of grimdark Squads and customize your tactics.I thought the story was good but it does contain some deeper references into the VAST lore of the 40k universe. And it might be hard for some to follow. But the Voice acting brings the narrative to life, and even if some details might seems obscure to casual fans of the IP, it's stil a FUN tale of heroism and sacrifice in the face of galactic horror.My only REAL gripe? It could really have used more playable factions with their own stories and missions. The Two it launched with were well balanced and excellent, but the 40k universe begs for more. And even though the online community is still pretty active the limited  army choices means that fans of the IP, who would love Battlesector, might give it a pass since their favorite armies are not represented. Expansions or multiplayer modes offering more factions would be a big plus. But once i finish my current play through and a few online matches, i don't know if ill re-download this in the future to check out the new content unless its a NEW full campaign with a new story.Overall, Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector is a a FUN game and a pleasant surprise. It nails the tabletop feel, offers strategic depth, and delivers pure, grimdark fun. If you're a fan of the franchise or turn-based strategy, this is worth checking out. Just be warned: you might end up wanting to paint some miniatures by the end of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great tbs game. Don't expect too much in the way of deep narrative as even in the sole sp campaign the story comes across largely as throwaway gibberish. Despite this, Battlesector's primary strength remains its campaign as each map is well designed and interesting with new army upgrades and/or new units being awarded at the end of each. This progression gives the campaign a satisfying and utterly absorbing feel. There are 3 other game modes one being a fairly standard skirmish mode which can be played against AI but I'm certain is primarily there for the inclusion of PvP; a survival mode where you just try to outlast wave after wave of enemies, and the other is a new hex map conquest game called Planetary Domination and it's quite fun.Regarding DLC - unless you intend to play lots of skirmish and multiplayer there is currently no reason to buy any of the dlc beyond the Blood Angels Elites one - which is a great dlc. Sadly, none of the other dlc add any campaign content and you can't run the main campaign with anything other than those it offers you as standard and those that come as part of the Blood Angels Elite pack.The game is still actively being worked on and improvements to all aspects of the game (including the new Planetary Domination mode itself) are evident. A future new campaign is also in the works. It's a shame the devs haven't (yet?) found a way to let you take your dlc units into the main campaign as this would have greatly added to both the value of the dlcs themselves and created a lot more replay value for those not too interested in PvP or survival mode.NB: Keep in mind that creator content IS available through a weird in-game interface rather than through the external workshop and that you do not see this until you agree to the online part of the EULA via the "custom" menu.

_childDocuments_.review: It's turn based, so just be warned if that's not your bag. Otherwise, this might be the most enjoyable and most Warhammer40k of the WH40k games I've played, and that includes the entire RTS series of Dawn of War, Space Marine, and the other turn based WH40K games, which I have here on Steam or other services.   That said, this is more along the lines of a budget to mid-range title, as opposed to AAA. There are only Blood Angel space marines(and some Sisters) and Tyrannids in the campaign, no other races or even other chapters.  I got about 20 hours out of the campaign, and I was taking my time. 20 Missions total?  There are some rumors of the developers making a more open ended campaign with a map, which would be amazing, but currently you just have the single path of missions campaign, just vs Tyrannids.  It feels like some of the upgrades for single units (Warhammer for your main NPC, for example) are WAY too expensive, 65 points, when plasma marines are 110 points and are 10 times more useful.  The Pistol and Melee weapon upgrades for most of the HQ units should be far cheaper, that's really my only gripe.  I  would like a way to upgrade the regular marines (Intercessors) and Sisters to have plasma or something, because late game they are basically useless against higher level enemy troops, but that's game balance for you. It's true to the lore, I'd assume, but shooting armies are far better than trying to go melee vs the Tyrannids, especially later in the campaign.  I dropped all my Librarians and even Dreadnoughts for just tanks and plasma troops, and wiped the floor with the highest level enemies.  Missions design was overall very enjoyable, with only 1 mission where you're designed to lose surrounded troops really annoying me, as I could not figure out how to save all 7 surrounded troops!@#!  It's okay though, lore wise; humanity is always getting slaughtered by the xenos, until overpowered Space Marines show up.I would love to see this game added to with additional campaigns and races, the core engine here is great, and the voice acting and writing was even acceptable, which I was not expecting, hehe.  Additional DLC campaigns with more races, get to it, Developers! :)tl,dr: If you enjoy turn based games (on the slightly simpler side) and enjoy the Warhammer 40k universe, pick this up.   Also, plasma is your friend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is certainly not a AAA title. It's not bad. But it's not great. It's snugly right in decent territory. The campaign is so-so. It's honors the Warhammer 40k aesthetic really well. Everything looks good. Models are good. It's kinda cool seeing it on the screen in 3d. I really like the presentation. Angels look great, the Tyranids look great. Although, hive fleet leviathan isn't the coolest color scheme. But good god the callouts, and the Tyranid roars sound awful. "They will fear to tread close" is an awful sentence, and I hear it ♥♥♥♥♥♥ constantly. It's only in there because of the Sanguinius book Fear to Tread. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate that. There are like 3 tyranid pain roars, and they play on repeat, and are shared between creatures. So a Trygon sounds exactly like a hormagaunt sounds exactly like an Exocrine sounds exactly like a Warrior. It's awful.Some of the music is ok. But some of it is AWFUL. The Astropathic Relay map has teh worst music hands down. I turned it off. The AI is ok, but sometimes it is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid. I had a Trygon crawl just far enough into my bolter battle line to activate every single Overwatch. Then it burrowed 3 spaces back, then forward to. Why did it do that? I had an exocrine walk between 3 of my melee guys triggering Zone of Control and taking a lot of damage. Then it burned it's AP to take one more step. It didn't even attack. This leads me to my next complaint. I'm playing on Hard (Lieutenant) difficulty. And so far the grand strategy is to just pile up all your Blood Angels into a Big Blob of Bolters and just march across the map. Sprinkle in a few jet pack dudes to close the gap between you and the artillery. That's all you need to do to win every mission. The tyranids have such ♥♥♥♥ ranged weapons that they pose zero threat to you. Just keep marching forward firing with all your bolters and you'll win. There's not much tactical skill required to be successful. It's really difficult to recommend this game, but given that it's only 40 bucks, it may be worth it for you if you love Blood Angels. If they add mod support in the future then buy this for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be a record for the quickest game I’ve ever uninstalled. In lieu of an in-depth review, I’m going to give you a rundown of my experience with the first 30 minutes or so of gameplay and the impression I got.First of all, I was greeted by a not-very-impressive title screen that looks like something off a 90’s game like  or , accompanied by unpleasant, faux-epic music with a distractingly farty-sounding bass horn. Perhaps the orchestra needs to stay off the baked beans. It then segues into bad church organ playing and one minute of what sounds like someone throwing a basketball against a wall in an empty sports hall, concluding with some dot matrix printer noises.The title screen isn’t the only thing that looks dated either – the in-game graphics do too: Even on the highest settings, they look like something out of  – currently approaching it's 20th birthday. Why so much oversaturation? Every single space marine has identical scratches on their armour, which doesn’t look like it’s been maintained for centuries (I thought these primaris were supposed to be brand new recruits) Something just seemed “off” about them – perhaps it was the textures or lighting.The voice acting sounded okay for the most part, just the usual stuff you might expect space marines to say although there were a few “Bane” moments where you couldn’t understand what was being said because they're talking through a mask. There is a subtitle option though, although the writing is small and often disappears before you’ve had chance to read it. Some of the dialogue choices were poor too. “Your eyes may deceive you, your ears may deceive you,” says the tutorial marine “but the Emperor is always the truth. Trust your auspex [i.e. scanner] to guide you.” What? Is my auspex the Emperor? Was this line intended for a mechanicus priest? It doesn't sound right.I’m told to “not waste rounds on cowards who hide behind walls”. I’m sure that’s very useful advice against the Tyranids (i.e. the original Zerg), given that they’re literally fearless and renown for their swarming tactics – not their use of cover. They certainly made no attempt to use it during the game. And since when have space marines ever regarded the use of cover as cowardice? Maybe there’s some new lore I’m unfamiliar with.I didn’t like the GUI either – the controls are clunky and the writing on the screen not only blends into the background, but at one point it was obscuring the command tooltip the tutorial was asking me to use so I couldn’t read it.As for the gameplay, it’s a fairly simple move-shoot turn-based tactics game, very similar to . The usual mechanics, such as “overwatch” are there, but  has some new features, such as being able to issue a “fall back” order if the enemy is at close range, which makes your space marines walk backwards in slow motion, shooting at the enemy until they reach the square behind them. The enemy may also attack while they’re doing this – also in slow motion. It's good idea, but it looks weird to be honest. The tutorial will invite you to try this out – . Other units and a sanguinary priest just appear out of nowhere. The priest is a special unit that can use “command points” to perform some a strafing run special attack, which hits four squares in a row, but I kept getting a message saying “ability out of range” (or something) every time I tried to activate it, with my other units gaining an action point for no apparent reason and shouting “for the Emperor” even though nothing seemed to happening on the screen at the time (bug?) You can’t fire your tank’s main weapons separately; the turret assault cannons and the heavy bolter sponsons shoot together and their shots look exactly the same. The tank apparently can't turn its turret and can only shoot at things right in front of it.  didn't have these problems. Troops can shoot through a tank just fine without hitting it. The Dreadnought’s close combat attack looks ridiculous and cartoony; it spins its power fist around during its idle animation like it weighs nothing.The game cost me £31 and it’s been out for about 18 months now. For the price, I wasn’t very impressed. And don’t get me started on the price of the DLC – I suspect it’s more of the same. Maybe  has a really interesting story, but having just read other people’s reviews, it doesn’t sound like I’m missing a lot. I could easily be accused of not giving it a fair chance, but all of the stuff I’ve described occurred within the first thirty minutes and I’ll be damned if I’m playing through several hours of this (or however long the game is). It’s just not entertaining and from what I’ve seen of other people’s footage, if you’ve played the tutorial, you’ve pretty much seen it all.And having learned my lesson from , I requested a refund immediately. If you’ve played , there really isn’t any point playing this game. I suggest you play that instead - it's cheaper. Alternatively, there's , which is just a better game in general.

_childDocuments_.review: The good: -Plays much closer to the Warhammer 40K tabletop game in that positioning and movement of units is much more involved and skills and abilities are essential to winning battles-The campaign is fairly streamlined and if you want to skip the cutscenes (they're still photos mostly with voice over) or aren't super familiar with the lore or story, it doesn't really impact the fun of the battles-It is much harder even on normal difficulty than other WH40K games released recently.  This is good because there is an actual challenge to the battles and they take strategy to complete-Having the "momentum" aspect of the units forces you to not just have them sit in overwatch for the entire battle.  The more enemy units they kill and movement they take they gain momentum, which improves their stats during battle.  -The HQ units are fun to play with and have skills that can really impact the battle.  They never feel like they're just extra units that need to be kept alive, they NEED to be used to keep units alive and the battle in your favor. -The point limit on battles makes the need for selecting units strategically important.  The Bad: -The enemy AI has some issues at times and it doesn't always move or attack in a logical way.  This can make the ends of some battles boring-The line-of-sight for units can be an issue because sometimes they will just shoot into an obstacle that doesn't necessarily look like it should be a huge obstacle to getting hits -The ends of the battles tend to be "kill the remaining enemy units" situations.  When its really close and they keep spawning units this can be kind of annoying.  An example is when it says "eliminate the remaining 7 units" then 5 more pop up on the side of the map.Final Thoughts: I hope they release additional campaigns with different armies (Tyrannids, Eldar, etc.) because the Blood Angels are cool, but I'd love to play more (and I believe they are doing this and it's on the roadmap).  This is definitely one of my favorite 40K games I've played since Dawn of War II.  It really gets the need for strategy that exists in the tabletop game right and you can tell the developers really wanted to make sure the game had that feel.  It isn't easy and there are missions that were really hard initially where I didn't really use good tactics, but after learning more about movement and abilities it was easier and more fun.   Many times I loaded up on units for a battle only to realize I should have selected a different army composition, and I haven't gotten bored with going back and replaying campaign missions.  Would definitely recommend for anyone who likes the 40K universe or loves the tabletop.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the closest any game I've played comes to the experience of playing table top. The models all look great and are fun to fight with. This is the one area the developers really nailed.I enjoyed the story but actually playing the campaign wasn't much fun. Every single mission in the campaign can be boiled down to: 1) get a specific unit to an objective on the other side of the map, 2) hold that objective for X rounds or get to a different objective, 3) kill all the enemies. The computer will spawn reinforcement units every single turn (including from behind your deployment zone) until the objective is complete so there's no point in taking a slow and steady approach to the objective while killing everything in your path. The only way to play is to rush the objective. Rush rush rush the entire game otherwise you'll end up fighting an insanely large horde.Fighting the tyranids doesn't feel dangerous, it's annoying. There are so many termagants, hormagaunts, and gargoyles running around that it often feels like you're spending most of your actions to swat away bugs so that you can actually fight the things that are scary. Since the computer is constantly spawning more of these units every turn it can sometimes feel like fighting through a never ending swarm of gnats. Exocrines: I hate these more than anything else in the game. It's an artillery unit that can shoot way further than anything you have access to and way further than any of your units can move in a turn, can shoot through terrain/buildings, can one shot your units, and is built like a tank. This means it will be raining down death on your army for 2-3 turns minimum before you can even start to fight it. It just feels cheap, there's no way to counter it other than spending multiple turns running to it, and when you finally get to it it can take a lot of punishment and has a surprisingly hard hitting melee attack so you have to run it down with multiple units. It's pretty normal to have to fight multiple exocrines for most missions through the campaign.The game has a deployment phase in which you can move your units around in a small grid but you don't get to know what the overall objective of the mission is, where the objectives are on the map, or which specific unit has to get to the objective so there's not much point to the deployment phase. The game also uses a fog-of-war so you can't even use enemy position to make informed decisions during deployment.There's a skill tree you can unlock unit upgrades with points earned completing missions and bonus objectives but different units are unlocked gradually throughout the campaign and the talent tree sections are not viewable until the unit is unlocked. If you're going into the game blind you can end up like me having dumped a bunch of points to upgrade a unit I didn't deploy after the first few missions. There's no way to respec so you're just stuck with what you pick. Trying out new units without dumping points into them first feels bad because they can become so much stronger with the upgrades and there's really no way to know without putting the points in. Unlocking every upgrade for a unit can take it from "why would I ever deploy this??" to "this is one of the strongest units in my army" but without the ability to respec the tree it feels like a gamble.

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing experience this game is. I've had it wishlisted probably since it showed up but there it fell under my radar since its release. It may or may not have caught some sales in that time but again it went unnoticed and what an absolute crime that is. Released in 2021, it recently just came out with the T'au army which put the rest of the game and its various army packs on sale to an agreeable level, and putting it back on my radar.Many Warhammer games usually nail the aesthetic, themes, diction, and storylines but very few capture the actual feel of playing on tabletop. There was Dawn of War which depicted swaths of armies cutting across the landscape but it was all in real time, the only methodology there was making sure your travelling teams had all the right counters to vehicles and infantry and after that you basically just let it go.What we have here is a unique XCOM-like that may very well be the closest many of us will get to playing the actual tabletop game. We have a campaign (just one; following a Blood Raven chapter of the space marines) and two extra modes. Demonic Invasion is a wave based king of the hill type thing where you hold off for as long as you can as every round will continually spit the chaos god's minions at you. There's Planetary Supremacy, which is a sort of Catan/Risk style hex board that players of Dark Crusade or Soulstorm may be familiar with. It's the mode most of my hours have been played on. My only wish is that it could go for just a bit longer, maybe a bigger map, more enemies fighting each other, better node control.In extension, there's also custom campaigns players can build as well as skirmishes for you to play against AI or other players. As of this writing there is no Co-op and that's quite a shame. So there's a lot to do here. Some of the more mixed reviews, especially targetting the new armies, are complaining that there's not a super special story campaign for each and every single one of them. That is frankly not so much a problem for me, as I immediately gravitated towards the hex board game mode and just enjoyed having my hands on the Necron for the first time in many years. Now in HD with reflections! My dead bois are beautiful!There's plenty to learn as well. Even on the easiest difficulties, the AI can route you. My Necron have units called Warriors, basically the equivalent to shotgunners. They also have the slowest movement of my army so it's difficult to get them into position and keep my general army momentum going. Sometimes they fall behind and I lack the much needed damage against enemy swarm units, and I've lost some good troops because I didn't have enough people shooting back. It's how I nearly lost against the Tyranids one game despite outnumbering them by 500 army points. Tactics very much matter here.There's also a photo mode which is a bit fickle. The camera is locked at certain height over the floor tile so it's difficult to get sweeping, heroic visions of your armies from foot-level. You're more or less stuck staring at them from head-on. It's fun to play around with, though.So while there is a campaign (just the one), this game could be treated more like a sandbox than anything else. I'm told from the game's discord they plan on releasing free units over the coming months. This is good, because that's one of my chief complaints about the game. There's a significant lack of versatile units to play with. Each faction gets around a dozen to fifteen to allocate with your army point cap (another staple of Tabletop that most games don't quite capture), with Khorne getting the shortest end of the stick (and the cheapest DLC) whom only have eight units to choose from. There's a significant lack of Kroot and vehicles here, and foot troops seem to be a choice between three different things. There's a lot more than that on tabletop.Not that I expect this to be the tabletop simulator but it cuts real damn close. Closer than most games in this franchise. A must have if you like turn-based XCOM-likes.

_childDocuments_.review: The core gameplay is quite masterful.  The combat, mission structure, and sheer number of units under your control tend to make the game feel more like Chess than XCOM.   Strategically planning your advance so as not to leave troops exposed, yet moving quickly so as not to time-out the mission or allow your position to become surrounded.  Then, baiting the Tyranid hordes into a hail of Bolter fire as they swarm your units by using clever tactics and area denial zones has never felt better with weighty sounds and hit registrations that leave dozens of Tyranid corpses eviscerated on the battlefield.  Units are also quite diverse with wargear selections and even Sororitas that show up a few missions into campaign, without spoiling too many fun surprises.  In conclusion: If you're even a passing fan of 40k, or a fan of this turn-based, isometric view style of game this is a MUST BUY.

_childDocuments_.review: Warhammer 40K Battlesector is a good game.  The core gameplay is good enough that it could be any science fiction setting and still be satisfying but we have been blessed by the Emperor and we got a 40k game that is enhanced by the setting rather than the setting being the only reason I'd try it in the first place.Between missions you get filled in on the story which itself is pretty generic.  Apparently a tyranid hive fleet got sucked into the warp and if you don't kill the ones who remain they will form enough synaptic nodes to create a beacon to bring the hive fleet back.  It's about what I'd expect from a 40k game, what I didn't expect is how character driven it felt at times.  A lot of this will probably be lost of people who don't already know about the Blood Angels and the Sororitas and the universe as a whole, but it was clear these characters were written by fans.The game is basically broke up into two sections.  Missions are traditional turn based you move and shoot with your army, the opponent does the same with theirs.  Individual units are infantry or vehicles/monsters made up of 1-5 models (1-8 or 10 for the tyranids).  Each model in a unit has their hp tracked individually which heavily influences what kind of weapons you want to use against the different enemies... for example using a multi-melta that fires once for 150 damage against high model count unit you'll do 150 damage to one model. This mechanic (along with character progression) basically keeps even your starting units very viable the whole game because you're trying to find the right mix of anti-armor and anti-horde.The action is well animated and the game mostly rewards aggression with its momentum system but it doesn't prevent you from playing other styles you'll just be missing out on certain strategic options like calling in reinforcements, strafing runs, or a missile strike.  You are often walking on a knife's edge though because if you make one wrong move, say jet packing with your commander into an area you haven't scouted yet might see you landing in a horde of enemies that absolutely will overwhelm and kill you next turn... but this can be fun too because now your carefully planned turn is rushing as many friendly units as you can to take pressure off your commander so he just might survive the turn and extract.There are some elements of the game I don't fully understand.  For example the game tracks how many battles your individual units have survived but it's unclear to me if there's any veterency benefit for that or if it's just a "good to know" kind of thing.  I'm leaning towards there being no actual benefit in terms of statistical improvement as near the end of the game I'd shuffle my entire army into the reserves and recruit new armies to test out on the battlefield for fun.The other section of the game is the prep in between missions.  Here you you set your army composition of 20 units you bring with you to the battle however once you are in the battle you can't necessarily use all 20 units, you are gated by points.  Each unit costs points based around upgrades and it's relative power level and the 20 units kind of serves as a side bar so once you arrive in battle you see the initial few enemies you'll face which might inform you a bit on which of the 20 you want to actually use.The most important part of the mission prep though is upgrading your characters.  You get upgrade points for beating missions and can spend them on your characters.  Each character has various skills they can unlock, or skills they can unlock for the various units.  You eventually get enough points to get almost every upgrade on most of the characters, but what you get early can have a real impact.I rushed unlocking the auto-bolter for my tactical squads (intercessors?) and turned my functional anti-horde starter units into tyranid mulchers, but this diminished what they could do against higher armored targets.  Every squad gets different upgrades that can either further specialize them into their role, or diversify their capabilities which I had a lot of fun with.  The personal upgrades for characters can be quite satisfying as well, for example upgrading your commander's chainsword to a thunderhammer was incredibly satisfying... and actually is a rare case of an upgrade being a straight upgrade with no downside somewhere else.Over all I'd give this game a 9.5 out of 10, maybe an 8.5 if I remove my 40k bias.  I didn't really know what I was expecting coming in but his game greatly exceeded them.  Perhaps the most exciting element of the game for me is seeing space marines, adepta sororitas, and tyranids represented which to me means this game is template.  I would love to see it build out like Dawn of War did and want to eventually see all the races represented ideally with their own campaigns.  I see the potential and can hardly wait to see where they go next.

_childDocuments_.review: My kind of game, I enjoyed it a lot. I do not see myself replaying it. Playing the whole campaign took me around 40+ hours. I see that quite a few players said that they needed only 25 hours to complete the campaign - I'm not that good :) + my game style = do not loose not even a unit from my army (some soldiers may die, but not a whole unit). I didn't encounter big problems - I've had only some very minor issues with the view, easily resolved by moving and rotating the camera (wasd - qe). The game experience is not extremely polished, for example I can watch the map (key m) but I do not know how to click and see a specific area, when I get out of the map view I am seeing the same area as when I initiated the map view.I finished and won the campaign at Lieutnant difficulty from the first go (not the most difficult, 1 level of difficulty below). I'm not the "ultimate game perfection" type of player, I'm doing some mistakes, I'm using saves and load games. I didn't loose any unit from my own army until the last battle in the campaign (20 battles/scenarios/campaign episodes) - I played extremely defensive. I guess that even in the last battle this can be achieved as the last scenario is the only one where the goal is not to kill every enemy, but 4 main enemy units. I had to destroy a lot more than those 4 mission-objective units. Thinking about this last mission, it is just a massive "all-enemies-attack" that mission, not really too many choices of saving own attacked units. I've lost 2 units in that mission (I started with 16).Game similar to Panzer General and others of the same genre, with some more detailed rules. There are control zones (please read "if you try to pass through control zones, all the enemies controlling that zone will attack you" - I think that control zones are only for melee attacks). There are bonuses for attacking from the side or from behind: the damage is significantly higher if attacking from behind the enemy unit, a rare possibility because most of the time it would mean that your unit will be attacked by other enemy units coming in the next wave and most often it will be destroyed. Do I recommend the game? Absolutely, if you like Panzer General you most probably will like Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector. It is not the best game of this type, but it is not bad either. Very dark game, generally very simple ("Kill the swarm, kill'em'all"). Complete the indicated objectives, receive some bonus points that you can use to gain a few more abilities or to improve stats, NEXT MISSION! Note: there are 2 different missions from the achievements point of view, all the other 18 are "regular". A "regular" mission is "complete objectives and THEN kill everything left". Well, in 1 mission there is the objective to bring/move Brother Quindar to a specific location on the map. If you do not get Quindar there and activate the objective before exterminating the swarm, you will not complete that objective (you will loose some bonus points useful for new stats/abilities), so you will have to first get Brother Quindar and activate that objective and AFTER that kill all the swarm units (thanks for the saves :) ). The other different mission is the last mission, "kill 4 objective swarm units", all the other dead swarm units (I'll let you guess who did it, who ordered it and why) - as many as possible if you wish - are a necessity, in the wrong place at the wrong time on your way to the 4. The 4 which actually are galloping to get to you and do the very same to your beloved psycho-kill'em'all-army. Meaning that in 2-3 rounds you will have a stare contest (and some swords and chainsaws to add to the atmosphere) with the 4 who came from the other side of the big map "just to".To not forget to mention, although I think that you will discover everything and more by yourself: you can recruit a lot more units than you can actually have in the allowed army for a mission, so you will have to select what will stay in reserves and what will be actively participating. Any unit participating in a mission gets +1 to accuracy and chance to critical damage (I'm not sure if it is chance or +1 to critical damage, I didn't try to find either = moar missions, moar bonuses, good enough). I found that the "big health-points units" are the best for me, fewer to recruit, taking more  army points (hence I had 16 units in my army, not the maximum 20 possible), but more resilient (as opposed to 1-shot/attack-killable). I will not present the army composition that I used, enjoy your army mix :) Although the enemies/swarm has a very basic approach (all units focus on 1 of your units to destroy it), depending on your play style, you may find that it is difficult to keep all your units alive, sometimes the AI just "knows" what it wants, and it wants it bad. Bad for your too (saves or approach change required).I wish you a nice army-against-swarm campaign :) and to enjoy the game at least as much as I did, you will have fun even if it is a dark game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:  There is no replayability in this game.  It's no Soulstorm.Browsing through the lack-luster menu only really gives you two main options:  Campaign which dumps you directly into the linear Blood Angels campaign, or the (Beta) Planetary Conquest which dumps you into a 1:1:1 FFA as the race of your choice (Blood Angels, Tyranid, or Necrons).I bought the Necron expansion pack but Planetary Conquest is the only way for me to actually play the Necrons.  I haven't defeated the Blood Angels campaign to see if it gives me a Tyranid campaign (and perhaps a Necron campaign afterwards) but I have no intention of doing that. Oh yea, there is Skirmish mode, in which you dispense with all sense of purpose and plot and simply kill enemies, you can play Necrons there too.The controls were designed by an alien race that has neither used a mouse or met a human before.  You select actions (hot key or clicking) and then you right click to do the action, left click to do nothing whatsoever, and hit escape to either cancel that action or deselect your unit, dealer's choice, it seems to be entirely random as far as I can tell.There is facing, line of sight, fog of war, cover, and all of that, but it's pretty poorly implemented.  There is no real concept of elevation and the LOS/FOW has you feeling like you're wandering around blind.  Putting your units behind cover seems to protect the enemy more than it does you, because everything in front of you gets "full cover" but things can flank and shoot you just fine.  I guess no one programmed in the "shoot around the obstacle you are standing behind" subroutine.  Honestly, other units make for better cover than anything else.Units can awkwardly move and shoot (sometimes shoot twice) unless you move that magical "one more square" and then you sacrifice all of your attacks.  Some skills and abilities take up singular or multiple actions but all of them seem to allow you to move your full speed - 1 square, and either shoot twice or shoot and use an ability, unless you're summoning necron warriors, that takes 1 action but sacrifices both of your attacks and spawns necron warriors with no actions.  In short, the action count has no real relevance to what you can actually do in a single turn.Unit purchasing is similarly convoluted:  All units have a unit cost which builds up as you play (so you can, for example, field a 1000 point army and a necron warrior is worth 55 points), some units cost a requisition point of which you have 2 which replenishes after every battle, in addition to their point cost, so you can't hire too many high priority units at once, I suppose.  Some really valuable units have a cooldown in addition to their requisition cost that stops you from buying them even if you do have requisition points available.  Then there is a reserve list which does NOT allow you to place extra units in battle after some of them die, it seems to only be a placeholder to store excess units that I can only imagine is meant to allow you to manage requisition and cooldown so you are not wasting valuable recruitment opportunities.Units can "overwatch" which basically means if something enters your line of fire, you shoot it.  Except, ranged units can only overwatch a particular square, so it's more of a trap than it is a defensive zone, but the game sometimes ignores that and shoots some of anything that moves in that general direction.  Sometimes overwatch triggers multiple times, sometimes not at all.  Melee fighters do not get an overwatch ability, unless you try to end your turn with an action point available, then it will ask you to overwatch and end turn.  I don't think it actually works though.The range of weapons is a mystery.Speaking of commanders, there aren't any.  In the campaign you get certain "leader" types which you can upgrade using HQ points in a kind of tech-tree fashion, and about half of them upgrade your leader and the other half directly upgrades the equipment of your units.  Why does your leader type upgrade the weapons of your units...I do not know.  There is no clear documentation on which thing upgrades what because half of them upgrade keywords like "mechanical" or "librarians" and while the one dreadnought is definitely a mechanical and your one "Librarian" is definitely a librarian, it's not at all clear which if your other units fit into those keywords because those keywords are not documented or flagged anywhere else in the game.Necrons are even worse, only the Overlord gets any "HQ points" at all, and it appears that those are one-shots that you accumlated in battle rather than any actual upgrade.Honestly, from my writhing pile of Warhammer nonsense you would think I would have learned my lesson by now with Games Workshop but here I am with Warhammer number 8 still wishing it was Soulstorm.Also, with the number of times they have put out basically the same game, you would think they would be able to put out a game with all the races included and sell us on content other than races we've already played the previous eight times.I should have known better.  I really have no excuse for myself.

_childDocuments_.review: A really good strategy game. I enjoyed my time with this quite a bit. Lining up your units for ideal ranges, figuring out ideal activation orders, and keeping your units in cohesion all tickled my brain in the right places. It almost plays like XCOM, but on a grander scale. I have one, and only one critique. Throughout the first twelve missions of the game, all the missions end with the objective "Kill Remaining Tyranids." This REALLY slows the game down to a crawl as you have to scrounge around the map, searching for just one or two remaining Tyranid units hidden in the fog of war. It turns fast-paced and exciting missions into an extra ten minutes of slogging through the map. The game also doesn't really give an indication of when this objective will or won't be there. For instance, the final mission of the game just ends as soon as the boss is killed, it does not have that objective. This completely caught me off-guard, as I had very carefully placed my units in positions to deal with the other threats on the map as well. Otherwise, this is a fantastic game well worth every penny. I look forward to seeing what new factions they add, and the campaign/map maker has a lot of potential. I've played around with it in beta as well as the full release. The addition of pre-mission and post-mission text really helps players make custom campaigns, not just maps strung together.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the weakest Warhammer 40k game I have played recently. And it features Primaris Marines. Must be a coincidence huh?After having played through four maps, I see there is ZERO design behind them. Each map features Blood Angels vs Tyranids, each map features the same scenario: get to the objective point, when enemy forces randomly spawn around the map in undiscovered regions. Objectives so far are 'go to point A" and "defend for X turns". Then, when you do the objectives, you... have to "eliminate all remaining Tyranid forces". I have played through the second map going to the 4th objective in a big circle, killing 'nids.... whole 67 of them units spawned total. On map 4 there was one hand-spawned boss unit, the rest spawns randomly and continously.I'm sorry, this is garbage. It could maybe work with more variety of enemies. I mean, let's take Gladius, another hex strategy Warhammer 40k game. You have many many many more factions there, instead of just TWO here. Not to mention that continous spawning of enemies makes sense (a Tyranid horde, okay), but until you complete an objective? But what would Tyranids care that I found 4 of my dead gene brothers and gathered their geneseed? *Now* they'd stop their assault?I like mechanics otherwise - attacks are nice, I like how they are calculated between models. Too bad the entire strategy layer is nonexistent.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very hesitant at first to give this game the light of day. Nothing particularly earth shattering about the game, however I think it's a very solid core game. It falls short in terms of scope (ie focused on one very specific faction which is the Blood Angels) as opposed to Dawn of War Soulstorm. This can be a bit frustrating if you're like me and not a Space Marine player. However, as far as a 40k strategy game, I find this game to be an extremely welcome change after the disaster that was Dawn of War 3. Visually the game is well done and is in keeping with the gothic elements of 40k.In terms of the story, if you're familiar with the developments within the tabletop over the past few years, it's very easy to tell from the introduction when and where the campaign takes place.As far as gameplay, it is a turn based game which isn't common these days. I won't say this is a pro or a con, it just is what it is. I do admit that in video game format, I'm more partial to real time, but as someone who also enjoys the tabletop game, it works. As with a lot of 40k games, it centers around Space Marines in one form or another. Personally for me that was a turn off, however since the core game seems solid, there is plenty of room for growth and it looks like the developers recognize that so I'm looking forward to future content. In fact it was the news that they are working on additional factions that finally convinced me to get the game.Overall, I'm loving the game. It's not what I think a lot of Dawn of War fans such as myself were hoping for, but it is a wonderful game in its own right and I think should be taken as such.

_childDocuments_.review: In typical 40K licensed game fashion, Battlesector is a mashup of ideas, some good, some bad, poorly executed. The Blood Angels units are well developed, playing as the faction in the campaign feels satisfying. The Tyranid units feel like the developer has no familiarity with and doesn't understand the faction at all. They've demonstrated this lack of understanding in discussions with users in the steam forums as well.The Nids pretty much just spawn in across the map for 4-6 rounds in pre-scripted fashion, regardless of your actions. They outnumber your units 6 to 1 but they can't overwhelm you...they're just tedious to fight.Even if they do slaughter a few of your units there's no sense of risk or loss- you just replace that unit next mission. The missions then a) don't feel like 40K tabletop as far pacing or structure and b) aren't particularly fun. The devs announced this week they'll be adding a new faction next year but at this point I'm not hoping for much given their 50-50 success rate with factions so far.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a phenomenal Warhammer turn-based tactics + strategy game. I regret not licking it up sooner. I'd put it just after Chaos Gate and Mechanicus in my personal ranking.The mechanics are smooth and balance is well-thought out. Unlike the other two games I mentioned, this one gives you the feeling of commanding a full batallion & has some decent-ish character development. It's rare to get either of those from a WH40K game without being either a RTS or ARPG — getting both in one game is exceptional.The only thing holding this game back, for me, is that I'm in these games for the single player campaigns. I don't really care about PVP or sandbox/survival modes. Which means I sadly don't see any point in purchasing the DLCs, which unlike a new faction. If each of those DLCs had a campaign like the mainline Blood Angels campaign, I would buy them at full price in a heartbeat. Heck I'd buy them all of they had campaigns *half* as good as the Blood Angels Carleon campaign. It would be awesome to have campaigns for the Orks & Necrons & Sororitas. Heck, even the mainline Tyranid's could have their own campaign.As it stands, as much as I want to support the dev's for making an awesome game, I just can't justify buying all the DLC, even on sale, when their only purpose really is for PVP and skirmish modes.TLDR: if you like Warhammer or turn-based tactics games, absolutely buy this. If you like single player campaign & stories like I do, you can skip the DLCs.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say Battlesector targets a very specific playerbase of the 40K fandom: people who want to play a good 40K strategy game, yet don't want it to feel too RTS-y like the Dawn of War or Total War series, but more like actual tabletop.Of course, you don't have to know about 40K or even know the tabletop rules to play this game: you can go in blind and still have a great experience, since the game holds your hand long enough to teach you about its mechanics, and then has you figure out your own composition for future missions, letting you customize your troops and deciding what approach you will take to complete the mission you are given.It's overall a very solid experience, and one that you can replay to test multiple builds across the single-player campaign... or you can head over to multiplayer and feel like you're playing some sort of digital version of the tabletop experience, either against AI or other players.My only critique would be the lack of more factions for multiplayer, but there's no way Games Workshop would be ok with you paying a couple bucks and playing a tabletop version of the game they can charge you hundreds for the physical pieces.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:++ Good graphics++ The ability to zoom all the way in on a model and see the detailCons:-- The game needs to be polished more-- Game play and campaign is not engaging in my opinionOverall:First off, I love the models in this game. The model designers did a great job capturing the look of the tabletop models and the ability to zoom all the way down and see them up close is awesome. However, that's all I can really say positive about this game because honestly... the game was not engaging for me. When it comes to game play, I definitely did not "feel" every "bone-rattling explosion and soul-crushing charge" the description reads out. Game play was slow; You move your units, they shoot at the bugs or the bugs shoot you and there is no wow factor. The speed of the bullet effects are slow and the effects themselves definitely do not feel like the speed and punch of the 41st millennium. I wanted the bullet effects and explosion effects to really be something memorable, but they designers didn't take it to 11 where Warhammer exists.The sound is also left to be desired. The music and sound effects did not put me in a future where there is only war. I really wanted some dark Gothic music that was memorable or sound effects from weapons that let me know that this next shot was really going to hurt, but it was good at best.Then there is the campaign; I play 40K games for the narrative just like any 40K fan enjoys the lore of 40K, but the campaign is a bit lack luster. The game does not focus as much as it should on characters and I honestly didn't care who died or not as long as the mission was over.In the end, there were more than a handful of times I stopped playing in the middle of battle because I simply got bored because the game play was just not exciting. If you've come from playing Warhammer 40K Mechanicus, which is one of the top 3 best 40K games out there, you will not nearly have the same good time that game provides. Warhammer 40K Battlesector just does not really engage you in the 40K universe. Put your Money into 40K Space Marine, 40K Mechanicus, 40K Dawn of War 1, 2 or 3, or even 40K Gladius. You will be much happier.

A lot of the units feel like the same thing with different model on it (Intercessors and Sisters of battle for example feel almost identical, as well as Agressors and Dreadnoughts). The enemy is always tyranid and there is only so many hormagaunts you can obliterate, before it starts feeling old.So if you are a 40k nut and love turn-based strategy, go for it - you will get your moneys worth. _childDocuments_.review: Warhammer 40K: Battlesector is a Turn Based Tactics game with a moderate length linear campaign as well as online multiplayer and a single player skirmish mode. The campaign follows the Blood Angels, now reinforced with Primaris Marines, as they attempt to secure their home world in the aftermath of the Cicatrix Maledictum and in preparation for the Indomitus Crusade that occupies much of current Warhammer 40K lore.Unlike many contemporary 40K strategy games, Battlesector has no base building or unit production. Upgrades for units can be purchased between missions, but the units you take into combat are for the most part all you will get. While units lost in combat are irrecoverable, you have an essentially limitless supply to reinforce with between missions. Missions have a unit price cap, limiting the types of units you bring into combat. The more powerful, the more it costs.The rules for combat borrow heavily from the tabletop, encouraging careful use of equipment and abilities as well as proper matching of opposing units.Pros:-Models and effects are fantastic. -Sound, dialogue and music are great. Particularly Sargent Carleon, who blends the bombast of 40k with compelling delivery.-Engaging if limited and straightforward campaign.Cons:-Eliminating the few remaining enemies at the end of particularly large missions can be a slog to find them.-A speed option for your units movements would be appreciated.To the Devs:Take this game, expand the units and factions, make the campaign open ended and let us choose our chapter. I'll pay full price for that game in a heartbeat. You have a real gem with Battlesector.

_childDocuments_.review: Giving this a "No" recommendation because there are just too many nagging flaws that undermine a really great effort. If you want this type of game in the 40k universe, play Sanctus Reach (from the same publisher) first. Read on for more details:I've played through the campaign on Astartes (normal) difficulty and Company Captain (highest) difficulty. I didn't lose a single mission on any playthrough. I rarely lost even a single unit in a mission.PRO:+ In-game production value. Art, voice acting, animations, and models are all very good. There are nice touches, like the way models within a unit flow around each other as they move through/between other units.+ Core combat system. Movement Points, Action Points, activated abilities, chance to hit, damage ranges/types, etc. It all works fairly well.+ Warhammer 40k feeling. This is the story of a Blood Angels sergeant, recently reinforced with Primaris marines after the Devastation of Baal, and his small war band clearing out the remainder of Hive Fleet Leviathan so the Crusade can move on. The units feel true to tabletop, the story centers on the Black Rage (a unique BA flaw), and it generally fits. The story writing isn't super deep, but I think it makes a fair arc, and there's nice little details acknowledged in tech trees and tooltips and voice lines that show the team cared about the 40k Universe.+ It feels like Sanctus Reach. Which is good, because Sanctus Reach is the best adaptation of 40k as a turn-based wargame on PC.CON:- Mission designs. They tried to make the missions thematic to the story, I will give them that. The aesthetics change a very small bit, but there are really only three mission types: go to a place and activate an objective, defend an area for a number of turns, and ensure X survives. This is uninspired (and pretty low-hanging fruit to just crib from the tabletop game) but serviceable, except that every. single. mission. concludes with "Kill all Tyranids." Every mission is literally the same. It appears the only distinction is on some missions, completing the initial objective triggers/stops Tyranid unit spawns, allowing you to kill the remainder (because of Fog of War--see below--there's no way to verify this behavior.) With the exception of the two "ensure X survives" missions where the surviving units begin on the other side of the map, this means that there is absolutely zero incentive to take any risk in achieving the primary objective. If you rush forward and/or overextend to complete an objective, you still have to kill everything else anyway. Might as well just walk forward slowly and fight everything with your full army, meaning you have NO macro map strategy. This is a huge, unforgivable miss for this kind of game. There are a couple missions where having specific units makes the primary objective much easier, but naturally the pre-mission briefing doesn't indicate this in any way. "Have fun scaling the castle walls!"- The AI is a moron. Other reviews complain about the AI charging headlong into you and dying. If it were only that bad, the game would be fine. The AI is bad at so much basic wargame logic: focusing targets, prioritizing the biggest threats, finishing kills, minimizing overkill/overshooting, contesting objectives, locking up targets in melee, positioning around AoE weapons, etc. It also consistently fails to maximize Tyranids' "swarm tactics" ability, which gives bonus damage based on the number of adjacent swarms. I believe this is because it activates each unit once and does not split activation (such as moving all your swarms together and then shooting them all at once). For most missions, the only Tyranid win condition is to kill a Blood Angels character, and the AI will consistently prioritize good shots on bad targets over game-winning shots on characters. Horrible.- The combat system is opaque AF. There's no way to see the stats of Tyranid weapons short of LOADING A CUSTOM GAME AS TYRANIDS TO HOVER THEM. There's no way to see the AP cost of abilities or army points cost of wargear upgrades in the Tech Trees. There's no way to tell if you can shoot through a piece of terrain, or how exactly people/vehicles/terrain impact cover short of move-and-find-out. I've played through the max difficulty and I'm still not sure why you aren't able to attack Hormagaunts back in melee, or when I'm in range of an Exocrine cannon and how it can target me from multiple squares beyond my fog of war, or the cooldown of Gargoyle debuff. Of course, it doesn't really matter, because the game is so stupidly easy that I never had to bother figuring it out.- The difficulty (Unit Balance). In single player, some units absolutely trivialize the challenge, while others are practically unplayable. Dreadnoughts in general are OP, but with Heavy Flamer are a cheat code. Meanwhile, the bread-and-butter Blood Angels unit, Assault Marines, are just liability even when fully teched. The tech tree also has several trap options (Inferno Pistols lol), while Aggressors are basically a lifeline in one early mission on Company Captain and then obsolete within a couple missions. On one hand, there are several strong units to build an army around. On the other, there are several very bad units you shouldn't bother with. For a game with a dozen units, that's not great. Of course, when you do find the mix of units that's really your cup of tea, you never have to change them because the game requires no macro strategy.- The difficulty (Company Captain difficulty, specifically). OK, fine. The main game is a little easy. The AI is a little dumb. But you've beaten the game and unlocked Nightmare mode, where the enemies are buffed and you'll really be challenged. Right? Wrong. Company Captain is indistinguishable from any other difficulty once you have even modest tech upgrades, which means it's fun for the second mission (where you meet the Sanguinary Priest and recover three gene-seeds) and absolutely nothing else. This is because the main difficulty spike comes from buffing Tyranid damage and durability, but the AI is still moronic. And since you must have completed the game to unlock the difficulty, assuming you aren't brain dead, you already know the challenging parts of each mission and can just tech your army for the upcoming mission (mobility, durability, horde killing, monster hunting, whatever). Of course, after a few units unlock, you don't even have to bother with that any longer. This is SUCH a missed opportunity to actually introduce unexpected challenges, as simple as moving Exocrines to different parts of the map so they attack from unexpected areas. Maybe artificially limiting your unit selection (infantry only? herohammer?) makes it tolerable.- Fog of war. This is a hallmark of video game adaptations that really undermines a lot of the systems here. Every unit has a vision cone (despite allowing for free rotation of units at any time) that is supposed to do... I dunno, something? There's no benefit to shooting from the enemy fog of war that I can tell, and no penalty if you're attacked by an unseen enemy. Nothing is fast enough to charge from beyond fog of war, I dunno. But the fact it exists just makes the game SO INCREDIBLY REPETITIVE. Combined with the mission design issues (above), it means the optimal strategy on literally every map and mission is to form a gun line and walk up the field a square at a time until you make contact, then orient your gunline and blow it up. This feature single-handedly destroys any hope of macro strategy. The fact that some of your units have vision of enemy positions is why the Ensure X Survives missions stand above the rest.- The momentum system. Good idea, lousy execution. Doesn't reward aggression sufficiently to outweigh the boring gunline strategy, and not worth the work to aggressively micro last-hits. Also surging is full of dumb traps.- Army building. No unit XP, no veteran advancement. Why do reserves exist?

_childDocuments_.review: I've come to love Warhammer 40,000 in the past couple of years, and I've played other games in this style (XCOM in a different universe and Mechanicus in the same universe). This is a solid game with high potential for improvement. Aside from some UI issues in the campaign and army-builder menus, I have little to complain about. I'm mainly writing this because, due to some unfortunate release timing, people have been criticizing this game (a bit unfairly in my opinion) for it's new Planetary Supremacy game type. Because the release of this new game type (which was a free update for all players who own the base game) coincided with the release of the Necron race pack paid DLC, the new game type was set against "Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War - Dark Crusade" (which added the Necrons and a Planetary Supremacy-like game mode to Dawn of War) for comparison. I think this is a brutal comparison *at present* and ignores a lot of the good will shown by the Battlesector devs and their intent to support, update, and improve this game into the future. If the recent reviews on this topic have been making you waver on your purchase of the game, I would encourage you to take the recent criticism with a grain of salt. It's a good game, and scratches the 40k itch if you like this strategic genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This is almost a great game.  I did somewhat enjoy the single-player campaign however it lacked depth.  The planetary supremacy was a step in the right direction but lacked any significant value.  Both of these could be easily improved and the game made substantially better and worth the $$ (keeping in mind they're probably planning on adding more races for $15 a pop).In regards to the single-player campaign, there is just no vested interest in your units.  It doesn't matter if you lose one or all of your units, it will have absolutely no effect on subsequent battles.  A veteran system was added after release, but other than seeing the ribbons on your units a 1% increase in hit chance doesn't really make any difference.  There are many ways this could be addressed.  One simple way would be to enhance the requisition system.  Based on using an army with a requisition total lower than the scoped battle could provide additional bonuses to your next battle.  This could take on the form of allowing additional units or special equipment for your units.  This would result in some battles being easier, but the truth is, they're all pretty easy anyhow.  In short the single-player campaign needs to better draw our interest and get us vested into our units.Planetary supremacy was my big hope for this game.  I am an avid lover of Soul Storm.  Unlocking heroic units was greatly rewarding.  While supremacy adds requisition or action points, they really don't do much for the play through.  That is, once you've played it there's really nothing pulling you back to playing it again.  The battles are really just skirmishes that don't require much thought.  This is also something that could be fixed from a multitude of options.  One way might be to grant unit upgrades through the requisition system.  Units that truly change the tide of battle in your favor but is painful when the AI or other player focus fires them so that they are gone.  Being able to configure different equipment within a single unit would also add depth, especially when you see a unit from your squad that you've augmented drops from enemy fire so that you lose the requisition or upgrades that you've spent.I wouldn't say the game is bad but it just lacks in drawing any interest in your units.  The inclusion of additional races and small (or large) improvements in the campaigns or Planetary supremacy could make this my all time favorite strategy game.  But for now I just consider the game 'meh'..  I hope they invest a little more into the development of the title.  I think it really does have a lot of potential.

_childDocuments_.review: As is, this is a good turn-based strategy game. Especially if you're into Warhammer. That said, it's nothing you likely haven't seen before from the genre of hex-based (squares, technically) combat games, it's really just the 40k version of all of that. That said, I prefer this style to Dawn of War because you can actually slow down and smell the roses, so to speak. All of the clicking and building and recruiting of DoW meant I rarely got to just sit back and enjoy all that Grimdark goodness, and the graphics in this are certainly on par. Unit customization and advancement follows you through the campaign, writing and flavor are good - TL:DR it's worth the money. ESPECIALLY after they add Necrons and an expand the campaign.I mention the last bit because this sucker does get repetitive. SO many Zer-er, Tyranids. Just waves and waves and endless waves and mostly the same enemies. But that's really the only downside if you're a fan of this genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: (Mid-campaign review)Neat little tactics game with great VA and appropriately bombastic music, but the constant requirement of clearing the map of enemies to end a mission even after the other, more interesting objectives have been fulfilled makes almost every mission a chore to finish, and bingeing a difficult prospect. The slow animations, while cool, don't help with the grind. The vast open maps are pretty and a nice contrast to the claustrophobic corridors of the other Blood Angels vs Tyranids tactics game, Space Hulk Tactics (which I also like), offering a wider range of tactical possibilities; but again, they exacerbate the grind. I suspect this is to pad out what is going to be a pretty short campaign.It's good to see the Red Thirst playing some role in both the gameplay and the narrative. The Blood Angels are my favourite Space Marine chapter, and Sanguinius' genetic flaw is one of the cooler aspects of their lore - something I missed in Space Hulk Tactics.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. It's basically Sanctus Reach 2.0Edit:Having played this game for a while now, I still recommend and enjoy it, but I find that I prefer Sanctus Reach! Why? Because there is only one playable campaign for this game, and I've beaten it. But for some reason, I have something like 1,500 hours played of Sanctus Reach, and I don't get tired of it. I wish this game had more factions WITH CAMPAIGNS. I've downloaded all these DLCs but what am I supposed to do with them? They have no single player campaign!
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review: Great game for fans of WH40K and especially fans of the Blood Angels, who are obviously the greatest and coolest of all the Chapters and Space Marine Legions (Suck it, Smurfs and Space Puppies). The game involves Blood Angels lore, including their flaws, and doesn't over-explain things, which is very nice for someone who knows the stories well.The turn based combat works well, the units and abilities are varied, fun and interesting to play around with. Compared to other games from this developer, it feels a bit on the "light" side, both in terms of complexity and difficulty. Not necessarily a bad thing, though. I enjoyed the game very much, but if you're after a more hard-core turn-based experience, this might not be your game. Unless you're a WH40K nerd like me, then I'd still say you should get it.The sound effects and voice acting are great also, so the mood of the game is very enjoyable and immersive.
_childDocuments_.name: Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector

_childDocuments_.review:
In the grim darkness of the far future, there is only war. Experience every bone-rattling explosion and soul-crushing charge in Warhammer 40,000: Battlesector, the definitive battle-scale game of turn-based strategy and fast-paced combat that takes you to the battlefields of the 41st Millenium. 

Experience an epic twenty mission single-player campaign that explores the aftermath of the Devastation of Baal. Help Sergeant Carleon and his allies purge the Tyranid infestation on Baal Secundus, and preserve the honour of the noble Blood Angels.

name: The Longest Road on Earth
detailed_description: Play in a song. The Longest Road on Earth is a deeply personal and meditative narrative title. Play in the songs of four short stories featuring stripped down mechanics and no words. Each story is up for interpretation – what story lives inside you for each character and the world around them? Be swept away by the haunting and sentimental lyrics of over twenty-four original, emotionally charged songs, sung by one of the developers. Walking down The Longest Road on Earth will only take you two hours, and it’s worth every step. THE SONGS OF LIFE An original, intimate soundtrack with themes and lyrics that seek the serenity and simplicity of life is included in each ticket to ride on The Longest Road on Earth. Feelings, emotions, situations, and perceptions that aren't extraordinary yet define us as human beings, our stories, and how we share our lives with each other. EVOKE MEMORIES Play through four chapters that capture the essence of everyday life and skip through the snapshots of moments both meaningful and mundane — All set to a nostalgic soundtrack. No dialogue or text means that you can share moments of time with the characters and create your interpretations. Though the experience is short (under 3 hours) The Longest Road on Earth allows you to wrap yourself like a cozy blanket in the beauty of small joys like blowing dandelion seeds, collecting seashells, sledding on the first day of winter, and riding a bike on a summer day. THE QUIET, SIMPLE MOMENTS In The Longest Road on Earth, there are no challenges to tarnish the experience, no fail-states to punish you. Players of all ages, levels of ability, known language, or backgrounds can participate with simple controls and a relaxed pace.
