_childDocuments_.review: debut is loosely based off a real-life tragedy where a neighbor of game director Arash, took his own life. The incident left family and friends lost for words as everything seemed fine with the victim. And to think I only got knee deep in research because  offered it to me- otherwise I wouldn't even realize I already possessed it from a previous sale XD. Granted, themes dealing with mental health are more widespread in video games. Though they tend to revolve around fictional premises (up for debate) such as in .Usually handled with respect and educate us on lesser known intricacies of mental disorders but others exploit or phone it in by slapping them with "psychological horror."  is smack dab in the middle of that spectrum. It began with great intentions except it didn't stick the landing after all the huffin' and puffin', believe me it's a lot~Stiles is your everyday angst-filled and depressed teen trying to survive going through the motions in high school. For the past year however, things have been escalating and on one fateful day- he spirals. A dear old companion, cheerleader and devil's advocate emerges and together they go on a trip of deja vu.Not much in way of gameplay and so it's fair to call it a [/i]drug simulation[/i]. Your alter ego being your guide on what to do, judging you and taunting you- the bumbling introvert. There are venting journal entries to be found too, shedding light on his struggles. Pretty soon, he descends into incoherence and tasked with locating light bulbs while getting lost in the maze that is the drug-addled mind.There aren't a lot of ways to die but when you do, you enter multiple versions of "Limbo" and you have to seek the way out. Ultimately, the endings are the incentives to continue playing and they can actually be achieved in one go, provided you inspect carefully! Fortunately for me, I managed to uncover the alternate "bad endings" and then I simply 'continued' from the main menu.Now, the sheer amount of time, hard work that went in to the design of the school is obvious. Be it the variety of posters plastered throughout or props that cater to different classrooms! All wonderfully detailed and I must've spent the first hour admiring them. It's a living, breathing school so kudos!! The creative input is just nothing short of endless, creating almost unique set pieces to throw at you that you can't help but stop and stare. Since Stiles' school acts as his anchor, it only makes sense to revisit it a lot and it's spruced up each time to convey a different state of mind. Another gorgeous illustration of its visuals go into the  manipulation of "reality" where once you reach a dead end, you turn around and something's changed! This is done a lot and I couldn't keep up. It's sure to leave you satisfied!! The mirrored effects of drugs kicking in start off slow and psychedelic-like but amp up in intensity. So just take a break every now and then~In keeping with the theme of the game, I'll let you find out WH for yourself! Instead, I'll go into what I liked a.k.a. what I found scary~ Firstly, the idea of a darker version of yourself is very much a nightmare. It knows everything about you, it ridicules, second guesses and clouds your thoughts. Technically it's still you in control but we all have our fair share of the bad, don't we?Secondly, I have to point out a character that I just loved; whose performance was natural and sweet. It's Rose! I absolutely fell head over heels because of what she and the flower represents. You'll see single roses throughout the ugly tripping and it's somehow reassuring. The phrase 'every rose has its thorn' couldn't be more true because like just don't appreciate what you do have. Thirdly, I liked how it was on the nose about the people's tendency to overreact and replay that same moment of regret. It's tough to see someone going through it but what about those who keep it hidden? Makes you wonder... Finally the title, "WH" depending on the intonation or punctuation can imply many nuances. Is it out curiosity, a blaming tone or just explanatory? Disorienting is an understatement for that initial gimmick of colors grows into unbearable and nausea-inducing the further you go. It's like they wanted to see how many filters and novel ways to rotate the camera could be fit in until people hurl. Then the angle suddenly zooms and jerks all shaky cam to direct your attention. Oh and head bob can't be toggled off so rest up every hour.Stiles is the protagonist but he's...bland and reserved. I liked the "Mind" / alter ego but he's just dying to be edgy and dark, comes off as a try hard. Other characters were standard teenage drama fodder, who we don't learn enough of to actually see them favorably... Also, the depiction of self-harm got so gratuitous. I'd rather not be shown any and just told (on second thought, talked my ears off too). Moderation, that was missing!!Alter Stiles is like a preacher- that is if they were the ones telling you to give in to . What we are treated to, is preachy, beating that dead horse over. Kid you not, by the end- I questioned what was the point of everything?! The game was better off cutting its price and runtime by half, which I think would have conveyed its message just as fine.Some nitpicks are the notes which are somehow randomly generated? Because every time I locate one, I make a habit to leave that drawer open. But next time I came back, it was moved to a different drawer!? Plus, an achievement bug, where it said I "collected all notes" but then being the rebel I am- I found more!The amount of phasing objects were off-putting. A note standing on its own protruding out the cabinet or grass and other foliage coming through drawers. The game may question reality but that's just sloppy. Even some objects are placed too close to another and when you open the drawer, it goes into the other object. Little things like these can be damning!Prognosis? WH came from a wholesome, noble place by not victimizing those who have considered suicide. Bringing that vision to life proves arduous- ending up mundane, overstretched for the most part though it has its moments of clarity. I am an immense advocate for mental health so I can appreciate the sentiment and was really hoping it'd be something special (which it is, just not all the way). What it did exceptionally is in its breathtaking visuals of a life-like school setting and unpredictability of Stiles' being under the influence. However, such a momentous stride to mental health awareness calls for impeccable execution and a certain degree of sensitivity that was just not present. And with a dull and one-dimensional cast, it's challenging to like let alone care for them... The same goes for the at first alluring transitions that became obnoxious and induced in me enough motion sickness for my lifetime. Though I "don't recommend it", I'd advise picking it up when its price is slashed as it's still fairly enjoyable and an innovative piece of entertainment- I guess that's why it hurt even more~

_childDocuments_.review: Creative and immersive, that's how I'd describe . This game is a journey through anxiety and depression of a high school student, Stiles. From a gameplay perspective it's a Walking Simulator/Psychological Horror. What Remains of Edith Finch is probably the closest similar game that I remember, but What Happened is definitely a unique project.Pros:+ A lot of creative decisions for visuals/atmosphere/gameplay. Intuitive level design.+ Great visuals/sounds and technical part as a whole. Good voice acting.+ A solid lenght (5+ hours) for a game of this genre, with a great variety of events/locations.And a few words about the story before mentioning things that I didn't like. This story is about anxiety and depression, bullying in school and personal tragedies, friendship and betrayal, your own demons and suicide. While all these topics are rather serious and were depicted quite well in the game, personally, I did not get enough details of the story to dive into it more fully and to understand the characters (and game ending didn't help me at all).Cons:- I didn't like all the characters. I wasn't able to empathize MC while I totally understand the game's message. From the store page - "The empathy you show for the character will subtly affect the outcome of his journey." Yeah, I got a bad ending, heh.- A common issue for any walking simulator - replayability. I've missed some achievements and there's 2 other endings, but replaying the whole game while being unable to even skip cutscenes would be too much for me, at least for now. I actually started a new game after completing my first run and I had some hopes that it's possible to at least get a different ending faster somehow. But it seems like there's no way.All in all,  will be interesting for people who like walking simulators and psychological horrors. I enjoyed it mostly because of an impressive technical part and creative game design decisions, while the story itself wasn't that interesting for me. 8/10P.S. I don't think that it was an actual reference but a couple of scenes heavily reminded me of a "house" from Lars von Trier's "The House That Jack Built".

_childDocuments_.review: After about seven hours of play I was asking myself the same thing so read the entire review.I disliked this game when I started it – and yet, I kept playing. I wanted to know more, the art and stunning visuals kept me going. Stiles kept me playing.The game opens with a teenager in high school dropping acid. Then he gets a swirly and is beaten up. So yes, the subject matter is very dark: suicide, bullying, depression, drugs. Just being a teenager is hard enough. Add all those things together and it is not going to be an easy comfortable play.The game takes you on a bad trip from the perspective of a depressed teen. He has had a very good run of bad luck.Some scenes are tortuous. You see how mean kids can be in high school; hopefully actions you see are no longer tolerated. I really felt for Stiles, the teen.This is an Objet d'art in so many ways. You are forced to go slowly at times and see… what did I see?  You will ask yourself that too.You are forced to experience hallucinogenic effects. Synapses on drugs are misfiring and taking you deeper into his mind and witnessing the things he has been going through.At some point in the game you are told the outcome of the game is dependent on how well you “treat Stiles”. I guess I missed the memo on how you control that. You do not click a dialogue choice or select an action. Was it bad when I didn’t run fast enough through the burning forest and dodge a tree that fell? Is it bad because I still have not managed to out-swim the shark and make to the safety of a classroom I have to find only by trial and error?There is a lot of trial and error in the game. You are lacking clear direction in where you will find what. You must enter every room you have access to in the high school over and over and trigger memories. That does get tedious, but the amazing visuals kept me plodding alongThere are some clever unique puzzles, they may feel overused after a while. There are notes to read, items that will jog a memory.  Some memories are good; some are not. You question if what you saw was even the real memory.There is an utterly unique way you access menu features. That is a hint on how you will proceed at times. The start feature is so appropriate. Perfect for this game.You have the usual set-up options, the game autosaves after a chapter/memory. You will know when you have completed it.Traditional WASD movement. A right click flips you around; that was a nice addition. I doubt I will be able to progress because I am not good at action and speed. In fact, I just received an achievement for being eaten by a shark 20 times.I wish I could though...I had no screen tearing, no lag. no problems running it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard pass.What Happened is a directionless, nauseating experience, with overly long cutscenes, that just go on and on without any creative storytelling or competent dialogue. The game is just a mess, with very little gameplay, confusing narrative and distracting visual effects. I have no idea how this happened, because the general art direction is commendable and the environments look fantastic, and clearly whoever made the cutscenes knew what they were doing. However, I just couldn't bare the game anymore. It was frustrating, disorienting and vomit inducing. I couldn't care less about the unlikeable characters or the plot that didn't go anywhere. The game is like that scene in mother! where we follow Jennifer Lawrence while her house collapses. It works in a movie, but it sure as hell doesn't work in a game.Maybe that was the point considering this was someone's acid trip. But I'd rather sniff glue than have this on my hard drive.

_childDocuments_.review: On a positive note, this game has a very strong visual style and interesting scenes. The game goes on and on from one anguished scene to the next without bringing anything to the table plot wise.I wish there was an option to "maybe" recommend the game, since it has its moments and it manages to capture a certain dreamlike atmosphere. I'm giving this one a thumbs down because there aren't enough puzzles or action elements to make up for the mediocre storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a mixed bag of elements on complete opposite ends of the spectrum. Some of it's textures, lighting, and level designs are super unique and quite frankly, amazing. But the character models, animations, voice acting, and writing are not at all anything I enjoy. I don't believe it's worth the $25 price tag considering I really had to push myself to play it, but just an hour in and the harsh flashing lights and strange FOV makes me a bit motion sick to play this game. Pros: The attention to detail and lighting is really solid. But what really shines here (see what I did there?) is the level design. These set pieces are mind bending and things are constantly shifting and they're really trippy (also saw what I did there?) Because your character is on acid. He's a high school student and while I know that's a real thing, I'd say it's at least uncommon enough to say it's not really relatable for me at all. One because I'm much older now and my emo angsty days are (right) behind me and I've never had an acid trip. Although I imagine this is exactly what it's like. Cons: Here comes a mountain so prepare yourself. The writing in this is that of an angsty teenager that's mad his girlfriend is with his best friend or something. I dunno. You're tripping on acid, it's sometimes a little weird to grasp what's going on. Like, you might feel bad for the main character if he developed an addiction to drugs because his best friend slept with his girlfriend, but from what I can gather, your girlfriend left you because you have an addiction. So...that makes sense to me. It's also the little romantic dialogue bits that feel like Star Wars Episode I quality. Like any moment the game is going to cut to Naboo, but whatever. The character models are not quite as detailed as the environment and the animations are really stiff. It just feels out of place given the amazing set design. Voice acting is pretty rough. Pretty safe to say English is a 2nd language here and there's probably translation pains from the script, but all of the dialogue feels really unnatural. I honestly think this game would've been better off with just text and no voice acting at all. It's just really distracting. Yeah I know I'm only an hour in and if it was strictly just "This game is slow paced" or something. Sure. I'd probably spend more time on this. But unless the voice acting, writing, dialogue, and character animations drastically improve out of nowhere, it's safe to say this isn't a game I find enjoyable. Despite the fact that the levels are truly, really, jaw droppingly cool.

_childDocuments_.review: If "Life is strange 1" and "Layers of fear" had a baby it would probably look like "What happened". I'm amazed at the game's visual design, the amount of detail is insane (for an indie developer), As for the atmosphere and the plot, the developers also did a very good job depicting a teenager's pain and loneliness, which are very intense. Some reviewers complained about the game being too high-school: well, guess what, it's a high school story, but quite mature and dark. When it comes to the puzzles, some of them are really imaginative and fun. Now, the cons. I'm all in when it comes to surreal scenes and creepy metaphors. "What happened" in that sense may stretch the formula a bit too much, being almost like a parody of walking simulators. Sometimes it seems like going deep into your own psyche means going underwater, to hell, to the jungle and to a library, and then falling through walls and walls, falling through pipes and walking down stairs and then being hunted by a shark. There's where some restraint would benefit the game big time. It seems as if the developers couldn't keep the core of the plot safe and sound while still exploring the depths of its ideas. They got lost on their way.At the same time, despite the game being bonkers and hallucinatory, it's also quite repetitive and exhausting when it comes to its dialogues and monologues. The game is way too self-explanatory and obvious, as if scared of not being clear enough. Consequently, while on the one hand it goes way too far exploring new landscapes (to the point when drug abuse, bullying, depression and suicidal thoughts seem like playing a dark Mario Bros parody), on the other hand the game suffers from being to plain, obvious and simplistic. The game is both too metaphorical and overly verboseThirdly, "What happened" would also benefit from having better human figures and facial expressions. It's hard to sympathize with Pixar like, unrealistic creatures that still want to show cruel and violent animosity against the main character. Never too human, never too fake, stuck in an unsatisfactory middle ground, the characters lack the depth or the originality to be truly remarkable. They fail to carry the pathos and tragedy of the plot.Nevertheless, I still think "What happened" is an interesting addition to a long list of walking simulators dealing with mental health and self- /drug abuse. It definitely has its amusing moments, despite the formula being a bit too unbalanced. And the darkness it portrays is as real as can be.

_childDocuments_.review: A unique limbo nightmare with some cool ideas and some things that do not work very well. But I will say one section in particular is rather scary. Lots of secrets to find and multiple endings. A decent length if you try to go for everything. I have put some hours in and I still find myself finding new things to add to the experience. While not for everyone this game is at least memorable with its shifting limbo mechanics. The voice acting at times can be a little much lol but it conveys the nightmare good enough I suppose. All in all worth a try if you like silent hill type narratives with some general spookiness and cheese added on top. My favorite part of this game is the atmosphere of the shifting limbo sections. For example the school setting goes through multiple changes that give each one a separate feel and design. Of all the ideas thrown at the wall for this project that is perhaps the one that actually stuck the landing. The game received some updates and changes after launching in 2020 but as of now I think the updates have stopped coming but still worth the try for achievements or if you enjoy nightmarish scenarios. Hope this review helped you and try this game if this all sounds interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Full Review: Score - 8/10Conclusion (although I advise you read the full review above):What Happened was confusing, shocking, depressing, and increased my anxiety, which I believe was its goal from the start. Step into the shoes of a young mentally ill teenager who has just lost his father and finds comfort in drugs, it’s an experience unlike any other as you delve into his thoughts and emotions, visualising his fears and paranoia as disturbing manifestations. Although I found it hard to understand what was happening at times, the game made me feel lost, confused, helpless and alone, pulling me further into the world of Stiles and how he was feeling. The story felt like it was a little too long as there were a few sequences which dragged out the game without adding context, but overall it was a thought-provoking game which I can’t wait to re-experience on consoles in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: A game for the ages. Some games are played for fun. Others played for the sake of escapism. Once a generation however a game comes along with social commentary so powerful that it rocks the very foundation of the fabric we consider to be reality. What Happened? The titular theme theme of the game in question. Now a personal anecdote. I was at my wits end. I make content that no one watches. Unsure of where to go or what to do I decided to stream a video game and it was to be my last stream ever. That was, until I discovered What Happened. So many people showed up to my stream that evening with positive messages of kindness and affection that it turned my life around as well as my stream. God bless you devs and God bless America. A life of crime and drugs is not a life worth living and I see this now. Take care of yourself and each other. Urinary Tract Infector out. Thanks again.

_childDocuments_.review: It's quite a shame that this has so few reviews and not the highest score either when it's clearly a labor of love and has been expertly crafted.  I did balk at the price to be fair but the steam winter sale made it affordable.I'll start with the positives.  The world looks great.  It really does.  The fidelity and realisticness of the school setup you start in was fantastic.  Granted the characters animate a bit stiffly but still much much better than most indies and not too far behind some triple A stuff.  And the story in general is executed well.  Basically the whole aim of the game is to tell a story of regret and sorrow and self-pity through the lens of a grief-strucken teenager going on a drug-fuelled bender.  Quite a unique premise, and the environments and scenes you pass through reflect that.  I won't elaborate much more than saying this game takes you to some dark places and some trippy places, often at the same time.Where I do have complaint is that I feel that this game was put together by far too many artistic designers rather than game designers.  I'm struggling to think back now even though I've just completed it, as to what gameplay mechanics and activities I engaged with beyond switching on and off lightbulbs, and moving lightbulbs around.  Now that's not the biggest critique as some walking simulators have even less gameplay.  But in addition, for the length of the game I sure felt I spent a serious portion of that trapped in cutscenes, with these edging more towards a movie at times than a game.And speaking of length, sometimes I felt some points were overlabored and scenes.  Granted likely this is part of the artistic vision of this game, they want to show how being stuck in the head of somewhere where their brain hates them and constantly reminds them of awful things, is certainly not a nice place to be.  And that there is no break to this spiraling repetition of awfulness.  But when you do that to the extent where the player is actively being put off your game is to the game's detriment.  Honestly I think they could have trimmed it a bit more to allow you to complete the game in a single sitting.   As I found going back to it the second night I wasn't overly relishing going back to that same negativity over again.  But I'll allow it given what the story is trying to convey, and also because the game had sunk enough of a hook in me that I was able to grit my teeth and sink back into the grim and bleak murkiness of it all.And speaking of story, I thought it was an odd choice to focus on a love-sick teenager to tell a story about depression.  I'm sure most people go through teenage blues, some worse than others.  But I'm not sure how relevant this would be to most players who play this who will likely be adults and will have left this part of their life far behind.  I think they could have taken even a similar story and worked it in to an adult's telling and I think that would have found more common ground with players.  As there were at times when the character was being a bit over melodramatic, and like a typical teenager and my reaction in my head was more or less "grow up".  I think I would have been more able to empathise with someone who has reached emotional maturity but is still cripplingly depressed and is having a hard time.But those critiques aside, it's clear there was so so much effort put in to this, and it is quite a treat for the senses altogether, so I strongly recommend you to pick this up.

name: Archvale
detailed_description: A malicious and cruel king once ruled the land and terrorized all who faced him. He along with the fabled arch to Archvale have become the fodder for ghost stories and passed down myths. All that remains of him are the Undying; beings whom the king cursed with immortality to live out their eternity in his prisons. You and you alone can defeat the Undying and rid the world from the dark shadow the king has left. Journey across diverse regions, looting and crafting your way to better weapons and equipment. Through these upgrades you will be able to succeed against the host of enemies that await you and stand between you and the truth about the said-to-be-mythic arch to Archvale. Key Features: Play Your Way. Augment your character via badges, allowing you to create a build that suits your playstyle. Mastery is Key. Skill-based bullet hell combat will put your weapons of choice to the test and require precision and speed to succeed. Build Your Arsenal. Craft over 200 weapons and armor using items gathered from the environment and from slaying enemies. Explore the World. A host of enemies across diverse environments and classic-inspired dungeons will take you across an ever changing map where you will find unique resources needed to complete your journey. Discover the Truth. Uncover the dark lore of the world on your quest to unearth the arch to the fabled world of Archvale.

_childDocuments_.review: Fans of the Bullet Hell genre will love this game. Fans of Enter the Gungeon will love this game. Fans of RPGS WITHOUT stat min maxing will love this game. Fans of RPGS WITH min maxing will love this game.The gameplay consists of traveling from "room" to "room" in an interconnected world. You can go anywhere at any time, but some areas are clearly meant for later. The game doesn't hold your hand in where to go next, but it does have a map that allows you to see everything you've done, and pathways you have not been to. Since the loop here is "room" to "room", you can be sure that you will always clearly tell what you have and have not done. I can't stress that enough, as somebody who generally hates getting lost in games.Along the way, you will encounter enemies who, more often than not, shoot projectiles. And this is where I 100% recommend the game. There is not a single enemy that shoots stuff just to shoot it because bullet hell. Every enemy is crafted to fulfill a specific role on the battlefield. Every attack is not only well telegraphed, but very learnable. You will, after only meeting the enemy a few times, know exactly what to take out first and why. Speaking of enemies, the variety here is great. Blobs, bugs, beetles, skeletons, a... mage... thing, and more. You don't level up in this game, but you do find Fountains. These Fountains act as a full heal, refill all of your potions, and allow you to fast travel between them. On death, you lose gold (used to purchase items from vendors). Gold is valuable, but since enemies respawn on statue use, it can be obtained. I don't back track in games, but the combat in this one is superb and I have no problem farming some gold. HOWEVER, if you don't want to, you can fast travel to a town and store gold in a bank, making it safe even if you fall in battle. This is especially wise to do before boss fights.Bosses in this game are not HP sponges that clutter the screen with jank. They are, as the enemies that came before them, carefully thought out and well designed. Some are harder than others, but that is subjective. The overarching point is that everything that damages your HP can be learned, avoided, and eventually conquered. Speaking of avoiding bullets, you have 3 dashes that recharge. The cooldown starts when you dash once, but you can do up to 3 in a row. The cooldown period is very short, but just long enough to catch you if you "panic dodge", as in, just spam the button while panicking. Weapons and items will be found on your journey. Magic weapons, melee weapons, and a lot of "what the hell is that, oh wow cool!" weapons. These can be upgraded via a Forge in town. Town is also there to sell (you can't sell weapons or items) special treasures you find along your path, and buy badges. Badges act as a "perk" system. You can equip only so many, and each one tells you just how much space it will take to equip. Eventually you can upgrade your capacity for these. Badges range from stat upgrades all the way to having an adorable creature float around enemies and lower their defenses. Every badge is thought out, and players who love to make "builds" will enjoy mixing and matching the dozens upon dozens of badges to achieve their desired result.These badges are obtained by entering special areas you encounter along the way and dodging some bullets. You can't fire in these areas, and they are all about being able to maneuver around the threat while collecting little blue crystals. There are three waves, but getting hit only takes off a tiny sliver of health, and you start on the same wave you failed at. I could go on and on about what this game offers, but I think I've given a good overview. All in all, the people who made this very obviously love video games. Better yet, they also play them, and that grants them the knowledge of what playing a game should be like. Functional, responsive and most importantly, fun. And this game is all of those things, and the $15 asking price is an absolute steal.

_childDocuments_.review: This is unironically Game of the Year 2021 for me. This little indie title, made by just five people, including all the art, sound, and music, is such a fantastic combination of the thrills of bullet-hell shooters, roguelike combat, and RPG exploration.From start to finish, it's about 10-12 hours, depending on how hard you find it, and every step through the semi-procedurally-generated open world is as exciting as the last.There are ten unique areas, each with a plethora of aesthetic design elements and enemies to fight, from the green forest of Cradlewood to the icy mountain of Pine Peak, to the windswept Dustcrag desert.The bosses spread around the world and at the end of each dungeon all feel unique and fairly difficult in their own right, ramping up to the final boss—a grueling ruthless fight to the bitter end.The list of armour, weapons, and perk-providing badges to unlock and equip and mix and match is long and colourful, with many different kinds of weapons to choose from, ranging from slimy flails to hellfire crossbows to laser-beam-shooting magic scepters.And the graphics! The music! The game is visually and auditorially beautiful from start to finish, featuring a timeless 16-bit retro aesthetic with a gorgeous soft colour palette and stunning lighting effects.All in all, if you like bullet hell shooters and RPGs, this is the game for you.10/10 would play again and again and again.

_childDocuments_.review: 10h 7/10 1 Not really, but you don't need a guide No No No No No No No No, you can play on easy and still get all the achievements NoI first notice "Archvale" because of the looks, it looks beautiful in my opinion. I got even more interested when I heard from others the game is good, and let me tell you... they were right! I have finished this game within 1 day because I couldn't stop playing. Took some necessary breaks for food and some work-related things, but in the end, kept going back. A part of this addictive feeling is that you always make progression. even if you would spend a few minutes, you could make some progression. If it is getting some resources to craft armor or weapons, or if you can get from one save spot (a fountain) to another fountain, you get further because they are teleport points, so you now don't have to do that part of the map anymore. Even if faced with a challenging boss, you can go another route and maybe do that boss first, or get some better armor/weapons that suit your playstyle. (Melee, ranged, or magic). Other things you will collect are health upgrades and more healing potions, which get reset when you activate a fountain. You can also boost those to be better, so not only can you have more healing potions, but also boost how good to heal you. About the achievements, this game has no missable achievements and you can even unlock them all on the easiest difficulty.  I would suggest that when you play through the game, to just explore everything, as you just need loads of resources but also will find that way the challenges rooms and the extra bosses. If you're close to a city I would go first to there, to unlock a new bank upgrade. In the bank, you can store your money because when you die you lose half of the money you have in your pockets. But there is a maximum you can store. In every city is a bank and when you activate those you increase the amount of money you can store. (There is also an achievement for storing the maximum amount of 10k, but this isn't that hard if you first store your money in the last city you'll enter before buying any upgrades). It is a very modern bank... it wouldn't give you any profit, just the option to store and to pay for things you don't even have to withdraw (I think the shops in this game accept a  bank card or credit card, to make it easy for you.The achievement for completing all challenges might sound hard but it is a very doable one. You will find those challenges all over the map and you'll get teleported to a room with a round floor. There you have to avoid any damage during 3 stages in which it gets harder and harder, but the good thing is when you finish a stage, you will only reset back to the beginning of that stage and don't have to start over from the beginning. some of those can be challenging, as the name implies, but with practice and a bit of luck, you'll be fine. For me the real challenge where the dungeons where you get the arch pieces... not because of the monsters but because most of them have some sort of "dash challenge" where you have to navigate through a parkour with your dash ability... This was horrible and by far the worst part of this game (but gladly the only part that was bad). The ones in the jungle dungeon and the ice dungeon were the most challenging, but I believe the developer is still tweaking them and hopefully, they will get easier... if you just have a second more to react, would already make a lot of a difference. I can't tell you how horrible the dash parkour is in the fire dungeon, as I skipped it.. didn't want to do it anymore and gladly for the achievements I didn't have to (I was afraid I would have but then I would come later back, didn't want to torture myself when it wasn't needed). Those dash parkours are the only reason I would say this game is challenging to complete, all the rest is very very doable and I would give the difficulty a 4/10 instead of the 7/10 I have given it now. Another minor annoyance I had in this game is throwing away armor you don't need anymore... you have to click the armor and then move your cursor (I used a gamepad which made this harder) to the trash and click again, you have to do this for every piece you want to throw away. I would love to see just a "trash" button when playing with a controller, but maybe even when playing with mkb. If this game looks fun to you, I would highly suggest giving Archvale a try, because it is an amazing game, and if you enjoy the challenge... even better! You don't need to look up anything before you start this game, just press play and enjoy :D

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale is a fun game, but unfortunately suffers in that it feels unfinished.The graphics in the game are lovely, and the art can range from silly to adorable. All of the items will change your character's appearance, which was a very nice touch.The sound design is amazing. There's more than one banger track, and the sounds in the game feel so satisfying.The systems in the game are where it starts to suffer. The crafting system feels unfinished, there isn't much to it. You can't even vendor extra gear, you have to destroy it(which is a bit of a pain on controller). There's technically gathering in the game, but it's really just attacking ore on the map. The only gear adjustment is basically just to upgrade your weapon up to 5 levels.The gameplay itself is fun. It's a bullet-hell game in which you have 3 dashes by default, that work similar to a roll in most games with one. The weapons don't feel balanced, but there is a large variety, and they've done a decent job providing lots of options of attack. However, due to the lack of balance, the variety feels a bit underwhelming. Still, the game rewards skill and practice, which generally feels good.The biggest issue I had is that the world feels unfinished. Early on there's a bunch of bosses on the map, or special events. Later on there isn't much on the map, just rooms full of enemies. They either ran out of time or money, or stopped caring. I stopped feeling rewarded for exploring. The end of game felt super rushed, and while the last boss wasn't a bad fight, there should have been something more with it.Overall, it was quite fun! Worth playing, but wait for a sale. It definitely has its downsides, but has enough going for it to be worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give this a negative review. I followed the game's development for years. And yet, here I am, unable to recommend it to pretty much anyone. It looks and sounds great. But that's about it! When I think back on this game, everything starts blending together. Its world is huge, but empty and lifeless. Procedural generation really does more harm than good here: there is little to no point in deviating from the main path, there are no secrets to uncover, just more of the same. The game makes itself seem open to exploration, but is actually extremely linear. It's fights are way too busy to reliably dodge everything, so your progress mainly relies on you being tanky enough to take an occasional hit here and there. If you stray from the path, you'll die left and right, otherwise you'll plow through waves of enemies without much thought. Bosses aside you approach every room exactly the same, the level and enemy design does absolutely nothing to force you to adapt or strategize. There is plethora of gear and weapons to craft, but realistically you'll stick to the same stuff for most of the game because nothing will come close to their stats. And that's actually a positive, as the interface for crafting is horrible! If you're playing in coop, don't get your hopes up for synergies either: most weapons don't even have an effect aside from raw damage. Ultimately "Archvale" is really repetitive, lacks depth and puts you pretty much on rails. It's not terrible. But it isn't nowhere near great either.

_childDocuments_.review: This is WORTH every money I spent on. I've been watching the Dev Log since the very first time and I am very satisfied with the result.But this is by no means a perfect game. Sometimes you get overwhelmed by the amount of bullet the moment you step into a room. So maybe the dev can tweak that a little bit so the enemies doesn't shower you with a screen full of bullets the moment players enter a room.If you're not a bullet hell enjoyer, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND you play the Easy Mode. I finished the game in Normal Difficulty and there are times that I think it's very hard to pass a room or defeat a boss.Correct pathing is the way to go, if you go to a room in a certain area and you think that it is too hard to clear that room. Then maybe that area is not meant for you yet, explore and search the area you think is the correct difficulty for your current equipment.Because I struggled in an area, but I forced my way through that area. Then collect and craft equipment from that area. The moment I go to another area it becomes too easy, because maybe I should come here first then come to the previous area. But that is the beauty of RPG and Adventure game, you just explore all the area, no order needed. Unless you can't progress anymore.Edit: The best way I can think of to tackle the "showered by bullets the second get into the room" are :1. giving a delay between player enter the room and enemies start attacking.2. giving the enemy a aggro radius, so if the player doesn't get inside a certain radius of an enemy, they will not attack the player (because many cases where when I enter the room, even the enemy that doesn't appear on my screen still attacks me, and it's kinda busted)

_childDocuments_.review: The art style's cool but at this point I'm playing the game to complete it as I've gone past the refund point. I heard there was an update coming to the game and I *might* check it out at that point for the sake of giving the game another (hopefully better) review, but what I got was ultimately pretty disappointing.It's clear that the game doesn't really understand how to properly pace itself by seemingly promoting an open world at first and then ruthlessly crushing you with incredibly spongy, highly-damaging enemies if you step out of the developer-intended progress route. If you headbutt the wall enough you can walk out of said areas with equipment so powerful you'll use it for most of the game. This game would have benefited a lot from having a straight forward path than one you can sequence break constantly, but instead it chose to have what appears to be a procedural approach to generation. This bit me in the ass when most of a major area's fountains spawned right next to each other, side-by-side.I'm not sure why the developer chose to have difficulty be locked per-save when modern games have had interchangeable difficulties for 2 decades. The game unfortunately has the classic, underwhelming "Hard means tedious" approach to difficulty and my experiences with the game when I set to the hard difficulty have been disappointing at best and downright frustrating at worst when the enemy placements bunch up in an awful way (happens a lot later on, when there are a lot more enemies per room spamming gigantic amounts of bullets) and you have effectively have to tank an undodgeable bullet pattern. When coupled with the game's awfully short immunity frames on hit, you can easily die in less than half a second even on *easier* difficulties later on.Melee in this game is a non-choice. I don't understand why it's in the game with such atrocious range when so many enemy bullet patterns are nigh-instantaneous. Granted, some enemies do have a wind up period, but this so far has been inconsistent. You aren't even benefiting from this high-risk playstyle, because the other two combat styles deal so much more damage and have far greater range before their projectiles dissipate anyways. Like, why does the emblem for ranged arrows to be on fire on a % chance not require being at full health, whereas the melee one does in exchange for fire as long as you have full health? I would really rather the melee one be chance-based too. The full-health melee damage emblem was one of the first emblems I had gotten in the game. Defense in this game barely seems to matter, so the extra 'tankiness' I got from having melee armor on meant little to no change in damage taken when I equipped a ranged set of armor.

_childDocuments_.review: Every aspiring game dev should play this.This is one rare instance of a non-linear game that doesn't waste half the time you put in it.- No secrets, fake walls, unrewarding backtracking or anything like that. Missables are locked behind challenge rooms, so you don't have to engage in tedious second job-like wallpoking to find them. Instead, you get to actually play the game.- No items that may or may not be useful in 50 hours, or any kind of inscrutable mechanics. The game is very rich, but also straightforward and consistent. Nothing feels out of place.- A sensible amount of crafting. Making new gear is quick, and happens naturally when you enter a new area, no excessive farming sessions required.A very refreshing surprise of a game, given what today's standards are. These devs understand that you don't buy an action game (any game, actually ?) to bump your head against every wall, or collect a bunch of useless stuff so you can follow cooking recipes.So there is that. But the game is also just great in every department.The soundtrack and graphics are lovely, Bosses are amazing, enemies are quite creative, and the amount of weapon types gives a lot of  freedom in how you can approach fighting. Melee, ranged, bit of both, doesn't matter. There's a lot of fun to be had with everything, and a lot of attention was obviously put into every single playstyle, so that it never feels dull, or trivializing, which is really impressive.I was also actually surprised at how on-point the difficulty feels. The game just kept delivering the right amount of challenge at every point.In short, Archvale combines great design choices and perfect execution, and I can't wait to see what's next.

Average Playtime: 6-8hrs for 100%Achievements: Easily done on first play-through.PC Requirements:☐ Intel® Pentium☑ Entry Level☐ Mid to High level Gaming PCPrice:☑ Worth the full price☐ Wait for a sale☐ Not even for freeGame play: ☐ God-like, can't put it down☑ Not unique, but very fun☐ Average☐ UnderwhelmingStory:☐ Non-existent☐ Basic and boring☑ Better than expected☐ Really sucks you inSoundtrack:☐ Mute it☐ Average☑ Decent☐ AmazingDifficulty:☐ Too Easy☑ Decent (Some trails may be very annoying.)☐ Nightmare☐ Go to Steam Support", Go to "Products", Click "I want to permanently remove this game from my account".Replay value:☑ One and done (New runs can be fun with friends or for a different generated map.)☐ Replay for missed items, endings, or achievements☐ EndlessBug:☑ Perfection (Can't think of any bugs I encountered.)☐ Minor bugs, tolerable☐ Broken, unplayableOverall Rating(8/10):    The first impression of this game was a fun pixel, action, rpg, semi-roguelike. The art style, game play, and mechanics weren't super special, but felt like a fresh take on similar games. The map layout being procedurally generated did keep it fresh when replaying with friends, but you still knew what to expect. The bosses were similar to other games, but did require you to either min-max your build or hunt for better equipment. The fountains (way-points) around the map allowed for easier travel, which made it easier when you had to backtrack to further progress in other area's before you could proceed in others. Trials were fun bonus puzzle games that rewarded you with some good, some maybe useless items. As well as some of the trials felt extremely hard while some were very simple and easy.     Overall, this is a very good game worth full price and definitely a steal on a sale, although I didn't crave for multiple play-throughs, some may. If you have never played a game like this, it is definitely one to pull you into them.

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale is a top-down Bullet Hell game in a beautiful pixel-style graphics. In this game you have to explore a procedurally-generated world and rooms to find items, materials, badges, upgrades and what not to help you in your quest of finding the seven arch pieces in order to face the final boss.I loved the freedom of exploring whichever sides you wanted first, the thrill of doing a zone way too hard for your character in hope of getting something good, vs playing it safe but proceeding a little slower and incrementally in strength instead. You can even create your own build with a mix of gear, badges and weapons, choosing your own playstyle.I would say one of the weakness of the game is the story, but it isn't too bad either, just not enough plot development to my tastes. However, this isn't the main point of the game, so it doesn't really matter. The graphics and animated are super well made, the music is totally awesome and the mechanics are on point. Most of the dialogues are worth reading and are funny, especially the town NPCs and the guard of the arena.The difficulty on normal is just right, having looked up videos on easy and hardcore, this is the best mode to play I believe. Easy if you have no experience with Bullet Hell games/are more casual, normal for a challenge, hard for a punishing challenge. As far as the balance goes, the last weapons do way too much damage in my opinion and makes the last 2-3 bosses almost trivial.Another brief rant, THE TRIALS and the DASHING ROOMS in dungeons. Some of them are just so unfair and really took the fun out of the game for me at times. The trials were harder than the dashing rooms for me, even if some of them were absurd especially in Brinkreef.Overall, I could go on for hours about how awesome this game is but I would just suggest you to just play it instead. The price point of $15 is OK if you plan to do more than one playthrough or want to play with friends, otherwise you might want to wait for a sale. The game does last a solid 10 hours on a single playthrough, so honestly for how good the game is, I'd still say it's worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a bad game by any means, and there's a good chance you might enjoy it, but I do think it has some serious problems that will be very frustrating to a lot of players. The biggest issue is just a basic design decision around difficulty and enemy damage. Simply put, it's just impossible to avoid getting hit in this game. By the halfway point, pretty much every encounter will have a moment or two where the screen is just *so* full of projectiles and the action is *so* busy that you're going to take some damage. The game is obviously designed this way, because by the end you can take at least a dozen or so hits before dying; in other words, it's balanced towards "You'll get hit a lot, but you have a lot of health" as opposed to "you can avoid getting hit at all, but if you are hit, it'll really hurt you." I found this extremely unsatisfying - it rewards a sort of tank-y approach where you just run in, take the hits, and heal afterwards that felt really at odds with the finesse and agility that traditional bullet hells rely on. I think it would have been much better to reduce the number of enemies and projectiles, but make them really count. Otherwise, there isn't a ton of variety in your attacks and all of the weapons end up feeling the same. There are tons of them, but much like the enemy attacks, it feels very "quantity over quality" in its approach. There are also some major difficulty spikes and issues with how the world is navigated - I ended up missing two entire sections until the very end, which meant the ones I did beforehand were harder than they should have been while the last two were way too easy. The game could definitely use some guidance for the player rather than just plopping them into the map. Finally, there's not a lot of story to keep you going and the towns, while charming, don't have any real character.With all this said, the game is still fun to play - but it's just good enough to be disappointing, imo, and I'd maybe wait for some balancing and other updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale is great in terms of combat mechanics, art style, music, sound design, and oomf factor. Not to mention that there are some rooms that really challenge your parkour/platforming skills which I find really cool!I have played mainly on Hard mode, but I have also completed the game on Easy mode in local multiplayer with some of my relatives. I have played on controller, and mouse and keyboard as well. You are able to finish the game from 8 to 20 hours depending on the difficulty and experience you have.However, I will now dictate some of my frustrations throughout my experience in the 20 hours I've played Archvale:Overall, I had a fun experience! If you have an itch for something similar to Enter the Gungeon, I think this is one of the closest games in terms of mechanics that's currently out there. I enjoyed all the hours I've spent on Archvale and I hope you will too! Rounds of applause to all the devs and the team that worked on this game, thank you for the experience. :)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a genuinely excellent little game. The gameplay is tight and fun and the production oozes charm. Everything feels slick and well thought out.Gameplay is a Gungeon- or Isaac-esque bullet hell with an invincible dodge roll, but it takes place as a campaign rather than a roguelike, collecting the 7 pieces of the triforce or whatever. There are a lot of different weapons and weapon types and gradually powering yourself and playing with different weapons is a blast. That said, despite their being tons of melee weapons, it feels nearly impossible to play with them as getting in an enemy's face in a bullet hell game is a recipe for death. They also don't present the variety found in the ranged and magic weapons.My biggest issue with this game is that it feels unfinished. It feels like an early access title that skirted early access. Where the game starts with all sorts of mini-bosses, complex dungeons, and lots of interesting weapon crafting combos to discover (Bag of Knives -> Bag of Poison Knives -> Bag of Frozen Poison Knives), by the end of the game the dungeons become entirely linear affairs (or an infamous dungeon which is simply just a single boss room), the weapon crafts all but disappear (except for a few ultimate weapons), and mini-bosses cease to exist. It's a shame, because the dungeon design in the completed dungeons is excellent, and more bosses are always fun, and I found a certain joy in discovering new weapons and combos until there weren't any anymore.There's also just a lot of stuff that seems like it's missing. There are no secrets in this game. You get bombs but they're only for DPS, you can't use them to blow up walls. You get a lot of equipment and are usually a bit starved for cash, but you can't sell anything, you just have to junk a lot of stuff because you'll run out of storage space. There are treasure chests in dungeons that give you nothing but sellable treasures, but the value of those treasures is a pittance compared to the gold you gather just playing the game. And the interface for crafting weapons will make you grind your teeth.But as much as I have to say about its feeling of incompleteness, I genuinely enjoyed the game and really want to shout of how excellent it it. Any gripes fall squarely in the category of "more! I want more!"

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale was my first bullet hell. And oh boy, what a wild ride it was.The premise is simple. You are a child with the ability to kill the undying, and you must reassemble the Arch. Fight your way through rooms of enemies, dungeons, and bosses to eventually reach your objective. You get three classes of weapon to choose from, though I stuck to magic almost exclusively.Here are the pros:- The game is honestly pretty accessible to people who haven't played a bullet hell before. (like me!)- The world is vibrant, with unique enemies in each area and different vibes throughout.- Upgrades are not unbearably grindy to get. If you clean each room out of useful resources on your way through areas, by the time you reach the town of the area, you'll have enough to upgrade your armour and buy health upgrades and badges.- The soundtrack is great - most of the area themes absolutely slap.The cons:- The trials. Most of the trials are fine. They're not too hard, you can dodge the orbs easy enough. Then you get to some that just spit tons of them at you with no rhyme or reason and before you know it, you've touched one and have to start over. These were easily the most exasperating part of the game for me, and I'm not usually someone who has to step away from my system in frustration.My overall opinion of Archvale is that it's a solid little bullet hell, well-designed for the most part, with a few balance issues here and there.

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoyed the game, I cannot wholeheartedly recommend buying it.It doesn't have much replay value - or I am at least not drawn by the game to do a second run.What seems on the surface to be a game with choose your own path style is actually a game trying to rail you on a single path. This on its own wouldn't be an issue but I for example ended up choosing "wrong" path and ending up in a lot more difficult area than I was supposed to be in, with no apparent indication that I've done so. And then when I entered the area I skipped, I was utterly bored because I collected items that made it into a sleepfest.I think the game deserves some more content and perhaps rethinking the idea of (non)linearity as well as some kinda randomness in its generation to make reruns compelling.

_childDocuments_.review: Read this review and others I looked at Archvale for the first time and thought, “So cute!” With its very fun and colorful pixel art, it reminds a little of the first Legend of Zelda. Little did I know that I would devote hours and some gray hair, trying to discover all the corners present in the different worlds and consequent environments, of this title that stitches itself between lines of RPG and Bullet Hell.Well, the game is quite difficult to start with, but not at an unplayable level. It’s quite interesting to understand the mechanics of each enemy, how they move, and their attack times. This enriches the adventure and even though it is difficult, when you fail, it is possible to see what went wrong. I think this is the feeling you get from a Soulslike, although not so brutal, as there are checkpoints and fast travel abound.Archvale puts the player in the position of hero, on a quest to obtain the seven stones that form an arch/portal believed to be magical. Along the way, you will find different civilizations, where although they don’t deliver a great depth of story, they frame the player in their world. There is a main city, where you can upgrade weapons, build new weapons, store the money in the piggy bank, sell treasures found during expeditions, increase the amount of health potions. All other cities only have the possibility to store the money, build new weapons, and the seller.There is a wide variety of weapons, from magic wands, bows, and arrows to swords or spears. They all feature different attack distances and attack times, which can be improved in Blacksmith. Although this title does not have a “skill tree”, it is possible to make different types of builds with the help of passive skills. These abilities are captured throughout the game and can give the option of defense, assigning a small debuff to enemies or abilities that help the player’s attack. It is really important to keep focused on this option and adapt the style of play to different occasions.While navigating the world of Archvale it is possible to find sources that enable the recovery of health as well as health potions and checkpoints that work like fast travel. Believe that sometimes these can be as your best friends. This title can be completed without having to explore the world, but there is a lot of hidden objects that can be interesting for more complicated confrontations, such as against the Bosses present in each dungeon. Each zone has as its main point the Dungeon, which is the place where the stone needed to rebuild the magic arch is found and which culminates in the confrontation against the Boss. However, before reaching the final showdown chamber, there are a variety of challenges that can consist of dexterity, where you use the ability to dash as the main mechanic, or simply encounter enemies that can be no more complicated than the surrounding areas. from the Dungeon itself.The whole look of this title is quite interesting and with attention to the color distinction between enemy attacks and the environment itself, which helps a lot to keep the attention of the bullets that approach the little hero. The fact that the monitor shakes when attacking an enemy brings a very pleasant feeling of accomplishment. The character’s movement is quite smooth, both on the keyboard and on the controller and even the “dash” ability is well implemented without leaving the player confused as to their character’s position.Although this title screams for the exploration of new areas, it manages to delineate the point where the player shouldn’t be at the moment with the simple fact of introducing enemies that are more complicated to defeat. Still, it is possible to defeat them, from a trial and error perspective, but it will be much more complicated. In this sense, instead of continuing in that direction, the best thing to do is to explore in another direction.I haven’t been this attracted to a game since Death’s Door. Although I already have a few hours of gameplay (about 26 hours at the moment), I still haven’t completed the challenge. The exploration and the difficulty are getting the better of me. Archvale manages to compete head to head, with titles of the genre and without giving any weak parts. It is possible to attack this adventure with another friend, even if on the same system, making everything a little more chaotic, or simpler if that friend is the King of Bullet Hell.

_childDocuments_.review: Really wanted to give this game a positive review but in my opinion it got some flaws that are really annoying me and they keep me from enjoying it.One example is the fact that you enter a room and you get absolutely bombarded by projectiles. And I know this is a bullet-hell game but it's frustrating if you enter a room and EVERY enemy in the room is instantly targetting you. Quite I catch myself being caught in a room that gives me litterally no playroom. Many people would now say "well the game is just hard, git gud scrub!!". Well, I think a good difficult game gives you the chance to show your skills without being unfair or cheap. And sadly I sometimes got the feeling I died without being able to do anything against it. It didn't feel like I had other options and could have played it way better - no - it just feels like even if I had dodged perfectly I would have died anyways.Games that do difficulty well are imo for example the binding of isaac. The more you play the more used u get to the controls and the more u play the more u learn the room layouts and u start to gain that muscle memory that enables you to cleanly get through most of the rooms. And then when you think u mastered the game it gets more difficult by adding more stuff.This game starts pretty good. It's not a slow start, u get into the game and instantly start to learn the core gameplay stuff. But not too fast, it's all well paced... and then you get to the next areas and you start to notice that most of the time you run through rooms that have randomized enemies in it that attack you far before you can see them, so the first thing you have to do is dodge the first wave of bullets. You have no time to analyse the rooms and the enemies so you can't really do anything but pray that you three dashes are enough to dodge everything.Let's compare this to Isaac again: you get to a room and you have this brief moment where nothing attacks you and you can analyse the room and if you are a good player you instantly know how to handle the situation and that's really satisfying cause you can actually USE the skills you aquired during your time with the game.And yes they are different types of games but I think just popping random enemies into a room is kinda boring game design. Especially in Bullet Hell game in which you wanna prove and show your skills. But if the game doesn't let you do that it just feels wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Good game, if a little short. Will make you rage, but in a good way.Archvale is a short, cute game that will please fans of bullet hell RPGs. For me, it gave me an experience reminiscent of Enter the Gungeon. It is challenging but not too unfair on the hardest difficulty. The combat is fun, the music pleasant, and the enemies flavourful. Replayability comes in the form of speedruns or self-imposed challenges, such as restricting oneself to a single weapon type (out of melee, ranged, and magic).The game features a simple crafting mechanic, where you can create new weapons and armour from a) enemy drops, b) prerequisite equipment, and/or c) environmental drops (e.g. rocks that drop ore when destroyed). With access to most areas being gated by nothing more than the player's skill to survive rooms of enemies (as opposed to Metroidvanias that require you to possess a certain ability), there is little stopping a player from challenging an area earlier than intended and using the drops from said area to craft a powerful weapon.Such instances were where I enjoyed the game the most, as the constant failing and retrying of rooms of tanky enemies that two-shot me gave me the rage-filled joy familiar to fans of Soulslike games. And at the end of such tribulations, I was often rewarded with the materials necessary to create weapons stronger than I had any right to have.However, this mechanic runs into a slight problem in the mid-late game, where you are allowed to create what I deem to be a pair of overpowered magic weapons. They are so powerful that they render almost everything in the melee and ranged categories obsolete. This results in a fairly stale late game, as playing optimally requires you to use one of those two weapons, which also drastically limits build options.Lastly, a slight pet peeve I have is that, even when using a controller, you are limited to only moving - and dashing - in the eight cardinal directions. This was not an issue most of the time, but in particularly difficult fights where precise movement was necessary, there have been many instances where being able to dash in more than eight directions would have made it feel more like I was fighting the boss instead of the controls.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Game is pretty fun and charming for a short bit and could be accomplished in about 8 hour sitting. However there are two main topics about this game that needs to be addressed. One is progression, and the others is weapon balancing.Progression is not linear, you get to choose where to go and which paths to take which is definitely nice. But as you progress, mats are quite easy to obtain in a few rooms which opens the road to new weapons. It is quite easy to make any weapon you need, almost too easy. There's really no sense of achievement for gaining a new weapon. No boss mats, no mat grind, just see grab and build.Now as for weapons, it was very nice to explore different options early in the game. During that exploration I found myself with weapons that were clearly much better choices than others, making a lot of the weapons in the game inundated and weaker in comparison. This limiting choice in weapons and viability shy you away possible "fun" builds and into a more conventional build. Relics/Buffs were cool, but there wasn't really anything that cool you could put together, and I ended up going for straight damage. The game overall was great, bought it on sale and well worth my money. A few QOL changes, would be a sort function for the storage to sort into types of equipment for easier viewing. Mouse button mapping doesn't exist, wish it was there. I prefer my "dash" buttons to be on mouse buttons but found out I couldn't doing it without changing my mouse key to a keyboard input. Fullscreen windowed would be nice, and some sort of mat hole for all the extra mats to be useful would be nice as well. By end game you end up with a storage full of mats you more than likely will never use.Again if you are looking for a gem to enjoy that has all the charms, this game is it. Good luck and finesse them puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, it's definitely a Bullet Hell game. I really really do like this game. There just some aspects of this game that really draws it back for me to even consider recommending it to someone to play it. I went an 100% this game, and i definitely got some mileage out of it. Half of the playthrough was spent trying to make it to the next checkpoint. You play as a warrior taking down all these monsters, but of course these monsters are located in separate castles across the world map. Still as you go along the way in Archvale you have to fight minions, and if you die. Well, unfortunately you have to go back to the previous checkpoint. What's worse though is that these enemies respawn again. You practically have to get good. The game has a hard time explaining how you should go about this game in terms of upgrades, and crafting. i'll be honest, I've never been a fan of crafting in whatever game. Especially that you need to do it in this game to get better helmets, armor and even weapons. For the first half of the game i went through it without even knowing that you could use badges. I wish the game could have hinted to me or reminded me that I had badges which allows the character to get stronger, Aesthetically I have no complaints. This game looks like a Link to the past, with some metroidvania elements plus crafting. I just think this game has some really cheap enemy placements, and feeling desperate for a checkpoint is just not good game design. I know this is a bullet hell type game, but every screen you enter a new wave of enemies. Sometimes you'd have to go through 5 or even 6 areas in order to reach a checkpoint. this game is okay, there's really no build up to the story. You're the good guy, there a big monster wanting to erase the world. I've seen this type of story so many times in games. It's just unoriginal. But once you know what to do, and what weapons, badges, and armor to use. Some of the bosses are a joke and you can beat them very quickly. I gotta to say that the final boss, I did not like. But when i beat it. I had a sense of relief and I actually rejoiced a little bit. So i gotta give this game some credit. There is some fun factor to it. I wouldn't enjoyed it this much if I didn't go ahead and 100% this game. I don't usually 100% newer games, but you can tell that a lot of people have also 100% the game since there is about more than 35-40% of players who do them. I'll definitely recommend this game although I am very skeptical that a lot of people will get into it. I got into, and I've enjoyed my time even there were some annoying moments. But Games done, and this review is up to anyone to decide if they wanna get this game for themselves.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into Archvale expecting to really enjoy it. After playing through and doing everything the game has to offer, I can say that it's good, but not great. Going in I expected a bullet-hell similar to games like Enter the Gungeon, which I feel really nails a good balance in difficulty and fairness. In Archvale, towards the latter half of the game, it often felt like there were so many projectiles onscreen that dodging them just came down to dumb luck. Also, after a while, the combat starts to feel a bit repetitive, and some of the bosses became way easier or harder depending on what attacks they randomly choose to do, and it becomes a sort of trial and error. During my playthrough of the game I mainly stuck with ranged weapons. There are tons of weapons to choose from, however, so many of them are just not good compared to others in their gear range, which leads to just using one weapon until you get better materials to make the next one. Melee and mage might be better in this regard, this was just my experience from using only ranged weapons.If you're looking to buy Archvale, and expecting a groundbreaking game in the genre, this isn't it. However, it's not a bad game by any means. I did enjoy my time with the game, and might even revisit it some day to try a different class. At it's price point, it's worth it for what you get. I'd recommend waiting for a sale though.

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale immediately reminded me of many memorable gaming experiences, the developers have pulled game mechanics and inspiration from many other games that I have enjoyed in the past. I found the badge based character customisation that can be edited on the fly was reminiscent to Paper Mario style games, this adds the ability to change your builds while you're playing as you find new gear or smith a new weapon. Zelda-style plot driven game but on a map where you have a bit more purchase over where you choose to explore. I managed to completely 100% this game within ~8 hours of gameplay, although it was an enjoyable 8 hours.Using the healing flask reminded me of games like Dark Souls, where you must stop completely to take a full sip, often getting yourself hit for more damage than you're healing unless you find a safe corner to hide first. I wish there was a bit more content to be experienced for what I paid for the title at $20 CAD. I'm not sure there is a ton of replay value other than setting the difficulty higher, which would likely play out annoyingly given that it's slightly punishing to die to the area mobs(lose some held gold on death). I found the bosses too easy while I would often die to rooms filled with unpredictable enemies while exploring the map. Definitely worth picking up and playing if you can find a decent sale price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those times I wish there was a neutral rating. I 100% the game and had a lot of fun, so I'll give it a thumbs up. With that being said, this is a buggy mess, a lot of lag spikes and a lot of missed opportunity here. The weirdest bug I seen was trying to add something to the stash when the stash is full. Every time you try to add it the stats repeat and scroll off the screen. For instance, if a weapon has attack +10 then that will be repeated over and over (a little hard to explain). None of the bugs were breaking, but there are too many to list. It feels like this was someones first project and I'm not sure how so many bugs made it out past quality control. Some achievements could have been added (picked up all resources, visited all areas, etc.). However, they did add meaningless ones like putting on a shark helmet with a mermaid armor...A lot of things don't matter... I didn't know you could upgrade your equipment until I was trying to get the "upgrade a weapon fully" achievement. I crafted several things and the rest of the gear I found. You pick up a ton of different resources for no reason. There are a ton of badges, which is not a bad thing, but they're meh at best. Once you pick a build and get badges for that build the rest are worthless.
