_childDocuments_.review: Damn, what a nice little game! If you're a fan of games like Gungeon, Zelda, Secret of Mana, the Y's series, Diablo, and so on, you'd probably like this bullet-hell action RPG fusion here!It's built the way I like it where the RPG side adds a little bit of build customization for spice and replayability, but the game is largely decided upon your own skill to dodge bullets and shoot accurately. The feeling of progression in this game is great and super addictive: not only is it great to keep getting new weapons, badges and other upgrades at a constant pace to change your build, the way every zone has brand new enemies with brand new patterns and behaviors to battle against shows that the developers are no slouch and don't just do copy-paste enemies with more health as a shoddy solution (seriously, many kudos to the devs for putting that work in!)The game ain't perfect though, and if I were to voice some complaints and cautionary messages, it'd be these:1) Difficulty spikes*The difficulty of the game can spike drastically on many occasions. Now don't get me wrong, I'm not talking about trying to sequence break by going to certain late game areas early: that's cool. Also, I do like a challenge, and understand that some spikes can add flavor. But this game can be pretty wack at times with how the RNG can create battle scenarios with some enemy compositions that really screw you over, and how some enemies can deceptively hurt way more than you'd think (a tackle from a huge beast? ok. a giant beam from a pharaoh? meh. a little worm bumping into you? instant death!)Also, the game can just be more bloody challenging in general that you might expect, with incredibly short hit invincibility and overall fast and crazy bullet patterns! That being said, the difficulty isn't too much of an issue because...2) Magic is way too good*Magic is just way too powerful, versatile, and safe as a combat option that it makes combat very repetitive and simple while making ranged and melee only viable for masochistic challenge runs. You'd think that melee would have very powerful attacks or cleaves or something to make up for the fact that you need to get dangerously close to enemies that can blast you at any time due to vague telegraphs Similarly, you might think that ranged would have the ability to pierce while magic can only hit one opponent or something of that nature: that way you have to change your weapons up based on the situation, yeah?NOPE! Magic not only does just as much damage as melee or ranged, but it also has homing shots that make aiming a non-issue and piercing beam shots that make crowd control easy-peasy: all you gotta do is focus on dodging and magic takes care of everything. Even more so, magic has a whole system to it where enemies drop mana stars that you can dive in to pick up to make magic even MORE powerful! Does melee or ranged get a cool system like that which rewards risky play? Take a wild guess.Again, you can make melee or ranged work with badges, armors and such to supplement for their weaknesses, but why bother? Magic works without any badges or whatever needed, so why wouldn't you just put your badges into magic to make it even more ridiculously powerful? It was just a bummer because I really wanted to have some dynamic play like jumping in with melee to make a powerful blow when I see a chance but then back off and switch to ranged at dangerous moments, but there's no reason: magic does it all.3) Bomb is a 'dud'*Not the biggest complaint, but I was really hoping the bomb would add something exciting to combat to spice it up, especially with the way you can get it back faster by doing damage. But, I found it incredibly boring and too risky, leaving it to just be a 'cracked wall clearing tool.' Maybe if it was more powerful or we could chuck the bomb a distance or use it to clear bullets in an emergency, it'd provide some nice spice to combat and make the cooldown something to want to strive for.4) Way too much combat, not much else*Don't get me wrong, I like the combat, and the game provides a great variety of enemies and bosses to fight! But other than some token easy platforming puzzles and the occasional key hunt on a forked path (which only happens in the dungeons, not the field), it is largely just blasting through enemies in small rooms over and over and over and over. Again, I love me some combat and its got good combat, but even for me, I felt like I wanted a bit more variety to palete cleanse, so I can't imagine what most people would feel, especially since the game gives Zelda-ish vibes.5) Incredibly uninformative UI*Weapons have a lot of properties to them, but the game will only tell you very simple stats that can give a false impression of the weapon. For example, you might say: "Oh, this magic rod is 30 damage and this magic rod is 60 damage, the 60 damage must be better!" but what you don't know is the 30 damage rod actually fires 3 piercing beams in a burst for 30 each while the 60 damage rod only fires 1 bullet. Later on you might get a shotgun that says 90 damage, so you might figure like the burst rod that it'd be the damage for each pellet, but nope, it's the total sum damage for all pellets! What the hell! And what the hell are these status effects and such: is there a glossary we can look these up in, or hover over tooltips?It's not that much of a problem since eventually you can learn the archetypes and the patterns, and it's pretty easy to collect and experiment with everything, but when resources are limited (such as in a new zone) and you're picking the one thing you can craft, it'd be helpful to know everything to make the best choice. A little blurb of special properties like '3 round burst', 'piercing beams', 'homing', etc, would help greatly.6) Other nitpicks*Would love it if the save slot told you more information about your session: right now it only displays time, but it'd be great to see number of pieces collected, what difficulty you're playing, etc.*In a similar vein to above, it'd be great if the game would let you see how many pieces you've gotten and what dungeons you've cleared and such on the map.*Would really like it if the game would let you fast travel to last checkpoint: sucks when you reach a dead end at a long branch and you just gotta hoof it back through cleared terrain.*Also, why the heck doesn't it automatically save you at a checkpoint you teleported to without having to manually do so? I keep getting teleported back to town and getting confused, haha.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game, I really did. But there are just so many design choices that make this game more infuriating than it is fun a lot of the time. The idea of a bullet hell RPG sounded right up my alley. It reminded me of another game that I am deeply fond of in Enter the Gungeon, however Archvale measures up quite unfavorably to it in my opinion.First let me start off with the things that it does well. The look of this game is absolutely fantastic, just so crisp and colorful. The world seems very charming and memorable with a variety of characters and beings. Each region is very distinct and there is never a feeling of the world feeling just all the same. Gameplay is very action packed and engaging with projectiles flying all over the place, both yours and the enemies. You are certainly forced to pay attention. Sadly, that now brings me to the criticisms I have with this game.With regards to the combat system, it is completely rage inducing at its worst and most awkward. Dashing is the main and most realistic means you have of avoiding heavy bullet clouds but that operates on a charge system so you can often find yourself in a situation where you literally cannot avoid an attack. You can use objects for cover but problem is there are enemy bullets that go through walls which means if you try avoiding them you open yourself up to yet other attacks. And when you get hit, unlike the majority of such games in this genre, there are no invincibility frames whatsoever meaning you can get hit repeatedly with no means of repositioning. This is especially atrocious in the sadly frequent scenario where you fall into a pit and respawn on the edge just to take a bullet to the face. And speaking of damage, this is one of those games where defense pretty much means nothing. No matter how much defense you have or how many buffs you've accumulated, enemies will frequently whack off multiple hearts from your total. And healing is another headache since each time you try to drink a potion it leaves you vulnerable for several seconds while your character is trying to drink it. Combine this with all the other problems mentioned with combat and it will make you want to tear your hair out at times. Oh one more thing about the combat system, one of the three classes of weapons is in essence completely useless. There are melee weapons, ranged, and magical attacks. Melee weapons are essentially worthless because of how short their range is so that's just asking for trouble. Why would a player ever use those when they can use ranged or magic weapons from a safer distance for just as if not way more damage potential. This game tries to emulate older titles such as the original Zelda game and open world RPGs. Normally I absolutely love when games give you the freedom to explore but there is a caveat here. It's clear there was some kind of intended order in mind with the regions and their difficulty and the game does not mention it in any way, shape, or form. I'm very certain I waltzed into and banged my head on a wall repeatedly in regions I was supposed to be looking at later on after getting more buffs and better equipment. It has made for some very bad times over the course of my adventures in playing it. In addition, the inventory system is a complete mess. There is no means of auto sorting, you can't sell equipment you don't want, and you have to manually move every last item into position when you move things into storage. There's just no excuse for that in this day and age in gaming. Nearly every RPG gives you the option to sort your inventory by time or auto move things for you into storage. It just feels like such a chore and takes time away from the other more engaging things. Like I said, I really wanted to enjoy this game, it had such potential to just be a grand slam for me. However, the borderline cheap shot nature of combat, the laborious handling of items, and tendency to run head first into a stone wall just really make this game more teeth gnashing than anything else. I may try to finish up everything in this game someday for the sake of completion but then I will put it away and never touch it again. It's clear that many people seem to enjoy this game but it's just not for me, there's many others on the market I'm more likely to actually love playing than merely suffer through.

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale is a great indie snack, and delicious little treat of pixel mayhem. While it looks like a rougelike it actually doesn't contain any random levels or weapons that I can remember. It takes the style from games like Nuclear Throne and Enter the Gungeon, but leaves the design choices often accompanying them. The gameplay is more like Heroes of Hammer Watch than Enter the Gungeon in actuality. It even has some metroidvania DNA as it will let you pick paths and biomes but they are organized by power level and you will have to find the weapons at the end of each area to move to the next usually. The combat is fast and punchy, though a tad but more random and chaotic than I prefer usually. Even so it's a fun bullet hell game that features great art and scale. It's fun (but even more chaotic) with a friend.  This is what I would call a great "7 out of 10" game. It's probably not going to be a 60 hour experience and the gameplay is consistent and simple. For the price I think it is very well made and worth a handful of hours for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game! it was super fun to play. If you like bullethell games but dislike the roguelike concept, look no further. Sure, this game has some roguelike elements but rather than starting over everytime, you respawn at checkpoints which are basically bonfires. upon activation, enemies spawn again in varying quantities and types. World is procedurally generated but it will remain the same untill you start a new game. if you explore enough, you'll have access to basically every item in the game towards the end of the game rather than relying on RNG which is a huge plus on my part. Soundtracks and graphics are lovely, enemy and weapon variation is decent and the boss fights are satisfying. Difficulty curve was on point IMO. If you are a roguelike enthuasist unlike me, you can always challenge yourself to start a new game everytime you die and turn the game into a true roguelike i guess. but i think the game is way too long to be played like that.

_childDocuments_.review: How come that only few know of the existence of this game? Only 40 minutes in and I'm already HOOKED.Play as the nameless hero as he uncovers the truth of the world during his travels, reaching the village of Timberwell, your character will, at first, get quests to help with the peasants... but upon completing them, he will find out that the characters behind the villagers' aches are only using them as a diversion, and there is a bigger plot afoot.Your character can, as in any Souls-like game, dodge, use potions to refill his health, get keys to unlock doors... however, unlike Souls-like games, your character has to move in between the bullets, to avoid getting hit and make short work of the enemies in a screen to advance to the next one. You can assume a number of builds, I'm guessing, since I'm already switching between long range weaponry that does little damage but has long range, on the expense of weapons that have short range and does tremendous damage... In a bullet hell, it's always good to keep your distance.Later on, you meet a cast of very peculiar characters that help you in your journey; an item collector, a merchant, a blacksmith and curiously, a banker... where you can save your money and trust me, you do want to do that because you will DIE, a LOT.Archvale is  pixel goodness with very uplifting soundtrack, good cryptic Souls-like narrative, and amazing Bullet Hell gameplay, I guess it will make for a lot of sleepless nights trying to take down that one particular boss... and it's October, I'm all for that lol

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game has difficulty issues that kill it for me.The enemies scale incredibly quickly on hard, but not fast enough on normal. They will deal half your hp in a hit when you first enter an area and will be fairly tanky. This would be fine if enemies had different abilities or there was a cover system. As an example, I entered an area where two shotgun style enemies rush me each time while a wave of projectiles approached with a variety of patterns. Nothing wrong with that. Except that there is nowhere to go. The dash is small so i can't dash through the wave. I can't bob and weave through the wave because it includes homing projectiles. I can't kill the shotgunners before they fire. I am stuck. I have beaten 6 bosses so far, but the scaling has finally gotten too high. This is the case no matter what direction I travel in. On normal, I can just tank the hits and walk through the area without using my dodge.

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale doesn't innovate all that much and wears all its influences on its sleeve, but executes that which it is aiming for perfectly. The game is a love letter to 2d shooters and dungeon crawlers, a deliciously functioning blend of Enter The Gungeon, The Binding of Isaac and Nuclear Throne, with exploration and Zelda-like dungeon crawling sprinkled in. The game is masterfully designed from the tiniest to the largest aspects. Game feel is on point with plentiful visual effects and impactful sound design. The loop of fighting and accumulating money and resources to then return to the cities for upgrades (maybe add Diablo to the list of influences) makes for excellent pacing on a macro scale, while bullet hell arenas and mobility challenges in the dungeons break up the room-clearing action every so often. The weapons have a commendable level of variance, with the game allowing you to lean into a particularly fond weapon or weapon type via upgrades, badges and equipment. Playing on normal the game is a solid challenge (coming from someone in hundreds of hours in all the aforementioned games), though the difficulty curve does somewhat of a jump as you leave the first zone, going from rather easy to suddenly challenging pretty quickly.Overall, Archvale is exactly what it looks to be: a 2d bullet hell shooter with roguelite elements, and it is very, very good in what it does.

I would love to interact a bit more with the NPCs. Also feel like the arch animation, when you obtain a piece of it, looked out of place. Other than those few bits, this game is wonderful. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a must-buy for Enter the Gungeon fans and top-down open-world enjoyers. The ending feels abrupt, but almost entirely because the game is not finished. There are so many areas that are clearly under development, however, there is plenty to do and see.I 100% completed this game in under 20 hours, and I do believe that it can be done in under 10 hours for bullet-hell veterans.One major complaint with the game so far is the lack of full-analog control when using a controller. I have often gotten myself stuck on objects because of the limited directional input, and don't even get me started on the bullet-hell trials you have to do for badges. (Speaking of which, those trials are some of the most fun I've ever had in a bullet hell.The music feels a little generic most times, but when it wants to, IT SLAPS! The jungle theme and main dungeon theme are instant bangers for me.My overall rating for Archvale is 7/10 as of writing this. While the game comes off as a generic open-world game frequently, there is some charm in the world when it presents itself. More updates to the game are coming later, so this may change. All in all, very good experience.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Super Nintendos "Legend of Zelda - A Link to the past" and "Enter the gungeon" mixed together.As a random nobody you melee, shoot, cast, dodge, craft, loot and puzzle your way through several unique and diverse biomes (which are each beautiful) to conclude your ultimate quest.Gameplay loop is addicting, music and sounds are pleasing to listen to and graphics are (let me call it this) pixel extended. _childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game but with a bunch of asterisks.The pixel art is fantastic. The enemy designs and attack patterns are plentiful. The NPCs are funny and cute. And most importantly of all, it's a bullet hell and gives you what you want from a bullet hell.However, there are so many little design choices in this game that baffle my mind. Why can't I sell my items? Why can I only destroy certain items? Why are melee items always way better than anything else? It makes the vast majority of items worthless. Why can't I hold the direction I want to go in my inventory instead of having to click over each item one at a time?Why are the gem quick platforming sections even in this game? And why in gods name do they need to be so done absolutely perfectly? I very rarely say this, but they're poorly designed i think they should have been cut. I honestly don't know what the developers were thinking. It's embarrassingly bad.The game has an inverted difficulty curve and gets incredibly easy near the end. I was just tanking everything with very little dodging because of the huge amount of potions and health I had.Despite all of these issues, I would recommend playing this game if you can get it on sale. It's absolutely not worth full price in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the game. Never really played a bullet hell type game. After playing and finishing the game, I am wanting more. Wish there was more content to still immerge myself into. Loved the rpg/Zelda feel with a great soundtrack, reminiscing of the Super Nintendo days. I am really hoping to see more of Archvale. I felt that traveling between areas freely was great. It allowed players to find out for themselves if they were ready to explore that area. Also the 2 checkpoints, HP check and dps check was a nice little touch that pushed the player to figure out how to get by those points. The variety of weapons and equipment was great. I felt that cycling through different builds was a must when you randomly find rings and weapons in the world, which lead to players experimenting with different builds and what players ultimately had fun playing. I do wish there was more of an expansion on upgrading gear. Upgrading your weapons to +5 was great but wish it was more in depth but still remaining simple. I found at the end of the game I had so much resources that I gathered from the different zones that just sat in my inventory. I wish there was more you can do with your resources that you collected. Crafting more items or using the resources to upgrade  or enchant would be more satisfying and have more meaning when making sure you clear each zone collecting certain resources. Thought the bank was a good idea, because when you died, the player faced consequences which the player lost their gold that the player was carrying. This made players think carefully before entering zones. It made players contemplate if they want to dump their pockets into the bank or just keep moving forward while exploring.The Badge system was a great addition which gave the interaction with enemies more depth.  It gave the player more control and experimentation on their builds. I felt the reward system was great. The player is constantly rewarded throughout their journey while exploring the world. Every 3 - 5 moves within each zone, the player was rewarded with either a fountain, which restored the players hearts and also allows the player to travel to other fountains in the world, or items which can vary from gear or weapons. The story-line was good, it reminded me of Zelda and Earthbound. Pretty simple and straight forward. Bosses were fun and for me at least, it took many attempts to figure out a way to defeat the bosses. I know there are a few more things that I am leaving out in this review, but the ones I mentioned really stuck out to me. Overall, I really enjoyed playing the game. When I defeated the last boss, I was left wanting more. Well done on the game and really look forward to more like Archvale. Thank you! :)

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: Great game for 15 bucks, or even 30 honestly. Cute art, addicting gameplay, and satisfying boss battles. Don't play on hard mode unless you wanna turn your mental anguish into physical pain when you punch the pixels off your monitor.As preface for my review and to give some context to what are obviously my personal opinions, let me start by saying this game would have had to try very hard to actually disappoint me. I love the hell out of Enter the Gungeon and when I'd heard this game was similar I was instantly hyped to play it. I love twin stick bullet hells and have been fairly of starved of them as of recently so finding out about this game was a godsend regardless of it's actual quality. That said, after finally beating the game on hard mode I feel like this game doesn't just live up to my admittedly low expectations, but completely blows them out the water... like twice or some ♥♥♥♥ I don't know how to quantify a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ metaphor.- The story is almost completely irrelevant to the rest of the experience. It's cute and simple, it doesn't waste your time or expect anything of you, it's just there. No complaints but no real props to give here either. - The art is super nice and of course super cute. I love it. For the most part everything on screen is easily readable besides two or three enemies who matched the color of the ground quite closely and two biomes  that simply had way too much decorative fodder. The locations look distinct from one another and are just some really nice takes on popular RPG environments. The artisan soup frog, literal piggy bank, and crocodile mages (or are they alligators) are some of my favorites from the collection of adorable little characters that this game has. Overall real good stuff.- The music in this game is overall just really nice as well. None of the tracks are genuinely bad or feel out of place. It all just plays well into the over the top fantasy excess that this game is. However, this does also mean that nothing really stands out as being that special or memorable. All except for the magic snek boss... his music was nice.Now onto the stuff that really matters- The exploration in this game feels so unique. The map is available in full from the start of the game. There's no wondering where to go and no secrets it's all just laid out. This one decision makes brings the pace and flow of this game to a whole new level. It's just so fun to leave your checkpoint and clear room after room without stopping for longer than what it takes to watch a small, but surprisingly satisfying, zoom-in when your character picks up an item praying that you find another checkpoint before you die. Then, when you do die, you take 30 seconds to teleport to town, buy items, drop off money, and upgrade weapons before going back out and doing it again. All the while never having to worry about finding secret rooms or creating some complex item build. It just feels so fluid and fast and it's so extremely addicting. The only issue I have with the map in this game is that special room placements can sometimes make zero sense. You can fight your way down a dead end 7 room hallway, finding a chest in room 3 and a health upgrade in room 4, and then go through rooms 5, 6, and 7 just to find nothing but enemies. Besides the satisfaction of seeing that no room has been left untouched the game generates no reason to go to those last three rooms. - The combat in this game is as addicting as it's exploration. The sounds are clear and satisfying, the bullets are highly visible, your hitbox is very consistent to the point that I cant recall even once where I thought "how the ♥♥♥♥ did that hit me," and the weapons are all fun to use. However, hard mode is absolute hell and I found so little success with any of the melee weapons that I basically gave up on them. Do they have the highest dps in most cases, yes, but when you take so much damage that every room can take you from full health to no health in less than a second having higher range becomes such a heavily weighed requirement that melee weapons simply cannot compete with the ranged and magic alternatives. Additionally, power creep in this game is actually insane. with enough patience and "determination" you can get weapons so far past where you actually are in the game as a whole that areas which should have been challenging become a complete cake walk. On one hand this is really is fun and a great way of handling difficulty. If an area is just too much, go somewhere else that you do better in and get stronger equipment. On the other hand though, there are 3 end game biomes. Two of which are locked off till a certain point in order to keep you where you need to be, but one is not locked off at all... not even behind a boss. This means you can bum rush to this area, grab on of the strongest weapons in the game with little issue, and then just destroy everything. Besides these difficulty related gripes though, the combat remains extremely strong.- The bosses are great. None of the bosses had unbearable gimmicks and were overall just a complete blast to fight. That said I did kinda cheese half of them using the aforementioned power creep but hey, hardcore don't play fair, so neither did I. Also it got my ass eventually. My playtime says 18 hours but it's more like 13 because I legit spent 5 whole grain hours of my life struggling against the final boss of this game. Sans can eat a bone, ultra instinct Old King is so damn hard.

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale is a great game overall, and I definitely recommend it, but the game does have two minor things that I think should change. There shouldn't be any spoilers in this reviewPros:- The game has a story that isn't straight up told, but isn't encrypted in a code that you have to spend hours to figure out. Every milestone you reach, you are informed a little bit of the story/lore.- The look and feel of the game is incredible. The color and lighting always matches the biome/section you are in, if your in a hot biome, you get a hot environment and warm lighting. If your in a dry biome, you get a dry environment, and so on for the other environments. Plus, there are satisfying effects, such as when you beat an area or when you defeat an enemy, that make every action feel like it has an impact.- There are a variety of upgrades that are different and unique in their own ways. There are basics such as armor and weapons, but there are also badges, rings, and other mechanics that make the game different than others.- There are little quality of life improvements, such as only needing stuff in your personal chest when crafting, but are great and help save time.Cons:In my opinion, there are two main problems that I see:1) Length: While this was a very fun game, it is quite short. I fully completed the game, got all achievements, badges, highest level weapons, and beat the final boss, on easy mode in 14 hours over the course of 3-4 days. I know this isn't something that is easy to fix, as you would have to add things that make the game longer, so this probably would have to be fixed over a long period of time.2) Mods: I love to play games with mods. Certain games feel like they have a mod for everything you need, like Minecraft. But I have looked at the community page, searched up on google, and even have looked up how to mod the game myself, and found only two mods and nothing on how to mod the game. One on the community page, being a save editor that allows you to change stuff in the game. And one on a website, which was a cheat mod, allowing you to change certain aspects about the game to make it easier. But, besides those two, there were no other mods that I found. And while I haven't played these mods yet, I was more looking for stuff that added new content, such as new biomes or weapons.Good News:One of the developers, IDoZ, posted a development log series on his Youtube channel that showed his process in making this game. And his latest video (As of the time of posting this) talks about videos he will be posting about starting a new game and updating Archvale. I really do hope that this update will either add more content, such as weapons, lore, armor, etc, or a easier way to mod, so that people can make many more mods for the game.Edit: Sadly, mods will most likely stay the same for a while. I asked about mods on IDoz's latest video and he (surprisingly) replied, saying that due to Archvale being a small community and that he would have to revamp Archvale's code to support mods, that he is not planning on adding something that makes modding easier.Conclusion:A great game. Archvale is polished, has great visuals, a whole bunch of content, and a good story. And while there are a few problems, such as how short the game is and the low amount of mods, the game is extremely fun and I would definitely recommend this game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games (minor spoilers ahead).Archvale is an indie adventure game with simple pixel graphics where you explore a map made of different biome areas, each with different “rooms” that vary between cities, regular combat levels, trails, bonus rooms and boss fights. In some rooms there will be a lot of projectiles flying around and it can get really hard especially in the harder difficulties (I’m guessing). I think my main save was on “easy”, given how fast I defeated the final boss after getting all the upgrades.You can also play the game with two players, but the file will be locked for two players only.The graphics are made with pixel art that still looks decent and colorful, the particles and visual effects are also ok. Despite the low resolution of the graphics, the enemies and weapons are varied and distinct from each other as well as the armor you wear. The OST is good and helps provide a different feel to each of the game areas/biomes.The gameplay, as mentioned, is bullet hell combat but you can pick between different weapons with different ranges, ranging from melee to very far range spells/tomes. The game also has a farming and crafting aspect that is necessary to make you stronger and able to endure more difficult game areas, just like the upgrades and badges (perks) you’ll be collecting and equipping.I think I played on easy, so the grinding was minimal, but after the first half of the game a cake walk, so if you want a tougher challenge you should pick at least normal, but expect a slow and grindy start.  40 Achievements. Around 7 hours on easy (I think), more on other difficulties. Easy, but varies with difficulty and number of players. Easy. If you completed every room in the map, just take a break before the final boss (or reload the game after) and craft and buy the items you’re missing to get the last achievements. You’ll also need to hoard a lot of money, but with the right badges and ring you can make the enemies drop a lot of money fast.  Archvale is a fun pixel art bullet hell indie game that can be played with another player, with a wide offer of biomes, enemies and types of weapons to pick from, and with that, it also offers different styles of play.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're trying to play co-op with two official wireless Xbox controllers on Windows 10, stop now and don't purchase.  Check the forums for confirmation because it didn't work for me in the demo and it didn't work for me on purchase.Update: I've given the game another chance and the official wireless XBOX controllers are working fine. I was able to finish the game in cooperative mode with the wife. I recommend the game but do so with some caveats.Hours -1The game is not a roguelite. It has virtually zero replay value and is pretty short overall (20Hrs Vs 1000+Hrs in e.g., Enter the Gungeon). There are some parts of the game so overwhelmingly frustrating it becomes a win to simply abandon them. At the end of the day, the game is worth something but 14.99 might be two thirds higher than its real value.Story -1 (Spoilers ahead)My partner and I have no idea what the story is and we finished it together. In fact, by the time we finished it the ending is just not what we thought. Are we the bad guys? What if I told you, we didn't see that one coming?Fights -1You have a limited number of dodges. You'll always need one more dodge than you've got. There are shots coming from everywhere and although the game takes place on an X and Y axis you will get shot from the Z axis because where the hell are those shots coming from? You will die and have no idea you were even close to death. There is cover but cover doesn't matter with half the barrage going through walls anyway. When going into a new area, you should probably learn how to fight enemy A, then B, then C, then D, then A and B, then C and D. Not here. You will always fight all enemies ASAP. It's a kaleidoscope of enemies and it feels a bit lazy.Challenges -1The challenges felt buggy, merciless and unforgiving. Dodging from diamond to diamond, if you had to go in a 45 degree angle, it feels like you can't push your stick 40 or 50 degrees, you'd better be at exactly 45 degrees or go straight to hell with that. Also at times, if you don't dodge within a 0.1 window, you'll just fall. When you're running around the little rock dodging bullets it feels like your hitbox is just massive. The challenges were almost all more stressful than they were a challenge.Inventory -1There is only one inventory. You find one weapon and you can share that at the same time but you can't share armor. That's OK. You don't ultimately build up an inventory of better and better gear, you build up a hodgepodge of gear that feels like hand-me-downs. The inventory is a pain to go through and the stuff you get will always be a trade off. You'll spend 95% of the game feeling UP and 5% feeling OP. Inventory management is just disastrous atm. It's boring to even think of inventory in this game.Bugs -1The game has very few bugs and I wouldn't say they're game breaking. In fact one bug felt like a blessing and probably saved us (the water currents affected me but not my partner). Only the main character can change outfits in town. If your partner dies taking a healing flask, you're left holding a flask above your head til you exit the room. There were bugs with money in the beginning or we didn't understand how the money worked (chances are high it's the latter).Promise  +1The game has promise. Everything seems to be in place to make this game huge. If they simply added a new game+ and found a way to make running through it more than once, it could be worthwhile. Game developers seem to be active on the game, hopefully they'll figure something out?ConclusionThe game was too quick to finish. The story isn't award winning. The fights are overwhelming. Challenges are stressful. Inventory is laborious and tedious. There's a few bugs but there is a whole lot of promise. I'm sure this game can be tweaked into something better, much better. At the moment it feels rushed and thrown together. But several good sessions at the development table could make this game amazing.I've been watching this game for a while and although it didn't meet my expectations, I'm certain it could if they kept at it. I don't want to give up on the game, I've paid full price for it and I have no regrets. It was fun while it lasted and I'm looking forward to updates that improve on any of the points above.

_childDocuments_.review: I kinda have a hard time giving this game a negative review but I have to, had fun for a good 17 or so hours but things just started falling apart. I guess I'll start with the general art and presentation because this is the hardest to explain bit about it. The easiest way to describe it it is that it's Nuclear Throne but without its energy, things bob and bounce constantly, fitting with the fast paced action, with either fittingly fast or moody westernish tracks. Things in Arch are a little smaller and less detailed, and more static, the music rarely ever stood out aside from the pit's theme and a few others, but that could be my own tastes. Everything in NT has the good kind of bassy what makes everything feel forceful and heavy when a lot of Arch sound effects aren't as heavy, but aren't particularly clean or beautiful either. Menu text looks slightly grimy and painted on, saving very simple blocky font for things you need to read fast or explains mechanics like your hp and character descriptions. While Arch used the exact same font for almost everything. The time the story actually starts going someplace actually interesting, its already over. Gameplay wise it's decent up to a point, but there are just too many little things that bugged me through the whole 100% hard mode completion of it.To start off, melee is absolutely painful to rely on in any way, I've experimented with some builds for it, but it's just so inferior to the other two options that unless you just like pain, there is no reason to use it. Barely does any more dmg than ranged or magic, but much riskier. You would think that the badge system, allowing you to spec into playstyles and optimize would make a major difference, but no. One dmg up is melee fire dmg at full hp, but going hitless in this game is borderline impossible for reasons I will elaborate on later, and other gear and badges that "negate" one hit a room or create a barrier don't work. They reduce an incoming hit to one dmg, meaning your fire will still be gone. You get another one that does bleed when you're in close range, but late game bosses will wreck your ♥♥♥♥ it you try it, you can't react to bullets that travel the whole screen in about 1 second from nearly point blank.It sometimes feels like melee was an after thought, because not only that, but you don't get gear and badges as consistently as other classes. you get one melee armor set early game and then you have to make due with sets that have no melee benefits, just some atk spd or something that does decreased dmg compared to your early game set but is necessary to not get two shot by mid game enemies. Your next melee specific set is literally the last set in the game. Other classes also get more and better badges.Even If you're not melee this game can be a bit cheap, as the game goes on the use of random spray gets worse. Hell has skelemages that do nothing but clutter the screen in random spray, and the hell boss can overlap some attacks over each other and make ok patterns way harder when he can box you in with slow bullets then send high speed explosion shots at you. Other areas like desert and jungle also have some random screen clutter enemies. The final boss feels like they ran out of ideas for fair attacks and just gave him 3 or 4 varieties of random reaction time test bullet hail between a harder version of an earlier boss and about 4 decent attacks. Hard mode late game in general just cranks enemy dmg up to where everything 4 or 5 shots you with tanky builds like blue heart badge set up, and normal builds get 3 shot with rare chances to heal. But yet in lower difficulties, tanky builds are barely necessary when you can just bulldoze the game with a dmg build anyways. Whats more, early game normal dmg is low enough to make defense worthwhile, but lategame bosses still just about 3 shot you with appropriate armor, so defense as a stat feels utterly useless when you spend most of the game taking mostly the same number of hits, and you never even have an option to sacrifice armor for power when all the lategame armor offers both the best defense and dmg. Stacking the two hit negating items makes both of them used by one hit, and waiting for the one that regenerates go back online by not getting hit is a big thing to ask with the randomness in hell and last two bosses, and even before then cover is sparse and sometimes enemies non random attacks can still be used at just the right times so that one will hit just as the other is dodged. Other games like EtG and NT, when they throw tons of goons with attacks that can overlap and be almost impossible to dodge, you can flip a table or retreat into a crevice or to the entrance to the room/level where you get have a sec to plan. Arch just has mostly open rooms where everything dogpiles you at once and maybe 1/4 of rooms have something you can use.You don't have much of a choice between weapons, if you stick to upgrading an early weapon you liked, it will cap and fall off. You have to move up to the next rarity or you're dmg will be unbearably low, in combination with what I said about combat in artstyle.TLDR A little bland, unbalanced and unfair, with little room for build variety. There is some polish and clearly effort was put into this, but in the end I just feel like it didn't do enough to differentiate itself from its inspirations or surpass them.

_childDocuments_.review: Micro-indie-team-approach on Enter The Gungeon especially suited for boomers and non-hardcore gamersObviously, this game is heavily inspired by Enter The Gungeon, but takes a fresh turn on it and boomerizes the game. No more grinding a gazillion times the same area to just get a tiny glimpse on the next floor before immediately dying: lots of variation, adjustable difficulty, well-known fighting mechanics, forgiving respawn mechanics and a general sense of acknowledgement for non-hardcore gamers that can not afford to spend hundreds of hours on practicing a game is packed into Archvale.This game has a steady progression, throws in quite a lot of variety regarding enemies, bullet patterns, weapons and attack techniques, small trinkets, level variation, scenery and even more. Small bullet-hell nano-dungeons every once in a while break up the repetition in fighting, small boss-fights and wave-based fights in small bandit camps carfully raise the tension every now and then. After 12-17 rooms, a new area throws in new scenery, enemies and crafting resources with lots of new and well-distinguishable weapons. This game takes a well executed more-of-the-same-but-for-boomers-approach on Enter The Gungeon that is easily accessible but still very interesting and fun to play. Of course, this game is not packed with super innovative features, nor features like Path of Exile sized skill trees.I have been following the 2-developer-indie-team on their YouTube-Channel for a while, so I am really happy that this game turned out that great. Unfortunately, a few UI-issues (overlaying and hard-to-read info when hovering over weapons, and no remapping for the map-button on controllers) still exist in this game and the polish is not comparable to a tripple A title before the days of Cyberpunk-Disasters like BF 2042. However, for a 15€ indie-title, this game is great fun for boomer-like people that find bullet-hell-shooters often too hard and repetitive. 9/10 would play indie-games like this again.

_childDocuments_.review: A mixed bag on this one because I really don't understand the developers logic. On one hand it is a fun and polished bullet hell game with lite RPG aspects. On the other hand it is a game with lite RPG aspects, which includes gold, shops and loot drops, yet you have absolutely no way to sell items. You can either throw the loot in the bin or store it in your always-bloated-with-junk stash, that's it, it makes no sense. It also doesn't support Steam cloud saves, so good luck if you want to play this on both your gaming PC and your laptop or Steam Deck. It also doesn't remember if you enable Windowed mode, so you have to toggle the setting every. single. launch. or it will start fullscreen.It's a little frustrating, and some of the dev choices are odd, but I'll just about recommend it because the game play is mostly fun.

The good: The bad: Ultimately, the core gameplay is solid enough that I, as a fan of the genre, wanted to play through the 6-8 hour campaign in a sitting or two. _childDocuments_.review: Tried this game for a few sessions with a friend, we played local co-op with controllers, with hard difficulty.The good:- gameplay loop works, basic movement and mechanics are quite fluid- boss fights are fun- bullet hell patterns are nice- precision dash challenges in dungeons are funThe bad:- combat is very confusing sometimes, it is easy to lose track of your position when the screen is full of your and enemy projectiles- most biomes are not very interesting- weapon upgrades and crafting are very straightforward and basic, quite boring tbh- dungeons felt too hard, meaning that we'd have to grind the rooms many times until we got them dialed down to a level in which we'd be able to survive to the next checkpoint- dungeons also usually had 3 waves of enemies in each room, it resulted in too much repetition in same environment- the non-stop grind resulted in a feeling, that after getting the next checkpoint we'd only feel relieved that we'd not have to play the earlier rooms ever again, so the fun quickly washed away from our experience- enemies don't telegraph their attacks clearly enough, it's hard to be preparedIn the beginning, our experience with this game was quite fun, but it quickly got very grindy and boring. Biggest thing that affected the core gameplay loop was the fact that the combat was so confusing. Maybe for people who enjoy the story aspect and the roleplaying elements more could enjoy this game more than us. We usually play roguelike games, like Enter The Gungeon and Spelunky HD/Spelunky 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Description:-Archvale is an action adventure bullet hell fusion of The Legend of Zelda and Enter the Gungeon.  On paper, this should be a perfect fit for me as I deeply love both of those games.  Unfortunately, after 4 hrs of banging my head against a wall on Hard Difficulty, I can't recommend this.  Not only are the difficulty spikes insane, but you can't switch difficulty settings once you start.  This is one of my bigger disappointments of the year as I was really excited to experience this gorgeous, top down, pixel art, bullet hell Zelda-style adventure.  Consensus:-Bottom Shelf (Tier 5 and makes up 10% of my reviews).  I am extremely experienced in both of these genres, but I still really struggled w/ the difficulty spikes.  It's brutally unforgiving b/c there are no invulnerability frames when you take damage and it feels like the entire screen is filled with projectiles in a matter of seconds.  I picked up every conceivable upgrade, damage boost, and defense that was available, yet I still felt like I facing 3 different paths of insta-death gauntlets.  This is a real shame, b/c this game looks great visually, has a ton of charm, has a bunch of unique and challenging bosses, and has an absurd amount of weapons to try out.  If you pick this up, I highly recommend to play it on Normal difficulty on your first run.  Imo, it's way better to have a slightly too easy experience than a way too difficult experience on your first playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Everything I do say in this review is how I feel. Archvale feels like a generic mashup of indie games. I do think it is enjoyable if you havent played many indie games, specifically roguelikes yet, and to reflect that I have changed my rating to "recommended".IF you have played a lot of indie games you will probably enjoy this game less.Let me preface this by saying how much I have wanted to like Archvale. I've been following the development since episode 2 of the devlogs, and was excited to get my hands on it.  But boy, do I find it hard to bring myself to like the game.  To quickly list the positives, the sound design is excellent, bullet patterns are unique and fun and enemies always feel fresh - contrary to items, I like the banking system, and Broaches are cool. However, while I hesitate to call it a bad game, I dont find it to be fun.As it stands only about 35% of players beat the second major boss and 10% of players have made it past the first "larger area". I find that to be indicative of issues with the game, even if those may not be the ones I have with the game.It is also worth mentioning that the story is interesting but I find the whole "save the world from the big bad doom" to be a rather generic and uninteresting inspiration for a story. I would have preferred a more isolated story that doesnt have to do with saving the world.There are a few small things that would be easy to fix.  Enemies attack the second you enter the room and give you little time to react.  Getting pelted immediately upon entering a room is a trick that gets tiring fast. The game also lacks any accessibility options aside from the option to lower screenshake. The art looks clean, but this is a chaotic game where the screen fills up quickly with particles and colors.  An option for more distinct outlines would help.  Lastly, it is difficult to tell when you take damage and the invincibility period is too short.  This is self-explanatory.However, those are minor gripes, and I feel Archvale is more fundamentally flawed—many of the unique things Archvale tries backfire and leave me scratching my head.  The sheer amount of inventory trash thrown at you is awful, for starters , and there is no "quick trash" feature, making inventory management a chore.  There isn't even basic inventory sorting. Every area also claims to have unique crafting materials, but these are hardly unique. Congrats, here's something to help you kill stuff faster. Oh? What's that? You already found that item in a chest ? Too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bad. I thought crafting was to get things you couldn't otherwise obtain, but nope. A ton of craftable items you can find in chests.This might not be so annoying if there were more effects. Unfortunately, the creativity budget must have run thin as it seems every item is just some variation on "+death%." Even exceptions like the Spider Octobow, which shoots two volleys of four piercing arrows, fail to stand out among the more generic damage ups. This compounds crafting feeling out of place as it is just another way to get the same generic items. Granted, at least most weapon projectiles have altered visuals.At the VERY least, we should have filters, a way to quickly discard trash, and if you MUST do this, enough inventory space to carry it!  It's a chore, and it weighs everything down.Moving on, the overworld. Even if I forgave the aforementioned immediate attacks, the overworld is just ... too open. There is no way to tell if you are in the area you should be in right now other than watching how much damage you are taking and estimating if it is too high. Rooms should break things up but feel reused and familiar quickly. At the very least, can we please zoom out and see a rough indicator of where we *should* be going?  The game is supposed to be open, cool, but open and aimless are not the same.An example of this is the desert area. Enemies in this area have rather difficult patterns but are far from impossible. However some of the enemies have very high defense and are difficult to kill without a weapon that pierces armor. This makes you wonder whether you should be elsewhere but when you enter the swamp area enemies deal a ton of damage on top of some of the hardest to dodge bullet patterns. Where to go is a little difficult to decide at that moment.It's too bad that the dungeons, bosses, and broach challenges are woeful. The bosses are challenging, but lean on that tired tactic of also being bullet sponges if you do not bring the right item. Why do I have to keep going for minutes if I know the patterns?  Dodging tricky bullets patterns is fine, but doing it while dealing morale-numbing chip damage just put me off.  And while dungeons themselves started promising, I will admit the first two were fun; this ends with the second (ice) dungeon while the fourth (mushroom) dungeon is just a series of wave spawning enemies. Unfortunately, the puzzle segment in the ice is obnoxious. The timings on your button presses are extremely tight and leave no room for error.  This is compounded by the controls, which feel unresponsive and sloppy.  This may be because I'm playing via Steam Play on Ubuntu, but consider my other complaints, and the controls are just smothering whatever fun I might have had, which greatly impacts the fun of broach challenges too.I really want to like Archvale. But, as it stands, it feels like a mix of better ideas from other games the developers just couldn't quite execute on, leaving a sloppy and eclectic mishmash of tedious gameplay.Lastly, there's few game breaking bugs that cannot be fixed without save file editing. As a fellow developer I sympathize and understand how difficult it is to rule those out in a procedually generated game, but as a customer this is unacceptable for a game.

Everything about this game is just solid.Definitely get it, it's a good 10 hours of entertainment. _childDocuments_.review: I've logged a few hours into this on Game Pass (I wanted to try it before purchasing a permanent copy)--needless to say, this is a game I  wanted to keep outside of Microsoft's subscription shenanigans, since I'm restarting mid playthrough just to have it on here.+ gorgeous pixel art and lively animations.+ lovely music.+ impactful sound effects.+ tight controls.+ top-notch bullethell combat.+ extremely rewarding--the game really douses you in rewards.+ can be pretty tough if you want, or much more accessible. while it doesn't have the extensive difficulty options of something like Unsighted or Hades, it's still a game that doesn't mind letting less experienced (or, in my case, less focused) gamers enjoy--which I appreciate.- having now gotten further into the game and seeing more of the dungeons, I find the dashing puzzles to be completely obnoxious rather than exhilarating. been playing on my PS5 controller--which generally works great in the game--but the dashing puzzles are infuriatingly precise and often back to back with no checkpoints in between. I ended up just throwing on Cheat Engine for the ice temple's puzzles, because they are so annoying.all in all, it's an outstanding outing, and one that has me craving for what idoz, phops, and their collaborators do next.for more thoughtful recommendations of the best games on Steam, check out my curator, .

_childDocuments_.review: QUICK NOTE: Do NOT pick hard mode, just save yourself the frustration and go on normal or easy.The game is really good, but it gets much and much worse the further you're in it, I speak from experience and I picked hard mode(worst mistake). The first three 'biomes' are pretty good and the first boss doesn't require as much skill, so it's still quite fun to play, but the further you go, the harder the whole thing is, also RNG is getting added to enemies' attacks. Everything in this game is just perfect, no bugs, no unbalanced stuff...until you get to the bosses. The bosses are so insanely RNG based, you literally cannot do anything if the attack is simply unavoidable. You think defense stat does something? Hah! It does barely anything! I treated this game like a game where you have only 3 hearts, because you can only take 3 hits on most of the hard mode. Atleast you get to heal in this game, which somewhat eased my nerves playing it on hard mode. I said everything I needed on this part, but the only part left is the final boss. The King is the worst crap I ever seen in this whole game, he's PURELY RNG based, even if you pray to all the gods possible in this world you'll STILL not get through the hard mode boss. You get to complete the game on hard mode ONLY if you're a second coming of RNGesus, which is what I am not. I am an expert in bullet hell games, but I've never been so infuriated playing a bullet hell game. Okay, the first phase of the king bossfight is bad, but the second phase is literally the easiest part of the whole bossfight. Why? Because you get time to HEAL in it. All the other phases leave you with no time to heal, and if you attempt to heal, you'll either not get a full heal or you'll die. Phase 3 is the worst part of it, again, PURELY RNG based fight. You don't need to be an expert to play this game or complete it, because you need only fraction of that expert skill, because everything else is just completely random. That's the review.

While not a dealbreaker given it's optional content, the bullet dodging trials ramp up in difficulty SIGNIFICANTLY faster than combat does, and eventually seeing one only inspires a feeling of dread due to not wanting to miss out on potentially good items, but also knowing I'll be spending anywhere from two minutes to two hours on the game's by far both least interesting and most frustrating aspect.2. Sound cues are lacking in necessary places. You can't afford to look at your HUD in the tougher boss battles or trials, and given your dashes refresh in a very unintuitive manner all at once, it'd be nice to have a sound cue when they all finish recharging. Things such as the ice shield ring could also do with a sound cue of some kind.3. The biggest complaint I have: optimization. I use a PC that's roughly average to above-average by current gaming standards but the game's performance begins to suffer very quickly with enough bullets on screen. Some enemies can single-handedly slow down the game's physics through certain attacks, such as the ents with their thorn lines, and while this seems beneficial at first for evasion it's actually more of a hinderance due to the timing of dodges being consistently inconsistent. Opening the pause menu seems to help but only briefly, and towns also seem to make the performance slow down.Overall: 6/10, my face is very bruised.

_childDocuments_.review: While I'm giving this game a thumbs up, I should note that there is a caveat for players who don't have lightning fast reflexes.This game will likely alienate players who haven't spent hours and hours honing their twitch reflex skills. (unless I'm missing something in the game mechanics that is making the game WAY harder for me than it should be)I'm at a point in the game where, try as I may, I just can't make any significant progress without slowly and painfully grinding up the money to upgrade weapons to do more damage. I can't see any other way (aside from "git gud") to get any further. I could spend gold to level up my weapon of choice, though each level becomes prohibitively more expensive, gold is hard to come by, and each upgrade is a micro-boost to the weapon's stats. There doesn't seem to be any clear way of my playing the game the way I like to play, upgrading till I'm OP and smashing through things regardless of my not having wicked fast reflexes.So, I'm at an impasse. I don't really want to push further, the towns I might be able to craft new recipes at are too many rooms away for me to make it to them, and without the stuff I can craft at them, I can't progress far enough to get to them. A catch 22, basically.I would imagine this would be acceptable for those who "like a real challenge" as it certainly SEEMS possible, it's just really REALLY hard. So, if that sounds like something you'd be able to look past (or if you're a dirty hedonist for pain and punishment), this game has lots of charm and enjoyable mechanics.If you're like me and don't want to spend possibly hours grinding the same three rooms over and over, each area in front of you being WAY too hard for you, this game might not be for you.I still recommend it for players better than me.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game, the items are neat, the enemies have some decent variety and its overall quite a pretty game to look at, but it gets stale quick due to the extreme difficulty ramp. I'm rather skilled at these types of games and from the some 13 hours I've played the difficulty for normal should be scaled up to hard and easy scaled up to normal. At least that's what I thought...The bigger issue is the world balancing on fountains (save stations) and dungeon room resets on death are way too brutal as-is. For example running through the over-world you can come across 6 extremely difficult rooms (for the difficulty level) and finish 5 of them and die. Problem is rooms reset when you die, making you do this all over again. And again and again. This wouldn't be a problem as much if the enemy spawns were constant, making the rooms predictable and learnable, but they aren't as enemies/positions can change each time you re-enter a room. This isn't a run based game where every room is expected to be different and every run is expected to be different. This is a story-driven game with a constant (albeit procedural) world and should behave as such.Here's where the difficulty becomes a problem: Some enemies' bullets fly through walls, some don't and visually you can't tell the difference. Some are orange/blue but notably don't have different behavioral patterns, while purple bullets follow you. This makes hiding behind pillars work on some enemies, not on others, but then not at all when both types spawn in one room. On top of this, the game suffers from bullet and enemy saturation. There's too much on screen, no where to walk and too much inconsistent distraction to enjoy the game.TL;DR I would not recommend this game to anyone. It's a semi-roguelike-souls-like-bullet-hell masquerading as an RPG. And anyone looking to enjoy this type of game shouldn't purchase this one. Get a bullet hell like Enter the Gungeon or get a souls game like Titan Souls. But don't get all of them squished into one game. Pick a genre or two not 7.

_childDocuments_.review: The bullet hell part is not my favorite genre. It's playable on easy at least where there are few to no one-shot situations. Progression is relatively linear and mechanically most of the weapons are indistinguishable from each other except for tiering, and getting to the next tier of gear is the way to break the balance of the game.The combat can be relatively trivialized and this is sorta a good thing. Really wish I didn't have to fight every  single room with enemies in it before progressing to the next area; the screenlock "you must fight to proceed" mechanic is one of my least favorites in the genre of action RPGs.The reason I am not recommending this though is that the dungeons have "puzzles" which are tests of player interface hardware and fast twitch response of the player. The puzzles are clearly designed and tested for controllers played by players used to fast-twitch precision platforming. This makes the game nearly unplayable in parts because of differences in response times, key sequences, and maximum number of keys pressed on a keyboard for example. Besides that it presents portions which are inaccessible to players.A word about the accessibility issues. This has a LOT of flashing, and there are virtually no warnings about it.Promising developer and game designer, but there's some QA problems that ought to have been tested and seriously reworked. Simple fix: get rid of the stamina token system for dashing; it clashes with the fast-twitch precision and I/O of the variety of UX that players will experience this on.

And if it stuck to that it would be a reasonable recommend.I quit at ten hours off one feature; "dash puzzles."  During normal combat you can dash which makes a lot of sense.  During certain sections there are dashing platform bits.  The first few are out of place, but very manageable.  I quit on the lava one; technically not required to my knowledge, but an obvious part.  To keep it simple the game can't handle it.  Sometimes my dash would fall short.  Other times I'd be too close to a wall and I'd dead stop.  The key to this is the ground is lava; if you don't dash the exact moment your current dash ends then you're dead.  And your dash must line up with the next crystal to refill your dashes.  You can't adjust mid dash so if your start wasn't aligned then it a complete waste.  There's also a cooldown on crystal use so if you fumble the first you'll be waiting a moment.  Sheer annoyance.As of writing this my fingers hurt from the attempts.  An hour of shots thwarted by my own fumbles and the game kneecapping me.  If the game was still early access I'd presume it was a hold over or test and mention it on the forums.  Since this is full release it gets the down vote.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game after seeing it in SplatterCat Gaming's reviews. At first, when I opened it up I thought, hmm, it seems pretty on rails, but I'm sure it'll open up soon. It's a small game in the style of what I saw classmates create in highschool using rpg maker or Stencyl, although a bit more polished than that, to be fair, in that there aren't any noticeable bugs. With that said, I thought there wasn't anything wrong with the game, it just lacked a lot of options/content. But then the "puzzles" really got to me. It just sticks you in this sphere and has these rotating orbs shoot dark balls at your position as you move around this small space trying to collect a sequence of stars. But it's mostly based on luck, and you can spend 20 minutes screwing around trying to beat the RNG on something stupid, but that you kind of need to do to advance a game with such little alternative content. These stars appear in random positions each time, and if you even graze one of these black balls the whole thing starts over from the beginning. And the balls are made to be faster than you, and it's not clear exactly where the hitbox is. This wouldn't be so bad if the game allowed better movement controls or ways to interact with the puzzle, but it doesn't. Only a dash that moves a fixed distance, often pushing you into the balls anyways. It's clearly meant to be a time sink, and makes the rest of the game much more frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this game on and off for a bit. I followed the devlogs on youtube and have finally figured out what I don't like: it isn't permadeath. This game was based loosely off of Realm of the Mad God (RotMG). RotMG was a serious grind and was devastating when you died. It meant that every fight mattered and your gear did too. Other bullet hells that capture this same idea are Nuclear Throne and Enter the Gungeon. What every one of these games has in common is death hurts. Archvale has none of that. It is a slog to push through levels and dying means nothing. You can just get the same weapons and badges every playthrough and you only lose half of your money when you die anyways. I really feel like this game would benefit greatly from reducing the size of the map, making new weapons harder to get, really leaning into different builds (they all feel the same), and punishing the player more for dying. Archvale is built like a bullet-hell, roguelike, permadeath but it's mechanics are stale. It also looks like the creator disappeared of of the face of the earth after release. Anyways, would not recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never been so bored in my life.  I often joke about "Indie: the game" but Archvale is so generic it might as well just be called "game."  The art style is bog standard low-resolution pixel art in a generic 16-bit fantasy style with slimes and butterflies and demons and I'm seriously going to pass out from sensory deprivation.  That's before I get to the generic template gameplay.  ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this game is boring.  Let me be clear, I'm not saying Archvale is terrible.  I'm saying Archvale is so generic and paint-by-numbers you'd swear it created by downloading library assets.  You've played this before.Let's describe it, shall we?  It's a choose-your-own-playstyle top-down shooter with crafting and collectibles.  Yup, another one of these.  Which weapon is your favorite?  The one that shoots projectiles or the one that shoots projectiles?  How about your favorite armor set?  Is it the one that boosts your preferred weapon, or the one that boosts your preferred weapon?  Why are we here?  Why is any of this here?  The enemy drops only exist to serve crafting, and the crafting only exists to give the enemies a reason to drop stuff.  Nothing in this game matters, it's a complete waste of time.I received this game from a friend, and all the points I've railed on here are precisely why I would never buy it.  You can tell it's a bog standard top-down pixel shooter from space. You might also think I hate this game but no, I'm trying to wring some level of enjoyment out it by writing this review.  Ben Croshaw said if you can't do anything new, you should at least do everything right and on that front I guess Archvale succeeds.  It's inoffensive, unchallenging and boring.  It asks nothing of the player, and offers nothing in return.  Thus, if you can get it for free like I did it might be worth uninstalling, but this is the example project that comes with the Game Creation Kit: it does nothing to stand out and can't even claim the title of the most recent top-down pixel art shooter on Steam.Go play Bastion.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty middling bullet-hell game. Combat is simple, equipment and badges equally so - you'll know what your next upgrades are, just go for big numbers. I'd say about 60% of the time the game feels pretty fun. The game's lacking in particular highs, but it also doesn't have any major lows either.The two highlights for me were the Frankenslime and Soul Serpent bosses, these two felt just right in terms of difficulty. The rest of the fights were too short, and no place is this more prominent than with the final boss. He should've had much more health, and should've given a bit more room for using health potions - the fight as it is gives you little to no room to get in any heals. You just rush him down, 15 seconds per phase, before the damage catches up to you.The partial heal with potions is an interesting idea for a mechanic if you really squint at it, but it doesn't really work in the game's favour - I never found myself in a position where a partial heal from having to stop drinking the potion felt like a tactical decision, because by the end of the game that partial heal won't be enough to cover even one hit you'll take (17 recovered VS 27-40 taken).Some of the more populated enemy rooms, mainly in the jungle area, felt a little unfair at times. Overall, the enemies were pretty good despite this, and generally I found fighting waves of enemies more fun than the bosses.Personally, if you're looking for a bullet-hell game, I think there's a lot better out there that you should play first. If you're already very familiar with most games like this, it's not a bad way to spend 6-8 hours.Get it on sale. I wouldn't recommend this game at full price, but having paid £5.99 for it, it's not too bad.

_childDocuments_.review: So glad I finally get to review this game. Seeing a game made by Phops and Idoz was surreal as I had met Phops through another community called Realm of the Mad God. Phop's did a tremendous job on the sprite work and you could tell there was passion put into the artwork everywhere.First thing's first, the gameplay. If you've ever touched a bullet hell game like Enter the Gungeon or Realm of the Mad God, you will see many similarities in this game. This game is a love letter to the bullet hell genre with a more focused story and play fantastic. If you enjoyed the previously mentioned games, you will love this one.The world map is pretty big, and exploring the map will reward the player in loot chests, perks, etc. I will say though, as someone like me who enjoys exploring and finding secrets, I was a little disappointed that there weren't hidden passages behind foliage/obstacles. It would have made the exploration for each tile more enjoyable. Even when I had approached the desert area, I was expecting to be able to interact with the shining statues for a hidden loot chest or something.The enemies are fantastic to fight against. They feel like the perfect challenge and never felt too difficult or too easy. Same with the bosses, they were even more fun figuring out their gimmick on how to damage them. When I fought the glowing snake inside the orb in the forest, I struggled to beat him until I had a weapon that made killing the flowers way quicker. It was seriously probably the most fun challenge I had.The badge and weapon system made for an extremely interactive set of decisions on what badge worked best for the player's playstyle. Prefer magic? Magic build! Prefer to be more up close and personal? Tank build! I would have loved to see more badges personally, as I love a great badge system, but overall the badges here work really well.Speaking of badges, scattered around the map are little bullet hell challenges for the player to complete. Complete three rounds of dodging while collecting the gem with each round getting gradually harder and you're rewarded with a cool to new badge to play around with! Some of these challenges are actually really difficult and require a lot of trial and error. It's a great challenge for someone who loves this genre. However, if you just aren't able to do it, no problem! It's not required to beat the game which is cool!Music wise, I would say the game does pretty well at matching each area to it's theme. I will say when I reached the bog region, I swear it gave me DK 64 vibes and I loved it. It definitely brought me back to a better time hearing tunes that remind me of those games. I won't say the music has those "stuck-in-your-head" catchy tunes like Undertale, but don't discredit the composer, they did great overall.This game has a system where you're penalized in losing half your money when you die. This system is great in the first half of the game because money is everything. Used for buying equipment, badges, etc, it's definitely needed. However, late game, losing money doesn't feel as much of a loss. Luckily, if money is a problem for you, there's plenty of banks to interact with so you don't lose all of your money.The equipment gets an A+++. If you've ever played Enter the Gungeon, you'll know that the different types of guns go crazy. There's so many different guns to play with and it feels like every run is new. This game has the same take. With new weapon types, shot patterns, debuffs, etc. The list goes on and on, it's been amazing seeing what new item was going to appear and how they would work. I especially liked the nod to the Realm of the Mad God Demon Blade item they added in the game. If you know, you know.Lastly, I want to touch on the boss and lore. To be completely honest, the lore seemed interesting at first, but the gameplay was so much more fun that I just ended up skipping past most of the dialogue. I hate to say it, but maybe some forced cutscenes would improve this? As for the boss, he's pretty tough if you don't have the top-of-the-line gear at your disposal. The fight was pretty good, but felt a little lackluster for the finale. With all that being said, Archvale 2 man, I need it. This was a fun game to just drop 12 hours into. If you're on the fence about purchasing this game, DO IT! The creators put a lot of effort and care into this game and it shows!

_childDocuments_.review: There's not really a lot to say about Archvale. You get what you see. Archvale is a bullet hell game with RPG elements. It plays similar to that of Gungeon or Nuclear Throne with generally similar mechanics such as a dodge roll. The rooms are seemingly randomly generated but are formed to make up a static map. I'm not sure if this changes on repeat playthroughs but I imagine it does. As you prgoress in the game you collect crafting ingredients and coins allowing you to buy and craft weapons which fall into melee, ranged and magical categories. As you explore you encounter a variety of enemy types based on the biome you are in as well as shrines for badges which give you special skills and chests and pedestals which provide upgrades. The main goal of the game is to locate dungeons which hold pieces of the arch. Collect them all and you face off against a big bad. Each of these dungeons contain some platforming sections as well as waves of mobs. Personally I like the platforming sections as 90% of the game is moving from room to room filled with enemies. The best part of the game however comes in the form of the bosses in said dungeons. They all provide a reasonable challenge yet feel far more balanced and deliberate than the rest of the game. I really wish the game were more structured. The general room to room nature gets rather tedious and once you've seen a new area a couple of times, there's not much else to see. The dungeons are fun because they provide far more variety which is generally lacking in the overworld. Whilst the game is by no means bad, it's just a bit bland.
