_childDocuments_.review: **UPDATE** As my time with Archvale draws to its imminent conclusion, I just wanted to update a few things whilst leaving my original review up for context - the positive reco remains the same;- There is a bit of Metroidvania-style gating, but it's the most minimal and forgivable gatekeeping you can think of. Ultra-basic damage/survival checks that can usually be cheesed by swapping some badges around.- There is an entire biome (water biome) that is weirdly obfuscated, making it entirely possible that you completely miss its existence for the entire length of the game. It's not that it is exceptionally well hidden - you simply talk to an NPC after collecting some resources, it's just that there is no other instance of game areas being gated this way, making you disinclined to look for it. The entire unlocked area doesn't even appear on your map until you visit it. In my case I had completely cleared every room of every other biome in the game, then wandered around aimlessly for an hour before I finally accessed the biome, which I massively out-scaled at this point in the game. This also hurts the pacing in other areas of the game as the intended flow of progression gets circumvented - I realised why I had so much more trouble in the land of fire than I had previously in any other area, not to mention there were a bunch of legendary weapons that became immediately craftable after visiting the water biome. Not a huge deal but it did seem weird that an entire, necessary area of the game is hidden in such a manner. I can't think of a single other NPC in the game that you  to talk to that doesn't automatically initiate dialogue within a cutscene. Some kind of map-marker in the town where you find the NPC that activates once you have collected the resources would be a nice unobtrusive push for players.- The final bossfight lays the moves on a little too thick. I can only assume this is deliberate to ensure the player has the best equipment in the game before challenging the fight, but it does come off as a bit cheap. Unlike other bosses in the game (and other games of the genre) I'm not entirely certain that it's possible to beat this fight without getting hit, which limits build variety quite a bit and will surely anger some purists.Other than that, the game remains the same tight and rewarding experience the whole way through. Incredibly polished hacknslash/bullethell game wrapped up in a 90's LoZ aesthetic.---ORIGINAL REVIEW:Challenging but rewarding game. Collecting the different weapons and badges is a lot of fun. I don't know how much story is here, and I haven't seen anything in the way of quests really. It appears to be pretty light on the RPG part, but there's a lot of diverse biomes to visit. Think "Link To The Past" on steroids, only there's no metroidvania-style gating with areas requiring you to meet specific requirements or possess a specific item - you're only gated by your gear and your skill, which will make speedruns of this game very entertaining to watch I'm sure.Worth full price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first review i'm making on a game so i'll try to keep this as constructed as i can.(FYI i played this because i can't get into ffxiv and play the endwalker expansion right now. Idk what that means for this review but wtv i'm sad) GAMEPLAY:The gameplay of Archvale is that of a room to room bullet hell dungeon crawler, similar to games like Enter the Gungeon. You go through these rooms fighting enemies, collecting resources and exploring the world in order to collect 7 pieces of a portal. You do this with various weapons like swords, bows, staffs and so on. You can talk to npc's, buy new items, as well as reforge the one's you already have. There are bosses to fight, trials to undertake, dungeons to explore and treasures to find as you progress in Archvale's world. This is the core gameplay of Archvale and it does not do much to stray from or expand upon this gameplay loop, except for introducing new enemy and weapon types. I found myself enjoying it, the gameplay felt very smooth and responsive and was like this from start to finish. However, towards the end of the game, it started to feel a little stale. ART/SOUND:The game has a very nice pixel art style and the colours are extremely vibrant. I was always excited to find the new zones because it introduced a new environment and enemies. The sound design was good. It does it's job, and the music is just fine. It doesn't do anything revolutionary imo, but some of the boss themes were quite nice. STORY:The story of Archvale is quite simple. It boils down to your character being thrown into this world where you must collect 7 pieces of a portal that will lead you to a world of peace. This is done by exploring the dungeons and defeating the various bosses. It does its job but honestly this game would've felt very similar without the story.DIFFICULTY:This is where i feel Archvale begins to falter gameplay wise. There are a few reasons for this. THE FIRST is the lack of any invulnerabilIty when you get hit by an attack. The only invulnerabilIty present in Archvale is when dashing and it is very brief. The lack of any sort of invuln mechanic when getting hit was EXTREMELY frustrating. You can get hit multiple times withing 1-2 seconds and your health just TANKS. (More on this mechanic in a bit.) THE SECOND problem with the difficulty is the inconsistent challenge within the zones. To access certain areas of the game, you need to go through certain zones. Once you go far enough, you will end up reaching a NEW zone. You would THINK that there would be a solid increase in difficulty as you go through each zone, but this is not the case. I actually found a certain zone named 'Murkmire' to be extremely tough compared to the zone that comes after it. This leads into my THIRD issue. A lot of the 'difficulty' feels extremely unfair at times. You'll find yourself very quickly overwhelmed in a room almost immediately. This is due to the amount of enemies and the SHEER amount of projectiles on screen. It can sometimes feel virtually impossible not to take damage and that felt incredibly frustrating. This issue is very prominent in the underwater and jungle zones where most of the challenges comes from the enemies flooding your screen with bullets. I am very aware that this is a 'bullet hell', but in games like Enter the Gungeon, they give you ways to deal with things if they get out of hand. These 3 points culminate into my fourth and final gripe with this game's challenge, and that is the insane difference between the difficulty modes. There are 3 difficulty options in Archvale. There is Easy, normal, and hardcore. I completed the game on normal mode and i got about 7 hrs in on hardcore mode. The issues here is, that there is no in between for this two difficulty modes. I found normal to be quite easy, and then found Hardcore to be COMPLETELY UNFAIR. Towards the later portions of normal mode, i could easily face tank 8-10 hits and still be fairly healthy. This does not translate whatsoever into hardcore. Now, maybe i was naive in thinking that it wouldn't be such a large difficulty increase but Jesus Christ this ♥♥♥♥ was so stupid. In hardcore, enemy damage has increased DRASTICALLY and their HP has also been increased. Instead of tanking 8-10 shots, you can maybe live 3-5 hits at most and can even die within 2 hits if they hit hard enough. This translates into my other points, remember the lack of invulnerabilIty when you get hit? Yea well you really start to notice it in hardcore mode. You can be killed almost instantly after you walk into a room if you aren't careful. I don't know how many times i would walk into a room and just die without even being able to understand what just happened. I couldn't even dash anywhere without being immediately CLAPPED by 2 shots and losing 70% of my health bar. Add this on to the fact that half the zones in the game decide they just want to FILL your screen with projectiles that you cannot dodge, and that will chain hit you. I found myself just calling ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on everything because you basically had to play perfectly if you wanted to make any sort of meaningful progression It is so so so frustrating that i simply can't recommend playing on this mode unless you are a masochist. I refuse to complete the game on this difficulty for now, maybe i will in the future but not for now. I haven't played on easy mode, but i imagine it's incredibly boring seeing as normal mode is already fairly easy.(TL;DR if you want to play, go normal mode cuz hardcore is BS.)OTHER ISSUES I HAVE: After that lengthy rant on the difficulty, i'll try to keep this short. Firstly I found the progression kind of boring. You find some mildly unique items around the world, but they aren't anything crazy and are replaced quite quickly. The main progression lies within collecting materials in the various zones. However, most of the time, you're just collecting a new ore that replaces the previous one. There are a decent amount weapons types but most of them do the same thing, just at varying speeds and damage. For example an Iron sword will pretty much be exactly like the Gold sword, the only difference being the gold sword's damage and speed. (SPOILERS FOR THE FINAL BOSS) IN CONCLUSION:Archvale is a fun game that has some issues, but i still recommend it if you're looking for decent indie purchase. I enjoyed my time playing it, even if i was raging like the little manchild i am.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really everything I could ask for in a bullet-hell. It has a unique gathering and crafting system. The progression is skill based, which means you can theoretically beat the game with the beginning gear, and the replay ability of the game is nice. The graphics are clean and smooth and oddly enough, the ghetto arch that looks like it has 1970s graphics is one of my favorite parts after you beat a tough boss and get to see the rainbow colored arch made on a potato. It isn't extremely hard, but it is tough enough where you will find yourself stuck eventually. It has no hand holding so you can go out of order and fight the hard bosses before easier ones. I have no issues with the game at all other than a few bugs, but that can be expected from a game that just released. I would say for $15 they set the perfect price and it is one of the best purchases i have made o steam yet.

_childDocuments_.review: All in all.. pretty solid! Not super lengthy but the devs have talked about NG+ and other such.The weapon balance/variety could use a little love - as usual ranged weapons are as good/better than anything close range, and it's FAR easier to dodge projectile spam from across the screen than it is up close. Some weapons feel a tad redundant or out of place (i.e. damage is way low by the time you get them, additional effects don't seem to do much, etc.) but overall it's pretty good. Nice variety of enemies, some enemies have rare drops, lots of weapons and such to craft, etc. I would like to see more crafting options that unlock as you progress but a lot of it feels up front and then you kinda just pound through a bunch of the game.A few areas felt a tad heavy handed in damage/difficulty - the trouble is your health is measured in hearts, but a hit taken is not a heart lost.. sometimes it's 4 hearts and there seem to be basically no i-frames so with bullet hell projectile spam some areas get you dead shockingly fast. But still, overall, pretty fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Archvale is a lot of fun! The open world really is only gated by your ability and defense level, which you gradually pickup both exploring/fighting. Each area sets you up with some unique weapons and new crafting materials that will last you well into the next. Fighting is mixed up for the occasional challenge room where you put down the weapons and try to survive an onslaught of various bullet patterns. Every boss in dungeons and the various areas are quite the challenge with bullet hell madness.I really only have a few minor gripes with the game. The first is that since each area has it's own set of crafted armor/weapons etc. you tend to not hold onto gear for long. The pace is quick going from area to area and I wanted to spend a bit more time with each tier...but when it' so easy to upgrade to the next you tend to craft a piece or two then drop very quickly into the next zone. This also kinda makes a bit of a mess with the inventory that you have to go stack things in a chest and even then that runs out of space. The second thing is that during my play through, I had made it through one of the last zones before exploring some of the earlier areas. Coming out with weapons and armor from that high level zone going into the lower level zones the challenge became trivial. I think it would be neat to have some sort of gear scaling affect on mobs/bosses so that it's still a bit of a challenge when going back to lower level zones. There are a couple gates already in the game that check if you're ready to be in the next zone so I know it's definitely on the developers mind.Anyways, regardless of these issues the game is still a blast from start to finish. It's impressive how much content was fit into the game with such a small team! It's definitely worth picking up if you enjoy bullet hell games with a sense of exploration and some fun RPG stats and crafting.As a side note, I've been following this games development through IDoz' dev vlogs for quite a long time now. It's so exciting to see the game be released and be so fun! Congratulations on the release and all the hard work you and the team put in! As a fellow dev it's a great inspiration to see Archvale finished and released :]

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost: why are you reading this review. JUST BUY IT. It's worth it. ARCHVALE's main gameplay loop is the bullet hell combat. At first its easy, but an area and a half later and I find myself really challenged to stay alive. It has the perfect difficulty so far, and the curve is finely designed so as to really test your skill at any given moment. The main way to upgrade is through the gathering and crafting and buying systems. Money is collected just by killing enemies, but the gathering is more interesting. You have to manually mine things, but its quick and fun, and even grinding doesn't feel like a chore.The combat is the main thing, and its juicy and polished to shining perfection, and the weapons are so varied and cool to use. I never really got confused or stuck, and the mechanics are fluid and well-explained. Overall, a fantastic game, and I am disappointed it doesn't get the attention it deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: So, this game has a couple of problems, and before I talk about the good stuff, let me get on with the negatives first.Negatives:1) Balance, this is getting fixed, but the bosses are too easy2) I heard there are major controller issues so wait to buy this game if you plan to play on some controllers.3) This is not a multiplayer game, it only is if both people have good internet for steam remote play to work.4) Length (this is just a joke, but this game is so good i want it to be longer)5) The small amount of levels per area, there should be just more.Now, all the other negative reviews talking about the game being too hard are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and enemy patterns being ♥♥♥♥ are just rage comments imo. So let me talk about the positives.Positives:1) Music, Sound Effect and Art are amazing and make the game super satisfying to play.2) The game is polished and juicy.3) Quality > Quantity. Boss and Enemy design is nicely done.4) The open world map is super fun to go explore, sometimes you are not in the right area, but because of difficulty, you know it is not where you are supposed to go. The locks and keys of this game are well done and pretty creative.5) The amount of weapons, armours, rings and badges is great for easy build making.Now. Do not expect this game to be a complex rpg with a skill tree and complex build making, because it isn't. This is a open world bullet hell game with item progression. Do not go into this game thinking it is going to have complex systems>If you played any topdown roguelike, or any bullet hell game, you will enjoy this short and sweet adventure.The dev promised free content updates and balance patches later down the line, will update this review every single update the game gets.There are still a few crashes and bugs that the dev is fixing, but it should be mostly fine.

Take up your weapon in this RPG bullet-hell world and embark on a journey to defeat the evil forces of the Undying guardians and reunite the world with the fabled Archvale. A malicious and cruel king once ruled the land and terrorized all who faced him. He along with the fabled arch to Archvale have become the fodder for ghost stories and passed down myths. All that remains of him are the Undying; beings whom the king cursed with immortality to live out their eternity in his prisons.

You and you alone can defeat the Undying and rid the world from the dark shadow the king has left. Journey across diverse regions, looting and crafting your way to better weapons and equipment. name: Dust & Neon
detailed_description: Death is just the beginning in Dust & Neon, an action-packed twin-stick roguelite shooter set in a post-apocalyptic Wild West overrun by villainy. Play as the mysterious gunslinger as he embarks upon an epic quest filled with twitch-trigger precision gunplay, armies of menacing robots, and incredible boss fights. If at first you don’t succeed, try again with dozens of unlockable abilities, thousands of unique weapons, and game-changing performance boosts, all of which transform your hero into an unstoppable force. Be warned: Dust & Neon isn’t easy. But if you’re up for a robust challenge designed to test your skills, you’ve found your game. A seriously robust and challenging twin-stick roguelite shooter with visceral reload mechanics—pop each bullet into the chamber during the heat of battle. Best-in-class controls allow for twitch speed and precision gunplay, and a dynamic power-up boost system will have you mowing down mechanical menaces with non-stop action. Dive, slide and seamlessly take automatic cover as you reload and strategize your next move. Choose your arsenal from an unlockable selection of nearly 2,000 wholly unique revolvers, shotguns and rifles. 1,600 unique tonics allow you to temporarily change or enhance your gunslinger’s abilities on the battlefield, crack open hundreds of loot boxes filled with money, weapons and upgrades. Upgrade your gunslinger with 24 unique skills that fundamentally change the way the game plays. An action-packed 10-plus-hour campaign awaits for those daring enough to accept the challenge! Completionists will find many, many more hours of adventure at their disposal. Explore a huge, varied world with four unique regions, shoot it out against an impressive roster of robot enemies with unique strengths and weaknesses, and claim the bounties on a sinister cast of villains in epic boss fights.

_childDocuments_.review: Dust and Neon is a fun game. The wild west theming is perfect, and the characters are authentic. I enjoy Dust and Neon for what it is but I have some issues with the game that I hope are addressed in the future. Buying Dust and Neon right now is a mistake. Despite having a slick art style, cool characters, and a rad premise the gameplay needs to catch up on many levels. I found the cover system to be lacking and often I would have to go out of my way to take cover. The enemy AI would either back up too far or come too close while I was taking cover: This would not be a problem however, I found the controls to be unintuitive and often, unresponsive. One thing I like about this game is the gunplay. Despite having a poor cover system, shooting the guns feels alright. The reloading animation on your screen is neat and I have not seen that done before. You can switch to auto-reloading in the options menu if you would prefer. You get a healthy variety of weapons as well: Revolvers, shotguns, and sniper rifles are most of the guns you can choose from. I appreciate that Dust and Neon does not try and punish you for trying new weapons. The best part of the game for me is the boss fights, I only got to try one before putting the game down but it was fun. So why did I put the game down? The lack of key binding is extremely annoying. It is one of the first features a development team should consider, in my opinion. Some of the post-processing effects can’t be turned off. The game feels horribly balanced. All of the weapons are overpriced for what you receive. The guy who gives you an upgrade chip for the run you’re about to do is also overpriced. Leveling up your cyborg is not fulfilling: One of my biggest issues is I don’t look forward to advancing my character. Many upgrades feel like they're not giving you enough bang for your buck. Finally, the price tag for this game is a bit steep. The gameplay loop is not as efficient as in other roguelites and you are not nearly as rewarded for your time as in other games. In a way, calling this a roguelite feels like a lie. I can only recommend this game if you pick it up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Dust & Neon

_childDocuments_.review: I was in the mood for a good rogue-like, so when sales came on I bought a bunch of them.Honestly, I am a bit surprised by some of the reviews, although I note they were written before the latest major update in June.First off as a rogue-like, I am surprised at people commenting that you lose your guns when you die. Guns are pretty much the only progression that resets in this, and the point of rogue-likes IS that some progress is reset. Everything else stays, you are not starting over the map, you keep your base upgrades and your spec. You lose the loot in the mission you fail, but you keep the rest.The other thing I am surprised to see is people saying this is difficult, and I was actually put off from buying this by those comments. The game has difficulty modes. Just put it on easy. Maybe it didn't exist before the June update? As I have some other games I invested a lot of time in which are difficult, I didn't want this to be also difficult, but I am finding the easy mode is challenging enough while staying on the casual side, and might make me want to sink my teeth in the harder mode later. If I had ignored the reviews saying this was too difficult, I'd saved a bunch of money buying the other rogue-likes, as I had my eye on this for a while. Please understand I am not saying I am amazing, I am just pointing out there are diffculty modes.Another good thing that this has is that it doesn't seem to fill the screen with special effects. Some others games do it (especially the bullet hell rogue-likes) and after a while those games can make me feel ill, because too much is going on. But this one does not.The guns feel meaty and satisfying to use, the gameplay loop can be digested in small chunks which is not always the case and I wish more rogue-likes were like this. One obstacle this genre has for me is not being able to pause and come back later, but this is one of those games that doesn't have this issue.Like others have said, I think the cover system needs some improvement. My characters also seems to get stuck at the bottom of stairs for no reason. I noticed one keybind reset after a gaming session.I like the progression so far, but I think I need more hours to comment on it. But it's rather intuitive and you can respec, so if you weren't sure where to invest your points at the beginning you can quickly fix your build.Overall this and Hades are my favourite two rogue-likes that I got during the sale, and I see myself coming back to this game often.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on sale for $8, and after 100%'ing it I can say it was a pretty worth while purchase. I can see why people wouldn't recommend it if they bought it for the original $30 it released at, but I think its a nice little game for around $10. The game starts off pretty strong, giving me vibes very similar to Synthetik - running around blasting robots while dodging bullets and having to manually reload your weapons all in the name of humanity. The very unique reloading mechanic and animations is what caught my eye and is probably my favorite aspect of the game. I enjoyed having to manually load my weapons mid fight, and pick between fully reloading but risk being shot or partial loading and get that last bullet in. Playing this game fast paced and hyper-aggressive was really fun and very rewarding. The first 3 bosses weren't that difficult, but were pretty fun, introducing you to certain mechanics (explosive shots, shield orbs, explosive barrels, shield walls, etc). The last 3 bosses however....W. Elder's fight is straight up not fun. The game up until this point can be as fast or slow as you want, and as someone that played it hyper aggressive; this fight sucked. Dodging traps in of it self was janky - I would over shoot my dodge most of the time and hit another laser, forcing me to have to diagonal dodge. On top of that, my character sometimes crouched under the lasers (which made the fight bearable) but other times he wouldn't, making me wonder if it was a bug or not. It wouldn't be nearly as bad if the boss teleported around more often, but he seemed to only teleport after taking a certain amount of damage, leading to situations where he would move to the opposite side of the area and force you to take a solid minute or two to reach him, only to for him to repeat the process. This was the first boss I died to, and actually died so many times it was the one and only time I reset my skill points to make a new build. Its a difficult fight, but I feel like its difficult for the wrong reasons. You spend half the fight not even shooting anything or getting shot at because he doesn't fire at you, and only sends 2 waves of Adds. I feel the the fight would be better if he teleported more, or switched periodically between traps phase and Add phase (or another phase entirely).Sharpshot was actually my favorite fight. My only complaint with him is that you get almost 0 indication on what you need to do to damage him. The game doesn't feature barrels triggering anything up until this point in the game (as far as I remember) so I just ended up shooting the barrels and happened to see it trigger one of the green buttons.The final boss was actually pretty underwhelming, it was fun and almost reminded me of a Souls-like boss were he actually switched between phases mid fight, and did different things at lower health. Even though it's cliche and every game seems to have it nowadays, I was a little disappointed there wasn't a phase 2. The gun brands don't have enough to distinguish them between each other. Some guns had more "critical" than others, but I didn't know if this meant crit chance or damage, or both. Without more information on each weapon, I just ended up not taking pistols with less than 6 bullets, or shotguns that had lower damage even if the other stats were higher. Infact, I saw almost no reason to take any pistol other than the one with the "magazine" and 100 crit once I unlocked it. Which leads me to my next topic: the buy back feature is a neat idea, but just made me end up not using 90% of the weapons I came across. I just got dropped god-tier weapons and used them until I got one with marginally better stats, and bought them back when I died. I think it would be better to have a storage, and allow you to store up to, lets say 6 guns, so that you could store them for harder missions, and have a reason to use weaker weapons.Couple more things I felt worth mentioning: the keycards, insta-kill beams, and perk points. I felt like the keycards were severely underused, and just felt like a reason to extend the mission length. I think it would've been neat to have a special mission type where you needed to find all the keycards to get to the end, maybe make it an infiltrate/semi-stealth mission. You could even have the keycards be used in W. Elders fight as a way to disable his traps or something. They just felt like nothing, especially since I didn't even see every card color while playing. Mini-gun and W. Elder for some reason feature insta kill beams in their boss lair, despite not being shown anywhere else in the game (as far as I remember). This is extremely minor since after I ran into them for the first time I just learned to avoid them, but I felt that they could've been replaced with something else that didn't 1 shot you.I was looking forward to maxing out all the perks and becoming all powerful, but since you only get 1 point instead of 2 past level 30, I deemed it too grindy and didn't bother. Would've been nice, but not a necessity. I hope my criticism didn't come off too harsh, since at the end of the day I thought this game was very fun and charming for $8 and would actually come back to it if it got any major updates/content.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Good Art, Fun but repetitive gameplay, too pricey for what you get.Q: Hows the art?A: If you like the look of borderlands you will like the look of this game. I like the look of borderlands.Q: What about the story?A: Non-existent. They set up a small story to give you context and that is really it.Q: Is it fun?A: Yes and No. The arcadey style loot and shoot gameplay is enjoyable, but it's not very deep. Enemies do not vary greatly, and the roguelite elements are extremely... lite. This leads to fairly repetitive gameplay.Q: Is there replayability?A: Not really unless you just purely enjoy the lootin' and shootin' for the hell of it.Q: Is it worth the price?A: Not even close. _childDocuments_.review: Played the game. Dropped it for some time. Picked it back up some time later. Remembered why I dropped it. The core of Dust and Neon's game-play is solid. Running for cover, manual reloads, and shooting at enemies are fun mechanics in their own right. Using your different types of weapons for different situations is good too. However, that's where the fun factor stops. Progressing in this game is extremely grindy. You not only have to grind missions for levels to take on bosses, you need to grind for good weapons too.Here is a situation I found myself in several times: I have collected a good variety of strong weapons. I play a difficult mission and end up dying. No biggie, I'll just buy back my good weapons. But it turns out I don't have enough money to buy them all back. So I buy back the better 2 of the 3 and am forced to take a free weapon that is almost useless. I go into another mission to hopefully find a better replacement, or gather enough money to buy one. Problem is, all the available missions are stuck at max difficulty. So I go in, and get killed due to a lack of damage. Now I have no good weapons and no money to buy back my originals. I then had to grind back up to some decent weapons. It's like falling into a pit and the only thing you are given to climb out is a bar of soap.Another problem that is enhanced by this is enemy scaling. Enemies scale their health with your level. So when you have low damage weapons, you now have to shoot more to kill them. This wouldn't be an issue if ammo wasn't finite. As a result you die because the enemies have too much health an you chewed through your ammo to kill them.This game just misses all the marks for replayability and it's a shame.
_childDocuments_.name: Dust & Neon

_childDocuments_.review: Repetitive shooter with not a lot going for it+ shooting + reloading stuff is fun- far too much artificial gatekeeping- itemization serves no real purpose- bad boss designI feel like this game could be something good with a few more design iterations - overall almost all of the systems just seem to be lacking purpose and are just... there. I don't think I used a single shop outside of the "tutorial" style usages, and the shop that sold guns had items that were complete downgrades 99.9% of the time.In terms of "itemization", there are 3 different types of guns in the game (pistol, shotgun, rifle) and a loot system that has different stats for each however at no point did I ever really feel like any weapon upgrade mattered. The enemies all use "dynamic scaling", yet they literally never feel any different at rank 30 than they do at rank 1. Spending cores is literally never worth it (even "upgrading" the meta systems (e.g. shopkeeper) seems nothing short of pointless as the upgrades are meh so I don't think I ever spent money on anything aside from buying back guns from the clone shop after dying. The 2 temporary buff shops just seemed completely worthless (both giving forgettable bonuses that weren't worth the cost) and re-rolling stock in any of the shops seemed just like a waste of cores (which are slow enough to acquire as is).Enemy design is extremely simplistic, with only a small handful different types of enemies and a couple that have variants that only differ in aesthetics and HP. The bosses in the game aren't much better and half of them will just be infuriating when they kill you in 2 hits. Thankfully the levels are extremely short so losing progress is just more of an annoyance than anything, but none of them are procedurally generated so you'll get used to the layouts and tire very quickly.My biggest frustration with the game, however, is the sheer amount of artificial gatekeeping it does to inflate play time. Realistically this game in its current incarnation should only be 3-4 hours of playtime, but each boss is gated behind a level requirement so you can't even attempt them until you grind out arbitrarily defined level requirements (which, again, don't matter since dynamic scaling makes everything feel exactly the same anyway). It would be one thing if you could gain more than a single rank in any given level, however no matter how close you are to leveling when you start the game will only let you gain a single rank each time - yes, that means even if you have 99.9% on your XP bar you can only get 0.1% more XP and all that extra XP gained is wasted. On top of all that, if you die in a boss level the boss "goes into hiding" thus forcing you to play other levels before attempting it again - hopefully you're not bored of the repetition yet but thankfully the game is short so you don't have to suffer too much before it's done.

_childDocuments_.review: Played it on Next Fest. Bought it. Played an hour. Refunded. It feels like a REALLY REALLY polished alpha build. The gunplay is absolutely fantastic. The reload mechanic is very well implemented. The styling and colors of the game are really cohesive and looks great. It feels like it needs a LOT more to be a really good game. The upgrades are all functionally pointless numbers. The differences between the guns in the game are almost meaningless. There's some serious potential to have an absolutely fantastic game here, but it's not here yet. Also, 39 bucks CAD is easily twice what this game should cost.

_childDocuments_.review: Dust & Neon's aesthetics, music, and weaponry evokes the spirit of Borderlands within the world of Pandora. It feels like a top-down rendition of Borderlands, infused with elements of roguelite gameplay,  which contributes to both its strengths and weaknesses.On the positive side, the combat is engaging, featuring a fun reload mechanism and good boss encounters. However, after beating all the bosses few times it starts to wear its magic down, and certain events devolve into a repetitive grind, primarily preparing to face these bosses again.Despite its shortcomings, the game offers enjoyable moments, making it a worthwhile experience, especially when on sale. 7/10.Follow my Steam Curator for more:

_childDocuments_.review: Likes: Cool Art style. First 90 minutes of missions were enjoyable. I would have been happy to pay $5 this game, but no more than that. Dislikes: Replay loop is too limited, with only a few variations on missions that stop feeling fresh after the first hour. The duck--and-cover based combat system is clunky and has a low skill cap. Weapon variety is severely limited and there's no real strategy for choosing which new weapon to pick up beyond checking the damage and ammo capacity. Manually reloading each bullet sounds like a interesting idea until press "R" hundreds of times in a single mission. Leveling system is underwhelming, with the improvements too marginal to really notice. The cash system feels pointless, especially because the guns and items in shops are rarely useful unless you are just buying back the items you lost in a previous run. That said, I never had that issue, because there were always enough health drops and the combat system was too straight forward. Becoming bored or impatient is the real enemy here, and is the only reason I died. The only way to make the game feel difficult was to be overly aggressive. The most disappointing aspect of the experience was that the game didn't really even feel like a Roguelite due to the lack of variety, low difficulty, and absence of real risk/reward. I will keep an eye out for future gameplay updates, but the last two patches were underwhelming and do not give me much hope. I imagine it would take a total rework of most game systems, for me to want to play. And I realize that I'm basically saying it would need to be a different game altogether which is not not really fair of me, but I guess it speaks to my disappointment regarding how much it cost vs. how much fun I had.

_childDocuments_.review: Dust & Neon is a roguelike twin-stick shooter set in a futuristic wild west filled with robots! As a robot yourself, you will go on an epic quest to fight armies and partake in insane boss fights, all while unlocking abilities and finding the right weapons amongst thousands of different ones. Dying and coming back stronger with passive ability upgrades to beat the missions in front of you will be imperative as well. Now pick up your guns and get ready for a challenging top-down shooter that will keep you on your toes.I first played Dust & Neon during the Steam Next Fest last week and it quickly became one of my favorite demos. The visual aesthetic of the game is right up my alley, vibrant and simple, while the gameplay loop is engaging and addicting. I do love randomized items/weapons and roguelike systems in games and I feel this one does it really well too. The randomized weapons keeps me trying to crawl up the power while managing if I will need a certain capacity or accuracy, while the passive upgrades I get after dying influence some of my choices in terms of spending money to get certain weapons initially.You do have to reload your gun manually by pressing the X button, which some might not like, but I feel it adds to the challenge and charm of the game (also the gun showing on the right side when reloading is awesome). Combine the aiming, shooting, rolling, sliding to cover, and swapping between equipped weapons, Dust & Neon is such a fun game to play. And what makes it even better is how well it runs on the Steam Deck!Booting up Dust & Neon, I noticed it was automatically set to the highest graphical quality. Luckily, the game runs fairly well at max! 60 FPS with the max settings brings in around 13W - 17W battery drain depending on the location and amount of enemies on the screen. While this is fantastic, there is a change or 2 that we can make to really get the maximum battery life out with the game still looking wonderful.In this case, I wanted to retain the pleasing visuals and their crispness while bringing battery drain down. Luckily, I was able to do this just by turning the graphics down to medium. This primarily got rid of some detailed shadows, but overall kept battery drain around 11W - 12W. I did see once or twice where drain went a little above 13W, but this was far and few and overall added an extra hour or so of battery life. This is easily the recommended build I would say others should use.For a battery build, I elected to keep the graphics settings the same to keep the better shadows, but use Steam to force a 1024x600 resolution. This keeps the game looking quite nice still, with a slight bit of bluriness, but ends up saving around 2W drain with a stable 60 FPS. It looks a little worse, but if you're saving as much battery as possible without compromising visuals, this will be the way to do it! Other than that, I had no controller issues or visual bugs. The game also displays at a full 1280x800 resolution and has cloud saves!Dust & Neon is an incredible top-down shooter that shines with its gorgeous visuals and addicting gameplay. The game can get really intense in fights and feels quite rewarding when getting a new weapon that starts killing enemies in 3 hits instead of 4 or an overpowered shotgun that one-taps some enemies. Switching from actively shooting robots to rolling for cover to reload, then rushing around the corner and emptying the revolver's ammo into a group of bots feels fantastic. And while our recommended settings change the graphics quality, the game can be fully enjoyed and played without changing anything, making this our newest Best on Deck game! As one of my favorite Next Fest games, this is one I highly recommend adding to your Steam Deck library.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. It caught my attention when it released about a year ago, but I held off based on some of the reviews I read. After a year of patches, a significant 75% discount led me to finally try out Dust & Neon today, and I'm sad to say I've had a very mixed experience.Let's start with the good: when you're in the thick of combat, dodging for cover, blasting at enemies, and frantically reloading, the game feels utterly fantastic. There is no denying that the core gameplay of Dust & Neon is simply FUN -- it genuinely gives the best twin-stick shooters around a run for their money in terms of game feel and handling. The combat toes a perfect line between methodical elimination and explosive termination, with the pace ready to switch on a dime, and excellent sound design makes shooting, swapping, and reloading guns feel impactful. The pistol/shotgun/rifle trifecta works well, providing you with just the tools you need in any combat situation, and a variable accuracy system urges you to be deliberate with your shooting when you really need to land those crucial shots. The game also looks fantastic -- it's maybe not the most original, but the Borderlands-esque aesthetic is crisp and clean, serving the setting well. Now let's touch on the bad: literally everything else. The music during missions, as far as I can tell, is a SINGLE generic western track. The metaprogression is utterly abysmal -- an endless sea of +5% this, +5% that, pushed slowly upward by a Skinneresque drip-feed of currency. Not once did unlocking anything actually feel significant or interesting. The game also calls itself a roguelite, but it has none of the cool itemization, buildcraft, or synergy systems the genre has come to be known for. The only 'upgrades' to be had are temporary stat modifiers that last for a single mission (or two, if you're really lucky). They're so boring I never bothered to purchase a single one --more +5% XYZ, whoopee. The biggest letdown of all of this, though, is the guns: despite leaning into procedurally generated firearms, every single weapon in a given class feels EXACTLY The same. Different manufacturers, affixes, and traits do little more than tweak stat numbers on the guns. There was a huge opportunity to take inspiration from games like Borderlands, Gungeon, and Voidigo to create cool and unique guns, but every weapon, be it common or legendary, does absolutely nothing to change gameplay. They're indistinguishable from one another.There IS an excellent core at the heart of Dust & Neon. I cannot deny that there are moments of brilliance during combat and a pristine sense of polish to the overall controls and gunplay. The sad truth, though, is that you will see everything the game has to offer within 15 minutes of playtime. All of the systems built onto the core combat are uninspired, sluggish, and banal, and that's a damn shame considering how fun the combat really is. I would gleefully welcome a Dust & Neon 2, overhauled to be a true roguelite or a bespoke, hand-crafted campaign instead of the sad, weird middle ground the current mission system finds itself in. Until then, though, we only have Dust & Neon 1, and it's sadly not very good.I simply cannot recommend the game for the full $20 retail price. I purchased the game for $5, and I don't feel bad about that, but I would avoid this game unless it's on sale for 50% or more -- and only if you're really interested in it. I may or may not revisit this for a mission or two here and there, but, after beating the second boss, I really have no urge to keep playing. Dust & Neon absolutely has its high moments, but they're too few and far between to spend that much time chasing. There is an absolute wealth of excellent twin-stick shooters and roguelites out there -- in the current landscape, Dust & Neon simply doesn't cut it.

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool twin stick roguelike shooter. Graphics (definitely got inspired by Borderlands^^), movement, reload & cover systems are awesome. Gun sounds are on top. Also love these physics where robots dropping dead/flying away from your bullets like they were hit by a truck, pretty funny. The start might be tough, but after you unlock some healing skills (killing enemies or opening chests) it gets much easier. The money system needs some balancing I guess, cuz like scrapping legendary weapon gives you only around $10-20 while opening tiny money box gives you $20-40+ (btw holding R to scrap takes too much time imho, wish it would be like 0,5-1sec). Supersampling: on, brings constant FPS drops (RTX 3080, Ryzen 9), if disabled runs pretty smooth.I like how they put such small details like bullet casings staying on the ground for the entire time and they are also real objects which you can move if you step on them, same goes to oil footprints. The AI is pretty good, not that stupid like in AC or COD games, they hiding, they waiting for a moment etc., not just rushing straight to you. At the beginning I thought the levels were pros. generated, but they all are handmade, so you might see them again (based on count in game folder, there are 64 levels). Got it on sale for $5, which is surprisingly cheap for this quality they put in here. I remember this game had mixed reviews for a long time and after devs replying and fixing it,  I wanted to check  this out. Overall I really enjoyed this game as it is now. Took me around 18h to 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game at the end of 2023 for the first time, on mouse and keyboard. I think it is very fun. I read some comments and thought it may be pretty bad, but I found most of them are not completely accurate. Could be because there was some quality of life updates recently.  It reminds me of The Ascent, but done slightly better IMO. Some of the criticism I see:You die and lose your guns: Yes, you will lose your guns but if you didn't there would be very few gun drops, limiting the legendary possibility and variation chances, also there would be no downside to dying. I am completely fine with this. Aiming is poor: Yes, it can be, and when it is, it is brutal, and close to not playable, but I've only found that I had a inferior gun for one mission that I have played so far.  It was right after I died and the revolver they gave me was doo doo. It was very hard to hit anything, and was not fun. Luckily it only happened the one time. I have spec'd into aiming to limit this possibility. Even a 51 accuracy gun is good enough to get the job done. Maze like missions: The only one I found semi-confusing was the timed bomb mission. Combo'd with a gun that couldn't shoot, it made that mission impossible. I just avoid the bomb diffusal missions. This is the only time you will feel lost...because there is no guidance as to where the bomb is, so you just wander around and have to kill all the enemies, and hope you picked one of the right paths. In my one attempt at this, I couldn't kill anything because of the accuracy of my gun at the time (again, this was the only time I had this) and I timed out and still at the end after just hoofing it to try and find the bomb, I still had no idea where it was at.  So, just avoid the bomb missions if you don't like this. I think the cover system is nice. It's also nice that you don't have to hit a button to get behind cover, the character will automatically do it.  Reloading was interesting right away, I didn't think I would like it but after a while it becomes pretty second nature and adds enjoyment. The shotgunners seem a little OP, because they can hit you from anywhere, their distance needs to be nerfed, but you can deal with them if you just are patient, have cover and don't get snuck up on by melee bots. They reload after 3 shots, thats when you attack.  The game also prioritizes strategy and placement in the combat, as well as, shooting. It works well, you just have to take the time to understand how to avoid getting hit.  I am not sure if I like this version of a roguelite better than normal kinds...this game you slowly make progress without having to "start at the beginning" after dying. You maintain your levels and your place in the world when you die you just lose your equipment.  It seems like once you beat a boss you don't have to beat that boss ever again...maybe there is a second loop, IDK.  It would be interesting to see how they could make it where it was more a traditional rogue lite like hades or similar. Like I mentioned, I am not sure which would be better. All in all, get the game its worth a try. I got it for $5 but after playing it I still would have been happy if I paid full price.

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly fun and well-made gun-slinging action game!The most important part of this game - the combat - is incredibly well made. This really needs to be expanded upon by other developers, but having range, manual reload, auto-cover the way this game does it makes for a very enjoyable and satisfying experience.Also, most complaints from older reviews have obviously been fixed. The game is actually not punishing at all anymore, and there's quite a bit more variety in missions.Unfortunately, I think this game would have benefited from being a campaign like experience instead of the current design of redoing missions in different areas concept and difficulties. This game needs progress and different areas and more enemy types, unique guns, and a bit of a story. The stores are pointless and the guns offered are just +x in whatever.I highly recommend picking this up to try the gun combat and I hope the developers make a sequel and that other games pick up on these fun mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: There's something about the mechanics of Dust & Neon that makes this game very appealing to me. It's the most fun I've had with a twin stick shooter since Hotline Miami I think. There's definitely a challenge here, but you do get used to it rather quickly and reloading those guns and counting your shots becomes a second nature. Other people mention that it is punishing; yes, it might be but at the same time it makes you feel like the stakes are high, so you'll learn to be careful and methodical. I've only died twice in 6.5 hours of playtime, but each time it wasn't disastrous for my progression. You can unlock stuff that makes dying a lot less annoying along the way too, if you so desire. It might become a little bit grindy sometimes but that really depends on you and your confidence in your skills. I like to have an edge before I go into a boss fight, so maybe I grind a little more than I should. Speaking of which; the boss fights are super cool and feel very different from one another and from what you're used to seeing in between. Another review mentioned that there's only 3 types of guns like that's a bad thing; funny I hadn't even noticed because there's TONS of variety among those 3 types that you can buy/loot. Anyway as you probably can tell by now, I really like this game. If you watch some gameplay and you think that it looks fun, grab it. I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dust & Neon

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good twin-stick shooter/rogue-lite with a fun aesthetic. I guess you could call is cowboy cyberpunk. Right on the line between a 7/10 and an 8/10.It lives in the same space as games like Enter the Gungeon, Voidigo, and West of Dead. If you've liked any of those games and are looking for something broadly similar, then Dust & Neon could be right for you.The biggest mark against it, unfortunately, is that it never manages to give me as much variety as a Voidigo or a Gungeon. The guns are pretty straightforward -- everything is either a pistol, a shotgun, or a rifle. There are no machine guns, bazookas, grenades/bombs, or really off-the-wall weapons like a gun that shoots bees. You won't be seeing any elemental or special variants either. Imagine how interesting it would be to have an ice rifle that freezes enemies in place, a lightning pistol that slows down enemy reload speed, or a shotgun with low power in exchange for a burning damage-over-time effect. You won't find any of that here. The most variation you will see in D & N's guns are the stats, but to the game's credit, it tries to do a lot with very little.One of the big standout mechanics is the active reload. If your shotgun holds three shells, you have to tap reload three times while an image of your shotgun pops up on the right side of the screen to show you the reload in progress. This can lead to some fun cost-benefit analysis like the time I found an incredibly powerful two-shot pistol. It was a bit of a drag to reload so often, but I eventually fell into a rhythm. By the time I found a six shooter in a weapons chest, I was pretty attached to the two shots/reload style and the sheer power of the pistol. I wasn't willing to cut my attack power in half in exchange for three times the ammo capacity. It's a rogue-lite, so it offers some progress between runs. The two main branches are the Skill points used to buy defensive perks (more HP, less damage in cover, etc.) and offensive perks (more damage with guns of a certain weapon class, heal on kill, etc.), and the blue canisters used to buy things like better guns in the gun shop or the "Buy-Back-O-Matic." Tip:  Sinking resources into the gun shop is generally a waste. You will find better stuff out in the world on your runs. But Buy-Back-O-Matic memorizes the guns you were using when you died and gives you the chance to purchase them again at the start of a new run. If you've absolutely fallen in love with a certain loadout, you can upgrade the BBOM to remember all three of your guns (it starts with just the pistol) and selling them back to you at cheaper and cheaper prices. I never start a run without my Legendary-grade two-shot super pistol. Short version:  It makes for a fun weekend if you've already tried out the big name twin-stick rogue-likes and rogue-lites.
_childDocuments_.name: Dust & Neon

_childDocuments_.review: This plays a lot slower than what the previews show. From the artstyle and everything, it feels like the game should be a lot more dynamic and chaotic, but the game is very simplistic, where you're just moving and shooting. Not even a melee attack, any throwables, or any kind of ability. Reloading feels slow, and your other guns don't automatically reload when unequipped. Navigating the home base also feels very slow, with interactables placed far from one another. You'd be walking for like 10 seconds every time just to get to the mission select.The actual shooting gameplay does feel good once you get used to the isometric view, but this gets boring fast when the game expects you to do the same thing for hours and hours.The game's structure is honestly just bad. It has a mission select for you to do randomly generated missions, so the game expects you to play the same missions, albeit with slightly different layouts. This would have been fine if it were a roguelike, where each playthrough of the mission would feel different, but the game doesn't have any of that. The game quickly feels repetitive because of how simple the gameplay is, and no effort was made to mix up the gameplay.What makes this even worse is how grindy the game is designed. Each boss is locked behind a required rank, and if you fail to defeat them, you can't just try again immediately as the boss "goes into hiding" and their mission is inaccessible until you finish another normal mission.I get the idea this game is going for. It wants you to prepare before facing a boss by arming yourself with better weapons, but that should be an option, not something forced on players. Players should be free to challenge bosses however they want. But since there's not even a lot of preparation you can do aside from getting better weapons, this mechanic just falls flat and feels more like an artificial way of padding out the game.Once I saw this mechanic with the first boss, I honestly just didn't have the motivation to play again. This game feels like it would be a lot better as an open world where enemies can respawn. This makes it optional to replay the areas again rather than a necessity. Being able to stumble into a boss anytime and see how stronger they are would give players more motivation to grind to be on the same level.The game can still be serviceable if you're just looking for a simple twin-stick shooter, but there are a lot better games in that genre.
