_childDocuments_.review: Reading a review is not enough? Want to see some footage? Check the link and watch some game footage for yourself and decide if this game is worth your time:The Shore is a running simulator with most of the mandatory Lovecraft Creatures (the old ones) and a protagonist who will not die automatically by looking at them.This is the first game developed by Ares Dragonis who is entering the world of Steam with this game.Stranded hm? Hope your mind is strong for the world you are about to enter my Friend.Lovecraft theme, Why? Why me? My Issue with Love Craft? I played the Call of Cthulhu pen and paper for more than 10 years. They say you either love or hate it, I feared it and still do.You start as a guy who searches for his daughter stranded on an Isle. The Game itself is good at creating an oppressive atmosphere with the visuals and the sound. The big part in this game are that you are an actual immune sentient being and the game allows you to see one of the Old ones like Shoggoth or Dagon, even old Cthulhu. And this is the best and the worst part in one. Yes I feared it when I had to run into a giant mouth underwater and run away from a monster, no it was not scary rather more frustrating due to the lack of knowledge where to go and not much time to run away from the beholder. The runaway segments are the weakest part in this game, but the strong ones are the creatures. The Living monolith? It's there, looks a bit clumsy, let me not get to detailed to the Monsters. They are there, and they are horrifying, it's to bad it's too bright in the game. The horror is starts once you get in the darker spots and meet the beholder or the guy who tries to eat you and the level you are in. Its great and its fun to see these sizes. The End has a great twist, two bad besides the parts where you face the Monsters and watching Dagon ride the monolith, the game is lacking content. It is a straight forward game, and you get in to great and big levels, but why are you here for? You are here for to sink into the madness of the world and this happens to less, your character is so strong bond to his daughter he cares for nobody else. Even I had to take a few minutes when the giant Cthulhu merges from the ocean. You can't get into the madness when the playable character is not getting any anxiety by looking into a skyscraper big eye.- Big Lovecraft canonical behaving monsters- a few spaces are spot on pure horror- the narration is great- Visuals look amazing- great Lovecraft atmosphere- the soundtrack is spot on- Enemies are simple attack monsters without any horror behavior (teleporting around, screaming and doing horrific things)- not the typical madness you get from other Lovecraft inspired games- the story itself makes no senseThe Shore  offers a great visual game with the Lovecraft monsters and references, a lot of references to the Lovecraft universe. You will like it like I did when you love to see the Lovecraft Monsters animated in a game. It feels great to see them, takes a bit out of the horror, but it is great!So who will enjoy this game? Do you like Eternal Darkness sanity's Requiem? Have you ever felt the Monsters deserve more screen time? Now it's your time to play and see them all.

_childDocuments_.review: Putting aside the clunky mechanics and awkward movement, this game is incredible. Reminiscent of old explorer games such as Myst or Riven, it feels more like an art project than a game, and offers beautifully designed assets, a rich and compelling narrative, and an environment and atmosphere that rivals that of AAA games. I remember after first playing, I had to sit down for an hour and just process everything I had experienced - it remains to this day the only game that has had that profound of an effect on me. I find myself wishing to play it again for the first time, to feel that unparalleled and unique Lovecraftian atmosphere. Almost every minute of the 3 hours it took to complete was interesting in some way, which for a heavily visual-focused game is quite impressive. My only complaint is that I found some of the puzzles to be frustratingly unintuitive - having to google walkthroughs on some sections, but overall it is a masterpiece of environment art, accompanied with a beautifully written story.

_childDocuments_.review: Great atmospheric exploration, 3 hours long game, in the world of Lovecraft with 2 majors flaws. First the atmosphere and music are spot on, many small items to discover and some messages to read about the Cthulhu mythos. Discovering some strange monoliths and anomalies on this forsaken island are really well-made and super fun. The story could have been more defined rather then you wake up on a beach, now find some missing generic family member the player have no attachment to. The walking feel sluggish like stuck in jello and it's pretty hard to tell if you are running or not. There is a few kind of puzzles but they are not really satisfying nor intuitive, pick the right head from the ground was a bit boring and shoot the beams in the right order or die too.All of this could have been forgiven, but its a major component for fleeing and fighting the various denizens of the island. Fleeing is a terrible mechanic of the game, it seems like all the monster go at the same speed of you, took a wrong turn, or got stuck into a  wall corner ? too late your dead. You eventually get a strange item that allows you to stun some monsters, then the game become a repetition of : Run, stop, freeze the monster, run a short while ... rince and repeat for the whole level.I really hope for a deeper sequel in the same universe, but without combat or running. Actual working puzzles would be a lot more fitting to this kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall "The Shore" is a pretty good cosmic horror game with an excellent soundtrack and tons of awesome Lovecraftian references and aesthetics which are really brought to life with incredible detail. The setting and scenery is fantastic and dimly vibrant with lots to look at and inspect as you slowly descend into insanity in a typical Lovecraft fashion. Story wise, it is basic yet incomprehensible at the same time. Many appearances and themes leave you confused and inquisitive as to what has happened, what you are witnessing, what you have witnessed and what is real and what is not real. My only gripe with the game is the combat, the only reason it is tense is due to how irritating it is. I would have much preferred more complicated and in depth puzzles instead of tedious combat scenes which just consist of beings chasing you and outrunning you while you try and find the exit, barely getting the chance to fight back. Most of the time you can outrun certain enemies, but it is just boring. It isn't a very long game and you can easily get all the achievements and complete it in a few hours or less. Definitely a good Sunday afternoon game as you don't need to apply yourself too much as most of first half of the game is just exploring. As for whether or not it is worth the price... On one hand I would say yes because the creator has done a fantastic job making the game and deserves the support. Perhaps he will eventually create a longer eldritch horror game with more puzzles and more story, as I didn't find myself too invested in the main character. So on the other hand I would say it is more worth the sale price as the combat is tedious, the voice acting is average and the character isn't very interesting.But, credit where credit is due. I thoroughly enjoyed the game

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore is a somewhat short, 2-3 hour, Lovecraftian horror title that straddles a line between being a walking simulator and casual survival game. You play as a fisherman named Andrew, who finds himself washed ashore on a strange island filled with cosmic horrors and eldritch relics after his boat capsizes. You start out exploring this shore, and learning about the island's prior inhabitants, before falling down the void of the Elder Gods.First and foremost, this game has some amazing visual aesthetics. The graphics are absolutely cream of the crop, although the first half of the campaign is filled with stuttering issues even after turning on an option to increase texture cache size. These stuttering issues seem to be due to texture loading and not actual FPS optimization, as the FPS stays at a solid 60 the entire time. The sound design also beautifully captures and instills emotions such as a foreboding sense of dread, omnipresent feelings of insanity, and a sense that everything around you is much bigger and greater than your inconsequential existence. The further you continue into the story, the smaller and more insignificant you feel, as the Elder Gods make themselves and their powers known. If there's one thing this game does well, is that it brings to life H.P. Lovecraft's visions of massive cosmic entities that control not only our very existence, but the universe itself.While The Shore has phenomenal visual and audio design, it's the gameplay that will make-or-break this experience for all players; you'll either love it, or hate it. At around the halfway point of the playthrough, the entire game shifts its focus from walking simulator to somewhat survival horror, wherein you'll be fending off eldritch monsters with an artifact that sends out a lazer-beam stream. These abominations are invincible and the beam merely stuns them and slows them down, which grants you a very minimal amount of time to run ahead and find an exit before having to turn around and stun them again. Sandwiched between these encounters you'll be solving some novel, but objectively mundane, puzzles that require little to no thought to complete.By the end of The Shore you'll feel as though you started and finished two entirely different games. It's as though the developer changed his mind on exactly what type of game he wanted to create, and did a complete 180 around the halfway point. This isn't always a bad thing to do, and in most cases it prevents a game from becoming repetitive and stale, but unfortunately in doing this the developer actually introduced repetition and predictability. Taking out the frustrating fighting mechanics and instead keeping this title a simple walking simulator would've fared better by having players focusing more on the story and visuals, rather than an annoying gameplay mechanic that was implemented poorly. It's really a shame, as Ares Dragonis really captured the pure essence of H.P. Lovecraft's brilliant tales of cosmic horror. This one isn't going to be for everyone, and while it didn't quite hit the spot for me, if you can see through the poorly crafted combat and drab puzzles, you may enjoy it more.The Horror Network  |  Click for Gore

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels unfinished. Uneven audio levels on the voieovers; lots of places where the level geometry didn't match the visual geometry; objects floating in midair or with textures only half drawn; often there is no back-side to papers, just the mirror image of the front texture; if you press "Tab" you activate some kind of developer overlay with invisible text boxes. Just... lots of stuff that I feel like should have been caught and addressed before the game was released.Subjective gripes: not a fan of the control scheme used when rotating objects. Would appreciate a "Cancel" button on the settings menus instead of "Accepting" the settings you already had. Would like better signposting on where to proceed. Some of the environments, the way to progress felt like I was skyrimming, not following the intended path.Silly things: Pretty sure some of the assets chosen are anachronistic. _childDocuments_.review: Well this was a surprise in many ways. The premise is quite simple. A man wakes up on a beach looking for his lost daughter. After a small stroll along the shoreline utterly weird stuff starts to happen.. This is a very serene and strange game at its start only to drastically ramp up half way through into a tale of cosmic horrors and macabre discoveries knee deep in madness.. If you are a fan of cosmic horror and a weird walking simulator hybrid with a peculiar emerging narrative this is quite a hidden gem. However I will be a bit critical and say that the first half of the game is a brilliant piece of suspenseful mystery and serene atmosphere. As the story progresses it becomes a bit on the nose in the Lovecraftian fanfiction. The ending was a bit anticlimactic but in the end I had a good time with the game. And it offers a lot of eldritch sightseeing! It is not a Call of the Sea, but honestly it is a fine game standing on its own merits, had it been another setting than the Cthulhu Mythos it might have felt even better! I encountered a few bugs but nothing game breaking. Get it at a discount and immerse yourself in a strange journey.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has gorgeous visuals and interesting non linear writing in the form of notes in a bottle that one finds while exploring the world, it is well put together, no bugs or glitches that I remember (Apart from the game not responding when trying to start a new game from the pause menu).Sadly that's where the positives end for me, as a story there is not much to take home, it feels more like an "H.P. Lovecraft Bingo'' than anything else, the gameplay is not innovative, I understand that not every game has to innovate, but even as a walking sim it felt really lackluster, I'm a really big fan of non linear storytelling, especially if it's in form of collectibles scattered around the game’s world, but in most cases this collectibles will be nowhere to be found until you enter one specific area that has 3 of them one next to the other, it really takes me out of the whole "explore to find clues" idea that a Lovecraftian inspired walking sim should heavily use to its advantage, the voice acting was fine until the end where some exposition is being given by a woman and you can barely hear what she is saying.I did actually enjoy this game, even if it was because I spent more time taking pictures than actually playing it, but I wouldn't really recommend it, that being said, I'm interested on what the future holds with our developer.We will watch your career with great interest!

_childDocuments_.review: Contains very minor spoilers:This game is good, but it has a lot of issues that can easily be ironed out over the course of a few updates. First, the game is too short to warrant a $25 dollar tag. Around two and a half hours of content on my playthrough, for example. I'd say to drop the price from $25 to around $15.The game is absolutely stunning, visually. I found myself just looking around the island seeing how good it could look. Unfortunately, on my decently powerful rig, I noticed more than a few frame drops. This was the most noticeable during the chase sequences and any time I used the artifact. A benchmarking tool would be a very nice addition for those who don't know what graphics they can comfortably set it to.The acting and animations are all very well done, but the subtitles use a lot of incorrect grammar and spelling. This is very apparent in the late game, as most sentences have at least one mistake in the subtitles.The controls are fine but I would've liked key bindings or controller support. Making 'i' the inventory is a very minor issue, but I found myself locking the cursor far too many times.I followed the game's progress on itch.io and I am very glad it got its full release, and I want it to be the best it can be. _childDocuments_.review: Creepy Lovecraftian walking simulator.The video game industry of Greece is dead. Games have been banned from 2002 till 2011.No wonder they haven't produced anything worthwhile.So when a Greek indie studio made this game, we can be more lenient to its more amateurish aspects."The Shore" got a lot of exposure when the youtuber IGP released his 2.4 mil video.That's how I found this game and was intrigued.The sound design is good. The game is beautiful.The voice acting is amateurish, but as mentioned before we can overlook the smaller issues.Two Lovecraftian games of recent times are "The Sinking City" and "Call of Cthulhu".Both games are famously lacking, but I personally believe that having more atmospheric exploration like in The Shore would have enhanced these games."The SHORE" is basically "Grey Dawn" mixed with "Lust from Beyond" but shorter.

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore has what you would expect from an H.P. Lovecraft story.  The protagonist is an insignificant human that finds himself in the middle of a major cosmic event while searching for his daughter.  If you're a fan of H.P. Lovecraft and cosmic horror, this game is a must-buy, as long as you can overcome a few caveats.  The things this game does right, it does wonderfully, but it has some technical problems, and some pacing problems.The graphics are great, especially considering the island is little more than a desolate, rocky reef breaking the surface of the ocean.  The creature design is fantastic and their animations are fluid, bizarre, and organic.  The audio and music really stand out and sell the atmosphere and mood of the game.  The voice acting is decent enough.  Overall it's a well designed game.There's a few problems with it though.  First is that the controls are hard coded, including the mouse buttons.  This made it extremely frustrating during the escape sequences in the second half of the game because I could not rebind my keys and mouse to my typical, comfortable control scheme.  This is something that I usually refund a game for right away, but as a Lovecraft fan, I really wanted to experience this game so I made a go at it.  Second, the optimization is not great.  Although I had a decent enough framerate at 4k resolution and max settings, there were problems with sound crackling and stuttering and I had to turn down the sound quality in windows as well as close pretty much every background program and process that I could to keep the sound from going bad.  Last thing, the game could be longer... it took me about 2 hours to complete going at a leisurely pace, but that would have been at least 30 minutes shorter if I'd had my own control scheme to use.  There are a lot of mythos deities and beasties in this game, as well as a lot of connections to other mythos stories, but the game is too short to really delve into each of them properly.  The narrative escalates too quickly and could easily be expanded to a 15 to 20 hour game to really flesh everything out.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a mixed bag to me. It's a walking sim throughout a Lovecraftian showcase set on an island which exists seemingly outside of time. It is interesting at first but does not feature much in the way of plot, quests or other characters to interact with. The game is quickly revealed to be marred by bad, poor and uninspired design at all times. The movement, "combat", puzzles and VO are all subpar, sometimes infuriatingly so. Even taking a "less is more" interpretation with regards to the island itself, doesn't do it any favors as there just isn't all that much to it at all.I don't really know who to recommend this to... I don't even think I can recommend the source material after playing this game. The collected works are far more detailed, intricate and focused than anything this game tries to do. The game just seems to lump in a bunch of stuff in the hopes that there's some semblance of a worthwhile experience. And in my opinion, there isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore Review- Before reading I did win this game in a instagram drawing, but this did not change my experience in any way.This game was a well designed Lovecraftian homage walking simulator with all the tentacled creatures, occult ritualistic items, mystery and tension one might expect. Being an early access game, it did have some slight technical bugs and issues, but all in all I greatly enjoyed my experience and will be replaying this game to explore for anything I may have missed in my initial frightful awestruck playthrough. The game took me three and a half hours to complete without any knowledge about the game prior; other than it took great inspiration from HP Lovecrafts’ work. Using my wit and curiosity I held my own against what seemed to be impossible odds to help the main character, a fisherman named Andrew, find his missing daughter, Ellie, in a malevolent and hallucinatory adventure through the mundane. Gameplay: The Shore leaves players to their own devices when it comes to exploration and storytelling. Whether that's rushing to get to the next story set piece to find your favorite of Lovecrafts’ fantastical beasts or scouring the land for every unturned stone and item to truly understand what was going on this damned Island. I can see this being quite frustrating, boring or annoying to players who just want to experience horror survival scenarios, jump scares, or simply shoot a gun. This is especially apparent when things start to get a little confusing and they would want to be shown where to head next. Being lost on a mysterious desolate island with no HUD, waypoints or tips; I did feel at moments disoriented and slightly agitated. As some locations are so massive or so dark, this lack of direction can have you wander around aimlessly looking for a path or item that may have been just behind you or by your feet when you first entered the area. I ran into this issue when dealing with a door unlocking puzzle in a small dark cave, with no explanation or game dialog. You are just there in this dark room with no way to go back and reenter. You need to know how to activate the alters to open the door, so figure it out or...die there. This took me a minimal but frustrating amount of time; however upon completion of these challenges, wow. These gave me an overwhelming sense of achievement even on small tasks like finding the lock a rusty old key goes to or finding the path that leads me to the next story set or cinematic. I was filled with pride and sometimes a stroke of genius for my progress without the game holding my hand and guiding me. Since I was the master of Andrews’ destiny, I could have given up and let him perish to the lovecraftian horrors or to my own shortcomings.   Atmosphere: The atmosphere of The Shore is almost a being of its own; vast black stoned misty shore lines, Shipwrecks, deserted lighthouses and lush palm tree clusters are just a few of the scenes you will come across. All filling the player with a sense of bewilderment as they explore and discover the horrific mysteries that lie ahead. The island feels dead as you trudge along seeing no other person but only the places and items they left behind. Letters, manuscripts, and idols lend to the overall sense of macabre and loss. They also help build up the atmosphere and tension as you explore. Finding a note explaining a grotesque creature or a photo of a lost crew you truly gain an appreciation and fear of the story that has been laid out before you. This atmosphere was unfortunately broken at moments, by coming across floating rocks, invisible walls holding me back from climbing off a very small pile of rocks to my next path, and the odd seagull standing there, floating (not flying) high above the rocks. These small glitches though are easily overlooked as slight blemishes on an overall fantastic game.Sound and Music: The music and sound design was implemented to stunning effect; the footsteps’ sound while walking on the beach, seagulls calling in the distance. Especially impressive was the movement of metallic and stone objects which sound heavy as you place them down. This felt very impactful and “realistic” for such a new early access game. While  Playing with studio headphones, I truly felt moments of anxiety and dread from the sound alone. While exploring the island I came across a shimmering obelisk in the middle of a path. As I approached a deep swell started to grow, high pitches and other notes began to creep in causing the hairs on the back of my neck to begin to stand up and as I spun my character around to confront the creature I assumed was right behind me....there was nothing there. This clever use of sound design kept me in a constant state of tension as the fear of some unknown phantasmagoric creature or oddity showing up was ever present on my mind during exploration. Critically some characters' voices though were too altered or deep. When they would speak the deep unearthly rumble behind their voices would make it sometimes near impossible to understand. Though in the context of unimaginable beasts and gods speaking with a mere mortal this is totally plausible, just needs to be overlooked or I suggest to turn on subtitles so you can gain the full experience of their words. Final Thoughts: The Shore, even with its slight bugs, minute imperfections and overall short story, can and will be credited as a HP Lovecraft walking simulator, even by those who wanted a jolting zombie slaying shoot out. Taking into account that Lovecraftian horror finds terror in the unknown, especially if that unknown is hidden by the ordinary, common or mundane; this game does exactly that. It creates tension in the drag of exploring a lifeless beach and lighthouse with clever sound design. Creates fantastical, awe-striking moments with slumbering deities, and beasts from Lovecraft's work while still being its own story. Not some kind of knock off of every other Lovecraft inspired games of a grizzled, tired smoking detective trying to quelch the horrid and vivid dreams of the occult and visions of cthulhu. I give this title an 7/10 as I can only hope these small issues will be solved by developers in the future as the game becomes more polished.

_childDocuments_.review: The Shore was fascinating, curious and overall a frustrating and disappointing experience. For such a small, independent development team, the game is quite good overall, but the good bits are so vastly overshadowed by the bad that I simply can't recommend this game.For a fan of Lovecraft and Cthulhu lore, the storyline feels cobbled together from various bits and pieces of the lore. Almost as if it were created with an effort to check off as many boxes from the various mythos sources as possible. The overall plot feels very nonsensical and contrived. After the first half of the game, the gameplay takes a rather abrupt shift from calm exploration and investigation of the mysterious island to a fast-paced 'run-and-gun' frenzy interspersed with simple yet nonsensical puzzles. I am a staunch supporter of 'walking simulators' as a way to tell a story in a video game medium, and it at first it seemed like The Shore would be similar to Dear Esther or other atmospheric and surreal video games. I really enjoyed the calm atmosphere of the island during the first act. Each turn presented me with tantalizing tidbits of information that helped unravel just how much of a mystery the island was. Just how many people had been washed up upon those shores? How did they get there? What WAS this place, where the sun sets in the east and the mist draws all who sail out back once again to its rocky shores?Unfortunately, the storyline eventually takes a sharp turn. There are no further mysteries to unravel, just a series of alien corridors, monster chases, and frustrating semi-puzzles. -  Brandon Fague, is fantastic. His deep, grizzled voice is the perfect fit for the gritty, determined and resolute protagonist. Unfortunately we don't get to hear much of his voice during the gameplay, but I loved hearing his voice every time he got to speak. - . One word: phenomenal. Thanos Zampoukas created several pieces that evoke incredible sensations and emotions. The calm and peaceful island exploration songs during act one are beautiful yet haunting; it lets you feel almost safe, but hints at something terrible yet to come.  The bizarre synth and drum songs bring about a feeling of unease and alien presence. And the orchestrated pieces really bring out a sensation that truly cataclysmic and universe-scaling events are taking place. - . While The Shore has more than its fair share of broken textures and missing polygons, it shows a world of creatures and vistas that are both breathtaking and mystifying to behold. Combined with excellent sound design, there are encounters and scenes throughout the game that evoke a sense of mystery, dread, and things that are utterly alien to our mundane world. The Shore does a fantastic representation of cosmic, other-worldly landscapes that left me wanting for more.- . While the protagonist has a breadth of emotion and a deep, soulful voice, the rest of the voice actors leave much to be desired. Aside from the protagonist, the majority of the voice acting comes in the form of an unknown, disembodied voice, whose thick nordic accent oftentimes betrays the serious and otherworldly atmosphere. It's hard to take elder gods serious when they have difficulty pronouncing most words.  The remainder of the voices we hear sound like they were recorded through someone's speakerphone with a complete lack of audio balancing. Hearing the rich and crisp voice of the protagonist speaking alongside someone who sounds like they're talking into a tin can ten feet away was.. incredibly jarring.- . Calling them puzzles is a bit of a stretch, as the majority of them come down to 'click thing until it works' or 'poke three runes to proceed'. There is little to no indication of how to proceed with most of them, leading to many situations of confused running about and backtracking. Sometimes you find yourself transported to a single room to solve a single puzzle before proceeding. These really did a number on the pacing and left me feeling exhausted, confused and disappointed. - . Even taking into account all of the nooks and crannies I explored and the numerous deaths to frustrating enemies, the game only took about three hours. Not really worth the price of admission, overall.- . This is a game about cosmic horror. A game about otherworldly entities that exist so far removed from our mundane world that to behold them is to drive one insane! To even speak their name is to invite ruin! And yet, in this game, when the protagonist summons Cthulhu -  - we are treated to a twenty second monologue about the end of the human race before the big guy just sort of.. slowly stomps off down the coast. No fanfare, no reaction from the protagonist.. just a long look at Cthulhu's butt as he slowly meanders away.-  While the majority of the plot was pretty nonsensical and contrived, the ending is what really did this game in for me. After all of the trials the protagonist overcomes in order to achieve his goal of , we never get a payoff of whether it happens or not. Simply a cut away to the credits as we see him running into the distance.Overall, The Shore was mostly a letdown. A handful of fascinating, mysterious and immersive scenes were ruined by an inconsistent tone, frustrating mechanics, and a plot that left me scratching my head. Fans of Cthulhu lore and the Lovecraftian mythos might find the visuals and sound design fun for a while, but overall I feel like this is probably one to avoid unless it comes at a significant sale.

_childDocuments_.review: While I know one of the biggest complaints about the game will be its price for its length however for fans of Lovecraft and Cosmic horror that is a small price to pay. So many elements from the Cthulhu mythos went into this game and the visuals and game play have little to no flaws. it is a beautiful game and the world you are plunged into is bizare and disturbing to say the least. Some sections can be quite challenging and demand some very fast thinking on the part of the player. You will die at certain points if you are like me and require a minute to get your bearings. Don't let those parts discourage you. The monsters in this game are no joke and it is best to run from them as much as possible. Many of them will be able to out run you but you will have the tools to fight back. name: Olija
detailed_description: Olija is a game about Faraday's quest, a man shipwrecked then trapped in the mysterious country of Terraphage. Armed with a legendary harpoon, he and other castaways try to leave this hostile country to return to their homelands. Through adventurous exploration, narration and razor sharp combat, the player will discover a strange world and its inhabitants, including Olija, an enigmatic lady that Faraday finds himself bound to over time. Inspired by swashbuckling tales and cinematic adventure games, Olija is a story about facing the unknown in adversity. Features: Explore a mysterious and handcrafted world inspired by sailor's legends and Asian fantasy. Wield the Harpoon of legend and rethink movement through platforming, puzzle and combat. Rescue fellow castaways and meet curious characters to learn more about Terraphage and the enigmatic Olija. Beautiful melancholic soundtrack inspired by Flamenco, lo-fi and traditional Japanese music. Craft magic hats!

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing I noticed when starting the game was the pixel art. The hardcore pixel art. The closest good game with a similar visual style that I remembered was Songbringer. You have to like that style, or  you won't like the game. I liked it.You play a Lord of an impoverished fishing village who decides to lead his people into a brighter future in a far away land. He doesn't get very far. A terrible thunderstorm and a giant whale sink the ship, the villagers drown or get caught by the natives, and Lord Faraday is rescued by an old man and brought to a small island where he meets a bunch of desperate castaways. Here the adventure starts and the old man transports Faraday to different islands to explore and search for three magical keys to open a door that leads back home. The game plays like an easy platformer with frequent, again easy, fights. The other islands are inhabited by strange people (and animals) and harbour quite a few secrets. Faraday rescues a hatmaker who makes magical hats (if he brings him the required parts), a very mysterious princess and some of the crewmates from his sunken ship. He finds a cursed harpoon, that always returns back to him and allows him to instantly teleport to it. Other sideweapons like a musket round out his equipment. Soon the island with the castaways springs back to life and gives Faraday a base for his expeditions.What I really loved about Olija were the constant surprises, the constant new discoveries while you explore the islands. Strange inhabitants, collectibles, a few pieces of new equipment, story twists... it never gets boring. It is neither extremely challenging nor very long, but it is really good as long as it lasts. There are bossfights, but even they can be won without burning up one controller for one boss in hundreds of retries.Not extremely challenging hardcore pixel art action platformer with a focus on exploration and story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite interesting. At first I took it for an adventure platformer. Then I thought maybe it was more akin to exploration but it's not quite that either. It wasn't really until I was near the end that I decided it was a lite hack and slash story focused primarily on the main character's journey to find his way back to his world. Don't get me wrong, this game was alright but if you're looking for a metroidvania, hack and slash exploration type of game you're probably going to be a little bit disappointed. But what you will find is a short and sweet story in a strange world with retro graphics and some lite platforming.Olija takes place in the world of Terraphage, which is a series of islands. There's a few factions at play here and you find yourself thrust into a position of power when you discover a legendary mystical harpoon. You will gain access to various weapons throughout the game but the harpoon is your multipurpose swiss army knife. Battle is skin deep. The sporadic frequency of bag guys isn't terribly difficult to overcome and only the final boss did I have find a bit challenging. It's a bit odd that this game markets itself as an "adventurous exploration" because it actively discourages exploration. There's a number of dungeons that you can only experience once and then they're pretty much closed to you the entire remainder of the game. Boasting exploration when you can only move forward is a little bit deceiving. And while there are multiple islands you can explore gameplay is largely linear. You can't get further in island C with completing islands A and B type of deal. There's also no incentive to revisit any of the previously explored locations. This is one of those times where I wish Steam had a neutral recommendation. The game isn't good or bad but it's not as deep as it wants you to think it is. Not to mention with all the lore that might have inhabited this world was a bit of a missed opportunity to discover some cool things about it and the enemies or factions that inhabit it. You're purposed with a singular focus and that's what keeps this good narrative experience from being a great one.

_childDocuments_.review: FULL REVIEWSo I've finished the main part of the game which took around 6 - 7 hours according to my steam playtime, definitely didn't feel like that (which is a good thing). I've still got a few more achievements to go, which should give me an hour or so more of the game. Story: I'm gonna be honest here, After the initial intro and such I wasn't really paying attention on what was happening in the story. It's fully subtitled and I missed a few, so I was kinda out of luck on knowing what was fully going on.  That aside, it's still beautifully told with fantastic cutscenes, characters & excellent audio / music which all ooze atmosphere. Platforming: So In my initial review I said it was a pretty basic 2D hack n slash platformer at it's core, which isn't entirely wrong. What I mean by that is yes you jump around from platform to platform, but at times as you also use your harpoon to traverse areas (think of it like grappling hook in Sekiro). There's also some puzzles at time which aren't too hard, but certainly aren't straight forward. I enjoyed these as they made good use of your harpoon and one of your secondary weapons.  They even put in one stealth section, which makes sense when you get to the part.  Combat: The combat goes into more depth that I expected, though not an insane amount or anything. During the game you acquire a harpoon as your main weapon and 4 secondary weapons. I don't want to spoil what they are, as one was a total surprise and I'd like to leave it as that. I will say, they add a bit of depth to the game.  Also during the game you collect money which can be used to buy upgrades for the main hub (a sailor to go and find items for you and an alchemist that can upgrade your max health). As well as items that can be used to unlock hats. They've each got a skill, these can be switched out before each level, instead of having to go back to the main hub and change it, definitely helpful Overall the combat is very fluid and enjoyable with good animations. There's just a one downside which I think is the worst part of the game. The awful dodge mechanic, at first I completely forgot it was even a thing and wasn't really using it. But the more I used it, the more I realised how bad it is (especially during a boss fight). It completely ruins the fluidity of the combat by making your character have to stop for at least a second and get up. Wasn't a fan of thatBoss Fights: The boss fights can be fun or can be frustrating. They were a bit of both for me. They aren't hard, but that is once you've actually figured out how to beat it them. Some were straightforward and killed in one go, while others took a bit to finally figure out how to beat it.  Glitch I got in the final boss: Verdict: Pretty much the same as my initial review. I had a blast playing, didn't feel like I played as long as I did. Definitely worth the price, since it's pretty cheap. Easy recommendation if you like action 2D platformers________________________________________________________INITIAL REVIEWSo here's my initial review after playing about half an hour of the game. At it's core it's a pretty basic 2D hack n slash platformer, but it's story and style brings out so much more than that. Fantastic artistic direction, great story (so far), excellent audio / music & enjoyable combat. All of this being made by one person, makes it that much more impressive.I'm having a blast and I've hardly even started. If you enjoy 2D action platformers, I'd highly suggest giving the demo a go to see if it's for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Olija is a great little action platformer that doesn't completely gel as a game but excels at feeling like a grand adventure. Poor Lord Faraday. Trying to lead his impoverished domain to a better future, he gets all his men lost in a Bermuda-triangle-like mysterious sea where a shadowy entity holds sway. Soon he establishes a settlement among the shipwrecks, finds a magic harpoon and starts travelling to the different islands to fight back back the darkness and recover his men. And maybe find love. You do this by exploring small-ish levels composed of a dozen or so interconnected rooms depicted in very chunky but evocative pixel art (I got flashbacks of old C64 platformers, though of course this is way more colorful.) The platforming and combat are simple but pacey, and you soon find a harpoon that allows you to grapple onto enemies in combat or special environment objects to solve some simple traversal puzzles. There are also a few side weapons and ability-adding hats to add a bit more gameplay variety. Every island has its own personality, a few bits of plot or backstory, and most get some unique gameplay elements. There’s a few more things you can do, too. Your home base grows as the story unfolds, you can craft different hats, and spend what money you find in a couple of ways, but this is very undercooked and soon you’ll run out of things to do; Suikoden, this ain’t. Still, not bad for what’s essentially set dressing. I especially enjoyed the music, which is a wonderful blend of orchestral adventure music and flamenco stylings. The romantic elements are also outstanding; I found the love story more involving than anything Bioware have ever done… not bad when neither of the lovers get any dialog!   So the mechanics are fun and varied, combat is sufficiently fluid, and the difficulty is easy enough for the roughness of some of the elements not to grate. And if that feels like qualified praise… it kind of is; there's just not enough depth to make anything stand out, which is a shame. Even the story and setting, the game’s greatest strengths, are a bit light on detail and incident; I liked that the gaps and lack of detail leave behind a good sense of mystery, but it could easily come across as undercooked. Oh, and it’s a pretty short game, but that’s a plus as far as I’m concerned as it never overstays its welcome. On the balance it’s the storytelling and sense of adventure that carries this game for me; complaining about any of the small disappointments along the way just feels a bit churlish given how much I enjoyed my time trying to escape the Land Eater.

_childDocuments_.review: Olija is another game that's been sitting on my wish list for years; when faced with a choice between Olija or another game on my list, I've always bought the other game. When faced with a choice between Olija or going to the sub shop of my choice for dinner...Club Sub or Philly Steak? All the reviews said the game was too short, too easy, and just generally not all that interesting.Well, I finally got to the point where very little else on my list seemed as appealing, so I asked for it for Christmas. Was it good? Not particularly. Was it awful? No. Now that I've played it though, I can guarantee that I would've enjoyed a good sub sandwich and 4 hours of anime instead of the 4 hours I put into this. Essentially, Olija is a fairly bare bones platformer with some light combat elements. The player controls Lord Faraday, a man who oversees a poor fishing village on the brink of starvation. He sets out to find a way to save his village, he and his crew get shipwrecked in what is basically the Bermuda Triangle, and a bunch of the natives are possessed by shadow things. Early on, Faraday finds a cursed harpoon with the power to transport itself to its wielder or its wielder to itself, and using this to fight the crazy shadow-possessed natives and solve basic teleportation puzzles makes up most of the hook of the game (no pun intended). Other small additions include a *very* light town-development element, the inclusion of a crossbow and musket as optional secondary weapons, and the ability to passively collect crafting resources throughout the game which can be used in a hat shop to unlock 8 different hats which grant the player a unique ability (though I just used the first hat you can make for most of the game). You also get a sword that acts as a secondary teleport gimmick and (very briefly) a key and a light bulb.The game's controls are smooth, if slightly awkward for me; I never map a game's directional inputs to the left side of my keyboard, but that is what this game has them set to. You've got WASD for movement, Spacebar for jump, and JKL for primary weapon, the harpoon, and secondary weapon respectively.Minor issues:-Right after getting the harpoon, players are given an on-screen prompt that tells them that D+K will allow players to zip to the harpoon's location after they throw it. That is specific to that one context, and it took me a few minutes of confusion before I realized that you're actually just supposed to use the same key you use to throw/recall the harpoon together with the key for the direction of the location of the harpoon to pull Faraday to it. The prompt easily could've said "WASD+K" or "Directional input+K", and I wouldn't have been confused about how to use the harpoon at all.-If the game ever explains that you can cycle between secondary weapons using the Tab key, I must have missed it. I figured that out when my keyboard almost fell off my lap and one of the keys I pressed when I grabbed it was the Tab key. -The art style works for what it is, and everything is well animated, but I feel like the game would've looked a lot better if the sprites were at least double the resolution the devs went with. They put really nice cut scenes in here, so they absolutely could've had better in-game sprites. This art style choice was deliberate, and it hurts the game's presentation. -On a similar note: who decided the color palette for the entire game needed to be various shades of brown? Why did you think people would want to look at that? That's stupid. You can create an oppressive, hopeless-feeling atmosphere and still use more colors.  -There's a barely present/out of place love angle with Lady Olija, thus the name of the game. The naming convention for this game was kind of like having "Legend of Zelda" before "Majora's Mask", if there was only ever one LoZ game and Zelda was even less relevant. Would I recommend this? If you've run out of other games like it, you could do worse. But as I said, you'll enjoy a good sub-$10 meal more (pun fully intended).
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: Olija is one of those games that is solid yet doesn't wow: it's not like the game has major problems, and you're going to get a bit of fun out of it. Yes, the publisher of devolver digital seems a little odd at first as it's not hyper stylized from a neon/colorful/playful perceptive, but again, don't let that turn you away from the game's solid combat mechanics and nice movement system. The harpoon gimmick is a good one despite it being almost a bit overpowered in some cases, and some good enemy variety does help the game take advantage of it's nice animation quality despite being able to count the pixels on things at times. The hat system is a nice reward for collecting in the world, and some of the more subtle storytelling at display here goes a long way in making the game feel like it's made with heart and bone: it's structurally sound and is out to show what it has.The main problem with the game is mainly it's lack of an over the top feature: the driving force that would seperate it from the pack. Level design is great but like many other elements in the game, nothing truly stands out. Great music to listen to, but not amazing. Sound design is there, but not on part with the best of the genre has to show. For you wrestling fans out there, Olija is the definition of the B+ player: it's great at what it does but it just doesn't have what it takes to stand with the elite among its genre, despite not really having anything too “wrong” with it.Good for the price. Not something you need right away, but worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly a phenomenal game. It is very well made with care; which can be seen in the pixel art present in the beautiful areas you get to explore. In addition, this game has  a really fun combat system, as all the weapons feel really good to use. As well, as you can  explore in these areas to look for extra materials to craft new hats to wear that give special abilities, in the range of being able to siphon hp from enemies or to shoot out acid. My only complaint is that I wish it was longer. Would highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: Loading times are absolutely atrocious, to the point where it got into the way of my enjoyment. There's a long loading screen when starting up the game, but then there are also long loading screens for each level transition, and even going from screen to screen hitches noticeably.Question is: with graphics like these, what on earth is being loaded all the time? The game is only 340 MB, you could probably load the whole thing into RAM uncompressed on any toaster.And this is when playing from an SSD. I'm scared to think how this would fare on a hard drive.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: If you can get it on sale for ~$5, go for it, otherwise, skip.Combat is decent hack & slash with neat harpoon dashing/teleportation. The harpoon also makes platforming quick & interesting.A constant annoyance is how slow all the loading & unskippable transitions are.Starting the game takes a few secs; followed by unskippable logos. More loading to get into the game.Calling the old man on the boat, sailing, returning to your base, entering certain doors.So. Much. Wasted. Time.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: Cool Iberian music.  A fantasy-Irish protagonist with a torc of bondage clamped about his neck.  A Japan-like Lost World culture in a watery land that retains its mystery by dragging in sailors who get too close and not letting them escape.  A gooey demon lord with a fanged mask for a head who commands an army of lost souls.  General atmosphere, conception is A-1!  Would like some fill-in on the finer story points, however -- in the end it's way too misty for my tastes, and I could certainly have done with a few more  cutscenes like we get at the beginning (I'm not even talking about the exquisite hand-drawn promotional thing, in case you haven't played that ancient game I just mentioned, but the simple pixel graphic cinemas).  Fighting with the cursed interdimensional grapple-spear, though it  manage to be somewhat cool anyway, comes off way too sloppy to ever let you feel like you're a true martial arts master -- mostly the graphics are too crunchy and earth-toned to let you see much of what you're doing when things really heat up, so you'd better just go nuts with your arsenal and hope for the best.  And that's not too unlikely an outcome, seeing as how the game is a little on the easy side, ramping up a bit on the boss end of things.So!+Great music, interesting world+Well-conceived combat mechanics (in the rough cut)+Smooth platforming, responsive-Narrative too vague-Not enough crunchy cutscenes-Battles too often devolve into a spear-flailing, grapple-zipping mess with little room for actual masteryI enjoyed this, and I do not regret buying it in a bundle of Devolver platformers, but I don't think it's quite worth full price.  Needed a few more squirts of juice.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm admittedly not too far into the game but I'd like to share some initial impressions:Incredible atmosphere in this game, the top notch sound design in this title caught me by surprise as I didn't have such high expectations on that front. I've been playing this on my TV with a full receiver setup and while this game doesn't offer surround sound (no surprises there), the stereo quality is excellent with a lot of lovely sound effects and music that really pulled me into the game. In my experience, it's somewhat rare for an indie title to flex in this area, so it's a nice treat.Presentation is also really good, no menu overload here to get lost in. The overall world design appears to contain a central hub area with different merchants etc.. that you can unlock and upgrade via collectibles/currency but I won't dive too far into that to keep the surprises alive for anyone interested in playing. Main takeaway here is that on first glance there appears to be some decent progression paths. Getting into the gameplay means interacting the boat man at the edge of the hub area, which will bring up the world map, you choose a destination and set sail. Levels are laid out nicely as well, so far I haven't encountered any mazes which is actually a plus in my books. Combat is really really good, incredibly fluid with lovely animations and a bit more fast paced than I was expecting, which again, is a nice treat. It's giving me a mixed vibe of The Eternal Castle and Hyperlight Drifter, both excellent games to draw inspiration from.Occasional jank during some of the early cut scenes I've seen so far, nothing earth shattering or game breaking. Hopefully an update at some point will address that but if not, it's not really a big deal. An example of this would be after the intro cut scene, having my character standing in the first level, unable to move and then suddenly a cut scene starts, then finishes and I continue on my way. Maybe I'm nitpicking here but it stood out.So there you go, my initial impressions so far. I expect I'll be playing it for a decent amount of time this evening and I'm really happy I picked it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: Pros- nice pixel artwork and fluid animation- simple, yet very cool combat mechanics- good story- good soundtrack- Not in-game related, but the art style in the trailer is so good, they should have made a short film or somethingCons- Not a big con, but the devs could have fleshed out some game mechanics and areas to make it lengthier and more challenging. _childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: A solid four-ish hour Saturday afternoon romp. Very strong Another World and Flashback vibes - a few sequences near the end in particular really nailed that brand of storytelling.The puzzle-platforming and combat is just challenging enough to keep you engaged, but not hard enough for you to have to repeat any sequence more than maybe once or twice. There is one short segment of a level where you get a glimpse of what this game would've been if they'd leaned into some more brutal Celeste-tier challenge, but the game immediately snaps back to its much simpler brand of gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: Olija immediately reminded me of older cinematic platformers like Flashback and Another World. Those games have a reputation of being very difficult, but Skeleton Crew Studio has kept the difficulty accessible in order to focus on the atmosphere and gameplay. While the graphics are minimal, leaving much to the imagination, I really enjoyed the sound design. The creak of the wooden dock in the hub world, the whooshing spin of your magically returning harpoon, the otherworldly growl of the bad guy's voice (he sounds incredible). Bits of dialogue and moody music draw you into this mysterious world dotted with strange islands.Combat with your harpoon and choice of sub-weapon is easy, but fun. Animations look smooth and you have a variety of flashy moves that combo into each other. Certain enemies and bosses can be a little challenging, and the warping puzzles are snappy and engaging. In addition to running through the levels and brutalizing your foes, there are a handful of surprising moments. It's the presentation and the game's flair for the dramatic that really makes it memorable. Olija doesn't overstay its welcome - you can beat it in a few hours - and it tells a complete story with mystery, thrills, and romance in equal measure.I think we forget that games don't have to be long to be good. Certain moments will stick with me, and that's enough to give it a high recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Olija

_childDocuments_.review: I got Olija on sale as part of a bundle. It was enjoyable, but left me wanting more. The movement and game-feel are top notch; it's super satisfying to dash around with your spear, whether you're just platforming or closing the gap on an impaled enemy. The controls are tight and responsive, the combat is engaging and weighty, and the visuals and sound design do a lot to pull you into the experience. All that said, I'm left with a bittersweet feeling as I wrap up the story, since Olija doesn't feel terribly interested in fully exploring these fun, polished mechanics. I've never seen a game nail the game-feel this well, only to fumble on level design. Imagine if Celeste ended on Chapter 3 and had no B-sides. That's Olija, in both length and depth. Lovely to play, but there's just something missing from this 5-hour playthrough.Most of the challenges in Olija are simple and straightforward; even the secrets I found mostly just consisted of throwing my spear offscreen in a different direction from the beaten path. The most engaging parts were the boss fights, and while those were exciting and did take me a few tries, they ultimately boiled down to learning simple patterns and throwing/dashing to your spear accordingly. It just wasn't a very challenging or deep experience, which is a shame, because it definitely had the potential to be something you could really sink your teeth into.Olija is a nice little indie game, and while I really wish it offered a bit more to chew on, I enjoyed getting to know it. It was a nice 5 hours. If you enjoyed the demo (play the demo! it's great!), I would recommend picking it up on sale or as part of a bundle. But I don't think it's worth paying full price for, when the free demo is about as deep and challenging as the gameplay ever gets.
